additional_notes: Literally “good God.” Often used as an exclamation to show surprise, frustration, or emphasis (similar to “Good God!”). It can also refer to God in a religious or traditional way (“the Good Lord”). Tone depends on context: it can sound old-fashioned or mildly strong; in casual speech you may also hear softened forms like “Bon Dieu !”.
target_language_example: Bon Dieu, qu’est-ce qui se passe ici ?
native_language_example: Good God, what’s going on here?

additional_notes: Used to express relief that something bad didn’t happen or that something turned out well. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence (“Dieu merci, …”) or used alone as a quick reaction. It’s fairly common and not rude, though in very secular contexts you can also hear “heureusement” (“fortunately”).
target_language_example: Dieu merci, personne n’a été blessé.
native_language_example: Thank God, nobody was hurt.

meaning: “God knows” (used to say you don’t know, or that something is unknown).
additional_notes: Used as an exclamation to express uncertainty or to emphasize that something is hard to know: "Dieu sait !" = “God knows!” / “Who knows!” Often followed by a question word: "Dieu sait combien..." = “God knows how many/how much...”, "Dieu sait où..." = “God knows where...”. Tone is neutral to slightly emphatic; not slang.
target_language_example: Dieu sait quand il va revenir.
native_language_example: God knows when he’ll come back.

additional_notes: A set expression meaning you’re relieved or grateful that something turned out well. Literally “God be praised” (subjunctive of être: soit). Often used in a slightly formal, old-fashioned, or religious tone; in everyday speech people more commonly say « Dieu merci » or « Heureusement ».
target_language_example: Dieu soit loué, tout le monde est sain et sauf.
native_language_example: Thank God, everyone is safe and sound.

additional_notes: Mostly used in Christian contexts as a title for Jesus (often written with capitals). You may also see it in set phrases like "Jésus-Christ, Fils de Dieu". In everyday non-religious conversation it’s uncommon.
target_language_example: Dans la Bible, Jésus est appelé le Fils de Dieu.
native_language_example: In the Bible, Jesus is called the Son of God.

meaning: Great Britain (the island: England, Scotland, and Wales).
additional_notes: Geographic term for the island containing England, Scotland, and Wales. It is not the same as the United Kingdom (Royaume-Uni), which also includes Northern Ireland. Often used in country contexts in French, but if you mean the state, “Royaume-Uni” is more precise.
target_language_example: La Grande-Bretagne comprend l’Angleterre, l’Écosse et le pays de Galles.
native_language_example: Great Britain includes England, Scotland, and Wales.

additional_notes: Proper name used in Christian contexts (religion, history, culture). It can also be used as an exclamation to show shock or frustration (similar to “Jesus Christ!” in English), which some people may find rude or offensive depending on the situation.
target_language_example: Pour les chrétiens, Jésus-Christ est une figure centrale.
native_language_example: For Christians, Jesus Christ is a central figure.

meaning: fishing; also (with context) a peach (the fruit).
additional_notes: Usually means “fishing” (the activity): *faire de la pêche* = “to go fishing.” The same spelling *pêche* can also mean “peach” (fruit), so context matters (e.g., *une pêche* = “a peach”). In the expression *avoir la pêche*, it means “to feel full of energy / to be in great shape” (informal).
target_language_example: Le week-end, je fais de la pêche au bord du lac.
native_language_example: On weekends, I go fishing by the lake.

additional_notes: Used for a queen in a monarchy (often followed by a name or country, e.g., « la reine Élisabeth », « la reine d’Angleterre »). It can also refer to a queen in games (like chess or playing cards) or the queen bee (« la reine des abeilles »). Note: « reine » is feminine; the masculine is « le roi » (the king).
target_language_example: La reine arrive au palais.
native_language_example: The queen is arriving at the palace.

meaning: “The Blues”: the French national team (especially the men’s national football/soccer team).
additional_notes: A common nickname for French national sports teams, based on the traditional blue jersey color. In everyday French, “Les Bleus” most often refers to the French men’s national soccer team, especially during big tournaments (World Cup, Euros). Not the same as English “the blues” (sadness/music).
target_language_example: Ce soir, je regarde le match : les Bleus jouent contre l’Allemagne.
native_language_example: Tonight, I’m watching the match: the French national team is playing against Germany.

additional_notes: Capitalized, it can be a proper name (e.g., a place, a neighborhood, a hotel, a restaurant). Without context, it most commonly means “the sources” (information sources) or “the springs” (water sources). In French, “source” can mean a source of information, an origin/cause, or a natural spring; plural: “sources.”
target_language_example: Peux-tu me donner les sources de cet article ?
native_language_example: Can you give me the sources for this article?

additional_notes: Proper noun used the same way as in English. In French it usually doesn’t take an article (you say "à Los Angeles", not "au Los Angeles"). Often abbreviated "L.A." in informal contexts. Pronunciation in French is typically close to "loss an-jell-ess".
target_language_example: Je vais à Los Angeles la semaine prochaine.
native_language_example: I’m going to Los Angeles next week.

additional_notes: A formal greeting used to address an audience (e.g., at speeches, announcements, ceremonies, or presentations). It’s the plural of “Madame” and “Monsieur.” Often followed by a comma and a statement.
target_language_example: Mesdames et Messieurs, bienvenue à notre conférence.
native_language_example: Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to our conference.

meaning: New York (a city and a U.S. state).
additional_notes: Used as a proper noun in French just like in English. In French, you often add a preposition: « à New York » (in/to New York City) and « dans l’État de New York » (in New York State). If you mean the city specifically, you can also say « la ville de New York ».
target_language_example: J’habite à New York depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: I’ve lived in New York for two years.

meaning: “Our Lady” (a title for the Virgin Mary); often used in names of churches/cathedrals (e.g., Notre-Dame de Paris).
additional_notes: Literally means “Our Lady.” In French, it’s a common religious title for the Virgin Mary and appears in many place names and church names. With a capital N and D, it usually refers to a specific place or institution (most famously the cathedral in Paris). Pronounced roughly “notruh dahm.”
target_language_example: Nous avons visité Notre-Dame de Paris.
native_language_example: We visited Notre-Dame de Paris.

additional_notes: A proper noun (country name). Often used with the preposition “en” to mean “in/to New Zealand”: « en Nouvelle-Zélande ». Also used as an adjective in phrases like « néo-zélandais / néo-zélandaise » (New Zealander / New Zealand).
target_language_example: J’habite en Nouvelle-Zélande.
native_language_example: I live in New Zealand.

additional_notes: A proper noun (country name). It’s plural in French ("les Pays-Bas"), so you usually say: "aux Pays-Bas" (in/to the Netherlands) and "des Pays-Bas" (from the Netherlands). The demonym is "néerlandais(e)" (Dutch).
target_language_example: J’habite aux Pays-Bas depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: I’ve been living in the Netherlands for two years.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the Christmas gift-bringer in French-speaking cultures. It’s capitalized as a proper name. Often used with "le" ("le Père Noël") and in common holiday phrases like "lettre au Père Noël" (letter to Santa) or "le Père Noël apporte des cadeaux" (Santa brings gifts).
target_language_example: Les enfants ont écrit une lettre au Père Noël.
native_language_example: The children wrote a letter to Santa Claus.

additional_notes: Used mainly in formal or official writing (invitations, protocols, news) when referring to a king or queen. You’ll often see it as « S. M. le Roi… » (His Majesty the King) or « S. M. la Reine… » (Her Majesty the Queen).
target_language_example: S. M. le Roi arrivera à 18 heures.
native_language_example: His Majesty the King will arrive at 6 p.m.

additional_notes: A formal way to refer to a monarch (king/queen). Capitalized in writing. The possessive changes with the monarch’s gender: Sa Majesté = His/Her Majesty (generic), Son Majesté = His Majesty (male), Sa Majesté = Her Majesty (female). Often used with a title or name: Sa Majesté le roi / Sa Majesté la reine.
target_language_example: Sa Majesté le roi arrive au palais.
native_language_example: His Majesty the king is arriving at the palace.

meaning: Western Sahara (a region in North Africa).
additional_notes: Proper noun used in geography and news. Often capitalized: « le Sahara occidental ». « Occidental » means “western” (as in west). Not usually used as a common everyday phrase unless talking about places, politics, or current events.
target_language_example: Le Sahara occidental se trouve au nord-ouest de l’Afrique.
native_language_example: Western Sahara is located in northwest Africa.

additional_notes: A proper noun (place name). In French, it’s used just like in English; you can say "à San Francisco" (in/to San Francisco) and "de San Francisco" (from San Francisco).
target_language_example: Je vais à San Francisco demain.
native_language_example: I’m going to San Francisco tomorrow.

additional_notes: A compass direction meaning the area between south (sud) and east (est). Often used on maps, weather forecasts, travel descriptions, and to indicate where something is located (e.g., dans le Sud-Est de la France). Also used as an adjective: la région sud-est (the southeast region).
target_language_example: Lyon se trouve dans le Sud-Est de la France.
native_language_example: Lyon is located in the southeast of France.

additional_notes: Same word as in English; used for a short-sleeved casual shirt. Commonly masculine: un T-shirt (plural: des T-shirts). You may also see it written “tee-shirt” in French.
target_language_example: J’ai acheté un T-shirt noir.
native_language_example: I bought a black T-shirt.

additional_notes: Used mainly in religious contexts as a title for God: « le Tout-Puissant » (“the Almighty”). It can also be used more generally as an adjective meaning “all-powerful” (often with a somewhat literary or dramatic tone). Often written with a hyphen and capital letters when it’s a title; without capitals it can simply describe someone/something as very powerful.
target_language_example: Que le Tout-Puissant te bénisse.
native_language_example: May the Almighty bless you.

meaning: Your Highness (a formal title of address).
additional_notes: Used to address a member of royalty or a high-ranking prince/princess. Very formal and respectful; you would normally capitalize it. As direct address, it can be used alone (“Votre Altesse !”) or in sentences. In indirect reference (“His/Her Highness”), French often uses “Son Altesse” (masculine) or “Son Altesse” (feminine as well), depending on context; “Votre” is specifically for speaking to the person.
target_language_example: Votre Altesse, puis-je vous présenter nos invités ?
native_language_example: Your Highness, may I introduce our guests?

meaning: “Your Excellency” (a very formal title of address).
additional_notes: Used to address or refer to high-ranking officials (especially ambassadors and some senior clergy). Capitalized in writing, and typically preceded by a form of address like « Bonjour, Votre Excellence. » Very formal and not used in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Bonjour, Votre Excellence, je suis ravi de vous rencontrer.
native_language_example: Hello, Your Excellency, I’m delighted to meet you.

meaning: “Your Majesty” (a formal way to address a king or queen).
additional_notes: Very formal and used when speaking directly to a monarch (or in historical/ceremonial contexts). It’s written with capital letters in formal writing. Often used with the third person and formal phrasing (e.g., « Votre Majesté souhaite… »).
target_language_example: Votre Majesté, je vous remercie de votre accueil.
native_language_example: Your Majesty, I thank you for your welcome.

additional_notes: Common, neutral term used in news, reports, and everyday speech for an accident on the road involving vehicles (cars, motorcycles, etc.). You can also say « accident de voiture » (car accident) for something more specific. Plural: « des accidents de la route ».
target_language_example: Il y a eu un accident de la route sur l’autoroute ce matin.
native_language_example: There was a road accident on the highway this morning.

additional_notes: Used for someone who likes or is romantically interested in a person but doesn’t reveal their identity. Often appears in a romantic context (e.g., a note, flowers, a message) and is common around Valentine’s Day. You may also see the feminine form: « une admiratrice secrète ».
target_language_example: Elle pense qu’elle a un admirateur secret, parce qu’elle reçoit des fleurs anonymes.
native_language_example: She thinks she has a secret admirer because she’s receiving anonymous flowers.

additional_notes: Used to ask for, give, or write an email address (often on forms). Also commonly written/said as "adresse mail" or simply "e-mail" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Quelle est votre adresse e-mail ?
native_language_example: What is your email address?

additional_notes: Usually used with an indirect object: « adresser la parole à quelqu’un » = to speak to someone (often meaning to start talking to them, sometimes formally or deliberately). Common in negative sentences: « Je ne lui ai pas adressé la parole » = I didn’t speak to him/her.
target_language_example: Je ne lui ai pas adressé la parole depuis hier.
native_language_example: I haven’t spoken to him/her since yesterday.

additional_notes: A fixed expression used to say you’ll do something or continue despite uncertainty about the outcome. It has a slightly formal/literary tone. It’s built from the subjunctive of "advenir" (to happen): "advienne" = “may it happen,” and "que pourra" = “what can (happen).”
target_language_example: Je vais tenter ma chance, advienne que pourra.
native_language_example: I’m going to take my chances, come what may.

meaning: in order to; so as to.
additional_notes: Used to express purpose, often in more formal writing or speech than "pour". It is followed by an infinitive (verb in the "to + verb" form), e.g., "afin de + manger / faire / partir". If you need "in order that" + a clause, French typically uses "afin que" + subjunctive instead.
target_language_example: Je prends des notes afin de mieux comprendre.
native_language_example: I take notes in order to understand better.

additional_notes: Used to express purpose/goal, followed by the subjunctive (e.g., afin que tu viennes). More formal than "pour que" in everyday speech, but common in writing and careful speech.
target_language_example: Je te l’explique afin que tu comprennes.
native_language_example: I’m explaining it to you so that you understand.

additional_notes: Used for someone whose job is to keep a place safe (a building, store, event, airport, etc.). Often shortened in speech to "un agent de sécu" (informal). The plural is "des agents de sécurité".
target_language_example: Un agent de sécurité vérifie les sacs à l’entrée.
native_language_example: A security guard checks bags at the entrance.

meaning: “Oh really?” / “I see.” (reaction showing surprise or interest).
additional_notes: Common conversational reaction. Intonation matters: rising intonation often means genuine surprise or a question (“Oh really?”); flatter intonation can mean acknowledgment (“I see/okay”). Can also be slightly skeptical depending on tone/context. Often used alone as a short response.
target_language_example: — Je déménage à Lyon. — Ah bon ?
native_language_example: — I’m moving to Lyon. — Oh really?

additional_notes: Used to express liking something/someone without the stronger sense of "aimer" (which can mean "to love"). Often used with the conditional for a polite request: "J’aimerais bien…" = "I’d like to…". When talking about a person, it usually means you like them (not necessarily romantic love).
target_language_example: J’aime bien ce film.
native_language_example: I quite like this movie.

additional_notes: Used to add another person/thing to a list, similar to “and” but with the idea of “in addition”. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., « moi », « toi », « lui/elle »). In writing it can feel slightly more formal than plain « et ».
target_language_example: J’ai invité Paul ainsi que sa sœur.
native_language_example: I invited Paul as well as his sister.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a place or vehicle having (or using) air conditioning. Common with verbs like "avoir" (to have) and "mettre"/"allumer" (to turn on): "Il y a l’air conditionné ?" (Is there A/C?). Often abbreviated in speech as "la clim" (informal).
target_language_example: Est-ce qu’il y a l’air conditionné dans la chambre ?
native_language_example: Is there air conditioning in the room?

additional_notes: Used to say you are going to bed (to sleep or to lie down). Often appears in the near future: « Je vais aller au lit » (I’m going to go to bed). Also common with an earlier bedtime: « Aller au lit tôt » (go to bed early). Not the same as « se coucher » (to go to sleep/lie down), though both are frequently used for “go to bed.”
target_language_example: Je vais aller au lit maintenant.
native_language_example: I’m going to go to bed now.

meaning: to go with; to match; to suit (something).
additional_notes: Used to say that one thing matches or pairs well with another (clothes, colors, food, etc.). Often followed by a noun or pronoun: « Ça va avec … » / « Ça n’allait pas avec … ». In the literal sense, it can also mean to accompany someone: « Je vais avec toi. »
target_language_example: Cette veste va bien avec ce pantalon.
native_language_example: This jacket goes well with these pants.

meaning: to go get; to fetch (go and pick up).
additional_notes: Used when you leave to get someone or something and bring it back. Often followed by a direct object: aller chercher + noun/pronoun (Je vais chercher mon frère). In everyday French, it can also mean “to get/pick up” in contexts like picking up a child or an order.
target_language_example: Je vais aller chercher les enfants à l’école.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick up the kids from school.

additional_notes: Used mainly for clothes, shoes, or anything that fits very well. You conjugate *aller* to match the subject: *Ça me va comme un gant* (It fits me perfectly), *Cette robe lui va comme un gant* (This dress fits her perfectly). Often said with *aller à quelqu’un* (“to suit/to fit someone”).
target_language_example: Ce pantalon me va comme un gant.
native_language_example: These pants fit me like a glove.

meaning: to move forward; to go ahead; to proceed.
additional_notes: Used to talk about making progress or continuing despite difficulties (also figuratively, like after a problem or breakup). Often appears with "il faut" (we must) or in the imperative: "Allons de l'avant !".
target_language_example: Malgré cet échec, il faut aller de l'avant.
native_language_example: Despite this setback, we have to move forward.

meaning: to be obvious; to go without saying.
additional_notes: Used to say something is self-evident or naturally expected. Often appears as "ça va de soi" ("that goes without saying") or in the negative: "ça ne va pas de soi" ("it’s not obvious / it’s not a given").
target_language_example: Ça va de soi qu’on doit respecter les règles.
native_language_example: It goes without saying that we must respect the rules.

additional_notes: Used as an imperative to urge someone to act, continue, or stop hesitating; the tone can be encouraging or impatient depending on context. Common in spoken French. Often appears as “Allez donc !” (vous-form) or “Va donc !” (tu-form).
target_language_example: Allez donc, dis-moi la vérité !
native_language_example: Come on, tell me the truth!

meaning: to come and go; to go back and forth.
additional_notes: Used to describe repeated movement between places (people going in and out, traffic moving back and forth). It can also be used more generally for things that fluctuate or change over time (the “ebb and flow” of something), but the core idea is back-and-forth movement.
target_language_example: Toute la journée, il y a des gens qui vont et viennent dans le magasin.
native_language_example: All day long, there are people coming and going in the store.

meaning: to go far; to go a long way.
additional_notes: Used literally for physical distance (going far away) and figuratively for progress or ambition (going far in life/career). Often appears in phrases like « aller loin dans ses études » (to go far in one’s studies) or « ça va aller loin » (this will go far / go a long way).
target_language_example: Avec du travail, tu peux aller loin.
native_language_example: With hard work, you can go far.

meaning: to go without saying; to be obvious.
additional_notes: Used to say something is so obvious or expected that it doesn’t need to be stated. Very common in the form “Ça va sans dire” (“That goes without saying”). Often followed by “que + clause”: “Ça va sans dire que…”
target_language_example: Ça va sans dire que je suis d’accord.
native_language_example: It goes without saying that I agree.

meaning: to go and get something done (to yourself).
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nous/vous) + an infinitive to say you go somewhere to have a service done to you: « aller se faire + infinitive » (e.g., haircut, nails, a massage). In some fixed expressions it can introduce an insult (e.g., « va te faire voir / foutre »), but by itself it’s neutral and usually needs the following verb.
target_language_example: Je vais me faire couper les cheveux cet après-midi.
native_language_example: I’m going to get my hair cut this afternoon.

meaning: “go fuck yourself” / “go to hell” (very rude, vulgar).
additional_notes: A very strong insult used to tell someone off or express anger. It’s extremely impolite and vulgar in most situations (avoid in polite conversation, work, or with strangers). Often used as an imperative: « Va te faire foutre ! ».
target_language_example: Va te faire foutre !
native_language_example: Go fuck yourself!

meaning: “Get lost!” / “Go to hell!” (rude way to tell someone to go away).
additional_notes: Very informal and often offensive. Used as an angry dismissal (similar to “get out of here” but harsher). Often appears in the imperative: « Va te faire voir ! » You may also hear the longer euphemistic version « Va te faire voir ailleurs ! » (“…somewhere else!”).
target_language_example: Tu m’énerves — va te faire voir !
native_language_example: You’re annoying me—get lost!

additional_notes: Used mainly for travel tickets (train, plane, bus). Most often you’ll hear or say it with a ticket: « un billet aller simple » (a one-way ticket). The opposite is « aller-retour » (round trip/return ticket).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un billet aller simple pour Lyon, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a one-way ticket to Lyon, please.

meaning: to go by yourself; to go alone.
additional_notes: Used when someone goes somewhere without anyone accompanying them (often said about a child). "Tout seul" emphasizes being alone; it can change for gender/number: "toute seule" (feminine), "tout seuls / toutes seules" (plural).
target_language_example: Il peut aller tout seul à l’école maintenant.
native_language_example: He can go to school by himself now.

meaning: to go too far; to overstep the limit.
additional_notes: Used when someone has crossed a boundary (in words, behavior, jokes, criticism, rules, etc.). It can be literal (going too far physically) but is very often figurative ("That’s taking it too far"). Common in the past: "Tu es allé(e) trop loin" (You went too far).
target_language_example: Tu es allé trop loin avec cette blague.
native_language_example: You went too far with that joke.

meaning: 'to go and see' / 'to go to see (someone or something)'.
additional_notes: Used to say you will go somewhere to check something, see something, or visit someone. Often followed by a person, a place, or an infinitive: « aller voir un ami » (go see a friend), « aller voir le médecin » (go to the doctor), « aller voir si... » (go see if...). In the imperative it can mean “go and check”: « Va voir ! ».
target_language_example: Je vais aller voir si le magasin est ouvert.
native_language_example: I’m going to go see if the store is open.

meaning: to go (and) look elsewhere; to go somewhere else.
additional_notes: Often used to mean “look somewhere else” or “go elsewhere instead.” Depending on tone and context, it can also be dismissive, like telling someone to go away or stop bothering you (e.g., « Va voir ailleurs ! »).
target_language_example: Si tu ne trouves pas ta taille ici, tu peux aller voir ailleurs.
native_language_example: If you can’t find your size here, you can go look somewhere else.

additional_notes: Imperative of "aller" (to go) + the pronoun "y" (there). Literally it can mean “go there,” but very often it’s used to encourage someone to start or continue an action (like “go ahead”). Also used when inviting someone to enter first or proceed: "Allez-y, entrez." For one person: "Vas-y !"
target_language_example: Tu peux commencer — allez-y !
native_language_example: You can start—go ahead!

additional_notes: Used mainly for transportation to mean going there and coming back. Common on tickets and in travel situations: "un billet aller-retour" (a round-trip/return ticket). Opposite: "aller simple" (one-way).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un billet aller-retour pour Lyon, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a round-trip ticket to Lyon, please.

additional_notes: Fixed expression used to say that you don’t know the answer (and often that it’s impossible to know). It can sound a bit resigned or mildly dismissive depending on tone. Often used on its own as a reaction, or inserted into a sentence: “Il est parti, allez savoir pourquoi…”
target_language_example: Il n’est pas venu ; allez savoir pourquoi.
native_language_example: He didn’t come; who knows why.

additional_notes: Common in spoken French to show resignation or mild encouragement, like giving in or telling someone to proceed. Often said as "Allez, va" (with a pause/comma) and can sound a bit dismissive depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Bon, allez, va, je te le prête pour aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Alright, fine then, I’ll lend it to you for today.

additional_notes: Extremely vulgar insult used to tell someone off. Avoid in polite conversation; it can easily start or escalate a conflict. Literally uses “aller” (go) + “se faire foutre” (to get fucked), but it’s best understood as a fixed insult rather than translated word-for-word. You may also hear the singular form: “va te faire foutre.”
target_language_example: Il m’a dit : « Allez vous faire foutre ! »
native_language_example: He said to me, “Go fuck yourself!”

additional_notes: Imperative form of "aller" + "y" (“there” / “to it”). Commonly used to encourage someone to start or continue: “Go on!”, “Go ahead!”. Can also be a direct instruction to go somewhere already mentioned. Often said on its own; can be strengthened with "Allez-y !" or softened with "Allez-y, s’il vous plaît."
target_language_example: Allez-y, je vous écoute.
native_language_example: Go ahead, I’m listening.

additional_notes: Common encouragement to start or leave. Literally “let’s go there,” using the imperative of aller (“to go”) with y (“there/it”). Often said on its own, or followed by something you’re about to do: « Allons-y, on commence. »
target_language_example: Allons-y, on est en retard !
native_language_example: Let’s go, we’re late!

additional_notes: Used to link two clauses and show contrast (“whereas/even though”) or two actions happening at the same time (“while”). Often placed between the two clauses: A …, alors que B ….
target_language_example: Il est sorti alors qu’il pleuvait.
native_language_example: He went out even though it was raining.

additional_notes: Used both literally (a spiritual being believed to protect someone) and figuratively for a person who helps, watches over, or “saves” you. Often appears with possessives: « mon/ton/son ange gardien ». As a job title (in museums/stores), it can also mean an attendant/guard, but beginners most often meet the “guardian angel” meaning.
target_language_example: Elle dit que sa grand-mère est son ange gardien.
native_language_example: She says her grandmother is her guardian angel.

additional_notes: Used to talk about animals kept at home for companionship (dogs, cats, etc.). Often used with verbs like avoir (to have) and with possessives: mon/ton/son animal de compagnie. Commonly shortened in everyday French to « un animal de compagnie » rather than naming the species.
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu as un animal de compagnie ?
native_language_example: Do you have a pet?

additional_notes: Used to talk about animals kept at home (cats, dogs, etc.). In everyday French, you’ll often hear just "un animal de compagnie" for “a pet,” but "animal domestique" is also common, especially in more general or official contexts (rules, housing, travel).
target_language_example: Les animaux domestiques sont acceptés dans cet hôtel.
native_language_example: Pets are accepted in this hotel.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a year with an extra day (February 29). Common in calendar/date contexts: « En année bissextile… », « 2024 est une année bissextile ».
target_language_example: 2024 est une année bissextile, donc février a 29 jours.
native_language_example: 2024 is a leap year, so February has 29 days.

additional_notes: Used to talk about braces or other orthodontic devices worn on the teeth (sometimes removable). In everyday speech, people also say simply "des bagues" (braces).
target_language_example: Elle porte un appareil dentaire depuis six mois.
native_language_example: She has been wearing braces for six months.

additional_notes: Common way to say “camera” in French (especially for a still-photo camera). You can add a possessive: « mon appareil photo » (my camera), « ton appareil photo » (your camera). For a video camera/camcorder you may also hear « caméra ».
target_language_example: J’ai oublié mon appareil photo à l’hôtel.
native_language_example: I forgot my camera at the hotel.

additional_notes: Used to talk about realizing or understanding something only later, once an event has already happened. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence: "Après coup, ..." or after the verb: "Je m’en suis rendu compte après coup." It’s close to "a posteriori" but more common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Après coup, je me suis rendu compte que j’avais eu tort.
native_language_example: Afterwards, I realized that I had been wrong.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an action/event that happens later than another one: "after (someone) does/did..." It’s followed by a subject + verb (a full clause). In careful/standard French, the verb after « après que » is in the indicative (not the subjunctive), e.g., « après qu’il est parti ».
target_language_example: On est sortis après qu’il est parti.
native_language_example: We went out after he left.

additional_notes: Used to politely let someone go first (through a door, into an elevator, etc.). Often said on its own, or with “Non, après vous” for extra politeness (vous-form). Literally “after you.”
target_language_example: Vas-y, après toi !
native_language_example: Go ahead, after you!

additional_notes: Used to add a final thought, justification, or conclusion—often meaning you’ve reconsidered or want to emphasize that something makes sense in the end. Can appear at the start, middle, or end of a sentence: « Après tout, ... » / « ..., après tout. »
target_language_example: Après tout, on a le temps.
native_language_example: After all, we have time.

additional_notes: Used as a polite phrase to let someone go first (through a door, into an elevator, ahead in line). Often said while gesturing or holding a door. You can also use it to insist politely if someone hesitates.
target_language_example: Après vous, je vous en prie.
native_language_example: After you, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific day two days from now. Often appears with "(d’)" + time: "après-demain matin" (the morning after tomorrow), "après-demain soir" (the evening after tomorrow). Hyphenated form is standard.
target_language_example: On se voit après-demain ?
native_language_example: Are we seeing each other the day after tomorrow?

meaning: postwar; the period after a war.
additional_notes: Used as a noun (often with an article: "l’après-guerre") or as an adjective to describe things from the postwar period (e.g., "la période après-guerre", "les années d’après-guerre"). Common in history and news contexts. Usually refers to a specific war understood from context (often World War II).
target_language_example: Dans l’après-guerre, le pays a été reconstruit rapidement.
native_language_example: In the postwar period, the country was rebuilt quickly.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the time after midday (after 12:00). Often appears with a preposition: "cet après-midi" (this afternoon), "cet après-midi-là" (that afternoon), "l’après-midi" (in the afternoon/afternoons), "dans l’après-midi" (sometime during the afternoon). It’s masculine: "un après-midi".
target_language_example: On se voit cet après-midi à 15h ?
native_language_example: Shall we see each other this afternoon at 3 p.m.?

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for the decorated tree used during the Christmas season. Usually masculine: « un arbre de Noël ». You can also say « le sapin de Noël » (often more common), especially because people typically use a fir tree.
target_language_example: On a décoré l’arbre de Noël hier soir.
native_language_example: We decorated the Christmas tree last night.

additional_notes: A masculine noun: un arc-en-ciel. It can be used literally (a rainbow in the sky) or figuratively (a range/variety of colors). In French it’s usually singular, even though English often says “a rainbow” as well; the plural is des arcs-en-ciel.
target_language_example: Après la pluie, on a vu un arc-en-ciel.
native_language_example: After the rain, we saw a rainbow.

additional_notes: Used for weapons that shoot bullets using an explosion (e.g., a pistol, rifle). Often seen in news, laws, and security contexts. Plural: « des armes à feu ». Not the same as « arme blanche » (knife/other bladed weapon).
target_language_example: La police a trouvé une arme à feu dans la voiture.
native_language_example: The police found a firearm in the car.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: "arriver à + infinitif" to express achieving something after effort or difficulty. In everyday French it often means "to manage to" rather than the literal "to arrive at". Common in negative and questions: "Je n’arrive pas à..." / "Tu arrives à...?"
target_language_example: J’arrive à comprendre, mais c’est difficile.
native_language_example: I can manage to understand, but it’s difficult.

meaning: to measure up to someone; to be as good as someone.
additional_notes: Usually used in the negative: « ne pas arriver à la cheville de quelqu’un » = “not to be a patch on someone / not to hold a candle to someone.” Literally “to reach someone’s ankle,” meaning you’re not at their level. Often used to compare skills, talent, or success.
target_language_example: Il est bon, mais il n’arrive pas à la cheville de sa sœur.
native_language_example: He’s good, but he doesn’t measure up to his sister.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the place where you wait for a bus. Often used with prepositions like « à l’arrêt de bus » (at the bus stop) or « près de l’arrêt de bus » (near the bus stop). You may also hear « arrêt de bus » vs. « arrêt d’autobus » (more formal) depending on region.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à l’arrêt de bus à 8 h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the bus stop at 8 o’clock.

additional_notes: Usually used in the plural: « les arts martiaux » (martial arts). You can talk about practicing it with « faire/pratiquer un art martial » (to do/practice a martial art).
target_language_example: Je pratique un art martial deux fois par semaine.
native_language_example: I practice a martial art twice a week.

additional_notes: Used to stop a conversation and move on (often: “let’s act now”). It can sound firm or slightly impatient depending on tone; common in spoken French. Often followed by “passons à…” (let’s move on to…) or “au travail !” (back to work!).
target_language_example: Assez parlé, passons aux choses sérieuses.
native_language_example: Enough talking—let’s get down to business.

additional_notes: Common in spoken French as a shortened form of « attendre et voir » or « attendre de voir ». Used when you don’t want to decide yet and prefer to see what happens first.
target_language_example: On va attendre voir ce qui se passe.
native_language_example: We’ll wait and see what happens.

additional_notes: A very formal, legal phrase used at the start of clauses that state the reasons/background facts in contracts, court decisions, or official statements (similar to English "Whereas..."). Commonly followed by a full clause: "Attendu que + [fact/reason]". Not used in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Attendu que les parties souhaitent conclure le présent contrat, elles conviennent de ce qui suit.
native_language_example: Whereas the parties wish to enter into this contract, they agree to the following.

meaning: "Watch out for" / "be careful of" / "pay attention to".
additional_notes: Used to warn someone about a possible danger or problem (often like “watch out for…”). It can also mean “pay attention to…” in a more neutral sense. Common pattern: « Attention à + noun » or « Attention à ne pas + infinitive » (be careful not to…).
target_language_example: Attention à ne pas glisser sur le sol mouillé !
native_language_example: Be careful not to slip on the wet floor!

additional_notes: Used for drawing attention to yourself, something happening, or an important point. Often followed by "sur" + a topic: "attirer l’attention sur quelque chose" = "to draw attention to something". Can also be used in the negative: "ne pas attirer l’attention" = "not to draw attention".
target_language_example: J’essaie d’attirer l’attention du serveur.
native_language_example: I’m trying to get the waiter’s attention.

meaning: to catch a cold; to get chilled (from being cold).
additional_notes: Used when someone has been exposed to cold weather/air and you warn they might get sick: « Tu vas attraper froid. » It’s also commonly phrased as « attraper un rhume » (“to catch a cold” literally, with a runny-nose cold). Often used without an article before « froid ».
target_language_example: Mets une veste, tu vas attraper froid.
native_language_example: Put on a jacket, you’re going to catch a cold.

additional_notes: Used to say something will be done only if it becomes necessary. Common in more formal or written French, often followed by a verb: « au besoin, je peux… ». Close in meaning to « si besoin » (more common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Au besoin, je peux vous rappeler demain.
native_language_example: If needed, I can call you back tomorrow.

meaning: at the right time; at a good moment.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens at an appropriate or opportune time. Often paired with "au bon endroit" (in the right place): "au bon moment, au bon endroit". Also used after verbs like arriver, venir, tomber (e.g., "tomber au bon moment" = to come at just the right time).
target_language_example: Tu es arrivé au bon moment : le dîner est prêt.
native_language_example: You arrived at the right time: dinner is ready.

meaning: at the edge of; on the verge of.
additional_notes: Used literally for being next to a physical edge (a river, a cliff, the sea) and figuratively for being close to a state or event (often something negative): « au bord de la faillite » (on the verge of bankruptcy), « au bord des larmes » (on the verge of tears). Usually followed by a noun (often with an article): « au bord de la mer », « au bord du lac ».
target_language_example: Il était au bord des larmes.
native_language_example: He was on the verge of tears.

additional_notes: Common everyday way to talk about going to work or being at work. Often used with verbs like aller/être/retourner: « Je vais au boulot » (I’m going to work), « Je suis au boulot » (I’m at work). More formal/neutral: « au travail ». « Boulot » is slightly informal, like “work/the job.”
target_language_example: Désolé, je peux pas, je suis au boulot.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t, I’m at work.

meaning: "at the end of"; "after" (a period of time).
additional_notes: Used mainly in two ways: (1) location/sequence: "at the end of" a street, a line, a process, etc. (2) time: "after" a duration (often with "au bout de + number + minutes/heures/jours"), meaning when that time has passed. Commonly followed by a noun (au bout de la rue) or a time expression (au bout de deux jours).
target_language_example: Au bout de deux semaines, il a trouvé un appartement.
native_language_example: After two weeks, he found an apartment.

meaning: at the end of your rope; exhausted (physically, mentally, or financially).
additional_notes: Common idiom meaning you’ve reached your limit and can’t keep going. Often used about being extremely tired, burned out, or even broke. Used with "être" (e.g., "Je suis au bout du rouleau").
target_language_example: Après cette semaine de travail, je suis au bout du rouleau.
native_language_example: After this week of work, I’m at the end of my rope.

additional_notes: Used to express a precaution or contingency: you do something now because a situation might happen later. It’s often followed by the conditional in French when referring to a possible future situation (e.g., "au cas où tu aurais besoin de moi"), even though English typically uses the present tense (“in case you need me”).
target_language_example: Je te donne mon numéro au cas où tu aurais un problème.
native_language_example: I’m giving you my number in case you have a problem.

meaning: in a warm place; somewhere warm (warm and sheltered).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is warm, protected from the cold, or indoors. Often appears with verbs like rester/mettre/garder (rester au chaud = stay warm/stay inside; mettre au chaud = put/bring somewhere warm). Can also be used more figuratively to mean “safe and comfortable.”
target_language_example: Reste au chaud, il fait froid dehors.
native_language_example: Stay warm (stay inside), it’s cold outside.

additional_notes: Used with "être" to say someone is unemployed: "Je suis au chômage." It can also describe someone receiving unemployment benefits in some contexts, but it mainly means not currently employed. Related: "le chômage" = unemployment (noun).
target_language_example: Il est au chômage depuis trois mois.
native_language_example: He has been unemployed for three months.

meaning: clear; understood; up to date (on something).
additional_notes: Usually used with "être" and often with "sur" + topic: "être au clair sur (un sujet)" = to have things straight / to be clear about something. It can also mean "to be in the clear" (no longer suspected/in danger), depending on context.
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas encore au clair sur les détails, mais je te tiens au courant.
native_language_example: I’m not clear on the details yet, but I’ll keep you posted.

meaning: 'at the corner' (street corner) or 'in the corner' (of a room).
additional_notes: Literally "to the corner" = à + le → au. Used for locations: with streets/shops it usually means "at/on the corner" (Au coin de la rue). With rooms or objects it often means "in the corner" (au coin de la pièce). Often followed by "de" + a place.
target_language_example: La boulangerie est au coin de la rue.
native_language_example: The bakery is on the corner of the street.

meaning: 'at the corner of the street' (around the corner).
additional_notes: Used to give directions or describe a location near an intersection. Often followed by a landmark: "au coin de la rue, il y a…". "Au coin" = at the corner; "de la rue" = of the street.
target_language_example: La boulangerie est au coin de la rue.
native_language_example: The bakery is at the corner of the street / around the corner.

meaning: to the account of (in banking/accounting); in the name of.
additional_notes: Used mainly in formal contexts (bank transfers, accounting records) to indicate which person or organization an amount is credited/debited to. Often appears with verbs like « virer » (transfer), « verser » (pay), « créditer/débiter » (credit/debit). Related expression: « mettre au compte de » = to attribute/blame something on (more figurative).
target_language_example: Veuillez virer la somme au compte de Mme Durand.
native_language_example: Please transfer the amount to Mrs. Durand’s account.

meaning: on the contrary; quite the opposite.
additional_notes: Used to contradict what was just said or to emphasize the opposite idea. Often appears after a negation (e.g., « Ce n’est pas facile. Au contraire, c’est très difficile. »). Can be used on its own as a short reply meaning “Actually, no—it's the opposite.”
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas fâché ; au contraire, je suis content.
native_language_example: I’m not angry; on the contrary, I’m happy.

additional_notes: Most often used with the verb "être": "être au courant (de ...)" = to be aware of / to know about / to be up to date on something. Very common in everyday French, for news, plans, changes, or information. Not usually translated word-for-word as "to the current" in English.
target_language_example: Je suis au courant de la réunion de demain.
native_language_example: I’m aware of tomorrow’s meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens within a period of time (often followed by a noun phrase): au cours de la journée (during the day), au cours de l’année (during the year), au cours du voyage (during the trip). Slightly more formal than pendant in many contexts, but very common in writing and speech.
target_language_example: Au cours de la réunion, j’ai pris des notes.
native_language_example: During the meeting, I took notes.

additional_notes: Used to reject something, express irritation, or tell someone/something to go away (similar to "to hell with it" or "go to hell"). Often appears as "Au diable !" or "Au diable + noun" (e.g., "Au diable les devoirs !"). Can sound rude/harsh depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Au diable les papiers, je pars en vacances !
native_language_example: To hell with the paperwork, I’m going on vacation!

meaning: at the beginning; in the beginning (of something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the start of a time period, event, story, or process. Often followed by “de” + a noun: “au début de la journée” (at the beginning of the day). For contrast, “au début” focuses on the start, while “d’abord” means “first/first of all” (sequence of actions).
target_language_example: Au début du film, on voit la mer.
native_language_example: At the beginning of the movie, we see the sea.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the beginning of a situation, plan, or story, often to contrast with what happens later (e.g., «Au départ…, mais ensuite…»). It can also mean “at departure” in travel contexts (e.g., at the time of leaving).
target_language_example: Au départ, je voulais rester une semaine, mais finalement je suis resté un mois.
native_language_example: At first, I wanted to stay a week, but in the end I stayed a month.

meaning: "by the way"; "actually" (to bring up a new point or return to a topic).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to introduce something you just remembered, change the subject, or get back to the main point. Often comes at the start of a sentence: "Au fait, ...". It can also mean "informed/aware" in expressions like "être au fait de" (to be up to date on / aware of).
target_language_example: Au fait, tu as des nouvelles de Paul ?
native_language_example: By the way, have you heard from Paul?

additional_notes: Used as a warning/cry to signal a fire (or that something is burning). Commonly heard as in "Au feu !" or "Au feu, les pompiers !". In everyday conversation, you’ll more often describe the situation with "Il y a le feu" (There’s a fire) or "Ça brûle" (It’s burning).
target_language_example: Au feu ! Appelez les pompiers !
native_language_example: Fire! Call the firefighters!

meaning: over the course of; as time goes by (throughout).
additional_notes: Used to show that something changes or happens gradually during a period of time. Very common with time words like "les années", "le temps", "les semaines". Often followed by a noun phrase ("au fil des années") or by "au fil du temps". Note the form changes with the article: "au fil du" (de + le) and "au fil des" (de + les).
target_language_example: Au fil des années, j’ai appris à parler français.
native_language_example: Over the years, I learned to speak French.

additional_notes: Used to sum up or give the final outcome after considering everything (similar to "au bout du compte"). Common in both speech and writing, often to introduce a conclusion: "Au final, ...". Don’t confuse with "la finale" (the final/match).
target_language_example: Au final, on a décidé de rester à la maison.
native_language_example: In the end, we decided to stay home.

meaning: at the bottom; at the back; basically/deep down.
additional_notes: Literal meaning is physical location ("at the bottom" / "at the back"), often used for rooms/places: "au fond de la salle" (at the back of the room) or "au fond du sac" (at the bottom of the bag). Figuratively, it can mean "deep down" or "basically/when you think about it" to express someone’s true feeling or the essential point.
target_language_example: Au fond, je pense que tu as raison.
native_language_example: Deep down, I think you’re right.

additional_notes: Used to locate something far inside a place or container (the back of a room, the bottom of a bag, the far end of a hallway). It can also be used more abstractly to mean 'deep inside' someone/something (e.g., a feeling). Often followed by a noun: au fond de la salle, au fond du sac, au fond de moi.
target_language_example: Les clés sont au fond du sac.
native_language_example: The keys are at the bottom of the bag.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like mettre (to put) and être (to be) to talk about food or dishes cooking/baking. Literally “to the/in the oven,” but in English you usually say “in the oven.”
target_language_example: Mets le plat au four pendant 20 minutes.
native_language_example: Put the dish in the oven for 20 minutes.

additional_notes: Literally “at the gallop.” Used with verbs like aller/partir/arriver (“to go/leave/arrive”) to describe moving quickly, especially (but not only) on horseback. It can also be used figuratively to mean something is happening very quickly.
target_language_example: Il est parti au galop pour rattraper le bus.
native_language_example: He left at full speed to catch the bus.

meaning: at the whim of; depending on; according to.
additional_notes: Used to say something changes or happens depending on circumstances, someone’s wishes, or chance. Common with words like le vent (the wind), le hasard (chance), or les envies de quelqu’un (someone’s desires). Often implies little control: things go one way or another “as X dictates.”
target_language_example: Nous changeons nos plans au gré de la météo.
native_language_example: We change our plans depending on the weather.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done without a plan or selection (randomly). Often used with verbs like choisir (to choose), prendre (to take), tirer (to draw), or trouver (to find).
target_language_example: J’ai choisi un livre au hasard.
native_language_example: I chose a book at random.

meaning: day by day; from one day to the next.
additional_notes: Used to describe living or managing things without long-term plans, focusing on immediate needs and daily changes (often with the idea of uncertainty or short-term thinking). Common with verbs like vivre (to live), gérer (to manage), and suivre (to follow).
target_language_example: En ce moment, on vit au jour le jour.
native_language_example: Right now, we’re living day to day.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or give a more exact detail, often after something was said in a vague way. Very common in questions: "C’est quoi, au juste ?" = "What exactly is it?" You can also use it to clarify numbers, times, or reasons: "trois, au juste" = "three, exactly".
target_language_example: Tu veux dire quoi, au juste ?
native_language_example: What exactly do you mean?

meaning: offshore; out at sea (away from the coast).
additional_notes: Used to describe something located or happening out at sea, not near the shore. Common with verbs like « être », « naviguer » (to sail), « partir » (to head out), and with weather/sea contexts. Not to confuse with « large » meaning “wide/broad” in other contexts; in « au large » it specifically refers to being out to sea.
target_language_example: On a aperçu un bateau au large.
native_language_example: We spotted a boat offshore.

meaning: 'off' / 'off the coast of' (out at sea near).
additional_notes: Used mainly with places to say something is out at sea, not near the shore, but in the waters near that location. Common in news, geography, and travel contexts. Often follows a verb like être/se trouver (to be/to be located): « Le bateau est au large de… ».
target_language_example: Un cargo est au large de Marseille.
native_language_example: A cargo ship is off the coast of Marseille.

additional_notes: Used to show a substitution: one thing happens or is chosen rather than another. It’s followed by a noun or an infinitive (verb): « au lieu de + nom » or « au lieu de + infinitif ». If you need to follow it with a conjugated verb, you often use « au lieu de + infinitif » (e.g., « au lieu de venir, il reste… »).
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un thé au lieu de café.
native_language_example: I’m going to have tea instead of coffee.

additional_notes: Literally “to the bed.” Used after verbs like être (to be) to mean “in bed” (Il est au lit), and after aller (to go) to mean “to bed” (Je vais au lit). Also common in phrases like mettre quelqu’un au lit (“to put someone to bed”).
target_language_example: Je vais au lit.
native_language_example: I’m going to bed.

meaning: along; all along; throughout (often in “tout au long de”).
additional_notes: Means “along the length of” something (a road, a river, etc.) or “throughout” a period of time. In everyday French, you’ll much more often see or hear **le long de** (“along”) for places and **tout au long de** (“throughout”) for time. It’s followed by a noun: au long de + la route / la journée.
target_language_example: Nous avons marché tout au long de la plage.
native_language_example: We walked all along the beach.

additional_notes: Used to express an upper limit (“no more than”) or the highest possible level. Common with quantities and time: « deux fois au maximum » (twice at most), « dix minutes au maximum » (ten minutes at most). In instructions or settings it can mean “as high as possible”: « Mets le volume au maximum. »
target_language_example: On reste dix minutes au maximum.
native_language_example: We’re staying ten minutes at most.

meaning: 'as best as possible' / 'to the best of one's ability'.
additional_notes: Used to describe doing something in the best possible way given the circumstances. Often follows a verb (e.g., faire au mieux, s'organiser au mieux) and can also mean 'at best' when giving an upper limit or optimistic estimate (e.g., Au mieux, ça prendra deux jours = At best, it’ll take two days).
target_language_example: Je vais faire au mieux pour être à l’heure.
native_language_example: I’ll do my best to be on time.

additional_notes: Used to locate something/someone at the center of a place or group. Followed by a noun: « au milieu de + nom » (often with a plural to mean “among”). Can also be used more figuratively for being in the midst of an activity or situation: « au milieu d’une conversation ».
target_language_example: Il y a une fontaine au milieu de la place.
native_language_example: There is a fountain in the middle of the square.

additional_notes: Used to say a place is very remote/isolated, far from towns and people. Often used with verbs like être/se trouver (to be/be located) and vivre (to live).
target_language_example: On s’est perdus au milieu de nulle part.
native_language_example: We got lost in the middle of nowhere.

additional_notes: Used to express a minimum quantity, time, or requirement (the lowest acceptable amount). Often followed by a number or amount: "au minimum trois jours" (at least three days). It can also be used alone to mean "at the very least" in a more general sense.
target_language_example: Il faut au minimum deux jours pour finir ce travail.
native_language_example: It takes at least two days to finish this work.

additional_notes: Used to express a minimum quantity/degree (often with numbers) or to soften a statement by pointing to a minimum positive fact. Can also introduce a correction or limitation: “at least / anyway / in any case.”
target_language_example: J’ai au moins vingt minutes de retard.
native_language_example: I’m at least twenty minutes late.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause that marks the exact time something happens (often like “just as”). It can refer to the present (“right when”) or to the past in narration (“when”). Often followed by the imperfect or past tenses depending on the context.
target_language_example: Au moment où je suis arrivé, il pleuvait.
native_language_example: When I arrived, it was raining.

additional_notes: Usually used after a superlative or an expression like "the best/most/only" to emphasize something (e.g., "the best in the world"). In negatives, it can mean "(not) ... at all" / "(not) ... in the slightest" (e.g., "rien au monde" = "nothing in the world").
target_language_example: C’est le meilleur restaurant au monde.
native_language_example: It’s the best restaurant in the world.

additional_notes: Formal/prepositional phrase used to indicate the instrument, method, or intermediary used to do something. Often followed by a noun (e.g., un outil, un système, Internet). In everyday speech, people also use "avec" or "par" depending on context.
target_language_example: Il a ouvert la porte au moyen d’un tournevis.
native_language_example: He opened the door using a screwdriver.

meaning: in the name of; on behalf of.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is acting with someone else’s authority or representing them ("on behalf of"), or to justify something by referring to a principle/cause ("in the name of"). Common in formal contexts (letters, announcements, official speech): "Au nom de l’équipe, je vous remercie."
target_language_example: Au nom de toute l’équipe, je vous remercie.
native_language_example: On behalf of the whole team, I thank you.

additional_notes: Used to give a total count, often in formal or written French. It usually comes before a number: « au nombre de + chiffre » (e.g., « au nombre de 20 »). Similar in meaning to « en tout » or « au total », but « au nombre de » specifically introduces the number of people/things.
target_language_example: Les participants étaient au nombre de trente.
native_language_example: There were a total of thirty participants.

meaning: at a walking pace; at a walk (especially for a horse).
additional_notes: Common in horseback riding to describe the slowest gait: « marcher (son cheval) au pas » = to walk (a horse). By extension, it can describe moving very slowly: « avancer au pas » (to move along at a crawl/very slowly).
target_language_example: Après le galop, on est repassés au pas.
native_language_example: After the gallop, we went back to a walk.

additional_notes: Used to add something as an aside (a small extra comment) while talking about something else: « Au passage, … ». It can also be used more literally to mean “as (someone) passes by,” especially in the longer structure « au passage de + [person/thing] » (e.g., “when/while [someone] passed”).
target_language_example: Au passage, tu peux acheter du pain ?
native_language_example: By the way, can you buy some bread?

meaning: at the foot (of); at the base (of).
additional_notes: Usually used with "de": "au pied de" + place/thing (e.g., a mountain, a building) to mean "at the foot/base of". It can also be used as a dog-training command: "Au pied !" = "Heel!" (walk right next to me).
target_language_example: On s’est retrouvé au pied de la tour.
native_language_example: We met at the foot of the tower.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the most negative possible outcome, often to reassure: if things don’t go well, this is the fallback. Commonly paired with other options: « Au mieux…, au pire… » (“Best case…, worst case…”).
target_language_example: On essaie maintenant ; au pire, on le fera demain.
native_language_example: We’ll try now; at worst, we’ll do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used as a friendly, polite sign-off meaning “until next time / see you soon.” Often implies you expect to meet again or repeat the activity. You can also hear it with a verb: « Au plaisir de te revoir / de vous revoir » (“Looking forward to seeing you again”).
target_language_example: Merci pour ce café, au plaisir !
native_language_example: Thanks for the coffee—looking forward to next time!

additional_notes: Used to set an upper limit on a quantity, time, or number. Often followed by a number: "au plus trois" (at most three). You’ll also see it in set phrases like "au plus tard" (at the latest).
target_language_example: Je peux rester dix minutes au plus.
native_language_example: I can stay ten minutes at most.

meaning: no later than; at the latest.
additional_notes: Used to give a deadline (the latest acceptable time). Often followed by a day/time: "au plus tard lundi" / "au plus tard à 18 h". Common in writing (emails, notices), but also used in speech.
target_language_example: Merci de m’envoyer le document au plus tard vendredi.
native_language_example: Please send me the document no later than Friday.

meaning: as soon as possible; at the earliest.
additional_notes: Used to indicate the earliest possible time something can happen. Common in requests and scheduling (emails, appointments, deliveries). Often paired with a future tense or with verbs like « possible »: « au plus tôt possible ».
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me répondre au plus tôt ?
native_language_example: Can you reply to me as soon as possible?

meaning: as quickly as possible; as soon as possible.
additional_notes: Used to insist on speed or urgency, often with verbs like revenir (to come back), répondre (to reply), or faire (to do). It’s similar to “le plus vite possible,” and in many everyday situations it can also imply “as soon as you can.”
target_language_example: Réponds-moi au plus vite, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Reply to me as quickly as possible, please.

additional_notes: Colloquial/informal idiom meaning something is exactly right or flawless. Often used after "c'est" or "être" ("C'est au poil", "Tout est au poil"). Not a literal phrase (it doesn’t mean “to the hair” in normal use).
target_language_example: On a fini à temps, tout est au poil !
native_language_example: We finished on time—everything is perfect!

meaning: ready; in order; properly set up.
additional_notes: Often used with être: « être au point » = to be ready/working properly/in good shape (for a plan, a machine, preparations, or even a person’s knowledge). Related pattern: « au point de + infinitive » means “to the point of (doing something)” (e.g., « fatigué au point de s’endormir » = “so tired as to fall asleep”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tout est au point.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything is ready.

meaning: to the point of; so ... that (it leads to).
additional_notes: Used to indicate degree or intensity that reaches a consequence, often followed by an infinitive: « au point de + infinitif » (e.g., « au point de pleurer » = “to the point of crying”). It can also introduce a result clause with « que »: « au point que + phrase » (“so much that ...”). Common after adjectives or expressions of intensity (fatigué, stressé, énervé, etc.).
target_language_example: Il était fatigué au point de s’endormir dans le métro.
native_language_example: He was so tired that he fell asleep on the subway.

additional_notes: Used mainly in politics to say who is currently governing or holding authority. Often used with verbs like « être » (to be), « arriver » (to come), « rester » (to stay), « revenir » (to return): « être au pouvoir » = to be in power. Can also refer more generally to being in a position of authority, but the political meaning is most common.
target_language_example: Depuis 2017, ce parti est au pouvoir.
native_language_example: Since 2017, that party has been in power.

meaning: 'at the cost of' / 'at the price of'.
additional_notes: Used to express what must be sacrificed, paid, or endured to get something. Often used figuratively (efforts, sacrifices, risks), not just for money. It can imply the cost was high or difficult.
target_language_example: Il a obtenu ce poste au prix de beaucoup d’efforts.
native_language_example: He got this job at the cost of a lot of effort.

additional_notes: Used in formal or written French to mean something must happen first (a prerequisite step). Often appears with verbs like « vérifier », « demander », « informer »: « au préalable, il faut… » or « il faut… au préalable ».
target_language_example: Vous devez vous inscrire au préalable.
native_language_example: You must register beforehand.

meaning: on a daily basis; in everyday life.
additional_notes: Used to talk about routine, day-to-day life (habits, work, practical reality). Often paired with verbs like vivre, utiliser, gérer, or nouns like la vie, le travail: « dans la vie au quotidien ». More formal/neutral than « tous les jours » (every day).
target_language_example: Au quotidien, je prends le métro pour aller au travail.
native_language_example: On a daily basis, I take the subway to go to work.

meaning: at low speed; in slow motion.
additional_notes: Used to describe something happening slowly (a machine, a car, a process) or to say a video is being played in slow motion. Common with verbs like « rouler » (to drive), « tourner » (to run/operate), or « passer » (to play/show).
target_language_example: La voiture roulait au ralenti dans les embouteillages.
native_language_example: The car was moving slowly in the traffic jam.

meaning: in light of; considering; with regard to.
additional_notes: Formal-ish prepositional phrase used to introduce a comparison or evaluation based on a fact, context, law, or criterion. Common in writing and official/administrative French. Often followed by a noun phrase: « au regard de la loi », « au regard des résultats ». близ to « compte tenu de » (“given”) and « par rapport à » (“compared to”), but « au regard de » sounds more formal.
target_language_example: Au regard de la situation, il vaut mieux attendre.
native_language_example: In light of the situation, it’s better to wait.

additional_notes: A standard, polite way to say goodbye in most situations. Literally means “until seeing again,” implying you may see the person again. Often shortened to “’revoir” in casual speech.
target_language_example: Au revoir, à demain !
native_language_example: Goodbye, see you tomorrow!

meaning: Help! / Help me! (an urgent cry for help).
additional_notes: Used when you are in trouble or in an emergency; it’s a common exclamation to call for help. Often said alone (“Au secours !”) or with a short detail (“Au secours, je suis perdu(e) !”).
target_language_example: Au secours ! On m’a volé mon sac !
native_language_example: Help! Someone stole my bag!

additional_notes: Used mostly in formal or written French to mean "within" a group or structure (a company, team, family, committee, society). It’s common with abstract nouns and institutions: « au sein de l’entreprise », « au sein du gouvernement ». In everyday speech, people often use « dans » instead (e.g., « dans l’équipe »). Literally « sein » means "breast/bosom", but in this expression it means the "heart" or "midst" of a group.
target_language_example: Au sein de l’équipe, chacun a un rôle important.
native_language_example: Within the team, everyone has an important role.

meaning: 'to the sound of' / 'to the music of'.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens while hearing a particular sound or music. Often followed by a noun (au son de la musique, au son des cloches) or a musician/instrument (au son du violon). Note the contraction: à + le = au, à + les = aux.
target_language_example: Ils ont dansé au son de la musique.
native_language_example: They danced to the sound of the music.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic of what you’re talking, asking, writing, or thinking about. Common in more neutral or slightly formal contexts (emails, explanations). Often followed by a noun or pronoun: « au sujet de ce problème » (about this problem), « au sujet de ça » (about that). Similar to « à propos de ».
target_language_example: Je vous écris au sujet de votre annonce.
native_language_example: I’m writing to you about your ad.

meaning: "in the time of" / "back in the days of" (during a past period).
additional_notes: Used to place something in a historical period or in someone’s era (often with a person, ruler, or past time). It typically refers to the past: « au temps de Napoléon » = during Napoleon’s time. Also commonly appears as « au temps où… » (“at the time when…”).
target_language_example: Au temps de mes grands-parents, il n’y avait pas d’Internet.
native_language_example: In my grandparents’ time, there was no internet.

meaning: at work; to work (as an instruction).
additional_notes: Literally “to the work.” Used to say someone is at their workplace/working (Il est au travail) or as an encouragement/command meaning “Get to work!” (Au travail !). Often contrasts with being at home: Je suis au travail / Je suis à la maison.
target_language_example: Je suis au travail jusqu'à 18 h.
native_language_example: I'm at work until 6 p.m.

meaning: through; across (often: through something with obstacles).
additional_notes: A more formal/less common variant of "à travers". Used for moving through something (a forest, traffic, crowds) and can also be used figuratively (through experiences/events). In everyday speech, learners will more often hear "à travers".
target_language_example: Il a couru au travers de la forêt malgré la pluie.
native_language_example: He ran through the forest despite the rain.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is currently talking on the phone (Il/Elle est au téléphone) or that something is done by phone (On peut le faire au téléphone). Often contrasts with en personne (“in person”).
target_language_example: Je suis au téléphone, je te rappelle dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: I’m on the phone; I’ll call you back in five minutes.

meaning: on the fly; in mid-air (without stopping).
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like prendre/attraper/saisir (to catch), répondre (to answer), or improviser (to improvise). It suggests doing something immediately, as it happens, without preparation, or catching something while it’s moving through the air. You’ll also see it in sports contexts (frapper au vol = to hit on the volley).
target_language_example: Il a attrapé la balle au vol.
native_language_example: He caught the ball in mid-air (on the volley).

additional_notes: Used to say someone is driving a vehicle (car, bus, etc.). Often follows verbs like être (to be) or prendre (to take): « Il est au volant » (He’s driving), « Elle a pris le volant » (She took the wheel / started driving). Can also be used in warnings like « Ne téléphonez pas au volant » (Don’t use your phone while driving).
target_language_example: Je suis au volant, je te rappelle plus tard.
native_language_example: I’m driving; I’ll call you back later.

additional_notes: Used as an alarm cry when you see someone stealing or running away with stolen goods. Often said loudly and repeated: « Au voleur ! Au voleur ! ». You may also hear « Au voleur ! À l’aide ! » (“Thief! Help!”).
target_language_example: Au voleur ! Il m’a pris mon sac !
native_language_example: Thief! He took my bag!

additional_notes: Often used to talk about something further than a limit or point: au-delà de = “beyond” / “past” / “more than.” It can be literal (distance) or figurative (limits, expectations). Also appears as a noun in expressions like l’au-delà (“the afterlife”), but beginners most often meet it in au-delà de + noun/number.
target_language_example: Au-delà de 30 euros, c’est trop cher pour moi.
native_language_example: Beyond 30 euros, it’s too expensive for me.

additional_notes: Used to express going past a limit (physical, time, or abstract). With a noun or pronoun: au-delà de la ville (beyond the city), au-delà de minuit (after midnight), au-delà de 100 euros (more than 100 euros). Often followed by a noun phrase; can also be used figuratively (au-delà des apparences = beyond appearances).
target_language_example: Au-delà de 18 ans, l’entrée est gratuite.
native_language_example: Over 18, admission is free.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position at a lower level: *au-dessous de* + noun/pronoun ("below/under"). Often contrasts with *au-dessus* (above). Note: *en dessous* is also common and means "below/under" too; *au-dessous* can feel a bit more formal or written.
target_language_example: Le parking est au-dessous de l’immeuble.
native_language_example: The parking lot is below/under the building.

additional_notes: Used for position: something is physically higher than something else (often with "de": "au-dessus de" = "above/over"). Can be used literally (a shelf above the bed) and sometimes figuratively ("au-dessus de ça" = "above that / beyond that"). Often contrasts with "au-dessous" (below).
target_language_example: Le tableau est au-dessus du canapé.
native_language_example: The painting is above the couch.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a higher position than something/someone, either physically or on a vertical scale (often with a number: temperature, level, etc.). Usually followed by a noun or pronoun: au-dessus de la table (above the table), au-dessus de moi (above me). Not the same as "sur" (on top of, in contact with).
target_language_example: Le tableau est au-dessus de la cheminée.
native_language_example: The painting is above the fireplace.

meaning: "near" / "close to" (a person or place); also "with" (someone) or "from" (an organization).
additional_notes: Often used to talk about being physically close to someone, spending time with them, or being in their company: "rester auprès de quelqu’un" (stay close to someone). It can also mean "from" when referring to contacting or requesting something from an institution: "se renseigner auprès de la mairie" (ask the city hall for information). The sense is usually "in the presence of / with" (people) or "through / from" (official sources), rather than simple location like "à côté de".
target_language_example: Je me suis renseigné auprès de la mairie.
native_language_example: I asked the city hall for information.

additional_notes: Used to show that one action happens immediately after another. It’s a conjunction followed by a clause (subject + verb). Often interchangeable with « dès que » in everyday French.
target_language_example: Je t’appelle aussitôt que j’arrive.
native_language_example: I’ll call you as soon as I arrive.

meaning: "as much as" / "as many as"; sometimes "as ... as".
additional_notes: Used to compare quantities (autant + noun) or to compare actions/degree before que (as much as). In negatives, it often means "(not) as much as". Common patterns: "autant que + subject + verb" (as much as...), and "autant ... que" with an adjective/adverb (e.g., "autant bien que" = as well as).
target_language_example: Je veux autant de café que toi.
native_language_example: I want as much coffee as you.

meaning: as much as possible; as far as possible.
additional_notes: Used to say you’ll do something to the maximum extent you can. Common in polite requests and advice. It can modify a verb (e.g., "venir autant que possible"), and it’s often used as a set phrase after an instruction (e.g., "Répondez autant que possible").
target_language_example: Essayez de le faire autant que possible.
native_language_example: Try to do it as much as possible.

additional_notes: Used for (1) physical position/movement around something ("around the house"), and (2) an approximate quantity or time ("around 5 o’clock", "about 10 euros"). Often followed by a noun or number: "autour de la table", "autour de 20 minutes".
target_language_example: On se retrouve autour de 18 h.
native_language_example: We’ll meet up around 6 p.m.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or mention an alternative. Often appears as "autre chose ?" ("anything else?") or "Je veux autre chose" ("I want something else"). You’ll also hear the more emphatic "quelque chose d’autre" (also "something else").
target_language_example: Vous voulez autre chose ?
native_language_example: Do you want anything else?

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like aller (to go) or chercher (to look): « aller autre part » / more commonly « aller ailleurs » (“to go elsewhere”). Don’t confuse with « d’autre part », which means “on the other hand / besides.”
target_language_example: On peut aller autre part si tu préfères.
native_language_example: We can go somewhere else if you prefer.

meaning: “else to … / another … to …” (used before an infinitive).
additional_notes: Usually appears in patterns like **(quelque chose / rien) d’autre à + infinitive** (“something/nothing else to + verb”): *rien d’autre à faire* = “nothing else to do”, *quelque chose d’autre à dire* = “something else to say”. On its own, **autre à** is uncommon; you’ll more often see it with **d’** (d’autre à). Don’t confuse with **autre que** (“other than / except”).
target_language_example: Il n’y a rien d’autre à dire.
native_language_example: There’s nothing else to say.
