additional_notes: Used to rephrase or clarify what you just said, often introducing a simpler explanation or a summary. Common in both spoken and written French. It can appear at the start of a sentence or after a pause: "..., autrement dit, ...".
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas venir demain ; autrement dit, je viendrai après-demain.
native_language_example: I can’t come tomorrow; in other words, I’ll come the day after tomorrow.

meaning: near; in the vicinity of; on the outskirts of.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a location close to a place (often just outside it). Slightly formal and common in news, signs, and written descriptions. Typically followed by a noun place: « aux abords de la ville / de la gare / du stade ».
target_language_example: La police a renforcé la sécurité aux abords du stade.
native_language_example: The police increased security around the stadium.

additional_notes: Used to give an approximate time or location. With time it often means “around/at about” (aux alentours de 18 h = around 6 p.m.). With a place it can mean “in the area/vicinity of” (aux alentours de la gare = around the train station).
target_language_example: On se retrouve aux alentours de 18 h, aux alentours de la gare ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet around 6 p.m., near the train station?

meaning: "To arms!" (take up weapons; rally to fight).
additional_notes: A very formal, historical rallying cry meaning people should arm themselves and prepare to fight. Most commonly recognized from the French national anthem, *La Marseillaise* (e.g., "Aux armes, citoyens !"). In everyday French, you wouldn’t normally say this unless quoting/evoking that context.
target_language_example: Aux armes, citoyens !
native_language_example: To arms, citizens!

additional_notes: Used for someone who is literally operating a vehicle/machine (pilot, driver) or figuratively leading/managing something (a team, a company, a project). Often follows a verb like être/prendre/rester: « être aux commandes », « prendre les commandes ».
target_language_example: C’est elle qui est aux commandes du projet.
native_language_example: She’s the one in charge of the project.

meaning: beside; alongside; at the side of (someone).
additional_notes: Used to show physical proximity or being together with someone in a supportive/associated way (often in formal contexts like working or standing with someone). It agrees with nothing and is followed by a noun or pronoun: « aux côtés de Marie », « aux côtés de lui/elle ».
target_language_example: Il est resté aux côtés de sa sœur pendant toute la cérémonie.
native_language_example: He stayed by his sister’s side throughout the ceremony.

additional_notes: Used mainly in food contexts to describe something made with apples or flavored/filled with apples. Often follows the noun: tarte aux pommes (apple pie), compote aux pommes (apple compote), jus aux pommes (apple juice). Here, "aux" = "à + les" (with/to the).
target_language_example: Je voudrais une tarte aux pommes, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like an apple pie, please.

additional_notes: Most often used in the set expression « être aux trousses de quelqu’un » (“to be after someone / to be chasing someone”), meaning to pursue or hunt for someone (police, creditors, an enemy, etc.). It can also be used more generally for something that’s closely following you (problems, deadlines).
target_language_example: La police est aux trousses du suspect.
native_language_example: The police are on the suspect’s heels.

meaning: in the eyes of; in someone’s view/opinion.
additional_notes: Used to give a point of view or judgment from a specific person or group. It often comes before a noun/pronoun (e.g., aux yeux de mes parents / aux yeux de tous) and can be followed by something that is considered true or important from that perspective.
target_language_example: Aux yeux de Marie, ce film est un chef-d’œuvre.
native_language_example: In Marie’s eyes, this movie is a masterpiece.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an action that happens earlier than another. In French it’s typically followed by the subjunctive: « avant que tu partes » (“before you leave”). Often used with « ne » (called the *ne explétif*) in more formal French: « avant qu’il ne parte »—this « ne » doesn’t mean “not.”
target_language_example: Finis tes devoirs avant que tes parents arrivent.
native_language_example: Finish your homework before your parents arrive.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize what matters most or what should be done first. Common at the start of a sentence or after the verb: « Avant tout, ... » or « ... avant tout ». Literally “before everything,” and it closely matches the English phrasing.
target_language_example: Avant tout, je veux te remercier.
native_language_example: Above all, I want to thank you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened two days ago. It’s a single word in French and is commonly used with the past tense (passé composé or imparfait).
target_language_example: Je l’ai vu avant-hier au café.
native_language_example: I saw him the day before yesterday at the café.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens gradually as time passes (learning, healing, changes, habits). Often paired with verbs like "changer", "s'améliorer", "se calmer", "se passer". Can also mean "in time" in the sense of eventually (e.g., "Avec le temps, tu verras").
target_language_example: Avec le temps, tu vas t’habituer à la ville.
native_language_example: Over time, you’ll get used to the city.

meaning: "With pleasure" / "gladly" (a friendly way to say yes or you're welcome).
additional_notes: Used to accept a request or invitation (similar to “gladly” or “sure!”). It can also be used to respond to “merci” as “my pleasure/you’re welcome.” Common in polite, everyday conversation.
target_language_example: — Tu peux m’aider ? — Avec plaisir !
native_language_example: — Can you help me? — Gladly!

additional_notes: Used for an official notice (often by police) stating that someone is wanted or being sought. Common in news reports and on posters: « Un avis de recherche a été lancé contre… » / « diffuser un avis de recherche ». Also used more broadly for an announcement looking for someone or something (e.g., a missing person or lost pet).
target_language_example: La police a lancé un avis de recherche après la disparition de l’enfant.
native_language_example: The police issued a wanted notice after the child’s disappearance.

additional_notes: Used to say you are able/allowed to enter, use, or reach something (a place, a service, information, etc.). It is usually followed by "à" + noun: "avoir accès à Internet", "avoir accès au bâtiment". Negative: "ne pas avoir accès (à...)".
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas accès à mon compte.
native_language_example: I don’t have access to my account.

meaning: to have to deal with; to be dealing with.
additional_notes: Used with a person or thing: « avoir affaire à + quelqu’un/quelque chose ». It often suggests you’re facing a situation (sometimes difficult) or interacting with someone in a professional/official way. Note the false friend: it does NOT mean “to have an affair (romantically)” in French.
target_language_example: Vous avez affaire à un expert, écoutez-le.
native_language_example: You’re dealing with an expert, listen to him.

additional_notes: Used as a set expression: "avoir beau + infinitive" to say that despite efforts, the result doesn’t change. Often followed by a contrasting clause (frequently with "mais" or just implied): "Tu as beau + infinitif, ..." = "No matter how much you ..., ...". Common in everyday French but not slang.
target_language_example: Tu as beau essayer, tu n’y arrives pas.
native_language_example: No matter how much you try, you can’t manage it.

meaning: to need; to have to have something.
additional_notes: Very common way to express “need” in French. It’s built with avoir (to have) + besoin (need) + de (of). Conjugate avoir: j’ai besoin de…, tu as besoin de…, il/elle a besoin de…, nous avons…, vous avez…, ils/elles ont…. Use de before a noun (J’ai besoin de temps) and before an infinitive (J’ai besoin de partir). De becomes d’ before a vowel or silent h (J’ai besoin d’aide, d’eau).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de ton aide.
native_language_example: I need your help.

meaning: to be right; to have the correct answer.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is correct, often in contexts like quizzes, schoolwork, games, or checking an answer. It’s common in some regions (especially Swiss French) and informal/colloquial in many places; in standard French you’ll more often hear "avoir raison" (to be right).
target_language_example: Tu as bon : la réponse est 42.
native_language_example: You’re right: the answer is 42.

meaning: to look well; to look healthy/rested.
additional_notes: Used to comment on someone’s appearance in a positive way (they seem healthy, rested, or in good shape). Often used with "Tu as bonne mine" (informal) or "Vous avez bonne mine" (more formal). Can also be used in past tense: "Tu avais bonne mine" (You looked well).
target_language_example: Tu as bonne mine aujourd’hui !
native_language_example: You look well today!

additional_notes: Used to talk about how you feel, not the temperature of an object or the weather itself. Literally “to have hot,” but in French you say you “have” heat: J’ai chaud (I’m hot), Tu as chaud ? (Are you hot?). For the opposite, use avoir froid (to be cold).
target_language_example: J’ai chaud, on peut ouvrir la fenêtre ?
native_language_example: I’m hot—can we open the window?

additional_notes: Used to express trust in a person or confidence in something. Often followed by "en" + a person/thing: "avoir confiance en quelqu’un/quelque chose" (to trust someone/something). You can also specify the area of confidence with "dans": "avoir confiance dans l’avenir" (to feel confident about the future).
target_language_example: J’ai confiance en toi.
native_language_example: I trust you.

meaning: to be aware of; to know about (to have knowledge of).
additional_notes: Often used in a more formal or administrative style. Most commonly followed by "de" + noun: "avoir connaissance de quelque chose" = to be aware of something / to have knowledge of something. In the negative: "Je n’en ai pas connaissance" = I’m not aware of it / I don’t know about it.
target_language_example: J’ai eu connaissance de ce problème hier.
native_language_example: I became aware of this problem yesterday.

additional_notes: Often used with "de" + noun/infinitive: "avoir conscience de quelque chose" (to be aware of something) or "avoir conscience de faire/avoir fait..." (to realize you are doing/have done...). It’s common in more formal or thoughtful contexts (awareness, responsibility).
target_language_example: J’ai conscience de mes erreurs.
native_language_example: I’m aware of my mistakes.

meaning: to have class; to have lessons (school/university).
additional_notes: Used to say you have scheduled classes (often without an article): « J’ai cours aujourd’hui. » You can add a time: « J’ai cours à 8h. » It can also mean “to be in effect/valid” in more formal contexts (e.g., « avoir cours légal »), but beginners most often use it for school classes.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : j’ai cours cet après-midi.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I have class this afternoon.

meaning: to be lucky; to have luck.
additional_notes: Common way to say someone is lucky or fortunate. Used with a subject: "J'ai de la chance" (I'm lucky), "Tu as de la chance" (You're lucky). Can also be used with "de + infinitive" to mean "to be lucky to...": "J'ai de la chance de te connaître" (I'm lucky to know you).
target_language_example: Tu as de la chance : il reste encore des places.
native_language_example: You’re lucky: there are still seats left.

meaning: to look great; to have style/impact.
additional_notes: Informal. Used to say someone or something has a striking look, strong presence, or impressive appeal (often visual): a person, an outfit, a car, a building, a project, etc. Literally “to have some mouth/mug,” but the real meaning is closer to “to have wow factor.”
target_language_example: Avec ta veste en cuir, tu as vraiment de la gueule !
native_language_example: With your leather jacket, you really look great!

meaning: to be lucky; to have good luck.
additional_notes: An idiomatic, fairly informal way to say someone is lucky. Often used with "Tu as de la veine !" (“You’re lucky!”). More neutral alternatives: "avoir de la chance" or "être chanceux/chanceuse".
target_language_example: Tu as de la veine d’avoir trouvé un billet si bon marché !
native_language_example: You’re lucky to have found such a cheap ticket!

meaning: to be educated; to be learned.
additional_notes: A somewhat old-fashioned expression meaning someone has a good education or literary learning ("a man/woman of letters"). Not about receiving letters/mail. Often used in phrases like « un homme de lettres » (a literary person/writer).
target_language_example: Il a des lettres, il a beaucoup lu.
native_language_example: He’s educated; he’s read a lot.

meaning: to be entitled (to); to have the right (to).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has a legal or official right/eligibility to something. Most often followed by "à" + noun/infinitive: "avoir droit à" (to be entitled to / to qualify for), e.g., "avoir droit à une réduction". The negative "ne pas avoir droit" means "not to be allowed" / "not to be entitled".
target_language_example: Tu as droit à une pause après le cours.
native_language_example: You’re entitled to a break after the class.

meaning: to be lucky (to have good luck).
additional_notes: Informal expression. Literally “to have (a) bowl,” but it really means to have good luck. Often used in the present or past: « J’ai du bol ! » (I’m lucky!), « Tu as eu du bol » (You were lucky). Can also be used with « Quel bol ! » (What luck!).
target_language_example: Tu as du bol d’avoir trouvé une place si vite !
native_language_example: You’re lucky to have found a spot so quickly!

meaning: to have some good in it; to have its good points.
additional_notes: Used to say that something has advantages, often despite drawbacks. Commonly used with an impersonal subject: « Ça a du bon » (“That has its good points”). You can also use « Il y a du bon à + infinitive » to mean “There’s something good about doing…”.
target_language_example: Travailler à la maison, ça a du bon : je gagne du temps.
native_language_example: Working from home has its good points: I save time.

meaning: to have difficulty; to struggle (to do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something is hard to do: « avoir du mal à + infinitive ». Very common in everyday French. In the negative, it can mean you do something easily: « Je n’ai pas de mal à… » = “I have no trouble …”.
target_language_example: J’ai du mal à comprendre cette phrase.
native_language_example: I’m having trouble understanding this sentence.

avoir du pain sur la planche

target_language_multi_word_term: avoir du pain sur la planche
meaning: to have a lot to do; to have your work cut out.
additional_notes: Common idiom used to say you have plenty of work/tasks ahead of you. It can refer to work, school, or personal to-dos. Not meant literally (“having bread on the board”). Often used in the present tense: « J’ai du pain sur la planche ».
target_language_example: Cette semaine, j’ai du pain sur la planche avec tous ces dossiers.
native_language_example: This week, I’ve got my work cut out for me with all these files.

additional_notes: Common, fairly informal idiom meaning someone has good luck (often in a specific situation). It does not literally mean “to have pot” (and it’s not about marijuana). You’ll often hear it in the present: « Tu as du pot ! » = “You’re lucky!”
target_language_example: Tu as du pot : il restait une table libre !
native_language_example: You’re lucky: there was a free table left!

avoir du sang sur les mains

target_language_multi_word_term: avoir du sang sur les mains
meaning: to have blood on one’s hands (to be responsible for deaths or serious harm).
additional_notes: Used figuratively to accuse someone of causing or being complicit in deaths or major violence (directly or indirectly). It’s strong language and common in political/moral contexts. Also used with other subjects: "Il a du sang sur les mains" / "Ils ont du sang sur les mains".
target_language_example: Après cette décision, beaucoup disent que le gouvernement a du sang sur les mains.
native_language_example: After that decision, many say the government has blood on its hands.

meaning: to make sense; to be meaningful.
additional_notes: Used to say something is logical/understandable (Ça a du sens) or that something has meaning/purpose (C’est important que ça ait du sens). Very common in everyday speech. Often used in questions/negatives: « Est-ce que ça a du sens ? » / « Ça n’a pas de sens. »
target_language_example: Ce que tu dis a du sens.
native_language_example: What you’re saying makes sense.

meaning: to have in mind; to be thinking of.
additional_notes: Used to say something is in your thoughts or memory, or that you’re considering a plan/idea. Often followed by a noun or an infinitive: « J’ai en tête une idée » (I have an idea in mind), « J’ai en tête de… » (I’m thinking of / planning to…).
target_language_example: J’ai en tête de partir plus tôt demain.
native_language_example: I’m thinking of leaving earlier tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common way to express desire or inclination. Most often used as: "avoir envie de + noun" (J’ai envie de chocolat) or "avoir envie de + infinitive" (J’ai envie de dormir). With people, it can also mean sexual desire ("avoir envie de quelqu’un"), so context matters. Often used with "ne... pas": "Je n’ai pas envie" = "I don’t feel like it."
target_language_example: J’ai envie de sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: I feel like going out tonight.

additional_notes: Literally “to have hunger,” but it’s the normal way to say “to be hungry” in French (you use avoir + noun for many feelings/needs). You can intensify it: « avoir très faim » (very hungry), « avoir faim de… » can also mean “to crave/long for…” in a broader sense.
target_language_example: J’ai faim. On mange ?
native_language_example: I’m hungry. Shall we eat?

additional_notes: Used to express faith or strong belief, often in a religious sense (foi = faith), but it can also mean believing in a person, an idea, or a project. Common patterns: "avoir foi en Dieu" (have faith in God), "avoir foi en quelqu’un" (have faith in someone). More formal than simply "croire" in many contexts.
target_language_example: J’ai foi en toi.
native_language_example: I have faith in you.

meaning: to be cold; to feel cold.
additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir (to have) in French, where English uses “to be” (“I am cold”). You can change the subject and tense: j’ai froid (I’m cold), tu as froid (you’re cold), il/elle a froid (he/she’s cold), nous avons froid, etc. To emphasize, you can add très: j’ai très froid (I’m very cold).
target_language_example: J’ai froid, peux-tu fermer la fenêtre ?
native_language_example: I’m cold—can you close the window?

additional_notes: Literally "to have shame," but in English you usually say "to be ashamed." Used to express embarrassment, guilt, or shame about something. Common patterns: "avoir honte de + noun/verb" (J’ai honte de mon erreur / J’ai honte d’avoir menti) and "avoir honte de + person" (Elle a honte de lui).
target_language_example: J’ai honte de ce que j’ai dit.
native_language_example: I’m ashamed of what I said.

meaning: to hate; to be horrified by.
additional_notes: Used to express a very strong dislike or aversion to something (stronger than "ne pas aimer"). It’s usually followed by "de" + noun/verb: "avoir horreur de + nom/infinitif". Example: "J’ai horreur des araignées" (I hate spiders), "J’ai horreur de mentir" (I hate lying).
target_language_example: J’ai horreur de parler en public.
native_language_example: I hate speaking in public.

meaning: to look forward to; to be eager (to).
additional_notes: Used to express excitement or impatience about something in the future. Often followed by de + infinitive (J’ai hâte de te voir = I can’t wait to see you) or que + subjunctive (J’ai hâte que tu viennes = I can’t wait for you to come). Very common in everyday French.
target_language_example: J’ai hâte de partir en vacances.
native_language_example: I can’t wait to go on vacation.

meaning: to be in one’s interest; to have something to gain/benefit.
additional_notes: Often used as « avoir intérêt à + infinitive » meaning “to be better off doing (something)” or “it would be in your interest to…”. Don’t confuse with « être intéressé(e) » (“to be interested/curious”); « avoir intérêt » is about advantage/benefit.
target_language_example: Tu as intérêt à étudier si tu veux réussir.
native_language_example: You’d better study if you want to succeed.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s or something’s apparent state or appearance. Common patterns: « avoir l’air + adjective » (Il a l’air fatigué. = He looks tired.), « avoir l’air de + infinitive » (Elle a l’air de comprendre. = She seems to understand.), and « avoir l’air de + noun » (Ça a l’air d’une bonne idée. = That looks like a good idea.). Often used as « avoir l’air » without naming the subject: « Ça a l’air… » = “It seems/looks…”.
target_language_example: Tu as l’air content aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: You look happy today.

meaning: to hold a grudge (usually: « avoir une dent contre quelqu’un »).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as « avoir une dent contre + [person] », meaning you have resentment or a “bone to pick” with someone. You’ll also often hear it in the plural: « avoir une dent contre quelqu’un ». On its own, « avoir la dent » is uncommon; the idiomatic meaning is tied to « contre » + a person.
target_language_example: Il a une dent contre son collègue depuis la réunion.
native_language_example: He’s held a grudge against his coworker since the meeting.

additional_notes: Very common but informal: "gueule" is a slangy/rough word for "mouth/face" (more polite: "avoir la tête qui tourne", "avoir mal à la tête", etc.). Used with the verb "avoir" in many tenses: "J’ai la gueule de bois" (I have a hangover), "J’avais la gueule de bois" (I had a hangover).
target_language_example: Ce matin, j’ai la gueule de bois après la soirée d’hier.
native_language_example: This morning, I have a hangover after last night’s party.

meaning: to feel dizzy; to have your head spinning.
additional_notes: Used to describe dizziness or lightheadedness (e.g., from heat, hunger, standing up too fast, fatigue, illness). Often said with the subject: « J’ai la tête qui tourne. » You can also hear « Ça me donne la tête qui tourne » (It makes me dizzy).
target_language_example: J’ai la tête qui tourne, je vais m’asseoir un moment.
native_language_example: I feel dizzy, I’m going to sit down for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re romantically interested in someone, often in a light, not-too-serious way (a “crush”). Common pattern: « avoir le béguin pour + person » (e.g., « J’ai le béguin pour lui/elle. »).
target_language_example: J’ai le béguin pour Clara depuis la rentrée.
native_language_example: I’ve had a crush on Clara since the start of the school year.

meaning: to have the final say; to get the last word in.
additional_notes: Used when someone makes the final decision in a discussion (or when someone insists on speaking last in an argument). Often about authority (who decides) or stubbornness (who "wins" the exchange). Common in both everyday and formal contexts.
target_language_example: C’est le chef qui a le dernier mot.
native_language_example: It’s the boss who has the final say.

additional_notes: Used to say an event happens/occurred/will occur (often for scheduled or formal events). Conjugate "avoir" to match the tense: present "a lieu" (is taking place), past "a eu lieu" (took place), future "aura lieu" (will take place). Often followed by a time/place phrase (e.g., "demain", "à Paris").
target_language_example: La réunion aura lieu demain à 10h.
native_language_example: The meeting will take place tomorrow at 10 a.m.

meaning: to hurt; to be in pain.
additional_notes: Used with a body part to say what hurts: « J’ai mal à + [body part] » (e.g., « J’ai mal à la tête » = “My head hurts / I have a headache”). Without a body part, it means you’re in pain in general (« J’ai mal »). Note: French uses « avoir » (to have) where English often uses “to hurt.”
target_language_example: J’ai mal au dos depuis hier.
native_language_example: My back has been hurting since yesterday.

meaning: to look unwell; to look tired/ill.
additional_notes: Used to comment on someone’s appearance (not how they actually feel): they look pale, tired, or sick. Common with the verb in the present (Tu as mauvaise mine) or past (Il avait mauvaise mine). Often followed by a cause with « à cause de… » or « avec… » (e.g., with a cold).
target_language_example: Tu as mauvaise mine aujourd’hui—tu es sûr(e) que ça va ?
native_language_example: You look unwell today—are you sure you’re okay?

meaning: to have a share/part in something; to be involved.
additional_notes: Often used with "à": "avoir part à [qqch]" = to take part in / to have a role in something. It can also mean having some responsibility or involvement (sometimes in a negative context: not being involved). Common pattern: "avoir (une) part dans/à".
target_language_example: Il n’a eu aucune part dans cette décision.
native_language_example: He had no part in that decision.

meaning: to be afraid; to feel scared.
additional_notes: Literally “to have fear.” Common structure: avoir peur de + noun (“to be afraid of …”) and avoir peur de + infinitive (“to be afraid to …”). Often used with ne…pas to reassure: “N’aie pas peur” / “N’ayez pas peur” (“Don’t be afraid”).
target_language_example: J’ai peur des chiens.
native_language_example: I’m afraid of dogs.

meaning: to be able to stand (in water); to touch the bottom.
additional_notes: Used mainly when talking about water depth: if you "as pied", the water is shallow enough for your feet to reach the bottom so you can stand. Often used with negation: "Je n’ai pas pied" (= it’s too deep, I can’t touch the bottom). Can also be used figuratively to mean “to have a foothold / feel on solid ground” in a situation.
target_language_example: Ne va pas plus loin : ici, je n’ai plus pied.
native_language_example: Don’t go any farther: here, I can’t touch the bottom anymore.

meaning: to feel pity (for); to take pity (on).
additional_notes: Used to express feeling compassion for someone/something. Most often followed by "de" + a person/thing: "avoir pitié de quelqu’un/de quelque chose". Common in requests or pleas as "Ayez pitié !" / "Ayez pitié de moi" (formal/plural imperative).
target_language_example: Ayez pitié de lui, il est épuisé.
native_language_example: Have pity on him; he’s exhausted.

meaning: to be right; to be correct.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is correct in an argument, opinion, or situation. Often used as « Tu as raison » (You’re right). The opposite is « avoir tort » (to be wrong).
target_language_example: Tu as raison, c’est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: You’re right, it’s a good idea.

meaning: to be right to (do something); to be right about.
additional_notes: Used after a person (subject) to say they’re correct or justified. Very common with an infinitive: « Tu as raison de + infinitive » = “You’re right to + verb.” It can also be used with a noun/pronoun to mean “be right about” something: « Il a raison de s’inquiéter » / « Elle a raison de ça ». Note: don’t confuse it with English “have reason to” (which is more like « avoir une raison de »).
target_language_example: Tu as raison de partir maintenant.
native_language_example: You’re right to leave now.

meaning: to have an appointment; to be meeting (someone) at a set time.
additional_notes: Used for scheduled meetings (doctor, hairdresser, business) or arranged meet-ups with someone. Common patterns: « J’ai rendez-vous à 15 h » (at 3pm), « J’ai rendez-vous avec le médecin / avec Marie » (with the doctor / with Marie). In speech, you may also hear « J’ai un rendez-vous » (I have an appointment).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : j’ai rendez-vous avec le dentiste à 16 h.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I have an appointment with the dentist at 4 p.m.

additional_notes: Literally “to have thirst,” but in French you use avoir (to have) for thirst (and also hunger: avoir faim). Common in everyday situations like ordering a drink or saying you need water.
target_language_example: J’ai soif, je voudrais un verre d’eau, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’m thirsty; I’d like a glass of water, please.

meaning: to be sleepy; to feel like sleeping.
additional_notes: Literally “to have sleepiness.” In French you use avoir (to have) to express states like hunger/thirst/sleepiness: avoir faim (be hungry), avoir soif (be thirsty), avoir sommeil (be sleepy). Often used with a person: J’ai sommeil, Il/Elle a sommeil, On a sommeil. Can be strengthened with très: J’ai très sommeil (I’m very sleepy).
target_language_example: J’ai sommeil, je vais me coucher.
native_language_example: I’m sleepy, I’m going to bed.

meaning: to have had enough; to have gotten one’s fill.
additional_notes: An idiom used when someone feels they’ve had enough of something (often something unpleasant): « J’en ai eu mon compte » = “I’ve had enough.” It can also mean someone got what they deserved after a bad action: « Il a eu son compte » = “He got what was coming to him.” Often appears in the past (a eu son compte).
target_language_example: Après cette journée, j’en ai eu mon compte.
native_language_example: After this day, I’ve had enough.

meaning: to have on your conscience; to feel guilty (about something).
additional_notes: Used to say you feel moral responsibility or guilt for something you did (or failed to do). Often followed by what you feel guilty about: « J’ai ça sur la conscience » / « J’ai sur la conscience la mort de… ». Commonly used with « avoir quelque chose sur la conscience » (to have something on your conscience).
target_language_example: Depuis cet accident, il a ça sur la conscience.
native_language_example: Since that accident, he’s had it on his conscience (he’s felt guilty about it).

additional_notes: Used to say someone is mistaken or incorrect. Often contrasted with "avoir raison" (to be right). Common patterns: "Tu as tort" (You’re wrong), "J’ai tort" (I’m wrong), "avoir tort de + infinitive" (to be wrong to do something).
target_language_example: Tu as tort : ce n’est pas ouvert aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: You’re wrong: it isn’t open today.

meaning: to be one step ahead; to have an advantage.
additional_notes: Idiom meaning you’re ahead of others (in progress, information, preparation, strategy, etc.). Often used with “sur” to say who you’re ahead of: “avoir une longueur d’avance sur quelqu’un.” Common in sports, business, competition, and everyday planning.
target_language_example: Grâce à sa préparation, elle a une longueur d’avance sur les autres candidats.
native_language_example: Thanks to her preparation, she’s one step ahead of the other candidates.

meaning: to hear about (something); to get wind of (something).
additional_notes: Usually used as **avoir vent de + noun/phrase** (e.g., *avoir vent d’un projet*). It means learning something indirectly (through rumors, news, or someone telling you), often before it’s officially announced. Somewhat formal/idiomatic.
target_language_example: J’ai eu vent de votre déménagement.
native_language_example: I heard about your move.

meaning: to have to; to need to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity, followed by an infinitive: "avoir à + verb". Common in spoken and written French (similar to "devoir" but often a bit less like a duty and more like something that needs doing). In questions/negatives: "Tu as à… ?" / "Je n’ai pas à…".
target_language_example: J’ai à finir ce travail avant demain.
native_language_example: I have to finish this work before tomorrow.

meaning: to keep an eye on; to watch (closely).
additional_notes: Used to say you are monitoring someone/something carefully, often because it might cause trouble or needs attention. Commonly used with a direct object: « J’ai à l’œil les enfants » (I’m keeping an eye on the kids). Also appears as « garder à l’œil » with the same meaning.
target_language_example: J’ai à l’œil ton sac pendant que tu vas payer.
native_language_example: I’ll keep an eye on your bag while you go pay.

meaning: 'to have to do with' / 'to be related to'.
additional_notes: Most often used in the structure « avoir … à voir avec … » (= to have something to do with / be connected to). Very common in the negative: « ne rien avoir à voir avec » (= to have nothing to do with).
target_language_example: Ça n’a rien à voir avec mon travail.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with my job.

meaning: a beneficiary; a person entitled to a benefit/right (legal/administrative).
additional_notes: Used in official, legal, and administrative contexts (health insurance, social security, inheritance, contracts) for someone who has a right to receive something through their own status or through another person (e.g., a spouse/child covered under someone’s insurance). Often seen in the plural: « les ayants droit ».
target_language_example: Vous devez déclarer vos ayants droit auprès de votre assurance maladie.
native_language_example: You must declare your dependents/beneficiaries with your health insurance.

additional_notes: Common borrowed English word in French. Used mainly as a noun: "une/un baby-sitter" (a babysitter). You can also use it as a verb in casual speech: "baby-sitter" = "to babysit" (e.g., "Je baby-sitte ce soir."). Plural: "des baby-sitters".
target_language_example: On a engagé une baby-sitter pour ce soir.
native_language_example: We hired a babysitter for tonight.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: “magic stick/wand.” Common in fairy tales, fantasy, kids’ stories, and costumes. Also used figuratively for a “magic solution” (e.g., there’s no quick fix).
target_language_example: Il n’y a pas de baguette magique pour résoudre ce problème.
native_language_example: There’s no magic wand to solve this problem.

meaning: a bloodbath; a massacre (a lot of bloodshed).
additional_notes: Used to describe a very violent event with many deaths/injuries. Can be literal (a scene covered in blood) or figurative in journalism/politics (e.g., warning of possible violence). Strong, dramatic expression; avoid in casual conversation. Literally “bath of blood.”
target_language_example: Le conflit a dégénéré en bain de sang.
native_language_example: The conflict escalated into a bloodbath.

meaning: to lower your tone; to calm down (in how you speak).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to speak less loudly or less aggressively, often in an argument. It can be a command ("Baisse d’un ton !") or used about someone ("Il a baissé d’un ton"). More common than the literal-sounding "baisser d’un ton" in English; the idea is to tone it down.
target_language_example: Baisse d’un ton, s’il te plaît : on n’est pas obligés de se disputer.
native_language_example: Lower your voice, please—we don’t have to argue.

meaning: to give up; to stop trying.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression meaning you stop fighting/working toward a goal because you feel it’s hopeless. Often used with "ne pas" to encourage someone: "Ne baisse pas les bras !" (Don’t give up!).
target_language_example: Même si c’est difficile, ne baisse pas les bras.
native_language_example: Even if it’s hard, don’t give up.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to talk about a group of people or things: une bande de copains (a group of friends), une bande de voleurs (a gang of thieves). In speech it can also be used in insults before a negative word (e.g., bande d’idiots). In the sense of “strip of” it can refer to a long narrow piece of something: une bande de papier (a strip of paper). Note the spelling change: bande de + vowel sound often becomes bande d’ (bande d’amis).
target_language_example: C’est une bande de copains du lycée.
native_language_example: They’re a group of friends from high school.

additional_notes: Used for comics in general (newspaper strips, comic books, graphic novels). Often shortened to “une BD” in everyday speech and in bookstores/libraries. It’s feminine: une bande dessinée / des bandes dessinées.
target_language_example: J’adore lire des bandes dessinées, surtout Astérix.
native_language_example: I love reading comics, especially Asterix.

additional_notes: French uses the English loanword for the sport, usually written with a hyphen (base-ball). You’ll also see it without a hyphen (baseball). Common with verbs like jouer au base-ball (“to play baseball”) and with parler de / regarder le base-ball (“to talk about / watch baseball”).
target_language_example: Je joue au base-ball le week-end.
native_language_example: I play baseball on the weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the sport; you’ll often also hear just « basket » in casual speech. In French it’s commonly written with a hyphen (« basket-ball »), though « basketball » is also seen. You can say « jouer au basket(-ball) » (to play basketball) and « un match de basket(-ball) » (a basketball game).
target_language_example: Je joue au basket-ball le samedi.
native_language_example: I play basketball on Saturdays.

additional_notes: Used literally for birds/insects (and sometimes for a person miming wings). In everyday French, the idiom is more often "battre de l’aile" (singular), meaning “to struggle / to be in trouble” (a plan, business, relationship, etc.).
target_language_example: L’oiseau battait des ailes pour s’envoler.
native_language_example: The bird was flapping its wings to take off.

additional_notes: A fairly formal expression, used in military or tactical contexts (soldiers/armies), and sometimes figuratively in everyday speech to mean backing off, withdrawing, or giving up ground. It uses the verb *battre* (“to beat”), but the overall meaning isn’t simply “to beat in retreat” in English—think “to retreat.”
target_language_example: Face à l’ennemi, les soldats ont battu en retraite.
native_language_example: Facing the enemy, the soldiers retreated.

meaning: (for the heart) to pound / race (with emotion).
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used when you’re very excited, nervous, scared, or in love—your heart is beating very fast. Most often used with "mon/son cœur" (my/his/her heart): "Mon cœur bat la chamade."
target_language_example: Quand je l’ai vu arriver, mon cœur battait la chamade.
native_language_example: When I saw him arrive, my heart was pounding.

additional_notes: Used to congratulate or compliment someone on work they’ve done (can be said sincerely or sometimes sarcastically depending on tone). Often used as an interjection: « Beau boulot ! ». Note: « boulot » is informal for “job/work,” so the whole expression sounds casual.
target_language_example: Beau boulot ! Tu as fini bien plus vite que prévu.
native_language_example: Nice job! You finished much faster than expected.

additional_notes: Informal, common in everyday speech. Often used as a compliment or to describe someone attractive. Literally it’s closer to “handsome kid,” but in practice it can refer to a young man or just “a handsome guy.” You may also hear it used playfully or flirtatiously: « Salut, beau gosse ! »
target_language_example: Il est vraiment beau gosse.
native_language_example: He’s really handsome.

additional_notes: Used to congratulate or praise someone for what they did (work, effort, result). Often said on its own as an exclamation: « Beau travail ! ». You can also say « C’est du beau travail » (“That’s good work”). Note that French more commonly uses « Bon travail » for “good job,” especially at work; « Beau travail » sounds a bit more emphatic/admiring (“nice work”).
target_language_example: Beau travail ! Tu as fini beaucoup plus vite que prévu.
native_language_example: Nice work! You finished much faster than expected.

additional_notes: Family term for a man who is related to you by marriage: either your spouse’s brother or your sibling’s husband. In some contexts it can also mean “stepbrother,” but “brother-in-law” is the most common meaning. Feminine equivalent: "belle-sœur" (sister-in-law).
target_language_example: Mon beau-frère habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: My brother-in-law lives in Lyon.

additional_notes: Can mean either your spouse’s father (father-in-law) or your parent’s husband (stepfather). Context usually makes it clear. Plural: beaux-pères.
target_language_example: Mon beau-père vient dîner ce soir.
native_language_example: My father-in-law/stepfather is coming for dinner tonight.

additional_notes: Literally “beautiful days.” Used to talk about pleasant weather (often spring/summer) or better times. Common in expressions like « aux beaux jours » (“when the weather is nice,” “in the summertime”) and « le retour des beaux jours » (“the return of fine weather”).
target_language_example: Avec le retour des beaux jours, on mange souvent dehors.
native_language_example: With the return of fine weather, we often eat outside.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is true or confirmed, often as a correction or to insist on a fact. It can strengthen a statement ("It really is...") or confirm a conclusion ("So it is indeed..."). Often appears with verbs like être/avoir/faire: « C’est bel et bien… », « Il a bel et bien… ». The phrase is fixed: you usually don’t change the word order.
target_language_example: C’est bel et bien toi sur la photo.
native_language_example: It really is you in the photo.

additional_notes: Meaning depends on context: (1) your spouse’s mother = “mother-in-law” (Ma belle-mère). (2) your parent’s wife (not your biological mother) = “stepmother” (Ma belle-mère). You can clarify by saying “la mère de mon mari / de ma femme” or “ma mère (biologique) / ma mère adoptive” if needed. Plural: belles-mères.
target_language_example: Ma belle-mère vient dîner ce soir.
native_language_example: My mother-in-law is coming for dinner tonight.

meaning: sister-in-law (your spouse’s sister, or your sibling’s wife).
additional_notes: Used to talk about family by marriage. The plural is usually "belles-sœurs". Note that French "belle-" is part of several in-law terms (e.g., "beau-frère" = brother-in-law).
target_language_example: Ma belle-sœur habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: My sister-in-law lives in Lyon.

additional_notes: A common dog breed name. In French, animal breeds are usually not capitalized unless they include a proper adjective used as a noun; you’ll often see it written in lowercase: « un berger allemand ». The adjective « allemand » agrees with gender/number (allemande/allemands/allemandes), but in the fixed breed name it commonly stays « allemand ». Also note: « berger » can mean a shepherd (person) or a sheepdog depending on context; here it’s the breed.
target_language_example: Ils ont un berger allemand très gentil.
native_language_example: They have a very friendly German shepherd.

additional_notes: A food item. Also commonly said as "beurre de cacahuètes" (plural) or "beurre d’arachide". In everyday French, "beurre de cacahuète" usually refers to the spread (not an actual butter).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un sandwich au beurre de cacahuète, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a peanut butter sandwich, please.

additional_notes: Most commonly used when ordering food, especially steak: "un steak bien cuit". It can also describe food that is thoroughly cooked (sometimes implying it’s more cooked than ideal). Related levels: "saignant" (rare), "à point" (medium).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un steak bien cuit, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a well-done steak, please.

additional_notes: Used to agree with or praise what someone just said (like “exactly” or “good point”). Often said on its own as a reaction, or followed by a name/pronoun (e.g., « Bien dit, Marie ! » / « Bien dit, toi ! »).
target_language_example: — On devrait partir plus tôt pour éviter les embouteillages. — Bien dit !
native_language_example: — We should leave earlier to avoid traffic. — Well said!

additional_notes: Common in spoken and written French to agree, confirm, or emphasize that something is obvious/expected. Often used as a standalone reply: « Bien entendu ! ». It can also mean “clearly/obviously” in a sentence (more formal tone). Note: « bien sûr » is a very close everyday synonym for “of course.”
target_language_example: Bien entendu, je peux t'aider demain.
native_language_example: Of course, I can help you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to react to someone’s attempt that didn’t work (a failed excuse, a trick, an unsuccessful try). It can be genuine encouragement, but very often it’s said with irony to mean “I’m not fooled.” You’ll also hear: « Bien tenté. »
target_language_example: — Je n’ai pas de devoirs, je te jure ! — Bien essayé, mais je sais que tu en as.
native_language_example: — I don’t have any homework, I swear! — Nice try, but I know you do.

additional_notes: Often used to congratulate or praise someone: « Bien fait ! » You can also use it sarcastically to mean “serves you right” after someone has a bad outcome (context and tone matter). As an adjective, it can mean “well-made / well done,” e.g., « un travail bien fait » (a job well done).
target_language_example: — J’ai réussi l’examen. — Bien fait !
native_language_example: — I passed the exam. — Well done!

additional_notes: Used to congratulate someone for doing something well (a good move, good idea, good job), especially in games or sports but also in everyday situations. You can also use it sarcastically depending on tone. Often said alone as an exclamation: « Bien joué ! »
target_language_example: Bien joué ! Tu as trouvé la bonne réponse.
native_language_example: Well done! You found the right answer.

additional_notes: Used as an adjective or a noun to describe people, opinions, or attitudes seen as conformist, socially acceptable, and morally ‘proper’. It’s frequently pejorative/ironic, implying someone is narrow-minded or follows mainstream views to look respectable. Often written with a hyphen: « bien-pensant » (also « bienpensant »).
target_language_example: Il se croit très bien-pensant, mais il juge tout le monde.
native_language_example: He thinks he’s very respectable/right-thinking, but he judges everyone.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize a comparison or an increase. Often followed by de + noun/infinitive (e.g., bien plus de temps, bien plus intéressant) or used with a comparative (bien plus grand, bien plus cher). It adds emphasis compared with just plus.
target_language_example: Ce livre est bien plus intéressant que le film.
native_language_example: This book is much more interesting than the movie.

additional_notes: Most often used with "être": "Il/Elle est bien portant(e)" = "He/She is healthy." It can sound a bit formal or old-fashioned, and in some contexts it can imply someone is a little plump/well-built (a polite way to say "sturdy" or "on the heavier side").
target_language_example: Malgré son âge, il est encore bien portant.
native_language_example: Despite his age, he is still in good health.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast. It’s followed by the subjunctive (e.g., bien que je sois…, bien qu’il fasse…). Often interchangeable with « quoique » in meaning.
target_language_example: Bien qu’il pleuve, on sort quand même.
native_language_example: Even though it’s raining, we’re going out anyway.

additional_notes: Very common phrase to express agreement or confirmation. Often used as a polite, friendly answer to a request or question. Can be used alone ("Bien sûr !") or followed by a clause ("Bien sûr que oui/non").
target_language_example: — Tu peux m’aider ? — Bien sûr !
native_language_example: — Can you help me? — Of course!

additional_notes: Used to praise an idea, phrase, or solution as clever or fitting. Often said as a short comment: « Bien trouvé ! » It agrees in gender and number when used like an adjective: « une remarque bien trouvée », « des idées bien trouvées ».
target_language_example: — Tu devrais l’appeler « Le Petit Paris ». — Bien trouvé !
native_language_example: — You should call it “Little Paris.” — Clever idea!

additional_notes: Used to react to something someone said or noticed, meaning you agree it’s a smart observation (similar to “good catch”). It can also mean “well thought out / well seen” about an idea or solution. Often used as a short standalone comment: « Bien vu ! ».
target_language_example: — Il manque une page au dossier. — Bien vu !
native_language_example: — There’s a page missing from the file. — Good catch!

additional_notes: Used to describe a person (often a child) who has good manners and was raised properly. Also said as a compliment: « Il est très bien élevé. » The opposite is « mal élevé » (rude, badly behaved). Often used with « être »: « être bien élevé ».
target_language_example: Cet enfant est bien élevé : il dit toujours bonjour et merci.
native_language_example: This child is well-behaved: he always says hello and thank you.

additional_notes: Often used as an adjective before or after a noun (e.g., « mon bien-aimé », « ma ville bien-aimée »). Can refer to a romantic partner, a family member, or something cherished. In writing it’s frequently hyphenated (« bien-aimé »), but you may also see « bien aimé ».
target_language_example: Je te présente mon bien-aimé.
native_language_example: Let me introduce you to my beloved.

additional_notes: Used to talk about overall health, comfort, and quality of life (physical and mental). Common in phrases like « le bien-être », « le bien-être au travail » (well-being at work), and « bien-être mental/physique ». It’s a noun and usually takes a hyphen: « bien-être ».
target_language_example: Le bien-être est important pour la santé.
native_language_example: Well-being is important for health.

meaning: “blah blah”; meaningless talk / etc. (often implying boredom or annoyance).
additional_notes: Used to dismiss what someone is saying as unimportant or repetitive (like “blah blah blah” or “yada yada”). Can be said on its own (“Bla bla.”) or after a summary (“Il a parlé de son travail, bla bla.”). Often written with hyphens too: « blabla » / « bla-bla ».
target_language_example: Il a encore parlé pendant une heure, bla bla, et on n’a rien décidé.
native_language_example: He talked again for an hour, blah blah, and we didn’t decide anything.

additional_notes: Literally compares something’s whiteness to snow. Figuratively, it can describe someone as completely innocent or above suspicion (often used ironically depending on tone/context).
target_language_example: Il dit qu’il est blanc comme neige, mais la police n’est pas convaincue.
native_language_example: He says he’s as innocent as can be, but the police aren’t convinced.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who looks extremely pale, often because of fear, shock, illness, or bad news. Common with the verb « être »: « être blanc/blanche comme un linge ». Literal image: white linen (like a sheet).
target_language_example: Quand il a entendu la nouvelle, il était blanc comme un linge.
native_language_example: When he heard the news, he was as white as a sheet.

meaning: to drink a lot; to drink heavily.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression meaning someone drinks excessive amounts of alcohol. Common in spoken French and fairly informal; it can sound judgmental or rude, so avoid it in polite/company settings. Often used with a subject: « Il/Elle boit comme un trou. »
target_language_example: Depuis qu’il a perdu son travail, il boit comme un trou.
native_language_example: Since he lost his job, he’s been drinking heavily.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for the small storage compartment in a car’s dashboard. Usually used with the verb "mettre" (to put) or "chercher" (to look for): "mettre les papiers dans la boîte à gants". Note the spelling: "boîte" often has a circumflex (^) but you may also see "boite" without it.
target_language_example: Les papiers de la voiture sont dans la boîte à gants.
native_language_example: The car’s papers are in the glove compartment.

meaning: toolbox; (by extension) a set of tools/resources.
additional_notes: Literally “box of tools.” Used for an actual toolbox, and also figuratively (especially in tech/training) for a “toolkit” of methods, features, or resources (e.g., une boîte à outils pédagogique). Often written without the accent in casual typing: “boite à outils,” but the correct spelling is “boîte à outils.”
target_language_example: J’ai besoin d’une boîte à outils pour réparer le vélo.
native_language_example: I need a toolbox to fix the bike.

additional_notes: A common, neutral term for an atomic/nuclear bomb. Often used in news, history, and discussions about war or nuclear weapons. It can also be used figuratively to mean a "bombshell" (shocking news), especially in expressions like « lâcher une bombe atomique » (to drop a bombshell).
target_language_example: La bombe atomique a été utilisée pendant la Seconde Guerre mondiale.
native_language_example: The atomic bomb was used during World War II.

additional_notes: Literally “good God.” Can refer to God in a religious sense (often with an article: « le bon Dieu »), or be used as an emotional exclamation expressing surprise, annoyance, relief, etc. As an exclamation, it’s fairly informal and can be considered a mild oath.
target_language_example: Bon Dieu, j’ai oublié mes clés !
native_language_example: Good God, I forgot my keys!

meaning: “so then… / alright then…” (a filler to move on or conclude).
additional_notes: Used mainly in spoken French to introduce what comes next, wrap up a topic, or show you’re about to act/decide. Often said with a pause: “Bon, alors…” It can sound slightly impatient or like “well, anyway…” depending on tone.
target_language_example: Bon alors, on y va ?
native_language_example: Alright then, shall we go?

additional_notes: Used to wish someone a happy birthday. You can say it directly to the person, write it on a card, or use it in a message. Often followed by a person’s name (Bon anniversaire, Marie !). In France you may also hear “Joyeux anniversaire”, which means the same thing.
target_language_example: Bon anniversaire ! J’espère que tu passeras une super journée.
native_language_example: Happy birthday! I hope you have a great day.

additional_notes: Very common informal abbreviation in texts/messages. Full form: "Bon appétit !" Said to someone who is about to eat, similar to "Enjoy your meal" or "Enjoy". Literally it’s "good appetite," but in English you wouldn’t normally say that.
target_language_example: Bon app ! On se reparle après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: Enjoy your meal! We’ll talk again after lunch.

additional_notes: A very common, polite phrase said to someone who is about to start eating (at home or in a restaurant). Also used as a toast-like remark when food is served. Literally means “good appetite,” but in English it’s usually translated as “enjoy your meal.”
target_language_example: Bon appétit !
native_language_example: Enjoy your meal!

additional_notes: Used as a polite wish when someone is leaving or as a greeting during the afternoon. Similar to "bonsoir" (good evening). You’ll also hear "Bonne après-midi"; both are common in everyday French.
target_language_example: Bon après-midi ! À tout à l’heure.
native_language_example: Have a good afternoon! See you later.

additional_notes: Used to say something costs little or is affordable. It can be neutral (“inexpensive”) or imply good value for the price. Often used after the noun: « un restaurant bon marché » (an inexpensive restaurant). Don’t confuse with « le Bon Marché », a famous department store name in Paris.
target_language_example: On cherche un hôtel bon marché près de la gare.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a cheap hotel near the train station.

meaning: a witty remark; a clever one-liner.
additional_notes: Used to praise something someone said as clever or amusing. Often found in more formal or literary contexts (you might also hear it in English as a borrowed French expression).
target_language_example: Il a sorti un bon mot pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: He came out with a witty remark during the meeting.

meaning: a good deal; a great tip/idea (a “good plan”).
additional_notes: Very common in everyday French. Often means a bargain (cheap price) or a useful recommendation (“I’ve got a good tip for you”). In the plural: des bons plans. Often used with avoir/trouver: J’ai un bon plan / J’ai trouvé un bon plan.
target_language_example: J’ai un bon plan pour un resto pas cher près d’ici.
native_language_example: I’ve got a great tip for a cheap restaurant near here.

additional_notes: Used to express annoyance, impatience, surprise, or emphasis. Literally means “good blood,” but it functions like an exclamation. Often appears in phrases like “Bon sang !” or “Bon sang, dépêche-toi !”. Milder than stronger swear words, but still an expletive.
target_language_example: Bon sang, qu’est-ce que tu fais ?
native_language_example: For goodness’ sake, what are you doing?

additional_notes: Used to talk about practical, reasonable thinking. Often appears with articles: "le bon sens" (common sense) or in phrases like "avoir du bon sens" (to have common sense) and "c'est du bon sens" (it’s just common sense).
target_language_example: C’est du bon sens : il faut regarder avant de traverser la rue.
native_language_example: It’s common sense: you have to look before crossing the street.

meaning: "the good old days" (times in the past you remember fondly).
additional_notes: Most often used in the plural: « le bon vieux temps » (“the good old days”), or « le bon vieux temps de… » (“the good old days of…”). It expresses nostalgia for the past and is common in casual conversation. You may also see it in « au bon vieux temps » (“back in the good old days”).
target_language_example: Ah, le bon vieux temps… quand on jouait dehors jusqu’à la nuit !
native_language_example: Ah, the good old days… when we played outside until night!

additional_notes: A common, friendly wish said to someone who is leaving to travel (by plane, train, car, etc.). Used on its own as a farewell or written on cards/messages. You can also say it to a group: Bon voyage !
target_language_example: Tu pars demain ? Bon voyage !
native_language_example: You’re leaving tomorrow? Have a good trip!

additional_notes: A strong insult used to say someone is useless or incapable. Often used as a noun phrase ("un bon à rien") or as a description ("Il est bon à rien"). Avoid in polite conversation; use softer alternatives like "inutile" (useless) or "pas très compétent" (not very competent).
target_language_example: Arrête de me traiter de bon à rien !
native_language_example: Stop calling me a good-for-nothing!

meaning: a good student; a well-behaved/polite pupil.
additional_notes: Literally “good student.” Used for someone who studies well, gets good grades, follows instructions, and behaves in class. In French it can also imply “a model student” (serious, diligent), not just academically strong.
target_language_example: C’est un bon élève : il écoute en classe et fait toujours ses devoirs.
native_language_example: He’s a good student: he listens in class and always does his homework.

additional_notes: The standard, common term for a snowman. Literally “good man/little man of snow,” but it just means “snowman.” Often used with the verb faire (“to make”): faire un bonhomme de neige.
target_language_example: On va faire un bonhomme de neige dans le jardin.
native_language_example: We’re going to make a snowman in the garden.

meaning: a good deed; an act of kindness.
additional_notes: Used to talk about doing something helpful or kind for someone (often small, everyday acts). In French you can say "faire une bonne action" (to do a good deed). It can also be used in a moral/charity context (helping others, volunteering, donating).
target_language_example: J’essaie de faire une bonne action chaque jour.
native_language_example: I try to do a good deed every day.

additional_notes: Used as a New Year greeting, especially around January 1st and during the first days/weeks of January. Often said as part of "Bonne année !" or "Bonne année et bonne santé !" (Happy New Year and good health!). You can also say "Bonne année à toi/vous" (to you).
target_language_example: Bonne année ! Je te souhaite plein de bonheur.
native_language_example: Happy New Year! I wish you lots of happiness.

additional_notes: A polite expression used when parting ways during the afternoon. Often said as a farewell (similar to "bonne journée" for "have a good day"). You can also say "Bon après-midi"; both are common, and "Bon" matches the masculine noun "après-midi". Typically used from after lunch until early evening.
target_language_example: Bon après-midi, à tout à l’heure !
native_language_example: Have a good afternoon, see you later!

additional_notes: Used to wish someone luck before an exam, interview, trip, performance, etc. You can also say "Bonne chance !" on its own as an exclamation. Similar phrases: "Bon courage" (more like 'hang in there/you've got this' for something difficult) and "Je te souhaite bonne chance" (more formal/complete: 'I wish you good luck').
target_language_example: Bonne chance pour ton entretien !
native_language_example: Good luck with your interview!

meaning: an old woman; (sometimes) a simple, ordinary woman.
additional_notes: Often used to mean “old woman” in everyday speech, but it can sound dismissive or rude depending on tone and context (similar to “old woman” or “woman” said in a scornful way). In some contexts it can simply mean “a good woman / simple woman,” but beginners should be cautious using it; prefer "une femme" (a woman) or "une vieille dame" (an elderly lady) if you want to be polite.
target_language_example: Il a traité la bonne femme de manière impolie.
native_language_example: He treated the old woman rudely.

meaning: a good-natured, kind (often simple/naive) girl or young woman.
additional_notes: Literally “good girl,” but it usually means someone who is easygoing and kind rather than “well-behaved.” It can sound a bit old-fashioned or patronizing, especially if said about an adult woman. Often used with "une" ("C’est une bonne fille").
target_language_example: C’est une bonne fille, elle aide toujours les autres.
native_language_example: She’s a good-natured girl; she always helps others.

meaning: "good faith" (honest intentions; not trying to deceive).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is acting honestly or sincerely, often in formal/legal contexts (e.g., contracts, disputes). Common phrases: « de bonne foi » = in good faith; « agir de bonne foi » = to act in good faith. Opposite: « de mauvaise foi » = in bad faith (dishonestly).
target_language_example: Il a agi de bonne foi.
native_language_example: He acted in good faith.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone well on their “fête” (celebration day). In many regions it’s commonly said on someone’s birthday, and it can also refer to a saint’s day/name day (especially in more traditional contexts). Similar in spirit to “Joyeux anniversaire,” but “bonne fête” can be broader than just birthdays. Often said directly to the person: « Bonne fête ! » or « Bonne fête, Marie ! »
target_language_example: Bonne fête, Papa !
native_language_example: Happy birthday, Dad!

additional_notes: Used to describe a generally positive, cheerful state of mind. Common in expressions like « être de bonne humeur » (to be in a good mood) and « mettre quelqu’un de bonne humeur » (to put someone in a good mood).
target_language_example: Aujourd’hui, je suis de bonne humeur.
native_language_example: Today, I’m in a good mood.

additional_notes: A common polite phrase used when saying goodbye. Often said as a wish: « Bonne journée ! ». With « passer », it becomes « Passe une bonne journée ! » (Have a nice day!). More formal than « bonne journée »: « bonne journée, Monsieur/Madame ». Similar expressions: « bonne soirée » (have a nice evening).
target_language_example: Merci, bonne journée !
native_language_example: Thanks, have a nice day!

additional_notes: Used to announce or refer to positive information. Often appears with the verb "avoir" (J’ai une bonne nouvelle) or in the plural (de bonnes nouvelles).
target_language_example: J’ai une bonne nouvelle : j’ai trouvé un appartement.
native_language_example: I have good news: I found an apartment.

additional_notes: Used to say goodnight when someone is going to sleep or when you’re leaving in the evening. Commonly said as a farewell at bedtime (often to family, friends, or a partner). You can also say “Bonne nuit !” on its own; “Bonne soirée” is more like “have a nice evening” (not specifically for sleeping).
target_language_example: Je vais me coucher. Bonne nuit !
native_language_example: I’m going to bed. Good night!

additional_notes: Used to wish someone well when they’re leaving and will be traveling (by car, train, etc.). Often said as a friendly send-off, similar to “Bonne journée” but specifically about the journey. You may also hear “Bonne route !” in writing (texts, messages) when someone is driving.
target_language_example: Tu pars déjà ? Bonne route !
native_language_example: Are you leaving already? Have a good trip!

additional_notes: A common, polite way to wish someone a pleasant evening, often when saying goodbye in the late afternoon/evening. It can be used with friends, coworkers, or strangers. You’ll also hear it with vous: « Bonne soirée, Madame/Monsieur. » (Note: « Bonsoir » means 'good evening/hello/good evening (as a greeting)', while « bonne soirée » is a wish as you leave.)
target_language_example: Merci, bonne soirée !
native_language_example: Thanks, have a nice evening!

additional_notes: Used to talk about a positive, cooperative attitude or readiness to make an effort. Common in expressions like « avec toute la bonne volonté du monde » (“with all the goodwill in the world”) and « faire preuve de bonne volonté » (“to show goodwill”). It can describe either friendliness toward someone or simply being willing to try.
target_language_example: Avec un peu de bonne volonté, on peut trouver une solution.
native_language_example: With a bit of goodwill, we can find a solution.

additional_notes: Used to talk about etiquette and how someone is expected to behave politely (at home, at school, in public, etc.). Often appears in expressions like « avoir de bonnes manières » (to have good manners) or « apprendre les bonnes manières » (to learn good manners).
target_language_example: Il faut avoir de bonnes manières à table.
native_language_example: You need to have good manners at the table.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone a good vacation/holiday period. Often said when someone is about to leave for time off or at the start of a holiday season. You can also hear similar forms like “Bonnes vacances !” (plural) and “Bonne vacances !” is less common; the standard is plural because vacances is usually plural in French.
target_language_example: Bonnes vacances ! Profite bien et repose-toi.
native_language_example: Have a nice vacation! Enjoy yourself and get some rest.

additional_notes: A very strong, vulgar swear phrase used to express anger, frustration, or pain (similar force to “for fuck’s sake” or “fucking hell”). Avoid in polite company, at work/school, or with strangers. Note: "bordel" literally means “brothel,” and in everyday speech it can also mean “mess/chaos,” but in this phrase it functions mainly as an intensifier.
target_language_example: Bordel de merde ! J’ai encore raté mon train.
native_language_example: For fuck’s sake! I missed my train again.

additional_notes: Used to describe being so surprised, amazed, or shocked that you can’t speak. Often follows verbs like « rester » or « être »: « rester bouche bée » (to be left speechless). The word « bée » is not common on its own; you’ll mostly see it in this fixed expression.
target_language_example: Quand il a annoncé la nouvelle, tout le monde est resté bouche bée.
native_language_example: When he announced the news, everyone was left speechless.

additional_notes: Most commonly the literal object: a ball of snow you can throw or roll. Also used in the expression « effet boule de neige » (“snowball effect”), meaning something that grows quickly as it continues.
target_language_example: Les enfants se lancent des boules de neige.
native_language_example: The kids are throwing snowballs at each other.

meaning: the end of the world; the middle of nowhere.
additional_notes: Usually used in the expression « au bout du monde » to mean a very far-away place (sometimes exaggerating for effect). Literally « end of the world », but often just means “really remote.”
target_language_example: Ils habitent au bout du monde, on met deux heures pour y aller.
native_language_example: They live in the middle of nowhere; it takes two hours to get there.

additional_notes: Used for the box where you put outgoing mail or where you receive mail. In France it can mean a home/apartment mailbox, a building’s group of mailboxes, or a street mailbox (often La Poste yellow boxes). Also used in the phrase “boîte aux lettres électronique” for “email inbox.”
target_language_example: J’ai laissé la lettre dans la boîte aux lettres.
native_language_example: I left the letter in the mailbox.

additional_notes: A common, neutral term for a place where people go at night to dance, drink, and listen to music. Often used with verbs like « aller en boîte » (to go clubbing) or « sortir en boîte » (to go out to a club). You can also say « une boîte » informally to mean a nightclub when context is clear.
target_language_example: On va à la boîte de nuit ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we going to the nightclub tonight?

additional_notes: Refers to the storage compartment in the dashboard of a car. Literally “glove box.” Commonly used with the article: « la boîte à gants ».
target_language_example: Les papiers de la voiture sont dans la boîte à gants.
native_language_example: The car documents are in the glove compartment.

meaning: toolbox; a set of useful tools or resources.
additional_notes: Literal meaning is a physical toolbox (a box for tools). It’s also commonly used figuratively (especially in work/tech/training contexts) to mean a collection of methods, documents, or resources you can use to solve problems (like a “toolkit”).
target_language_example: J’ai une boîte à outils pour réparer mon vélo.
native_language_example: I have a toolbox to fix my bike.

additional_notes: Literally “right arm.” Used for someone’s most trusted helper or second-in-command (often in work or politics): « C’est mon bras droit. » You can add a possessive: « mon/son bras droit ».
target_language_example: Claire est le bras droit du directeur.
native_language_example: Claire is the director’s right-hand person.

additional_notes: Used both literally (in a romantic sense) and more generally for causing deep sadness or disappointment. Often appears as “Tu m’as brisé le cœur” (You broke my heart) or “Ça me brise le cœur” (It breaks my heart). The verb can be conjugated: briser / brise / a brisé / brisera, etc.
target_language_example: Tu m’as brisé le cœur quand tu es parti(e).
native_language_example: You broke my heart when you left.

additional_notes: A common everyday noun. Usually feminine: **une brosse à dents**. Plural: **des brosses à dents**. Often used with **se brosser les dents** (“to brush your teeth”).
target_language_example: J’ai oublié ma brosse à dents.
native_language_example: I forgot my toothbrush.

additional_notes: Used for the place where you mail letters/packages, buy stamps, and use postal services. Often appears with the verb "aller à" (to go to): "Je vais au bureau de poste." In everyday speech, people also say "la poste" to mean the post office/service.
target_language_example: Je vais au bureau de poste pour envoyer un colis.
native_language_example: I’m going to the post office to send a package.

additional_notes: Contraction of "ce" + "est" ("ce est" is not used). Very common for identifying or introducing something: "C'est + noun" (often with an article) or "C'est + adjective". For people: "C'est Marie" (identifying) but often "Il/Elle est + adjective" for describing: "Elle est gentille." Plural is "Ce sont" ("Ce sont mes amis.").
target_language_example: C'est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: It's a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to confirm or agree with what someone just said (“Exactly”). It can also mean “that’s what it is” when clarifying something. Often said on its own as a short response; close in meaning to “c’est ça” (more common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: — Donc, tu viens demain ? — Oui, c’est cela.
native_language_example: — So, you’re coming tomorrow? — Yes, that’s right.

meaning: "which is to say" / "that says a lot" (emphasizes what comes before).
additional_notes: Used after a fact or situation to underline its importance or to suggest a conclusion is obvious. Often translated as “which is to say…”, “that’s saying something,” or “so you can imagine…”. Common in writing and formal speech; in casual speech you might also hear “autant dire” (“so basically”).
target_language_example: Il travaille 70 heures par semaine, c’est dire à quel point il est débordé.
native_language_example: He works 70 hours a week, which tells you how overwhelmed he is.

additional_notes: Used to say that a woman or a feminine noun (or something referred to with a feminine word, like "la solution") is the best. Often said as a compliment (about a person) or to recommend something. For a man/masculine noun: "c'est le meilleur". If you mean "it’s the best (thing)" without specifying gender, French still follows the noun’s gender.
target_language_example: Essaie cette boulangerie : c'est la meilleure du quartier.
native_language_example: Try this bakery: it’s the best in the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Used to express resignation or acceptance when something goes wrong or can’t be changed. Often said with a shrug, and can sound lightly philosophical or mildly ironic depending on tone. Literally "it’s the life," but it corresponds to the idiom "that’s life."
target_language_example: On a raté le train… c’est la vie !
native_language_example: We missed the train… that’s life!

additional_notes: Used to identify yourself (answering the door/phone, introducing yourself, or saying you’re the person being talked about). Also used when recognizing yourself (e.g., in a photo or description): “That’s me.”
target_language_example: — Qui est là ? — C’est moi !
native_language_example: — Who is it? — It’s me!

additional_notes: Common expression said when something is beginning (a trip, an activity, a meeting, a process). Literally “it has left,” but idiomatically it means “we’re off” or “it’s underway.” You can also use it to hype yourself/others up before starting something.
target_language_example: Tout le monde est prêt ? C’est parti !
native_language_example: Is everyone ready? Here we go!

additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason or explanation for what was just said (cause → consequence). Often followed by a clause: "C'est pourquoi + subject + verb". It’s close to "donc" (so) but a bit more explicit: it points back to the reason.
target_language_example: Il pleuvait, c’est pourquoi je suis resté à la maison.
native_language_example: It was raining; that’s why I stayed home.

additional_notes: Said when something starts up again (an activity, a trip, a problem, an argument, noise, etc.). Often used with a resigned or slightly annoyed tone: "here we go again." Literally "it’s started again" (from repartir = to set off/leave again).
target_language_example: Le bébé recommence à pleurer… c’est reparti !
native_language_example: The baby is starting to cry again… here we go again!

additional_notes: Used to say something is finished or there is nothing more to add. Often comes at the end of an explanation or list. Can also be used to politely refuse additional help/information ("Non merci, c’est tout.").
target_language_example: Je voudrais un café, s’il vous plaît. C’est tout.
native_language_example: I’d like a coffee, please. That’s all.

additional_notes: Very common in conversation to confirm something is correct (“Yes, that’s right”), to indicate you’ve understood, or to wrap up (“That’s it / that’s all”). It can be said with different intonation: rising to confirm, firm to agree, or final to end a point.
target_language_example: — Donc on se retrouve à 18 h ? — Oui, c’est ça.
native_language_example: — So we’re meeting at 6 p.m.? — Yes, that’s right.

additional_notes: "C'est-ce" isn’t standard spelling; you’ll almost always see "c'est ce" (no hyphen). It’s used to point to something specific and is very often followed by a relative word like "que/qui/dont" (e.g., "c'est ce que…" = “that’s what…”).
target_language_example: C’est ce que je voulais dire.
native_language_example: That’s what I meant to say.

additional_notes: Used to clarify, rephrase, or give a more precise explanation of what you just said. Very common in both speech and writing. Often followed by a pause/comma in writing: "..., c'est-à-dire ...". Similar to "autrement dit" (in other words).
target_language_example: Il est végétarien, c'est-à-dire qu'il ne mange pas de viande.
native_language_example: He’s vegetarian, that is, he doesn’t eat meat.

meaning: "those were the good old days" / "that was the good time(s)."
additional_notes: Used to look back nostalgically on the past. Literally "it was the good time," but in English it often corresponds to "those were the good old days." Commonly said after remembering something from earlier in life. Note: you’ll also hear the plural: « C’était le bon temps » can sound regional/old-fashioned; « C’était le bon temps, ça » or « C’était le bon vieux temps » are also common.
target_language_example: Quand on jouait dehors toute la journée sans téléphone… c’était le bon temps.
native_language_example: When we played outside all day without a phone… those were the good old days.

additional_notes: Written abbreviation of « c’est-à-dire ». Used to clarify or restate something more precisely, like English “i.e.” or “that is to say.” It’s mainly used in writing; when speaking, you usually say « c’est-à-dire » in full.
target_language_example: Il viendra demain, c.-à-d. vendredi.
native_language_example: He’ll come tomorrow, i.e., Friday.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "jouer" (to play): "jouer à cache-cache". Also said as "un jeu de cache-cache". Common in everyday speech, especially with kids.
target_language_example: On joue à cache-cache dans le jardin ?
native_language_example: Do we play hide-and-seek in the garden?
