additional_notes: Used when ordering coffee to specify you want it without milk or cream. It may still be served with sugar on the side unless you say you want it unsweetened (e.g., « sans sucre »).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un café noir, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a black coffee, please.

additional_notes: Literally “box for tools.” Commonly used for a physical toolbox, and also figuratively for a set of methods/resources (e.g., “a toolbox” of techniques). Often seen with possessives: ma/ta/sa caisse à outils.
target_language_example: J’ai rangé le marteau dans la caisse à outils.
native_language_example: I put the hammer away in the toolbox.

additional_notes: Used to describe a quiet period that you expect will be followed by trouble, tension, or a busy/chaotic situation. Often said about relationships, work, or the atmosphere before an argument, crisis, or big event. Usually with the definite article: « le calme avant la tempête ».
target_language_example: Ne te fie pas à ce silence : c’est le calme avant la tempête.
native_language_example: Don’t trust this silence: it’s the calm before the storm.

additional_notes: Used for cameras that monitor an area for safety or security (shops, streets, buildings). In French, "surveillance" often means monitoring/being watched, not just "watching over" in a caring sense. You may also see: "caméra de sécurité" (less common) or "caméras de surveillance" (plural).
target_language_example: Il y a une caméra de surveillance à l’entrée du magasin.
native_language_example: There is a security camera at the entrance to the store.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a single written character/symbol in Chinese writing (or by extension, any logographic character). Plural: « des caractères chinois ». Often seen in contexts like fonts, language learning, or writing systems.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas écrire ce caractère chinois.
native_language_example: I don’t know how to write this Chinese character.

additional_notes: Refers to an official identity document. In France, it often means the national ID card (CNI), but it can also mean any ID card depending on context. Common with verbs like « montrer » (to show) and « demander » (to ask for).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me montrer votre carte d'identité, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you show me your ID card, please?

additional_notes: Used for paying in shops/restaurants or online. Common phrases: « payer par carte de crédit » (to pay by credit card), « Vous acceptez les cartes de crédit ? » (Do you accept credit cards?). Often you’ll also hear « carte bancaire » as a general term for bank card (debit or credit), depending on the country and context.
target_language_example: Je vais payer par carte de crédit.
native_language_example: I’m going to pay by credit card.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a business card you give someone with your name and contact details. You’ll also see it on signs like « Cartes de visite » (business cards available). It can sometimes mean a “calling card” (a card left to introduce yourself), but in modern everyday French it usually refers to a business card.
target_language_example: Voici ma carte de visite.
native_language_example: Here’s my business card.

additional_notes: In France, the "carte grise" is the official document proving a vehicle is registered (today officially called the "certificat d’immatriculation"). You often need it when buying/selling a car, dealing with insurance, or if the police ask for your papers. Despite the name, it’s not necessarily gray anymore. Not the same as a driver’s license ("permis de conduire").
target_language_example: Vous avez la carte grise du véhicule ?
native_language_example: Do you have the vehicle’s registration document?

additional_notes: Used for a postcard you send by mail (often a photo card) to write a short message while traveling. You can buy one and then add a stamp: « une carte postale » / « des cartes postales ».
target_language_example: J’ai acheté une carte postale et je vais l’envoyer à mes parents.
native_language_example: I bought a postcard and I’m going to send it to my parents.

additional_notes: Used for a (paper or digital) map designed for driving, showing roads and routes. Often heard with verbs like « consulter » (to consult) or « utiliser » (to use).
target_language_example: On a consulté la carte routière pour trouver le meilleur itinéraire.
native_language_example: We checked the road map to find the best route.

meaning: (very vulgar) to annoy someone / to be a pain in the ass (literally: “to bust someone’s balls”).
additional_notes: Very rude and vulgar expression in French. Used to complain that someone/something is really bothering you. Often appears with an indirect object pronoun: « Tu me casses les couilles » (You’re really annoying me), « Ça me casse les couilles » (This is really pissing me off). Avoid in polite situations; use something like « m’énerver » or « m’agacer » instead.
target_language_example: Arrête, tu me casses les couilles !
native_language_example: Stop it, you’re really pissing me off!

meaning: to annoy someone; to be a pain (to someone).
additional_notes: Very common informal expression, often used as "Tu me casses les pieds !" (= "You’re annoying me!"). Also used with a subject: "Ça me casse les pieds" (= "That annoys me / That’s a pain"). You can replace "les pieds" with a more vulgar word in slang, but "casser les pieds" is the safer version.
target_language_example: Arrête de me casser les pieds avec tes questions !
native_language_example: Stop annoying me with your questions!

meaning: "what" / "that which" (as the object of de: "of which", "that ... about").
additional_notes: Used to refer to a thing/idea previously mentioned or understood, when the verb/adjective needs the preposition **de**. Often translates as **"what"**, **"what ... about"**, or **"that which"**. Common with verbs like **avoir besoin de** (to need), **parler de** (to talk about), **se souvenir de** (to remember), **rêver de** (to dream of). Pattern: **C’est ce dont + subject + verb...**
target_language_example: C’est ce dont j’ai besoin.
native_language_example: That’s what I need.

additional_notes: Used to link an action to its consequence or to introduce what happens as a result. Common in written or formal French (less common in everyday conversation). Often refers back to the previous clause: *Il a changé de travail ; ce faisant, il a déménagé.*
target_language_example: Il a accepté l’offre et, ce faisant, il a pris un risque.
native_language_example: He accepted the offer and, in doing so, he took a risk.

additional_notes: Polite, somewhat formal way to say you enjoyed meeting/helping someone. Uses the past historic tense (fut), which is common in set phrases like this even in everyday speech. Often used when saying goodbye or after finishing a service. More casual alternatives: « Ça a été un plaisir » or « Avec plaisir » (you’re welcome / with pleasure).
target_language_example: Merci pour votre aide, ce fut un plaisir de travailler avec vous.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help, it was a pleasure to work with you.

additional_notes: A fairly formal way to mean “the thing(s) for which” or “what ... for.” It’s built from **ce** (“that/what”) + **pour** (“for”) + **quoi** (“what”). Often used in writing or careful speech; in everyday French you may also hear **ce pourquoi** (as one word) or rephrasing like **la raison pour laquelle** (“the reason why”).
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce pour quoi ils se battent.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what they are fighting for.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause referring to something (often unknown) as the object of a verb ("what I want", "what you said"). Common after verbs like dire (to say/tell), savoir (to know), vouloir (to want), comprendre (to understand). Often becomes "ce qu’" before a vowel or silent h: "ce qu’il…".
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce que tu veux.
native_language_example: I don’t know what you want.

meaning: 'what' / 'which' / 'that which' (as the subject of a verb).
additional_notes: Used to refer to an idea or thing, and it functions as the subject of the following verb (literally “that which”). Often contrasted with "ce que", which is used when it’s the object of the verb. Common in sentences like "Ce qui est important, c'est..." (What’s important is...).
target_language_example: Ce qui m'intéresse, c'est la musique.
native_language_example: What interests me is music.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the evening of today (often meaning “tonight”). Common in plans and invitations. It can refer to a time later today/tonight: ce soir, je sors (tonight I’m going out).
target_language_example: On se voit ce soir ?
native_language_example: Shall we see each other tonight?

additional_notes: Used when a verb/adjective/noun requires the preposition "à" and you want to refer to an idea or thing: "ce" (what/that which) + "à" (to/at) + "quoi" (what). Common with verbs like "penser à" (to think about), "s’attendre à" (to expect), "tenir à" (to care about), "se préparer à" (to prepare for), "renoncer à" (to give up). Often translates as “what …” or “what … to/at,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce à quoi il pense.
native_language_example: I don’t know what he’s thinking about.

meaning: "what I’m thinking about" / "the thing I’m thinking of."
additional_notes: Used to refer to an idea or thing you have in mind. It uses the relative structure “ce à quoi …” (= “that which …” with à + quoi), which is common after verbs that take “à” (penser à, s’attendre à, tenir à, etc.). Often appears with verbs like: « Ce à quoi je pense, c’est… » (“What I’m thinking about is…”).
target_language_example: Ce à quoi je pense, c’est notre voyage de demain.
native_language_example: What I’m thinking about is our trip tomorrow.

additional_notes: A fairly formal transition used to qualify what you just said or to introduce a concession (similar to "however" or "still"). It’s often followed by a comma. Very common in the fuller expression "ceci étant dit" (= "that being said").
target_language_example: Ceci étant, je comprends ton point de vue, mais je ne suis pas d’accord.
native_language_example: That being said, I understand your point of view, but I don’t agree.

additional_notes: Common in cars, buses, and planes. Often used with the verbs "mettre" (to put on) and "attacher" (to fasten): "Mettez votre ceinture de sécurité" / "Attache ta ceinture". You may also hear "boucler sa ceinture" (to buckle your seat belt).
target_language_example: Attache ta ceinture de sécurité, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Fasten your seat belt, please.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast, limitation, or nuance after what you just said (similar to "however" or "still"). Common in both speaking and writing, often followed by a comma: "Cela dit, ...".
target_language_example: Je n’aime pas trop le froid. Cela dit, la montagne en hiver est magnifique.
native_language_example: I don’t really like the cold. That said, the mountains in winter are gorgeous.

additional_notes: Used to acknowledge what was just said and then add a consequence, limitation, or contrasting point—often like “however,” “still,” or “that said.” Common in more formal speech/writing. You’ll often see it in the full phrase “Cela étant dit,” but “cela étant” can stand alone.
target_language_example: Cela étant, je préfère attendre avant de décider.
native_language_example: That said, I’d rather wait before deciding.

additional_notes: Demonstrative pronoun used to point to a specific masculine noun/person/object close to the speaker or just mentioned. It often contrasts with "celui-là" (that one). Feminine forms: "celle-ci"; plural: "ceux-ci" (masc.), "celles-ci" (fem.).
target_language_example: Je préfère celui-ci, il est plus simple.
native_language_example: I prefer this one; it’s simpler.

additional_notes: Demonstrative pronoun used to point out a specific masculine person or thing, often contrasting with another option (e.g., celui-ci = “this one”). The hyphen is standard. The feminine form is celle-là; plurals: ceux-là (masc.), celles-là (fem.).
target_language_example: Tu vois deux manteaux ? Celui-là est moins cher.
native_language_example: Do you see two coats? That one is cheaper.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize total certainty or full agreement, like “100%” in English. You can use it as an adverb (Je suis cent pour cent d’accord) or after a noun/adjective to mean “completely” (C’est vrai à cent pour cent). Also written: « 100 % ».
target_language_example: Je suis cent pour cent d’accord avec toi.
native_language_example: I 100% agree with you.

additional_notes: Used to state an age or a duration. In French, numbers like 107 are often said as separate words: "cent sept" (no "et"). Add "ans" for years (age/time).
target_language_example: Mon arrière-grand-mère a cent sept ans.
native_language_example: My great-grandmother is 107 years old.

additional_notes: A noun phrase for a facility that produces electricity (e.g., a nuclear, hydroelectric, wind, or gas power plant). Often used with a type: « une centrale nucléaire », « une centrale hydroélectrique ». Don’t confuse with « central électrique » (incorrect) or « centre électrique » (different meaning).
target_language_example: Cette centrale électrique fournit de l’électricité à toute la région.
native_language_example: This power plant supplies electricity to the whole region.

additional_notes: A common place name for a mall. In French it’s usually masculine: (le) centre commercial. You’ll often see it on signs or in directions, and it can be followed by a name (ex. le centre commercial Les Halles).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au centre commercial cet après-midi ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at the shopping mall this afternoon?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the central part of a town/city where shops, restaurants, and main streets are. Often used with "en centre-ville" (downtown) or "dans le centre-ville" (in the city center).
target_language_example: On se retrouve en centre-ville à 18 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet downtown at 6 p.m.?

meaning: a vicious circle; a self-reinforcing negative cycle.
additional_notes: Used to describe a situation where one problem causes another, which then makes the first problem worse, creating a repeating loop. Often used with verbs like « entrer dans », « tomber dans » (to get into) or « sortir de » (to get out of) un cercle vicieux.
target_language_example: Avec le stress et le manque de sommeil, je suis dans un cercle vicieux.
native_language_example: With stress and lack of sleep, I’m in a vicious circle.

additional_notes: A common noun for a kite you fly in the wind. It’s masculine: un cerf-volant. Plural: des cerfs-volants. Despite the literal parts (“flying deer”), the meaning is simply “kite.”
target_language_example: On fait voler un cerf-volant à la plage.
native_language_example: We’re flying a kite at the beach.

meaning: “the icing on the cake”; an extra bonus that makes something even better.
additional_notes: Common idiom used to describe a final positive detail that tops off an already good situation. Often introduced with “Et/Et en plus, la cerise sur le gâteau…” or “C’est la cerise sur le gâteau.” It’s generally neutral (not slang).
target_language_example: On a eu une réduction, et la cerise sur le gâteau, la livraison est gratuite.
native_language_example: We got a discount, and the icing on the cake is that delivery is free.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the current period of time (recently, nowadays), not a specific day. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence: “Ces jours-ci, …” or “…, ces jours-ci.”
target_language_example: Je suis très occupé ces jours-ci.
native_language_example: I’m very busy these days.

additional_notes: Used to say that everyone acts in their own interest and helps themselves rather than cooperating. Often describes competition, lack of solidarity, or a situation where people stop working together (e.g., in a crisis, at work, in politics). Can also be used as a warning or resigned comment: "Bon, chacun pour soi !"
target_language_example: Quand la panne a commencé, c’était chacun pour soi : tout le monde a cherché une solution de son côté.
native_language_example: When the breakdown started, it was every man for himself: everyone looked for a solution on their own.

meaning: goosebumps (often from cold, fear, or emotion).
additional_notes: Very common expression. Used with the verb "avoir": "J’ai la chair de poule" = "I have goosebumps." You can also specify the cause: "à cause du froid" (because of the cold), "quand j’ai peur" (when I’m scared).
target_language_example: J’ai la chair de poule à cause du froid.
native_language_example: I have goosebumps because of the cold.

additional_notes: Very informal, spoken contraction of « je ne sais pas » (often also written « ché pas »). Used in casual conversation; avoid in formal situations or writing. Common pronunciation: /ʃe pa/.
target_language_example: Tu viens ce soir ? Chais pas, on verra.
native_language_example: Are you coming tonight? I don’t know, we’ll see.

meaning: a vault; a strong room (secure room for valuables).
additional_notes: Used for a highly secure room in a bank, hotel, museum, or company where money, documents, or valuable items are stored. Often used with definite articles (la chambre forte) and verbs like déposer/mettre/être dans. Not the same as a regular “chambre” (bedroom).
target_language_example: Les bijoux sont dans la chambre forte de la banque.
native_language_example: The jewelry is in the bank vault.

additional_notes: A common, neutral term for a bedroom in a home or apartment. Often shortened to just chambre when the context is clear. Not usually used for hotel rooms (you’d more often say une chambre d’hôtel).
target_language_example: La chambre à coucher est au deuxième étage.
native_language_example: The bedroom is on the second floor.

additional_notes: Used literally for the place where a battle happens (historical or modern). Also used figuratively to describe any area of intense conflict or competition (e.g., politics, business): «Le marché est un champ de bataille.»
target_language_example: Cette colline était un champ de bataille pendant la guerre.
native_language_example: This hill was a battlefield during the war.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone (or a team) who has won a world championship in a sport or competition. Often follows the noun it describes (e.g., "Il est champion du monde"), and can be made feminine/plural: "championne du monde" (female), "champions/championnes du monde" (plural).
target_language_example: Il est champion du monde de judo.
native_language_example: He is the world judo champion.

additional_notes: A common, neutral term used in news, science, and everyday conversation to talk about long-term changes in Earth’s climate (often linked to global warming). Often used with verbs like « lutter contre » (fight against), « parler de » (talk about), and « agir face à » (act in response to).
target_language_example: Le changement climatique a des effets sur la météo et les océans.
native_language_example: Climate change has effects on the weather and the oceans.

additional_notes: Used when someone revises their opinion, decision, or plan. It’s very common in everyday French. You can specify about what: "changer d’avis sur quelque chose" (change your mind about something). The "d’" is the contraction of "de" before a vowel.
target_language_example: J’ai changé d’avis : je ne viens plus ce soir.
native_language_example: I changed my mind: I’m not coming tonight anymore.

additional_notes: Used for someone who tracks down a person (often a criminal or someone who skipped bail) in exchange for a reward (une prime). Common in movies/TV; in everyday French you may also see "chasseur de têtes" (headhunter) but that refers to recruiting, not bounties.
target_language_example: Dans ce film, un chasseur de primes poursuit le fugitif pour toucher la récompense.
native_language_example: In this movie, a bounty hunter chases the fugitive to collect the reward.

additional_notes: A feminine noun: une chauve-souris (plural: des chauves-souris). The literal components mean “bald” + “mouse,” but it refers to the flying mammal (a bat). You’ll see it in everyday contexts (nature, Halloween, etc.).
target_language_example: Il y a une chauve-souris dans le grenier.
native_language_example: There is a bat in the attic.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a TV channel you watch, whether over-the-air, cable, or satellite. Often shortened to "une chaîne" when context is clear. Common with "sur" + channel number/name ("sur la chaîne 2", "sur TF1") and with verbs like "regarder", "mettre", "changer" (de chaîne).
target_language_example: Sur quelle chaîne de télévision passe le match ce soir ?
native_language_example: Which TV channel is the match on tonight?

meaning: a masterpiece; a work of outstanding quality.
additional_notes: Used for art, books, films, music, architecture, etc. You’ll often see it with an article: « un chef-d’œuvre ». In plural: « des chefs-d’œuvre » (the first part becomes plural).
target_language_example: Ce film est un chef-d’œuvre.
native_language_example: This movie is a masterpiece.

additional_notes: Often used for the rail system in general. Literally “iron path,” and you’ll also see it in set phrases like "gare de chemin de fer" (railway station). In everyday speech, people also say "train" for a trip by rail.
target_language_example: Il travaille pour la compagnie de chemin de fer.
native_language_example: He works for the railway company.

meaning: to nitpick; to look for something to criticize.
additional_notes: An idiom used when someone keeps hunting for tiny faults or problems, often unnecessarily (e.g., in an argument, a review, or a complaint). It implies being overly picky rather than genuinely trying to help. Commonly used with "arrête de" (stop) or to describe someone: "Il cherche toujours la petite bête."
target_language_example: Arrête de chercher la petite bête : tout est correct.
native_language_example: Stop nitpicking: everything is correct.

meaning: to try to; to seek to (do something).
additional_notes: Followed by an infinitive verb: « chercher à + infinitive ». It expresses an attempt or effort to achieve something (often with the idea of aiming for a result), not the physical act of searching for an object/person (that’s « chercher + noun »). Common in more formal or written French; in everyday speech you’ll also hear « essayer de » for “to try to.”
target_language_example: Je cherche à comprendre ce problème.
native_language_example: I’m trying to understand this problem.

additional_notes: Refers to hair that has turned white/gray, often because of age. Usually used with a possessive (mes/tes/ses cheveux blancs) or with the verb "avoir" (to have). Note: "blanc" agrees in number with "cheveux" → "cheveux blancs" (plural).
target_language_example: Mon grand-père a les cheveux blancs.
native_language_example: My grandfather has white/gray hair.

meaning: at our place; at home (for us).
additional_notes: Used to talk about where you/your group lives or the place that feels like home. It can mean your physical home (“come to our place”) or, more broadly, your country/region/culture (“back home/where I’m from”). Often contrasts with chez vous (“at your place”) or chez eux (“at their place”).
target_language_example: Ce soir, on dîne chez nous.
native_language_example: Tonight, we’re having dinner at our place.

additional_notes: Uses the stressed pronoun (moi/toi/lui/elle/nous/vous/eux/elles) to mean “at my/your/his/her/our/your/their home.” Common with verbs like être, rester, rentrer, and se sentir: « Je suis chez moi » (I’m at home), « Je rentre chez moi » (I’m going home). Not the same as « à la maison », which also means “at home” but doesn’t specify whose home.
target_language_example: Après le travail, je rentre chez moi.
native_language_example: After work, I go home.

additional_notes: A noun phrase meaning a dog used for hunting (e.g., tracking, pointing, retrieving). Often used generically, but it can also refer to a specific breed trained for hunting. Plural: chiens de chasse.
target_language_example: Il a un chien de chasse très bien dressé.
native_language_example: He has a very well-trained hunting dog.

additional_notes: Used to refer to numbering written with Roman numerals (I, II, III, IV, V, etc.), often seen in book chapters, centuries, monarchs’ names (Louis XIV), clocks, or outlines. Note: in French, *chiffre* often means a numeral/digit (not necessarily “cipher”).
target_language_example: Le chapitre est numéroté en chiffres romains.
native_language_example: The chapter is numbered in Roman numerals.

additional_notes: Used to name the type of chocolate (as an ingredient, flavor, or item). You’ll often see it on menus and packaging: gâteau au chocolat blanc (white-chocolate cake), mousse au chocolat blanc, tablette de chocolat blanc.
target_language_example: Je prends une glace au chocolat blanc.
native_language_example: I’ll have a white chocolate ice cream.

additional_notes: A common drink, especially in winter. You can order it in a café: « Un chocolat chaud, s’il vous plaît. » Note that « chocolat » can mean chocolate (the ingredient) or a hot chocolate drink depending on context; « chocolat chaud » is unambiguous for the drink.
target_language_example: Je voudrais un chocolat chaud, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a hot chocolate, please.

additional_notes: A common phrase for a castle-shaped structure made out of sand, typically at the beach. Often used with verbs like "faire" or "construire" (to make/build).
target_language_example: Les enfants font un château de sable sur la plage.
native_language_example: The children are making a sandcastle on the beach.

meaning: 'below' / 'below this' (in a document or on a page).
additional_notes: Used mostly in writing (emails, instructions, forms) to point the reader to information that appears later on the page or further down. Often seen in phrases like « voir ci-dessous » (see below) or « comme indiqué ci-dessous » (as indicated below).
target_language_example: Vous trouverez les détails ci-dessous.
native_language_example: You will find the details below.

additional_notes: Used in formal writing (letters/emails) to refer to a document you are sending along with the message. Often appears in set phrases like « Veuillez trouver ci-joint… » (“Please find attached…”) or « Vous trouverez ci-joint… » (“You will find attached…”). It usually agrees with what is attached: « ci-jointes » (feminine plural), « ci-joints » (masculine plural).
target_language_example: Veuillez trouver ci-joint le contrat signé.
native_language_example: Please find attached the signed contract.

additional_notes: Used to say the number 500 (in counting, prices, amounts, etc.). Unlike some numbers, it’s straightforward: cinq (five) + cent(s) (hundred). Note: when "cent" is multiplied and not followed by another number, it usually takes an -s (e.g., "cinq cents"), but it loses the -s if another number follows (e.g., "cinq cent un" = 501).
target_language_example: Ça coûte cinq cents euros.
native_language_example: It costs five hundred euros.

additional_notes: Used to say you can hear/understand someone perfectly, especially on the phone, in radio/aviation/military-style communication, or jokingly in everyday speech. Literally "five out of five," but it functions as a fixed expression meaning the signal is perfect.
target_language_example: — Tu m’entends ? — Oui, cinq sur cinq !
native_language_example: — Can you hear me? — Yes, loud and clear!

additional_notes: Cardinal number used for counting and giving quantities. Hyphenated in standard French spelling. Often used for ages, prices, dates, and numbers in general.
target_language_example: J'ai cinquante-deux euros sur moi.
native_language_example: I have fifty-two euros on me.

additional_notes: A common, neutral expression for the light from the moon (often in poetic or romantic contexts). You can use it with verbs like « admirer » (to admire) or « se promener au clair de lune » (to walk in the moonlight). Also used in titles (e.g., « Clair de lune »).
target_language_example: On s’est promenés au clair de lune.
native_language_example: We went for a walk in the moonlight.

additional_notes: Refers to the social/economic group between the working class and the upper class (income, lifestyle, education). Often used with articles: « la classe moyenne » (the middle class) or « les classes moyennes » (the middle classes). Common in discussions about society, taxes, housing, and politics.
target_language_example: La classe moyenne a du mal à payer le loyer dans certaines grandes villes.
native_language_example: The middle class has a hard time paying rent in some big cities.

additional_notes: Common with the verb "cligner" + "des yeux" (often used as "cligner des yeux" = blink). Also used figuratively in "en un clin d’œil" (“in the blink of an eye”). You may also see "cligner de l’œil" meaning “to wink.”
target_language_example: Je n’arrive pas à cligner des yeux avec ces lentilles.
native_language_example: I can’t blink with these contact lenses.

meaning: a wink; a playful hint or nod.
additional_notes: Literally “blink of the eye.” Most often means a wink (a quick closing of one eye), used to show humor, friendliness, or a shared secret. By extension, it can mean an allusion/nod to something (like a reference in a film or speech): “un clin d'œil à…”
target_language_example: Il m’a fait un clin d'œil pour me dire que c’était une blague.
native_language_example: He winked at me to tell me it was a joke.

additional_notes: Refers to an improvised incendiary weapon, typically a glass bottle filled with flammable liquid and a cloth wick. Often used in news reports, history, or discussions of riots/war. In French, it’s usually written “cocktail Molotov” (sometimes with a lowercase m: “cocktail molotov”).
target_language_example: La police a trouvé des cocktails Molotov près de la barricade.
native_language_example: The police found Molotov cocktails near the barricade.

meaning: the Highway Code (traffic laws/rules of the road).
additional_notes: Refers to the official set of road traffic rules and regulations in France, often mentioned in driving contexts. You’ll see it in phrases like « apprendre / réviser le code de la route » (study for the theory test) and « le code de la route interdit / autorise… » (the traffic code forbids/allows…).
target_language_example: Je révise le code de la route pour passer le permis.
native_language_example: I’m studying the Highway Code to take the driving test.

meaning: a safe (secure metal box for valuables).
additional_notes: Used for a secure container where you keep money, jewelry, documents, etc. Common in homes, hotels, banks, and offices. In a hotel you might hear: « coffre-fort dans la chambre » (in-room safe).
target_language_example: J’ai mis mon passeport dans le coffre-fort de l’hôtel.
native_language_example: I put my passport in the hotel safe.

meaning: street corner (the corner of a street).
additional_notes: Often used as part of the very common expression "au coin de la rue" (at the street corner / just around the corner). Note that "coin" usually means "corner" in French (not a "coin" like money).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au coin de la rue.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the street corner.

additional_notes: Literal meaning is the spinal column in your body. It’s also used figuratively to mean the “backbone” of something: its main support or central structure (e.g., the backbone of an organization, system, or argument).
target_language_example: Le bénévolat est la colonne vertébrale de cette association.
native_language_example: Volunteering is the backbone of this organization.

additional_notes: Common way to ask the price of something in shops, markets, or restaurants. Often followed by a noun: « Combien ça coûte, ce livre ? » You may also hear the slightly more formal « Combien ça coûte ? » / « Combien ça coûte, s'il vous plaît ? »
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, combien ça coûte ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how much does it cost?

additional_notes: Used to describe how something is done or how something is. Often interchangeable with the more common spoken form "comme ça". It can refer to something you’re pointing at or something already understood from context.
target_language_example: Fais-le comme cela, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Do it like that, please.

additional_notes: Informal abbreviation of « comme d’habitude ». Used in casual speech, texts, and messages to say something is happening the normal way or routinely. Avoid in formal writing; use « comme d’habitude » instead.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à 18 h, comme d'hab ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at 6 p.m., as usual?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like « se vendre » or « partir » to say something is being bought very fast because it’s popular or in high demand: « Ça se vend comme des petits pains. » Literally “like little breads,” but the natural English equivalent is “like hotcakes.”
target_language_example: Les billets se vendent comme des petits pains.
native_language_example: The tickets are selling like hotcakes.

meaning: proper(ly); as it should be; decent/respectable.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done the right way, in a correct or socially acceptable manner. Often implies good manners or being respectable ("bien comme il faut"). It can modify a verb (doing something properly) or a noun (a respectable person).
target_language_example: Il faut s’habiller comme il faut pour l’entretien.
native_language_example: You need to dress properly for the interview.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a common expression, proverb, or a familiar way of putting something. Literally “as one says,” with the general subject “on” meaning “people/they.” Often used as a parenthetical (set off by commas).
target_language_example: C’est, comme on dit, la cerise sur le gâteau.
native_language_example: It’s, as they say, the icing on the cake.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened suddenly, surprisingly, or effortlessly—often with a hint of amazement or irony. Common in storytelling and everyday speech. Often follows a verb like apparaître (to appear), disparaître (to disappear), se résoudre (to get resolved), or fonctionner (to work).
target_language_example: Et puis, comme par magie, le problème a disparu.
native_language_example: And then, as if by magic, the problem disappeared.

meaning: like crazy; extremely; a whole lot.
additional_notes: Informal intensifier used after a verb to mean “a lot/very strongly,” often implying something is excessive (e.g., working, partying, sweating, raining). Literally it’s “as not allowed,” but it’s not used with that literal meaning.
target_language_example: Il a travaillé comme pas permis cette semaine.
native_language_example: He worked like crazy this week.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone does something exceptionally well or in a unique way. Often appears after a verb: « Il cuisine comme personne » = “He cooks like nobody (else).” Similar in meaning to « comme nul autre » / « comme personne d’autre ».
target_language_example: Elle danse comme personne.
native_language_example: She dances like nobody (else).

meaning: “as for” / “like for” / “as with” (when comparing or saying something is the same for someone/something else).
additional_notes: Used to draw a parallel or say the same situation applies to another person/thing. Often followed by a noun or pronoun: « comme pour moi », « comme pour les enfants ». In many contexts it matches English “as for…” or “as with…”.
target_language_example: Comme pour moi, il préfère partir tôt.
native_language_example: As for me, he prefers to leave early.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened according to the plan or expectation. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence: « Comme prévu, … » / « …, comme prévu. » Common in emails and updates to confirm things went normally.
target_language_example: Comme prévu, la réunion commence à 9 h.
native_language_example: As planned, the meeting starts at 9 a.m.

meaning: "which goes to show" / "so" (introduces a conclusion or what something proves).
additional_notes: Often used in speech to draw a conclusion from what was just said, similar to “which just shows that…” or “so…”. It can also introduce reported information with a slightly doubtful tone (“apparently / seems like”): *Il paraît comme quoi…* (common but informal/redundant; *il paraît que…* is more standard).
target_language_example: Il a réussi sans réviser, comme quoi tout est possible.
native_language_example: He passed without studying, which just goes to show anything is possible.

additional_notes: Used to compare something to an imagined or unreal situation. It’s often followed by the imperfect (l’imparfait) to express something contrary to reality: « Il parle comme s’il savait tout. » (“He talks as if he knew everything.”). It can also be followed by the conditional in more formal/literary French.
target_language_example: Il me regarde comme si je n’existais pas.
native_language_example: He looks at me as if I didn’t exist.

meaning: as if it were yesterday; as if it happened yesterday.
additional_notes: Used to say you remember something very clearly, even though it happened a long time ago. Often follows verbs like « je m’en souviens » (I remember it) or « je m’en rappelle » (I recall it). It can also express nostalgia.
target_language_example: Je m’en souviens comme si c’était hier.
native_language_example: I remember it as if it were yesterday.

meaning: as if nothing happened; as if nothing were wrong.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone acting normally and ignoring an incident, problem, or awkward situation. Often follows verbs like "agir" (to act), "faire" (to do), or "continuer" (to continue): "Il a continué comme si de rien n’était." The fuller common form is "comme si de rien n’était" (as if nothing had happened).
target_language_example: Elle est revenue comme si de rien n’était.
native_language_example: She came back as if nothing had happened.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone acting normally after something unusual, embarrassing, or serious—ignoring it or pretending it didn’t happen. Often suggests a deliberate attempt to act unaffected.
target_language_example: Après l’accident, il est revenu au bureau comme si de rien n’était.
native_language_example: After the accident, he came back to the office as if nothing had happened.

meaning: really; very; incredibly (used to intensify an adjective).
additional_notes: Used after an adjective (often a positive one) to mean “so/very/really.” Common in spoken French: "gentil comme tout" (so nice), "mignon comme tout" (so cute). It doesn’t usually mean the literal “like everything” in this expression.
target_language_example: Ton chien est mignon comme tout !
native_language_example: Your dog is so cute!

additional_notes: Used to agree to someone else’s preference or decision (often meaning “up to you”). Depending on tone, it can sound neutral, accommodating, or slightly dismissive (“fine, whatever”). In more formal/polite situations, you might say “comme vous voulez”.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à 18 h ? Comme tu veux.
native_language_example: Shall we meet at 6 p.m.? Whatever you want.

meaning: "like that" / "that way" (referring to how something is done).
additional_notes: Used to describe the manner or way of doing something. Often said while showing or pointing: « Fais-le comme ça » (“Do it like this/that”). It can also be used vaguely to mean “like that / sort of” when you don’t want to give details: « Je l’ai fait comme ça » (“I did it like that”).
target_language_example: Fais-le comme ça, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Do it like that, please.

additional_notes: A polite way to ask someone’s wellbeing. Uses the formal/plural “vous,” so it works for strangers, people you don’t know well, or when speaking to more than one person. Common replies: « Ça va, merci. Et vous ? » (I’m fine, thanks. And you?).
target_language_example: Bonjour, comment allez-vous ?
native_language_example: Hello, how are you?

meaning: "How so?" / "How is that?" (asking for an explanation).
additional_notes: Used as a short question—often expressing surprise or confusion—when reacting to what someone just said. It’s a shortened form of questions like « Comment cela se fait-il ? » (“How come?”). On its own, it’s mostly conversational rather than formal writing.
target_language_example: — J’ai déjà fini le travail. — Comment cela ?
native_language_example: — I’ve already finished the work. — How so?

meaning: "how is …?" / "how is … going?" (asking how someone/something is doing).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question, followed by a subject (person/thing): « Comment va ta mère ? » (How is your mother?). Very common with « ça »: « Comment ça va ? » (How are you?/How’s it going?). The verb « va » is from « aller » (to go).
target_language_example: Comment va ton travail en ce moment ?
native_language_example: How is your work going at the moment?

additional_notes: Used to ask how someone is doing when talking to one person you address as "tu" (a friend, someone your age, a child). In more formal situations or with strangers, use "Comment allez-vous ?". You may also hear the shorter "Ça va ?".
target_language_example: Salut ! Comment vas-tu ?
native_language_example: Hi! How are you?

additional_notes: Used to ask for clarification or express surprise about what someone just said. Often comes with a questioning tone: « Comment ça ? » You can also use it in a longer question: « Comment ça se fait ? » (How come?) or « Comment ça va ? » (How are you?) but on its own it usually means 'how so/what do you mean?'.
target_language_example: — Je pars demain. — Comment ça ?
native_language_example: — I’m leaving tomorrow. — What do you mean?

meaning: How are you? / How’s it going?
additional_notes: Common, friendly way to ask how someone is doing. Often shortened to “Ça va ?” or expanded to “Comment ça va ?”. A typical reply is “Ça va.” (I’m fine / It’s going OK), or “Ça va bien / pas mal / comme ci, comme ça.”
target_language_example: Salut ! Comment ça va ?
native_language_example: Hi! How are you?

additional_notes: A common travel term for a business that operates flights. Often used with a specific airline name or with articles: « une compagnie aérienne », « la compagnie aérienne ».
target_language_example: Quelle compagnie aérienne as-tu prise ?
native_language_example: Which airline did you take?

additional_notes: Used for an account you have at a bank to deposit money, pay bills, receive salary, etc. Common in administrative/banking contexts. You’ll often see it with verbs like "ouvrir" (to open) and "fermer" (to close): "ouvrir un compte bancaire". In French, "compte" can also mean other kinds of accounts (online account, customer account), so "bancaire" specifies it’s a bank account.
target_language_example: J’ai ouvert un compte bancaire dans cette banque.
native_language_example: I opened a bank account at this bank.

additional_notes: Used for counting down from a number to zero before an event (a launch, a deadline, New Year’s, etc.). Often used with the verb "commencer" (to start) or "lancer" (to begin): "Le compte à rebours commence !"
target_language_example: Le compte à rebours a commencé : plus que dix secondes !
native_language_example: The countdown has started: only ten seconds left!

meaning: a bill to pay; the check (at a restaurant).
additional_notes: Used when talking about paying what you owe, especially in restaurants (similar to “l’addition”). It can also be used more generally for an unpaid bill/invoice. Literally “account to settle,” but in everyday use it’s about paying the bill.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, il y a un compte à régler, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Excuse me, we need to pay the bill, please.

meaning: a report; a written summary (e.g., meeting minutes).
additional_notes: Used for an official or structured summary of what happened or what was said, often after a meeting, event, or appointment ("un compte-rendu de réunion" = meeting minutes). You can also use it for a medical summary ("compte-rendu médical"). Common verb: "faire/rédiger un compte-rendu" = to write up a report.
target_language_example: Je vais rédiger un compte-rendu de la réunion et te l’envoyer.
native_language_example: I’m going to write up a report of the meeting and send it to you.

meaning: to plan to (do); to intend to (do).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (compter faire + verb) to express an intention or plan, often similar to “I’m planning to…” or “I mean to…”. It does not mean “to count.” You can also add a time phrase: « Je compte le faire demain. »
target_language_example: Je compte faire les courses après le travail.
native_language_example: I’m planning to do the shopping after work.

meaning: to count for; to matter to.
additional_notes: Used to say that something has value/importance in someone’s eyes (compter pour quelqu’un) or that it is included as part of a total (compter pour X % / compter pour une part). Often appears in negatives like « ne compter pour rien » (“to not matter at all”).
target_language_example: Tu comptes beaucoup pour moi.
native_language_example: You mean a lot to me.

meaning: to count on; to rely on.
additional_notes: Used when you depend on someone/something: « Je compte sur toi » (“I’m counting on you”). It can also mean “to be planning/intending to” + infinitive: « Je compte sur venir demain » (“I’m planning to come tomorrow”), though « je compte venir demain » is more common.
target_language_example: Je compte sur toi pour m’aider demain.
native_language_example: I’m counting on you to help me tomorrow.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used to talk about someone’s confidence in their own abilities or worth. Often used with verbs like "avoir" (to have), "manquer de" (to lack), "prendre" (to gain), or "perdre" (to lose): "avoir confiance en soi", "manquer de confiance en soi".
target_language_example: Elle a beaucoup de confiance en soi quand elle parle en public.
native_language_example: She has a lot of self-confidence when she speaks in public.

additional_notes: A formal meeting where a public figure or organization speaks to journalists and answers questions. Often used with verbs like "donner" (to hold/give) or "organiser" (to organize): "donner une conférence de presse".
target_language_example: Le ministre va donner une conférence de presse à 15 h.
native_language_example: The minister is going to hold a press conference at 3 p.m.

meaning: to know (someone) by sight; to recognize (someone) but not know them personally.
additional_notes: Used when you’ve seen someone before (in the neighborhood, at work, on the bus, etc.) and you would recognize them, but you haven’t really met or spoken much. Often followed by a contrast like « mais je ne le/la connais pas » (“but I don’t know him/her”).
target_language_example: Je le connais de vue, mais je ne sais pas comment il s’appelle.
native_language_example: I recognize him, but I don’t know what his name is.

meaning: to know the drill; to know the usual story/excuse.
additional_notes: Often used when something is familiar or predictable (you’ve heard it all before). It can imply skepticism, like “Yeah, I know how this goes.” In the negative, it can mean you don’t know what’s going on: « Je ne connais pas la chanson. »
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je connais la chanson : il va encore être en retard.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I know the drill: he’s going to be late again.

meaning: to know the ropes; to be familiar with how it works (often from past experience).
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used when someone has seen a situation before and isn’t easily fooled or surprised. Often implies: “I know this story already / I know what to expect.” It can also be used literally about actually knowing a piece of music, but the idiomatic meaning is common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je connais la musique : ils vont encore nous demander de patienter.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I know the drill: they’re going to ask us to wait again.

additional_notes: Refers to the elected governing body of a municipality (town or city) that votes on local decisions (budget, urban planning, local rules). Often used with a specific place: « le conseil municipal de Lyon ». In France it’s distinct from « mairie » (the town hall building/administration) and from the person « le maire » (the mayor).
target_language_example: Le conseil municipal a voté le budget de la ville.
native_language_example: The city council voted on the city’s budget.

additional_notes: Used to talk about looking directly into someone’s eyes, often in social situations, presentations, interviews, or when discussing confidence/respect. You can use it with verbs like « établir », « maintenir », or « éviter » (to make/keep/avoid eye contact).
target_language_example: Il est important de maintenir le contact visuel pendant un entretien d’embauche.
native_language_example: It’s important to maintain eye contact during a job interview.

additional_notes: Means a traditional children’s story with magic, fairies, princes/princesses, etc. In standard French you’ll usually see the plural: « un conte de fées » (a fairy tale) / « des contes de fées » (fairy tales).
target_language_example: Le soir, elle lit un conte de fées à son fils.
native_language_example: In the evening, she reads a fairy tale to her son.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for traditional magical stories (princesses, witches, etc.). Also used figuratively to describe an unrealistically perfect or dreamy story/situation (like “a fairy tale”). Often appears with an article: « un conte de fées », « les contes de fées ».
target_language_example: Quand j’étais petit, ma mère me lisait un conte de fées avant de dormir.
native_language_example: When I was little, my mother read me a fairy tale before I went to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to contrast two things. It’s followed by a noun/pronoun (e.g., contrairement à moi, contrairement à cette idée) or can refer back to a whole statement (e.g., Contrairement à ce que tu penses… = Contrary to what you think…). Often used in formal or neutral writing/speech.
target_language_example: Contrairement à mon frère, je préfère rester à la maison.
native_language_example: Unlike my brother, I prefer to stay at home.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened even though it seemed unlikely. Common in written French and formal speech, but also understood in everyday conversation. Often placed at the start of a sentence or between commas.
target_language_example: Contre toute attente, il a réussi son examen.
native_language_example: Contrary to all expectations, he passed his exam.

meaning: to counterattack; to hit back after an attack.
additional_notes: Used in sports, military contexts, debates, or any situation where you respond to an attack/criticism with your own attack. Often followed by "contre" + person/opponent (e.g., "contre-attaquer contre son adversaire") or used on its own ("Ils ont contre-attaqué").
target_language_example: Après avoir encaissé un but, l’équipe a contre-attaqué immédiatement.
native_language_example: After conceding a goal, the team counterattacked immediately.

meaning: against the current; going against the flow (literal or figurative).
additional_notes: Often used in the set expression « à contre-courant » (“against the current/against the tide”). Can be literal (water, traffic flow) or figurative (ideas, fashion: doing the opposite of what most people do).
target_language_example: Il nage à contre-courant pour traverser la rivière.
native_language_example: He’s swimming against the current to cross the river.

additional_notes: Literally “setting of the sun.” Used to talk about the time of day when the sun goes down or the view/colors in the sky at that moment. Commonly used with verbs like regarder/voir (to watch/see) and expressions like au coucher du soleil (“at sunset”).
target_language_example: On va regarder le coucher de soleil sur la plage.
native_language_example: We’re going to watch the sunset on the beach.

additional_notes: Used to mean taking a brief look at something (information, a document, a place, etc.). Very common in set phrases like "jeter un coup d'œil" (to take a quick look) and "au premier coup d'œil" (at first glance).
target_language_example: Tu peux jeter un coup d'œil à mon CV ?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at my résumé?

additional_notes: Used for a brief, fast look at something. Common with verbs like "jeter" (to throw) or "donner" (to give): "jeter un coup d'œil" / "donner un coup d'œil" = "to take a quick look." Can also refer to an overall view at a glance: "un coup d'œil sur" = "a quick look/overview of."
target_language_example: Tu peux jeter un coup d'œil à ce document ?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at this document?

meaning: a stroke of luck; a lucky break.
additional_notes: Informal expression used to say something good happened by chance. Often used with « Quel coup de bol ! » (“What luck!”) or « C’est un coup de bol » (“It’s a lucky break”).
target_language_example: J’ai trouvé 20 euros par terre : quel coup de bol !
native_language_example: I found 20 euros on the ground: what a stroke of luck!

meaning: a stroke of luck; a lucky break.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a fortunate event that happens unexpectedly. Very common in everyday French. Often used with avoir (to have): « J’ai eu un coup de chance » (I got lucky).
target_language_example: J’ai eu un coup de chance : le train avait du retard, alors je ne l’ai pas raté.
native_language_example: I got lucky: the train was late, so I didn’t miss it.

meaning: a gunshot; (also) a sudden rush/busy moment.
additional_notes: Most commonly means “gunshot” in everyday news or police contexts: *Il y a eu un coup de feu* (“There was a gunshot”). In restaurants, *le coup de feu* can mean the peak rush (the busiest moment of service).
target_language_example: On a entendu un coup de feu dans la rue.
native_language_example: We heard a gunshot in the street.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase meaning “a quick call.” Often used with verbs like donner/passer (to give/make) or recevoir (to receive): « Je te donne un coup de fil. » / « Passe-moi un coup de fil. » It’s informal but not slang; in more formal contexts you can say « un appel (téléphonique) ».
target_language_example: Je te donne un coup de fil ce soir.
native_language_example: I’ll give you a call tonight.

meaning: love at first sight; a sudden (often romantic) crush.
additional_notes: Literally means “bolt of lightning.” Very common to describe falling in love instantly (un coup de foudre), but it can also mean a sudden strong enthusiasm for something (e.g., a place or an idea). Often used with the verb “avoir” (to have): « J’ai eu un coup de foudre pour… » or « Ça a été le coup de foudre. »
target_language_example: Quand je l’ai vu, ça a été le coup de foudre.
native_language_example: When I saw him, it was love at first sight.

additional_notes: Most often used in the phrase « donner un coup de main » (“to give a hand / to help out”), usually for practical, short-term help (moving, carrying, setting up, etc.). You can also say « un petit coup de main » for “a quick little help.”
target_language_example: Tu peux me donner un coup de main pour déménager samedi ?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand moving on Saturday?

meaning: a kick (a blow with the foot).
additional_notes: Literally “blow of foot.” Used for a physical kick (in sports, fighting, or accidents). Common in set phrases like « donner un coup de pied (à…) » = “to kick (something/someone)” and « au coup de pied » in some contexts (e.g., “by kicking”).
target_language_example: Il a donné un coup de pied dans le ballon.
native_language_example: He kicked the ball.

additional_notes: Used for a hit delivered with the fist, in sports or in a fight (e.g., boxe). Can be literal (a physical punch) or sometimes figurative in fixed phrases like « un coup de poing dans l’estomac » (“a gut punch,” meaning a shocking or upsetting impact). Plural: « des coups de poing ».
target_language_example: Il lui a donné un coup de poing.
native_language_example: He punched him.

additional_notes: Used for the skin burn you get from being in the sun too long. You typically say "avoir un coup de soleil" (to have a sunburn) or "attraper/prendre un coup de soleil" (to get a sunburn).
target_language_example: J’ai attrapé un coup de soleil à la plage.
native_language_example: I got a sunburn at the beach.

meaning: a clap of thunder; (figuratively) a shock/bombshell.
additional_notes: Literal meaning is “clap/strike of thunder.” It’s used for a loud thunderclap in weather, and very commonly in a figurative sense for sudden, startling news or an event that causes surprise (like “a bombshell”). Often used with verbs like « être », « tomber » (as in « c’est tombé comme un coup de tonnerre »), or « faire l’effet d’un coup de tonnerre ».
target_language_example: La nouvelle est tombée comme un coup de tonnerre.
native_language_example: The news hit like a bombshell.

additional_notes: Literally “a hit/strike of telephone,” but it simply means “a (quick) phone call.” Very common with the verb “donner” (to give): “donner un coup de téléphone” = to give/make a call. Also used with “passer” or “faire” in some contexts.
target_language_example: Je te donne un coup de téléphone ce soir.
native_language_example: I’ll give you a call tonight.

meaning: a headbutt; also an impulsive action/decision.
additional_notes: Literally “a blow of the head,” but in English you usually say “headbutt.” By extension, it can mean doing something on impulse (a spur-of-the-moment decision), often without thinking about consequences. Context makes the meaning clear: physical action in sports/fights vs. a sudden decision in everyday life.
target_language_example: Sur un coup de tête, j’ai acheté des billets pour Paris.
native_language_example: On a whim, I bought tickets to Paris.

meaning: a set-up; a framed job; a plot (often to trick someone).
additional_notes: Used when something was planned in advance to deceive someone or make them look guilty (e.g., a trap, a sting, or being framed). Often heard in news, crime stories, or everyday speech: « C’est un coup monté ! » = “It’s a set-up!”
target_language_example: Il dit que son arrestation était un coup monté.
native_language_example: He says his arrest was a set-up.

meaning: to interrupt (someone); to cut someone off while they’re speaking.
additional_notes: Used when someone starts speaking before another person has finished. Often followed by an indirect object: « couper la parole à quelqu’un ». It can be neutral (describing what happened) or negative (criticizing rude behavior). Common in polite corrections: « Pardon de vous couper la parole… ».
target_language_example: Pardon de te couper la parole, mais je ne suis pas d’accord.
native_language_example: Sorry to interrupt you, but I don’t agree.

meaning: to take someone’s breath away; to leave someone breathless.
additional_notes: Often used for something impressive or shocking (a view, a performance, unexpected news). Common pattern: « Ça m’a coupé le souffle » (“It took my breath away”). Can also be used more literally for something that makes it hard to breathe (e.g., running, a blow).
target_language_example: La vue du sommet m’a coupé le souffle.
native_language_example: The view from the top took my breath away.

additional_notes: Common in everyday situations (home, car, office) to talk about air coming in through an open window/door and making you feel cold. Very often used with verbs like « il y a » (there is), « éviter » (to avoid), « attraper » (to catch), or « faire » (to cause): « Il y a un courant d’air. », « Évite les courants d’air. »
target_language_example: Ferme la fenêtre : il y a un courant d’air.
native_language_example: Close the window: there’s a draft.

additional_notes: An idiomatic (often negative) way to describe a man who constantly flirts with or pursues women. Literally “runner of skirts/petticoats,” so it can sound old-fashioned or judgmental; in more neutral contexts you might say "un séducteur" or "un dragueur" (more informal).
target_language_example: Tout le monde sait que c’est un coureur de jupons.
native_language_example: Everyone knows he’s a womanizer.

meaning: to run after; to chase; to pursue.
additional_notes: Used literally (running after someone/something) and very often figuratively (trying hard to get something or keep up), e.g. courir après le bus (run after the bus) or courir après le temps (race against time). It’s followed by a noun or pronoun: courir après lui/elle/eux.
target_language_example: Je cours après le bus !
native_language_example: I’m running after the bus!

additional_notes: A formal/neutral way to say “email” in French (often shortened to “courriel,” especially in Canada). In everyday speech, people also say “un mail” or “un e-mail,” which are more informal/borrowed from English. Used with verbs like “envoyer” (to send) and “recevoir” (to receive): envoyer un courrier électronique, recevoir un courrier électronique.
target_language_example: Je vous enverrai le document par courrier électronique.
native_language_example: I will send you the document by email.

additional_notes: Used to talk about running as a sport or workout. Often appears in phrases like "faire de la course à pied" (to go running) or "une course à pied" (a run). Not the same as "course" meaning a shopping errand ("faire les courses").
target_language_example: Je fais de la course à pied trois fois par semaine.
native_language_example: I go running three times a week.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the place where you play tennis. In French, the English word “court” is commonly used for sports playing areas (court de tennis, court de basket). Also note: “le cours de tennis” (with an s) means “a tennis lesson/class,” which is different from “court.”
target_language_example: On se retrouve au court de tennis à 16 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at the tennis court at 4 p.m.?

meaning: a boost up; a leg up (helping someone climb or reach something).
additional_notes: Usually used in the expression « faire la courte échelle à quelqu’un »: you put your hands together or support someone so they can step up and climb over/reach something. It can also be used figuratively to mean helping someone get ahead (e.g., by giving support or connections).
target_language_example: Tu peux me faire la courte échelle pour que je passe par-dessus le mur ?
native_language_example: Can you give me a boost so I can get over the wall?

additional_notes: A general word for anything worn on the head (e.g., a hat, cap, helmet, headscarf). Often used in more formal contexts, in signage, or in rules (e.g., in a church, at school, in the army). Plural: des couvre-chefs.
target_language_example: Veuillez retirer votre couvre-chef à l’intérieur.
native_language_example: Please remove your headwear indoors.

meaning: cowboy (a cattle herder; also the Western-style character).
additional_notes: A borrowing from English; also commonly written without a hyphen: « cowboy ». Used for the real job (in the American West) and more generally for anything with a “Western” vibe (hat, boots, films).
target_language_example: Il est déguisé en cow-boy pour la fête.
native_language_example: He’s dressed up as a cowboy for the party.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how expensive everyday life is in a place (housing, food, transport, etc.). Common in comparisons: « le coût de la vie est plus élevé à… » (“the cost of living is higher in…”).
target_language_example: Le coût de la vie est très élevé à Paris.
native_language_example: The cost of living is very high in Paris.

meaning: no matter what; at all costs.
additional_notes: Fixed expression meaning you will do something regardless of difficulties, consequences, or price. Often used after a verb to emphasize determination: « Je le ferai, coûte que coûte. »
target_language_example: Je finirai ce projet, coûte que coûte.
native_language_example: I will finish this project, no matter what.

meaning: to cost (someone) their life; to be fatal.
additional_notes: Used to say that an action, accident, illness, or situation caused someone to die. Often appears as "coûter la vie à quelqu’un" (to cost someone their life). Common in news and serious contexts.
target_language_example: L’accident a coûté la vie à deux personnes.
native_language_example: The accident cost two people their lives.

coûter les yeux de la tête

target_language_multi_word_term: coûter les yeux de la tête
meaning: to cost a fortune; to be extremely expensive.
additional_notes: A common idiom used to complain that something is overpriced. It literally means “to cost the eyes from the head,” but you use it like “it costs an arm and a leg.” Often used with the subject “ça” (that/it): « Ça coûte les yeux de la tête ! »
target_language_example: Je voulais acheter ce téléphone, mais il coûte les yeux de la tête.
native_language_example: I wanted to buy that phone, but it costs a fortune.

meaning: to spill the beans; to confess; to tell the truth (often after pressure).
additional_notes: Informal idiom. Used when someone finally reveals a secret or admits something, often because they’re being questioned or pressured. You can also use it as an order: « Allez, crache le morceau ! » (“Come on, spill it!”).
target_language_example: Après des heures d’interrogatoire, il a fini par cracher le morceau.
native_language_example: After hours of questioning, he finally spilled the beans.

additional_notes: A formal term for a person accused or convicted of serious crimes committed during a war (for example, against civilians or prisoners). Often used in news, history, and legal contexts. Plural: « criminels de guerre ».
target_language_example: Le tribunal a jugé plusieurs criminels de guerre.
native_language_example: The court tried several war criminals.

additional_notes: A medical term used for a sudden, serious heart problem. In everyday conversation, people also say “faire une crise cardiaque” (to have/suffer a heart attack). You may also hear “infarctus” in more technical contexts.
target_language_example: Il a fait une crise cardiaque pendant la nuit.
native_language_example: He had a heart attack during the night.

meaning: to take (someone) at their word; to believe without proof.
additional_notes: Used when you trust what someone says and don’t ask for evidence. Often used with a pronoun object: « Je te crois sur parole » (I’ll take your word for it). Not to be confused with English “parole” (early release from prison); here « parole » means “word” in the sense of what someone says.
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas de preuves, mais je te crois sur parole.
native_language_example: I don’t have any proof, but I’ll take your word for it.

meaning: to believe in; to believe that something is real/true.
additional_notes: Used with a noun or pronoun after it: croire à quelque chose / croire à ça. Often means believing in an idea, plan, or possibility ("I believe in it"), not believing a person (that’s usually "croire quelqu’un"). In the negative, "ne pas croire à" = "not to believe in" / "not to buy the idea."
target_language_example: Je crois à ton projet.
native_language_example: I believe in your project.

meaning: to cross your fingers (to hope for luck).
additional_notes: Used to express that you hope something will happen, often for luck or a good outcome. You can say it about yourself (Je croise les doigts.) or for someone else (Je croise les doigts pour toi.). Also commonly used as a standalone wish: Croise les doigts !
target_language_example: Je croise les doigts pour que tout se passe bien.
native_language_example: I’m crossing my fingers that everything goes well.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something surprising or hard to believe. It’s the imperative form addressing “you” (plural/formal): literally “believe it or not.” Often followed by a comma. You can also say “Crois-le ou non” when speaking to one person informally (tu).
target_language_example: Croyez-le ou non, je n’ai jamais goûté de café.
native_language_example: Believe it or not, I’ve never tasted coffee.

additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about the dessert. Often shortened in everyday speech to just "une glace" (an ice cream). You can specify a flavor with "à" (e.g., "crème glacée à la vanille").
target_language_example: Je voudrais une crème glacée à la fraise, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a strawberry ice cream, please.

additional_notes: Used for a cream/lotion you put on your skin to protect it from the sun. Common in summer, at the beach, or when traveling. Often used with a sun protection factor (SPF): « crème solaire SPF 30 » / « indice 50 ». Also: « mettre de la crème solaire » (to put on sunscreen), « en mettre » (to apply some).
target_language_example: N’oublie pas de mettre de la crème solaire avant d’aller à la plage.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to put on sunscreen before going to the beach.

additional_notes: Used in cooking to mean the measurement “tablespoon” (often written “c. à s.” or “càs”). Literally “spoon for soup,” but in recipes it usually indicates a quantity rather than the utensil.
target_language_example: Ajoute une cuillère à soupe d’huile d’olive.
native_language_example: Add a tablespoon of olive oil.

meaning: a dead-end street; (also) a dead end.
additional_notes: Used for a street that doesn’t go through (no exit). In French it can also be used more generally for a situation with no way out (figuratively). The term exists in English too (“cul-de-sac”), so the meaning is often the same.
target_language_example: Cette rue est un cul-de-sac.
native_language_example: This street is a dead end.

additional_notes: A common noun for the small stick used to remove food from between teeth, typically after a meal. Usually masculine: un cure-dent; plural: des cure-dents. Often used in restaurants: « Vous avez des cure-dents ? »
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous avez un cure-dent ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have a toothpick?

additional_notes: Used in formal/professional contexts (job applications, internships, academic programs) to mean a document summarizing your education, work experience, and skills. In French you can also say "un CV" (often pronounced like the letters) and write "CV" in ads and emails.
target_language_example: Je vous joins mon curriculum vitae et ma lettre de motivation.
native_language_example: I’m attaching my CV/résumé and my cover letter.

additional_notes: Used in formal contexts (jobs, internships, applications) to mean a document summarizing your education and work experience. In French, people most often say "CV" (pronounced “cé-vé”). You may also see the spelling "curriculum vitae" (without the ligature).
target_language_example: Je vous envoie mon CV (curriculum vitæ) en pièce jointe.
native_language_example: I’m sending you my résumé (CV) as an attachment.

additional_notes: Used for people or things that are positioned directly next to one another, often emphasizing closeness or parallel placement. It can describe standing, sitting, or being arranged (e.g., houses, photos, cars).
target_language_example: Ils marchaient côte à côte dans la rue.
native_language_example: They were walking side by side in the street.

additional_notes: Used to talk about deep sadness, especially after a breakup or unrequited love. Often appears with the verb « avoir » (to have): « avoir le cœur brisé » = “to be heartbroken.” You can also use it as an adjective after « être »: « être le cœur brisé » (less common) or more naturally « être brisé(e) » in context.
target_language_example: Depuis la rupture, j’ai le cœur brisé.
native_language_example: Since the breakup, I’m heartbroken.

meaning: a heart of stone; someone who is cold-hearted.
additional_notes: Used (often with "avoir un cœur de pierre") to describe a person who shows little compassion or emotion. It can be critical or exaggerated for emphasis in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Il a un cœur de pierre : il n’a même pas essayé d’aider.
native_language_example: He has a heart of stone: he didn’t even try to help.

additional_notes:
Common everyday phrase with several meanings depending on context and tone. 
- About food or something you’re tasting: “It’s good.” (also “That tastes good.”)
- To accept or approve something: “OK / That’s fine / All good.”
- To say you have enough or you’re finished (often at a table or when someone offers more): “No thanks, I’m good / I’m done.”
Also used as a quick “OK!” to move on. (If you want to stop someone or say “enough!”, you might hear the stronger "Ça suffit !")
target_language_example: — Tu veux encore du café ? — Non merci, c’est bon.
native_language_example: — Do you want more coffee? — No thanks, I’m good.

additional_notes: Used to exclude everything except what follows. Common after pronouns like "personne" (nobody), "rien" (nothing), "quelqu’un" (someone), or after a noun: "Je ne connais personne d’autre que…" = “I don’t know anyone other than…”. Often appears in negative sentences to mean “no one/nothing else but…”.
target_language_example: Je ne vois personne d’autre que toi.
native_language_example: I don’t see anyone other than you.

additional_notes: Often used to describe something happening instantly or unexpectedly. Very common with verbs like arriver, partir, changer, s’arrêter, etc. Also appears in expressions like « tout d’un coup » (“all of a sudden”).
target_language_example: D’un coup, il s’est mis à pleuvoir.
native_language_example: All of a sudden, it started to rain.

meaning: at any moment; from one moment to the next (very soon, unpredictably).
additional_notes: Used to say something could happen very soon and without much warning. Common with verbs like arriver (to happen/arrive), changer (to change), tomber (to fall), or partir (to leave).
target_language_example: Il peut arriver d'un moment à l'autre.
native_language_example: It could happen at any moment.

meaning: at any moment; from one minute to the next.
additional_notes: Used to say something can change or happen very suddenly, with little or no warning. Common with verbs like changer (to change), arriver (to happen/arrive), or basculer (to shift).
target_language_example: Tout peut changer d'une minute à l'autre.
native_language_example: Anything can change at any moment.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a situation that was just mentioned, often as a response or to introduce a consequence/next step. Common in conversation: “Dans ce cas, …” = “In that case, …”.
target_language_example: Tu n’as pas de voiture ? Dans ce cas, on prend le métro.
native_language_example: You don’t have a car? In that case, we’ll take the subway.

meaning: in the air; (figuratively) in the air / going around (a feeling, idea, rumor).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: something is physically in the air (e.g., a smell, smoke). Very commonly used figuratively to mean a general feeling or trend is noticeable, or that something is being talked about (sometimes implying a rumor). Often appears with verbs like « sentir » (to feel/smell), « flotter » (to float), « être » (to be), or « il y a … dans l’air » (there’s … in the air).
target_language_example: Il y a un parfum de fête dans l’air.
native_language_example: There’s a festive feeling in the air.

meaning: in the hope of; hoping to.
additional_notes: Used to express an intention or action done with the hope of achieving a result. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., « dans l’espoir de + infinitive »). It’s fairly formal/written compared with « en espérant ».
target_language_example: Je t’écris dans l’espoir de te revoir bientôt.
native_language_example: I’m writing to you in the hope of seeing you again soon.

meaning: in order; in the right order; (also) OK / all set.
additional_notes: Literally “in the order.” Used to talk about sequence (“do it in order”), or to say that something is correct/organized (“everything is in order”). Often used in questions like “C’est dans l’ordre ?” meaning “Is that OK / Is everything good?” In that “OK” sense, it’s fairly informal but still common.
target_language_example: Tu peux me donner les documents dans l’ordre, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you give me the documents in order, please?

meaning: in deep trouble; in a mess (literally: “in shit”).
additional_notes: Very informal/vulgar. Used to say someone is in a bad situation (financial, practical, legal, etc.) or has a serious problem. Often used with être: « Je suis dans la merde », « On est dans la merde ».
target_language_example: Si le patron l’apprend, on est dans la merde.
native_language_example: If the boss finds out, we’re in deep trouble.

meaning: in nature; outdoors (and sometimes: out there / missing).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: “in nature” (outside, in the countryside/woods). It can also be used more figuratively to mean something/someone is “out there” or has disappeared, especially after verbs like laisser/mettre/partir: « laisser quelque chose dans la nature » (leave it lying around / abandon it), « être parti(e) dans la nature » (head off somewhere, disappear), « se retrouver dans la nature » (end up stranded/abandoned).
target_language_example: On a passé la journée dans la nature.
native_language_example: We spent the day outdoors (in nature).

meaning: in the pocket; (figuratively) in the bag / secured.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: something is physically in a pocket. Figurative use (often with verbs like "avoir" or "être"): something is guaranteed or already won (e.g., "C’est dans la poche" = “It’s in the bag”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : c’est dans la poche.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s in the bag.

meaning: in need; needy (lacking money or essentials).
additional_notes: Often used to talk about people who don’t have enough money or basic necessities ("people in need"). Common in charity/help contexts: "aider les personnes dans le besoin". You can also use it more generally for someone who needs help: "si tu es dans le besoin".
target_language_example: Cette association aide les familles dans le besoin.
native_language_example: This charity helps families in need.

additional_notes: Means something is in the local area or close by. It can also literally mean “in the corner” depending on context (e.g., in a room), but very often it’s used more generally to mean “near here / around.” Common with verbs like être/avoir/chercher: « Il y a un café dans le coin » (There’s a café nearby).
target_language_example: Il y a une boulangerie dans le coin ?
