native_language_example: Is there a bakery nearby?

meaning: in the loop; up-to-date; in on it.
additional_notes: Commonly used (often informally) to say someone knows what’s going on, understands what’s current/fashionable, or is involved in a plan. Often used with être: « être dans le coup » (to be in the loop / to be with it). Can also be negative: « ne pas être dans le coup » (to be out of the loop).
target_language_example: T’inquiète, je suis dans le coup : je sais ce qui se passe.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m in the loop: I know what’s going on.

additional_notes: Used to say you will explain something thoroughly, or that you don’t want to go into specifics. Common with verbs like « expliquer », « entrer », « parler », « détailler »: « entrer dans le détail » = “to go into detail.”
target_language_example: Je peux t’expliquer dans le détail si tu veux.
native_language_example: I can explain it in detail if you want.

additional_notes: An idiomatic expression meaning you’ve guessed or said the correct thing (like ‘right on the money’). Often used after someone makes an accurate guess or identifies the real reason for something. Usually appears with verbs like « tomber dans le mille » (to be spot on) or « être dans le mille » (to be exactly right).
target_language_example: Tu as deviné son âge ? Oui, je suis tombé dans le mille !
native_language_example: Did you guess her age? Yes, I was spot on!

meaning: in the past; in former times.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a time earlier than now. Often contrasts with the present (maintenant/aujourd’hui). Can refer to your personal past or historical times, and it commonly appears with past tenses like the imparfait or passé composé.
target_language_example: Dans le passé, je voyageais beaucoup pour le travail.
native_language_example: In the past, I used to travel a lot for work.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "être" ("être dans le pétrin" = to be in trouble). Literally "in the dough/trough," but it’s an idiom meaning you’re stuck in a difficult situation.
target_language_example: Si tu rates ce train, tu seras dans le pétrin.
native_language_example: If you miss this train, you'll be in trouble.

additional_notes: Often used as an idiom to say something is already won or certain: « C’est dans le sac ! ». It can also be used literally to mean something is physically inside a bag (e.g., keys, phone).
target_language_example: T’inquiète, avec ce candidat, l’élection est dans le sac !
native_language_example: Don’t worry— with that candidate, the election is in the bag!

meaning: over time; in the past (back then).
additional_notes: Meaning depends on context. (1) With verbs like "changer / évoluer / s’améliorer": "over time" (gradually). (2) When talking about earlier days: "in the past / back then". It’s common in spoken French, and often similar to "au fil du temps" (over time) or "à l’époque" (back then).
target_language_example: Dans le temps, on n’avait pas Internet.
native_language_example: Back then, we didn’t have the Internet.

additional_notes: Used to say something (clothes, music, an activity, a person’s style) is currently popular or fashionable. Often paired with the opposite: « pas du tout dans le vent » (“not trendy at all”). Literally “in the wind,” but it’s an idiom in French.
target_language_example: Ces baskets sont vraiment dans le vent en ce moment.
native_language_example: These sneakers are really trendy right now.

meaning: into the void; into thin air (with no effect or no one listening).
additional_notes: Used to describe words, efforts, or actions that have no result or seem pointless—like speaking when nobody listens ("parler dans le vide"). It can also be more literal: doing something with nothing underneath/around ("sauter dans le vide" = to jump into empty space).
target_language_example: J’ai l’impression de parler dans le vide : personne ne m’écoute.
native_language_example: I feel like I’m talking into the void: nobody is listening to me.

meaning: in the smallest details; in every detail.
additional_notes: Used to say something is explained, described, examined, or planned very thoroughly. Common with verbs like expliquer, décrire, raconter, connaître, and analyser. Often implies “nothing is left out.”
target_language_example: Elle a tout expliqué dans les moindres détails.
native_language_example: She explained everything in the smallest details.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is in the vicinity, without being very specific. Often used with verbs like être/se trouver (to be/to be located) or passer (to come by).
target_language_example: Il y a un bon café dans les parages ?
native_language_example: Is there a good café nearby?

meaning: out of it; dazed; not paying attention.
additional_notes: Informal idiom. Used with verbs like « être » or « tomber » to say someone is spaced out, confused, or mentally “not there” (sometimes after a shock or feeling unwell). Literally means “in the apples,” but that’s not how you translate it.
target_language_example: Après la chute, il était complètement dans les pommes.
native_language_example: After the fall, he was completely out of it.

meaning: properly; by the rules; as it should be done.
additional_notes: Means something is done correctly and in compliance with rules/procedure (officially, fairly, or the right way). Often used with verbs like faire (to do), jouer (to play), and être (to be): « faire les choses dans les règles », « jouer dans les règles ».
target_language_example: On va faire ça dans les règles.
native_language_example: We’re going to do this properly / by the rules.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done by the expected time or before a deadline. Often with verbs like être/arriver/finir/rendre: « Je suis dans les temps », « On arrivera dans les temps », « Tu rendras le dossier dans les temps ». Closely related to « à l’heure » (on time, especially for appointments), but « dans les temps » is very common for meeting a time limit or schedule.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, on finira dans les temps.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we’ll finish on time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something considered in its entirety (not in detail). Often placed after the noun it describes: « le pays dans son ensemble » (“the country as a whole”). « Ensemble » here means “whole,” not “together.”
target_language_example: Le projet, dans son ensemble, est une réussite.
native_language_example: The project, overall, is a success.

meaning: "In your dreams!" (No way; not going to happen.)
additional_notes: Used as a sarcastic or teasing reply to say something is very unlikely or impossible. Common in spoken French. Often appears as "dans ton rêve" (singular) or "dans vos rêves" (more formal/plural). Can also be used after a statement: "Tu vas gagner ? Dans tes rêves !"
target_language_example: — Tu vas sortir avec lui ? — Dans tes rêves !
native_language_example: “You’re going to go out with him?” “In your dreams!”

meaning: in a corner; off to one side.
additional_notes: Used to describe something or someone located in a corner of a room/space or tucked away out of the way. Often paired with verbs like « être » (to be), « se mettre » (to go/put oneself), « ranger » (to put away), or « rester » (to stay).
target_language_example: Le chat est dans un coin de la pièce.
native_language_example: The cat is in a corner of the room.

meaning: in a sense; in one way.
additional_notes: Used to qualify what you’re saying: it suggests something is true from a particular perspective, but not completely or not in every respect. Often followed by a clarification (e.g., "dans un sens, oui, mais...").
target_language_example: Dans un sens, tu as raison, mais ce n’est pas si simple.
native_language_example: In a sense, you’re right, but it’s not that simple.

additional_notes: Used to qualify a statement: you agree or something is true, but only partially (not completely). Often followed by a comma and then a nuance or limit (e.g., "..., mais..."). Common in both spoken and written French and can sound slightly formal depending on context.
target_language_example: Dans une certaine mesure, je suis d'accord, mais il faut aussi penser au coût.
native_language_example: To a certain extent, I agree, but we also need to think about the cost.

additional_notes: Used on forms and in official contexts to ask for or state someone’s birth date. Often appears as « Date de naissance : » and is commonly abbreviated « DDN » in administrative paperwork. You can answer with « Je suis né(e) le… » (I was born on…) or simply give the date.
target_language_example: Quelle est votre date de naissance ?
native_language_example: What is your date of birth?

additional_notes: Used for the last day/time something must be done (pay a bill, submit an application, turn in work). Often appears as "date limite" or "date limite de + noun" (e.g., "date limite d’inscription"). Also common: "avant la date limite" (before the deadline), "après la date limite" (after the deadline), and "prolonger/repousser la date limite" (extend/postpone the deadline).
target_language_example: Quelle est la date limite pour envoyer le dossier ?
native_language_example: What is the deadline for sending the file/application?

meaning: 'from A to Z' (completely; from beginning to end).
additional_notes: Means doing or explaining something thoroughly, covering everything. Often used with verbs like lire (to read), expliquer (to explain), apprendre (to learn), or refaire (to redo): « lire un livre de A à Z ». It’s a common, neutral expression.
target_language_example: Je vais te l’expliquer de A à Z.
native_language_example: I’m going to explain it to you from A to Z (from start to finish).

additional_notes: Used to indicate origin or association. Often follows a noun: "un plat de Grèce" (a dish from Greece), "la mythologie de Grèce" (Greek mythology). With people, you’ll more commonly hear "grec/grecque" (Greek): "Il est grec".
target_language_example: Ce vin vient de Grèce.
native_language_example: This wine comes from Greece.

additional_notes: Common in everyday French. Often used to mean “basically” when explaining something (De base, je n’aime pas le café.), or “by default / originally” (De base, le logiciel est en français.), or “standard/basic” after a noun (un modèle de base = a basic model). More informal than "en principe" or "à l’origine" in some contexts.
target_language_example: De base, je travaille à la maison, mais aujourd’hui je vais au bureau.
native_language_example: Basically, I work from home, but today I’m going to the office.

additional_notes: Means “early” as in early in the morning/early in the day. Commonly used with the verb "se lever" (to get up) or to say you arrived/left early: "Je me suis levé(e) de bonne heure." Note: "bonne heure" also appears in "de bonne heure à bonne heure" (from early to early), but on its own "de bonne heure" just means early.
target_language_example: Je me suis levée de bonne heure pour prendre le train.
native_language_example: I got up early to catch the train.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify something is done/used with the mouth (often in medical or technical contexts). Common in expressions like « de bouche à oreille » (word of mouth) and terms like « thermomètre de bouche » (oral thermometer).
target_language_example: Il faut prendre ce médicament par voie de bouche.
native_language_example: You have to take this medicine orally (by mouth).

meaning: with character; strong-willed; (of a person) with a strong personality.
additional_notes: Used after a noun (often a person) to describe someone who is strong-minded, determined, and not easily influenced: "une femme de caractère". It can be positive (strong, confident) and sometimes suggests someone can be tough or difficult. Commonly used with "avoir du caractère" (to have a strong personality).
target_language_example: C’est une femme de caractère, elle sait ce qu’elle veut.
native_language_example: She’s a strong-willed woman; she knows what she wants.

additional_notes: Used to explain or describe how something is done. Often answers the question "Comment ?" (How?). Common near-synonyms: "comme ça" (more casual) and "de cette manière" (a bit more formal). Can also refer back to a previously mentioned method: "De cette façon, on gagne du temps" (That way, we save time).
target_language_example: Fais-le de cette façon, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Do it this way, please.

additional_notes: Used to describe the manner or method of doing something (how something is done). It often refers back to what was just said or shown. Also common: "de cette façon" (same meaning).
target_language_example: Fais-le de cette manière, c’est plus simple.
native_language_example: Do it this way; it’s simpler.

additional_notes: Placed after a noun to mean something intense or extreme: mesures de choc (drastic measures), thérapie de choc (shock therapy). In everyday speech it can also be used as an emphatic compliment meaning “really great / impressive”: une équipe de choc, une soirée de choc.
target_language_example: Le gouvernement a annoncé des mesures de choc.
native_language_example: The government announced drastic measures.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean “chosen/selected” or “of the best quality,” often implying something is excellent or premium (e.g., "un vin de choix" = a fine wine). Common with things like products, guests, locations, etc. Can sometimes be translated as “choice” in the sense of “choice cuts” or “choice ingredients.”
target_language_example: Nous avons sélectionné des ingrédients de choix pour ce plat.
native_language_example: We selected top-quality ingredients for this dish.

additional_notes: Used to describe something (a remark, a gift, an outfit, an excuse, etc.) that fits the current circumstances. Often appears after a noun: "une remarque de circonstance" (a fitting remark). Can also be used in set phrases like "un discours de circonstance" (a speech for the occasion).
target_language_example: Il a fait une remarque de circonstance pour détendre l’atmosphère.
native_language_example: He made a fitting remark to lighten the mood.

additional_notes: Used to say that people or groups act together toward the same goal, often with the idea of coordination or agreement. Common with verbs like agir/travailler/œuvrer/décider (e.g., « agir de concert » = to act in concert). More formal than « ensemble ».
target_language_example: Les deux pays ont agi de concert pour résoudre la crise.
native_language_example: The two countries acted together to resolve the crisis.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean “trusted” or “reliable” (often implying you know the person/thing well). Common in phrases like « une personne de confiance » (a trustworthy person), « un ami de confiance » (a trusted friend), and « un site de confiance » (a trusted website).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin d’une personne de confiance pour garder les enfants.
native_language_example: I need a trustworthy person to watch the kids.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe its color: "une voiture rouge" = a red car, but you can also say "une voiture de couleur rouge" (more formal/less common). Very common in fixed phrases like "une photocopie de couleur" (a color photocopy) or "une image en couleur". Often followed by a specific color: "de couleur bleue" (blue-colored).
target_language_example: Je voudrais une photocopie de couleur, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a color photocopy, please.

additional_notes: Used to express sincere emotion or intention (gratitude, support, affection). Often appears in set phrases like « de tout cœur » (“with all my heart / wholeheartedly”) or « du fond du cœur » (“from the bottom of my heart”). By itself it sounds a bit literary; it’s more common as part of a longer expression.
target_language_example: Je te remercie de cœur pour ton aide.
native_language_example: I thank you from the bottom of my heart for your help.

additional_notes: Used to specify that something is chosen or counted from a set of two, often with "l’un / l’une" ("one of the two"). You also see it in the fixed expression "de deux en deux" meaning "in steps of two / every other."
target_language_example: Je voudrais l’un de deux billets, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like one of the two tickets, please.

meaning: by law; legally; rightful (as of right).
additional_notes: Used to say something is the legal/rightful result or status (not just in practice). Often found in set phrases like "de plein droit" (automatically, by operation of law) and in contrasts like "de fait" (in practice) vs "de droit" (in law).
target_language_example: De droit, il a la garde de son enfant.
native_language_example: Legally, he has custody of his child.

meaning: "in fact" / "in reality"; "as a matter of fact".
additional_notes: Used to confirm or emphasize what is actually true in reality (often after a statement or to correct an impression). Somewhat formal in tone. Can also mean "in practice" or "effectively" (e.g., something is true or happening even if not officially). Distinct from "en fait" (also "in fact" but very common in conversation).
target_language_example: Il disait qu’il n’était pas intéressé, mais de fait, il l’était.
native_language_example: He said he wasn’t interested, but in fact, he was.

meaning: 'of iron' (made of iron; also figuratively: iron/very firm).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe what something is made of (un anneau de fer = an iron ring). It’s also common in fixed expressions to mean “iron/unyielding,” especially about strength or strictness (une volonté de fer = an iron will; une main de fer = an iron hand).
target_language_example: Elle a une volonté de fer.
native_language_example: She has an iron will.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something fundamental or happening in the background. Common collocations: "un problème de fond" (an underlying/fundamental problem), "un débat de fond" (an in-depth debate), "un travail de fond" (groundwork/long-term work), "un bruit de fond" (background noise).
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas un détail : c’est un problème de fond.
native_language_example: It’s not a detail: it’s an underlying problem.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done using physical force or against someone’s will. Often placed after the verb: "entrer de force" (break in), "ouvrir de force" (force open). Also appears in the fixed expression "un tour de force" meaning an impressive feat/achievement.
target_language_example: La police a dû entrer de force dans l’appartement.
native_language_example: The police had to force their way into the apartment.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something improvised because there’s no proper option available (e.g., un lit de fortune = a makeshift bed, des toilettes de fortune = temporary/makeshift toilets, un abri de fortune = a makeshift shelter). It does not mean “of fortune” in the sense of wealth or luck.
target_language_example: On a dormi sur un lit de fortune.
native_language_example: We slept on a makeshift bed.

additional_notes: Informal intensifier meaning “really/so” or “unbelievably.” Often follows a noun phrase: "un truc de fou" (something crazy), "une ambiance de fou" (an amazing/crazy atmosphere). It can also emphasize an adjective or amount in casual speech: "cher de fou" (insanely expensive).
target_language_example: Il y avait une ambiance de fou hier soir.
native_language_example: There was a crazy/amazing atmosphere last night.

additional_notes: Used to describe something positioned or approached directly in front, or an encounter done directly (without turning aside). Common with verbs like « regarder », « faire face », « attaquer », « affronter ». Can also mean “directly/front-on” in descriptions (e.g., a photo taken from the front: « de front »).
target_language_example: Il m’a regardé de front et m’a dit la vérité.
native_language_example: He looked me straight in the eye and told me the truth.

meaning: on duty; on call (available to work if needed).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say someone/something is providing duty coverage: "médecin de garde" (on-call doctor), "pharmacie de garde" (pharmacy on duty). Also used with "être" or "faire" + garde: "Je suis de garde" / "Je fais la garde" = "I’m on duty". Meaning is about being responsible/available during a specific shift, often nights, weekends, or emergencies.
target_language_example: Ce week-end, c’est le docteur Martin qui est de garde.
native_language_example: This weekend, it’s Dr. Martin who’s on call.

additional_notes: Used to beg or insist, often in a dramatic, serious, or polite way. Common in phrases like « Je vous en prie, de grâce » or « De grâce, écoute-moi ». Less common in everyday casual speech than « s’il te plaît / s’il vous plaît ».
target_language_example: De grâce, ne pars pas tout de suite !
native_language_example: Please, don’t leave right away!

meaning: during the day; on the day shift.
additional_notes: Often used to contrast with « de nuit » (at night / on the night shift). You’ll see it after a noun to specify that something or someone is for daytime (e.g., « infirmier de jour » = day-shift nurse, « gardien de jour » = daytime guard). It can also be used after a verb like « travailler »: « travailler de jour » = to work days.
target_language_example: Je travaille de jour, pas de nuit.
native_language_example: I work during the day, not at night.

meaning: day by day; from one day to the next.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that changes gradually over time, often becoming more noticeable. Common with verbs like « changer », « s’améliorer », « empirer », « augmenter », « diminuer ».
target_language_example: De jour en jour, il se sent mieux.
native_language_example: Day by day, he feels better.

meaning: just barely; by a narrow margin.
additional_notes: Used to say something almost didn’t happen, but it did (often implying it was close, lucky, or last-minute). Common with verbs like réussir (to manage/succeed), arriver (to arrive), éviter (to avoid), or with winning/qualifying by a small margin: « Il a réussi de justesse. », « On l’a évité de justesse. »
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé de justesse à l’heure.
native_language_example: I arrived just barely on time.

meaning: some (partitive), or “of the” before a vowel/silent h.
additional_notes: This is the elided form of "de le" or "de la" → "de l'" used before a singular noun that starts with a vowel sound (including silent h): de l’eau, de l’argent, de l’hôtel. Most often it’s the partitive article meaning “some” with uncountable or general amounts (Je bois de l’eau = I drink some water). It can also mean “of the” in expressions like parler de l’amour (to talk about love).
target_language_example: Je voudrais de l’eau, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like some water, please.

additional_notes: Used to locate something across a street, river, wall, border, etc. Often follows a verb like « être », « se trouver », or « habiter »: « Il est de l’autre côté de la rue. » You may also hear « de l’autre côté » on its own when the object is understood from context.
target_language_example: La boulangerie est de l’autre côté de la rue.
native_language_example: The bakery is on the other side of the street.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun. As a partitive article, it often means “some” with uncountable things (food, drinks, etc.): de la soupe, de la musique. It can also mean “of the” in phrases showing belonging/origin: la couleur de la voiture (“the color of the car”). Before a vowel or silent h, it becomes de l’ (de l’eau). In negative sentences, it often changes to de: Je ne veux pas de soupe.
target_language_example: Je voudrais de la soupe, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like some soup, please.

meaning: “of the Tower” (often part of a surname or place name).
additional_notes: Usually seen as a name element rather than a standalone phrase (e.g., a family name like « Marie de la Tour »). « de la » is a common name particle meaning “of the,” and « Tour » is typically capitalized in names. In regular, non-name sentences you’d more often say « de la tour » (lowercase) to mean “of the tower” literally.
target_language_example: J’ai rendez-vous avec Madame de la Tour.
native_language_example: I have an appointment with Mrs. de la Tour.

additional_notes: Informal slang. Literally "some of the good," but it’s used on its own (without naming the noun) to mean a high-quality product—very often drugs (e.g., weed/coke), depending on context. You’ll also hear it in the longer phrase "de la bonne qualité" (good quality), which is neutral—not slang.
target_language_example: Il dit qu'il a de la bonne.
native_language_example: He says he has the good stuff.

meaning: from (on behalf of), from the part of.
additional_notes: Used to say who a message, gift, invitation, or action comes from (or who is sending it). Common in phrases like “Un message de la part de …” (a message from …) or “De la part de toute l’équipe” (from the whole team).
target_language_example: J’ai un message de la part de Mme Dupont.
native_language_example: I have a message from Ms. Dupont.

additional_notes: Means “in that manner” (similar to « de cette manière » / « comme ça »). Often refers back to what was just said or done. Slightly formal/literary compared with « comme ça ».
target_language_example: Ne parle pas de la sorte.
native_language_example: Don’t talk like that.

meaning: from head to toe; from top to bottom.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone/something completely or entirely, often about appearance (clothes, getting wet/dirty) or a full-body feeling. Literally means “from the head to the feet.” Often used with verbs like être, trempé(e), mouillé(e), habillé(e), couvert(e).
target_language_example: Après l’orage, je suis trempé de la tête aux pieds.
native_language_example: After the storm, I’m soaked from head to toe.

additional_notes: Often means physical distance (“from afar”), but it’s also used for emphasis to mean “by far” (the clear winner/best/worst). In comparisons it commonly appears with a superlative: « de loin le/la/les + superlative » (e.g., « de loin le meilleur » = “by far the best”).
target_language_example: C’est de loin le meilleur restaurant du quartier.
native_language_example: It’s by far the best restaurant in the neighborhood.

meaning: back and forth; up and down (moving around a space).
additional_notes: Used to describe walking or moving repeatedly across an area, often while searching, pacing, or exploring. Often follows verbs like marcher, aller, se promener, parcourir. Roughly “from end to end” / “lengthwise and crosswise,” but the natural English is usually “back and forth.”
target_language_example: Il a marché de long en large dans la chambre pendant des heures.
native_language_example: He paced back and forth in the room for hours.

additional_notes: Used after a noun (often in ads/descriptions) to say something is luxurious or top quality: «hôtel de luxe», «voiture de luxe». It can also be used more loosely to mean “fancy” or “extra nice.”
target_language_example: Ils ont réservé une chambre de luxe.
native_language_example: They booked a deluxe room.

additional_notes: Placed after a noun (often an insult) to add contempt or frustration: « espèce d’idiot de malheur », « ce téléphone de malheur ». It literally means “of misfortune,” but in everyday use it’s closer to “wretched/damn.” Tone is negative and can be rude; it can also sound a bit old-fashioned.
target_language_example: Espèce d’idiot de malheur !
native_language_example: You wretched idiot!

meaning: "so as to" / "in order to" (often with an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to express purpose or intended result. Common pattern: "de manière à + infinitive" ("De manière à éviter les erreurs..."). It can also be followed by "ce que" + subjunctive: "de manière à ce que + (subjunctive)" ("...de manière à ce que tout le monde comprenne"). Slightly formal; in everyday speech you often hear "pour" or "afin de" instead.
target_language_example: Je parle lentement de manière à ce que tout le monde comprenne.
native_language_example: I speak slowly so that everyone understands.

additional_notes: Literally means “of marble” (used to describe an object’s material). Very common in the expression « rester de marbre », meaning to show no reaction (to stay impassive, as if made of marble).
target_language_example: Quand elle a entendu la nouvelle, elle est restée de marbre.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she didn’t react (she stayed stone-faced).

additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used after a noun to insult it or say it’s bad/low-quality: "un film de merde" (“a shitty movie”), "une journée de merde" (“a shitty day”). It can also be used in insults like "espèce de merde" (“you piece of shit”). Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: J’ai passé une journée de merde.
native_language_example: I had a shitty day.

meaning: a rude, dismissive add-on meaning “my ass” / “bullshit” (said to show contempt).
additional_notes: Informal and vulgar-ish slang (a euphemism for “de mes deux couilles”). It’s used after a noun to insult or dismiss it, like “X, my ass” / “your X is bullshit.” Common patterns: “un/une + noun + de mes deux” (e.g., “un héros de mes deux”), or “X de mes deux !” as an exclamation. Avoid in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Ton excuse de mes deux, je n’y crois pas.
native_language_example: Your bullshit excuse—I don’t believe it.

meaning: better and better; improving more and more.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that is gradually improving over time. Often goes with verbs like « aller » (to be doing), « se sentir » (to feel), « s’améliorer » (to improve), or « devenir » (to become). The pattern « de + comparative + en + comparative » expresses progressive change (e.g., « de plus en plus » = more and more).
target_language_example: Ça va de mieux en mieux depuis que je fais de l’exercice.
native_language_example: It’s getting better and better since I started exercising.

additional_notes: Most often used in the expression « être de mise » (= to be appropriate/expected). Common in slightly formal contexts: manners, dress code, behavior, what is considered proper. Often translates as “in order” or “called for” rather than word-for-word.
target_language_example: Dans ce genre de cérémonie, une tenue sobre est de mise.
native_language_example: At this kind of ceremony, subdued/formal clothing is expected.

additional_notes: Used to show a gradual decrease over time or as something continues. Often placed near the verb: Je travaille de moins en moins (I work less and less). Can also modify adjectives/adverbs: Il est de moins en moins patient (He is less and less patient). Common pair with its opposite: de plus en plus (more and more).
target_language_example: Je sors de moins en moins le soir.
native_language_example: I go out less and less in the evening.

additional_notes: Used to show you’re relying on what you remember rather than checking facts (similar to “if I remember correctly”). Often placed at the start of a sentence: “De mémoire, …” or after a statement: “…, de mémoire.”
target_language_example: De mémoire, le musée ouvre à 10 h.
native_language_example: As far as I remember, the museum opens at 10 a.m.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the same as what was just mentioned, or to respond politely with “you too” (often in the form “Moi de même.”). Can also mean “in the same way” before a verb: “Il a fait de même” = “He did the same.”
target_language_example: — Bonne journée ! — Merci, à vous aussi. — De même !
native_language_example: “Have a nice day!” “Thanks, you too.” “Likewise!”

additional_notes: Used to say something is true from the moment someone was born (origin, nationality, a condition, etc.). Often follows a noun/adjective: "Français(e) de naissance" (French by birth), "aveugle de naissance" (blind from birth). Not the same as "naissance" alone (birth) or "depuis la naissance" (since birth).
target_language_example: Elle est Française de naissance, mais elle vit au Canada.
native_language_example: She is French by birth, but she lives in Canada.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the present time in general (modern life), often to contrast with the past. Common at the start or in the middle of a sentence: "De nos jours, ..." or "..., de nos jours."
target_language_example: De nos jours, beaucoup de gens travaillent à distance.
native_language_example: Nowadays, many people work remotely.

additional_notes: Means something is happening again or being repeated. Often interchangeable with "encore" for 'again', but "de nouveau" can sound a bit more formal and can emphasize starting over (doing it anew). Can appear at the end of a sentence or near the verb: "Je recommence de nouveau" / "De nouveau, il pleut."
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous répéter ça de nouveau, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you repeat that again, please?

additional_notes: Often used after a noun to mean “nighttime” (e.g., un train de nuit = a night train; une garde de nuit = a night shift; un vol de nuit = a night flight). Also used with verbs to mean “at night” (e.g., travailler de nuit = to work at night/on the night shift).
target_language_example: Je travaille de nuit cette semaine.
native_language_example: I’m working at night (on the night shift) this week.

meaning: true to one’s word; who keeps promises.
additional_notes: Usually used after a noun, especially in the set phrase « un homme/une femme de parole » meaning someone reliable who does what they say. Related expressions: « tenir parole » (to keep your word) and « donner sa parole » (to give your word/promise). Note that French « parole » means “word/speech,” not English “parole” (release from prison).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : c’est un homme de parole.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’s a man of his word.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is in a place only for a short time (not living there). Often used with être: « Je suis de passage (à Paris) » = “I’m just passing through (in Paris).” Can also describe a temporary visitor: « un ami de passage » = “a friend passing through.”
target_language_example: Je suis de passage à Lyon pour le week-end.
native_language_example: I’m just passing through Lyon for the weekend.

additional_notes: Used as a polite reply after someone says “merci.” Most often heard as “Je t’en prie” or “De rien,” but “de peu” is also correct (a bit old-fashioned/formal in some contexts). Literally “of little,” implying “it was nothing.”
target_language_example: — Merci pour votre aide. — De peu.
native_language_example: — Thank you for your help. — You’re welcome.

meaning: of one’s own free will; willingly.
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something voluntarily, without being forced. Often appears as "de mon/ton/son plein gré" (of my/your/his/her own free will). Common contrast: "contre mon gré" = against my will.
target_language_example: Je l’ai fait de mon plein gré.
native_language_example: I did it of my own free will.

additional_notes: Used to add another point or item. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence to mean “besides/what’s more” (De plus, …), or after a noun to mean “extra/additional” (une heure de plus = an extra hour). Common in writing and formal speech; in everyday conversation you’ll also hear “en plus”.
target_language_example: De plus, je n’ai pas le temps.
native_language_example: Besides, I don’t have time.

meaning: even more; even harder (with increased intensity).
additional_notes: Used to say something resumes or continues more strongly than before (often after a pause), or intensifies. Common with verbs like "reprendre" (start again), "redoubler" (intensify), or with weather and emotions: "pleuvoir de plus belle" (rain even harder), "se disputer de plus belle" (argue even more).
target_language_example: Après une courte accalmie, il s’est remis à pleuvoir de plus belle.
native_language_example: After a short break, it started raining even harder.

additional_notes: Used to show that something is growing over time (frequency, intensity, amount). Often placed before an adjective/adverb (e.g., « de plus en plus important », « de plus en plus vite ») or with a verb (e.g., « Il pleut de plus en plus » = it’s raining more and more).
target_language_example: Il fait de plus en plus froid en soirée.
native_language_example: It’s getting colder and colder in the evening.

additional_notes: Goes after a noun to mean a small, easy-to-carry version: un dictionnaire de poche (a pocket dictionary), une lampe de poche (a flashlight/torch). Also in the fixed expression "un livre de poche" = a paperback (pocket edition).
target_language_example: J’ai acheté un dictionnaire de poche pour le voyage.
native_language_example: I bought a pocket dictionary for the trip.

additional_notes: Used after a noun (often with an indefinite article) to mean “weighty” in the sense of “significant.” Common collocations: une raison de poids (a compelling reason), un argument de poids (a strong argument), des preuves de poids (solid evidence). It’s more formal than everyday “important.”
target_language_example: Il a une raison de poids pour refuser.
native_language_example: He has a compelling reason to refuse.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something very advanced or at the forefront of its field. Common in phrases like « technologie de pointe » (cutting-edge technology), « équipement de pointe » (state-of-the-art equipment), and « recherche de pointe » (advanced research).
target_language_example: Cet hôpital utilise des équipements de pointe.
native_language_example: This hospital uses state-of-the-art equipment.

additional_notes: Used to describe something as being in first class (especially travel: train/plane tickets, compartments) or as being of the highest quality (often shorthand for « de première qualité »). You’ll most often see it after a noun: « un billet de première », « une cabine de première ». More formal/explicit: « de première classe ».
target_language_example: J’ai pris un billet de première pour le train.
native_language_example: I got a first-class ticket for the train.

additional_notes: Used after a verb to mean doing something closely/at close range (e.g., observe, follow, watch). Common in the fixed expression « de près ou de loin » (“from near or far” = “in any way”). Often contrasts with « de loin » (“from far away”).
target_language_example: Je veux voir le tableau de près.
native_language_example: I want to see the painting up close.

meaning: "By what right?" / "Who gave you the right?"
additional_notes: Used to challenge or question someone’s authority or permission to do something; often sounds indignant or accusatory (stronger than a neutral question like "Pourquoi ?"). Often followed by a verb: "De quel droit tu me parles comme ça ?"
target_language_example: De quel droit tu entres ici sans frapper ?
native_language_example: Who gave you the right to come in here without knocking?

additional_notes: A common prepositional pronoun that replaces “de + a thing/idea.” Use it after verbs that take “de,” especially in questions: “De quoi parles-tu ?” = “What are you talking about?” With “avoir de quoi + infinitive,” it means having something or enough (money/food/etc.) to do something: “J’ai de quoi manger” = “I have something/enough to eat.” You’ll also hear it in “Il n’y a pas de quoi,” meaning “You’re welcome / Don’t mention it.”
target_language_example: Tu parles de quoi ?
native_language_example: What are you talking about?

additional_notes: Most commonly used for animals to say they are a specific, recognized breed: «un chien de race», «un chat de race». It often implies the animal has pedigree papers. Be careful using it about people—talking about humans in terms of «race» can sound outdated or offensive in French; for people, you’d usually talk about origin/nationality instead.
target_language_example: Ils ont adopté un chien de race.
native_language_example: They adopted a purebred dog.

meaning: (of) rank; in rank; (restaurant) for the dining room/floor.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify rank/status (often in formal contexts): "officier de rang", "un poste de rang supérieur". In Québec restaurant French, "serveur/serveuse de rang" means a waiter responsible for a specific section of tables (a station) in the dining room.
target_language_example: Au restaurant, c’est la serveuse de rang qui s’occupe de notre table.
native_language_example: At the restaurant, it’s the station waiter who takes care of our table.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has come back (often after being away or after an action). Common with verbs like être/revenir: « Je suis de retour » (I’m back) or « Il sera de retour demain » (He’ll be back tomorrow).
target_language_example: Je suis de retour à la maison.
native_language_example: I’m back home.

additional_notes: Used as a reply when someone says « merci ». Literally “of nothing,” meaning “don’t mention it.” Common in everyday, polite French; slightly more casual alternatives include « pas de quoi » and « t’inquiète » (more informal).
target_language_example: — Merci beaucoup ! — De rien.
native_language_example: — Thank you very much! — You’re welcome.

meaning: required; expected (the proper thing to do).
additional_notes: Used to say something is customary or socially expected in a situation (e.g., clothes, manners, rules). Often follows the noun it describes: "tenue de rigueur" (required dress), "politesse de rigueur" (expected politeness). In English, "de rigueur" is also used, so it may look familiar.
target_language_example: Dans ce restaurant, une tenue correcte est de rigueur.
native_language_example: In this restaurant, proper attire is required/expected.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is the normal practice or the expected rule in a situation. Often found in the pattern « Il est de règle de + infinitive » (“It is customary/standard to…”), or « C’est de règle » (“That’s the rule / That’s standard practice”).
target_language_example: Il est de règle d’arriver à l’heure.
native_language_example: It’s customary to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something as wonderful, ideal, or magical: "des vacances de rêve" (dream vacation), "un appartement de rêve" (dream apartment). It can also mean literally "dreamlike" depending on context (a "paysage de rêve" can be breathtaking or surreal).
target_language_example: On a passé des vacances de rêve en Bretagne.
native_language_example: We had a dream vacation in Brittany.

additional_notes: Placed after a noun to mean “emergency” or “for use in case of need.” Common in set phrases like « sortie de secours » (emergency exit), « numéro de secours » (emergency number), « roue de secours » (spare tire), and « solution de secours » (backup plan).
target_language_example: Il y a une sortie de secours au fond du couloir.
native_language_example: There is an emergency exit at the end of the hallway.

meaning: on duty; for service (as a replacement/backup).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe a person or thing assigned for service or duty (often temporary): un médecin de service (the doctor on duty), un agent de service (staff member), une voiture de service (company/service vehicle). It can also mean “as a stand-in/backup” in expressions like un remplaçant de service (the usual stand-in).
target_language_example: Le médecin de service arrive dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: The doctor on duty will be here in five minutes.

meaning: Not a standard French expression; usually you want “de sorte que” (so that) or “de sorte à” (so as to).
additional_notes:
“De sorte de” is generally considered incorrect in modern French. Use:
- “de sorte que” + indicative to introduce a result/consequence: “..., de sorte que ...” = “..., so that ... / with the result that ...”.
- “de sorte à” + infinitive to express purpose: “..., de sorte à + verb” = “..., so as to ...”.
Tip: “que” is followed by a full clause (subject + verb); “à” is followed by an infinitive.
target_language_example: Il a parlé très clairement, de sorte que tout le monde a compris.
native_language_example: He spoke very clearly, so everyone understood.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a consequence or result. Often followed by the indicative: "Il pleuvait, de sorte qu’on est restés à la maison." It can also appear after an intensifier for a strong result: "si… de sorte que" / "tellement… de sorte que". In many cases, it’s close in meaning to "donc" or "alors".
target_language_example: Il a raté le bus, de sorte qu’il est arrivé en retard.
native_language_example: He missed the bus, so he arrived late.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something that comes from a ready-made supply rather than being custom-made. Common in set phrases like « photo de stock » (stock photo) and in product contexts to mean the standard version/configuration. Don’t confuse with « en stock » = “in stock / available.”
target_language_example: Ce site utilise des photos de stock.
native_language_example: This site uses stock photos.

additional_notes: Used mostly in informal spoken French to mean “straight away.” It’s often interchangeable with « tout de suite », but « de suite » can also mean “in a row / consecutively” depending on context (e.g., « deux jours de suite » = “two days in a row”). In formal writing, « tout de suite » is usually preferred for “immediately.”
target_language_example: J’arrive de suite.
native_language_example: I’ll be there right away.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something meant to be used/served at the table, often in everyday contexts: sel de table (table salt), vin de table (table wine), eau de table (table water). It’s a common descriptive phrase, but English usually doesn’t translate it word-for-word as “of table.”
target_language_example: Pour la recette, prends du sel de table.
native_language_example: For the recipe, use table salt.

additional_notes: Used to describe dimensions or magnitude, often after a noun: "une ville de taille moyenne" (a medium-sized city). Frequently appears with adjectives like "petite", "moyenne", "grande" or with measurements: "de taille 42" (size 42). In clothing, you’ll also see "taille" alone meaning "size" ("Quelle taille ?").
target_language_example: C’est une entreprise de taille moyenne.
native_language_example: It’s a medium-sized company.

additional_notes: Common way to say something happens sometimes but not regularly. It can go at the beginning or end of a sentence: « De temps en temps, … » / « …, de temps en temps. » Similar in meaning to « parfois » (sometimes) and « occasionnellement » (more formal: occasionally).
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma de temps en temps.
native_language_example: I go to the movies from time to time.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens sometimes but not regularly. It’s fairly neutral and common in speech and writing. Similar in meaning to « parfois » (sometimes) and « occasionnellement » (occasionally).
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma de temps à autre.
native_language_example: I go to the movies from time to time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that is habitual or unchanged ("as always"), or something that has existed for a very long time ("long-standing"), or sometimes something permanent ("forever"). Often appears in phrases like "comme de toujours" (as always) and "depuis toujours" (always/for as long as I can remember).
target_language_example: Il est gentil, comme de toujours.
native_language_example: He’s kind, as always.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something that is part of daily life (not special, not fancy). Often translates as “everyday” or “day-to-day.” Example: “la vie de tous les jours” = “everyday life.”
target_language_example: Je préfère des vêtements de tous les jours, pas des vêtements de fête.
native_language_example: I prefer everyday clothes, not party clothes.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is the best/worst/biggest, etc. in history or in someone’s experience (often after a superlative: "le meilleur de tous les temps"). It can refer to all of history or more loosely to “ever.”
target_language_example: C’est le meilleur film de tous les temps.
native_language_example: It’s the best movie of all time.

additional_notes: Used to express sincere, warm feelings—often to congratulate, thank, encourage, apologize, or wish someone well. Common patterns: « Je te remercie de tout cœur » (I thank you with all my heart), « Je suis de tout cœur avec toi » (I’m with you wholeheartedly / my heart is with you), « Je te souhaite de tout cœur… » (I sincerely wish you…).
target_language_example: Je te remercie de tout cœur pour ton aide.
native_language_example: I thank you with all my heart for your help.

additional_notes: Used to say something has been true for a very long time, traditionally, or as far back as people can remember. Common in general statements and often followed by a present tense verb: « De tout temps, on a… ». More emphatic and formal than just « toujours ».
target_language_example: De tout temps, les gens ont cherché à comprendre le monde.
native_language_example: Since forever, people have tried to understand the world.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true or will happen regardless of other facts, objections, or what was just said. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence: "De toute façon, ..." or "..., de toute façon."
target_language_example: De toute façon, je dois partir à 18 h.
native_language_example: Anyway, I have to leave at 6 p.m.

additional_notes: Used to say that what comes next is true regardless of the situation, or to return to your main point (“anyway…”). Common variant: « de toute façon » (same meaning). Often placed at the start or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: De toute manière, on n’a pas assez de temps.
native_language_example: Anyway, we don’t have enough time.

additional_notes: Used to express that something comes or happens from many directions/places at once. Often appears with verbs like venir/arriver (to come/arrive), entendre (to hear), regarder (to look), or with ideas like attacks, criticism, or noise coming in from all directions. Also common in the plural form “de toutes parts,” which has the same meaning.
target_language_example: Les critiques venaient de toute part.
native_language_example: The criticism was coming from all sides.

additional_notes: Used to say something is evident based on facts or what you can see. Common in written and formal spoken French, similar to “clearly” or “evidently.” It often comes at the beginning of a sentence but can also be inserted mid-sentence.
target_language_example: De toute évidence, il a oublié notre rendez-vous.
native_language_example: Obviously, he forgot our appointment.

meaning: from all sides; from every direction.
additional_notes: Used to describe something coming, happening, or being attacked/criticized from every direction. Often used with verbs like venir (to come), arriver (to arrive), attaquer (to attack), or être entouré (to be surrounded).
target_language_example: Les critiques venaient de toutes parts.
native_language_example: The criticism was coming from all sides.

meaning: with all one’s strength; as hard as possible.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize maximum physical effort (often with verbs like pousser, tirer, courir, crier). It agrees with the subject via the possessive: de toutes mes/tes/ses/nos/vos/leurs forces.
target_language_example: Il a poussé la porte de toutes ses forces, mais elle ne s’est pas ouverte.
native_language_example: He pushed the door with all his strength, but it didn’t open.

meaning: crooked; not straight; the wrong way.
additional_notes: Used to describe something positioned incorrectly (tilted, uneven, askew) or done the wrong way. Common with verbs like être, mettre, regarder: « C’est de travers », « Tu l’as mis de travers ». It can also mean “in a bad way” when talking about seeing/understanding something: « Tu vois ça de travers » (you’re taking it the wrong way).
target_language_example: Tu as mis le tableau de travers.
native_language_example: You hung the painting crooked.

additional_notes: Used after a noun or pronoun to say something/someone is in excess or not needed. Common with expressions like « en trop » (extra/left over) and « être de trop » (to be one too many / to feel unwelcome). It often carries a negative or awkward tone when referring to people.
target_language_example: Il y a une chaise de trop dans la salle.
native_language_example: There is one chair too many in the room.

meaning: from memory; off the top of one’s head.
additional_notes: Used to say you know or can say/do something without checking notes, a document, or looking it up. Common with verbs like savoir, connaître, réciter, calculer, dire: « Je ne sais pas de tête » (I don’t know offhand).
target_language_example: Je ne connais pas son numéro de téléphone de tête.
native_language_example: I don’t know their phone number by heart / off the top of my head.

additional_notes: In French, **de + un** almost always contracts to **d’un** before a masculine singular noun (or adjective) beginning with a vowel sound (including mute **h**). You’ll see it in meanings like “of a/from a,” and also after many expressions that require **de** (e.g., *avoir besoin de* → *J’ai besoin d’un…* = “I need a…”).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin d’un stylo.
native_language_example: I need a pen.

additional_notes: Used after a noun (or with the pronoun "rien") to describe something that has value—often monetary ("valuable") but also figurative ("worthwhile"). Common pattern: "un objet de valeur" (a valuable item). You can also say "ce n’est rien de valeur" to mean "it’s nothing valuable."
target_language_example: Ne laisse pas d’objets de valeur dans la voiture.
native_language_example: Don’t leave valuable items in the car.

additional_notes: Literally "de" (of/from/about) + "ça" (that). Very common after verbs that take "de" (e.g., parler de = to talk about, avoir besoin de = to need, se souvenir de = to remember). Often refers to something previously mentioned: "J’ai besoin de ça" = "I need that"; "Je parle de ça" = "I’m talking about that." In everyday speech, "de ça" is frequently shortened to "d’ça".
target_language_example: Je me souviens de ça.
native_language_example: I remember that.

additional_notes: Used for the act of asking someone to marry you. You’ll often see it with the verb "faire" (to make): "faire une demande en mariage" = to propose (marriage). The article can vary depending on context: "une demande en mariage" (a proposal), "la demande en mariage" (the proposal).
target_language_example: Il a fait sa demande en mariage hier soir.
native_language_example: He proposed (asked her to marry him) last night.

additional_notes:
Very common verb for asking/requesting something.
- Ask for something: « demander + noun » → « Je demande un renseignement. »
- Ask someone (to do something): « demander à quelqu’un de + infinitive » → « Je demande à Paul de venir. »
- Ask a question: « demander + question / si… » → « Je demande si c’est possible. »
Note: looks like English “to demand,” but French « demander » is usually softer (ask/request). For a strong “demand,” use « exiger ».
target_language_example: Je voudrais demander un café, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like to order (ask for) a coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used when you seek someone’s guidance or opinion. Often followed by "à" + a person: "demander conseil à quelqu’un" (to ask someone for advice). You can also specify the topic with "sur" or "pour": "demander conseil sur/pour…".
target_language_example: Je vais demander conseil à mon médecin.
native_language_example: I’m going to ask my doctor for advice.

meaning: to propose (ask someone to marry you).
additional_notes: Used when someone asks their partner to marry them. The person you propose to is introduced with "à": "demander quelqu’un en mariage" or "demander à quelqu’un de vous épouser". The noun is "une demande en mariage" (a marriage proposal).
target_language_example: Il l’a demandée en mariage hier soir.
native_language_example: He proposed to her last night.

meaning: to apologize; to ask for forgiveness.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re sorry for something you did. Very common and polite; you can also use the shorter phrase "Pardon" to apologize briefly (e.g., when you bump into someone). Often followed by "de" + infinitive ("demander pardon de..." = to apologize for doing something).
target_language_example: Je te demande pardon d’avoir oublié ton anniversaire.
native_language_example: I’m sorry for forgetting your birthday.

additional_notes: Used mainly for quantities, especially when ordering or counting items. Often appears with “une” (une demi-douzaine de…) and can mean exactly six or roughly six depending on context.
target_language_example: Je voudrais une demi-douzaine d’œufs, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like half a dozen eggs, please.

additional_notes: Used for a brother you share only one parent with (same mother or same father). Feminine form: « demi-sœur » (half-sister). Often used with possessives: « mon demi-frère », « son demi-frère ».
target_language_example: C’est mon demi-frère : on a le même père.
native_language_example: He’s my half-brother: we have the same father.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a 30-minute duration or a time interval. Often appears with durations: « une demi-heure » (half an hour), « deux demi-heures » (two half-hours = one hour), « une demi-heure de plus » (half an hour more). Note the hyphen in the usual spelling.
target_language_example: J’arrive dans une demi-heure.
native_language_example: I’ll be there in half an hour.

meaning: half-sister (a sister you share one parent with).
additional_notes: Used for family relationships when you have the same mother or the same father, but not both. Feminine noun; masculine is "demi-frère". Often used with possessives: "ma/ta/sa demi-sœur".
target_language_example: J’ai une demi-sœur du côté de mon père.
native_language_example: I have a half-sister on my father's side.

meaning: a U-turn; turning back the way you came.
additional_notes: Often used with the verb faire: faire demi-tour = “to make a U-turn / turn around.” Common in driving directions and everyday speech to mean reversing direction or going back.
target_language_example: On s’est trompés, il faut faire demi-tour.
native_language_example: We made a mistake; we need to turn around (make a U-turn).

additional_notes: Used for a woman who takes part in a wedding ceremony as the bride’s attendant. Today it can refer to any bridesmaid (not necessarily unmarried), though literally it suggests a young woman (“demoiselle”). Masculine equivalent: « garçon d’honneur » (less common) or « témoin » for a wedding witness/best man role.
target_language_example: Ma sœur sera ma demoiselle d'honneur au mariage.
native_language_example: My sister will be my bridesmaid at the wedding.

additional_notes: A common everyday term for the third molar, often mentioned at the dentist or when talking about tooth pain or extraction. Usually used in the singular for one tooth (une dent de sagesse) and in the plural for multiple (des dents de sagesse).
target_language_example: Je dois me faire enlever une dent de sagesse.
native_language_example: I have to get a wisdom tooth removed.

meaning: for a long time; since it’s been so long.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is long overdue or that a long time has passed. Often appears with verbs like « attendre » (to wait) or in exclamations: « Depuis le temps que j’attends ! » = “I’ve been waiting forever!” It can also imply “at long last” when something finally happens.
target_language_example: Depuis le temps que je t’attends, j’allais partir !
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for you for so long, I was about to leave!

meaning: for a long time; for a long while.
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to say something started in the past and is still true now (duration up to the present): « Je l’attends depuis longtemps. » It can also mean “long ago” (something that started far back in the past), often with past tenses depending on context.
target_language_example: Je te connais depuis longtemps.
native_language_example: I’ve known you for a long time.

additional_notes: Used to say something started not long ago and is still true now. Often follows the verb: « Je travaille ici depuis peu. » Similar to « depuis peu de temps ». Not used for a completed past action (for that you’d use « il y a peu » = “a short time ago”).
target_language_example: J’habite à Lyon depuis peu.
native_language_example: I’ve been living in Lyon for a short time (since recently).

meaning: since when? / how long (has it been) since…?
additional_notes: Used to ask from what point in time something has been true, often with the present tense in French (present meaning “has been”). Can also express surprise or disbelief (“Since when…?!”). Common pattern: « Depuis quand + verbe au présent ? »
target_language_example: Depuis quand tu habites à Paris ?
native_language_example: How long have you lived in Paris?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause (subject + verb) to say something has been true starting at a specific moment/event in the past and continues to the present. Typically followed by the present tense in French: « Depuis que je suis ici, ... » = “Since I’ve been here, ...”.
target_language_example: Depuis que j'habite à Paris, je prends le métro tous les jours.
native_language_example: Since I’ve lived in Paris, I take the метро every day.

meaning: since always; for as long as I/you/etc. can remember.
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true for a very long time, from the earliest point you can refer to (often “as long as I can remember”). It’s common with the present tense to describe a state that started in the past and continues now: « Je vis ici depuis toujours. » It can also be used more generally to mean “always/forever,” especially in set phrases like « depuis toujours et pour toujours » (“forever and ever”).
target_language_example: Je te connais depuis toujours.
native_language_example: I’ve known you forever / as long as I can remember.

meaning: the last word; the final say.
additional_notes: Used literally for the final word in a text or conversation, and very commonly in the expression « avoir le dernier mot » (“to have the last word,” i.e., to get the final say in an argument or decision). You can also say « le dernier mot revient à… » (“the final decision rests with…”).
target_language_example: Dans cette discussion, c’est elle qui a eu le dernier mot.
native_language_example: In this discussion, she had the last word.

meaning: the final stretch (the last stage before finishing).
additional_notes: Used literally for a race (the last straight section before the finish line), and very often figuratively for the final phase of a project, studies, a deadline, etc. Usually appears with verbs like « être dans la dernière ligne droite » (to be in the final stretch) or « entrer dans la dernière ligne droite » (to enter the final stretch).
target_language_example: On est dans la dernière ligne droite avant la date limite.
native_language_example: We’re in the final stretch before the deadline.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something done or decided just before a deadline or right before something happens. Common in phrases like "à la dernière minute" (at the last minute) and "réserver à la dernière minute" (to book at the last minute).
target_language_example: Il a annulé son rendez-vous à la dernière minute.
native_language_example: He canceled his appointment at the last minute.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is in jail/prison or imprisoned. Literally “behind the bars,” where *barreaux* refers to the metal bars of a cell. Often used after verbs like *être* or *finir* (e.g., *être derrière les barreaux*, *finir derrière les barreaux*).
target_language_example: S’il est reconnu coupable, il finira derrière les barreaux.
native_language_example: If he is found guilty, he will end up behind bars.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to emphasize that it’s impressive, intense, or on a large scale (often implying “a real ___”, “a ___ like no other”). Common with things like: une fête des familles (a huge party), un match des familles (an epic match), un embouteillage des familles (a massive traffic jam). It’s not about actual families here; it’s an idiomatic expression.
target_language_example: On a fait une fête des familles pour ses 30 ans.
native_language_example: We threw a huge party for his 30th birthday.

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech as a shorter alternative to « parfois ». It can go at the beginning or end of a sentence (or after the verb) to mean something happens occasionally.
target_language_example: Des fois, je vais au café après le travail.
native_language_example: Sometimes I go to the café after work.

additional_notes: Used to express a precaution or to prepare for a possible situation. Often followed by a clause in the subjunctive (des fois que + subject + verb): « Des fois qu’il pleuve… » = “In case it rains…”. In everyday speech you’ll also hear the variant « au cas où » with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Prends un parapluie, des fois qu’il pleuve.
native_language_example: Take an umbrella, just in case it rains.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the good times and bad times in a situation, relationship, job, etc. Often follows a phrase like « Il y a / On a connu / Ça a été » to describe a period with both successes and difficulties. The adjectives « haut » (high) and « bas » (low) are used here as nouns.
target_language_example: Dans notre relation, il y a eu des hauts et des bas, mais on est toujours ensemble.
native_language_example: In our relationship, there have been ups and downs, but we're still together.

meaning: loads of; tons of; a lot (of).
additional_notes: Informal/colloquial intensifier meaning “in large quantity.” Often placed after a noun: « des gens des masses » (loads of people), « des devoirs des masses » (tons of homework). You can also use it more generally to mean “a lot”: « Il a plu des masses » (It rained a lot).
target_language_example: J’ai des devoirs des masses ce soir.
native_language_example: I’ve got tons of homework tonight.

additional_notes: Used for the number 200. Note the spelling: *cent* takes an **-s** (*cents*) when it is multiplied and **not** followed by another number (*deux cents*), but it stays singular when followed by another number (*deux cent un* = 201). Also, liaison is common: *deux cents* sounds like "deu san".
target_language_example: J’ai dépensé deux cents euros.
native_language_example: I spent two hundred euros.

additional_notes: Literally “two or three.” Often used to mean “a few / a couple of” in an approximate, casual way (not necessarily exactly 2 or 3). Can be followed by a noun: “deux ou trois minutes / questions”.
target_language_example: Attends deux ou trois minutes, j’arrive.
native_language_example: Wait a couple of minutes, I’m coming.

meaning: 'two pairs' (two sets of two matching items).
additional_notes: Used when counting or ordering items that come in pairs (e.g., shoes, socks, earrings). Often followed by "de" + item: "deux paires de chaussettes" (two pairs of socks). Note: French uses "paire" (pair) where English sometimes uses a plural-only noun like "pants"—for example, "une paire de pantalons" (a pair of pants).
target_language_example: Je voudrais deux paires de chaussettes, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like two pairs of socks, please.

additional_notes: Used for the punctuation mark “:” in writing. You’ll hear it when someone dictates an email address, a URL, times, or lists (e.g., « http deux points barre barre… »). Also used in school contexts when talking about punctuation.
target_language_example: Dans l’adresse, écris « http deux points barre barre ».
native_language_example: In the address, write “http colon slash slash.”

additional_notes: Used for an opportunity to try again after a failure or problem. Common in everyday speech (school, work, relationships). Also used in the phrase « donner une deuxième chance à [quelqu’un] » (“to give [someone] a second chance”).
target_language_example: Je veux te donner une deuxième chance.
native_language_example: I want to give you a second chance.

additional_notes: Used to introduce surprising or exciting news, often at the start of a sentence. Also common as a question: « Devine quoi ? » In writing you’ll see both « Devine quoi ? » and « Devine quoi ! ».
target_language_example: Devine quoi ? J’ai trouvé un nouvel appartement !
native_language_example: Guess what? I found a new apartment!

meaning: to owe someone a big debt of gratitude; to be very grateful to someone.
additional_notes: Usually used with an indirect object: « Je te/lui/vous dois une fière chandelle » (“I really owe you/him/her a lot”). It means someone helped you a lot (often in an important situation), so you feel you owe them a big thank-you or favor in return. Somewhat old-fashioned but still understood.
target_language_example: Je te dois une fière chandelle : sans toi, je n’aurais jamais réussi.
native_language_example: I really owe you a lot: without you, I would never have succeeded.

additional_notes: Means literally “to say farewell.” It’s often used in emotional contexts (leaving for a long time, a breakup, or a death), so it can sound more final than just "dire au revoir." You can use it with a direct object: "dire adieu à + [person/thing]."
target_language_example: Il a dû dire adieu à sa famille avant de partir.
native_language_example: He had to say goodbye to his family before leaving.

additional_notes: Used when leaving or ending a conversation. You can say it to one person or a group. Often shortened to just « Au revoir ! » (more common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Je dois y aller, je vais dire au revoir à tout le monde.
native_language_example: I have to go; I’m going to say goodbye to everyone.

meaning: to speak badly about; to badmouth.
additional_notes: Usually followed by "de" + a person/thing: "dire du mal de quelqu’un/de quelque chose". It means criticizing someone (often behind their back), saying negative things about them.
target_language_example: Il ne faut pas dire du mal des autres.
native_language_example: You shouldn’t speak badly about other people.

meaning: to say that; (exclamation) to think that…!
additional_notes: Most often you’ll see it with a conjugated form of *dire*: *je dis que…, il dit que…* (“I/he says that…”). It can also appear after another verb in the infinitive: *Je voudrais te dire que…* (“I’d like to tell you that…”). As an exclamation at the start of a sentence—*Dire que…!*—it expresses surprise, disbelief, or regret and is closer to “To think that…!” than the literal “To say that…”.
target_language_example: Je voulais te dire que je pars demain.
native_language_example: I wanted to tell you that I’m leaving tomorrow.

meaning: to say something; to tell something.
additional_notes: Uses the verb dire (irregular) with a direct object (quelque chose = “something”). Often followed by à + person to show who you’re telling it to: dire quelque chose à quelqu’un (“to tell someone something”). For “to say (a word) in French,” use dire ... en français.
target_language_example: Je dois te dire quelque chose.
native_language_example: I have to tell you something.

additional_notes: Used mostly in spoken French as a short follow-up question when you didn’t hear, didn’t understand, or want the other person to clarify. Often appears as « Tu veux dire quoi ? » (“What do you mean?”) or just « Dire quoi ? » meaning “Say what?” It can sound a bit blunt depending on tone.
target_language_example: — On devrait annuler. — Dire quoi ? Pourquoi ?
native_language_example: — We should cancel. — Say what? Why?

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase: dire = “to say/tell” + toujours = “always.” In real sentences, toujours usually comes right after the conjugated verb (e.g., il dit toujours…, je dis toujours…). You can use it for habits or things someone says repeatedly.
target_language_example: Il dit toujours la vérité.
native_language_example: He always tells the truth.

meaning: "hey," "wow," or "say," (used to react or get someone’s attention).
additional_notes: Literally “say then,” but it’s mainly an interjection in conversation. It can express surprise, emphasis, mild annoyance, or be used to call someone’s attention (a bit like “hey!”). Often followed by a question or comment: “Dis donc, tu viens ?” The tone depends on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Dis donc, tu as changé de coiffure !
native_language_example: Hey, you changed your hairstyle!

additional_notes: Common computing term for the storage device in a computer. Often used with verbs like "sauvegarder" (to back up/save), "installer" (to install), or "être plein" (to be full): "Mon disque dur est plein." Also seen as "disque dur externe" (external hard drive).
target_language_example: J’ai sauvegardé mes photos sur mon disque dur externe.
native_language_example: I backed up my photos onto my external hard drive.

additional_notes: Used in France for a bank machine where you withdraw cash with a bank card. You may also see or hear the abbreviation “DAB” (distributeur automatique de billets).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, où est le distributeur de billets le plus proche ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the nearest ATM?

meaning: “Say,” / “Tell me,” (to get someone’s attention or show surprise).
additional_notes: Polite form (vous) of “dire” used as a set phrase. Often expresses mild surprise, emphasis, or a gentle reproach, similar to “Well!” or “Hey!” in English depending on tone. Can be followed by a question or a comment: “Dites donc, vous avez vu l’heure ?”
target_language_example: Dites donc, vous avez changé de coupe de cheveux !
native_language_example: Hey, you changed your haircut!

additional_notes: The number 18. Used for counting, age, dates, and quantities. Spelled with a hyphen: dix-huit. The final “t” in dix is usually silent here (sounds like “dee-zweet”).
target_language_example: J’ai dix-huit ans.
native_language_example: I’m eighteen years old.

additional_notes: The French number 19, formed from dix (10) + neuf (9). Used for counting, age, dates, prices, etc. Hyphenated in standard spelling.
target_language_example: J’ai dix-neuf ans.
native_language_example: I’m nineteen years old.

additional_notes: Used to say the number 17. In French, numbers 17–19 are formed as “ten-seven/ten-eight/ten-nine”: dix-sept (17), dix-huit (18), dix-neuf (19). Often used for age, dates, prices, quantities, etc.
target_language_example: J’ai dix-sept ans.
native_language_example: I’m seventeen years old.

meaning: to entitle (someone) to; to give the right to.
additional_notes: Used to say that something (a ticket, a subscription, a situation) grants a right or benefit. Common pattern: « donner droit à + noun/infinitive » (e.g., donner droit à une réduction / à entrer / à voter). Often used in formal or administrative contexts.
target_language_example: Cette carte donne droit à une réduction de 10 %.
native_language_example: This card entitles you to a 10% discount.

meaning: to make (someone) want to; to make (someone) feel like.
additional_notes: Usually used with "donner envie de" + infinitive: "Ça me donne envie de partir" (It makes me want to leave). You can also use it with a noun: "Ça donne envie" (It makes you want some / It’s tempting). Note: "envie" often means "desire/craving," not "envy" (that’s usually "jalousie").
target_language_example: Cette photo me donne envie de voyager.
native_language_example: This photo makes me want to travel.

additional_notes: Used to say that a person, event, first remark, or general attitude establishes the mood/style for what follows (a meeting, conversation, speech, relationship, etc.). Often said about the beginning of something: « Dès le début, il a donné le ton. »
target_language_example: Son discours a donné le ton de la réunion.
native_language_example: His speech set the tone for the meeting.

additional_notes: Used for childbirth (people/animals), often followed by "à" + the baby/young: "donner naissance à un garçon". Can also be used figuratively for creating something new: "donner naissance à une idée/un mouvement" (to give rise to). More formal than "accoucher" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Elle a donné naissance à une petite fille en mai.
native_language_example: She gave birth to a little girl in May.

meaning: to say someone is right; to agree with someone.
additional_notes: Used when you acknowledge that another person’s opinion or argument is correct. Often followed by « à + person »: « donner raison à quelqu’un » (to agree with someone / to say someone is right). Commonly appears as « Tu as raison » (“You’re right”) or « Je te donne raison » (“I agree with you / You’re right”).
target_language_example: Je te donne raison : ce n’est pas une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I agree with you: it’s not a good idea.

meaning: to face / to overlook (a place); to open onto.
additional_notes: Used mainly for rooms, windows, balconies, buildings, or streets to say what they look out onto or where they open. Common with views: « donner sur la mer », « donner sur la cour », « donner sur la rue ». It does not mean “to give on”.
target_language_example: La chambre donne sur la mer.
native_language_example: The room faces the sea / has a sea view.

meaning: to teach someone a lesson; to give a lesson (class).
additional_notes: Meaning depends on context. In a learning/teaching context, it’s literal: to give a lesson (e.g., music, driving). In a conflict or punishment context, it means “to teach someone a lesson” (make someone learn from their mistake), often with a negative tone. Common pattern: donner une leçon à quelqu’un.
target_language_example: Il a voulu me donner une leçon, mais il s’est trompé.
native_language_example: He wanted to teach me a lesson, but he was wrong.

meaning: to sleep like a baby (to sleep very well/deeply).
additional_notes: A common idiomatic way to say you slept extremely well. Used with conjugated forms of "dormir": "J’ai dormi comme un bébé" (past), "Je dors comme un bébé" (present). Also often said as "dormir comme un loir" (to sleep like a dormouse).
target_language_example: Après la randonnée, j’ai dormi comme un bébé.
native_language_example: After the hike, I slept like a baby.

meaning: to sleep very soundly (sleep like a log).
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression meaning someone is in a deep sleep and is hard to wake up. Literally “to sleep with closed fists,” but you should translate it as “sleep soundly” or “sleep like a log.” Often used with "je/il/elle dors" (present) or "j'ai dormi" (past).
