target_language_example: Après le voyage, il a dormi à poings fermés toute la nuit.
native_language_example: After the trip, he slept like a log all night.

meaning: a double life (living two separate lives).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has a secret second life (for example, another relationship, identity, or activities) that they hide from others. Often appears with verbs like "mener" (to lead) or "avoir" (to have): "mener une double vie".
target_language_example: Il menait une double vie : le jour, il était professeur, et le soir, il jouait dans un groupe.
native_language_example: He led a double life: by day he was a teacher, and at night he played in a band.

meaning: “Good Lord!” / “Sweet Jesus!” (an exclamation of surprise, shock, annoyance, etc.).
additional_notes: Used as an interjection, often with an exclamation mark: « Doux Jésus ! ». It’s a mild religious oath; common in informal spoken French, but can sound old-fashioned or dramatic depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Doux Jésus ! Tu m’as fait peur !
native_language_example: Good Lord! You scared me!

meaning: 'straight to the point' / 'get right to it'.
additional_notes: Used to say you want someone to be direct, without long explanations or small talk. Often used as an instruction or request: "Allons droit au but." / "Va droit au but."
target_language_example: Allons droit au but : combien ça coûte ?
native_language_example: Let’s get straight to the point: how much does it cost?

meaning: the right to vote; voting rights.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s legal right/eligibility to vote (in a country, an election, an organization, etc.). Often appears with verbs like avoir (to have), accorder (to grant), retirer (to take away), and with articles: le droit de vote (the right to vote), un droit de vote (a voting right/a vote).
target_language_example: Tous les citoyens majeurs ont le droit de vote.
native_language_example: All adult citizens have the right to vote.

additional_notes: Used right before a noun to describe something as odd/strange (most common meaning) or amusing/funny depending on context and tone. Often expresses mild surprise or disapproval: "drôle d’idée" = "a strange idea." Note the form changes before a vowel sound: "drôle d’..." (e.g., drôle d’histoire).
target_language_example: C’est une drôle d’idée.
native_language_example: That’s a strange idea.

additional_notes: “Du” is a partitive article meaning “some,” and “bon” means “good.” You use “du bon” to mean “some good-quality (thing),” often with the noun understood from context (e.g., food, wine). With a noun, it commonly becomes “du bon + noun” (e.g., du bon fromage = some good cheese). In casual speech, “C’est du bon !” can mean “It’s the good stuff!”
target_language_example: On a acheté du bon pain.
native_language_example: We bought some good bread.

additional_notes: Literally “some good time.” Used with verbs like passer (to spend) or s’amuser (to have fun): “passer du bon temps” = “to have a good time.” Contrast with “le bon temps,” which can mean “the old days” or “good weather,” depending on context.
target_language_example: On a passé du bon temps ensemble hier soir.
native_language_example: We had a good time together last night.

additional_notes: Used as an exclamation to ask someone to relax or stop getting angry/excited. Often said on its own (Du calme !) or with a polite addition (Du calme, s'il te plaît.). Literally it’s “some calm,” but it’s used like an imperative in English.
target_language_example: Du calme, s'il te plaît, tout va bien.
native_language_example: Calm down, please, everything is fine.

meaning: "near" / "in the area of"; or "on the side of" (supporting).
additional_notes: Literally “on the side of.” Very common to give an approximate location: « J’habite du côté de Lyon » (“I live near/in the Lyon area”). It can also mean taking someone’s side in a disagreement: « Je suis du côté de Marie » (“I’m on Marie’s side”). Often used with places, neighborhoods, or landmarks for “around there.”
target_language_example: On cherche un restaurant du côté de la gare.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a restaurant near the train station.

additional_notes: A fairly formal way to give a reason for something. It’s followed by a noun or noun phrase (or by an infinitive introduced with "le" in more formal writing: "du fait de l’avoir oublié"). Often interchangeable with "à cause de" (more common) or "en raison de" (also formal).
target_language_example: Le match est annulé du fait de la pluie.
native_language_example: The match is cancelled because of the rain.

additional_notes: Used to say something changes very quickly and unexpectedly, sometimes literally from one day to the next. Often appears with verbs like changer, disparaître, perdre, devenir. Common pattern: « Du jour au lendemain, … » or « … du jour au lendemain ».
target_language_example: Du jour au lendemain, il a changé de travail.
native_language_example: Overnight, he changed jobs.

meaning: from morning to evening; all day long.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens continuously throughout the day. Literally “from the morning to the evening,” and often implies “all day (long).” You can use it with verbs like travailler (to work), pleuvoir (to rain), or regarder (to watch).
target_language_example: Il travaille du matin au soir.
native_language_example: He works from morning to evening / all day long.

additional_notes: Used to weaken or correct what you just said, similar to “at least / anyway” in English. Often comes after a statement as a clarification: “..., du moins, ...”. Can also introduce a minimum or fallback idea.
target_language_example: Je viendrai demain, du moins j’essaierai.
native_language_example: I’ll come tomorrow—at least I’ll try.

additional_notes: Literally “of the people,” but in everyday French it most often means “people” in the sense of a number of people present. Common in expressions like “Il y a du monde” (There are a lot of people / It’s crowded) and “avoir du monde” (to have people over / to have company). Also used to mean “(some) people” in general: “Il y a du monde qui pense que…” (Some people think that…).
target_language_example: Il y a du monde ce soir au restaurant.
native_language_example: It’s crowded at the restaurant tonight.

additional_notes: Used as an exclamation to urge someone to hurry up or to show more energy and determination. You’ll often hear it with « Allez »: « Allez, du nerf ! ». Related phrase: « avoir du nerf » = to have pep/energy (and sometimes strength/character). It looks like English “nerve,” but here it’s about energy, not audacity.
target_language_example: Allez, du nerf ! On est en retard.
native_language_example: Come on, get moving! We’re late.

meaning: "of the century" (the most important/best/worst of the century).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to emphasize that something is exceptional or unforgettable: "le match du siècle" (the match of the century), "la découverte du siècle" (the discovery of the century). It can be used seriously or ironically/exaggerated in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ils ont annoncé le match du siècle à la télé.
native_language_example: They announced the match of the century on TV.

meaning: in the time of; back in the days of.
additional_notes: Used to place something in the past, during the period when a person lived/ruled or when something existed/was common. It’s followed by a person, reign, era, or older period reference (e.g., du temps de Napoléon, du temps de mes grands-parents). Often implies “back then” compared to today.
target_language_example: Du temps de mes grands-parents, on écrivait plus de lettres à la main.
native_language_example: In my grandparents’ day, people wrote more letters by hand.

additional_notes: Colloquial intensifier meaning something is really great or impressive. Often used after a noun (e.g., "un film du tonnerre") or after a verb like "être" ("C’est du tonnerre !"). Literally means "of thunder," but it’s not translated that way in English.
target_language_example: On a passé une soirée du tonnerre !
native_language_example: We had an awesome evening!

additional_notes: Used with a negative phrase like ne...pas / ne...plus / ne...jamais to emphasize the negative: pas du tout = “not at all,” plus du tout = “not anymore at all,” jamais du tout = “never at all.” Often placed at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas faim du tout.
native_language_example: I’m not hungry at all.

additional_notes: Used with the partitive article (du) to talk about wind as an uncountable thing: Il y a du vent = “It’s windy.” Also appears in the idiom C’est du vent (“It’s just hot air / empty talk”).
target_language_example: Il y a du vent aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: It’s windy today.

additional_notes: Describes someone who is strict, shrewd, or uncompromising when dealing with money, contracts, prices, or negotiations. Often implies the person drives a hard bargain. You can also say "être dur en affaires".
target_language_example: Il est dur en affaires : il ne baisse jamais ses prix.
native_language_example: He’s tough in business: he never lowers his prices.

meaning: tough cookie; hard to deal with (stubborn, resilient).
additional_notes: Colloquial expression used to describe someone who is mentally or physically tough, stubborn, or not easily intimidated. Often said about a person (sometimes admiringly, sometimes critically). Literally means “hard to cook,” but it’s used figuratively.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas pour Léa : c’est une dure à cuire, elle va s’en sortir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about Léa: she’s a tough cookie, she’ll get through it.

meaning: tough; a tough cookie (hard to intimidate or defeat).
additional_notes: Colloquial idiom used to describe someone (or sometimes something) very tough, stubborn, or resilient. Feminine form: « dure à cuire » (for a woman/girl). Masculine: « dur à cuire » (for a man/boy). Often used with « être »: « Elle est dure à cuire. »
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas pour Léa : elle est dure à cuire.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about Léa—she’s tough.

additional_notes: Literally “duration of life.” Used for living things (a person’s/animal’s lifespan) and for objects/technology to mean how long something lasts before it wears out or needs replacement (battery life, shelf life, product lifetime). Often followed by "de" + noun: "la durée de vie d’une batterie".
target_language_example: La durée de vie de cette batterie est d’environ deux ans.
native_language_example: The lifespan (battery life) of this battery is about two years.

additional_notes: Used to show immediacy: one action happens right after another. Commonly followed by the present tense to talk about the future: « Dès que j’arrive, je t’appelle. » (= As soon as I arrive, I’ll call you). You can also use it for past events: « Dès que j’ai compris, je suis parti. »
target_language_example: Dès que tu as fini, on part.
native_language_example: As soon as you’re finished, we’re leaving.

additional_notes: Used to ask for something to be done at the earliest possible time. Common in both spoken and written French, including polite requests (often with “s’il vous plaît”).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me rappeler dès que possible, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you call me back as soon as possible, please?

additional_notes: Means starting immediately at the present moment and continuing into the future. Often used in formal speech or writing (announcements, emails, rules). Similar in meaning to « à partir de maintenant ».
target_language_example: Dès à présent, il est interdit de fumer ici.
native_language_example: From now on, it is forbidden to smoke here.

meaning: 'already seen' (the feeling you’ve experienced something before).
additional_notes: Used as a noun in French (often masculine: "un déjà-vu") to describe the sensation that a new situation feels familiar, as if it has happened before. Also commonly used in English with the same meaning.
target_language_example: J’ai eu un déjà-vu en entrant dans cette rue.
native_language_example: I had a déjà vu when I walked into this street.

additional_notes: Used literally in math (the denominator shared by fractions) and figuratively to mean the one thing different people/situations have in common. Often used with trouver/chercher: « trouver un dénominateur commun » (“to find common ground”).
target_language_example: On a essayé de trouver un dénominateur commun entre nos deux projets.
native_language_example: We tried to find common ground between our two projects.

meaning: to go too far; to cross the line.
additional_notes: Used when someone’s behavior or words are unacceptable and exceed limits (social rules, respect, patience). Often said as a reproach: « Tu dépasses les bornes ! » It can apply to a comment, an attitude, or an action. Literally “to go beyond the boundary markers,” but the natural meaning is idiomatic.
target_language_example: Tu dépasses les bornes : tu n’as pas le droit de lui parler comme ça.
native_language_example: You’re going too far: you don’t have the right to talk to him/her like that.

additional_notes: Used for a professional hired to investigate (e.g., missing persons, fraud, infidelity). Often shortened to “un privé” in speech. Plural: “des détectives privés.”
target_language_example: Elle a engagé un détective privé pour retrouver son frère.
native_language_example: She hired a private detective to find her brother.

additional_notes: Used like the English word. Also commonly written "email" or "mail". The noun is masculine: "un e-mail". You can say "envoyer un e-mail" (to send an email) or "recevoir un e-mail" (to receive an email).
target_language_example: Je t’envoie un e-mail ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m sending you an email tonight.

additional_notes: Used to describe water from rivers, lakes, and streams (as opposed to "eau salée" = saltwater/sea water). You’ll see it in nature contexts (fish, habitats) and everyday contexts like "piscine d’eau douce" (freshwater pool).
target_language_example: Ce poisson vit dans l’eau douce.
native_language_example: This fish lives in freshwater.

additional_notes: Common in everyday contexts (restaurants, hotels, at home) to specify water from the faucet (as opposed to bottled water: « eau en bouteille » / « eau minérale »). Often used with « boire » (to drink) or « un verre d’ » (a glass of).
target_language_example: On peut boire l’eau du robinet ici ?
native_language_example: Can you drink the tap water here?

additional_notes: Used especially in formal contexts (travel, lost-and-found, police reports) to refer to someone's belongings. Often seen in the plural: « effets personnels » = personal belongings (e.g., in a bag, suitcase, or on a person). Not the same as « un effet » meaning an effect/result.
target_language_example: Veuillez garder vos effets personnels avec vous en tout temps.
native_language_example: Please keep your personal belongings with you at all times.

meaning: side effect (an unintended result, especially from medicine).
additional_notes: Common in medical contexts for unwanted effects of a drug or treatment: « effets secondaires ». Can also be used more generally for an unintended consequence of an action or decision. Often appears with « avoir » (to have) or « provoquer » (to cause): « Ce médicament peut provoquer des effets secondaires. »
target_language_example: Ce médicament peut avoir des effets secondaires.
native_language_example: This medicine can have side effects.

meaning: 'well…' (to react, pause, or introduce what you’ll say next).
additional_notes: Common discourse marker, often at the start of a sentence. Used to show hesitation, surprise, emphasis, or to respond before giving an answer or conclusion (similar to “well then” / “so” / “okay then” depending on context). Can be followed by a comma in writing: « Eh bien, … ».
target_language_example: Eh bien, je ne sais pas quoi dire.
native_language_example: Well, I don’t know what to say.

additional_notes: Emphatic pronoun used to insist that it’s the same person (not someone else): "she herself". Often comes right after the subject (Elle-même a appelé.) or after the verb/preposition (Elle l’a fait elle-même.; par elle-même). Hyphenated form; masculine is "lui-même"; plural "elles-mêmes".
target_language_example: Elle a réparé son vélo elle-même.
native_language_example: She fixed her bike herself.

additional_notes: Stressed pronoun used for emphasis or reflexive meaning with a feminine plural subject (elles = “they” for women/girls/things). Often appears after the verb or after a preposition: Elles le font elles-mêmes (“They do it themselves”); Elles parlent d’elles-mêmes (“They talk about themselves”). Not used as the regular subject pronoun (use elles, not elles-mêmes).
target_language_example: Elles ont préparé le dîner elles-mêmes.
native_language_example: They prepared dinner themselves.

additional_notes: Used for a planned set of activities/appointments (school, work, daily routine). Very common with school or university: you can ask for or consult your "emploi du temps". Often shortened to "EDT" in informal written contexts (especially among students).
target_language_example: Tu peux m’envoyer ton emploi du temps pour la semaine prochaine ?
native_language_example: Can you send me your schedule for next week?

additional_notes: Used for identification or security (unlocking a phone, police records, administrative documents). Literally “digital imprint” in French; here *digitale* means “of a finger” (a *digit*), not “digital” in the tech sense.
target_language_example: Pour déverrouiller le téléphone, il faut une empreinte digitale.
native_language_example: To unlock the phone, you need a fingerprint.

additional_notes: Used to say something exists or is available in large quantities. Common with verbs like "avoir" (to have), "trouver" (to find), "pousser" (to grow), or "être" (to be). Often implies “more than enough.”
target_language_example: Dans cette région, l’eau est disponible en abondance.
native_language_example: In this region, water is available in abundance.

meaning: as a friend; in a friendly way.
additional_notes: Used to show you’re speaking or acting from a friendly, non-hostile, non-professional point of view. Often appears after verbs like parler/discuter (to talk), venir (to come), saluer (to greet), aider (to help), or in set phrases like « en ami » / « en amis ». Can also imply doing something informally, without official status (e.g., visiting someone privately rather than in a work role).
target_language_example: Je viens en ami, je ne veux pas de problèmes.
native_language_example: I come as a friend; I don’t want any trouble.

additional_notes: Used literally for rivers/flows (upstream, toward the source) and very commonly in business/tech to mean something that happens earlier in a workflow or supply chain ("upstream" steps). Often contrasts with "en aval" (downstream / later in the process).
target_language_example: Il faut vérifier les données en amont pour éviter des erreurs plus tard.
native_language_example: We need to check the data upstream/earlier in the process to avoid errors later.

meaning: to end up (doing); to come to (do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (en arriver à + verb) to show a progression or escalation that leads to a final result, often surprising, negative, or inevitable. It’s close to “to get to the point of” or “to wind up” in English: « Il en est arrivé à mentir » = “He ended up lying.”
target_language_example: Avec le stress, j’en suis arrivé à oublier mon propre anniversaire.
native_language_example: With the stress, I ended up forgetting my own birthday.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or direction toward the back: « reculer / aller / marcher en arrière » (“to move/step backward”). Also used for something located behind: « derrière, en arrière » (“in back/behind”). Common in set phrases like « en arrière ! » (“Back up!”) and « en arrière-plan » (“in the background”).
target_language_example: Reculez un peu en arrière, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please move back a little.

additional_notes: Used to say what happens during the time before something else occurs. Often followed by "que" + a clause: "En attendant que tu arrives…" (while waiting for you to arrive). It can also be used alone as a transition meaning “in the meantime.”
target_language_example: Le train a du retard ; en attendant, on peut prendre un café.
native_language_example: The train is late; in the meantime, we can have a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say what happens in the meantime until something else happens. It is followed by a clause with a verb (often in the subjunctive, especially for future/uncertain events): « En attendant que tu arrives, je prépare le dîner. » For a noun or infinitive instead, use « en attendant »: « En attendant le bus… » / « En attendant de te voir… ».
target_language_example: En attendant que le médecin arrive, asseyez-vous ici.
native_language_example: While waiting for the doctor to arrive, sit here.

additional_notes: Used to say something is waiting to happen or be dealt with (often in admin, customer service, transport, or technology). Common in set phrases like « en attente de + noun » (waiting for) and « mettre/laisser en attente » (to put/leave on hold). Can describe a person (waiting) or a thing/request/file (pending).
target_language_example: Votre demande est en attente de validation.
native_language_example: Your request is pending approval.

additional_notes: Used to strongly forbid or rule something out. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis: "En aucun cas, ...". It can also follow a negative: "Je ne... en aucun cas". More formal/stronger than "jamais" in many contexts.
target_language_example: En aucun cas tu ne dois partager ce mot de passe.
native_language_example: Under no circumstances should you share this password.

additional_notes: A strong, formal-sounding negative expression meaning something is absolutely not the case. Often used with "ne" (e.g., "Je ne suis en aucune manière responsable"), and can be followed by "de" + infinitive ("en aucune manière de..." is rare; prefer "en aucune manière" + verb clause). Similar in meaning to "en aucun cas" (in no case) and "d'aucune façon" (in no way).
target_language_example: Je ne suis en aucune manière responsable de ce retard.
native_language_example: I am in no way responsible for this delay.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens before the planned time/deadline (in advance) or that someone arrives earlier than expected. Often with verbs like "arriver" (to arrive) and "payer" (to pay): "arriver en avance" = arrive early; "payer en avance" = pay in advance.
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé en avance pour le rendez-vous.
native_language_example: I arrived early for the appointment.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or direction toward the front (opposite of « en arrière » = backward). Also used on its own as an encouragement to start or continue: « En avant ! » = “Forward!/Let’s go!”
target_language_example: En avant ! On y va.
native_language_example: Come on! Let’s go.

meaning: to have had enough; to be fed up.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re tired of a situation or behavior and don’t want it to continue. The pronoun "en" refers to what you’re fed up with (often implied). Common patterns: "J’en ai assez" (I’ve had enough), "J’en ai assez de + noun/verb" (I’m fed up with…), and "En avoir assez !" as an exclamation. Often followed by "de" + noun or infinitive.
target_language_example: J’en ai assez de t’attendre tous les jours.
native_language_example: I’m fed up with waiting for you every day.

meaning: to be fed up (with it/with something).
additional_notes: Common, everyday expression meaning you’re tired/annoyed and want it to stop. Often followed by de + noun/verb: J’en ai marre de ce bruit / J’en ai marre d’attendre. The “en” refers to what you’re fed up with; you can also make it explicit with “de…”. Conjugates with avoir: j’en ai marre, tu en as marre, il/elle en a marre, on en a marre, etc.
target_language_example: J’en ai marre de travailler le week-end.
native_language_example: I’m fed up with working on weekends.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a lower position or level (the opposite of « en haut »). Common for directions and locations: « en bas » = downstairs; « en bas de… » / « tout en bas » = at the bottom of something. Often used with verbs like « descendre » (to go down), « être » (to be), and « aller » (to go).
target_language_example: Les toilettes sont en bas.
native_language_example: The toilets are downstairs.

meaning: at the bottom of (down at the bottom of).
additional_notes: Used to locate something lower down on a page, screen, sign, or physical object. Often followed by a noun or pronoun: « en bas de la page » (at the bottom of the page), « en bas du document » (at the bottom of the document). You may also hear « en bas » on its own meaning “downstairs/down below.”
target_language_example: Tu trouveras mon numéro en bas de la page.
native_language_example: You’ll find my number at the bottom of the page.

meaning: in style; beautifully; on a high note.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done with elegance or flair, or that something ends in an impressive way. Often follows a verb like finir/terminer ("to finish/end"), but can also describe how something is done in general.
target_language_example: On va finir en beauté avec un dernier morceau.
native_language_example: We’re going to finish in style with one last song.

meaning: favorably; in a positive way (often: “well” of someone).
additional_notes: Used especially after verbs like parler, dire, penser to mean speaking/thinking positively about someone or something: parler de quelqu’un en bien (“to speak well of someone”). Often contrasted with en mal (“negatively”).
target_language_example: Il parle de toi en bien.
native_language_example: He speaks well of you.

additional_notes: Literal use: made of concrete (material). Figurative use (common, informal): means something is very solid, sturdy, reliable, or excellent (e.g., "un plan en béton" = a rock-solid plan). Often used after a noun or with "c'est".
target_language_example: On a un plan en béton pour demain.
native_language_example: We have a rock-solid plan for tomorrow.

meaning: secretly; in hiding; on the sly.
additional_notes: Used to say an action is done without others knowing, often because it’s forbidden, surprising, or you don’t want to be seen. Common with verbs like faire (do), partir (leave), regarder (watch), manger (eat), and also with “se voir” (to meet) in a secret relationship: “Ils se voient en cachette.”
target_language_example: Il a mangé des bonbons en cachette.
native_language_example: He ate candy secretly (when no one was looking).

meaning: in case of; in the event of.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a possible situation/condition (often in instructions, warnings, or emergency info). It is followed by a noun or noun phrase: "en cas de problème", "en cas d’incendie". For "in case + clause" (e.g., "in case it rains"), French often uses "au cas où" + conditional: "Au cas où il pleuvrait".
target_language_example: En cas d’urgence, appelez le 15.
native_language_example: In case of an emergency, call 15.

additional_notes: Often used after a noun to refer to the person/thing being discussed or implicated: « la personne en cause » (the person concerned), « les faits en cause » (the facts in question). Common in formal contexts (news, legal/administrative). It doesn’t mean “the cause” (reason); it means the matter/person involved.
target_language_example: La personne en cause a été entendue par la police.
native_language_example: The person concerned was questioned by the police.

meaning: on the run; hiding (from the police or authorities).
additional_notes: Used when someone is fleeing and trying not to be found, often after escaping or doing something illegal. Common in news/crime contexts. Often appears with verbs like « être » (to be) or « partir » (to go).
target_language_example: Depuis son évasion, il est en cavale.
native_language_example: Since his escape, he’s been on the run.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what is happening currently (these days) or at this exact moment; context decides. Often paired with the present tense: « Je travaille en ce moment. » It can also answer a question like « Qu’est-ce que tu fais en ce moment ? »
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas te parler en ce moment.
native_language_example: I can’t talk to you right now.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a topic or specify what you’re talking about. Common in more formal writing and speech; in everyday conversation you can often use "pour" or "à propos de" instead. It is usually followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., "en ce qui concerne lui", "en ce qui concerne le travail").
target_language_example: En ce qui concerne le paiement, vous pouvez régler par carte ou en espèces.
native_language_example: Regarding payment, you can pay by card or in cash.

meaning: in those days; at that time (in the past).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a past period, often with a nostalgic or historical tone. It points to a specific time in the past that both speaker and listener can identify from context. Common in storytelling: «En ce temps-là, ...».
target_language_example: En ce temps-là, il n’y avait pas d’internet.
native_language_example: In those days, there was no internet.

additional_notes: Used with the verb « être » to say someone has responsibility for a task, project, or group: « être en charge de + noun/verb ». Common in workplaces and administration. For people, French often uses « s’occuper de » (to take care of) as a more everyday alternative.
target_language_example: Je suis en charge de l’organisation de la réunion.
native_language_example: I’m in charge of organizing the meeting.

meaning: chief; head (the main person in charge).
additional_notes: Used after a title to specify the top role in an organization or hierarchy. Common in set phrases like « rédacteur en chef » (editor-in-chief) and « commandant en chef » (commander-in-chief). It doesn’t usually stand alone; it follows the noun.
target_language_example: Elle est rédactrice en chef du magazine.
native_language_example: She is the editor-in-chief of the magazine.

meaning: on the way; on one’s way.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is currently traveling toward a place or is in transit. Often with verbs like être (Je suis en chemin), être + participle (Il est en chemin pour…), or as an adverbial phrase: en chemin vers/pour + destination. Can also mean “along the way” (En chemin, on a rencontré…).
target_language_example: Je suis en chemin, j’arrive dans dix minutes.
native_language_example: I’m on my way; I’ll be there in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "être" ("to be") to say someone is angry: "être en colère (contre quelqu’un)" = "to be angry (with someone)". It’s a fairly neutral/common expression (not slang).
target_language_example: Je suis en colère contre lui.
native_language_example: I’m angry with him.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something shared between people or things (ideas, interests, points, spaces). Very common in the phrase « avoir ... en commun » (“to have ... in common”). Often placed after the noun: « un point en commun » (“a point in common”).
target_language_example: On a beaucoup de choses en commun.
native_language_example: We have a lot in common.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with another person (or sometimes an animal) in a neutral or slightly formal way. Often appears with verbs like être, venir, partir, sortir: « Il est en compagnie de… » / « Je suis venu(e) en compagnie de… ». In everyday speech, « avec » is more common.
target_language_example: Je suis venu en compagnie de ma sœur.
native_language_example: I came with my sister.

meaning: knowingly; with full knowledge of the facts.
additional_notes: An adverbial phrase meaning you are fully aware of the situation (and often the consequences) when you act or decide. Common in formal or legal contexts. Often used after the verb: « choisir / décider / agir en connaissance de cause ».
target_language_example: J’ai signé le contrat en connaissance de cause.
native_language_example: I signed the contract knowingly (with full knowledge of the facts).

additional_notes: Used to link two ideas: one situation causes another. Common in writing and formal speech; in everyday conversation you might also hear "donc" or "du coup". Often follows a first clause and introduces the result: "..., et en conséquence, ...".
target_language_example: Il a oublié son passeport et, en conséquence, il n’a pas pu embarquer.
native_language_example: He forgot his passport and, as a result, he couldn’t board.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is romantically partnered (often in an exclusive relationship), whether married or not. Common with "être": "Je suis en couple" (I’m in a relationship). You can specify who with using "avec": "Elle est en couple avec…".
target_language_example: Ils sont en couple depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: They’ve been together (in a relationship) for two years.

additional_notes: Used to say something is happening now or underway (a process, event, project, class, etc.). Common in set phrases like « en cours de + noun/verb » (in the process of / being + past participle): « en cours de construction » (under construction), « en cours de préparation » (being prepared), « en cours de route » (along the way).
target_language_example: Les travaux sont en cours.
native_language_example: The work is in progress.

meaning: in the process of; currently (doing something).
additional_notes: Used to say an action is happening right now or is underway, usually followed by an infinitive verb: « en cours de + infinitive » (e.g., en cours de préparation). Often interchangeable with « en train de », but « en cours de » is slightly more formal and can also be used with nouns to mean “ongoing” (e.g., des travaux en cours = ongoing work/roadworks).
target_language_example: Je suis en cours de préparation d’un dossier.
native_language_example: I’m in the process of preparing a file.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is in a risky situation. Common with être: "être en danger" (to be in danger). You can also use it after a noun: "des espèces en danger" (endangered species).
target_language_example: Attention, cet enfant est en danger.
native_language_example: Careful, this child is in danger.

additional_notes: Often used with "de": "en dehors de" = "outside of" (physically) or "apart from/except for" (figuratively). Without "de", it commonly means being outside (not inside): "Je suis en dehors."
target_language_example: En dehors de ça, tout va bien.
native_language_example: Apart from that, everything is fine.

additional_notes: Often used to exclude something from a group or statement: « En dehors de X, … » = “Except for X, …”. It can also mean physically “outside of” (not inside): « en dehors de la maison » = “outside the house”. Usually followed by a noun or pronoun (moi, toi, lui/elle, nous, vous, eux/elles).
target_language_example: En dehors de Marie, personne ne connaît la réponse.
native_language_example: Except for Marie, nobody knows the answer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about position (physically under something) or a level/amount that is lower than a reference point. Often followed by a noun or number: « en dessous de la table » (under the table), « en dessous de 10 € » (under 10 euros). For comparisons in writing/speech you may also see « au-dessous de » with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Le chat est en dessous de la table.
native_language_example: The cat is under the table.

meaning: in the making; emerging; becoming (not finished yet).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe someone or something that is developing and expected to become something later (e.g., an "artiste en devenir" = an aspiring/emerging artist). Common in formal or written French. Similar idea to "en cours de" (“in progress”), but with a stronger sense of future potential.
target_language_example: C’est un artiste en devenir.
native_language_example: He’s an emerging artist / an artist in the making.

additional_notes: Used to describe a person, group, or situation that is having problems (financial, emotional, practical, etc.). Often used with "être" ("être en difficulté" = to be in trouble/struggling) or after a noun ("une entreprise en difficulté" = a struggling company). Can also be used in plural: "des élèves en difficulté" (students who are struggling).
target_language_example: Depuis la perte de son emploi, il est en difficulté financière.
native_language_example: Since he lost his job, he has been in financial difficulty.

meaning: to say a lot (about something); to speak volumes.
additional_notes: Used to mean that a fact, detail, or situation reveals a lot about someone/something, often without needing more explanation. Commonly appears as "Ça en dit long sur…" (That says a lot about…).
target_language_example: Son silence en dit long sur ce qu’il pense.
native_language_example: His silence speaks volumes about what he thinks.

additional_notes: Used for live TV/radio/streaming (“broadcast live”) and for anything happening in real time (e.g., a live update or live chat). Often appears with verbs like « être » (to be), « passer »/« diffuser » (to air/broadcast), or as an adjective-like phrase: « un match en direct » (a live match).
target_language_example: Le journal est en direct à 20 h.
native_language_example: The news is live at 8 p.m.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something in a calm, smooth, non-aggressive way (often “slowly and carefully”). Common with verbs like aller, commencer, se réveiller, atterrir, and expressions like "prendre les choses en douceur" (to take things easy). Depending on context it can mean physical gentleness (softly) or a gradual approach (ease into it).
target_language_example: On va y aller en douceur.
native_language_example: We’re going to take it easy / go gently.

additional_notes: A formal-ish prepositional phrase used to show contrast (something happens even though there is an obstacle or opposing fact). It’s followed by a noun/pronoun or an infinitive: « en dépit de la pluie », « en dépit de tout », « en dépit d’être fatigué ». Often interchangeable with « malgré » in everyday French.
target_language_example: En dépit de la pluie, on est sortis se promener.
native_language_example: Despite the rain, we went out for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to say you will explain something thoroughly, with specifics. Often follows verbs like expliquer (to explain), décrire (to describe), raconter (to tell), or parler de (to talk about). You can also use it in questions: « Tu peux me l’expliquer en détail ? »
target_language_example: Je vais t’expliquer ça en détail.
native_language_example: I’m going to explain that to you in detail.

additional_notes: Often used to agree with what was just said (like “that’s right/indeed”), or to introduce an explanation/justification. Common in both spoken and written French. Placement: frequently at the start of a sentence, but can also appear after a statement as a confirming tag.
target_language_example: — Il va pleuvoir demain. — En effet, ils annoncent de la pluie.
native_language_example: — It’s going to rain tomorrow. — Indeed, they’re forecasting rain.

additional_notes: Means something is complete, not cut/divided or not partially done. Common with nouns ("le gâteau en entier" = the whole cake) and with verbs like "lire" or "payer" ("lire en entier" = read all of it; "payer en entier" = pay in full).
target_language_example: J’ai mangé le gâteau en entier.
native_language_example: I ate the whole cake.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is directly in front of, or on the other side from, someone/something. Often used with "en face de" + place/person (e.g., "en face de la gare" = across from the station). You can also say "en face" alone when the other location is understood (e.g., "C’est en face" = It’s opposite/across the street).
target_language_example: La boulangerie est en face de la pharmacie.
native_language_example: The bakery is across from the pharmacy.

additional_notes: Used to say something is directly facing something else (often a place or building). It’s followed by a noun or pronoun: en face de la banque (opposite the bank), en face de chez moi (across from my place). Often used with être or se trouver.
target_language_example: Le café est en face de la gare.
native_language_example: The café is across from the train station.

meaning: to do some of it; to do it (with “en” = “some/of it”).
additional_notes: Used with the pronoun “en” (meaning “some,” “any,” or “of it/of them”) before the verb “faire.” It often appears in common patterns like “en faire trop” (to overdo it), “en faire partie” (to be part of it), or with “se” as “s’en faire” (to worry about it). On its own, “en faire” usually needs extra context (how much? what part?).
target_language_example: Je vais en faire une partie ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to do part of it tonight.

additional_notes: Very common discourse marker used to correct, clarify, or add precision (like “actually” in English). Often comes at the beginning of a sentence, but can also appear mid-sentence. In French it’s frequently used as a soft correction (“Well, actually…”) rather than a strong contradiction.
target_language_example: En fait, je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: Actually, I can’t come tonight.

meaning: in terms of; as regards; when it comes to.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic you’re talking about (often a bit formal). It’s close to “quant à / en matière de”. Don’t confuse it with “en fait” alone, which usually means “actually / in fact.”
target_language_example: En fait de budget, on doit faire attention cette année.
native_language_example: When it comes to the budget, we have to be careful this year.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something together with your family members, often meaning a family-only setting (no friends/coworkers). Common after verbs like être, aller, partir, rester, dîner, passer du temps. Similar idea: « en couple » (as a couple), « entre amis » (with friends).
target_language_example: On va au restaurant en famille ce soir.
native_language_example: We’re going to the restaurant as a family tonight.

additional_notes: Used to express support for an idea, proposal, person, or side in a debate. Often follows verbs like être (to be), voter (to vote), se prononcer (to come out), or arguments like un argument en faveur de (an argument in favor of). Opposite: contre (against).
target_language_example: Je suis en faveur de cette proposition.
native_language_example: I’m in favor of this proposal.

additional_notes: Used to say something is literally burning (a fire). You can also use it figuratively to mean someone/something is “on fire” (doing extremely well), but that’s more colloquial. Often used with the verb être: « être en feu » (to be on fire).
target_language_example: Attention ! La maison est en feu.
native_language_example: Watch out! The house is on fire.

additional_notes: Used to sum up the final result or conclusion after considering everything (similar to “after all” or “when all is said and done”). Often placed at the start of a sentence or after a short pause to introduce the conclusion.
target_language_example: En fin de compte, on a décidé de rester à la maison.
native_language_example: In the end, we decided to stay at home.

meaning: to be done with it; to put an end to it.
additional_notes: Often used to express wanting something to stop or be finished. Very common pattern: "en finir avec + noun/pronoun" (to be done with / finish with): "J’en ai fini avec ce travail" = "I’m done with this work." You can also use it as a request: "On en finit ?" = "Can we be done (now)?"
target_language_example: J’en ai marre : je veux en finir avec cette histoire.
native_language_example: I’m fed up: I want to be done with this whole story.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens extremely quickly or increases sharply. Common with verbs like "aller" (to go fast) and "monter" / "augmenter" (to rise), e.g. "aller en flèche", "partir en flèche", "monter en flèche". It’s idiomatic: it suggests movement like an arrow (straight and rapid).
target_language_example: Les prix sont partis en flèche cette année.
native_language_example: Prices have skyrocketed this year.

additional_notes: Used to express that something changes or is decided based on another factor (a condition, criterion, or variable). Very common in instructions, plans, prices, and decisions. Often followed by a noun or pronoun: "en fonction de la météo" (depending on the weather), "en fonction de ses besoins" (according to his/her needs).
target_language_example: On choisira le restaurant en fonction de ton budget.
native_language_example: We’ll choose the restaurant depending on your budget.

additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb être (être en forme) to say you feel well/energetic or are physically fit. It can describe general energy (today I feel great) or fitness level (she’s very fit). Can also be used with other verbs like se sentir: Je me sens en forme.
target_language_example: Je suis en forme aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I’m feeling fit/energetic today.

additional_notes: Used to warn someone to be alert, or as a set command in fencing meaning “ready/guard position” (often followed by « Prêts ? Allez ! »). Outside fencing it’s a quick warning similar to “careful!” or “look out!”
target_language_example: En garde ! Il y a une voiture qui arrive.
native_language_example: Watch out! There’s a car coming.

additional_notes: Common in spoken French to introduce a summary or simplify what you’re saying (similar to “basically” / “so, in short”). It can also mean “roughly/approximately” when giving an estimate. Slightly informal in tone, but very common in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: En gros, on se retrouve à 8 h devant la gare.
native_language_example: Basically, we’ll meet at 8 in front of the station.

meaning: as / in the form of; by way of (as a substitute).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to say something is used or given instead of something else, or to serve a particular role (often: “as a gesture”, “as a substitute”, “for lack of”). Common pattern: « en guise de + nom ». Example: « en guise de dessert » (for dessert / as dessert), « en guise de cadeau » (as a gift). More formal than casual speech.
target_language_example: En guise de dessert, on a pris un café.
native_language_example: For dessert, we had a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that is true most of the time or as a general rule (not an exception). Often placed at the beginning of a sentence or after the verb: « En général, … » / « …, en général. »
target_language_example: En général, je prends le bus pour aller au travail.
native_language_example: In general, I take the bus to go to work.

additional_notes: Used to say something is increasing, especially numbers, prices, rates, or trends. Often paired with verbs like « être » (to be) or « être en hausse » (to be rising), and commonly contrasted with « en baisse » (down, decreasing).
target_language_example: Les prix sont en hausse cette année.
native_language_example: Prices are rising this year.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a higher position or direction (opposite of "en bas"). Common for locations on a page/screen ("up there", "at the top") and for floors in a building ("upstairs"). Often used with verbs like "monter" (to go up) or "être" (to be located).
target_language_example: Les toilettes sont en haut, à droite.
native_language_example: The bathrooms are upstairs, on the right.

meaning: 'at the top of' / 'at the top end of'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a position higher up on something (a page, a list, a street, a hill, a piece of furniture, etc.). Commonly used with locations and objects: "en haut de la page" (at the top of the page), "en haut de la rue" (at the top of the street). Also appears with "en haut du" (masc. singular) and "en haut des" (plural).
target_language_example: Le titre est en haut de la page.
native_language_example: The title is at the top of the page.

additional_notes: Used to describe a movement, path, or shape that forms a figure eight (8). Often used with verbs like "tourner" (to turn), "rouler" (to drive), "patiner" (to skate), or "tracer" (to draw/trace): "tourner en huit" = to move in a figure-eight pattern.
target_language_example: Il patine en huit sur la glace.
native_language_example: He skates in a figure eight on the ice.

meaning: to be impressive; to have a lot of style (slang).
additional_notes: Informal expression used to say someone/something really stands out or looks great (often about appearance, clothes, a car, a place, etc.). Most common in the pattern “Ça en jette !” or “Il/Elle en jette !”. Not used for literally throwing something.
target_language_example: Cette voiture, elle en jette !
native_language_example: That car is really impressive!

additional_notes: Used to say something is involved in a situation and could be won, lost, or affected. Common with verbs like « être » (to be) and « mettre » (to put): « Ce qui est en jeu… » = “What’s at stake…”, « mettre sa réputation en jeu » = “to put one’s reputation on the line.”
target_language_example: Il y a beaucoup en jeu dans cette décision.
native_language_example: There’s a lot at stake in this decision.

meaning: in the air; (figuratively) up in the air/uncertain.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: something is physically in the air (floating, thrown, airborne). Common figurative use: a plan or decision is not settled yet ("still up in the air"). Also used in expressions like "jeter (quelque chose) en l’air" (throw up in the air) or "faire exploser / faire sauter en l’air" (blow up).
target_language_example: Pour l’instant, nos projets de vacances sont encore en l’air.
native_language_example: For now, our vacation plans are still up in the air.

meaning: free; at liberty; released (not in captivity).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is not locked up or confined (a prisoner released, an animal not in a cage). Often contrasts with "en prison" or "en cage". Also used in fixed expressions like "poulet/œufs en liberté" meaning free-range (raised without being kept in cages).
target_language_example: Après trois ans de prison, il est enfin en liberté.
native_language_example: After three years in prison, he is finally free.

additional_notes: Used to say something is stored/kept somewhere secure. Often appears with verbs like « mettre » (to put), « garder » (to keep), or « ranger » (to store/put away). « Sûr » agrees with the noun « lieu » (masculine singular), so it stays « sûr » here.
target_language_example: Mets tes papiers en lieu sûr.
native_language_example: Put your papers in a safe place.

additional_notes: Used for things that happen via the internet (shopping, services, meetings, accounts): acheter en ligne, cours en ligne, banque en ligne. It can also literally mean “in a line/queue” in some contexts (e.g., être en ligne = to be lined up / on the line), but the most common beginner meaning is “online.”
target_language_example: Je fais mes courses en ligne.
native_language_example: I do my grocery shopping online.

additional_notes: Used mostly in the set expression « être en mal de + noun » meaning “to be in need of / to be lacking / to be craving (something)”. Without « de », « en mal » is less common on its own and can sound incomplete; you’ll more often see « en mal de sommeil », « en mal d’argent », etc.
target_language_example: En ce moment, je suis en mal de sommeil.
native_language_example: Right now, I’m really lacking sleep.

meaning: longing for; craving; in need of (often emotionally).
additional_notes: Used before a noun (or infinitive) to express a strong desire or a felt lack: "en mal de reconnaissance" (seeking/need of recognition), "en mal d’affection" (needing affection), "en mal d’aventures" (craving adventure). It often suggests an unmet need or dissatisfaction, not just a simple, neutral “need.”
target_language_example: Après sa rupture, il était en mal d’affection.
native_language_example: After his breakup, he was craving/needed affection.

meaning: running; in operation; on the move.
additional_notes: Used to say a machine/device is operating (often like English “on” or “running”): « Le moteur est en marche. » It can also describe someone moving or a process that has started and is underway: « La réforme est en marche. » In everyday speech you may also hear « Ça marche » meaning “It works / OK,” but that’s a related expression.
target_language_example: L’ascenseur est en marche.
native_language_example: The elevator is running (in operation).

meaning: in a group; all together; in large numbers.
additional_notes: Used to say that many people (or things) do something at the same time, as a collective. Often seen with verbs like venir/arriver/partir (to come/arrive/leave) to emphasize a crowd or mass movement. In English you can also say “en masse,” so it’s a close match.
target_language_example: Les clients sont arrivés en masse après la pub.
native_language_example: Customers arrived in large numbers after the ad.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic or area you’re talking about, often in formal or written French (policy, law, work, school). It’s commonly followed by a noun or noun phrase: « en matière de sécurité », « en matière de droit », etc. Close to « en termes de » and « concernant », but slightly more formal.
target_language_example: En matière de sécurité, il faut suivre ces règles.
native_language_example: In terms of safety, you must follow these rules.

meaning: 'able to' / 'in a position to' (to do something).
additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to express capability or readiness, often in formal or written French: "être en mesure de + infinitive". It can imply having the means, authority, or opportunity to do something. Common in official statements and professional contexts.
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas en mesure de vous répondre tout de suite.
native_language_example: I’m not able to answer you right away.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very quickly, within a time limit of two units. In everyday speech it’s often short for “en moins de deux minutes” (or secondes), but you can also specify the unit: “en moins de deux minutes/heures/jours”. Common in offers or promises: “livré en moins de deux jours”.
target_language_example: J’arrive en moins de deux minutes.
native_language_example: I’ll be there in less than two minutes.

additional_notes: Used to say that something (a person, vehicle, object, or even a project/situation) is currently moving or active, as opposed to still (immobile). Common in signs and everyday speech: "Ne pas toucher (l’appareil) en mouvement" (don’t touch while it’s moving), "Le bus est en mouvement" (the bus is moving). Also works figuratively for things that are developing or changing: "un projet en mouvement".
target_language_example: Attention : le train est en mouvement.
native_language_example: Careful: the train is moving.

meaning: on average; on an average basis.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a typical/average amount or frequency, not an exact number. Often placed after a quantity or at the end of a sentence: "30 minutes en moyenne", "Je lis deux livres par mois, en moyenne." Also common in more formal contexts like statistics or reports.
target_language_example: Je fais du sport trois fois par semaine, en moyenne.
native_language_example: I work out three times a week, on average.

meaning: in memory of (as a tribute to).
additional_notes: Used to dedicate something (a ceremony, message, donation, plaque, etc.) to someone who has died, or sometimes to commemorate an event. Common in formal contexts (speeches, memorials, inscriptions). Often followed by a person’s name: « en mémoire de Marie ».
target_language_example: Nous avons planté un arbre en mémoire de mon grand-père.
native_language_example: We planted a tree in memory of my grandfather.

meaning: at the same time; at the same moment.
additional_notes: Used to say two things happen simultaneously. It’s also commonly used conversationally to mean “at the same time / however” when adding a nuance or mild contradiction (similar to “on the other hand”).
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué, mais en même temps, je veux sortir.
native_language_example: I’m tired, but at the same time, I want to go out.

additional_notes: Used to say that many people/things are present or arrive together. Common with verbs like « venir » (to come) or « être » (to be): « Ils sont venus en nombre. » It can also mean simply “in number” in a more neutral sense, but it often implies “a lot.”
target_language_example: Les supporters sont venus en nombre pour le match.
native_language_example: The fans came in large numbers for the match.

additional_notes: Used with “en + material” to describe what something is made of (especially jewelry or objects): « une bague en or » = a gold ring. Note: French « or » means “gold” (not the English word “or”).
target_language_example: Elle porte une bague en or.
native_language_example: She’s wearing a gold ring.

additional_notes: Used to say something is tidy/organized (often about a room, papers, etc.) or that something is in good working order / everything is OK. Common with verbs like « mettre en ordre » (to put in order/tidy up) and « être en ordre » (to be in order / to be OK). Also used for documents/administration: « être en ordre avec ses papiers » (to have one’s paperwork in order).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tout est en ordre.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything is in order.

meaning: broken down; out of order (not working).
additional_notes: Used mainly for machines, vehicles, or systems that stop working (car, elevator, internet, heating, etc.). Often with the verb « être »: « être en panne » = to have broken down / to be out of order. You can add what’s broken with « de »: « être en panne de batterie » (battery is dead).
target_language_example: Désolé, ma voiture est en panne.
native_language_example: Sorry, my car broke down.

additional_notes: Used to highlight one specific person/thing within a broader group or situation (similar to “especially”). Often follows a general statement: “... en particulier.” Can also be used before a noun phrase: “en particulier + noun” or after the item you’re emphasizing.
target_language_example: J’aime les fruits, en particulier les fraises.
native_language_example: I like fruit, in particular strawberries.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true only to some extent, not completely. Often followed by a phrase like “à cause de…” (because of) or used with verbs like “expliquer” (to explain) and “dépendre” (to depend): “en partie à cause de…”, “en partie parce que…”.
target_language_example: C’est en partie vrai, mais pas complètement.
native_language_example: It’s partly true, but not completely.

additional_notes: Used to mention something briefly without focusing on it. Commonly paired with verbs like « dire/mentionner/ajouter » (to say/mention/add). Can also appear after a noun phrase to mean “on the way/by the way,” but it usually keeps the idea of something said or done briefly.
target_language_example: Je te dis ça en passant, mais demain il y a une réunion à 9h.
native_language_example: I’m telling you this in passing, but tomorrow there’s a meeting at 9 a.m.

meaning: in the process of; on the way to; about to (become/do).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive or a noun to describe something that is developing and likely to happen soon. Often suggests a change that is underway (e.g., a project nearing completion, a company close to bankruptcy, someone about to become something). Similar in idea to "être sur le point de," but "en passe de" can feel a bit more like "well on the way to."
target_language_example: L’entreprise est en passe de faire faillite.
native_language_example: The company is on the verge of going bankrupt.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens without stopping or very frequently. Often follows the verb or appears at the end of the sentence: « Il travaille en permanence. » It’s common with verbs like être, travailler, parler, surveiller, changer.
target_language_example: Il regarde son téléphone en permanence.
native_language_example: He’s on his phone all the time.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically present (not by phone/email) or that you do something yourself. Common after verbs like « venir » (to come) and « rencontrer » (to meet): « venir en personne », « rencontrer qqn en personne ».
target_language_example: Je préfère te parler en personne.
native_language_example: I prefer to talk to you in person.

additional_notes: Used to mean “seen in relation to other things” (not in isolation). Common after verbs like mettre/garder/prendre: « mettre en perspective » (put into perspective), « garder en perspective » (keep in perspective), « prendre du recul et mettre en perspective » (step back and put things in perspective). Often used in more formal writing/speech.
target_language_example: Il faut mettre ce problème en perspective.
native_language_example: We need to put this problem into perspective.

additional_notes: Used to say something is already positioned correctly, ready, or already arranged/implemented. Common with verbs like être (to be), mettre (to put), and se mettre (to get). Examples: « tout est en place » (everything is in place/ready), « mettre en place » (to set up/put in place, e.g., a system or plan).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : tout est en place.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything is in place.

additional_notes: Used to say an activity happens outside (not indoors). Common with verbs like faire (faire du sport en plein air), manger (manger en plein air), or with nouns like cinéma/théâtre: un cinéma en plein air (an outdoor movie theater).
target_language_example: On va déjeuner en plein air s’il fait beau.
native_language_example: We’re going to have lunch outdoors if the weather is nice.

additional_notes: Very common phrase. Use it to add another piece of information ("besides/what’s more") or to talk about an extra quantity ("an extra one/more"). Often appears with quantities: "en plus" = "more", "deux en plus" = "two more". In negative sentences, French often uses "ne... plus" ("no longer"), which is different from "en plus".
target_language_example: Je veux un café, et en plus un croissant.
native_language_example: I want a coffee, and also a croissant.

additional_notes: Used to add an extra item to what’s already mentioned. Followed by a noun, pronoun, or an infinitive (en plus de + nom/pronom/verbe à l’infinitif). Often equivalent to 'as well as'. Example patterns: « en plus de ça » (besides that), « en plus de moi » (besides me), « en plus de travailler… » (in addition to working…).
target_language_example: En plus de son travail, elle suit des cours de français.
native_language_example: In addition to her job, she’s taking French classes.

meaning: in practice; practically; in real life.
additional_notes: Used to contrast theory/ideas with what actually happens or works in reality (often after talking about rules, plans, or principles). Common in explanations: “En théorie…, mais en pratique…”. It can also introduce a practical method or concrete steps.
target_language_example: En théorie, c’est simple, mais en pratique, ça prend du temps.
native_language_example: In theory, it’s simple, but in practice, it takes time.

additional_notes: Used to say what should be true according to rules, logic, or the plan, sometimes implying that reality may be different ("in theory"). Often followed by a contrast like "mais..." (but...).
target_language_example: En principe, le magasin est ouvert le lundi, mais aujourd’hui il est fermé.
native_language_example: In principle, the store is open on Mondays, but today it’s closed.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens away from other people (not in public), or in a private setting/message. Common with verbs like parler/discuter (to talk), rencontrer (to meet), and also to contrast with en public (“in public”).
target_language_example: On peut en parler en privé ?
native_language_example: Can we talk about it in private?

additional_notes: Used to say you’ll look at, study, or discuss something deeply and in detail (not just briefly). Common with verbs like analyser, étudier, discuter, examiner. Can also be used literally for physical depth (e.g., a wound or a drill hole), but it’s very often figurative.
target_language_example: On va analyser le problème en profondeur.
native_language_example: We’re going to analyze the problem in depth.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is physically there at the same time, often in more formal contexts. Very commonly appears as "en présence de + noun/pronoun" (in the presence of). Can also be used without "de" when the context is clear (meaning "when people are present").
target_language_example: Je n’en parlerai pas en présence de tes parents.
native_language_example: I won’t talk about it in front of your parents.

meaning: in the presence of; with (someone) present.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is there and able to see/hear what happens. Common in formal contexts (meetings, legal/official language), but also usable in everyday speech. Often followed by a person or group: en présence de ma mère, en présence des témoins.
target_language_example: Je préfère en parler en présence de tout le monde.
native_language_example: I’d rather talk about it in everyone’s presence (with everyone present).

additional_notes: Used to say something happens in front of other people (not in private). Often contrasted with « en privé » (in private). Common with verbs like « parler », « apparaître », « se disputer », « embrasser », etc. It can describe doing something where others can see or hear you.
target_language_example: Je n’aime pas parler de ça en public.
native_language_example: I don’t like talking about that in public.

meaning: as (in the capacity of); in the role of.
additional_notes: Used to state someone’s official role, title, or function (often in formal or administrative contexts). It’s commonly followed by a job/role noun: « en qualité de responsable », « en qualité de témoin ». Similar to « en tant que », but « en qualité de » sounds more formal.
target_language_example: Je vous écris en qualité de responsable du service client.
native_language_example: I’m writing to you in my capacity as the head of customer service.

additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify what you’re saying, meaning “kind of” or “more or less.” Often comes right after the verb or near the part you want to qualify. It can introduce an explanation, comparison, or approximation.
target_language_example: C’est, en quelque sorte, une solution provisoire.
native_language_example: It’s, in a way, a temporary solution.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the specific thing being talked about or considered (often in a slightly formal tone). Common in phrases like « la personne en question » (the person in question), « le document en question » (the document in question), or « le sujet en question » (the subject/topic in question).
target_language_example: La personne en question n’est pas encore arrivée.
native_language_example: The person in question hasn’t arrived yet.

additional_notes: Used to give the cause or reason for something. Usually followed by a noun or noun phrase (e.g., en raison de la pluie). It’s more formal than "à cause de" (which can sound more negative), and is common in writing, news, and official contexts.
target_language_example: Le match est annulé en raison de la pluie.
native_language_example: The game is cancelled because of the rain.

meaning: in a line; lined up (one behind the other).
additional_notes: Used to describe people or objects arranged in an orderly line, often for school, an event, entering somewhere, etc. Common with verbs like "se mettre" (to get into line) or "se ranger" (to line up): "Mettez-vous en rang !"
target_language_example: Les enfants se mettent en rang devant la classe.
native_language_example: The children line up in front of the classroom.

additional_notes: A fairly formal prepositional phrase used to compare two things or to set something “in relation to” something else. Often followed by a noun or pronoun: « en regard de + nom/pronom ». In everyday speech, people often use « par rapport à » instead.
target_language_example: En regard de l’an dernier, les prix ont augmenté.
native_language_example: Compared to last year, prices have gone up.

meaning: to leave it at that; to stop there.
additional_notes: Used to say you’ll stop a discussion, explanation, action, or conflict at that point (no further steps, details, or arguments). Often used with a subject like “On va en rester là.” It can sound neutral (ending politely) or firm (refusing to continue).
target_language_example: On va en rester là, d’accord ?
native_language_example: Let’s leave it at that, OK?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "être" to say you are late (e.g., "Je suis en retard"). It can refer to being late for an appointment/class, or to something running behind schedule ("Le train est en retard"). Common opposite: "en avance" (early/ahead of schedule).
target_language_example: Désolé, je suis en retard de dix minutes.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm ten minutes late.

meaning: in return; in exchange (for); back (as a reply/response).
additional_notes: Used to talk about reciprocity or what you get/give back. Common after verbs like donner (to give), recevoir (to receive), offrir (to offer), demander (to ask), or as a set phrase with merci: « Merci, en retour ! » (“Thanks, same to you!”). It can also mean “back” in the sense of a response: « Je n’ai rien eu en retour » (“I didn’t get anything back / in response”).
target_language_example: Je t’aide aujourd’hui, et en retour tu m’aideras demain.
native_language_example: I’ll help you today, and in return you’ll help me tomorrow.

meaning: set back; withdrawn; in the background.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something that is not in the foreground or not actively participating. It can be literal (physically set back: a house/building) or figurative (staying reserved or keeping a low profile). Common with verbs like être/rester (to be/stay): « rester en retrait » = to stay back / keep to oneself.
target_language_example: Pendant la réunion, il est resté en retrait.
native_language_example: During the meeting, he stayed in the background.

additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb être to say someone is retired (Être à la retraite is also very common). Not to be confused with une retraite (a pension/retreat) or une retraite spirituelle (a spiritual retreat).
target_language_example: Mon père est en retraite depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: My father has been retired for two years.

meaning: to get over it; to recover from it; (often) to be able to believe it again.
additional_notes: “En” refers to something already mentioned or understood (an event, shock, news, etc.). Very common in the negative expression “ne pas en revenir” = “can’t get over it / can’t believe it.” You’ll often see it with an indirect object: “s’en remettre” is similar, but “en revenir” is especially natural for surprise or shock.
target_language_example: Je n’en reviens pas !
native_language_example: I can’t believe it! / I can’t get over it!

additional_notes: Most often used with negation to mean “not at all / in no way”: e.g., « ne … en rien » = “not … at all.” It can also appear after verbs like « aider » or « changer » to emphasize “in any way.” Although it literally contains « rien » (“nothing”), the natural English translation is usually “at all,” not “in nothing.”
target_language_example: Ça ne m’aide en rien.
native_language_example: That doesn’t help me at all.

meaning: on the way; heading to (a place).
additional_notes: Used to say you are traveling toward a destination or that something is underway. Common in phrases like « Je suis en route » (I’m on my way) or « en route pour + place » (on the way to + place). It can also describe something starting/being in progress (« un projet en route »).
target_language_example: Je suis en route pour l’aéroport.
native_language_example: I’m on my way to the airport.

meaning: in order; up to date; compliant (with rules).
additional_notes: Used to say something is properly arranged or meets requirements. Common with documents, payments, paperwork, and legal/administrative situations: "être en règle" = to be in compliance; "mettre en règle" = to bring into compliance; "en règle avec" + organization/authority = up to date/registered/paid (e.g., with taxes, insurance).
target_language_example: Pour conduire, il faut être en règle avec l’assurance.
native_language_example: To drive, you need to be up to date with (have) insurance.

additional_notes: Used to correct, clarify, or contrast with what was just said or what people might think. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence ("En réalité, ...") or after the verb. Similar in meaning to "en fait," but "en réalité" can feel a bit more emphatic/formal.
target_language_example: En réalité, je n’ai pas le temps aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Actually, I don’t have time today.

meaning: in reserve; held back as a spare/backup.
additional_notes: Used to say something is kept aside and available if needed (extra supplies, spare players, backup money, etc.). Common with verbs like garder/mettre/avoir: « garder en réserve », « mettre en réserve », « avoir en réserve ». Also used in the expression « de réserve » (e.g., « roue de réserve » = spare tire), but « en réserve » emphasizes that it’s being kept aside.
target_language_example: J’ai de l’eau en réserve au cas où.
native_language_example: I have some water in reserve just in case.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a brief summary or conclusion of what was just said or written. Common in both speech and writing. Often followed by a comma: “En résumé, …”. Similar options: “Bref, …” (more informal: “in short”), “En bref, …”.
target_language_example: En résumé, on part demain matin.
native_language_example: In summary, we’re leaving tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done privately, without other people knowing. Common with verbs like faire (to do), garder (to keep), se voir (to see each other), or parler (to talk). You can often place it after the verb: « Ils se voient en secret. »
target_language_example: Ils se sont mariés en secret.
native_language_example: They got married in secret.

meaning: as a sign of; as a token of.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that an action or gesture shows a feeling, intention, or message. Often followed by a noun: en signe de respect / paix / gratitude (as a sign of respect/peace/gratitude).
target_language_example: Il a serré la main de son voisin en signe de paix.
native_language_example: He shook his neighbor’s hand as a sign of peace.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something without talking or making noise. Often follows a verb (e.g., attendre en silence, marcher en silence) and can also be used after nouns (un moment en silence). It’s neutral/formal enough for most situations.
target_language_example: Ils ont attendu en silence pendant quelques minutes.
native_language_example: They waited in silence for a few minutes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something considered on its own, independently of other factors ("as such"). Often appears in contrasts like "pas ... en soi" ("not ... in itself") or "rien en soi" ("nothing in itself"). Also common as "en soi-même" ("in itself").
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas une mauvaise idée en soi, mais c’est trop cher.
native_language_example: It’s not a bad idea in itself, but it’s too expensive.

meaning: in his/her/its time; back in the day (for that person/thing).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone or something as it was during the period when that person was active or when that thing existed/was popular. Often implies "at the time" or "back then" and is commonly used when comparing past and present. The possessive changes with the subject: en mon temps (in my day), en ton temps (in your day), en leur temps (in their day).
target_language_example: En son temps, il était un grand sportif.
native_language_example: In his day, he was a great athlete.

meaning: to get out (of it/there); to come out of something.
additional_notes: En refers back to a place, situation, or problem already mentioned (roughly “out of it/from there”). Very common in the reflexive form s’en sortir: “to manage,” “to cope,” “to make it through.”
target_language_example: Je veux en sortir, mais je ne sais pas comment.
native_language_example: I want to get out of it, but I don’t know how.

additional_notes: Used for things arranged/connected so they happen or are processed one after another (not in parallel), or for repeated actions done consecutively. Common in technical contexts (electronics: circuit en série; manufacturing), and also in everyday speech (travailler en série = do a bunch in a row). Contrast with « en parallèle » (in parallel).
target_language_example: J’ai enchaîné trois réunions en série ce matin.
native_language_example: I had three meetings back-to-back this morning.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a role, status, or function (who/what someone is in a given situation). Often followed by a noun or a stressed pronoun: « en tant que médecin », « en tant que responsable », « en tant que moi ». Common in formal or neutral contexts; in casual speech people may also say « comme » in some cases.
target_language_example: En tant que professeur, je dois être à l’heure.
native_language_example: As a teacher, I have to be on time.

meaning: in times of; during (a period of).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a situation or period characterized by something (often difficult): en temps de guerre (in wartime), en temps de crise (in times of crisis). It’s commonly followed by a noun (guerre, crise, pandémie, etc.).
target_language_example: En temps de crise, il faut économiser.
native_language_example: In times of crisis, you have to save money.

meaning: at the right time; when the time is right.
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen later, at an appropriate or planned moment (not necessarily soon). Common in formal or neutral contexts, often to reassure someone or to avoid giving a specific date/time.
target_language_example: Je te donnerai plus de détails en temps voulu.
native_language_example: I’ll give you more details when the time is right.

meaning: dressed / in an outfit (often for a specific occasion).
