additional_notes: Used with "être" to say someone is dressed a certain way or wearing a particular outfit, often implying appropriate attire (e.g., in uniform, in formalwear, in sportswear). Common patterns: "être en tenue" (be dressed), "en tenue de..." (in ... attire), "en tenue de sport" (in sportswear), "en tenue de soirée" (in evening wear). Not the same as "en train de" (in the middle of doing).
target_language_example: Je suis en tenue de sport, je vais courir.
native_language_example: I’m in sportswear; I’m going to go running.

additional_notes: Used to specify the aspect or criteria you are talking about (often in more formal or explanatory speech and writing). It’s frequently followed by a noun or noun phrase: « en termes de prix/de qualité/de sécurité ». You can often replace it with « concernant » or « au niveau de » (the latter is common but sometimes considered less formal).
target_language_example: En termes de prix, cet ordinateur est très intéressant.
native_language_example: In terms of price, this computer is very appealing.

additional_notes: Used to contrast an idea or rule with what happens in reality. Often implies that the practical situation is different: "En théorie, oui…" (= but in practice, not really). Can be placed at the start of the sentence or after the verb.
target_language_example: En théorie, ça devrait marcher, mais on verra.
native_language_example: In theory, it should work, but we’ll see.

additional_notes: Used to give the total amount/number after adding things up. Common in shopping, receipts, time or quantity summaries: « Ça fait 20 euros en tout. » It can be used alone at the end of a sentence to mean “altogether/overall.” Often interchangeable with « au total » or « en tout et pour tout » (more emphatic).
target_language_example: Ça fait trente euros en tout.
native_language_example: That comes to thirty euros in total.

additional_notes: Used to move the conversation along or to qualify what you just said. Common in speech to mean “anyway” (changing topic, concluding), or “at least” (setting a minimum or a sure point). Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence: “En tout cas, …” / “…, en tout cas.”
target_language_example: En tout cas, on se retrouve à 18 h.
native_language_example: Anyway, we’ll meet up at 6 p.m.

additional_notes: Used almost always with the verb **être**: **être en train de + infinitive** = ‘to be in the process of doing something (right now)’. It emphasizes that an action is happening at this moment (French often just uses the present tense without it). You can negate it: **Je ne suis pas en train de…**
target_language_example: Je suis en train de préparer le dîner.
native_language_example: I’m in the middle of making dinner.

additional_notes: Used to describe something positioned crosswise rather than straight (often with verbs like « mettre » / « se mettre »). Very common in the pattern « en travers de + [place/object] » = “across / across the way of”. Not the same as « de travers », which usually means “crooked / not straight” or “in a bad way”.
target_language_example: Il a mis une chaise en travers de la porte.
native_language_example: He put a chair across the doorway.

additional_notes: Commonly used in phrases like « avoir [quelque chose] en tête » (to have something in mind / to be thinking about something) and « être en tête » (to be in the lead / in first place). It can also refer to position at the front: « en tête de la file » (at the front of the line).
target_language_example: J’ai une idée en tête.
native_language_example: I have an idea in mind.

meaning: in the blink of an eye; very quickly.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens very fast, often unexpectedly. Common in everyday speech. Note the spelling: d'œil (with œ). Similar idea to English “in a blink.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : je reviens en un clin d’œil.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll be back in a blink.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a brief summary or a single-word description. Often followed by a colon or a short phrase (e.g., "En un mot : parfait."). Common in both speech and writing; slightly formal in tone.
target_language_example: En un mot, c’était incroyable.
native_language_example: In short, it was incredible.

additional_notes: Common expression to say something happens very fast. Literally “in a nothing of time,” but the natural English equivalent is “in no time.” Often used with the near future or past: "Je reviens en un rien de temps" (I’ll be right back), "Il a fini en un rien de temps" (He finished in no time).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je serai là en un rien de temps.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll be there in no time.

additional_notes: Used to qualify what you’re saying and show it’s true only from a particular point of view (not completely). Often followed by a contrasting idea: « en un sens…, mais… ». Also common: « en un sens, oui/non ».
target_language_example: En un sens, tu as raison, mais ce n’est pas si simple.
native_language_example: In a way, you’re right, but it’s not that simple.

meaning: “in one piece” (without being broken or harmed).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something arrived safely and undamaged, often after a trip, accident, or difficult situation. Literally “in a single piece,” and it can describe both people and objects.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je suis rentré en un seul morceau.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I got home in one piece.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens almost instantly. Literally “in a lightning bolt,” but in English it’s usually translated as “in a flash” or “in no time.” Often used with verbs like faire, partir, finir, comprendre, etc.
target_language_example: Il a fini ses devoirs en un éclair.
native_language_example: He finished his homework in a flash.

additional_notes: Used to say an effort or attempt didn’t work or had no result. Often follows a verb like essayer (to try), chercher (to look for), attendre (to wait), or appeler (to call): « J’ai essayé en vain. » It’s fairly formal/neutral in tone.
target_language_example: J’ai cherché mes clés en vain.
native_language_example: I looked for my keys in vain.

meaning: to get to the point; to come to the matter at hand.
additional_notes: Used when you want to stop introductions or side details and talk about what really matters. Often said as an imperative: « Venons-en au fait. » (Let’s get to the point). « Le fait » here means “the matter/issue,” not a literal “fact.”
target_language_example: Venons-en au fait : qu’est-ce que tu me proposes exactement ?
native_language_example: Let’s get to the point: what exactly are you proposing to me?

meaning: to come to (doing/saying something); to end up (doing something).
additional_notes: Used to show a progression or change that leads to a result, often after some time or difficulty. Common pattern: "en venir à" + infinitive (en venir à comprendre / en venir à dire / en venir à penser). Can also mean "to get to the point of" doing something.
target_language_example: Avec le temps, j’en suis venu à comprendre pourquoi il a fait ça.
native_language_example: With time, I came to understand why he did that.

additional_notes: Used after the verb (often with « être », « rester », « maintenir », « garder ») to say someone/something is alive or still exists. Often used in contrasts like « vivant » vs « mort ». Can also be used more broadly for things that are still active or functioning (e.g., a tradition, a project).
target_language_example: Il est toujours en vie.
native_language_example: He is still alive.

meaning: in effect; in force (currently valid, usually about laws/rules).
additional_notes: Used to say that a law, regulation, rule, policy, or agreement is currently active and applies. Common with verbs like « être » (to be) and « entrer » (to come into effect): « La loi est en vigueur » / « La loi entre en vigueur le 1er janvier ». Also used in « en vigueur dans… » (in force in…).
target_language_example: Cette loi est en vigueur depuis 2020.
native_language_example: This law has been in effect since 2020.

meaning: in town; downtown; in the city.
additional_notes: Used to say you are (or are going) in the town/city center, as opposed to being in the countryside or in the suburbs. Common with verbs like être (to be), aller (to go), sortir (to go out). Depending on context it can mean “in town” (any city) or specifically “downtown/city center.”
target_language_example: On va en ville ce soir.
native_language_example: We’re going into town tonight.

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech to say something is done fast or rushed. Often used with verbs like faire/prendre/manger: « Je le fais en vitesse » (I’ll do it quickly). Similar to « vite » or « rapidement », but can imply doing it a bit hastily. Also seen in « vite fait, en vitesse » (quickly, just to get it done).
target_language_example: Je mange un sandwich en vitesse avant de partir.
native_language_example: I’m eating a sandwich quickly before leaving.

meaning: on the way to; in the process of (becoming/doing).
additional_notes: Used with "être" to describe something that is developing or changing (often in formal/news style), e.g., "en voie de disparition" = "endangered" (lit. on the way to disappearing). Often followed by a noun ("en voie de disparition", "en voie de développement") or an infinitive introduced by "être en voie de + infinitive" in more formal contexts.
target_language_example: Cette espèce est en voie de disparition.
native_language_example: This species is endangered.

additional_notes: Used to point out or hand over something, often in response to a request. Very common with an implied noun: « En voilà ! » (“Here you go!”) or with a number/quantifier: « En voilà deux. » (“Here are two.”). It can also mean “There you have it/That’s it.” when concluding or confirming.
target_language_example: Tu veux des fraises ? En voilà !
native_language_example: Do you want some strawberries? Here you go!

meaning: to be angry at (someone); to hold it against (someone).
additional_notes: Used mainly in the pattern « en vouloir à [person] ». It means you blame someone or you’re upset with them. Common with « Je ne t’en veux pas » (“I’m not mad at you / I don’t hold it against you”). The « en » doesn’t translate directly; it refers to “it/that” (the thing you’re upset about).
target_language_example: Je ne t’en veux pas.
native_language_example: I’m not mad at you.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French to correct yourself, add emphasis, or introduce what you really think (similar to “actually” or “honestly” in English). Often placed at the beginning of a sentence: “En vrai, …”. More informal than “en réalité” or “à vrai dire”.
target_language_example: En vrai, je préfère rester à la maison.
native_language_example: Honestly, I’d rather stay at home.

additional_notes: Used to say something can be seen or is approaching: « être en vue » (to be in sight). Common in travel/transport contexts: « La gare est en vue ». Also appears in the longer expression « en vue de + infinitive/noun » meaning “in order to / with a view to,” and « avoir en vue » meaning “to have in mind / to be planning.”
target_language_example: La côte est en vue.
native_language_example: The coast is in sight.

meaning: 'with a view to' / 'for' (with the aim of).
additional_notes: Used to express purpose or intention, often in more formal or written French. It is commonly followed by a noun ("en vue de la réunion") or by an infinitive introduced by "de" ("en vue d’acheter"; note the apostrophe: "de" → "d’" before a vowel sound). Similar in meaning to "afin de" or "dans le but de".
target_language_example: Il étudie en vue de passer l’examen.
native_language_example: He is studying in order to take the exam.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something as the real truth or a correction/clarification (similar to “actually” or “in fact”). It sounds a bit formal or literary in everyday conversation; you’ll more often hear "en fait" for “actually.”
target_language_example: En vérité, je ne sais pas quoi faire.
native_language_example: Actually, I don’t know what to do.

meaning: old enough to; of an age to.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has reached the required/appropriate age to do something. Most often followed by an infinitive: « en âge de + infinitive » (e.g., en âge de conduire). Can also be used with a noun: « en âge de + noun » (e.g., en âge de voter).
target_language_example: Elle n’est pas encore en âge de conduire.
native_language_example: She isn’t old enough to drive yet.

additional_notes: Used to talk about giving, doing, or receiving something as a trade or return for something else. Commonly followed by "de" + noun or infinitive: "en échange de" (in exchange for). It can also stand alone when the other side of the trade is understood from context.
target_language_example: Je te prête mon livre en échange de ton stylo.
native_language_example: I’ll lend you my book in exchange for your pen.

meaning: in a state/condition; fit/capable (often: en état de…).
additional_notes: Often used with **de**: **en état de + infinitive** = “able to / fit to” do something (usually meaning physically/mentally capable): *Je ne suis pas en état de…* It can also mean “in working order / ready to use” for objects: *un appareil en état*. Common related phrases: **mettre/remettre en état** = “to put back in working order / restore.”
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas en état de conduire.
native_language_example: I’m not fit to drive.

meaning: in a state/condition to; able to (be in a condition to).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something’s condition, often followed by a noun ("en état de choc" = in shock) or by an infinitive with "être" ("être en état de + infinitive" = to be able/fit to do something). Common in formal or official contexts (health, safety, legal): "en état de nuire" (able to cause harm), "en état d’ivresse" (drunk), "en état de marche" (in working order). Note the fixed preposition: "en état de" (often becomes "en état d’" before a vowel).
target_language_example: Après l’accident, il n’était pas en état de conduire.
native_language_example: After the accident, he wasn’t in a condition to drive.

additional_notes: Used to say that a device, machine, system, or vehicle is functioning properly (the opposite of « en panne »). Often used with « être »: « Le chauffage est en état de marche. » You may also see « mettre/remettre en état de marche » (to start up / get working again).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, l’ascenseur est en état de marche.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, the elevator is working.

meaning: to be involved; to be at a certain point (in a process).
additional_notes: Uses the pronoun en (“of it / about it”) to refer back to something already mentioned (a project, task, story, etc.). Very common in questions like « Où en es-tu ? » (“How far along are you?”) and with a stage/limit: « J’en suis à… » (“I’m at…”). In spoken French, you may also hear it to mean “to be in / to join”: « T’en es ? » (“Are you in?”).
target_language_example: Où en es-tu avec ton rapport ?
native_language_example: How far along are you with your report?

meaning: a snack; a light bite to eat.
additional_notes: Used as a noun: « un en-cas ». It refers to something small you eat between meals (a quick snack). Don’t confuse it with « en cas de… » (without a hyphen), which means “in case of…”.
target_language_example: Je prends un en-cas avant le sport.
native_language_example: I’m having a snack before working out.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize repetition or something happening repeatedly. It can describe actions (doing something repeatedly), events (something keeps happening), or thoughts (going over something repeatedly). Often placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Il me pose la même question encore et encore.
native_language_example: He asks me the same question again and again.

additional_notes: Used to strengthen a negative statement or show something is even less likely/possible than what was just said, often after a negative: « Je ne… pas, encore moins… ». In English it’s frequently translated as “let alone.”
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas le temps de cuisiner, encore moins de faire un gâteau.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to cook, let alone make a cake.

additional_notes: Used to intensify a comparison. Often followed by an adjective/adverb in the comparative: « encore plus grand(e) » (even bigger), « encore plus vite » (even faster), « encore plus tard » (even later). You can also use it with « de » + noun to mean a greater amount: « encore plus de temps » (even more time).
target_language_example: Je veux encore plus de temps.
native_language_example: I want even more time.

additional_notes: Introduces a correction, limitation, or nuance to what was just said (similar to “mind you” or “that said”). Often followed by the subjunctive, especially when it expresses doubt or a restriction: « Encore que ce soit vrai… » (“Even if that’s true…”). In everyday speech, you may also hear it with the indicative, especially when the speaker treats the point as more factual. Don’t confuse with « encore » alone (“again / still / more”) or « bien que » (“although”), which is more standard and always takes the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Je peux venir demain, encore que je ne sois pas sûr d’avoir le temps.
native_language_example: I can come tomorrow, though I’m not sure I’ll have time.

additional_notes: Used to repeat something or do something again. Common in speech to mean “again” or “let me repeat,” and it can sound slightly insistent depending on tone. In formal writing, you may also see “encore une fois” used like “once again” to re-emphasize a point.
target_language_example: Encore une fois, je ne suis pas d’accord.
native_language_example: Once again, I don’t agree.

meaning: a spoiled child; (figuratively) a pampered favorite.
additional_notes: Literally “spoiled child.” Most often describes a child who gets everything they want (“spoiled brat”). It can also be used figuratively for a person who is treated as the favorite or is especially indulged (e.g., “the darling” of a group/company). The feminine form is *enfant gâtée* (same pronunciation).
target_language_example: Il est enfant gâté : ses parents lui achètent tout ce qu’il veut.
native_language_example: He’s a spoiled child: his parents buy him everything he wants.

additional_notes: Means a child with no brothers or sisters. Often used with “être” or in questions about family: “Je suis enfant unique.” / “Tu es enfant unique ?” You can also specify gender: “fille unique” (only daughter) or “fils unique” (only son).
target_language_example: Je suis enfant unique, donc je n’ai pas de frères ni de sœurs.
native_language_example: I’m an only child, so I don’t have any brothers or sisters.

additional_notes: Literally “to hear voices.” Very commonly used in a mental-health context to mean hearing voices that aren’t there (auditory hallucinations). You can also say “entendre une voix” (to hear a voice). In everyday context it can be literal too (e.g., hearing people talking from far away), but the plural often suggests hallucinations.
target_language_example: Il dit qu’il entend des voix depuis quelques jours.
native_language_example: He says he has been hearing voices for a few days.

meaning: to hear (it) said; to hear about (something) through others.
additional_notes: Used to report information you heard from other people (hearsay), often introducing a clause with "que": "J’ai entendu dire que..." (= I heard that...). Common with "on" to mean “people say / word is”: "On entend dire que...".
target_language_example: J’ai entendu dire que ce restaurant est très bon.
native_language_example: I heard that this restaurant is very good.

meaning: to hear (people) say that; to hear that.
additional_notes: Used to report hearsay or something you’ve heard from others, without guaranteeing it’s true. Often followed by a clause with "que" (e.g., "J’ai entendu dire que..."). In everyday English it’s close to "I heard that..." / "I’ve heard that...".
target_language_example: J’ai entendu dire que ce restaurant est très bon.
native_language_example: I heard that this restaurant is very good.

additional_notes: Very often used with **de**: **entendre parler de + noun** = “to hear about.” Example: *J’ai entendu parler de ce film.* Note: **entendre** usually means “to hear,” not “to understand” (that’s **comprendre**).
target_language_example: J’ai entendu parler de cette exposition, mais je n’y suis jamais allé.
native_language_example: I’ve heard about that exhibition, but I’ve never gone there.

meaning: to hear about; to hear of.
additional_notes: Used when you learn about something/someone indirectly (from other people, the news, etc.), not by meeting them or experiencing it yourself. It’s often followed by a noun or a person: «J’ai entendu parler de ce restaurant / de Marie.» In questions/negatives: «Tu as déjà entendu parler de… ?» / «Je n’en ai jamais entendu parler.»
target_language_example: J’ai entendu parler de ce film, mais je ne l’ai pas encore vu.
native_language_example: I’ve heard about that movie, but I haven’t seen it yet.

additional_notes: A set phrase meaning a party to celebrate a man’s last days as a single man before his wedding. Often shortened to "un EVG" (initialism). For a woman, you’ll hear "enterrement de vie de jeune fille" (often "EVJF").
target_language_example: On organise un enterrement de vie de garçon pour Julien samedi soir.
native_language_example: We’re organizing a bachelor party for Julien on Saturday night.

additional_notes: Used to mention one or more examples in a list without naming everything. It can refer to things (among other things) or people (among others). Often placed after what it qualifies: “J’ai acheté du pain, du fromage, entre autres.”
target_language_example: J’ai visité Paris et Lyon, entre autres.
native_language_example: I visited Paris and Lyon, among other places.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something confidential or private (like “off the record”). It can also mean “among ourselves” when speaking about a group. Often appears as “Entre nous, …” at the start of a sentence.
target_language_example: Entre nous, je n’aime pas beaucoup ce restaurant.
native_language_example: Just between you and me, I don’t like this restaurant very much.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens during the time between two events. Often placed at the start of a sentence (followed by a comma), but it can also appear mid-sentence. Common in both spoken and written French; note the hyphen in the usual spelling: « entre-temps ».
target_language_example: Je reviens dans une heure ; entre-temps, tu peux commencer le dîner.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in an hour; in the meantime, you can start dinner.

meaning: 'to come into play' (to start being involved or important).
additional_notes: Used when a factor, rule, person, or element starts to matter in a situation. Common in explanations and discussions: "Quand X entre en jeu..." Also used in the sense of "to come into effect" for rules or conditions.
target_language_example: À partir de maintenant, d’autres facteurs entrent en jeu.
native_language_example: From now on, other factors come into play.

meaning: to come on stage; to enter the scene (appear).
additional_notes: Used literally in theater/performance when someone comes onto the stage. Figuratively, it means someone or something appears and starts playing an important role (in a story, situation, politics, etc.). Often used with a person or idea as the subject: « Puis X est entré en scène… ».
target_language_example: À ce moment-là, le détective entre en scène et tout change.
native_language_example: At that moment, the detective enters the scene and everything changes.

additional_notes: Used when you have flowers delivered to someone (for a birthday, to say thank you, to congratulate someone, or as a sympathy gesture). You can specify the recipient with "à" (envoyer des fleurs à quelqu’un).
target_language_example: Je vais envoyer des fleurs à ma mère pour son anniversaire.
native_language_example: I’m going to send flowers to my mom for her birthday.

additional_notes: Literal sense is “species/type of,” used before a noun: « une espèce de + nom » = “a kind of + noun” (often meaning “something like…”). In insults, it’s said directly to someone: « Espèce de + nom ! » = “You (noun)!” and is rude/insulting (e.g., « Espèce d’idiot ! »). Note the form « espèce d’ » before a vowel or silent h (e.g., « espèce d’imbécile »).
target_language_example: C’est une espèce de café, mais plus doux.
native_language_example: It’s a kind of coffee, but milder.

meaning: to always try; to keep trying.
additional_notes: Compositional: "essayer" = "to try" and "toujours" = "always." In natural French, you’ll more often see the adverb placed after the verb in an imperative ("Essaie toujours de…" = "Keep trying to…") or before an infinitive ("toujours essayer de…" = "to always try to…").
target_language_example: Essaie toujours de garder espoir.
native_language_example: Keep trying to stay hopeful.

meaning: to try and see; to see if you can (do something).
additional_notes: Very common in casual spoken French as a shortened form of "essayer de voir" (or "essayer de" + verb). Used when you’re not sure yet and will check/attempt something (e.g., availability, possibility). In more careful or written French, prefer: "Je vais essayer de voir si…" / "J’essaie de voir…"
target_language_example: Je vais essayer voir si je peux venir demain.
native_language_example: I’ll try and see if I can come tomorrow.

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of **passer** with **être** (used for many movement/change-of-state verbs). It can mean that time has gone by (**Le temps est passé**), that an event is over (**La mode est passée** = “The trend is over/outdated”), or that someone came by briefly (**Il est passé chez moi** = “He stopped by my place”). With **être**, the past participle agrees with the subject: **est passé** (m. sg.), **est passée** (f. sg.), **sont passés** (m. pl./mixed), **sont passées** (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Le temps est passé très vite.
native_language_example: Time went by very quickly.

additional_notes: Used to form questions, most commonly in the structure **est-ce que + subject + verb**: *Est-ce que tu viens ?* (“Are you coming?”). It can also be used without **que** in short questions like *Est-ce possible ?* (“Is it possible?”). The hyphen is part of the spelling: **est-ce**.
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu comprends ?
native_language_example: Do you understand?

meaning: Question marker used to form yes/no questions (often like “do/does…?”).
additional_notes: Placed at the start of a sentence, followed by normal word order (subject + verb). It’s a common, neutral way to ask questions: “Est-ce que tu… ?” You can also use it with question words: “Où est-ce que tu vas ?” = “Where are you going?” In more informal speech, it’s often replaced by rising intonation: “Tu viens ?”
target_language_example: Est-ce que vous avez une réservation ?
native_language_example: Do you have a reservation?

additional_notes: Used in formal or written questions as subject–verb inversion of "il est" ("he/it is"). Common in phrases like "Est-il possible de… ?" (Is it possible to…?). In everyday speech, people often use "Il est… ?" or "Est-ce qu’il est… ?" instead.
target_language_example: Est-il prêt ?
native_language_example: Is he ready?

additional_notes: Often used in a neutral, general way (e.g., in science, philosophy, or formal speech). It can refer to humanity in general or to an individual person. Note the accent: « être » (to be) is usually written with a circumflex; without it (« estre ») is a misspelling in modern French.
target_language_example: Chaque être humain mérite le respect.
native_language_example: Every human being deserves respect.

additional_notes: Used at the end of a list to mean there are more similar items or details. Common in both speech and writing. Often shortened to “etc.” in writing. You can also say “et cetera” (more formal).
target_language_example: On a acheté du pain, du fromage, des fruits, et ainsi de suite.
native_language_example: We bought bread, cheese, fruit, and so on.

additional_notes: Used to react to what someone just said. Depending on tone, it can be neutral ("and then?", asking what happened next) or slightly confrontational/defensive ("so?", meaning "why does that matter?").
target_language_example: Il a oublié ? Et alors ? Ce n’est pas grave.
native_language_example: He forgot? So what? It’s not a big deal.

additional_notes: Often said as “Et comment !” as an emphatic reply meaning “of course” or “definitely,” sometimes with a slightly cheeky or enthusiastic tone. Used in spoken French more than in formal writing.
target_language_example: — Tu viens ce soir ? — Et comment !
native_language_example: — Are you coming tonight? — Absolutely!

additional_notes: Used when listing items and the next noun is plural: "et" = "and" and "des" is the plural indefinite article (often "some" in English, or just omitted in natural English). Common in shopping lists, menus, and descriptions: "du…, de la…, et des…"
target_language_example: J’ai acheté du pain, du fromage et des fruits.
native_language_example: I bought bread, cheese, and some fruit.

meaning: "and even then" / "and besides" / "what’s more" (depending on context).
additional_notes: Commonly used to add a correction or limitation ("and even then") or to add an extra point ("what’s more / besides"). Often comes after a statement: e.g., "Il a accepté, et encore…" to suggest doubt, or "Il faut être patient, et encore…" to mean "and even then" (it still might not be enough).
target_language_example: Il dit qu’il va venir, et encore, je n’en suis pas sûr.
native_language_example: He says he’s going to come, and even then, I’m not sure.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical idea or a suggestion. Very common in conversation: you can propose something (Et si on allait au cinéma ?), or wonder about a possibility (Et si je me trompais ?). Often followed by the imperfect (si + imparfait) for hypothetical situations, but it can also be followed by the present when making a simple suggestion.
target_language_example: Et si on prenait un café ?
native_language_example: How about we grab a coffee?

additional_notes: A formal, fixed expression (often in administrative or legal style) meaning “taking into account.” It’s typically followed by a noun phrase: « eu égard à + nom ». In everyday speech, you’ll more often hear « compte tenu de », « vu », or « étant donné ».
target_language_example: Eu égard à la situation, nous avons décidé de reporter la réunion.
native_language_example: Given the situation, we decided to postpone the meeting.

additional_notes: Stressed reflexive pronoun used for emphasis, meaning “they themselves.” Refers to a masculine or mixed-gender group (for an all-female group, use « elles-mêmes »). Often placed after the subject (« Ils l’ont fait eux-mêmes ») or after a noun to emphasize it (« les enfants eux-mêmes »). Hyphen is standard.
target_language_example: Ils ont réparé la voiture eux-mêmes.
native_language_example: They fixed the car themselves.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a woman someone was previously married to. Usually written with a hyphen (ex-femme). Commonly used with a possessive: « mon ex-femme » (“my ex-wife”). Note: many speakers also say « mon ex » (my ex), which can mean ex-wife or ex-girlfriend depending on context.
target_language_example: Mon ex-femme habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: My ex-wife lives in Lyon.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a man you were previously married to. Written with a hyphen (ex-mari). Feminine: ex-femme (ex-wife). Often used with a possessive: mon ex-mari, son ex-mari.
target_language_example: Mon ex-mari habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: My ex-husband lives in Lyon.

additional_notes: Used to apologize, to get someone’s attention, or to politely move past someone. Addressed to one person (“moi” = me). For more formal or for someone you don’t know well, use “excusez-moi”.
target_language_example: Excuse-moi, je suis en retard.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m late.

additional_notes: Formal or polite way to apologize, get someone’s attention, or politely interrupt. Literally “excuse me” (imperative + object pronoun). Often used with strangers, service staff, or in formal situations. More informal: « excuse-moi ».
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, où est la gare ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the train station?

meaning: speeding; going over the speed limit.
additional_notes: Used in formal contexts (police, road signs, insurance) to talk about speeding. Often appears with verbs like « faire un excès de vitesse » (to speed) or « être en excès de vitesse » (to be speeding). Not to be confused with « vitesse excessive » (excessive speed), a related but slightly different phrasing.
target_language_example: Il a reçu une amende pour excès de vitesse.
native_language_example: He received a fine for speeding.

meaning: to burst out laughing; to crack up.
additional_notes: Strong way to say you suddenly start laughing a lot (often because something is very funny). Used with a subject + conjugated verb: « J’ai explosé de rire », « Il explose de rire ». You can also use the simpler, more neutral « rire » if you just mean “to laugh.”
target_language_example: Quand il a raconté la blague, j’ai explosé de rire.
native_language_example: When he told the joke, I burst out laughing.

additional_notes: Used as a noun (un extra-terrestre / des extra-terrestres) or as an adjective (une vie extra-terrestre). Often shortened in informal speech to “un extraterrestre” (no hyphen) or “un extra” in sci‑fi contexts. Agreement: extra-terrestre is invariable in the singular; plural adds -s (extra-terrestres).
target_language_example: On dit qu’il y a des extra-terrestres dans ce film.
native_language_example: They say there are aliens in this movie.

meaning: hidden side; hidden face (the side you don’t see).
additional_notes: Used literally (the unseen side of an object) and figuratively (someone’s or something’s hidden side, secrets, or what is not obvious). Often appears with a possessive: « la face cachée de… » (the hidden side of…).
target_language_example: On va découvrir la face cachée de cette histoire.
native_language_example: We’re going to discover the hidden side of this story.

meaning: facing; opposite; in the face of.
additional_notes: Used to express (1) physical position: “opposite / facing” someone or something, and (2) a situation you must deal with: “faced with / in the face of” a problem, difficulty, etc. Common patterns: « face à + noun » (face à la mer = facing the sea; face à un problème = faced with a problem) and « faire face à » = to face/deal with.
target_language_example: Face à ce problème, on doit trouver une solution.
native_language_example: Faced with this problem, we must find a solution.

meaning: to get by; to manage (to keep things going).
additional_notes: Used especially in the set phrase « Je fais aller » meaning “I’m managing / I’m getting by” (often implying things aren’t great but you’re coping). Literally it’s “to make go,” but in everyday French it commonly expresses coping rather than physically making something go.
target_language_example: — Ça va ? — Bof… je fais aller.
native_language_example: — How’s it going? — Meh… I’m managing.

meaning: to allude (to); to refer to indirectly.
additional_notes: Usually followed by "à" + a person/thing: "faire allusion à quelque chose/quelqu’un". It means you mention something in an indirect or implied way rather than saying it clearly. In English it can be translated as "to allude to" or more simply "to refer to" depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu fais allusion à quoi ?
native_language_example: What are you alluding to?

meaning: to call on / to use / to seek (help), or to appeal (a decision).
additional_notes: Most often used as **faire appel à + someone/something** meaning “to call on” or “to use” (e.g., call on an expert, use a service). In a legal/administrative context, **faire appel** can mean “to appeal” a court decision (similar to English “appeal”).
target_language_example: On va faire appel à un expert pour résoudre le problème.
native_language_example: We’re going to call on an expert to solve the problem.

meaning: to be careful; to pay attention.
additional_notes: Very common phrase. Often followed by « à » + noun/pronoun: « Fais attention à la marche » (Watch your step) / « Fais attention à toi » (Take care of yourself). It can also be used with « de » + infinitive to warn someone: « Fais attention de ne pas tomber » (Be careful not to fall). In the imperative, you’ll often hear « Attention ! » alone meaning “Watch out!”
target_language_example: Fais attention à la circulation en traversant.
native_language_example: Be careful about traffic when crossing.

meaning: to pay attention to; to be careful about.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to watch out or to focus. Often as an imperative: « Fais attention à… » (“Be careful about…/Watch out for…”). Takes « à » before a noun or verb in the infinitive: « faire attention à la marche » (watch your step), « faire attention à ne pas… » (be careful not to…).
target_language_example: Fais attention à la marche !
native_language_example: Watch your step!

meaning: to do one’s best; to do as well as possible (given the situation).
additional_notes: Used to say you will try your best within limits (time, resources, circumstances). Similar to “faire de son mieux,” but “au mieux” often highlights adapting to constraints: “as best as we can.” Common in polite, professional contexts (emails, customer service).
target_language_example: Je ferai au mieux pour te répondre aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I’ll do my best to reply to you today.

meaning: to make do (with); to cope with.
additional_notes: Used when you accept a limitation and manage using what you have. Often followed by a noun (faire avec ce qu’on a = make do with what we have) or used alone meaning “cope/deal with it” (Il faut faire avec = we’ll have to manage).
target_language_example: On n’a plus de café, alors on va faire avec du thé.
native_language_example: We don’t have any more coffee, so we’ll make do with tea.

additional_notes: Used with impersonal “il”: “Il fait beau” = “The weather is nice.” Often contrasts with “Il fait mauvais” (bad weather) and pairs with other weather expressions like “Il fait chaud/froid” (it’s hot/cold). Not used to mean “to do/make beautiful.”
target_language_example: Aujourd’hui, il fait beau, alors on va se promener.
native_language_example: Today, the weather is nice, so we’re going for a walk.

meaning: to do well; to do something properly / in a good way.
additional_notes: Often used to talk about doing a task correctly or getting a good result: «faire bien son travail» (do your job well). You may also hear it in the impersonal form «ça fait bien» meaning “it looks good / it’s the proper thing to do” (socially appropriate).
target_language_example: Elle fait bien son travail.
native_language_example: She does her job well.

meaning: to be right to (do something); to do well to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to say that doing something is a good idea or the sensible/right thing to do. It’s followed by an infinitive: « faire bien de + infinitive ». Very common in the conditional to give advice: « Tu ferais bien de… » = “You’d better… / You should…”.
target_language_example: Tu ferais bien de prendre un parapluie.
native_language_example: You’d better take an umbrella.

additional_notes: Used almost always in the impersonal form: « Il fait bon » = “It’s nice out / the temperature is pleasant (often mild or warm).” Common with time/place: « Il fait bon aujourd’hui / ici / dehors ». Not the same as « faire beau » (sunny/nice weather) or « il fait bien » (rare).
target_language_example: Il fait bon dehors, on peut marcher un peu.
native_language_example: It’s nice out; we can walk a bit.

additional_notes: In practice, French usually says **faire un bon voyage** (with *un*). Most often, you simply wish someone well by saying **Bon voyage !**. *Faire* here means “to have/take” a trip, not literally “to make”.
target_language_example: J’espère que tu vas faire un bon voyage !
native_language_example: I hope you have a good trip!

additional_notes: Used to say you appear positively to someone (your behavior, look, or attitude gives a good first impression). Often used with “sur” (on) + a person: “faire bonne impression sur quelqu’un”. You can also use it with “vouloir” or “essayer de” when talking about wanting to impress someone.
target_language_example: J’essaie de faire bonne impression sur mes nouveaux collègues.
native_language_example: I’m trying to make a good impression on my new coworkers.

additional_notes: Commonly used with children and in casual, family contexts. It’s more childish than the neutral/standard "aller aux toilettes" (to go to the bathroom) and less formal than "déféquer" (to defecate). You can use it as an infinitive ("Je dois faire caca") or as a question ("Tu veux faire caca ?").
target_language_example: Je dois faire caca.
native_language_example: I need to poop.

meaning: to give (something) as a gift; to gift.
additional_notes: Used mainly in the pattern « faire cadeau de [something] à [someone] » (or « faire cadeau de [something] » with the receiver understood). It can also be used more figuratively to mean “to let someone have something” or “to waive/forgive” (e.g., a debt), and it can sound a bit formal compared with « offrir ».
target_language_example: Je te fais cadeau de ce livre.
native_language_example: I’m giving you this book as a gift.

additional_notes: Most often used as "faire chanter quelqu’un" = to blackmail someone (threaten them to get money, information, favors, etc.). The literal meaning “to make someone sing” also exists in a normal music context, but the idiomatic meaning is very common in news/crime contexts.
target_language_example: Il la fait chanter avec des photos.
native_language_example: He’s blackmailing her with photos.

additional_notes: Used with impersonal “il” to talk about temperature/weather: “Il fait chaud.” (It’s hot.). You can add intensifiers like “très” (very) or “trop” (too): “Il fait très chaud.” Not used for people (“Je suis chaud” is not the normal way to say you feel hot).
target_language_example: Aujourd’hui, il fait chaud, alors on reste à l’ombre.
native_language_example: Today, it’s hot, so we’re staying in the shade.

meaning: to piss (someone) off; to annoy (a lot).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar (uses the verb "chier," meaning "to shit"). Often used as "Ça me fait chier" (= "It pisses me off" / "It really annoys me") or "Tu me fais chier" (= "You’re pissing me off"). With an indirect object pronoun (me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur), it means “to annoy/piss off” that person. In polite situations, prefer "énerver" (to annoy) or "embêter" (to bother).
target_language_example: Ça me fait chier d’attendre ici.
native_language_example: It pisses me off to wait here.

meaning: to act as if; to pretend (that).
additional_notes: Used when someone behaves as though something were true (often to ignore or hide reality). Common pattern: « faire comme si + [clause] ». After « comme si », French often uses the imperfect (or past conditional) even when talking about the present: « Il fait comme s’il ne savait pas » (“He acts as if he didn’t know”).
target_language_example: Elle fait comme si tout allait bien.
native_language_example: She acts as if everything is fine.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "à" + a person/thing you trust: "faire confiance à quelqu’un" (to trust someone). Common in everyday French; it literally means “to make trust,” so you can’t translate it word-for-word into natural English. Can also be used in the negative: "Je ne lui fais pas confiance" (I don’t trust him/her).
target_language_example: Je te fais confiance.
native_language_example: I trust you.

meaning: to meet (someone) / to get to know (someone).
additional_notes: Used for meeting someone for the first time and beginning to know them. Common patterns: « faire connaissance avec + person » (to get to know someone) and « faire la connaissance de + person » (more formal). You can also say « On fait connaissance ? » (“Shall we introduce ourselves?”).
target_language_example: Enchanté, je suis Paul. On fait connaissance ?
native_language_example: Nice to meet you, I’m Paul. Shall we introduce ourselves?

meaning: to make (someone/something) known; to introduce; to publicize.
additional_notes: Often used when you help people discover or hear about someone/something (a person, a product, an idea, a place). Common patterns: « faire connaître quelque chose » = to publicize/promote something; « faire connaître quelqu’un » = to introduce someone / make them known; « se faire connaître » = to become known / make yourself known.
target_language_example: Cette campagne va faire connaître notre nouvelle application.
native_language_example: This campaign is going to publicize our new app.

additional_notes: Common, neutral expression. Uses a possessive: faire de mon mieux (my best), de ton mieux (your best, informal singular), de votre mieux (your best, formal/plural), de son mieux (his/her/its best), de notre mieux, de leur mieux. Often used to encourage someone: Fais de ton mieux ! / Faites de votre mieux !
target_language_example: Je vais faire de mon mieux pour arriver à l’heure.
native_language_example: I’m going to do my best to arrive on time.

meaning: to turn around; to make a U-turn.
additional_notes: Used when you reverse direction (walking, driving, etc.). In traffic, it often corresponds to “make a U-turn.” Can also be used figuratively to mean changing your mind and going back on a decision (e.g., "Il a fait demi-tour").
target_language_example: On s’est trompés de route, il faut faire demi-tour.
native_language_example: We took the wrong road; we need to turn around.

meaning: to make romantic/sexual advances (flirt with someone).
additional_notes: Used when someone comes on to someone else (in a welcome or unwelcome way). Often appears with an object: « faire des avances à quelqu’un ». Can imply unwanted advances depending on context. Not the same as « avancer » (to move forward).
target_language_example: Il lui a fait des avances pendant toute la soirée.
native_language_example: He made advances on her all evening.

meaning: to make a fuss; to cause trouble (about something).
additional_notes: Commonly used when someone is complaining, being difficult, or creating drama over a situation: often with "ne pas" to mean "don’t make a fuss" ("Ne fais pas d’histoires !"). You can add "pour" + noun/pronoun to specify what it’s about ("pour rien" = for nothing).
target_language_example: Ne fais pas d’histoires pour ça, c’est pas grave.
native_language_example: Don’t make a fuss about that, it’s not a big deal.

meaning: to cause devastation; to wreak havoc.
additional_notes: Used to say that something has caused a lot of damage or serious negative effects (a disease, a storm, war, alcohol/drugs, a trend, etc.). Often used with subjects like "la maladie", "la tempête", "la guerre", "l'alcool". Common pattern: "X fait des ravages (dans/sur Y)".
target_language_example: La tempête a fait des ravages sur la côte.
native_language_example: The storm wreaked havoc on the coast.

meaning: to create a distraction; to divert attention.
additional_notes: Used when someone deliberately draws attention away from something (a person, problem, or event). Often used in situations like avoiding questions, escaping, or changing the subject. Literal idea is “to make a diversion,” but in English you usually say “to create a distraction” or “to divert attention.”
target_language_example: Pendant que je fais diversion, prends les clés et sors !
native_language_example: While I create a distraction, take the keys and get out!

meaning: to donate; to give (as a gift), often formally.
additional_notes: Used in fairly formal contexts meaning to donate (money, goods) or to give something as a gift. Usually followed by a direct object: faire don de + noun (“donate/give” something). More common in everyday speech: faire un don (“make a donation”) or donner (“to give”).
target_language_example: Il a fait don de ses livres à la bibliothèque.
native_language_example: He donated his books to the library.

meaning: to go ahead and do it (then); used to urge someone to act.
additional_notes: Most often used in a conjugated form (especially the imperative): « Fais donc ! » = “Go on, do it then!” « donc » adds emphasis and can sound encouraging, insistent, or slightly impatient depending on tone. You can also hear « Faites donc » (polite/plural).
target_language_example: Tu hésites ? Fais donc !
native_language_example: You’re hesitating? Go on, do it!

meaning: to do good; to make someone feel better.
additional_notes: Used with an indirect object to say something is beneficial or soothing: « Ça me fait du bien » = “That does me good / That makes me feel better.” Also common in the infinitive after verbs like « ça va » or « ça peut »: « Ça va te faire du bien » (It’ll do you good). Not the same as « faire le bien » (to do good deeds in general).
target_language_example: Une promenade me fait du bien.
native_language_example: A walk does me good.

additional_notes: Used to talk about causing noise in general (often with the idea of being too loud). Common in everyday situations: at home, in class, at night, etc. You can also use it with a negative or command: « Ne fais pas de bruit ! » (Don’t make noise!).
target_language_example: Les enfants font du bruit dans le salon.
native_language_example: The children are making noise in the living room.

additional_notes: Used for physical pain (hurting someone) and emotional harm (hurting someone’s feelings). With an indirect object pronoun it often means “to hurt (someone)”: « Ça me fait mal » = “That hurts (me)” / “I’m in pain.” You can also use it for causing damage in general: « Ça fait du mal à l’environnement » = “It harms the environment.”
target_language_example: Ne me fais pas de mal !
native_language_example: Don’t hurt me!

meaning: to flirt with someone discreetly (often by touching feet/legs under a table).
additional_notes: Used for subtle flirting in a situation where you don’t want others to notice (e.g., at dinner, in a meeting). It can be playful, but it can also imply unwanted advances depending on context. Not the same as literally “to do some foot”; it’s an idiom.
target_language_example: Arrête de me faire du pied sous la table !
native_language_example: Stop flirting with me under the table!

meaning: to be missing; to be lacking; (also) to default (on a payment/obligation).
additional_notes: Used with the thing that is missing/lacking as the subject: « Le courage fait défaut » = “Courage is lacking.” Often appears in more formal French. In finance/legal contexts, it can mean “to default” (fail to pay/meet an obligation): « L’entreprise a fait défaut sur sa dette ».
target_language_example: Dans cette situation, le courage ne doit pas faire défaut.
native_language_example: In this situation, courage must not be lacking.

meaning: to have an effect; to work (have the intended impact).
additional_notes: Used for something that produces a noticeable result or impression. Common with things like medicine, alcohol, a speech, or a surprise: « Le médicament fait effet » (“The medicine is working”). Can also be used about impressing someone: « Ça fait de l’effet » (“That makes an impression / has an impact”).
target_language_example: Le médicament commence à faire effet.
native_language_example: The medicine is starting to work.

additional_notes: Commonly used with "que" + subjunctive to express ensuring an outcome: "faire en sorte que + [subjunctive]". Often followed by an infinitive with "de" in practice: "faire en sorte de + infinitive" (make sure to...).
target_language_example: Je vais faire en sorte que tout soit prêt demain.
native_language_example: I’ll make sure everything is ready tomorrow.

additional_notes: Literally "to make enter." Used when you cause someone/something to enter a place (opening a door, admitting someone, bringing an object inside). Often takes a direct object: « faire entrer quelqu’un » (let someone in) / « faire entrer quelque chose » (bring something in).
target_language_example: Je vais faire entrer les invités.
native_language_example: I’m going to let the guests in.

meaning: to be mistaken; to make a mistake.
additional_notes: Means that someone is wrong about something. In everyday French you more often hear "faire une erreur" (make a mistake) or "se tromper" (be mistaken). "Faire erreur" without the article is a bit more formal/literary and is often used in the pattern "faire erreur sur (qqch)" (be mistaken about something).
target_language_example: Je crois que tu fais erreur sur son âge.
native_language_example: I think you're mistaken about his age.

additional_notes: Used for trips by plane, train, or ship when you stop somewhere briefly before continuing to your final destination. Often followed by a place with "à" (faire escale à Paris) or used with "avec" to mention a stopover (un vol avec escale).
target_language_example: Nous faisons escale à Montréal avant d’arriver à Vancouver.
native_language_example: We have a stopover in Montreal before arriving in Vancouver.

meaning: to do it on purpose; deliberately.
additional_notes: Used to say an action was intentional (often implying it was annoying, mean, or not accidental). Common patterns: "Je l’ai fait exprès" (I did it on purpose), "Tu l’as fait exprès ?" (Did you do that on purpose?), "sans le faire exprès" (without meaning to / accidentally).
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas cassé ton verre exprès.
native_language_example: I didn’t break your glass on purpose.

meaning: to face; to deal with (a situation).
additional_notes: Used for confronting a problem, difficulty, or situation (often serious): *faire face à* + noun (“to deal with / to face”). Can also mean “to face (toward)” in a physical sense: *La maison fait face à la mer* (“The house faces the sea”), but the most common beginner use is with difficulties.
target_language_example: Je dois faire face à ce problème.
native_language_example: I have to deal with this problem.

meaning: to go bankrupt; to go out of business (financially).
additional_notes: Used for a person or a company that can’t pay its debts and must stop operating or declare bankruptcy. Very common with businesses (une entreprise fait faillite). In everyday speech you may also hear « déposer le bilan » (to file for bankruptcy), but « faire faillite » is the basic beginner-friendly phrase.
target_language_example: Si l’entreprise perd trop d’argent, elle risque de faire faillite.
native_language_example: If the company loses too much money, it risks going bankrupt.

meaning: to open fire; to shoot (with a gun).
additional_notes: Most common in news, military, or police contexts. Often used with a target: « faire feu sur [quelqu’un/quelque chose] » = “to fire at [someone/something]”. Not the usual everyday way to say “to make a fire” (you’d say « allumer un feu » or « faire un feu » for that).
target_language_example: Les soldats ont fait feu sur le véhicule.
native_language_example: The soldiers opened fire on the vehicle.

meaning: to make a fortune; to become very rich.
additional_notes: Used to mean becoming wealthy, often through success in business or a career. Common with the passé composé: « Il a fait fortune » (He made a fortune). The phrase is fairly literal, but in English you also often say “make a fortune.”
target_language_example: Il a fait fortune dans l’immobilier.
native_language_example: He made a fortune in real estate.

additional_notes: Used mainly in the impersonal weather expression « Il fait frais » (“It’s cool/chilly”). It describes a slightly cold temperature (cooler than « il fait bon »; usually less severe than « il fait froid »). You can add a place or time: « Il fait frais ce matin / dehors / ce soir ».
target_language_example: Il fait frais ce matin, prends une veste.
native_language_example: It’s chilly this morning—take a jacket.

additional_notes: Used mainly to talk about the weather, like English “it’s cold.” It’s impersonal (you can’t say *je fais froid*). Common forms: *Il fait froid* (It’s cold), *Il va faire froid* (It’s going to be cold), *Il faisait froid* (It was cold). Often used with temperature: *Il fait 5 degrés.*
target_language_example: Il fait froid aujourd’hui, prends un manteau.
native_language_example: It’s cold today—take a coat.

meaning: to send shivers down your spine; to be creepy/scary.
additional_notes: Used to say something is frightening or unsettling (a story, a noise, a place, an idea). It’s an idiomatic expression: literally “to make cold in the back,” but it means it gives you chills.
target_language_example: Ce film fait froid dans le dos.
native_language_example: That movie sends shivers down your spine.

meaning: to give a warm welcome to; to make a fuss over (someone).
additional_notes: Most often used as "faire fête à quelqu’un" (to welcome someone enthusiastically, show them a lot of attention). It’s common with pets or when greeting someone you’re happy to see. Don’t confuse with "faire la fête", which means "to party/celebrate."
target_language_example: Le chien fait fête à son maître quand il rentre.
native_language_example: The dog gives his owner a big welcome when he comes home.

meaning: to be careful; to watch out.
additional_notes: Informal spoken expression. Often used as an imperative: « Fais gaffe ! » (Watch out!/Be careful!). You can also use « faire gaffe à + noun/pronoun » to mean “to pay attention to”: « Fais gaffe à la marche. »
target_language_example: Fais gaffe, la route est glissante.
native_language_example: Be careful, the road is slippery.

meaning: to act like / pretend (to seem a certain way).
additional_notes: Informal, common in spoken French. Used when someone is putting on an attitude or trying to look a certain way (often with a slightly critical or teasing tone). Frequently followed by a description: “faire genre + cool / sérieux / surpris / je sais tout”. You can also say “faire genre de + infinitive” (e.g., “faire genre de pas entendre” = pretend not to hear).
target_language_example: Arrête de faire genre, tu as très bien compris !
native_language_example: Stop pretending—you understood perfectly well!

meaning: to do justice to; to honor (something/someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you are doing something in a way that shows it deserves respect or appreciation. Common patterns: “faire honneur à + noun/pronoun” (to honor/do justice to), and “faire honneur à un plat/un repas” meaning to enjoy/eat it with enthusiasm (to ‘do it justice’).
target_language_example: Tu fais honneur à ce repas !
native_language_example: You’re really doing this meal justice!

meaning: to shame; to make someone feel ashamed (or embarrassed).
additional_notes: Used with an indirect object to say who is being shamed: « faire honte à quelqu’un » (“to shame someone”). It can also be used without an object to talk generally about something shameful: « Ça fait honte. » Often expresses moral disapproval or social embarrassment.
target_language_example: Tu me fais honte devant tout le monde.
native_language_example: You’re shaming me in front of everyone.

meaning: to burst in; to break in suddenly.
additional_notes: Used when someone (or something) enters a place suddenly and unexpectedly, often in a dramatic or forceful way. Common with "dans" (faire irruption dans...) and with a subject like "la police", "un homme", "une idée". Slightly formal compared to "entrer".
target_language_example: La police a fait irruption dans l’appartement.
native_language_example: The police burst into the apartment.

meaning: to get light; to dawn (become daytime).
additional_notes: Used as an impersonal expression, most often in the form **il fait jour** (“it’s daytime / it’s light out”) or **il commence à faire jour** (“it’s starting to get light”). Common when talking about early morning and daybreak. Not usually translated word-for-word as “make day.”
target_language_example: Il commence à faire jour, on peut partir.
native_language_example: It’s starting to get light; we can leave.

meaning: to do the job; to be good enough; to work (for a purpose).
additional_notes: Used to say something is suitable or sufficient for what you need ("That’ll do"). Often with "ça" or a subject: "Ça fera l’affaire" (That will work / That’ll do), "Ce manteau fait l’affaire" (This coat will do). Can also describe a solution, plan, or option that is acceptable even if it’s not perfect.
target_language_example: Pas besoin d’un modèle cher : celui-ci fera l’affaire.
native_language_example: No need for an expensive model: this one will do.

additional_notes: A common and fairly neutral expression for having sex, often implying affection/romance. You can say it without specifying the partner ("Ils ont fait l’amour" = "They made love") or with "avec" + a person ("faire l’amour avec quelqu’un" = "to make love with someone"). In casual speech, people may use more direct verbs like "coucher avec", but "faire l’amour" is generally softer.
target_language_example: Ils ont fait l’amour pour la première fois.
native_language_example: They made love for the first time.

meaning: to act like a child; to be childish.
additional_notes: Used to criticize someone’s immature behavior (pouting, whining, fooling around, not taking things seriously). Often said as a suggestion or complaint: « Arrête de faire l’enfant » (“Stop acting like a child”).
target_language_example: Arrête de faire l’enfant et écoute, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Stop acting like a child and listen, please.

meaning: to go grocery shopping; to run errands (shopping).
additional_notes: Usually used in the plural: « faire les courses » = to do the shopping / grocery run. With the singular (« faire la course »), it can also mean “to race” (to run a race), but beginners will most often see the shopping meaning in everyday contexts.
target_language_example: Je dois faire les courses avant de rentrer à la maison.
native_language_example: I have to go grocery shopping before going home.

meaning: to make a difference; to tell the difference.
additional_notes: Common in two main uses: (1) "make a difference" = have an impact: « Ça fait la différence. » (It makes a difference.) (2) "tell the difference" (often with "entre") = distinguish: « Je ne fais pas la différence entre… » Also used as a noun phrase: « la différence » = the difference.
target_language_example: Je ne fais pas la différence entre ces deux mots.
native_language_example: I can’t tell the difference between these two words.

additional_notes: Common, neutral expression meaning to have a party or go out and enjoy yourself (often with friends, music, drinks, etc.). You can use it for a specific occasion (birthday, holiday) or just going out. Often used with "on" (we) or "je/tu" in conversation.
target_language_example: On va faire la fête ce soir pour son anniversaire.
native_language_example: We’re going to party tonight for his birthday.

meaning: to make a face; to grimace (show displeasure/disgust).
additional_notes: Used when someone twists their face (a frown, scrunched nose, etc.) to show they don’t like something, are annoyed, disgusted, or in pain. Often used with "quand" (when) or after seeing/tasting something. Literal idea: “to make the grimace,” but English usually says “make a face.”
target_language_example: Il a fait la grimace quand il a goûté la soupe.
native_language_example: He made a face when he tasted the soup.

meaning: to sulk; to pout; to be in a bad mood (and show it).
additional_notes: Informal expression. Used when someone is visibly annoyed or upset and is being cold/quiet (e.g., not talking much, giving short answers). Often used with reasons: « Il fait la gueule parce que… »
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu fais la gueule ?
native_language_example: Why are you sulking?

meaning: to read (something) aloud; to do a reading.
additional_notes: Used when someone reads a text out loud to others (e.g., to children, in class, at an event). Often appears as "faire la lecture de + [text]". Note that "lecture" in French means "reading" (not usually "a lecture" in the classroom sense), so this expression can be confusing for English speakers.
target_language_example: Le soir, je fais la lecture aux enfants avant de dormir.
native_language_example: In the evening, I read to the children before they go to sleep.

meaning: to do the laundry; to wash clothes.
additional_notes: A common everyday phrase for washing clothes (by hand or in a washing machine). You can also say "je fais une lessive" for “I’m doing a load of laundry.” Not used for dry cleaning (that’s "le pressing").
target_language_example: Je dois faire la lessive ce soir.
native_language_example: I have to do the laundry tonight.

meaning: to make the rules; to call the shots.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is acting like they have authority over others (at home, at work, in a group). It can be neutral (simply stating who’s in charge) but is often critical, implying the person is bossy or domineering. Common patterns: « Ici, c’est lui/elle qui fait la loi » (“Here, he/she makes the rules”).
target_language_example: À la maison, c’est toujours mon frère qui fait la loi.
native_language_example: At home, it’s always my brother who makes the rules.

meaning: to make a good match; to go well together (to form a pair).
additional_notes: Used for two things that match (shoes, socks, colors) or two people who “belong together” (as a couple, or sometimes ironically meaning they’re equally annoying or similar). Literally “to make the pair.”
target_language_example: Ces deux chaussures ne font pas la paire.
native_language_example: These two shoes don’t match (they’re not a pair).

additional_notes: Used when people stop fighting/arguing and become friendly again, or when groups/countries end a conflict. Common patterns: « faire la paix avec quelqu’un » (make up with someone) and « faire la paix » (make peace).
target_language_example: Après leur dispute, ils ont décidé de faire la paix.
native_language_example: After their argument, they decided to make up.

meaning: to wait in line; to queue up.
additional_notes: Used for standing and waiting your turn (in a shop, at a counter, for tickets, etc.). Often appears as: « Je fais la queue » (I’m waiting in line) or « Il y a une queue » / « Il y a la queue » (there’s a line). You can also say « faire la queue pour + noun/infinitive »: « faire la queue pour acheter des billets ».
target_language_example: On a dû faire la queue pendant vingt minutes pour entrer.
native_language_example: We had to wait in line for twenty minutes to get in.

meaning: To sulk; to be in a bad mood (often because you’re upset).
additional_notes: Common idiom for looking grumpy or refusing to talk because something annoyed you. Often used with "à cause de" (because of) or "contre" (at/with someone): "Il fait la tête contre moi."
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu fais la tête ?
native_language_example: Why are you sulking?

meaning: to make the front page; to be headline news.
additional_notes: Used mainly with news/media (newspapers, websites, TV) to say something is the main story everyone is talking about. Often used for events, scandals, big announcements, or anything that gets major media attention. Common pattern: « X fait la une ».
target_language_example: Le scandale fait la une des journaux ce matin.
native_language_example: The scandal is making the front pages this morning.

meaning: to do the dishes; to wash up.
additional_notes: Common everyday expression meaning washing dishes and kitchen utensils (usually after a meal). You can also say "faire la vaisselle" for the chore in general, even if using a dishwasher. Related: "la vaisselle" = (the) dishes/tableware; "faire" = to do/make.
target_language_example: Après le dîner, je dois faire la vaisselle.
native_language_example: After dinner, I have to do the dishes.

meaning: to do good; to do good deeds.
additional_notes: Means acting in a helpful, moral way (helping others, charity, kindness). Often used in a general sense (as a principle) rather than one specific act. Also appears in contrasts like « faire le bien / faire le mal » (“do good / do evil”).
target_language_example: Il essaie de faire le bien autour de lui.
native_language_example: He tries to do good around him.

meaning: to pull a trick/stunt (often a scam).
additional_notes: Used when someone does a sneaky or surprising move, especially a repeated “trick” like a scam. Very common with an object: “faire le coup de + noun” / “faire le coup du + noun” = “to pull the (specific) trick,” e.g., “faire le coup du pneu crevé” (the flat-tire scam). Often colloquial.
target_language_example: Il a encore fait le coup : il a dit qu’il avait oublié son portefeuille.
native_language_example: He pulled the same trick again: he said he’d forgotten his wallet.

meaning: to do the housework; to clean (the house).
additional_notes: A very common everyday phrase. It usually means cleaning and tidying at home (vacuuming, dusting, washing dishes, etc.). You can specify the place: « faire le ménage dans la cuisine » (clean the kitchen). It can also be used without specifying where: « Je dois faire le ménage. »
target_language_example: Je fais le ménage le samedi matin.
native_language_example: I do the housework on Saturday morning.

meaning: to do what’s necessary; to take the necessary steps.
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that you will handle a situation and take care of what needs to be done. Common in customer service, administration, and everyday polite speech. Often followed by "pour" + infinitive (purpose): "faire le nécessaire pour...".
target_language_example: Ne vous inquiétez pas, je vais faire le nécessaire pour résoudre ce problème.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll do what’s necessary to solve this problem.

meaning: to fill up (the tank); to get gas.
additional_notes: Most commonly used for refueling a car or motorcycle: « faire le plein d’essence ». By extension it can mean stocking up or filling up (e.g., batteries) depending on context. In everyday speech you’ll often hear it with « d’essence » or « avant de partir » (before leaving).
target_language_example: On doit faire le plein avant de partir.
native_language_example: We need to fill up (get gas) before leaving.

meaning: to take stock; to review where things stand.
additional_notes: Used when you want to assess a situation, recap progress, or clarify the current status before deciding what to do next. Common in work/project contexts and also in personal situations (e.g., in a relationship). Often appears as: « On fait le point ? » (Shall we take stock?) or « Faire le point sur [quelque chose] » (to review [something]).
target_language_example: On se retrouve demain pour faire le point sur le projet.
native_language_example: Let’s meet tomorrow to take stock of the project.

meaning: to make the first move; to take the first step.
additional_notes: Used when someone initiates contact or action (starting a conversation, reaching out, trying to reconcile) rather than waiting for the other person. Common in social and relationship contexts. Literally “to do the first step,” but in English it’s usually “make the first move/step.”
target_language_example: Si tu veux te réconcilier, fais le premier pas.
native_language_example: If you want to make up, make the first move.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a trip that goes to many countries/continents (a “round-the-world” trip). You can also use it more loosely to mean something that travels worldwide or becomes known everywhere (e.g., news). Related noun phrase: « le tour du monde » (a trip around the world).
target_language_example: Un jour, j’aimerais faire le tour du monde.
native_language_example: One day, I’d like to travel around the world.

meaning: to be good for business; to be profitable (for someone).
additional_notes: Often used as « faire les affaires de quelqu’un » = “to benefit someone / to be good for someone’s business.” The subject is frequently a situation or event (sales, tourism, a trend) that helps someone sell more. « affaires » here means “business,” not “(romantic) affairs.”
target_language_example: Les soldes font les affaires des magasins.
native_language_example: Sales are good for stores’ business.

meaning: to pace (up and down), often because you’re nervous or impatient.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression meaning to walk back and forth repeatedly (e.g., in a hallway or waiting room). It’s used when someone is anxious, worried, or impatient while waiting. Commonly used with "être en train de" (to be in the middle of) or in the imperfect to set a scene: "Je faisais les cent pas".
target_language_example: Il faisait les cent pas dans le salon en attendant le médecin.
native_language_example: He was pacing in the living room while waiting for the doctor.

meaning: to go grocery shopping; to run errands (shopping).
additional_notes: Very common everyday phrase meaning to go out and buy what you need (often food and household items). It usually implies shopping for necessities, not leisure shopping (that would often be "faire du shopping"). You can specify what kind of shopping: "faire les courses au supermarché" (at the supermarket), "faire les courses pour la semaine" (for the week).
target_language_example: Je vais faire les courses après le travail.
native_language_example: I’m going to do the grocery shopping after work.

meaning: to go shopping (to browse in stores).
additional_notes: Used for shopping as an activity—visiting/browsing different shops, often without a specific purchase in mind. More general “to shop” can also be expressed as "faire du shopping" (more modern/Anglicism) or "faire des courses" when you mean running errands/buying necessities (especially groceries).
target_language_example: On va faire les magasins samedi après-midi ?
native_language_example: Are we going to go shopping Saturday afternoon?

meaning: to have been a long time (usually: “Ça fait longtemps.” = “It’s been a long time.”)
additional_notes: Mostly used in the fixed expression “Ça fait longtemps (que…)” to say that a lot of time has passed, often since you last saw someone or since something happened. You can add “que + clause”: “Ça fait longtemps que je ne t’ai pas vu.”
target_language_example: Ça fait longtemps qu’on ne s’est pas vus !
native_language_example: It’s been a long time since we’ve seen each other!

additional_notes: Used to talk about physical pain (and sometimes emotional pain). Often appears as: « Ça fait mal » (“It hurts”), « J’ai mal » (“I hurt / I’m in pain”), or « Tu me fais mal » (“You’re hurting me”). For a specific body part, French usually uses « avoir mal à + body part » (e.g., « J’ai mal à la tête »).
target_language_example: Attention, ça fait mal !
native_language_example: Careful, that hurts!

additional_notes: On its own, **faire marche** is not the usual phrasing in everyday French. You’ll almost always hear **faire de la marche** (“to go walking / to do walking for exercise”) or **faire une marche** (“to go for a walk,” more specific/one walk). For “to back up / reverse,” French says **faire marche arrière**.
target_language_example: Le dimanche, on aime faire de la marche au parc.
native_language_example: On Sundays, we like to go walking in the park.

meaning: to reverse; to back up; to go back (on a decision).
additional_notes: Common with cars/vehicles (backing up) and also figuratively meaning to backtrack or reverse a decision ("to back down"). Often used with the auxiliary "avoir": "J’ai fait marche arrière."
target_language_example: En voyant le panneau, j’ai fait marche arrière.
native_language_example: When I saw the sign, I backed up / turned back.

meaning: to make (something) work; to get (something) running.
additional_notes: Most often used with a machine, device, app, etc.: « faire marcher l’ordinateur / l’imprimante ». In a more informal, idiomatic use, « faire marcher quelqu’un » can mean “to pull someone’s leg / to trick someone.”
target_language_example: Je n’arrive pas à faire marcher l’imprimante.
native_language_example: I can’t get the printer to work.

additional_notes: Used almost always with the impersonal subject: « Il fait mauvais » (= The weather is bad). This is part of the common weather pattern « il fait + adjective » (il fait beau, il fait froid, etc.). You can also say « Il fait mauvais temps » for extra clarity.
target_language_example: On reste à la maison : il fait mauvais aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: We’re staying home: the weather is bad today.

meaning: “to had better” / “to be better off (doing something)”.
additional_notes: Used to give advice or a warning, usually with the conditional: « tu ferais mieux de + infinitive » (“you’d better…”). Can sound firm, like telling someone what the smartest choice is.
target_language_example: Tu ferais mieux de partir maintenant.
native_language_example: You’d better leave now.

additional_notes: Usually followed by "de" + a noun (e.g., courage, patience): "faire montre de". It’s a fairly formal expression meaning to display or demonstrate a trait/attitude, often in writing or formal speech. Often used with abstract nouns rather than physical objects.
target_language_example: Il a fait montre de beaucoup de patience pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: He showed a lot of patience during the meeting.

additional_notes: Used about the weather/time of day to say it’s dark outdoors (e.g., at night or when it gets dark early). It’s often used with an impersonal subject: « Il fait noir. » You can also add time: « Il fait noir dehors. »
target_language_example: Il fait noir dehors, rentrons à la maison.
native_language_example: It’s dark outside; let’s go home.

meaning: to be dark; to be nighttime (used with « il »: « Il fait nuit »).
additional_notes: Used in the impersonal weather/time expression « Il fait nuit » meaning “It’s dark / It’s nighttime.” You normally don’t say « Faire nuit » on its own; you conjugate « faire » with « il » (il fait / il faisait / il fera nuit). Commonly paired with « quand » or « parce que » to explain why something is hard or dangerous (e.g., driving).
target_language_example: Dépêche-toi, il fait nuit.
native_language_example: Hurry up, it’s getting dark.

meaning: to serve as; to act as; to function as.
additional_notes: Used when something/someone takes the place of something else or is used as a substitute. Common pattern: “X fait office de Y” (X serves as Y). Often followed by a noun (un bureau, un lit, un guide, etc.).
target_language_example: Ce canapé fait office de lit d’appoint.
native_language_example: This sofa serves as a spare bed.
