meaning: to inform; to let someone know (about).
additional_notes: Usually used with "de" + the thing you are announcing: "faire part de quelque chose (à quelqu’un)". It’s a fairly formal way to announce information (news, a decision, a resignation, condolences, etc.). As a noun, "un faire-part" (often written with a hyphen: "faire-part") is a formal announcement card (e.g., a birth, wedding, or death announcement).
target_language_example: Je voudrais vous faire part de ma décision.
native_language_example: I would like to inform you of my decision.

meaning: to be part of; to belong to.
additional_notes: Most often used as **faire partie de + noun/group** (“to be part of/of the group”). You can also say **faire partie de [something]** to mean “to be among” (included in a list/category). In everyday speech, it’s a common way to say someone is a member of a team, organization, or group.
target_language_example: Je fais partie de l’équipe.
native_language_example: I’m part of the team.

meaning: to pass on/along; to put through; to administer (a test/exam).
additional_notes: Literally “to make (something) pass.” Common uses: (1) "faire passer un message" = to pass on a message; (2) "faire passer un examen/un test" = to give/administer an exam or test (the students take it: "passer un examen"); (3) sometimes "faire passer quelqu’un" = to let someone go through / show someone in.
target_language_example: Le professeur fait passer un examen demain.
native_language_example: The teacher is giving/administering an exam tomorrow.

additional_notes: Usually used with an indirect object pronoun: « Tu me fais peur » (You scare me). In the present tense it can also mean “to look scary” or “to be frightening”: « Ce film fait peur » (This movie is scary). Related: « avoir peur » = to be afraid.
target_language_example: Ce bruit me fait peur.
native_language_example: That noise scares me.

additional_notes: Common, child-friendly way to say someone is urinating. Often used with "aller" (to go): "Je vais faire pipi". More neutral/adult options include "uriner" (formal) and "faire ses besoins" (vague/polite).
target_language_example: Je vais faire pipi, j’arrive.
native_language_example: I’m going to pee, I’ll be right back.

meaning: to be pitiful; to inspire pity.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something makes you feel sorry for them (or seems pathetic). Often negative or judgmental, especially about something disappointing: "Ça fait pitié" = "That’s pathetic / That’s really sad." You can also use it about a person: "Il fait pitié" (he’s pitiful) or "Tu me fais pitié" (I feel sorry for you).
target_language_example: Franchement, ce que tu as fait, ça fait pitié.
native_language_example: Honestly, what you did is pathetic.

meaning: to make room; to step aside (make way).
additional_notes: Used when you want someone/something to move so there’s space. Often appears as an imperative: « Faites place ! » (“Make room!” / “Step aside!”). Very common with « à »: « faire place à + noun » = “to make room/way for” (often in the sense of replacing something: « Faire place au nouveau modèle. »).
target_language_example: Faites place, s’il vous plaît !
native_language_example: Make room, please!

meaning: to please; to make (someone) happy; to do a favor (for someone).
additional_notes: Commonly used with an indirect object pronoun: "Ça me fait plaisir" (That makes me happy / I'm glad). You can specify who you’re pleasing with "à" or a pronoun: "faire plaisir à Marie" / "lui faire plaisir" (to please Marie / to please her). Often used when accepting thanks or expressing appreciation: "Ça me fait plaisir" = "My pleasure" / "I’m happy to help."
target_language_example: Ça me fait plaisir de te voir.
native_language_example: I’m happy to see you.

additional_notes: Used when you talk about doing something for someone’s benefit. Very common in service situations and polite offers: « Qu’est-ce que je peux faire pour vous ? » (“What can I do for you?”). The person comes after « pour » (pour toi, pour vous, pour lui/elle, pour moi, etc.).
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que je peux faire pour toi ?
native_language_example: What can I do for you?

additional_notes: Usually used with "de" + a noun to say someone demonstrates a trait: "faire preuve de patience" (show patience), "faire preuve de courage" (show courage). Common in formal or written French. It doesn’t mean "to make proof" in the literal sense.
target_language_example: Il a fait preuve de patience pendant l’attente.
native_language_example: He showed patience during the wait.

meaning: to keep a low profile; to lie low.
additional_notes: Used when someone avoids attention, stays quiet, or doesn’t show off—often after a mistake, during a conflict, or to avoid trouble. Common in everyday speech. Conjugates like faire: je fais profil bas, il/elle fait profil bas, etc.
target_language_example: Après la dispute, il a préféré faire profil bas pendant quelques jours.
native_language_example: After the argument, he preferred to keep a low profile for a few days.

meaning: to blow up / make explode; also (informal) to pop open (e.g., champagne).
additional_notes: Literally “to make (something) explode.” In everyday informal French, it’s very common with things like bottles (“faire péter le champagne” = to pop open the champagne). It can also be used more literally for explosions (a bomb, a firecracker, etc.). The object is usually stated: faire péter + noun (faire péter une bombe / un pétard / le champagne).
target_language_example: Pour fêter ça, on va faire péter le champagne !
native_language_example: To celebrate that, we’re going to pop the champagne!

meaning: to be all the rage; to be very popular (at the moment).
additional_notes: Often used with a trend, fashion, or activity as the subject: « Les baskets blanches font rage. » It means something is extremely popular and talked about right now (like a craze). Not to be confused with « être en rage » (to be furious) or « faire rager quelqu’un » (to make someone mad).
target_language_example: En ce moment, les séries coréennes font rage.
native_language_example: Right now, Korean series are all the rage.

meaning: to bring/get (someone or something) in; to make (someone) come back in/go home.
additional_notes: A common causative structure: **faire + infinitive** = “to make/have someone do something.” So **faire rentrer quelqu’un** means you cause them to come in/come back (e.g., call the kids inside, send someone home). With objects, it can mean “to put/get something back inside” (**faire rentrer la voiture dans le garage**). It’s also used with money: **faire rentrer de l’argent** = “to bring in money.”
target_language_example: Il faut faire rentrer les enfants avant la nuit.
native_language_example: We need to get the kids inside before nightfall.

meaning: to refer to; to mention; to allude to.
additional_notes: Used with "à" to introduce what you’re referring to: "faire référence à + noun". Common in writing and formal speech (but not slang). Also appears as the noun phrase "une référence" (a reference).
target_language_example: Dans ce chapitre, l’auteur fait référence à plusieurs événements historiques.
native_language_example: In this chapter, the author refers to several historical events.

meaning: to pack (your) suitcase; to pack your bags.
additional_notes: Used when preparing for a trip or leaving somewhere (even figuratively: “pack up and leave”). Literally “to make one’s suitcase,” but in French it means to pack it. The possessive changes with the person: faire ma/ta/sa/notre/votre/leur valise.
target_language_example: Je dois faire ma valise ce soir pour partir demain.
native_language_example: I have to pack my suitcase tonight to leave tomorrow.

meaning: to do without; to manage without.
additional_notes: Used to say you can manage without something. Often followed by a noun or pronoun: "faire sans café" (do without coffee), "faire sans lui/elle" (do without him/her). You can also use it alone when the missing thing is understood: "Je peux faire sans."
target_language_example: On n’a plus de sucre, mais on va faire sans.
native_language_example: We don’t have any sugar anymore, but we’ll manage without it.

meaning: to make (something/someone) jump; also: to blow up / to sauté (cook quickly).
additional_notes: Literally “to make jump.” Very common with a direct object: faire sauter un enfant (make a child jump/bounce), faire sauter un pont (blow up a bridge), faire sauter des légumes (sauté vegetables in a pan). Figuratively, it can also mean “to skip” something: faire sauter une étape (skip a step).
target_language_example: Ils ont fait sauter le pont.
native_language_example: They blew up the bridge.

additional_notes: Used when you communicate information to someone, often in a polite or slightly formal way (emails, announcements, requests). Common patterns: « faire savoir à quelqu’un que… » (to let someone know that…), and « faire savoir quelque chose à quelqu’un » (to make something known to someone). Can also mean “to make known/publicize” in a broader sense depending on context.
target_language_example: Faites-moi savoir si vous pouvez venir demain.
native_language_example: Let me know if you can come tomorrow.

meaning: to pretend; to act as if something is true.
additional_notes: Used when someone is faking an action, feeling, or situation. Often followed by "de" + infinitive ("faire semblant de dormir" = to pretend to sleep). Can also be used alone ("Il fait semblant !" = He’s pretending!).
target_language_example: Elle fait semblant d’être malade pour ne pas aller à l’école.
native_language_example: She’s pretending to be sick so she doesn’t have to go to school.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to describe acting as if something is true when it isn’t (or when you don’t want to show the truth). Often implies faking or putting on an act: « faire semblant de dormir » = to pretend to be asleep. Can also be used without « de » when followed by a clause: « Il fait semblant qu’il ne sait pas » (less common in everyday speech than the infinitive form).
target_language_example: Il fait semblant de ne pas comprendre.
native_language_example: He’s pretending not to understand.

meaning: to say goodbye; to take leave (often for the last time).
additional_notes: Used when someone is leaving a place or separating from people, and can sound more formal or emotional than simply saying « au revoir ». It’s also common in serious contexts like leaving a job, moving away, or before death (e.g., « faire ses adieux à quelqu’un »). Literally “to make one’s goodbyes.”
target_language_example: Avant de partir, il a fait ses adieux à toute l’équipe.
native_language_example: Before leaving, he said goodbye to the whole team.

additional_notes: Used when someone is preparing to leave, usually for a trip or a move. Often appears in commands or near-future plans (e.g., « Il faut que tu fasses tes valises » / « Je vais faire mes valises »). You can change the possessive to match the subject: faire ma/tes/ses/nos/vos/leurs valises.
target_language_example: Je dois faire mes valises ce soir.
native_language_example: I have to pack my bags tonight.

additional_notes: Used when you communicate non-verbally (with your hand, head, eyes, etc.) to get someone’s attention or to indicate what they should do. Very common pattern: “faire signe à quelqu’un (de + infinitive)” = “to signal to someone (to do something)”. In the past: “il/elle m’a fait signe…”.
target_language_example: Il m’a fait signe de venir.
native_language_example: He signaled to me to come.

meaning: to be quiet; to fall silent.
additional_notes: A fairly formal/literary expression meaning to stop making noise or to stop talking. In everyday French, people more often say « se taire », « faire taire quelqu’un » (make someone be quiet), or « faire le silence » / « faire silence » as an instruction (e.g., in a meeting or classroom).
target_language_example: Quand le professeur est entré, tout le monde a fait silence.
native_language_example: When the teacher came in, everyone fell silent.

meaning: to keep it simple; to do something in a simple way.
additional_notes: Used when you want to avoid unnecessary complexity and choose the easiest, most straightforward option. Often appears as an instruction or suggestion: « On va faire simple » (“Let’s keep it simple”) or « Fais simple » (“Keep it simple”).
target_language_example: On va faire simple : tu m’envoies l’adresse et j’arrive.
native_language_example: Let’s keep it simple: you send me the address and I’ll come.

additional_notes: Literally “to do/make one’s bed.” Used for tidying your bed (pulling up sheets/blanket, arranging pillows). Often said as a daily chore: « Je dois faire mon lit. » You can change the possessive: faire mon/ton/son/notre/votre/leur lit.
target_language_example: Je fais mon lit tous les matins.
native_language_example: I make my bed every morning.

meaning: to take/bring someone or something out; to make (someone/something) go out.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "faire" + infinitive to show that you cause the action to happen (you make/let someone or something go out). Common with people and pets ("faire sortir le chien" = let/take the dog out) and also for making something come out or be released (e.g., "faire sortir l’argent" = get the money out).
target_language_example: Je fais sortir le chien.
native_language_example: I’m taking the dog out.

meaning: to resist; to stand up to (often: faire tête à).
additional_notes: Usually used with « à » + a person/thing: « faire tête à quelqu’un/quelque chose » = to face up to, resist, or withstand (pressure, an opponent, a problem). Common in contexts like competition, conflict, or difficulties. Not the same as « faire la tête » (to sulk).
target_language_example: Elle a su faire tête à la pression au travail.
native_language_example: She managed to withstand the pressure at work.

meaning: to sign/make a lease; (in « ça fait un bail ») it’s been a long time.
additional_notes: « Un bail » means a (rental) lease. Literally, « faire un bail » is to draw up/sign a lease, but beginners will very often hear it in the set expression « Ça fait un bail ! », meaning “It’s been ages / It’s been a long time!” This use is informal and common in conversation.
target_language_example: Ça fait un bail qu’on ne s’est pas vus !
native_language_example: It’s been ages since we’ve seen each other!

meaning: to do a lot of good; to feel really good.
additional_notes: Used to say something is extremely beneficial or makes you feel much better (physically or emotionally). Often used with an indirect object: « Ça me fait un bien fou » = “That does me a world of good.” « fou » here intensifies the idea (“crazy amount”), not “mad/crazy” literally. Common with rest, a walk, vacation, talking to someone, etc.
target_language_example: Cette promenade me fait un bien fou.
native_language_example: This walk does me a world of good.

meaning: to make a drawing; to draw a picture.
additional_notes: A common everyday way to say someone is drawing (often a simple sketch, e.g., a child’s drawing). You can also say "dessiner" (to draw). The object can change: "faire un dessin de ..." (make a drawing of ...).
target_language_example: Tu peux faire un dessin de ta maison ?
native_language_example: Can you draw a picture of your house?

meaning: to be a big hit; to be hugely successful.
additional_notes: Common idiom used for movies, shows, books, products, etc. It’s fairly informal/colloquial. In the past it could be linked to theater/box-office success, but today it’s used more generally for anything that “does really well.”
target_language_example: Son dernier film a fait un tabac en France.
native_language_example: His/Her latest film was a huge hit in France.

meaning: to take a walk/short trip; to have a quick look; to go for a spin.
additional_notes: Very common and flexible. Often means going somewhere briefly or casually (a walk, a short outing, a quick loop). With places: "faire un tour en ville" (go for a walk/short trip in town). With shops/events: "faire un tour au marché" (stop by the market). With "de" + place/person: "faire un tour de la ville" (tour the city) or "faire un tour chez un ami" (pop over to a friend’s). Can also mean to take a quick look: "Je vais faire un tour" = I’ll go have a look / I’ll step out for a bit.
target_language_example: On va faire un tour en ville ce soir ?
native_language_example: Shall we go for a walk/short trip in town tonight?

meaning: to cross off; (faire une croix sur…) to give up on something.
additional_notes: Literally “to make a cross.” In everyday French, it’s often used with "sur" + a noun/pronoun: "faire une croix sur X" = to stop hoping for it / abandon the idea (e.g., money you won’t get back, a plan that won’t happen). Without "sur", it can also be understood as marking something with an X (e.g., on a list).
target_language_example: Tu peux faire une croix sur ton argent : il ne te remboursera jamais.
native_language_example: You can kiss your money goodbye: he’ll never pay you back.

meaning: to do someone a favor (give them a special kindness).
additional_notes: Used when someone gives you a small advantage or kind gesture (often something they don’t have to do), like a discount, an exception to a rule, or extra help. Common pattern: « faire une fleur à quelqu’un » (do someone a favor). Not used literally about flowers here.
target_language_example: Tu peux me faire une fleur et me déposer à la gare ?
native_language_example: Can you do me a favor and drop me off at the station?

meaning: to use; to make use of.
additional_notes: Formal expression, most often used as **faire usage de + noun** (“to make use of…”). Common in official writing, instructions, and legal/administrative contexts; in everyday speech you’ll usually hear **utiliser** or **se servir de** instead.
target_language_example: Vous pouvez faire usage de cette carte pendant un an.
native_language_example: You can use this card for one year.

meaning: to have someone/something come; to send for (someone).
additional_notes: Used when you cause someone or something to come to a place (often by calling, ordering, or arranging). Common in service contexts: « Je vais faire venir un taxi. » It can take an object (person/thing) and often implies you requested or arranged it rather than going yourself.
target_language_example: Je vais faire venir un médecin.
native_language_example: I’m going to send for a doctor.

meaning: to show; to let someone see.
additional_notes: Used when you make something visible to someone (an object, a screen, a document, etc.). Common with an indirect object: « faire voir quelque chose à quelqu’un » (to show someone something). In speech, the imperative « Fais voir ! » often means “Let me see!” and is fairly informal.
target_language_example: Tu peux me faire voir ton billet, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you show me your ticket, please?

meaning: to make/take a vow (a solemn promise).
additional_notes: Often used in formal or religious contexts, frequently with "de" + infinitive or a noun: "faire vœu de silence" (take a vow of silence), "faire vœu de pauvreté" (take a vow of poverty). You may also see it as "faire un vœu" meaning "to make a wish" (different meaning).
target_language_example: Il a fait vœu de silence.
native_language_example: He took a vow of silence.

meaning: to team up; to work as a team.
additional_notes: Used to say people join together and cooperate toward a goal (sports, school projects, work). Often followed by "avec" + a person: "faire équipe avec quelqu’un" (to team up with someone). You can also use "On fait équipe !" to suggest teaming up.
target_language_example: On peut faire équipe pour ce projet ?
native_language_example: Can we team up for this project?

meaning: "sweet dreams" / "have nice dreams" (said to one person).
additional_notes: An affectionate good-night phrase. "Fais" is the informal singular (tu) form of "faire". For a more formal or plural version, use "faites de beaux rêves"; you can also hear "fais de jolis rêves".
target_language_example: Bonne nuit, fais de beaux rêves !
native_language_example: Good night, sweet dreams!

additional_notes: Colloquial way to ask someone to show you something (an object, a screen, a photo, a message, etc.). It’s the imperative of « faire » + « voir » (literally “make (me) see”), and it often implies “hand it to me / show it to me for a second.” You can also hear « Fais voir ! » by itself as a quick request.
target_language_example: Fais voir ton téléphone, deux secondes.
native_language_example: Let me see your phone for two seconds.

additional_notes: Used to describe food (and sometimes other products) prepared on-site rather than industrially made. Often appears on menus and labels: "tarte faite maison", "sauce faite maison". It agrees with the noun: "fait maison" (masc.), "faite maison" (fem.), "faits maison" / "faites maison" (plural).
target_language_example: Le gâteau est fait maison.
native_language_example: The cake is homemade.

additional_notes: A warm good-night wish. It uses the formal/plural command form of faire (faites), so it’s addressed to "vous" (one person formally or more than one person). For one friend/family member you’d usually say: "Fais de beaux rêves." Often said with "Bonne nuit" before or after.
target_language_example: Bonne nuit, faites de beaux rêves !
native_language_example: Good night, sweet dreams!

additional_notes: Fixed phrase used by a croupier/announcer in casinos or games of chance to tell players to make their wagers before betting closes. Literally “make your games,” but it means “place your bets.”
target_language_example: Mesdames et messieurs, faites vos jeux !
native_language_example: Ladies and gentlemen, place your bets!

meaning: to be necessary; to have to (impersonal).
additional_notes: This verb is almost always used in the impersonal form with a dummy subject: il faut… (it’s necessary / you have to). Common patterns: il faut + infinitive (Il faut partir. = We/You have to leave) and il faut + noun (Il faut du temps. = It takes time / You need time). Useful forms: il fallait (was necessary / had to), il faudra (will be necessary), il faudrait (would be necessary / should).
target_language_example: Il faut que tu étudies ce soir.
native_language_example: You have to study tonight.

meaning: "to have to / must"; literally "to be necessary that".
additional_notes: Used almost always in the impersonal form "il faut que + [subjunctive]" to express necessity/obligation: "Il faut que je parte" (I have to leave). You’ll also hear other tenses like "il fallait que" (had to) and "il faudra que" (will have to). In casual speech, people may drop "il": "Faut que j’y aille".
target_language_example: Il faut que tu viennes demain.
native_language_example: You have to come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech and on official forms to describe a household with several children; in France it can be linked to special discounts or benefits (e.g., for transport). Often used with être/venir d’: « Je viens d’une famille nombreuse ».
target_language_example: Je viens d’une famille nombreuse : nous sommes cinq enfants.
native_language_example: I come from a large family: there are five of us kids.

additional_notes: Medical/neutral term used to talk about an unintended loss of a pregnancy. Often used with the verb "faire": "faire une fausse couche" (to have a miscarriage). The adjective agrees: "une fausse couche".
target_language_example: Elle a fait une fausse couche il y a deux mois.
native_language_example: She had a miscarriage two months ago.

meaning: “we/you have to” / “might as well” / “it has to be done.”
additional_notes: Common spoken reduction of « il faut bien ». Used to express necessity or resignation (doing something because there’s no better option). It can also soften advice: « Faut bien essayer » = “You should at least try.” Often followed by an infinitive: « Faut bien partir » (“We have to leave / We might as well leave”).
target_language_example: Faut bien y aller, sinon on va être en retard.
native_language_example: We have to go, otherwise we’ll be late.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not available or not done, so another option happens instead. Often followed by a noun or an infinitive: « faute de temps » (for lack of time), « faute de preuves » (for lack of evidence), « faute de pouvoir venir » (failing to be able to come). Common in more formal/written French.
target_language_example: Faute de temps, je n’ai pas fini le rapport.
native_language_example: For lack of time, I didn’t finish the report.

additional_notes: Standard, neutral term for a wheelchair. Often used with the verb "être" or "se déplacer" (to get around): "Je suis en fauteuil roulant" (I use a wheelchair). In writing and conversation you may also see the shorter term "un fauteuil" when context is clear.
target_language_example: Elle se déplace en fauteuil roulant.
native_language_example: She gets around in a wheelchair.

meaning: “so to speak”; a figure of speech.
additional_notes: Used to signal that you don’t mean something literally, or that what you just said is an approximation/expression. Often follows a statement: “C’est une façon de parler.” It’s neutral (not slang).
target_language_example: Je suis mort de fatigue — enfin, c’est une façon de parler.
native_language_example: I’m dead tired—well, so to speak.

additional_notes: Used mainly in hotels to refer to the person who cleans guest rooms and changes linens. Today, "femme de ménage" is more general (cleaner/housekeeper in a home or office). "Femme de chambre" is fairly literal ("woman of the room"), but the natural English meaning is "housekeeper/chambermaid" rather than a direct word-for-word translation.
target_language_example: Je voudrais parler à la femme de chambre, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like to speak to the housekeeper, please.

additional_notes: Refers to a woman whose job is to clean (in a home, hotel, office, etc.). Common in everyday speech; a more gender-neutral option is "agent(e) d’entretien". For a male cleaner, you may hear "homme de ménage" (less common).
target_language_example: On cherche une femme de ménage pour deux heures par semaine.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a house cleaner for two hours per week.

meaning: to break someone’s heart; to be heartbreaking.
additional_notes: Literally “to split the heart.” Used for something very sad or moving that causes deep emotional pain or pity. Often appears in phrases like « Ça me fend le cœur » (It breaks my heart) or « C’est à fendre le cœur » (It’s heartbreaking). Also possible with other objects: « fendre le cœur à quelqu’un » (to break someone’s heart).
target_language_example: Ça me fend le cœur de le voir comme ça.
native_language_example: It breaks my heart to see him like that.

meaning: to close your eyes; (figuratively) to turn a blind eye.
additional_notes: Used literally for physically closing your eyes (e.g., to sleep, to avoid seeing something). Figuratively, it can mean to ignore something on purpose ("fermer les yeux sur" = "to turn a blind eye to").
target_language_example: Il a fermé les yeux sur leurs erreurs.
native_language_example: He turned a blind eye to their mistakes.

additional_notes: Used when you close something and lock it using a key (door, car, etc.). Common with the verb "fermer" (to close): "Ferme la porte à clef." Often written "fermer à clé"; both are accepted (clé is the modern spelling).
target_language_example: N’oublie pas de fermer la porte à clef.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to lock the door.

additional_notes: Used when you lock a door, window, or other opening using a key (not just closing it). Often used with an object: « Ferme la porte à clé » (“Lock the door”). You can also say « C’est fermé à clé » (“It’s locked”).
target_language_example: N’oublie pas de fermer la porte à clé en partant.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to lock the door with the key when you leave.

additional_notes: A literal “camp fire” (a fire made outdoors, typically for camping). Common with verbs like faire/allumer (to make/light) and around expressions like autour du feu de camp (around the campfire).
target_language_example: On a fait un feu de camp sur la plage.
native_language_example: We made a campfire on the beach.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a red traffic light, meaning you must stop: « être au feu rouge » (to be at the red light), « s’arrêter au feu rouge » (to stop at the red light), « griller un feu rouge » (to run a red light). It can also literally mean a red light in other contexts (a red lamp), but the traffic meaning is the default.
target_language_example: Arrête-toi au feu rouge.
native_language_example: Stop at the red light.

additional_notes: Used literally for a green traffic light ("Le feu est vert") and very commonly figuratively to mean you have authorization to start or proceed ("avoir le feu vert" = to get the go-ahead). You can also say "donner le feu vert" (to give the green light).
target_language_example: On a enfin le feu vert pour commencer les travaux.
native_language_example: We finally got the green light to start the work.

meaning: to leave (someone) alone; to stop bothering (someone).
additional_notes: Colloquial way to tell someone to stop annoying you or interfering. Often used as an imperative: « Fiche-moi la paix ! » (“Leave me alone!”). Can also be used with other objects: « Fiche-lui la paix » (leave him/her alone), « Fichez-nous la paix » (leave us alone). Similar in tone to « Laisse-moi tranquille ! ».
target_language_example: Fiche-moi la paix, je travaille !
native_language_example: Leave me alone, I’m working!

meaning: to get out of here; to clear off ("get lost").
additional_notes: Informal, often said as an order: "Fiche le camp !" = "Get out!/Get lost!" It can also mean "to run off/leave suddenly" when describing someone: "Il a fichu le camp." Stronger than "partir"; use with care.
target_language_example: Fiche le camp, je ne veux plus te voir !
native_language_example: Get out of here, I don’t want to see you anymore!

additional_notes: Literally “iron wire.” Used for metal wire in general (e.g., tying, hanging, fencing, crafts). Not usually used for electrical wire/cable (often "fil électrique", "câble").
target_language_example: J’ai besoin d’un fil de fer pour attacher le grillage.
native_language_example: I need some wire to tie the mesh fence.

meaning: the common thread; the main theme running through something.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the central idea or link that connects different parts of a story, speech, project, or discussion. Literally means “red thread,” but in English the usual translation is “common thread” or “main theme.” Often appears with verbs like « être » (to be) or « servir de » (to serve as): « Le fil rouge de ce livre, c’est… »
target_language_example: Le fil rouge de son discours, c’était l’importance de l’éducation.
native_language_example: The common thread of his speech was the importance of education.

meaning: a single-file line (one behind the other).
additional_notes: Used to describe people moving or queuing one behind another, especially in a narrow space (e.g., a corridor, stairs, a trail). Often used with verbs like « marcher en file indienne » (to walk single file).
target_language_example: Dans ce couloir étroit, on avance en file indienne.
native_language_example: In this narrow hallway, we move in single file.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has no sisters (and no other daughters in the family). Often appears with être: « Elle est fille unique ». Not to be confused with « enfant unique » (only child, no siblings at all) or « fille seule » (a girl/woman who is alone).
target_language_example: Elle est fille unique, mais elle a deux frères.
native_language_example: She is an only daughter, but she has two brothers.

meaning: "son of a bitch" (a very strong insult).
additional_notes: Highly offensive vulgar insult. Avoid in polite conversation; it can easily start a fight. In casual speech you may hear it used in anger or to insult someone directly ("Espèce de fils de pute !"). Not appropriate in most contexts.
target_language_example: Espèce de fils de pute, rends-moi mon portefeuille !
native_language_example: You son of a bitch, give me back my wallet!

meaning: only son (a family's only male child).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has no brothers. For “only child” (no siblings at all), French more often uses « enfant unique ».
target_language_example: C’est son fils unique.
native_language_example: He’s her only son.

additional_notes: Common in Canadian French to mean “the weekend” (often where France French would say « week-end »). Usually used with an article: « la fin de semaine » (the weekend) or « une fin de semaine » (a weekend). Can also mean the literal end of the week in context.
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que tu fais en fin de semaine ?
native_language_example: What are you doing this weekend?

additional_notes: Used literally for apocalyptic scenarios (the end of the world), and also exaggeratively to mean “it’s not the end of the world” (ce n’est pas la fin du monde) = “it’s not a big deal.” Can also describe a very remote place: au fin fond du monde (“in the middle of nowhere”).
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas la fin du monde si tu es en retard.
native_language_example: It’s not the end of the world if you’re late.

meaning: overly romantic; sentimental (often in a slightly teasing way).
additional_notes: Used to describe a person, attitude, or story that is very sentimental or dreamy about love. Usually said with gentle irony (not rude), e.g., someone who loves clichés, romance movies, love poems, etc. Often used with "être": "Je suis un peu fleur bleue." Can agree like an adjective: "fleur bleue" (invariable) after "être"; also common: "un(e) fleur bleue" (a sentimental person).
target_language_example: Il est un peu fleur bleue, il croit au grand amour.
native_language_example: He’s a bit overly romantic; he believes in true love.

additional_notes: Used to describe suddenly starting to cry (often from strong emotion like sadness, stress, or relief). It’s a fairly common, neutral expression (not slang). You’ll often see it with a subject pronoun: « Il/Elle a fondu en larmes ».
target_language_example: En entendant la nouvelle, elle a fondu en larmes.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she burst into tears.

additional_notes: Used to distinguish the U.S. sport from (European) football, which in French is usually called just « football » or « foot » (meaning soccer). You’ll also see « le football américain » with the article.
target_language_example: Mon frère joue au football américain le week-end.
native_language_example: My brother plays American football on weekends.

meaning: "it must be admitted" / "it has to be said".
additional_notes: A formal, somewhat literary set phrase used to introduce an unavoidable conclusion or a fact you have to acknowledge. Often followed by **de + infinitive** ("Force est de reconnaître que…") or by **que + clause** ("Force est que…"). Common in writing, less common in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Force est de reconnaître que tu avais raison.
native_language_example: It must be admitted that you were right.

meaning: to force someone’s hand; to pressure someone into doing something.
additional_notes: Often used figuratively when someone is pushed to make a decision or act sooner than they want (e.g., in negotiations, at work, in relationships). It can also be literal in rare contexts (physically forcing someone’s hand), but the common meaning is “to put pressure on someone.” Typically used as: « forcer la main à quelqu’un ».
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas te forcer la main, mais il faut qu’on décide aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I don’t want to force your hand, but we have to decide today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about forests in tropical climates (often humid, with lots of biodiversity). In everyday French it can refer specifically to a rainforest (especially if the context is the Amazon, Congo Basin, etc.), but it can also mean a tropical forest more generally.
target_language_example: La déforestation menace la forêt tropicale.
native_language_example: Deforestation threatens the tropical rainforest.

additional_notes: Used to express being extremely happy. It agrees with the person described: masculine singular "fou de joie", feminine singular "folle de joie", plural "fous/foll es de joie". Common with "être" ("Je suis fou/folle de joie") or "rendre" ("Ça me rend fou/folle de joie").
target_language_example: Quand j’ai appris la nouvelle, j’étais fou de joie.
native_language_example: When I heard the news, I was overjoyed.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize extreme anger. It often follows a form of “être” (to be): “Il/Elle est fou/folle de rage.” Note agreement: fou (masc.), folle (fem.).
target_language_example: Quand il a vu les dégâts, il était fou de rage.
native_language_example: When he saw the damage, he was furious.

additional_notes: Very informal and often vulgar because of "foutre". Used when something is spoiled, derailed, or messed up (a plan, a project, an arrangement). It can also be used literally as “to throw in the air,” but most commonly it means “to screw up/ruin.”
target_language_example: On avait tout prévu, mais la pluie a foutu la soirée en l'air.
native_language_example: We had everything planned, but the rain ruined the evening.

meaning: to scare (someone) a lot; to scare the hell out of (someone).
additional_notes: Very informal/vulgar because of « foutre ». Used with an indirect object: « foutre la trouille à quelqu’un » = to really frighten someone. Similar informal alternatives: « foutre les jetons à quelqu’un », « foutre la frousse à quelqu’un ». In more neutral French, you can say « faire peur à quelqu’un ».
target_language_example: Ce film m’a foutu la trouille !
native_language_example: That movie scared the hell out of me!

meaning: to get out / clear off; to leave (very informal, often rude).
additional_notes: Strongly informal and can sound aggressive, like “Get lost!” or “Get out of here!” depending on context. You’ll also see it used reflexively: « Je me suis foutu le camp » = “I got out of there / I left.” Use with caution (not polite in most situations).
target_language_example: Fous le camp !
native_language_example: Get out of here! / Get lost!

meaning: to scare someone a lot; to freak someone out.
additional_notes: Very informal/slang. Often used as « Ça me fout les jetons » (“It really scares me”) or « Ça fout les jetons » (“That’s scary”). « foutre » is a vulgar/informal verb in general, so avoid in formal contexts; a more neutral option is « faire peur ».
target_language_example: Ce film me fout les jetons.
native_language_example: That movie really freaks me out.

additional_notes: A common food item in France. Used on menus and in shops; you can also hear it shortened to just "chèvre" when the context is clearly cheese (e.g., a pizza or salad).
target_language_example: Je voudrais une salade au fromage de chèvre, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a goat cheese salad, please.

meaning: to frown; to furrow your eyebrows.
additional_notes: Describes the facial expression where you draw your eyebrows together, often showing worry, confusion, concentration, or disapproval. Common with verbs like « je fronce les sourcils » (I frown) or « il/elle a froncé les sourcils » (he/she frowned).
target_language_example: Elle a froncé les sourcils en lisant ce message.
native_language_example: She frowned while reading that message.

additional_notes: Usually used in the plural: « des fruits de mer » = seafood/shellfish (often as a platter: « un plateau de fruits de mer »). Not about sweet fruit—it's a set phrase meaning food from the sea (oysters, shrimp, mussels, etc.).
target_language_example: On va prendre un plateau de fruits de mer.
native_language_example: We’re going to have a seafood platter.

meaning: seafood (shellfish and other edible sea products).
additional_notes: Common on menus and in markets. Often refers especially to shellfish (oysters, mussels, shrimp), but can also include other seafood depending on context. You may also see it in "plateau de fruits de mer" (a seafood platter).
target_language_example: Je vais prendre les fruits de mer, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’ll have the seafood, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the local time in a region or country relative to others (useful for travel, scheduling calls, flights, etc.). Often used with a possessive or location: « mon/ton fuseau horaire », « le fuseau horaire de Paris ». You can also specify it with « GMT/UTC »: « le fuseau horaire UTC+1 ».
target_language_example: On n’est pas dans le même fuseau horaire, donc il est déjà tard chez toi.
native_language_example: We’re not in the same time zone, so it’s already late where you are.

meaning: livelihood; a way to earn a living.
additional_notes: A noun meaning your source of income or the work that provides it. Often used in phrases like « perdre son gagne-pain » (to lose one’s livelihood) or « assurer son gagne-pain » (to provide for oneself).
target_language_example: Il a peur de perdre son gagne-pain.
native_language_example: He’s afraid of losing his livelihood.

meaning: to save time; to buy time.
additional_notes: Used when you reduce the time something takes (“save time”) or when you delay something to give yourself more time (“buy time”). Often followed by « en + verb »: « gagner du temps en prenant le métro » (save time by taking the subway). In the “buy time” sense, it can imply stalling: « Il essaie de gagner du temps. »
target_language_example: On va prendre un taxi pour gagner du temps.
native_language_example: We’re going to take a taxi to save time.

meaning: to gain ground; to make progress.
additional_notes: Used literally for moving forward in physical space (especially in sports or the military) and very often figuratively for making progress, becoming more popular, or getting an advantage (an idea, a party, a team, etc.).
target_language_example: Ces derniers mois, notre projet a gagné du terrain.
native_language_example: In recent months, our project has gained ground.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone makes money for basic living expenses (their job or profession). Often appears with “Comment tu gagnes ta vie ?” (How do you make a living?) or “Je gagne ma vie en + verb” (I earn a living by...). The possessive changes with the subject: je gagne ma vie, tu gagnes ta vie, il/elle gagne sa vie, nous gagnons notre vie, vous gagnez votre vie, ils/elles gagnent leur vie.
target_language_example: Je gagne ma vie comme infirmière.
native_language_example: I earn a living as a nurse.

additional_notes: Refers to a person whose job is to protect someone (often a VIP). Usually used with an article (un garde du corps / le garde du corps). Plural: des gardes du corps (often pronounced the same).
target_language_example: La chanteuse a un garde du corps.
native_language_example: The singer has a bodyguard.

additional_notes: A legal term in France: someone is kept at a police station and questioned as part of an investigation (not the same as being convicted). Often used with verbs like « être placé(e) en garde à vue » (to be taken into police custody) or « mettre quelqu’un en garde à vue » (to place someone in police custody).
target_language_example: Il a été placé en garde à vue après l’incident.
native_language_example: He was taken into police custody after the incident.

additional_notes: Commonly refers to a wardrobe/closet where clothes are kept, or to someone’s collection of clothes (like “wardrobe” in English). In theater/film, it can also mean “costumes/wardrobe department” depending on context.
target_language_example: J’ai rangé mes manteaux dans la garde-robe.
native_language_example: I put away my coats in the closet/wardrobe.

meaning: to keep an eye (on); to watch carefully.
additional_notes: Often used as « garder l'œil sur + [something/someone] » to mean keeping something under observation or monitoring it (e.g., a bag, a child, a situation). You can also say « garder un œil sur… » which is very common and means the same thing.
target_language_example: Tu peux garder l'œil sur mon sac pendant que je vais aux toilettes ?
native_language_example: Can you keep an eye on my bag while I go to the restroom?

meaning: to keep a cool head; stay calm.
additional_notes: Used to say you should remain calm and think clearly in a stressful or tense situation. Often used as advice or encouragement (e.g., "Il faut garder la tête froide").
target_language_example: Même sous pression, essaie de garder la tête froide.
native_language_example: Even under pressure, try to keep a cool head.

meaning: to keep quiet; to remain silent.
additional_notes: A fairly formal way to say you are staying silent or not speaking (often by choice, in a serious or official context). Common with subjects like "je/il/elle" or as an instruction: "Gardez le silence" (Please keep quiet). You can also use it for not revealing information: "garder le silence sur" (to stay silent about).
target_language_example: Pendant la réunion, il a gardé le silence.
native_language_example: During the meeting, he remained silent.

additional_notes: Refers to a person who supervises inmates in a prison (a corrections officer). You’ll also see the plural "gardiens de prison". Not to be confused with "gardien" alone, which can mean a keeper/guardian (e.g., "gardien de but" = goalkeeper).
target_language_example: Le gardien de prison ouvre la cellule.
native_language_example: The prison guard opens the cell.

meaning: a tomboy (a girl who behaves or dresses in a typically boyish way).
additional_notes: Literally means “missed boy,” but it’s an idiomatic set phrase meaning a girl/woman considered boyish. It’s usually used for females: une fille / une femme, or a feminine person. As a noun phrase, it’s invariable in form (you still say une fille garçon manqué). Depending on context, it can feel old-fashioned or stereotypical, so use with care.
target_language_example: Quand elle était petite, c’était un vrai garçon manqué : elle jouait toujours au foot avec les garçons.
native_language_example: When she was little, she was a real tomboy: she always played soccer with the boys.

additional_notes: Used for the flotation device you wear for safety on a boat, during water sports, or on a plane. Also commonly said as "un gilet de sauvetage"; in everyday French you may also hear "un gilet de sécurité" depending on context.
target_language_example: Mets ton gilet de sauvetage avant de monter dans le bateau.
native_language_example: Put on your life jacket before getting into the boat.

additional_notes: Used for a mass of earth/rocks sliding down a slope, often after heavy rain or an earthquake. In news and warnings you may see it with verbs like "il y a eu" (there was), "provoquer" (to cause), or "évacuer" (to evacuate). Also used figuratively in politics to mean a "landslide victory" (une victoire par glissement de terrain).
target_language_example: Après les fortes pluies, un glissement de terrain a bloqué la route.
native_language_example: After the heavy rain, a landslide blocked the road.

additional_notes: Most often used in the set phrase « au grand air » (“outdoors / in the open air”). You’ll also hear « prendre le grand air » meaning “to get some fresh air / go outside.”
target_language_example: Après le déjeuner, on est allés se promener au grand air.
native_language_example: After lunch, we went for a walk outdoors.

meaning: a big day; an important/special day.
additional_notes: Used for a significant event (wedding, exam, moving day, etc.). Often appears with the definite article: « le grand jour » = “the big day” (the long-awaited day).
target_language_example: Le grand jour approche : on se marie samedi.
native_language_example: The big day is coming: we’re getting married on Saturday.

additional_notes: Used in accounting/bookkeeping for the record that summarizes all financial transactions by account. Also used in the more general sense of a big, important book (e.g., an old registry), but the accounting meaning is the most common fixed term.
target_language_example: Le comptable met à jour le grand livre chaque mois.
native_language_example: The accountant updates the general ledger each month.

additional_notes: Refers to a large store with many different departments (clothes, home goods, cosmetics, etc.). Often used with an article: « un grand magasin » (a department store) or « le grand magasin » (the department store). Common in shopping contexts; not the same as « magasin » alone (shop/store in general).
target_language_example: On va au grand magasin pour acheter des vêtements.
native_language_example: We’re going to the department store to buy clothes.

additional_notes: Used mainly after a noun (often a door or window): « la porte est grand ouverte ». It can also agree in gender/number: grand ouvert (masc. sing.), grande ouverte (fem. sing.), grands ouverts (masc. pl.), grandes ouvertes (fem. pl.). Means opened as much as possible (not just slightly open).
target_language_example: Laisse la fenêtre grand ouverte, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Leave the window wide open, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about watching a film in a movie theater (sur grand écran = on the big screen), as opposed to at home on TV or a phone. Also used more generally for any large display (e.g., a big TV), but the cinema meaning is very common.
target_language_example: J’aimerais voir ce film sur grand écran.
native_language_example: I’d like to see this movie on the big screen.

additional_notes: Also commonly spelled "grand-mère" (modern standard). Used with possessives like "ma grand-mère" (my grandmother), "ta grand-mère" (your grandmother). Plural: "des grands-mères".
target_language_example: Ma grand-mère habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: My grandmother lives in Lyon.

additional_notes: Most often used with negation to mean “much” or “anything”: « pas grand-chose » = “not much / not anything.” Also common in questions: « quelque chose ou grand-chose ? » Often follows the verb: « Je ne sais pas grand-chose. » In informal speech you may hear « pas grand-chose » without the full « ne ».
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas grand-chose à manger.
native_language_example: I don’t have much to eat.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your (or someone’s) grandmother. With the article: « ma grand-mère » (my grandmother), « sa grand-mère » (his/her grandmother). Plural: « grands-mères ». The word literally means “great mother,” but it’s the standard word for “grandmother.”
target_language_example: Je vais chez ma grand-mère ce week-end.
native_language_example: I’m going to my grandmother’s this weekend.

additional_notes: Refers to a grandparent (one of your parents’ parents). Singular: un grand-parent / une grand-mère / un grand-père. Plural: des grands-parents (“grandparents”). Often used with possessives: mes grands-parents (my grandparents).
target_language_example: Mes grands-parents habitent à Lyon.
native_language_example: My grandparents live in Lyon.

additional_notes: Family word meaning your parent's father. Often used with a possessive: « mon grand-père », « ton grand-père », etc. Pronunciation: the final “e” is silent, so it sounds like “grand-pair.”
target_language_example: Mon grand-père habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: My grandfather lives in Lyon.

meaning: a loudmouth; someone who talks big (often annoyingly).
additional_notes: Usually negative and informal. Describes someone who talks too much, speaks loudly, boasts, or makes big promises—sometimes without doing much. Can be said as an insult ("Quelle grande gueule !") or more casually about someone’s personality.
target_language_example: Arrête de faire la grande gueule et montre-nous ce que tu sais faire.
native_language_example: Stop talking big and show us what you can do.

additional_notes: Literally “big person,” but it’s commonly used (especially by or when talking to children) to mean a grown-up/adult, contrasting with a child (un enfant). Often used with an article: « une grande personne », « les grandes personnes ». Not the usual neutral adult word in formal contexts (where « un adulte » is more standard).
target_language_example: Quand je serai grand, je veux être une grande personne comme toi.
native_language_example: When I grow up, I want to be a grown-up like you.

additional_notes: Used for the big rotating wheel at a fair/carnival (une fête foraine) or amusement park. It’s feminine: une grande roue. Literal meaning is “big wheel,” which matches the idea, but in English you normally say “Ferris wheel.”
target_language_example: On a fait un tour de grande roue hier soir.
native_language_example: We went on the Ferris wheel last night.

meaning: an air of importance; putting on airs.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone acting pretentious or superior (often with verbs like "prendre" or "se donner": "prendre/se donner de grands airs"). It’s usually mildly negative or teasing. Literally "big airs," but in English you’d typically say "to put on airs" or "an air of importance."
target_language_example: Depuis qu’il a eu sa promotion, il se donne de grands airs.
native_language_example: Since he got his promotion, he’s been putting on airs.

meaning: "Good heavens!" / "For heaven’s sake!" (an exclamation of surprise, shock, or impatience).
additional_notes: Used as an interjection, often with an exclamation mark: « Grands dieux ! ». Literally means “great gods,” but it’s an idiomatic, mild oath (can sound a bit old-fashioned). You may also see stronger variants like « Par tous les grands dieux ! » (“For heaven’s sake!”).
target_language_example: Grands dieux ! Tu as vu l’heure ?
native_language_example: Good heavens! Have you seen the time?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the classical language (as opposed to modern Greek, "grec moderne"). Often appears in school/university contexts: "cours de grec ancien" (Ancient Greek class), "traduction du grec ancien" (translation from Ancient Greek). As an adjective phrase it agrees with what it describes: "la langue grecque ancienne" (the ancient Greek language).
target_language_example: J’étudie le grec ancien à l’université.
native_language_example: I study Ancient Greek at university.

additional_notes: Used to name the modern form of the Greek language (as opposed to ancient/classical Greek). Often seen in classes, books, and university course titles. Agreement: it stays masculine singular here because it refers to “le grec” (the Greek language).
target_language_example: Je prends des cours de grec moderne cette année.
native_language_example: I’m taking Modern Greek classes this year.

additional_notes: A common household noun for the electric appliance used to toast bread. It’s masculine: un grille-pain. Plural: des grille-pains. Often used with verbs like utiliser / brancher / réparer.
target_language_example: Je mets le pain dans le grille-pain.
native_language_example: I put the bread in the toaster.

additional_notes: An emphatic way to say “common sense” (bon sens) by adding gros (“big”). Often used with an article: du gros bon sens (“some plain common sense”) or le gros bon sens (“plain common sense”). Register is generally neutral/colloquial, not slang.
target_language_example: Il suffit d’un peu de gros bon sens pour résoudre ce problème.
native_language_example: A little plain common sense is enough to solve this problem.

meaning: a thug; hired muscle (a tough guy used for intimidation).
additional_notes: Informal. Used to refer to someone (often big/strong-looking) brought in to threaten, pressure, or physically intimidate others (e.g., by a boss, a club, debt collectors). Literal words mean “big arms,” but the usual sense is figurative.
target_language_example: Ils ont envoyé des gros bras pour le faire taire.
native_language_example: They sent some thugs/hired muscle to shut him up.

additional_notes: Literally “big dog.” « Gros » is an adjective meaning “big/large” (sometimes “fat”) and it comes before the noun here. If the dog is female, you’d usually say « un gros chien » (male dog) but « une grosse chienne » (female dog).
target_language_example: Il a un gros chien noir.
native_language_example: He has a big black dog.

additional_notes: Most common in lotteries, raffles, and contests. Often used with the definite article: « le gros lot » (“the jackpot”). Can also be used more generally to mean a big win or major reward.
target_language_example: Il a gagné le gros lot à la loterie.
native_language_example: He won the jackpot in the lottery.

meaning: a swear word; a curse word.
additional_notes: Used to refer to rude or offensive language (profanity). Often appears with verbs like dire (“to say”): « Ne dis pas de gros mots. » Literally “big word,” but it does not mean “a long/complicated word.”
target_language_example: Ne dis pas de gros mots devant les enfants.
native_language_example: Don’t swear in front of the children.

additional_notes: Common everyday body-part term. Usually used with a possessive: « mon/ton/son gros orteil » (my/your/his/her big toe). In French, « gros » means “big” and « orteil » means “toe.”
target_language_example: Je me suis cassé le gros orteil.
native_language_example: I broke my big toe.

meaning: a “big fish”; an important or powerful person (a big shot).
additional_notes: Can be literal (“a big fish”) or figurative (“a big fish” = someone important in a group, company, politics, etc.). Often used with verbs like « être » (to be) or « devenir » (to become): « C’est un gros poisson. »
target_language_example: Dans cette entreprise, c’est un gros poisson.
native_language_example: In that company, he’s a big shot.

meaning: headline; main title (especially in the press).
additional_notes: Used for the main, large title of a newspaper article, online news story, or magazine cover. You’ll also hear it about any big, attention-grabbing title (e.g., on a poster). In journalism, it contrasts with a smaller secondary title (a "sous-titre").
target_language_example: Le gros titre du journal annonce une hausse des prix.
native_language_example: The newspaper’s headline announces a price increase.

additional_notes: Used in medical contexts (doctor’s office, hospital, blood donation). Often followed by a letter and sign: A, B, AB, O, and +/− (e.g., « O négatif »). In French you may also hear « groupe sanguin » and « groupe sanguin (ABO) » or simply « groupe » in context.
target_language_example: Quel est votre groupe sanguin ?
native_language_example: What is your blood type?

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens due to a cause, often with a positive or appreciative tone. For a negative cause, French often prefers "à cause de" (because of). Followed by a noun/pronoun: "grâce à + nom" (e.g., grâce à toi, grâce à son aide).
target_language_example: Grâce à ton aide, j’ai fini à temps.
native_language_example: Thanks to your help, I finished on time.

additional_notes: Used to describe a war fought within a single country, usually between different groups of its own people (not between two countries). Often appears with a country name (e.g., « la guerre civile en Espagne »).
target_language_example: La guerre civile a duré plusieurs années.
native_language_example: The civil war lasted several years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the historical conflict; often appears with verbs like "pendant" (during), "après" (after), or in history/politics contexts. It’s a specific proper-name-style phrase: "guerre" (war) + "du" (of the) + "Vietnam".
target_language_example: Mon grand-père a vécu pendant la guerre du Vietnam.
native_language_example: My grandfather lived during the Vietnam War.

additional_notes: Informal. Literally “wooden mouth,” but it means the bad feeling after drinking too much alcohol. Often used with “avoir” (to have): « J’ai une gueule de bois » (I have a hangover). You can also say « avoir la gueule de bois ».
target_language_example: J’ai une gueule de bois ce matin.
native_language_example: I have a hangover this morning.

additional_notes: Usually means a person who shows visitors around (a tour guide): « un/une guide touristique ». It can also mean a book/app with travel information (a travel guide/guidebook): « un guide touristique (de Paris) ». The adjective « touristique » means “tourist”/“touristic,” so the phrase is fairly literal.
target_language_example: Nous avons engagé un guide touristique pour visiter la vieille ville.
native_language_example: We hired a tour guide to visit the old town.

additional_notes: Used to show you don’t know, don’t care, or can’t do anything about something. Often used with a subject: “Il/Elle a haussé les épaules” (He/She shrugged).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas quoi dire, alors j’ai haussé les épaules.
native_language_example: I didn’t know what to say, so I shrugged.

additional_notes: Used to describe products/services of premium quality (often more expensive). Common in shopping/marketing contexts. Can be used as an adjective phrase ("un hôtel haut de gamme") or as a noun phrase ("du haut de gamme" = high-end goods).
target_language_example: Ils cherchent une voiture haut de gamme.
native_language_example: They are looking for a high-end car.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who has an important role or a lot of authority (often in government, business, the police, etc.). It typically comes after the noun: « un responsable haut placé », « un fonctionnaire haut placé ». Feminine: « haut placée ».
target_language_example: Un responsable haut placé a confirmé l’information.
native_language_example: A high-ranking official confirmed the information.

additional_notes: A noun for a device that plays sound out loud (in a phone, computer, TV, or public address system). Often used with "un/une" depending on the model (in practice many speakers treat it as masculine: "un haut-parleur"). Common plural: "des haut-parleurs". Not to confuse with "écouteurs" (earbuds/headphones).
target_language_example: Le haut-parleur de mon téléphone ne marche plus.
native_language_example: The speaker on my phone doesn’t work anymore.

meaning: "moment of glory"; a short period of fame or success.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s (or something’s) brief time in the spotlight or biggest success. Often appears with "son/sa" (e.g., "son heure de gloire" = "his moment of glory"). Can be neutral or slightly ironic depending on context.
target_language_example: Cette chanson a eu son heure de gloire dans les années 90.
native_language_example: That song had its moment of glory in the 90s.

meaning: rush hour; peak time (when traffic/public transport is busiest).
additional_notes: Used for times of day when roads and public transport are most crowded, typically morning and evening commutes. Often appears with prepositions like « à l’heure de pointe » (at rush hour) or « aux heures de pointe » (during peak hours).
target_language_example: Le métro est bondé à l’heure de pointe.
native_language_example: The subway is packed at rush hour.

additional_notes: Used for hours worked beyond your normal schedule, often paid at a higher rate. Common in workplace contexts and with verbs like faire (to do/work) or payer (to pay): « faire des heures supplémentaires », « être payé(e) en heures supplémentaires ». Often shortened to « les heures sup » (informal).
target_language_example: Cette semaine, j’ai fait des heures supplémentaires.
native_language_example: This week, I worked overtime.

meaning: old story; ancient history (often: something from long ago that no longer matters).
additional_notes: Literally “ancient history.” Commonly used to say a past event is over and done with: « C’est de l’histoire ancienne » = “That’s old news / that’s in the past.” Can also refer literally to the subject of ancient history (as a school/university topic).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas pour ça, c’est de l’histoire ancienne.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about that—it’s in the past.

meaning: a love story; a romantic relationship/affair.
additional_notes: Often used for a romantic story (a book/movie) or to talk about two people’s relationship. You can also say "une histoire d’amour" (a love story) or "leur histoire d’amour" (their love story).
target_language_example: C’est une belle histoire d’amour.
native_language_example: It’s a beautiful love story.

additional_notes: Common way to express purpose or intention before an infinitive: "histoire de + infinitive" (often close to "just to" in English). It can also introduce a reason: "C’est une histoire de ..." = "It’s a matter of ..." (e.g., "une histoire d’argent" = "a money issue").
target_language_example: Je suis passé histoire de te dire bonjour.
native_language_example: I stopped by just to say hi.

additional_notes: A formal/common term for a man who works in business, often in management or running a company. Feminine form: "femme d'affaires" (businesswoman). You can also use the more general "un homme d'affaires" / "une femme d'affaires" for “a businessperson.”
target_language_example: C'est un homme d'affaires très connu à Paris.
native_language_example: He is a very well-known businessman in Paris.

meaning: the right person for the job (lit. “man for the situation”).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is particularly well-suited to handle a specific challenge or moment. Often used with “être” (to be): « Il est l’homme de la situation. » Can also be said about a woman in practice, but a more gender-neutral option is « la personne de la situation » or « la femme de la situation » depending on context.
target_language_example: Pour gérer cette crise, elle est l’homme de la situation.
native_language_example: To handle this crisis, she’s the right person for the job.

meaning: a strongman; the dominant/influential man (often in politics or an organization).
additional_notes: Used for someone who holds real power or control (an influential leader, boss, or political strongman). It can be neutral or slightly critical depending on context. Literally “strong man,” but the common sense is about power/influence rather than physical strength.
target_language_example: Dans ce parti, c’est lui l’homme fort depuis des années.
native_language_example: In that party, he has been the strongman for years.

additional_notes: A common neutral term for someone involved in politics (an elected official or political leader). It’s used in news and formal contexts. Can refer to any gender in practice, but for a woman you can also say "femme politique"; "politicien/politicienne" is another common word for “politician.”
target_language_example: C’est un homme politique très connu en France.
native_language_example: He is a very well-known politician in France.

additional_notes: A set phrase (especially in 17th–18th century contexts) describing an ideal man: morally upright, well-mannered, educated, and socially polished. It does not simply mean “an honest man” in the everyday sense (that would be more like « un homme honnête »). You’ll most often see it in literature, history, or formal discussion.
target_language_example: Au XVIIe siècle, l’honnête homme devait être cultivé et modéré.
native_language_example: In the 17th century, the honnête homme was expected to be cultured and moderate.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean “outside” or “not in.” Common fixed phrases include: "hors de question" (out of the question), "hors service" (out of order / not working), "hors de prix" (overpriced), and "hors de danger" (out of danger).
target_language_example: Ce sujet est hors de question.
native_language_example: That topic is out of the question.

additional_notes: Used for situations, emotions, costs, or events that can’t be managed or contained anymore. Often follows verbs like « être » or « devenir »: « C’est hors de contrôle » / « Ça devient hors de contrôle ». Can also describe something physically uncontrolled (e.g., a vehicle).
target_language_example: La situation est hors de contrôle.
native_language_example: The situation is out of control.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is no longer in immediate danger (often after an accident, illness, or emergency). Common with forms of "être": "Il/Elle est hors de danger."
target_language_example: Après l'opération, le médecin a dit qu'il était hors de danger.
native_language_example: After the operation, the doctor said he was out of danger.

meaning: "out of reach" / "out of range"; sometimes "beyond (someone’s) means."
additional_notes: Used literally for something you can’t physically reach or that’s too far away, and also figuratively for something inaccessible (e.g., too expensive: "hors de portée" or "hors de portée de + someone"). Common with verbs like "être" and "mettre" (e.g., "mettre hors de portée").
target_language_example: Ce livre est hors de portée des enfants.
native_language_example: This book is out of reach of the children.

additional_notes: A fairly formal expression used to say that a comment, question, or remark doesn’t fit the topic or situation. Often used with être: « C’est hors de propos » / « Votre remarque est hors de propos ».
target_language_example: Je suis désolé, mais votre question est hors de propos.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but your question is beside the point.

meaning: Out of the question; no way.
additional_notes: Used to refuse or reject something strongly (“absolutely not”). Often appears with "C’est" (C’est hors de question.) or "Il/Elle est" (Il est hors de question de + infinitive = There’s no question of / It’s out of the question to...). More emphatic than a simple "non".
target_language_example: C’est hors de question que tu partes tout seul.
native_language_example: There’s no way you’re leaving all by yourself.

meaning: out of order; not in service.
additional_notes: Used on signs/labels to say a machine, device, elevator, etc. is not working or unavailable. Often seen as: « En panne » (broken down) or « hors d’usage » (unusable), but « hors service » is very common for public equipment.
target_language_example: Désolé, l’ascenseur est hors service.
native_language_example: Sorry, the elevator is out of order.

additional_notes: Used for the fast-food item (a sausage in a bun). Common in casual speech and on menus; plural: « des hot-dogs ». You may also see « un hot dog » without the hyphen.
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un hot-dog, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’ll have a hot dog, please.

additional_notes: Used to say the number 800. In French, "cent" (hundred) takes an -s ("cents") when it is multiplied and not followed by another number ("huit cents"), but it stays singular when another number comes after it ("huit cent un" = 801).
target_language_example: Ça coûte huit cents euros.
native_language_example: It costs eight hundred euros.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens occasionally or by chance. Very often followed by the subjunctive: « Il arrive que + subjunctive ». Similar in meaning to « il se peut que » (it may be that). Note: « arriver » here means “to happen,” not “to arrive,” so it can be misleading for English speakers.
target_language_example: Il arrive que je sois en retard quand il pleut.
native_language_example: Sometimes I’m late when it rains.

additional_notes: Colloquial/spoken word order (literally “it’s what hour?”). More formal: « Quelle heure est-il ? ». Often used as a question with rising intonation, and you can add « s’il vous plaît » to be polite.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, il est quelle heure, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time is it, please?

meaning: it’s necessary; you have to; must.
additional_notes: Fixed impersonal expression using the verb *falloir*. Often followed by an infinitive: **il faut + verb** (“you/we must…”): *Il faut partir.* It can also be followed by **que + subjunctive**: *Il faut que tu viennes.* Even though **il** usually means “he,” here it doesn’t refer to a person; it’s like “it” in “it’s necessary.”
target_language_example: Il faut partir maintenant.
native_language_example: We have to leave now.

meaning: “You have to admit it” / “That’s something!” (often: “Well, that takes nerve!”).
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal expression « il faut » (“it’s necessary”) + « le faire » (“to do it”), but in real life it’s often said as a reaction meaning “you’ve got to hand it to them” or “can you believe it,” sometimes admiring, often ironic/critical depending on tone and context. Common in spoken French.
target_language_example: Il a menti devant tout le monde ; il faut le faire !
native_language_example: He lied in front of everyone; that takes nerve!

meaning: “it’s necessary / it has to be done.”
additional_notes: From the impersonal verb falloir (“to be necessary”). The pronoun le refers to something already mentioned (an action/plan): il le faut = “it must be done / it’s required.” Often used with si (“if”): s’il le faut = “if necessary.”
target_language_example: Je peux venir demain, s’il le faut.
native_language_example: I can come tomorrow, if necessary.

meaning: No way; absolutely not; that’s out of the question.
additional_notes: Used to refuse strongly or to say something won’t happen. Common in conversation and can sound firm/strict (depending on tone). Often followed by an infinitive: « Il n’en est pas question de + infinitive » (“There’s no question of… / We’re not going to…”).
target_language_example: — Tu peux me prêter ta voiture ? — Il n’en est pas question.
native_language_example: — Can you lend me your car? — No way.

additional_notes: Imperfect of "falloir" used to express past obligation/necessity, often with regret or criticism. Commonly followed by an infinitive: "Il ne fallait pas + infinitive" = “You shouldn’t have + verb” / “You didn’t need to + verb.” It can also be used on its own to react to what someone did: “You shouldn’t have (done that)!”
target_language_example: Il ne fallait pas acheter autant de nourriture.
native_language_example: You didn’t need to buy so much food.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or a conclusion after mentioning another point (often like “even so…”). It’s fairly formal and common in writing and careful speech. Usually followed by a clause: « Il reste que + subject + verb ».
target_language_example: Il a fait des efforts, mais il reste que le résultat est insuffisant.
native_language_example: He made efforts, but the fact remains that the result is insufficient.

additional_notes: Very common expression. Use it to say something exists or is present: "Il y a un problème" (There is a problem). It can also express how long ago something happened: "il y a deux jours" = two days ago. It’s invariable (doesn’t change for singular/plural): "Il y a un chat" / "Il y a deux chats".
target_language_example: Il y a un café près d’ici.
native_language_example: There is a café near here.

additional_notes: Used to indicate how long ago something happened, followed by a time expression (e.g., "trois ans", "quelques jours"). It’s a bit more formal/literary than simply "il y a" and often corresponds to English "... ago" rather than a literal translation.
target_language_example: Il y a de cela trois ans, j’ai déménagé à Lyon.
native_language_example: Three years ago, I moved to Lyon.

meaning: "about/roughly (that long) ago" (used with a time period).
additional_notes: Used to give an approximate time in the past, usually followed by a duration: « il y a de ça dix ans » = “about ten years ago.” Less commonly, it can also mean “there’s some truth in that / there’s something to that,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Je l’ai rencontré il y a de ça trois ans.
native_language_example: I met him about three years ago.

meaning: a long time ago; long ago.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened far in the past. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence (e.g., "Il y a longtemps, ..." or "..., il y a longtemps"). You’ll also see "il y a longtemps que + sentence" meaning “it’s been a long time since …”.
target_language_example: Je l’ai rencontré il y a longtemps.
native_language_example: I met him a long time ago.

additional_notes: Used when referring to an unspecified amount of something already mentioned. The pronoun “en” replaces “de + noun” (e.g., du pain, des pommes) or a quantity: “Il y en a trois” = “There are three (of them).” Often appears in answers or short statements.
target_language_example: Des croissants ? Oui, il y en a sur la table.
native_language_example: Croissants? Yes, there are some on the table.

il y en a des qui

target_language_multi_word_term: il y en a des qui
additional_notes: Common in spoken French to introduce a group within a larger set (often with a slightly critical, surprised, or joking tone). It’s an informal way to say "certains / certaines…" ("some…"). You’ll often hear it shortened in speech: "Y en a qui…"
target_language_example: Il y en a des qui se plaignent tout le temps.
native_language_example: There are some people who complain all the time.

additional_notes: A fixed storytelling opening used at the start of fairy tales and traditional stories. Literally “there was one time,” but in English it’s best translated as “once upon a time.” Usually followed by a description of the setting or characters.
target_language_example: Il était une fois une princesse qui vivait dans un grand château.
native_language_example: Once upon a time, there was a princess who lived in a big castle.

additional_notes: A very common way to talk about hunger. French uses “avoir” (to have): literally “I have hunger.” You can change the subject: “tu as faim” (you’re hungry), “il/elle a faim” (he/she is hungry), “nous avons faim” (we’re hungry).
target_language_example: J'ai faim, on mange ?
native_language_example: I'm hungry—shall we eat?

additional_notes: Very common way to express fear or being scared. Literally “I have fear,” but in English you usually say “I’m afraid/scared.” Often followed by de + infinitive (J’ai peur de tomber. = I’m afraid of falling) or que + subjunctive (J’ai peur qu’il pleuve. = I’m afraid it’ll rain).
target_language_example: J’ai peur du chien.
native_language_example: I’m scared of the dog.

additional_notes: Common way to ask for permission to speak or to introduce a question in class, at work, or in customer service. Often followed by "sur…" (about…) or "à propos de…" (regarding…). You can soften it with "Excusez-moi" / "Excuse-moi" (Excuse me).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, j’ai une question sur les devoirs.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have a question about the homework.

meaning: "I have (something) to do." / "I’ve got something to do."
additional_notes: Used to say you have tasks or obligations. Often followed by what you need to do (e.g., "j’ai à faire mes devoirs"), or used on its own to mean you’re busy (implied: "j’ai quelque chose à faire"). Similar to "je dois faire…" (I must do…), but "j’ai à faire…" can sound a bit more like “I have things to take care of.”
