target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : j’ai à faire ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I’ve got things to do tonight.

additional_notes: Very common informal spoken contraction of « je ne sais pas ». It often drops « ne » and shortens « je » to « j' »; you’ll also see « chais pas » in very casual speech. Use it in conversations, but avoid it in formal writing or polite situations (use « Je ne sais pas » or « Je ne sais pas, désolé(e). »).
target_language_example: J'sais pas où il est.
native_language_example: I don't know where he is.

meaning: “something or other” / “I don’t know what (exactly)” (an indefinable thing).
additional_notes: Very informal spoken сокращение of « je ne sais pas quoi ». Used when you can’t quite name or describe what you mean, or when something has an indefinable quality (often like “a certain something”). Can follow a noun: « un petit j’sais pas quoi ».
target_language_example: Ce film a un petit j’sais pas quoi que j’adore.
native_language_example: That movie has a certain something that I love.

additional_notes: A city-owned green space open to everyone (often with paths, benches, playgrounds). You can use it to ask where one is or suggest going there: « Il y a un jardin public près d’ici ? »
target_language_example: On se retrouve au jardin public après le déjeuner ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at the public park after lunch?

meaning: "I'm getting by" / "I'm managing" (not great, but OK).
additional_notes: Common spoken reply to « Ça va ? » or « Comment ça va ? ». It suggests you’re doing so-so—coping, but not amazing. Often also heard as « Ça fait aller. »
target_language_example: — Ça va ? — Bof… je fais aller.
native_language_example: — How are you? — Meh… I’m getting by.

additional_notes: Used to introduce yourself and say your name. It literally means “I call myself,” using the reflexive verb s’appeler. Follow it with your name (often without “:”): Je m’appelle Sarah. In questions you’ll often hear: Comment tu t’appelles ? / Comment vous vous appelez ?
target_language_example: Bonjour, je m’appelle David.
native_language_example: Hello, my name is David.

additional_notes: A very common phrase to say you didn’t understand what someone said. In speech, the “ne” is often dropped: “Je comprends pas.” You can also add “bien” to emphasize: “Je ne comprends pas bien” (“I don’t understand well/very well”).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne comprends pas. Vous pouvez répéter ?
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t understand. Can you repeat?

meaning: "I’m not saying (that)…" / "I’m not saying you’re wrong, but…"
additional_notes: Used to soften a statement, add a nuance, or introduce a disagreement politely. Often followed by a contrasting idea with « mais… » or by « que… » (e.g., « Je ne dis pas que… »). In casual speech, the « ne » is often dropped: « Je dis pas… ».
target_language_example: Je ne dis pas que tu as tort, mais je pense qu’on devrait vérifier.
native_language_example: I’m not saying you’re wrong, but I think we should check.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt or disagreement. Often followed by a clause with "que" ("Je ne pense pas que..." = "I don't think that..."). In everyday speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Je pense pas".
target_language_example: Je ne pense pas que ce soit une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I don't think that's a good idea.

additional_notes: Very common way to say you don’t know. Often heard (and said) as "je sais pas" in casual speech, where "ne" is dropped. You can add "désolé(e)" to soften it: "Je ne sais pas, désolé(e)."
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas où il est.
native_language_example: I don’t know where he is.

meaning: "I think so" / "I do think so" (often: "I think you're right").
additional_notes: Used to agree or confirm something, often with emphasis or certainty. In conversation it can sound a bit stronger than just « je pense » (closer to “I really do think so”). Depending on tone, it can also be slightly ironic (“Yeah, I bet!”).
target_language_example: — Il va pleuvoir demain. — Oui, je pense bien.
native_language_example: — It’s going to rain tomorrow. — Yes, I think so.

additional_notes: Used to announce or state a pregnancy. "Enceinte" agrees with the speaker: a woman says "je suis enceinte"; a man would say "ma femme/ma partenaire est enceinte" (“my wife/partner is pregnant”). The literal meaning of "enceinte" can also be “enclosed/walled in,” but in everyday conversation it commonly means “pregnant.”
target_language_example: Je suis enceinte de trois mois.
native_language_example: I’m three months pregnant.

additional_notes: Used to state your nationality or identity. "Je suis" = "I am". Make the adjective agree with the speaker: a woman typically says "Je suis française" (extra -e). You can also specify from where in France: "Je suis français, de Lyon."
target_language_example: Bonjour, je suis français.
native_language_example: Hello, I’m French.

additional_notes: Used to state nationality/identity. Add -e to “français” for a female speaker: “Je suis français.” (man) / “Je suis française.” (woman). Often followed by a place: “Je suis française, je viens de Lyon.”
target_language_example: Bonjour, je suis française.
native_language_example: Hello, I’m French.

additional_notes: A common way to express romantic love. "Je" = "I" and "t'" is short for "te" ("you") before a vowel. In everyday speech you may also hear "Je t’aime bien" ("I like you")—adding "bien" makes it less strong than "je t’aime".
target_language_example: Je t'aime, mon amour.
native_language_example: I love you, my love.

additional_notes: Very common polite phrase. Often used to respond to "merci" (like "you're welcome"). It can also mean "please" in the sense of "I beg you" / "please do" (more formal/insistent), e.g., asking someone to do something or to accept/refuse something politely. With "tu" (informal you); a more formal version is "je vous en prie".
target_language_example: — Merci pour ton aide. — Je t'en prie !
native_language_example: — Thanks for your help. — You're welcome!

meaning: “I’m going to go” / “I’m going to head off.”
additional_notes: Uses the near future (aller + infinitive): je vais + aller. In everyday French, people often avoid this repetition by saying “je vais y aller” (“I’m going to go there / I’m heading off”) or simply “j’y vais” (“I’m going”).
target_language_example: Je vais aller au supermarché après le travail.
native_language_example: I’m going to go to the supermarket after work.

additional_notes: Literally means you see something with your eyes, but very often it’s used like English “I see” to show you understand or you get the point (often followed by “ce que…” or “ce que tu veux dire”).
target_language_example: Je vois ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: I see what you mean.

meaning: "I love you" (to you, formal or plural).
additional_notes: Uses the object pronoun "vous" for either (1) one person you address formally/politely, or (2) more than one person ("you all"). With "aimer", this usually expresses romantic love; for non-romantic liking, French often uses "je vous aime bien" (I like you).
target_language_example: Je vous aime, madame.
native_language_example: I love you, ma'am.

additional_notes: Very common, formal/polite response to “merci” (especially to someone you address with vous). It can also be used to insist politely or to urge someone: “Je vous en prie, continuez / entrez.” Not the same as “s’il vous plaît” for everyday “please” (requests), though it can overlap in tone when urging someone.
target_language_example: — Merci beaucoup. — Je vous en prie.
native_language_example: — Thank you very much. — You're welcome.

meaning: to take a quick look; to glance.
additional_notes: Common everyday expression. Often used with "à" + the thing you’re looking at: "jeter un coup d’œil à". It suggests looking briefly (not studying carefully). You can also see the reflexive form: "Je vais y jeter un coup d’œil" = "I’ll take a quick look at it."
target_language_example: Tu peux jeter un coup d’œil à ce document ?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at this document?

meaning: to take a look; to have a quick look.
additional_notes: Common everyday expression meaning to look at something briefly (often as a favor or to check something). Usually used with "à" (jeter un œil à + noun) or with "sur" in some contexts. Often said as a polite request: "Tu peux jeter un œil ?"
target_language_example: Tu peux jeter un œil à mon CV ?
native_language_example: Can you take a look at my résumé?

additional_notes: Used to say something is extremely easy to do. Often appears with "C’est" (C’est un jeu d’enfant) or after "pour" (C’est un jeu d’enfant pour lui). Can also describe a task that is so simple it feels like a kid could do it.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, c’est un jeu d’enfant.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s child’s play.

additional_notes: Used to say something is easy to do, often with “C’est…” or “Ce n’est pas…”. Literally means “children’s game,” but it’s commonly an idiom meaning “no problem / very simple.”
target_language_example: Pour elle, résoudre ce problème, c’est un jeu d’enfants.
native_language_example: For her, solving this problem is child’s play.

additional_notes: Most often means a deck (pack) of playing cards: « un jeu de cartes ». It can also refer to a particular card game as an activity in some contexts, but « un jeu de cartes » usually = the physical deck. Plural: « des jeux de cartes » (decks / card games).
target_language_example: Tu as un jeu de cartes ? On peut jouer au poker.
native_language_example: Do you have a deck of cards? We can play poker.

additional_notes: Used for games where luck is the main factor (not skill), like roulette or slot machines. Often appears in the plural: « les jeux de hasard » (games of chance / gambling). Can also be used in legal or formal contexts about gambling.
target_language_example: Il dépense trop d’argent dans les jeux de hasard.
native_language_example: He spends too much money on gambling.

additional_notes: Used to describe humor or a clever effect based on words (similar sounds, double meanings, spelling, etc.). Often follows verbs like faire (faire un jeu de mots) or is used in comments like « C’est un jeu de mots. »
target_language_example: C’est un jeu de mots : « mer » et « mère », ça se prononce pareil.
native_language_example: It’s a pun: “sea” and “mother” sound the same in French.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for a video game. Masculine: un jeu vidéo; plural: des jeux vidéo. Often used with verbs like jouer à (to play): jouer à un jeu vidéo.
target_language_example: Je joue à un jeu vidéo après l’école.
native_language_example: I play a video game after school.

additional_notes: A common, neutral phrase for referring to a woman who is young (often roughly late teens to early 30s, depending on context). Used in everyday conversation and descriptions. Literally “young woman.”
target_language_example: Une jeune femme cherche son chemin.
native_language_example: A young woman is looking for her way.

additional_notes: Literally “young girl.” Common in more formal or traditional contexts (e.g., “une jeune fille de 16 ans”). It can also mean a young unmarried woman (“nom de jeune fille” = maiden name), which can sound old-fashioned in some contexts compared with “une fille” or “une jeune femme.”
target_language_example: C’est une jeune fille très gentille.
native_language_example: She’s a very nice young girl.

additional_notes: Common, neutral way to refer to a male youth/young adult. Often used with an article: « un jeune homme » (a young man), « le jeune homme » (the young man). Feminine equivalent: « jeune femme » (young woman).
target_language_example: Un jeune homme m’a aidé à porter mes valises.
native_language_example: A young man helped me carry my suitcases.

additional_notes: Literally “young married,” but it means a man who has just gotten married. Feminine form: « jeune mariée » (newlywed woman). Plural: « jeunes mariés » (newlyweds, can refer to a couple or to men). Often used with « les » to talk about the couple: « les jeunes mariés ».
target_language_example: Le jeune marié a remercié tous les invités.
native_language_example: The groom/newlywed thanked all the guests.

additional_notes: A fairly formal/plural way to refer to young people, often meaning young men specifically. Less common in everyday speech than "les jeunes" (young people/teenagers) or "les jeunes gens" (the young people). "Gens" is plural and uses the adjective before it: "jeunes gens".
target_language_example: Il y avait des jeunes gens devant le cinéma.
native_language_example: There were some young people in front of the movie theater.

additional_notes: Common idiom meaning to have just enough money to live on; often used with “avoir du mal à…” (to have trouble) or in the negative. You can also say “arriver à joindre les deux bouts.”
target_language_example: Avec l’augmentation des prix, on a du mal à joindre les deux bouts.
native_language_example: With rising prices, we’re having trouble making ends meet.

meaning: to play tricks on (someone); to prank (someone).
additional_notes: Usually used with an indirect object: « jouer des tours à quelqu’un ». It means doing something to fool someone or cause minor trouble as a joke (or sometimes in an annoying way). Can also be used about things like memory or luck: « ma mémoire me joue des tours » (“my memory is playing tricks on me”).
target_language_example: Arrête de me jouer des tours !
native_language_example: Stop playing tricks on me!

meaning: to play along; to go along with it (cooperate).
additional_notes: Used when someone cooperates with a plan, follows the rules, or goes along with a situation (sometimes even if they’re not fully convinced). Common in work, school, or social situations: "If you want this to work, you have to play along." Can also imply making an effort to participate or be fair.
target_language_example: Si tu veux que ça marche, il faut jouer le jeu.
native_language_example: If you want it to work, you have to play along.

meaning: 'day after day' (day by day; repeatedly over time).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize something happening continuously or repeatedly over many days. Often suggests routine, persistence, or something that keeps going. Can come at the beginning or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Jour après jour, il s’entraîne pour le marathon.
native_language_example: Day after day, he trains for the marathon.

additional_notes: Literally “day and night.” Used either in a literal sense (all the time, including daytime and nighttime) or figuratively to mean “non-stop/constantly,” often to emphasize sustained effort or activity.
target_language_example: Il travaille jour et nuit pour finir le projet.
native_language_example: He works day and night to finish the project.

additional_notes: Used for an official day off (often national or religious) when many businesses, schools, and public services may be closed or on a reduced schedule. Often used with verbs like « être » (C’est un jour férié.) or « tomber » (Le 1er mai tombe un jour férié.)
target_language_example: Demain, c’est un jour férié, donc les magasins seront fermés.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is a public holiday, so the shops will be closed.

additional_notes: Used for a regular, dated record of what happened (often on a ship, plane, project, or internship). More formal/technical than journal intime (personal diary). You can also say tenir un journal de bord (to keep a logbook).
target_language_example: Pendant le stage, on doit tenir un journal de bord chaque semaine.
native_language_example: During the internship, we have to keep a weekly logbook.

additional_notes: Refers to a private notebook where someone writes their thoughts, feelings, and daily experiences. Often used with possessives (mon/ton/son journal intime). Not the same as a newspaper (un journal).
target_language_example: Elle écrit dans son journal intime tous les soirs.
native_language_example: She writes in her diary every evening.

additional_notes: A common Christmas greeting used in December, often said to friends, family, coworkers, shop staff, etc. You can also write it on cards and messages. Capitalization varies (Noël is usually capitalized).
target_language_example: Joyeux Noël ! J’espère que tu passeras une belle journée.
native_language_example: Merry Christmas! I hope you have a lovely day.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone a happy birthday. Often said directly to the person, written in a card/text, or sung in “Joyeux anniversaire” (the French “Happy Birthday” song). You can add a name or “!” for emphasis: “Joyeux anniversaire, Marie !”.
target_language_example: Joyeux anniversaire ! J’espère que tu passeras une excellente journée.
native_language_example: Happy birthday! I hope you have an excellent day.

meaning: until the end; all the way (through).
additional_notes: Used to say something continues to the very end or is done completely. It can refer to time (“until the end”) or completion (“all the way through”), and also works in encouragement contexts (“go all the way / see it through”). Often used with verbs like aller, continuer, suivre, tenir.
target_language_example: Je vais continuer jusqu'au bout.
native_language_example: I’m going to keep going until the end.

additional_notes: Used to indicate an action continues up to the moment another action happens. It introduces a subordinate clause and is typically followed by the subjunctive: « jusqu’à ce que + [verb in subjunctive] ». Common pair: « attendre jusqu’à ce que… » (“to wait until…”).
target_language_example: Attends ici jusqu’à ce que je revienne.
native_language_example: Wait here until I come back.

meaning: "up to then" / "until then"; also "up to there" (to that point/place).
additional_notes: Used to mark a limit in time or in a sequence of events ("until then", "so far"), and sometimes a limit in space or extent ("up to there/that point"). Often appears as "jusque-là" with a hyphen, especially when used adverbially (e.g., "Jusque-là, tout va bien.").
target_language_example: Jusque-là, je n’avais jamais voyagé seul.
native_language_example: Up to then, I had never traveled alone.

meaning: 'up to then' / 'until then' / 'up to that point'.
additional_notes: Used to mark a limit in time or in a situation: everything that happened before a particular moment or point. Often appears with past tenses (e.g., imparfait or passé composé) when describing what was true/known/done up to that moment. It can also be used in a broader sense meaning 'so far' (up to now), depending on context.
target_language_example: Jusque-là, je n’avais jamais visité Paris.
native_language_example: Up to then, I had never visited Paris.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a recent day in the past without saying exactly which day. It often means “a few days ago” or “recently,” and can also be used with the meaning “some day” depending on context, though most commonly it refers to the past.
target_language_example: Je l’ai rencontré l’autre jour au supermarché.
native_language_example: I ran into him the other day at the supermarket.

meaning: one after the other; one by one.
additional_notes: Used to talk about things happening sequentially (in order), not at the same time. You can use it for people or things. Close equivalents: "l’un après l’autre" (one after the other) and "un par un" (one by one).
target_language_example: Ils sont entrés dans la salle l’un après l’autre.
native_language_example: They entered the room one after the other.

additional_notes: Used to express a reciprocal action between two people or things. Often follows the verb: « Ils se regardent l’un l’autre. » With a preposition (especially "de"), it becomes « l’un de l’autre » (= from each other / of one another): « Ils habitent près l’un de l’autre. » Can agree in gender/number: « l’une l’autre » (two females), « les uns les autres » (plural/mixed group).
target_language_example: Ils s’aident l’un l’autre quand ça ne va pas.
native_language_example: They help each other when things aren’t going well.

meaning: to shut up; to stop talking.
additional_notes: Very informal and often rude/harsh. Used to tell someone to be quiet (similar to “zip it” / “shut it”). Often appears in the imperative: « Boucle-la ! » (“Shut up!”). The « la » is a fixed pronoun in this expression (it doesn’t refer to a specific object you can identify in the sentence).
target_language_example: Boucle-la et écoute deux minutes.
native_language_example: Shut up and listen for two minutes.

meaning: to do it (with “la” = “it/her,” usually referring to something feminine).
additional_notes: “La” is a direct object pronoun placed before the verb/infinitive. It replaces a previously mentioned feminine noun (or sometimes “it” when the thing is understood). Example: « la tarte » → « Je vais la faire » (“I’m going to make it”).
target_language_example: Je vais la faire demain.
native_language_example: I’m going to do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Usually a noun phrase meaning a farm (a place where crops are grown or animals are raised). In spoken French, « La ferme ! » (with an exclamation mark) is also an informal way to say “Shut up!” / “Be quiet!”—use with caution because it can sound rude.
target_language_example: Ils habitent à la ferme.
native_language_example: They live on the farm.

additional_notes: Literally means “to close it,” but it’s used like “shut it / shut up.” Strongly informal and often aggressive; avoid in polite conversation. You may hear it in arguments or as an order. (More neutral alternatives: « tais-toi » / « taisez-vous ».)
target_language_example: Oh, la ferme !
native_language_example: Oh, shut up!

additional_notes: A common proverb meaning that a desired goal can be used to excuse the methods used to achieve it (often said critically or to debate ethics). It’s a set expression; you’ll usually see it with the definite articles: la fin / les moyens.
target_language_example: Il pense que la fin justifie les moyens, même si c’est injuste.
native_language_example: He thinks the end justifies the means, even if it’s unfair.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the feeling of being ashamed or embarrassed, or about something considered disgraceful. Common in expressions like "avoir honte" (to be ashamed) and "c'est la honte" (it’s so embarrassing / it’s a disgrace).
target_language_example: J’ai honte d’avoir dit ça.
native_language_example: I’m ashamed of having said that.

meaning: to act/pretend (often: “to play it” + an attitude, like cool or tough).
additional_notes: Usually used with an adjective or phrase describing the attitude you’re putting on: *la jouer cool* (act cool), *la jouer modeste* (act modest), *la jouer perso* (act selfish), *la jouer fine* (try to be clever). It often implies you’re putting on a show or not being sincere. The *la* doesn’t refer to a specific noun for beginners—it’s part of the fixed expression.
target_language_example: Arrête de la jouer cool : tu es stressé, ça se voit.
native_language_example: Stop acting cool: you’re stressed, it shows.

additional_notes: Used in music to name a key or chord quality. You’ll often see it with the preposition “en”: “en la majeur” = “in A major”. (Sometimes written with a capital in titles: “La majeur”.)
target_language_example: Ce morceau est en la majeur.
native_language_example: This piece is in A major.

additional_notes: Used to express that more than half of a group is included. It’s followed by a noun (often plural) or a pronoun: « la majorité des étudiants », « la majorité d’entre eux ». The verb after it is usually plural, but can be singular if you think of it as one group (more common: plural).
target_language_example: La majorité des gens préfèrent rester à la maison.
native_language_example: Most people prefer to stay at home.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the largest part of a group. Very often followed by "de" + noun or pronoun: "la plupart des gens" (most people), "la plupart d’entre eux" (most of them). It’s singular in form but usually refers to many people/things, so it commonly takes a plural verb: "La plupart sont…".
target_language_example: La plupart des gens aiment le chocolat.
native_language_example: Most people like chocolate.

additional_notes: Used to talk generally about the majority of people. Often followed by a verb in the plural (e.g., « La plupart des gens pensent que… »). You can also use it with other nouns: « la plupart des étudiants » (most students).
target_language_example: La plupart des gens aiment le week-end.
native_language_example: Most people like the weekend.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about what happens in general or in a typical situation. Often followed by a present tense verb: « La plupart du temps, je… ». You can also place it at the end of a sentence.
target_language_example: La plupart du temps, je prends le métro pour aller au travail.
native_language_example: Most of the time, I take the subway to go to work.

meaning: to show off; to mouth off (talk too much, in an annoying way).
additional_notes: Informal and often negative. Commonly used in the imperative: « Arrête de la ramener ! » meaning “Stop showing off / stop mouthing off.” The « la » doesn’t refer to a specific feminine noun here; it’s part of the fixed expression.
target_language_example: Arrête de la ramener, tu n’es pas le seul à avoir une idée !
native_language_example: Stop mouthing off—you’re not the only one with an idea!

additional_notes: Literal meaning is “the cow.” In everyday speech, especially as an exclamation (“La vache !”), it expresses strong surprise, admiration, or annoyance. It’s fairly informal. You can also hear it in expressions like “une vache de…” meaning “a hell of a…” (very intense, often negative).
target_language_example: La vache ! Il fait super froid aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Damn! It’s really cold today.

meaning: 'there it is' / 'here it is' (referring to a feminine noun or 'her').
additional_notes: Built from the direct object pronoun "la" ("it" for a feminine thing, or "her") + "voilà" ("there/here is"). Used when presenting, pointing out, or indicating that something/someone has arrived or been found. Choice of 'here' vs 'there' depends on context and distance; in everyday speech "voilà" often covers both. For masculine: "le voilà"; for plural: "les voilà".
target_language_example: Tu cherches la clé ? La voilà !
native_language_example: Are you looking for the key? Here it is!

meaning: to let go; to let things slide.
additional_notes: Often used as: (1) "laisser aller (qqch)" = to stop controlling or worrying about something (let it go). (2) "se laisser aller" = to let yourself go (stop making an effort, e.g., with your appearance or behavior), or to give in to emotions/impulses. Context decides whether it’s about relaxing control or about neglecting yourself.
target_language_example: Il faut parfois laisser aller les choses.
native_language_example: Sometimes you have to let things go.

meaning: to leave someone in the lurch; to abandon; to leave unfinished.
additional_notes: Used when someone leaves abruptly, doesn’t follow through, or stops in the middle of something (a person, a task, a project, an appointment). Often implies disappointment or inconvenience for the other person. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Il m’a laissé en plan au dernier moment.
native_language_example: He left me in the lurch at the last minute.

meaning: to let (someone/something) do; to let things happen without intervening.
additional_notes: Literally “to let do.” Used when you allow someone to act freely or you choose not to step in. Often appears as an instruction: « Laisse faire ! » (“Let it be / Leave it alone!”). In politics/economics, « le laissez-faire » refers to a hands-off approach (little government intervention).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, laisse faire, je m’en occupe.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, let me handle it.

meaning: to let (someone) speak/talk; to let them talk.
additional_notes: Often used literally to mean allowing someone to speak (e.g., in a discussion: “Laisse-le parler.”). It can also be used in the sense of “let people talk” (don’t worry about what others say): “Laisse parler, on s’en fiche.”
target_language_example: Laisse-le parler, il n’a pas fini.
native_language_example: Let him speak, he hasn’t finished.

meaning: to let (someone/something) pass; to let through.
additional_notes: Used when you allow someone or something to go by or go through a place. Often heard as an instruction: « Laissez passer ! » (“Let [me/us] through!”). Can be followed by a direct object: « Laissez passer la dame. » In noun form « un laisser-passer » means “a pass/permit” (e.g., to enter an area).
target_language_example: Pardon, laissez passer, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Excuse me, please let me through.

meaning: to leave for dead (to abandon someone, thinking they will die).
additional_notes: Used literally (after an attack/accident) or figuratively to mean someone was written off or abandoned with little chance of recovery/success. In real sentences it’s often conjugated and in the past participle: « laissé(e) pour mort » (agreeing with the person left): « Il a été laissé pour mort. » / « Elle a été laissée pour morte. »
target_language_example: Après l’agression, il a été laissé pour mort dans la rue.
native_language_example: After the assault, he was left for dead in the street.

meaning: to drop it; to let it go; to give up.
additional_notes: Literally means “to let fall,” but very often used idiomatically in everyday speech to mean “forget it / don’t worry about it,” or “give up on it.” Common in the imperative: “Laisse tomber !” (to one person) / “Laissez tomber !” (polite or plural).
target_language_example: Laisse tomber, ce n’est pas grave.
native_language_example: Forget it, it’s not a big deal.

meaning: to leave (someone) alone; to stop bothering (someone).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to stop annoying you or interfering, or to say you won’t disturb someone. Often appears as an imperative: « Laisse-moi tranquille ! » (Leave me alone!) or « Laissez-le tranquille. » (Leave him alone.) You can also say « laisser quelqu’un tranquille » (to leave someone alone).
target_language_example: Laisse-moi tranquille, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Leave me alone, please.

meaning: to let things happen; to wait and see (without forcing it).
additional_notes: Literally “to let come,” but it’s used to mean letting a situation develop naturally instead of pushing or rushing. Common in advice or planning: “Let’s wait and see how it goes.”
target_language_example: On va laisser venir et voir comment ça se passe.
native_language_example: We’ll wait and see and see how it goes.

additional_notes: Used literally for allowing visibility (e.g., allowing someone to see something), and often more generally to mean “to reveal” or “to show” (especially in writing): « Ça laisse voir que… » = “That shows/reveals that…”. Also commonly used with a reflexive pronoun: « se laisser voir » (“to let oneself be seen”, “to show oneself”).
target_language_example: La fenêtre laisse voir la mer.
native_language_example: The window lets you see the sea.

meaning: to leave something to be desired; to be not good enough.
additional_notes: Used to say that something isn’t satisfactory or could be much better (quality, performance, conditions, etc.). Often follows a subject like “ça” or “son + noun”: “Ça laisse à désirer” / “Son français laisse à désirer.”
target_language_example: Le service laisse à désirer.
native_language_example: The service leaves something to be desired.

additional_notes: Imperative of *laisser* (to let/allow/leave) + *faire* (to do/make). Used to tell someone not to interfere: “let it happen,” “don’t intervene,” or “let me handle it.” You’ll also see the related noun phrase *le laissez-faire* (hyphenated in English too) meaning a policy of non-intervention, especially in economics.
target_language_example: Laissez faire, je m'en occupe.
native_language_example: Leave it to me, I’ll take care of it.

additional_notes: Literally “pocket lamp.” Used for a portable light you hold in your hand; commonly with the verb "allumer" (to turn on/light) or "éteindre" (to turn off).
target_language_example: Tu as une lampe de poche ? Il fait trop sombre ici.
native_language_example: Do you have a flashlight? It’s too dark in here.

additional_notes: A common everyday noun for a portable light you hold in your hand. In French, it’s feminine: une lampe torche. You can also say une torche, but lampe torche is the standard, unambiguous term (especially since torche can also mean a burning torch).
target_language_example: Tu as une lampe torche ?
native_language_example: Do you have a flashlight?

additional_notes: Used to talk about computer coding languages (e.g., Python, Java, C++). Often used with common verbs like "apprendre" (to learn) or "utiliser" (to use): "apprendre un langage de programmation". In everyday French, you may also hear "langage informatique" (computer language), but "langage de programmation" is the standard, precise term.
target_language_example: J’apprends un langage de programmation pour créer des applications.
native_language_example: I’m learning a programming language to create apps.

additional_notes: Most often refers to the sign language used in a region/country. In France you’ll often see "la langue des signes française" (LSF) = French Sign Language. Usually used with the definite article: "la langue des signes".
target_language_example: Elle apprend la langue des signes.
native_language_example: She is learning sign language.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the first language someone learned as a child. Often appears with possessives (ma/ta/sa langue maternelle) or with the verb « être »: « Ma langue maternelle est l’anglais. » Not to be confused with « langue maternelle » meaning the language of someone’s mother specifically; it generally means your first/native language.
target_language_example: Quelle est ta langue maternelle ?
native_language_example: What is your native language?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a language that is not your native language (or not the main language of the country you’re in). Common in school and official contexts: "apprendre une langue étrangère" (to learn a foreign language), "cours de langue étrangère" (foreign language class). Often contrasted with "langue maternelle" (mother tongue/native language).
target_language_example: J’apprends une langue étrangère à l’université.
native_language_example: I’m learning a foreign language at university.

additional_notes: A common noun for the appliance that washes clothes. Often used with the article: "un/une lave-linge". Also commonly said as "machine à laver". The hyphenated form is standard in writing.
target_language_example: On a acheté un lave-linge neuf.
native_language_example: We bought a new washing machine.

additional_notes: A noun for the machine that washes dishes. Usually masculine: (un) lave-vaisselle. You’ll often see it with a hyphen; the plural is usually invariable in writing: des lave-vaisselle. Also used in the expression «mettre la vaisselle dans le lave-vaisselle» (to load the dishwasher).
target_language_example: Je mets les assiettes dans le lave-vaisselle.
native_language_example: I’m putting the plates in the dishwasher.

le beurre et l'argent du beurre

target_language_multi_word_term: le beurre et l'argent du beurre
meaning: Wanting to have it both ways (the best of both worlds), often unrealistically.
additional_notes: An idiom used when someone wants two incompatible advantages at the same time—like keeping something and also benefiting from selling it. Commonly appears in phrases like « vouloir le beurre et l'argent du beurre » (“to want both”). Similar to English “to have your cake and eat it too.”
target_language_example: Tu ne peux pas avoir le beurre et l'argent du beurre : soit tu le gardes, soit tu le vends.
native_language_example: You can’t have it both ways: either you keep it or you sell it.

meaning: to look for him/it; to go get him/it.
additional_notes: "Le" is a direct object pronoun meaning “him” or “it” (for a masculine noun). It comes before the infinitive: "Je vais le chercher". With verbs of movement (especially "aller"), "aller le chercher" often means “to go get/pick him/it up,” not just “to search.”
target_language_example: Je vais le chercher à la gare.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick him up at the station.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause as a fact, often with verbs like expliquer, prouver, montrer, nier, reconnaître. After "le fait que", French typically uses the indicative when stating a fact ("Le fait qu’il est ici...") and the subjunctive when the clause is judged/uncertain/triggered by emotion or doubt ("Le fait qu’il soit ici m’inquiète"). Common in more formal speech and writing.
target_language_example: Le fait que tu sois en retard m’inquiète.
native_language_example: The fact that you’re late worries me.

additional_notes: Used as a possessive pronoun (it replaces a noun), often after “être” or after “c’est…”. It agrees with the thing possessed (not the owners): le leur (m. sing.), la leur (f. sing.), les leurs (m. pl.), les leurs (f. pl.). Don’t confuse with “leur” as a possessive adjective before a noun (leur voiture = their car).
target_language_example: Ce sac est le leur.
native_language_example: This bag is theirs.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happens alongside something (a road, river, wall, beach, etc.). It often implies following the length of that thing. Common with movement verbs: marcher/courir/rouler le long de… It stays the same before vowels: le long de la rue, le long du fleuve, le long des quais.
target_language_example: Nous avons marché le long de la rivière.
native_language_example: We walked along the river.

additional_notes: A possessive pronoun that replaces a noun and agrees with the thing owned (not the owner). Use it for a masculine singular noun: *mon livre* → *le mien*. Often used after *c’est / ce sont*, or to contrast possessions: *le tien, le sien, le nôtre*, etc. Feminine singular: *la mienne*; masculine plural: *les miens*; feminine plural: *les miennes*.
target_language_example: Ce stylo est le mien.
native_language_example: This pen is mine.

meaning: when the time comes; when the moment arrives.
additional_notes: Used to mean “at the appropriate time” or “when it’s time to do something,” often referring to something planned for later. It’s a set phrase meaning “the moment having come” (with venu agreeing with moment). Commonly used with future actions: On en parlera le moment venu.
target_language_example: On prendra une décision le moment venu.
native_language_example: We’ll make a decision when the time comes.

additional_notes: Used when you unexpectedly meet someone you know, discover a surprising connection, or realize coincidences link people/places. Often said as an exclamation. Literally “the world is small,” and it matches the English expression closely.
target_language_example: Je viens de croiser mon ancien prof à Tokyo — le monde est petit !
native_language_example: I just ran into my old teacher in Tokyo — it’s a small world!

additional_notes: A possessive pronoun used to replace a noun already understood from context. It agrees with the thing possessed (not with the owners): le nôtre (masc. singular), la nôtre (fem. singular), les nôtres (plural). Often used in comparisons or to distinguish between items: "le vôtre" (yours), "le leur" (theirs).
target_language_example: Votre appartement est joli, mais le nôtre est plus grand.
native_language_example: Your apartment is nice, but ours is bigger.

meaning: "his" or "its" (the one that belongs to him/it).
additional_notes: A possessive pronoun used to replace a noun that’s already known from context. It agrees with the thing possessed (le = masculine singular), not with the owner. Variants: la sienne (fem. sg.), les siens / les siennes (plural). Often used after c’est or with comparisons: « C’est le sien. » / « comme le sien ».
target_language_example: Ce stylo est le sien.
native_language_example: This pen is his.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say there is enough time (often a short moment) to do something. Common pattern: "avoir le temps de + infinitive" = "to have time to"; also "le temps de + infinitive" = "the time it takes to" / "just enough time to". In English you often add "to" or "for" depending on context.
target_language_example: J’ai juste le temps de prendre un café.
native_language_example: I just have time to have a coffee.

meaning: "the time that" / "while" (as long as it takes).
additional_notes: Used to express duration needed to do something, often meaning “while” or “by the time that.” Common in phrases like: « le temps que + subject + verb » (e.g., le temps que je finisse = while/by the time I finish) or « le temps de + infinitive » (le temps de manger = time to eat). It can imply waiting or that something will happen during the time needed for another action.
target_language_example: Attends le temps que je revienne.
native_language_example: Wait while I come back / wait until I’m back.

additional_notes: A masculine singular possessive pronoun meaning “yours.” It replaces a noun already mentioned: "Ton livre ? — Oui, c’est le tien." Use it when what you’re talking about is masculine singular (or when the noun is implied and treated as masculine). Feminine: "la tienne"; plural: "les tiens / les tiennes." Often used after "c’est" or with "être" to show ownership.
target_language_example: Ce stylo est le tien ?
native_language_example: Is this pen yours?

meaning: "yours" (masculine singular; "the one that belongs to you").
additional_notes: A possessive pronoun used to replace a noun that’s already known from context. It agrees with the thing owned (not the owner): le vôtre (masc. sg.), la vôtre (fem. sg.), les vôtres (plural). Often used in comparisons or to avoid repeating the noun: "Mon livre et le vôtre" = "My book and yours."
target_language_example: Mon stylo est bleu, et le vôtre est noir.
native_language_example: My pen is blue, and yours is black.

additional_notes: A device for playing audio CDs. Often used with a possessive: « mon lecteur de CD ». In everyday speech today, you may also hear « lecteur CD » (without « de ») or more general terms like « lecteur audio » depending on the device.
target_language_example: Tu as encore un lecteur de CD ?
native_language_example: Do you still have a CD player?

additional_notes: Used for a single contact lens; the plural is usually "lentilles de contact". Often said with the verb "porter" (to wear): "Je porte des lentilles de contact."
target_language_example: Je porte des lentilles de contact aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I’m wearing contact lenses today.

additional_notes: Describes the posture of having your hands inside your pockets. Often suggests a casual or relaxed attitude; depending on context (e.g., in a formal situation), it can sound like someone is being too casual or not showing respect. Usually used with a verb like « avoir » or « mettre/garder »: « Il a les mains dans les poches. »
target_language_example: Il marche les mains dans les poches.
native_language_example: He’s walking with his hands in his pockets.

meaning: empty-handed (with nothing in your hands; without bringing anything).
additional_notes: Most often used with the verb "arriver" (to arrive) or "venir" (to come): "arriver/venir les mains vides" = to show up without anything (e.g., without a gift, food, or items you were supposed to bring). It can also be used more generally to mean leaving or returning with nothing.
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas arriver les mains vides, alors j’ai acheté des fleurs.
native_language_example: I don’t want to show up empty-handed, so I bought some flowers.

additional_notes: Used to point out that a group of people or things has arrived or is now visible. Built from object pronoun + voilà: “les” = “them” and “voilà” = “there/here is/are”. Often used when handing something over or when someone appears: “Les voilà !” = “There they are!” Similar forms: “le voilà” (there he/it is), “la voilà” (there she/it is), “les voici” (here they are, a bit more ‘right here’).
target_language_example: Tu cherchais les clés ? Les voilà !
native_language_example: Were you looking for the keys? Here they are!

meaning: with your eyes closed; easily, without effort.
additional_notes: Literally “(with) the eyes closed.” Used both literally (someone’s eyes are closed) and figuratively to mean doing something very easily or confidently, almost automatically. Often used with verbs like faire/réussir/conduire/jouer: “Je peux le faire les yeux fermés.”
target_language_example: Je peux réussir cet exercice les yeux fermés.
native_language_example: I can do this exercise easily (with my eyes closed).

additional_notes: A letter written to someone you love or are romantically interested in. Often refers to a personal, romantic letter (can be handwritten or not). In plural: "des lettres d’amour".
target_language_example: Il lui a écrit une lettre d’amour.
native_language_example: He wrote her a love letter.

additional_notes: Means the moment the sun rises. In standard French you’ll most often see **le lever du soleil** (with **du** = “of the”). You can use it with common phrases like **au lever du soleil** (“at sunrise”) or **se lever au lever du soleil** (“to get up at sunrise”).
target_language_example: On partira au lever du soleil.
native_language_example: We’ll leave at sunrise.

additional_notes: Means the moment the sun rises in the morning. Used in set phrases like « au lever du soleil » (at sunrise) and « se lever au lever du soleil » (to get up at sunrise). Also used in the fixed expression « du lever au coucher du soleil » (from sunrise to sunset).
target_language_example: On partira au lever du soleil.
native_language_example: We’ll leave at sunrise.

additional_notes: Used to refer to where someone works (an office, shop, factory, etc.). Often appears with possessives (mon/ton/son lieu de travail) or in phrases like « sur le lieu de travail » (at the workplace) and « se rendre sur son lieu de travail » (to go to one’s workplace).
target_language_example: Je vais au lieu de travail en métro.
native_language_example: I go to work by subway.

meaning: a straight line; straight ahead (in a straight line).
additional_notes: Literally “straight line.” Used for geometry (“draw a straight line”) and for movement/directions to mean going straight without turning. Often appears in phrases like “en ligne droite” (in a straight line) or “aller tout droit” (go straight).
target_language_example: Continuez tout droit : c’est en ligne droite.
native_language_example: Keep going straight: it’s in a straight line.

meaning: to read between the lines; to infer what is implied but not said.
additional_notes: Used when you understand the hidden meaning, subtext, or intention behind someone’s words (in a text, email, conversation, etc.). It’s a common, neutral expression (not slang). Often used with the imperative: « Lis entre les lignes ! »
target_language_example: Il n’a pas dit non, mais il faut lire entre les lignes : il n’est pas d’accord.
native_language_example: He didn’t say no, but you have to read between the lines: he doesn’t agree.

meaning: to lip-read; to read someone’s lips.
additional_notes: Used when you understand what someone is saying by watching their mouth (often because it’s noisy, you can’t hear well, or they’re speaking quietly). French commonly uses the structure “lire sur les lèvres de quelqu’un” (to read from someone’s lips).
target_language_example: Je n’entends rien ici, je vais essayer de lire sur tes lèvres.
native_language_example: I can’t hear anything here, I’m going to try to read your lips.

meaning: blacklist; list of people/things to avoid or ban.
additional_notes: Used in formal and informal contexts to mean a group that is excluded, banned, or not trusted. Often used with verbs like être sur (to be on), mettre sur (to put on), and figurer sur (to appear on). Can refer to people, companies, websites, email addresses, etc.
target_language_example: Son adresse e-mail est sur la liste noire, donc ses messages sont bloqués.
native_language_example: His email address is on the blacklist, so his messages are blocked.

additional_notes: A fairly formal/literary expression meaning the bed where someone is dying or has died. Often used when talking about someone’s last moments or final requests (e.g., « sur son lit de mort » = “on his/her deathbed”).
target_language_example: Sur son lit de mort, il a demandé à revoir sa famille.
native_language_example: On his deathbed, he asked to see his family again.

additional_notes: Literally “book of cooking.” Used to talk about a book that contains recipes and cooking instructions. Very common with acheter/avoir/chercher/consulter (to buy/have/look for/look up).
target_language_example: J’ai acheté un livre de cuisine pour apprendre à faire des plats français.
native_language_example: I bought a cookbook to learn how to make French dishes.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who learned a language from childhood and speaks it as their first language (often contrasted with "locuteur non natif"). You’ll see it in language-learning contexts: "un locuteur natif de français" = a native French speaker.
target_language_example: Je voudrais pratiquer avec un locuteur natif de français.
native_language_example: I’d like to practice with a native French speaker.

additional_notes: Used to describe a woman whose first language is the one being discussed. Often used in language-learning contexts (e.g., "une locutrice native de français"). For a man, you’ll see "locuteur natif"; for a mixed/unspecified group, "locuteurs natifs" or "locuteurs natifs et locutrices natives".
target_language_example: Je cherche une locutrice native pour pratiquer mon français.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a native (female) speaker to practice my French.

meaning: “far from it”; “not at all” (the opposite is true).
additional_notes: Used to strongly contradict or correct what was just said or implied. Often comes after a statement to emphasize that reality is the reverse. Can also be used with “être” (e.g., “Nous sommes loin d’être prêts” = “We’re far from being ready”).
target_language_example: — Tu es prêt ? — Loin de là !
native_language_example: — Are you ready? — Far from it!

meaning: "far from me" / "far be it from me" (I don’t mean to…; I’m not claiming…).
additional_notes: Often used at the start of a sentence to politely distance yourself from an idea or criticism: *Loin de moi l’idée de…* (“Far be it from me to…”). It can also be literal in context (physically far away), but the common phrasebook use is the set expression to soften what you’re saying.
target_language_example: Loin de moi l’idée de te critiquer, mais je pense qu’on peut faire mieux.
native_language_example: Far be it from me to criticize you, but I think we can do better.

meaning: wavelength; (figuratively) being on the same wavelength.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: the wavelength of a wave (light, sound, etc.), used in science/tech contexts. Figuratively, it means having the same way of thinking or understanding someone (often with "être sur la même longueur d’onde" = "to be on the same wavelength").
target_language_example: On n’est pas sur la même longueur d’onde sur ce sujet.
native_language_example: We’re not on the same wavelength about this topic.

additional_notes: This is the shortened form of « lors de » used before a vowel sound: « lors d’un… », « lors d’une… », « lors d’un accident… ». It introduces the time when something happened and is followed by a noun (not a verb).
target_language_example: Lors d’un entretien, je parle de mon expérience.
native_language_example: During an interview, I talk about my experience.

meaning: 'during' / 'at the time of' (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Used to locate something in time with an event or period: "lors de + noun" (often with an article), e.g., "lors de la réunion" = "during the meeting". It’s relatively formal; in everyday speech you’ll often hear "pendant" instead. Not followed by a verb directly—use "lorsque" or "quand" for "when" + clause.
target_language_example: Lors de la réunion, j’ai pris des notes.
native_language_example: During the meeting, I took notes.

additional_notes: A noun meaning a person who turns into a wolf (especially at night, in stories). Masculine: un loup-garou. Feminine: une louve-garou (also sometimes une femme-loup). Plural: des loups-garous. Common in folklore, books, movies, and Halloween-type contexts.
target_language_example: Dans ce film, le loup-garou apparaît la nuit.
native_language_example: In this movie, the werewolf appears at night.

additional_notes: Feminine form of « loup-garou » (werewolf). « Louve » means “she-wolf”; the whole expression refers to a person who turns into a wolf (often in folklore, at night or during a full moon). You may also see the plural « louves-garous ».
target_language_example: Dans ce film, la louve-garou se transforme à la pleine lune.
native_language_example: In this movie, the female werewolf transforms during the full moon.

meaning: to talk to him/her; to speak to him/her.
additional_notes: "Lui" is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him/to her” (or sometimes “to them” in formal singular). It comes before the verb: « Je vais lui parler » = “I’m going to talk to him/her.” In the affirmative imperative, it goes after the verb: « Parle-lui ! » = “Talk to him/her!”
target_language_example: Je vais lui parler après le cours.
native_language_example: I’m going to talk to him/her after class.

additional_notes: Stressed pronoun meaning “himself” (or “itself” for a masculine noun), used for emphasis or to show the subject did something personally. Often appears after a noun/pronoun: « le président lui-même » = “the president himself.” Feminine form: « elle-même » (herself). Plural: « eux-mêmes / elles-mêmes ».
target_language_example: Il l’a fait lui-même.
native_language_example: He did it himself.

additional_notes: Used for the trip or period right after a wedding (often with the verb « partir en lune de miel » = to go on a honeymoon). Also used figuratively for a “honeymoon period” at the start of a relationship, job, etc.
target_language_example: Après le mariage, ils sont partis en lune de miel en Italie.
native_language_example: After the wedding, they went on their honeymoon to Italy.

additional_notes: Literally “glasses of sun.” Used for sun protection; often shortened in speech to “des lunettes” when the context is clear.
target_language_example: N’oublie pas tes lunettes de soleil, il y a beaucoup de soleil aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Don’t forget your sunglasses; it’s very sunny today.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to sunglasses with dark-tinted lenses (what English usually calls “sunglasses”). In French, you can also say “des lunettes de soleil” for “sunglasses.” “Noires” agrees with “lunettes” (plural feminine).
target_language_example: Il porte des lunettes noires même quand il fait nuageux.
native_language_example: He wears dark sunglasses even when it’s cloudy.

meaning: 'over there' / 'there' (in a different place, not here).
additional_notes: Used to point to a place away from the speaker (often contrasted with ici, “here”). Can refer to a specific visible location (“over there”) or a general distant place (“there,” e.g., in another city/country). Often used with être/aller: être là-bas (to be there), aller là-bas (to go there).
target_language_example: On peut se garer là-bas, près de la pharmacie.
native_language_example: We can park over there, near the pharmacy.

additional_notes: Refers to something being inside a place, container, or situation already identified. It’s the adverbial form (more specific) compared with "dedans" alone; you can also say "là-dedans" to mean “in that (thing) there.” Often used in spoken French and can sound slightly emphatic.
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce qu’il y a là-dedans ?
native_language_example: What’s in there?

additional_notes: Very common in speech and writing. It can mean (1) "on that" in the sense of "on top of that" or "on that point" (e.g., giving an opinion or adding info), or (2) "after that / then" to move the story forward. Often used with verbs like dire (to say), revenir (to come back), ajouter (to add): "Là-dessus, il a dit…" = "At that point/then, he said…"
target_language_example: Là-dessus, il est parti sans rien dire.
native_language_example: After that, he left without saying anything.

additional_notes: Used to point to or refer to a place that is physically higher than where you are (a floor above, a mountain, the sky). It can also refer to 'up in the sky/heaven' depending on context. Often contrasts with "là-bas" (over there) or "en bas" (downstairs/down below).
target_language_example: Mon appartement est là-haut, au troisième étage.
native_language_example: My apartment is up there, on the third floor.

additional_notes: Informal idiom used to tell someone to stop pestering you or to back off. Often said as an irritated command: « Lâche-moi la grappe ! » (also « lâcher la grappe à quelqu’un »). Literally means “let go of the bunch (of grapes),” but the idiomatic meaning is what’s used.
target_language_example: Lâche-moi la grappe, j’ai besoin de calme.
native_language_example: Leave me alone, I need some peace and quiet.

meaning: to let go; to stop trying to control a situation.
additional_notes: Common in everyday speech and in self-help/well-being contexts. It means relaxing your “grip” on something mentally or emotionally—accepting what you can’t change, stopping overthinking, or easing pressure on yourself. Often used with "il faut" / "essaie de" (you should / try to) or in the imperative: "Lâche prise !".
target_language_example: Tu ne peux pas tout contrôler ; essaie de lâcher prise.
native_language_example: You can’t control everything; try to let it go.

meaning: a bootlicker; a brown-noser (someone who flatters people in power).
additional_notes: A pejorative, informal insult for someone seen as overly servile or trying to gain favor by flattering a boss/authority. Usually used as a noun (often masculine): « un lèche-bottes ». The plural is commonly invariable in writing: « des lèche-bottes ».
target_language_example: Arrête de faire le lèche-bottes avec le patron !
native_language_example: Stop brown-nosing the boss!

meaning: window-shopping (looking at shop windows without buying).
additional_notes: Commonly used as a noun (often with hyphens): *faire du lèche-vitrine* = “to go window-shopping.” It’s a fairly informal, everyday term; more neutral alternatives include *faire du shopping* (go shopping) or *regarder les vitrines* (look at shop windows).
target_language_example: On va faire du lèche-vitrine cet après-midi ?
native_language_example: Shall we go window-shopping this afternoon?

additional_notes: A noun for someone who gets up early. Used with an article: « un lève-tôt » (male/neutral), « une lève-tôt » (female). The plural is usually invariable: « des lève-tôt ». Often contrasted with « un couche-tard » (night owl).
target_language_example: Je suis plutôt un lève-tôt, donc je commence à travailler à 7 h.
native_language_example: I’m more of an early riser, so I start working at 7 a.m.

additional_notes: Used mainly in legal/police contexts to describe defending yourself in a way the law considers justified. Often appears with verbs like « invoquer » (to claim), « agir en » (to act in), or « être en » (to be in): « invoquer la légitime défense », « agir en légitime défense ». The everyday, non-legal phrase is often « se défendre » (to defend yourself).
target_language_example: Il a invoqué la légitime défense après l’altercation.
native_language_example: He claimed self-defense after the altercation.

additional_notes: Literally “to go away (myself) from there,” but used as a common verb meaning “to leave/go away.” It’s built from the verb aller (to go) with the reflexive pronoun me (m’) and the pronoun en (away/from here). Often used in the near future: « Je vais m’en aller » = “I’m going to leave.” Can also appear as an imperative: « Va-t’en ! » (informal) = “Go away!”
target_language_example: Je dois m’en aller maintenant.
native_language_example: I have to leave now.

additional_notes: Common in spoken French to express emphasis, mild surprise, resignation, or to introduce an opinion. Often used like a filler: "Ma foi, je ne sais pas" (“Well, I don’t know”). Can sound a bit old-fashioned or theatrical depending on tone and context. Literally “my faith,” but it’s not usually religious in everyday use.
target_language_example: Ma foi, c’est pas si mal !
native_language_example: Well, it’s not so bad!

meaning: 'my word!' / 'I swear!' (a strong promise or assurance).
additional_notes: Used to insist that you’re telling the truth or that you’ll do something. Commonly said as an exclamation: « Ma parole ! » (like “Honestly!” / “I can’t believe it!”). Also used in « Je te donne ma parole » (“I give you my word”).
target_language_example: Ma parole, je te promets que je serai à l’heure.
native_language_example: I swear, I promise I’ll be on time.

additional_notes: Informal, slightly joking way to refer to yourself, often implying “just me” or “me, all alone.” Common in phrases like « avec ma pomme » (“with little old me / by myself”) or « c’est ma pomme » (“it’s me”). Literally means “my apple,” but that’s not the intended meaning.
target_language_example: Je suis venu avec ma pomme.
native_language_example: I came by myself (just me).

additional_notes: Common way to refer to a coffee-making machine (at home, in an office, or a café). Also called « cafetière » in many contexts, especially for a drip coffee maker. Plural: « des machines à café ». The « à » indicates purpose: a machine for making coffee.
target_language_example: Il y a une machine à café dans la cuisine.
native_language_example: There is a coffee machine in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Common household noun. Usually feminine: une machine à laver. Also called un lave-linge (more common in France). Often used with faire la machine (= do a load of laundry).
target_language_example: La machine à laver est en panne, donc je vais à la laverie.
native_language_example: The washing machine is broken, so I’m going to the laundromat.

additional_notes: A noun phrase meaning a machine used to type text (before computers). In modern conversation you’re more likely to hear « ordinateur » (computer), but « machine à écrire » is still understood and used in historical contexts, museums, or when talking about old equipment.
target_language_example: J’ai trouvé une vieille machine à écrire dans le grenier.
native_language_example: I found an old typewriter in the attic.

additional_notes: Common term for swimwear (one-piece or two-piece) for any gender. Often used with "un" (masculine): "un maillot de bain". Plural: "des maillots de bain". You’ll also hear "maillot" alone in context, but "maillot de bain" is the clearest beginner-friendly form.
target_language_example: J’ai acheté un maillot de bain pour aller à la piscine.
native_language_example: I bought a swimsuit to go to the pool.

additional_notes: Used literally for people walking while holding hands, and figuratively to mean “together” or “in close cooperation” (often with verbs like aller, marcher, travailler).
target_language_example: Ils se promenaient main dans la main le long de la rivière.
native_language_example: They were walking hand in hand along the river.

meaning: 'now that' (introduces a reason or new situation).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that explains what has changed or why something is possible/true from this point on. It’s followed by a verb (often in the present or past, depending on context): « Maintenant que tu es là… » / « Maintenant qu’on a fini… ». Often implies a consequence in the main clause.
target_language_example: Maintenant que j’ai fini mes devoirs, je peux sortir.
native_language_example: Now that I’ve finished my homework, I can go out.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree, reassure, or confirm something. Depending on tone, it can also be slightly ironic or sarcastic (similar to 'yeah, sure'). Literally 'but (indeed) sure'.
target_language_example: — Tu peux m’aider ? — Mais bien sûr !
native_language_example: — Can you help me? — Of course!

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French to soften a disagreement, accept something reluctantly, or move the conversation on (often with a slight sigh or resignation). It can sound casual and mildly informal. Similar in tone to "but, well…" or "but still…" depending on context.
target_language_example: Je voulais venir, mais bon, j’ai trop de travail.
native_language_example: I wanted to come, but oh well, I have too much work.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm something, often in a reassuring or slightly emphatic way. Literally "but yes," so it can sound like "come on, yes" when responding to doubt or surprise. Tone depends on context: it can be warm and encouraging, or mildly impatient.
target_language_example: — Tu viens ce soir ? — Mais oui, bien sûr !
native_language_example: — Are you coming tonight? — Of course, definitely!

additional_notes: A residential care facility for older people. Common in neutral, everyday speech; you may also hear the more formal terms "EHPAD" (for a medicalized nursing home) or "résidence pour personnes âgées". Not the same as "maison de repos" (often a convalescent/rehab place).
target_language_example: Ma grand-mère vit dans une maison de retraite depuis l’année dernière.
native_language_example: My grandmother has been living in a retirement home since last year.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir: « avoir le mal de mer » = “to be seasick.” It literally means “sea pain,” but in everyday English you’d say “seasickness/seasick.”
target_language_example: J’ai le mal de mer sur les petits bateaux.
native_language_example: I get seasick on small boats.

additional_notes: Literally “pain of head.” Used with the verb avoir (to have): « J’ai mal à la tête » = “I have a headache / My head hurts.” You can also say « un mal de tête » for “a headache.”
target_language_example: J’ai mal à la tête depuis ce matin.
native_language_example: I’ve had a headache since this morning.

additional_notes: Used to talk about missing your home/country when you’re away (studying, traveling, living abroad). Often used with avoir: « J’ai le mal du pays » (“I’m homesick”). Also common: « avoir le mal du pays » and « souffrir du mal du pays ».
target_language_example: Depuis que je suis à l’étranger, j’ai le mal du pays.
native_language_example: Since I’ve been abroad, I’ve been homesick.

additional_notes: Used to describe a remark, action, or moment that doesn’t fit the situation (e.g., a joke at the wrong time). Often used after a form of “être” ("C’est mal à propos") or to describe something ("une remarque mal à propos").
target_language_example: Sa remarque était mal à propos.
native_language_example: His/Her remark was inappropriate.

additional_notes: Describes a person’s manners/behavior (not their school education). Often used as an insult or criticism: « Il est mal élevé » = “He has no manners.” Can agree in gender/number: mal élevé (m. sg.), mal élevée (f. sg.), mal élevés (m. pl.), mal élevées (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Ce garçon est vraiment mal élevé : il ne dit jamais bonjour.
native_language_example: That boy is really ill-mannered: he never says hello.

additional_notes: Feminine form of the adjective phrase (masc.: « mal élevé »). Used to describe a person’s manners or upbringing, often as a criticism: « Elle est mal élevée » = “She has bad manners / wasn’t raised well.” Can also be used with « être » or as an adjective before/after a noun: « une fille mal élevée ».
target_language_example: Je trouve qu’elle est mal élevée : elle ne dit jamais bonjour.
native_language_example: I think she’s ill-mannered: she never says hello.

additional_notes: Literally “mental sick,” used to describe someone who is mentally ill. In modern French it can sound harsh or stigmatizing; more neutral options include « une personne atteinte de troubles mentaux » (a person with mental health disorders) or talking about « une maladie mentale » (a mental illness). Agreement: « un malade mental » (a man), « une malade mentale » (a woman).
target_language_example: On évite de dire « malade mental » ; on dit plutôt « une personne souffrant de troubles mentaux ».
native_language_example: We avoid saying “mentally ill person”; we rather say “a person suffering from mental health disorders.”

additional_notes: Feminine form of « malade mental ». Used to describe a woman/girl with mental illness. In everyday conversation it can sound harsh or insulting, especially if used as a label (“Elle est une malade mentale”). In more neutral/medical contexts, French often uses « souffrir de troubles mentaux » or « avoir un trouble psychique ».
target_language_example: Cette patiente est malade mentale et elle a besoin de soutien.
native_language_example: This patient is mentally ill and she needs support.

additional_notes: Used to express contrast or persistence: something is true or will happen even though there are problems, objections, or negative circumstances. Often placed at the start or end of a sentence (e.g., “Malgré tout, …” or “…, malgré tout.”).
target_language_example: Il pleuvait, mais on est sortis malgré tout.
native_language_example: It was raining, but we went out anyway.

additional_notes: A legal document that authorizes the police to search a place (home, car, office) for evidence. Common in news, crime stories, and legal contexts. In French law, it’s typically used with verbs like « avoir/présenter un mandat de perquisition » (to have/show a search warrant) or « délivrer un mandat de perquisition » (to issue a search warrant).
target_language_example: La police a présenté un mandat de perquisition avant d’entrer dans l’appartement.
native_language_example: The police showed a search warrant before entering the apartment.

additional_notes: Used mainly when talking about driving or vehicles. You can say "mettre la marche arrière" (to put the car in reverse) or "faire marche arrière" (to back up / to reverse; also figuratively: to backtrack). Often written with a hyphen: "marche-arrière".
target_language_example: Mets la marche arrière et recule doucement.
native_language_example: Put it in reverse and back up slowly.

meaning: to step on someone’s feet; (figuratively) to step on someone’s toes.
additional_notes: Often used with an indirect object: “marcher sur les pieds à quelqu’un” (to step on someone’s toes / get in their way). Can be literal (in a crowd) or figurative (overlapping someone’s work or role).
target_language_example: Arrête de me marcher sur les pieds !
native_language_example: Stop stepping on my toes!

additional_notes: Literally “to walk on four paws/legs.” Used for babies and animals, or for an adult moving on hands and knees (often because something is hard, low, or they’re exhausted). In everyday English you usually say “to crawl,” but French often uses this longer phrase for clarity.
target_language_example: Le bébé marche à quatre pattes dans le salon.
native_language_example: The baby is crawling in the living room.

additional_notes: A neutral, standard term used in legal, political, and everyday contexts to refer to marriage between two people of the same sex. Often appears with the definite article: « le mariage homosexuel » (same-sex marriage, as a topic). You may also hear « mariage gay » (more informal) or « mariage pour tous » (a political slogan meaning “marriage for all”).
target_language_example: En France, le mariage homosexuel est légal depuis 2013.
native_language_example: In France, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013.

meaning: to score a point; to make a good point (figurative).
additional_notes: Used literally in sports/competition to mean “to score.” Often used figuratively in conversation to mean “to gain an advantage” or “to make a convincing argument.” In the figurative sense, English often uses “score a point” or “make a good point,” not “mark a point.”
target_language_example: Avec cet argument, tu marques un point.
native_language_example: With that argument, you score a point / you make a good point.

meaning: raw material; basic input used to make a product.
additional_notes: Used for manufacturing, industry, and economics to talk about materials before processing (e.g., wood, cotton, oil). Often appears in the plural: « matières premières ». Also used more broadly for a “starting ingredient” for a project (e.g., data as « matière première »).
target_language_example: Le pétrole est une matière première essentielle pour cette industrie.
native_language_example: Oil is an essential raw material for this industry.

meaning: a sore loser; someone who loses badly.
additional_notes: Describes a person who reacts badly when they lose (gets angry, complains, makes excuses). Can also be used more generally for someone who can’t accept losing. Often used with the verb "être": "Il/Elle est mauvais(e) perdant(e)." Make the adjective agree: "mauvais perdant" (male) / "mauvaise perdante" (female).
target_language_example: Arrête de râler, tu es un mauvais perdant !
native_language_example: Stop complaining, you’re a sore loser!

meaning: the evil eye; bad luck caused by jealousy or a curse.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a superstition: someone’s jealous look is believed to bring misfortune. Often appears with verbs like jeter/porter ("to cast/give") or attirer ("to attract") and in expressions like "avoir le mauvais œil" (to have the evil eye).
target_language_example: Elle pense qu’on lui a jeté le mauvais œil.
native_language_example: She thinks someone put the evil eye on her.

additional_notes: Literally “bad herb/plant.” Used for plants that grow where you don’t want them (in a garden, lawn, fields). Often used in the plural: "les mauvaises herbes" = weeds.
target_language_example: Il faut enlever les mauvaises herbes dans le jardin.
native_language_example: We need to pull up the weeds in the garden.

additional_notes: Common way to describe someone feeling irritable or unhappy. Often used with verbs like « être de mauvaise humeur » (to be in a bad mood) or « se mettre de mauvaise humeur » (to get into a bad mood).
target_language_example: Il est de mauvaise humeur ce matin.
native_language_example: He’s in a bad mood this morning.

additional_notes: This is the question form of "tu me diras" using inversion (verb + -tu). It’s a fairly formal/literary way to ask a question; in everyday speech you’re more likely to hear "Tu me diras ?" or "Est-ce que tu me diras… ?". Often used to request information or an explanation, sometimes with a slightly rhetorical tone depending on context.
target_language_example: Me diras-tu la vérité un jour ?
native_language_example: Will you tell me the truth one day?

meaning: "you will tell me" / "you might say (to me)".
additional_notes: Literally the future tense of « dire »: « vous me direz » (“you will tell me”), with the object pronoun « me » placed before the verb. Often used as a parenthetical or rhetorical phrase meaning “you might say/you may ask,” introducing a possible objection or question from the listener. Fairly formal in tone.
target_language_example: C’est cher, me direz-vous, mais la qualité est excellente.
native_language_example: It’s expensive, you might say, but the quality is excellent.

additional_notes: Means “best friend” when talking about a male friend. For a female friend, say “meilleure amie”. You can also use it as an adjective phrase: “mon meilleur ami” (my best friend). In French, “ami” can also mean “boyfriend” in some contexts, but “meilleur ami” usually means “best friend.”
target_language_example: Paul, c’est mon meilleur ami.
native_language_example: Paul is my best friend.

additional_notes: Feminine form: use about a female best friend or when the speaker is female and referring to her best friend in feminine terms. Masculine equivalent: « meilleur ami ». Often used with a possessive: « ma meilleure amie » (my best friend). In casual speech, French also says « ma meilleure pote » (more informal).
target_language_example: Ma meilleure amie habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: My best friend lives in Lyon.

meaning: Best wishes (often for the New Year).
additional_notes: A common greeting used to offer good wishes, especially at New Year’s. Often appears in the full phrase “Meilleurs vœux pour la nouvelle année !” It can be said or written on cards, emails, or messages. Similar in use to “Best wishes” or “Happy New Year.”
target_language_example: Meilleurs vœux pour la nouvelle année !
native_language_example: Best wishes for the New Year!

mener par le bout du nez

target_language_multi_word_term: mener par le bout du nez
meaning: to lead someone by the nose; to control/manipulate someone easily.
additional_notes: An idiom meaning someone is being easily influenced or fooled so that they do what another person wants. Often used with a direct object: « Il/Elle le/la mène par le bout du nez. » Also common in the passive: « Il/Elle se laisse mener par le bout du nez » (to let oneself be controlled).
target_language_example: Depuis qu’ils sortent ensemble, elle le mène par le bout du nez.
native_language_example: Ever since they started dating, she’s had him wrapped around her finger.

meaning: to successfully carry out; to see through to completion.
additional_notes: Used with a project/task/plan as the object: « mener qqch à bien ». It emphasizes finishing something successfully (not just starting or trying). Often used in formal or professional contexts.
target_language_example: Nous devons mener ce projet à bien avant la fin du mois.
native_language_example: We have to successfully complete this project before the end of the month.

additional_notes: A very common, polite way to thank someone. Often used on its own, or followed by something like « pour votre aide » (for your help). Slightly more emphatic than « merci ».
target_language_example: Merci beaucoup pour votre aide !
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help!

additional_notes: A slightly stronger, often more emphatic way to say « merci ». Depending on tone it can sound warmly appreciative, matter-of-fact, or even a bit sarcastic (like “yeah, thanks”). Common in everyday speech; « merci beaucoup » is more neutral and always polite.
target_language_example: Merci bien pour votre aide !
native_language_example: Thanks a lot for your help!

meaning: "please" (when asking someone to do something) / "thank you for".
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb: "Merci de + infinitive".
