In requests, it’s a polite, slightly formal way to mean “please” (common in signs, emails, instructions): "Merci de patienter" = “Please wait.” It can also mean “thank you for (doing something)” depending on context: "Merci de m’avoir aidé" = “Thank you for helping me.”
target_language_example: Merci de fermer la porte.
native_language_example: Please close the door.

meaning: "Damn!" / "Oh crap!" (an exclamation of surprise, annoyance, or frustration).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar because of "merde" (“shit”). Used as a standalone reaction (like “Well, damn!”). Avoid in polite/company settings; a milder option is "mince alors".
target_language_example: Merde alors, j’ai raté le bus !
native_language_example: Damn, I missed the bus!

additional_notes: Used to congratulate someone for an achievement or good news. Often said on its own as an exclamation. You’ll also hear/see: “Félicitations !” (most common) and “Toutes mes félicitations” (more emphatic/formal).
target_language_example: Tu as eu ton diplôme ? Mes félicitations !
native_language_example: You got your diploma? Congratulations!

additional_notes: Very common formal opening to address a group, especially in speeches, announcements, or when getting an audience’s attention (e.g., on a train or at an event). Often followed by a pause and then the message. Note the spelling: mesdames (plural of madame) and messieurs (plural of monsieur).
target_language_example: Mesdames et messieurs, le spectacle va commencer.
native_language_example: Ladies and gentlemen, the show is about to begin.

meaning: to inform; to bring up to date.
additional_notes: Used mainly as: « mettre quelqu’un au courant (de quelque chose) » = to let someone know / to keep someone informed (about something). Very common with pronouns: « Je te mets au courant. » You can also say « être au courant (de) » = to be aware (of).
target_language_example: Je vais te mettre au courant de la situation demain.
native_language_example: I’m going to bring you up to date on the situation tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when you provoke someone to prove they can do something, often with "de + infinitive" ("mettre quelqu’un au défi de faire…"). Can also mean "to dare" or "to defy" in the sense of challenging authority ("mettre au défi les règles"). Note: "défi" looks like English "defy" but usually means "challenge".
target_language_example: Je te mets au défi de finir ce puzzle en dix minutes.
native_language_example: I challenge you to finish this puzzle in ten minutes.

meaning: to bring to light; to uncover; to reveal.
additional_notes: Often used for discovering or revealing something that was hidden or unknown (facts, a scandal, evidence, archaeological remains). Common in news, research, and formal writing. Literally it means “to put into the daylight,” but in most contexts it’s an idiom meaning “to uncover/reveal.”
target_language_example: L’enquête a mis au jour de nouvelles preuves.
native_language_example: The investigation brought new evidence to light.

meaning: to give birth (to); to bring into the world.
additional_notes: Most often used for a mother giving birth to a baby; can be used with a direct object (mettre un enfant au monde) or without (elle a mis au monde). A more medical/neutral verb is « accoucher »; « mettre au monde » is common in everyday speech and slightly more descriptive/literary.
target_language_example: Elle a mis au monde une petite fille en juin.
native_language_example: She gave birth to a little girl in June.

meaning: to get (people) to agree; to reconcile.
additional_notes: Used when you help two or more people reach the same decision/opinion (often after a disagreement). It’s commonly used with direct objects like "mettre tout le monde d’accord" (get everyone to agree) or pronouns: "les mettre d’accord" (get them to agree). Not the same as "être d’accord" (to agree).
target_language_example: On va essayer de les mettre d’accord sur la date.
native_language_example: We’ll try to get them to agree on the date.

additional_notes: Used for setting something aside physically or figuratively (e.g., setting aside a topic or a disagreement). Very commonly means “to save up” money. In the figurative sense, you’ll often see it with “ses différences / ses désaccords” (set aside differences).
target_language_example: J’essaie de mettre de côté un peu d’argent chaque mois.
native_language_example: I’m trying to save a little money each month.

additional_notes: Often used as «mettre quelqu’un dedans» = to dupe someone (make them believe something false, sometimes causing trouble for them). Also «se mettre dedans» can mean to get it wrong/make a mistake (informal). Literal meaning is “to put inside,” but in everyday speech it’s commonly the figurative sense.
target_language_example: Je me suis mis dedans : le rendez-vous est demain, pas aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I got it wrong: the appointment is tomorrow, not today.

meaning: to put in danger; to endanger.
additional_notes: Used when someone/something is placed at risk (physical, legal, financial, etc.). Often followed by a direct object (mettre quelqu’un en danger) or used in passive voice (être mis(e) en danger). Close synonym: « mettre en péril » (more formal).
target_language_example: Ne mets pas les autres en danger.
native_language_example: Don’t put others in danger.

meaning: to doubt; to call into question.
additional_notes: Used when you question the truth, accuracy, or reliability of something (a statement, a fact, a decision). Often followed by a noun (mettre en doute ses paroles) or by a clause with “que” (mettre en doute que + subjunctive).
target_language_example: Je ne mets pas en doute ce que tu dis, mais j’ai besoin de preuves.
native_language_example: I’m not doubting what you’re saying, but I need proof.

meaning: to warn; to put on guard.
additional_notes: Used to warn someone about a danger or problem. Often followed by "contre" + noun (warn against something) or "de" + infinitive (warn someone not to do something). Common forms: "Je te mets en garde" (I’m warning you) and "être mis en garde" (to be warned).
target_language_example: Je te mets en garde contre les arnaques en ligne.
native_language_example: I’m warning you about online scams.

meaning: to put online; to upload; to post online.
additional_notes: Used for publishing or making something available on the internet (a file, photo, video, article, announcement, etc.). Common in everyday and professional contexts. Often followed by what you’re uploading: « mettre une vidéo en ligne », « mettre des documents en ligne ».
target_language_example: Je vais mettre les photos en ligne ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to put the photos online tonight.

meaning: to start; to switch on; to set in motion.
additional_notes: Used for starting a device, machine, or process (similar to “switch on/turn on” or “start up”). With appliances/vehicles you’ll often hear it with a direct object: mettre la machine en marche. Intransitively, it can also mean “to start working/running”: La machine se met en marche (= it starts up).
target_language_example: Peux-tu mettre la machine en marche ?
native_language_example: Can you start/switch on the machine?

meaning: to tear/smash to pieces; to destroy.
additional_notes: Used for physically breaking something into pieces (paper, a device, etc.), and sometimes figuratively for ruining something (a plan, an argument). Commonly used in the past tense (a été mis en pièces) to describe something that was completely destroyed. Not the same as "mettre la table" (to set the table).
target_language_example: Il a mis la lettre en pièces.
native_language_example: He tore the letter to pieces.

meaning: to set up; to put in place; to implement.
additional_notes: Used for organizing or establishing something (a system, plan, process, event). Common in formal/professional contexts. Can also be literal for physically positioning something (less common than the figurative use). Often followed by a direct object: mettre en place un système / une stratégie / des mesures.
target_language_example: On va mettre en place une nouvelle procédure.
native_language_example: We’re going to set up/implement a new procedure.

meaning: to put into practice; to apply (in real life).
additional_notes: Used for applying an idea, rule, method, or advice in a real situation (not just talking about it). Common with things like une méthode, une théorie, un conseil, des compétences. In the infinitive after a verb: essayer de mettre en pratique, pouvoir mettre en pratique. Often interchangeable with « appliquer », but « mettre en pratique » emphasizes real-world use.
target_language_example: J’essaie de mettre en pratique ce que j’ai appris en cours.
native_language_example: I’m trying to put into practice what I learned in class.

meaning: to start (a machine/vehicle); to set off.
additional_notes: Used for getting something running (a car, engine, device) or starting a process/project. Very common with cars: « mettre la voiture en route ». For people leaving, French often also uses « partir »; « se mettre en route » means “to set off / get going” (for a person or group).
target_language_example: On met la voiture en route et on y va.
native_language_example: We start the car and off we go.

meaning: to implement; to put into practice.
additional_notes: Used for carrying out a plan, policy, idea, or project (often in professional or formal contexts). You can also see it as a noun phrase: « la mise en œuvre » = “the implementation.”
target_language_example: Nous devons mettre en œuvre ce plan dès la semaine prochaine.
native_language_example: We have to implement this plan starting next week.

meaning: to end; to put an end to.
additional_notes: Usually used with "à" + noun or situation: "mettre fin à" (to put an end to something). Common in formal or neutral contexts (agreements, conflicts, problems). Often used as "mettre fin à [quelque chose]" or "mettre fin à [une relation]".
target_language_example: Le gouvernement veut mettre fin au conflit.
native_language_example: The government wants to put an end to the conflict.

meaning: to take one’s own life (to die by suicide).
additional_notes: A relatively formal, euphemistic expression used in news reports or serious conversation. It literally means “to put an end to one’s days,” but in French it specifically refers to suicide. You can change the possessive for the person: « mettre fin à ses jours » (one’s own life), « mettre fin à ses jours » can also be « mettre fin à ses jours » with the subject implied; « il/elle a mis fin à ses jours » = “he/she took his/her own life.”
target_language_example: Selon la police, il aurait mis fin à ses jours.
native_language_example: According to the police, he may have taken his own life.

meaning: to put your hand (on something); to get hold of (something/someone).
additional_notes: Often used with **sur**: **mettre la main sur + noun** = “to get hold of / find / catch” (e.g., documents, an object, a person). In the sense of “catch,” it can imply finally finding someone or something after searching. Without **sur**, it may appear in set expressions (e.g., **mettre la main à la pâte** = “to pitch in/help out”).
target_language_example: La police a finalement mis la main sur le suspect.
native_language_example: The police finally caught the suspect.

meaning: to get hold of; to find (after looking); to lay your hands on.
additional_notes: Used with a direct object (mettre la main sur + noun/pronoun). Often implies effort or success after searching, or finally obtaining something. Depending on context it can also mean tracking down/catching someone (e.g., the police). More informal synonym: « mettre la main dessus ».
target_language_example: J’ai enfin mis la main sur mes clés.
native_language_example: I finally found my keys.

additional_notes: Used for preparing a table for a meal (putting out plates, cutlery, glasses, napkins, etc.). Also commonly said as an instruction or chore at home: « Mets la table ! »
target_language_example: Tu peux mettre la table pendant que je prépare le dîner ?
native_language_example: Can you set the table while I prepare dinner?

meaning: to set fire (to); to light (something) on fire.
additional_notes: Used with "à" to say what is being set on fire: "mettre le feu à + noun" (e.g., mettre le feu à une maison). Very common in the past tense: "Il a mis le feu…". Can also be used figuratively to mean "to ignite" or "to spark" (e.g., a debate), but the literal meaning is most common for beginners.
target_language_example: Quelqu’un a mis le feu à la poubelle.
native_language_example: Someone set the trash can on fire.

additional_notes: Usually used with a place introduced by "à", "dans", or "chez" (e.g., "mettre le pied à Paris", "dans un musée", "chez quelqu’un"). Very common in the past tense: "Je n’ai jamais mis le pied…" = "I’ve never set foot…" It often implies going/entering somewhere (sometimes with emphasis: not going there at all).
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais mis le pied dans ce restaurant.
native_language_example: I’ve never set foot in that restaurant.

additional_notes: Often used with negation: "ne pas mettre les pieds (quelque part)" = "not to set foot (somewhere)" / "never to go there." You can add a place after it: "mettre les pieds dans + place" (in/into) or "mettre les pieds à + city/event" (in/at).
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais mis les pieds dans ce restaurant.
native_language_example: I’ve never set foot in that restaurant.

meaning: to put on the table; (figuratively) to put forward / bring up (an idea, topic, offer).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: physically place something on a table. Very common figurative meaning in discussions/meetings/negotiations: to introduce a subject, proposal, or offer for everyone to consider (similar to “put it on the table” in English). Often used with a noun like une idée, une proposition, un sujet, une offre.
target_language_example: On va mettre cette question sur la table et en parler franchement.
native_language_example: We’re going to put this issue on the table and talk about it honestly.

meaning: to put an end to; to bring to an end.
additional_notes: Often used with "à" + noun: "mettre un terme à" something (end something). Common in more formal or written French (news, official statements), but can be used in everyday speech too. It implies stopping something intentionally or officially.
target_language_example: Le gouvernement veut mettre un terme à cette pratique.
native_language_example: The government wants to put an end to this practice.

meaning: to carry out; to put into effect (a plan, a decision, a threat).
additional_notes: Used for turning an intention into action—often with nouns like un plan, une décision, une menace, une promesse. Slightly formal; common in news/legal contexts. Often appears as « mettre [quelque chose] à exécution » or « être mis(e) à exécution » (passive: to be carried out).
target_language_example: Ils ont mis leur plan à exécution.
native_language_example: They carried out their plan.

meaning: to update; to bring up to date.
additional_notes: Used for updating information, documents, schedules, software/apps, or your knowledge on something. Often followed by a direct object: mettre à jour le logiciel / les informations / mon CV. In computing, you also see the noun form “une mise à jour” (an update).
target_language_example: Je dois mettre à jour mon CV avant de postuler.
native_language_example: I need to update my résumé before applying.

meaning: to kick/throw someone out; to expel someone.
additional_notes: Used when someone is forced to leave a place (a house, a bar, a workplace). It often sounds harsh. Common forms: « On l’a mis à la porte » (They threw him out), « Le patron l’a mise à la porte » (The boss fired/booted her out). In a job context it can imply being fired, but the core idea is being made to leave.
target_language_example: Ils l’ont mis à la porte après la dispute.
native_language_example: They threw him out after the argument.

meaning: to put a price on; to place a bounty on (someone).
additional_notes: Often used in official or legal contexts. With an object like "une maison", it means setting an asking price (e.g., for sale). With a person ("mettre quelqu’un à prix"), it means offering a reward for capturing/killing them (a bounty), typically in historical or crime-related contexts.
target_language_example: Le bandit a été mis à prix par les autorités.
native_language_example: The authorities put a bounty on the bandit.

meaning: to make good use of; to take advantage of (something).
additional_notes: Used with an object: « mettre à profit + [time/opportunity/resource] ». Often followed by « pour + infinitive » to say the purpose: « mettre à profit son temps pour réviser ». Means using something effectively/beneficially, not exploiting in a negative sense.
target_language_example: Je vais mettre à profit mon temps libre pour apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I’m going to make good use of my free time to learn French.

meaning: to put on the ground; to knock down (floor).
additional_notes: Often used literally for objects (putting something down on the ground) and figuratively for people (knocking someone down) or things like machines/systems (bringing them down, stopping them). In sports or fights, it can mean to floor someone.
target_language_example: Le boxeur a mis son adversaire à terre.
native_language_example: The boxer floored his opponent.

additional_notes: Usually used with the preposition **à**: **à mi-chemin** = “halfway (there)” / “midway between.” It can refer to distance or progress in a task. Often followed by **entre ... et ...** (“between ... and ...”).
target_language_example: On s’est arrêtés à mi-chemin entre Paris et Lyon.
native_language_example: We stopped halfway between Paris and Lyon.

meaning: half-time; the break in the middle of a match.
additional_notes: Mostly used in sports to talk about the interval between the two halves of a game (football/soccer, rugby, etc.). You’ll also see it in the expression « à mi-temps » meaning “part-time” (working part-time).
target_language_example: À la mi-temps, le score était de 1 à 1.
native_language_example: At half-time, the score was 1–1.

additional_notes: In everyday French, the appliance is most often said as **un micro-ondes** (masculine), usually written with an **-s** even in the singular: *un micro-ondes*. You’ll also hear the verb phrase **mettre/passer au micro-ondes** (“to microwave (something)”).
target_language_example: Je réchauffe la soupe au micro-ondes.
native_language_example: I’m reheating the soup in the microwave.

additional_notes: Used to add a stronger, more attractive idea after the first one (“and even better…”). Often follows a statement and can be set off by commas: « …, mieux encore, … ».
target_language_example: On peut aller au cinéma, ou mieux encore, dîner au restaurant.
native_language_example: We can go to the movies, or better yet, have dinner at a restaurant.

additional_notes: Common phrase to say something is not ideal, but it’s still preferable to having nothing at all. Often used to accept a small advantage, a partial solution, or a minimal result (sometimes with a slightly resigned tone).
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas beaucoup, mais c’est mieux que rien.
native_language_example: It’s not much, but it’s better than nothing.

additional_notes: Common proverb used to say it’s preferable to do something late than not do it at all. Often said when someone finally arrives, responds, or completes a task after a delay.
target_language_example: Tu as enfin répondu ? Mieux vaut tard que jamais !
native_language_example: You finally replied? Better late than never!

additional_notes: A warm, emphatic way to thank someone (stronger than "merci"). Used in friendly and polite contexts, often in writing (texts, emails, cards) as well as speech.
target_language_example: Mille mercis pour ton aide !
native_language_example: Thanks a thousand for your help!

meaning: centipede (also used for millipede in casual speech).
additional_notes: A common noun for a many-legged crawling insect/arthropod. Literally means “thousand-legs,” but in French it most often refers to a centipede; some speakers also use it loosely for a millipede. Plural: des mille-pattes.
target_language_example: J’ai trouvé un mille-pattes dans la salle de bain.
native_language_example: I found a centipede in the bathroom.

meaning: staging; direction (of a play/film); how a scene is presented.
additional_notes: Used for theater, film, and sometimes events/exhibitions: it refers to the director’s choices (sets, lighting, actors’ movements, camera framing, etc.). Common with verbs like « faire la mise en scène » (to do the staging/directing) and « la mise en scène de + [work/event] » (the staging of…).
target_language_example: La mise en scène de ce film est impressionnante.
native_language_example: The direction/staging of this movie is impressive.

additional_notes: Used for software/app updates, updated information, or an update on a situation. Very common in tech: « faire une mise à jour » (to do/install an update). Also used in speech for a status update: « une mise à jour sur… » (an update on…).
target_language_example: Je dois faire une mise à jour de mon téléphone.
native_language_example: I need to update my phone.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone lives day to day (habits, routine, diet, work-life balance, values). Common with adjectives like « sain » (healthy), « actif » (active), « sédentaire » (sedentary), « moderne » (modern). Also used in public health and sociology contexts.
target_language_example: Elle a changé de mode de vie pour être en meilleure santé.
native_language_example: She changed her lifestyle to be in better health.

meaning: “my God!” (an exclamation of surprise, shock, worry, etc.).
additional_notes: Used as a standalone exclamation (often followed by !). It can express strong emotion (alarm, disbelief, annoyance, relief), similar to “Oh my God!” in English. Depending on tone and context, it may be considered mildly irreverent/religious language, so some speakers avoid it in formal or religious settings.
target_language_example: Mon Dieu ! Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ?
native_language_example: My God! What happened?

meaning: “my ass!” (a vulgar way to say “no way!” / “yeah, right!”).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used to express strong disbelief, rejection, or irritation at what someone just said (similar to “my ass,” “bullshit,” or “yeah, right” in English, depending on tone). Avoid in polite situations; it can easily sound rude or aggressive. You may hear it alone as a reaction, or in phrases like “X, mon cul !” to mock or deny X.
target_language_example: « Tu vas vraiment l’aider ? » — « Mon cul ! »
native_language_example: “You’re really going to help him?” — “My ass!”

meaning: “mate”, “buddy” (friendly way to address someone; literally “my old [friend]”).
additional_notes: Used mainly when speaking to a man, often with a warm, familiar, sometimes slightly nostalgic tone. Common in casual speech (e.g., between friends, or from an older speaker to a younger one). It can sound a bit old-fashioned depending on context. Not necessarily about age; it’s a term of address.
target_language_example: Ça va, mon vieux ?
native_language_example: How’s it going, mate?

additional_notes: Used as a skeptical or sarcastic reply to show you don’t believe what someone just said. It’s fairly informal and often said with a particular tone (rolling eyes, etc.). Literally means “my eye,” but that’s not how it’s used in English.
target_language_example: — Il a fait ça tout seul. — Mon œil !
native_language_example: — He did that all by himself. — Yeah, right!

additional_notes: Most often used in the plural to mean an amusement-park roller coaster: « On a fait les montagnes russes. » It can also be used figuratively to describe strong ups and downs (especially emotional): « C’est les montagnes russes en ce moment. »
target_language_example: J’adore les montagnes russes, mais ça me fait un peu peur.
native_language_example: I love roller coasters, but they scare me a little.

meaning: to stand guard; to keep watch.
additional_notes: Used for guarding a place, person, or entrance (often soldiers, police, security, or a dog). Literally “to mount the guard,” but in English you normally say “stand guard” or “keep watch.” Common with a location introduced by devant/devant la porte, à l’entrée, etc.
target_language_example: Des soldats montent la garde devant l’ambassade.
native_language_example: Soldiers are standing guard in front of the embassy.

meaning: to go to your head (alcohol, success, compliments).
additional_notes: Used when alcohol affects you quickly (“The wine went to my head”) or when power/fame/attention makes someone arrogant or overconfident (“Success went to his head”). Often used with a subject like l’alcool / le vin / la célébrité: « Le vin m’est monté à la tête. »
target_language_example: Après deux verres, le vin m’est monté à la tête.
native_language_example: After two glasses, the wine went to my head.

meaning: a sugar cube; a piece of sugar.
additional_notes: Used when talking about adding sugar to coffee or tea. In cafés you might hear or say: «Avec combien de morceaux de sucre ?» (“With how many sugar cubes?”). Also common with «un» or «deux» to specify quantity.
target_language_example: Je prends mon café avec un morceau de sucre, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I take my coffee with a sugar cube, please.

meaning: starved to death; dying of hunger.
additional_notes: Literally “dead from hunger.” Used to describe someone who actually died from lack of food, or more commonly as an exaggeration to mean “I’m starving” (e.g., "Je suis mort de faim"). You can also say "mourir de faim" (“to starve”).
target_language_example: Je suis mort de faim—on mange bientôt ?
native_language_example: I’m starving—are we eating soon?

additional_notes: Used for the password needed to log in to an account, access Wi‑Fi, unlock a device, etc. Often seen with verbs like « entrer » (to enter) and « réinitialiser » (to reset): « Entrez votre mot de passe. »
target_language_example: J’ai oublié mon mot de passe.
native_language_example: I forgot my password.

additional_notes: Used when you translate or repeat something exactly, sticking closely to the original wording (often implying a very literal translation). You can use it after verbs like traduire (“to translate”) or répéter (“to repeat”).
target_language_example: Ne traduis pas mot à mot, sinon ça sonne bizarre en anglais.
native_language_example: Don’t translate word for word, otherwise it sounds weird in English.

additional_notes: Used for online tools like Google, Bing, etc. Often appears with verbs like utiliser (to use), chercher sur (to search on), or as a noun phrase: un moteur de recherche. Example: sur un moteur de recherche = on a search engine.
target_language_example: J’ai trouvé cette information sur un moteur de recherche.
native_language_example: I found this information on a search engine.

additional_notes: Used for crossword puzzles in newspapers, magazines, or apps. Usually plural in French even when talking about one puzzle ("faire des mots croisés").
target_language_example: Je fais des mots croisés dans le train.
native_language_example: I do crossword puzzles on the train.

additional_notes: A noun meaning a mill powered by wind. Used literally for real windmills (common in the countryside, or in the Netherlands), and also for decorative/tourist windmills. Plural: des moulins à vent.
target_language_example: On a visité un vieux moulin à vent pendant les vacances.
native_language_example: We visited an old windmill during the vacation.

additional_notes: Literally “to die of hunger.” Commonly used as an exaggeration to say you’re extremely hungry; it can also be used literally in serious contexts. Often used with the imperfect for a past state: « Je mourais de faim ». Similar everyday option: « avoir très faim ».
target_language_example: On mange bientôt ? Je meurs de faim !
native_language_example: Are we eating soon? I’m starving!

meaning: means of transportation; mode of transport.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone travels (car, bus, metro, bike, etc.). Often appears with a possessive: « mon moyen de transport » (my way of getting around). Common question: « Quel est ton moyen de transport ? » (How do you get around?/What do you take to get there?).
target_language_example: Le vélo est mon moyen de transport pour aller au travail.
native_language_example: The bike is my means of transportation for getting to work.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the genre (Mozart, Beethoven, etc.). You can use it after verbs like aimer/écouter (to like/listen to) or with de to describe a type of concert: un concert de musique classique.
target_language_example: J’aime écouter de la musique classique le soir.
native_language_example: I like listening to classical music in the evening.

meaning: square meter (m²), a unit of area.
additional_notes: Used to measure surface/area, especially for apartments/rooms, land, and floor space in real estate listings. Often written as "m²" after a number: "50 m²". You can also say "au mètre carré" to mean "per square meter" (e.g., price per m²).
target_language_example: L’appartement fait 45 mètres carrés.
native_language_example: The apartment is 45 square meters.

additional_notes: Common in France in a healthcare/administrative context: the doctor you officially declare as your main doctor who coordinates your care and referrals (often a general practitioner). You can say “mon/ma médecin traitant(e)” depending on the doctor’s gender.
target_language_example: Je dois prendre rendez-vous avec mon médecin traitant.
native_language_example: I need to make an appointment with my primary care doctor.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something didn’t happen at all, or didn’t reach the smallest/expected amount. Very common in spoken French, often expressing surprise, annoyance, or disappointment. It can stand alone as a short reply meaning “Not even!” (e.g., to say you didn’t even get a chance).
target_language_example: Il n’a même pas dit merci.
native_language_example: He didn’t even say thank you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a concession (something is true or will happen despite another condition). Typically followed by the indicative (Je viens même si je suis fatigué). You can often translate it as “even if” (condition) or “even though” (fact) depending on context.
target_language_example: Je viendrai même si je suis fatigué.
native_language_example: I’ll come even if I’m tired.

meaning: to have nothing to do with; to be unrelated to.
additional_notes: Used to say there is no connection between two things. It’s the negative form of « avoir à voir avec » (“to have to do with”). Conjugate « avoir » to match the subject: « ça n’a rien à voir avec… », « je n’ai rien à voir avec… ». The structure is: ne + (conjugated avoir) + rien + à voir avec + noun/pronoun (or « ce que… »). In casual speech, « ne » is often dropped: « Ça a rien à voir avec… ».
target_language_example: Ça n’a rien à voir avec toi.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with you.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is no longer present. With a person, it can be neutral (“He’s not here anymore”) or a gentle euphemism meaning the person has died (“She is no longer with us”), depending on context and tone. Often refers back to someone already known in the conversation.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, il n’est plus là.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, he isn’t here anymore.

additional_notes: Used at the end of a statement to ask for confirmation or agreement. You match the English tag to the context (isn’t it?/aren’t they?/don’t you?/right?). Common in both spoken and written French and often said quickly.
target_language_example: Il fait froid aujourd’hui, n’est-ce pas ?
native_language_example: It’s cold today, isn’t it?

meaning: "were it not for" / "if it hadn’t been for".
additional_notes: A literary/formal expression used to introduce an exception or a factor that prevented something. It comes from the past subjunctive (plus-que-parfait du subjonctif) of « être » and is most often seen in writing, especially in the pattern « N’eût été + noun/pronoun… ». In everyday speech, people usually say « sans + noun » or « s’il n’y avait pas eu… ».
target_language_example: N’eût été la pluie, nous serions restés plus longtemps.
native_language_example: If it hadn’t been for the rain, we would have stayed longer.

additional_notes: Used to mean it doesn’t matter which one you choose. It’s the feminine form: use it with a feminine noun (e.g., une robe, une option). With a masculine noun, you’d say "n'importe lequel"; for plural, "n'importe lesquels / lesquelles". Often follows the noun or replaces it when the noun is understood from context.
target_language_example: Tu peux prendre n'importe laquelle de ces robes.
native_language_example: You can take any one of these dresses.

additional_notes: Used to say it doesn’t matter which one you choose. It can be a pronoun (meaning “any one”) or used before a noun (meaning “any”). It agrees with the thing chosen: feminine singular: "n'importe laquelle"; masculine plural: "n'importe lesquels"; feminine plural: "n'importe lesquelles".
target_language_example: Tu peux choisir n'importe lequel.
native_language_example: You can choose any one.

additional_notes: Used to say it doesn’t matter which specific ones you choose. It’s the feminine plural form to match a feminine plural noun (e.g., des chemises, des options). It replaces the noun and often corresponds to English “any of them / whichever ones.” (Masculine plural: « n’importe lesquels ».)
target_language_example: Prends n’importe lesquelles, elles sont toutes en solde.
native_language_example: Take any ones; they’re all on sale.

additional_notes: Used to say it doesn’t matter which items you choose. It’s the masculine plural form (for mixed or all-masculine groups): feminine plural is "n'importe lesquelles". Often used alone as a pronoun (“any ones”), or after a noun: "N’importe quels livres…".
target_language_example: Tu peux prendre n'importe lesquels, ça m'est égal.
native_language_example: You can take any ones you like; I don’t mind.

additional_notes: Used to say a place doesn’t matter or is unknown. Often placed after the verb: « Tu peux t’asseoir n’importe où. » It can also start a clause meaning “wherever”: « N’importe où tu vas, je te suis. »
target_language_example: On peut manger n’importe où dans ce quartier.
native_language_example: You can eat anywhere in this neighborhood.

additional_notes: Used to say there is no specific time, or that the time doesn’t matter. Often comes at the end of the sentence. You can also see it in questions and invitations: "Tu peux venir n’importe quand" (You can come anytime). Related forms: "n’importe où" (anywhere), "n’importe qui" (anyone), "n’importe quoi" (anything / nonsense depending on context).
target_language_example: Tu peux m’appeler n’importe quand.
native_language_example: You can call me anytime.

additional_notes: Used before a singular noun to mean “any” in the sense of “whichever you choose / it doesn’t matter which one.” It must agree with the noun: n’importe quelle (feminine singular), n’importe quels (masculine plural), n’importe quelles (feminine plural). Often used to emphasize that the choice doesn’t matter.
target_language_example: Tu peux choisir n’importe quel livre.
native_language_example: You can choose any book.

additional_notes: Used to mean any person at all, without specifying which one. Often appears in negatives and conditions (e.g., "Je ne le dirai pas à n’importe qui" = not to just anyone). Can also be used to mean “just anyone / some random person,” sometimes with a slightly dismissive tone depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu peux demander à n’importe qui, ils te diront la même chose.
native_language_example: You can ask anyone; they’ll tell you the same thing.

additional_notes: Literally “no matter what.” Used (1) neutrally to mean “anything” (“Choose anything you want”), and (2) very commonly as a reaction meaning “nonsense,” “that’s ridiculous,” or “what are you talking about?” depending on tone. Often said alone as an exclamation.
target_language_example: Tu dis n'importe quoi !
native_language_example: You’re talking nonsense!

meaning: to have nothing to do with it; to not be responsible.
additional_notes: Used to deny responsibility or involvement in a situation (often something negative). The "y" refers to the situation/thing being talked about. Commonly used with the person as subject: "Je n'y suis pour rien" (It’s not my fault / I had nothing to do with it).
target_language_example: Je n'y suis pour rien si le train est en retard.
native_language_example: It’s not my fault if the train is late.

additional_notes: Used to describe a military ship belonging to a navy. More general than specific types like "destroyer" or "battleship". Often appears in news or history contexts. Plural: "des navires de guerre".
target_language_example: Un navire de guerre patrouille près de la côte.
native_language_example: A warship is patrolling near the coast.

meaning: to become one; to be as one (act in perfect unity).
additional_notes: Used to say two people/things are so close or coordinated that they function like a single unit. Common with verbs like "être" or "ne faire plus qu’un" (even stronger), often in romantic, teamwork, or movement contexts: "Ils ne font qu’un" / "Le cheval et son cavalier ne font qu’un." Not the same as "ne faire qu’un(e) chose" (= to do only one thing).
target_language_example: Sur la piste, le danseur et sa partenaire ne font qu’un.
native_language_example: On the dance floor, the dancer and his partner move as one.

additional_notes: Used to make a sentence negative with the meaning “never.” In standard French, it’s split around the verb: **ne + verb + jamais** (e.g., *Je ne mange jamais de viande.*). In casual spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: *Je mange jamais de viande.*
target_language_example: Je ne voyage jamais seul.
native_language_example: I never travel alone.

meaning: "Don’t talk to me about it" / "Don’t mention it" (often: "Tell me about it!").
additional_notes: Literally means “don’t talk to me about it.” In real life it’s very often used to agree with someone’s complaint, meaning “Tell me about it!” or “Don’t get me started.” It can also be a direct request to stop discussing a topic. In speech you’ll commonly hear it without the “ne”: « M’en parle pas ! »
target_language_example: — J’ai encore raté mon train. — Ne m’en parle pas, ça m’arrive tout le temps !
native_language_example: — I missed my train again. — Tell me about it, it happens to me all the time!

meaning: “Don’t talk to me about it!” / “Don’t get me started (on that)!”
additional_notes: A strong, common reaction meaning you don’t want to discuss the topic—often because it annoys you, stresses you out, or brings back a bad experience. It’s the negative imperative of "m’en parler" (“to talk to me about it”), where "en" refers to the topic already mentioned. You may also hear the slightly shorter form "M’en parlez pas !" in speech.
target_language_example: Ne m’en parlez pas, j’ai passé une journée horrible au travail.
native_language_example: Don’t get me started—I had a horrible day at work.

additional_notes: Core French negation. With a conjugated verb, it usually goes around the verb: **ne ... pas** (often **n'** before a vowel sound): *Je n'aime pas.* With an infinitive, you often see **ne pas + infinitive**: *Ne pas fumer* (“Do not smoke”). In everyday spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: *J’aime pas / Je sais pas*.
target_language_example: Je préfère ne pas sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: I'd rather not go out tonight.

meaning: to not be able to get over it; to be unable to believe it.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used when you’re very surprised or shocked. Most commonly used in the present: « Je n’en reviens pas ! » (“I can’t believe it!”). « en » refers to the situation you’re reacting to (roughly “from it/over it”). You can add « de + infinitive » to specify the cause: « Je n’en reviens pas d’avoir gagné. »
target_language_example: Je n’en reviens pas : j’ai eu le job !
native_language_example: I can’t believe it: I got the job!

meaning: to not go easy on someone; to show no mercy.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is being very strict or tough and won’t give any special treatment or leniency (e.g., in competition, negotiations, grading, criticism). Often appears as a warning or description: « Il/Elle ne fait pas de cadeaux ». Not usually about literal gifts.
target_language_example: Le prof ne fait pas de cadeaux : il faut vraiment réviser pour réussir l’examen.
native_language_example: The teacher doesn’t go easy on anyone—you really have to study to pass the exam.

meaning: “no longer / not anymore” (used with a verb: ne … plus).
additional_notes: Used to form a negation meaning that something has stopped: ne + verb + plus. Example: Je ne fume plus = “I don’t smoke anymore.” In everyday spoken French, the “ne” is often dropped: Je fume plus. Note that without “ne”, plus usually means “more” (and is pronounced differently).
target_language_example: Je ne travaille plus ici.
native_language_example: I don’t work here anymore.

meaning: “nothing” (used with a verb to make a negative).
additional_notes: Used in French negation with a verb: ne + verb + rien. In everyday speech, “ne” is often dropped: Je (ne) vois rien. If there’s an object pronoun, “rien” usually comes after the verb: Je ne comprends rien. With an infinitive, it can be ne rien + infinitive: Ne rien dire (“to say nothing”).
target_language_example: Je ne vois rien.
native_language_example: I don’t see anything / I see nothing.

additional_notes: Used to say the number 900. Note the pronunciation: the final “f” in neuf is usually not pronounced before cents (often sounds like “neu”); and the final “s” in cents is silent. Also, cent takes an “s” (cents) when it is multiplied and not followed by another number (neuf cents), but no “s” when followed by another number (neuf cent un = 901).
target_language_example: Ça coûte neuf cents euros.
native_language_example: It costs nine hundred euros.

additional_notes: Used for a hole/depression in the road surface that can damage a car or make driving/biking uncomfortable. Often used with verbs like « éviter » (to avoid) or « tomber dans » (to hit/fall into). Plural: « des nids-de-poule ».
target_language_example: Fais attention, il y a un nid-de-poule juste après le virage.
native_language_example: Be careful, there’s a pothole right after the bend.

additional_notes: Used in geography, weather, and measurement contexts to talk about altitude/elevation relative to the surface of the ocean. Often appears in expressions like « au niveau de la mer » (at sea level) or « au-dessus du niveau de la mer » (above sea level).
target_language_example: Cette ville est à 300 mètres au-dessus du niveau de la mer.
native_language_example: This city is 300 meters above sea level.

additional_notes: Used for black-and-white photos, films, printing, or drawings. Also used figuratively to mean something is very clear/definite (written "in black and white") or seen in an overly simplistic way ("thinking in black and white").
target_language_example: J’aime les photos en noir et blanc.
native_language_example: I like black-and-white photos.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the fruit (and its flavor) in food and drinks. It’s usually feminine in French: une noix de coco. You may also see it in set phrases like lait de coco (coconut milk) and huile de coco (coconut oil).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un yaourt à la noix de coco, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a coconut yogurt, please.

additional_notes: Used on forms or in introductions to ask for or give your first name + last name (sometimes including any middle names). Often appears as: « Votre nom complet » (your full name) or « Quel est votre nom complet ? » (What is your full name?).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous écrire votre nom complet, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you write your full name, please?

additional_notes: An exclamation of anger, surprise, or frustration. Literally “name of God,” but it’s used like a blasphemous oath in French and can sound quite rude/offensive—avoid in polite settings. Often said on its own, sometimes with a pause: « Nom de Dieu ! »
target_language_example: Nom de Dieu ! J’ai encore oublié mes clés.
native_language_example: For God’s sake! I forgot my keys again.

additional_notes: Used on forms and in official contexts to mean your surname (the name you share with your family). Often contrasted with "prénom" (first name). You may also hear "nom" alone used to mean surname when the context is clear (e.g., "Nom :" on a form).
target_language_example: Quel est votre nom de famille ?
native_language_example: What is your last name?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a woman’s surname before marriage (or, more generally, her birth surname). Common on administrative forms and in official contexts. You may also see: « nom de naissance » (birth name; more neutral/official) and « née X » meaning “born X” in documents.
target_language_example: Quel est votre nom de jeune fille ?
native_language_example: What is your maiden name?

additional_notes: Used in grammar to talk about names of specific people, places, brands, etc. In French, a nom propre is usually capitalized and normally does not take an article (e.g., « Paris », « Marie »), though there are exceptions (e.g., « La France », « Les États-Unis »).
target_language_example: « Paris » est un nom propre.
native_language_example: “Paris” is a proper noun.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean “a number of” or “many/several,” often in a fairly formal or written style. It’s commonly used with a verb in the plural: « Un nombre de personnes sont venues. » Note: « nombre de » (without « un ») is also used in set phrases like « bon nombre de » (“a good many”). Don’t confuse with « le nombre de » (“the number of”), which usually takes a singular verb: « Le nombre de personnes est élevé. »
target_language_example: Un nombre de personnes sont venues à la réunion.
native_language_example: A number of people came to the meeting.

meaning: odd number (an integer not divisible by 2).
additional_notes: Used in math and everyday contexts (prices, counts, exercises). Opposite: « nombre pair » (even number). « Impair » agrees in gender/number: « un nombre impair », « des nombres impairs ».
target_language_example: 17 est un nombre impair.
native_language_example: 17 is an odd number.

additional_notes: Used in math and everyday contexts to say a number is divisible by 2 (0, 2, 4, 6, etc.). Note: French « pair » means “even” (as in even/odd), not “pair” (two things). The opposite is « nombre impair » (odd number).
target_language_example: Huit est un nombre pair.
native_language_example: Eight is an even number.

additional_notes: Used as a reaction to what someone just said or did. Often shows disbelief, annoyance, or emphasis, and it doesn’t always introduce a real contrast like English “no but.” Common in spoken French; intonation matters (can sound playful or irritated). Often followed by a statement or question: “Non mais ça va pas ?!”
target_language_example: Non mais tu te prends pour qui ?
native_language_example: Come on, who do you think you are?

additional_notes: A polite way to refuse or decline an offer. Often used on its own as a complete answer (e.g., when someone offers food, help, a bag, etc.). In very formal situations you can also say "Non, merci." with a slight pause, but it’s commonly said as one phrase.
target_language_example: — Tu veux un café ? — Non merci.
native_language_example: — Do you want a coffee? — No, thank you.

additional_notes: Used with negation to say something is also not true. Often follows another negative statement: « Moi non plus » = “Me neither.” Usually appears with « ne…pas » (or other negatives): « Je ne viens pas non plus » = “I’m not coming either.”
target_language_example: Je n’aime pas le café. — Moi non plus.
native_language_example: I don’t like coffee. — Me neither.

additional_notes: Used to add emphasis and introduce a second point. Very commonly appears in the structure "non seulement ..., mais aussi ...". It can also be used alone when the "but also" part is implied by context.
target_language_example: Non seulement il parle français, mais aussi espagnol.
native_language_example: Not only does he speak French, but also Spanish.

additional_notes: Used as an adjective or a noun to describe someone who doesn’t smoke or a place/option where smoking is not allowed. Common on signs and in bookings: "chambre non-fumeur" (non-smoking room), "zone non-fumeur" (non-smoking area). Feminine form: "non-fumeuse".
target_language_example: Je voudrais une chambre non-fumeur, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a non-smoking room, please.

additional_notes: Emphatic form of "nous" used to stress that it’s "we/us" personally (and not someone else). Often used after the subject or object: "Nous l’avons fait nous-mêmes" (We did it ourselves). Hyphenated and agrees with the pronoun: "moi-même" (myself), "toi-même" (yourself), "eux-mêmes" (themselves, masc.), "elles-mêmes" (themselves, fem.).
target_language_example: Nous avons préparé le dîner nous-mêmes.
native_language_example: We prepared dinner ourselves.

meaning: a fresh start; a new beginning.
additional_notes: Used to talk about starting over after a change or difficulty (moving, a breakup, a new job, etc.). Often appears with verbs like « prendre » (to take) or « offrir » (to offer): « prendre un nouveau départ », « offrir un nouveau départ à quelqu’un ». In French, « départ » is literally a “departure,” but in this phrase it commonly means starting anew.
target_language_example: Après cette période difficile, j’ai besoin d’un nouveau départ.
native_language_example: After that difficult period, I need a fresh start.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone who has recently arrived or joined a place, group, company, etc. Often written with a hyphen as "nouveau-venu" (masculine). Feminine: "nouvelle venue" / "nouvelle-venue". Plural: "nouveaux venus" / "nouvelles venues".
target_language_example: C’est un nouveau venu dans l’équipe.
native_language_example: He’s a newcomer to the team.

additional_notes: Used as a noun to refer to a baby that has just been born. Often appears with an article (un/une) or possessive (mon/son). Feminine form: "nouvelle-née". Common related phrase: "un bébé nouveau-né" (a newborn baby).
target_language_example: Le nouveau-né dort presque toute la journée.
native_language_example: The newborn sleeps almost all day.

meaning: dark/black cloud; (figuratively) a bad sign or gloomy mood.
additional_notes: Literally means “black cloud.” Used in weather contexts, or figuratively to talk about something hanging over a situation (bad luck, worry, negativity). Often appears with verbs like « avoir » or « planer »: « Un nuage noir plane sur… » (“A dark cloud hangs over…”).
target_language_example: Depuis cette annonce, un nuage noir plane sur l’équipe.
native_language_example: Since that announcement, a dark cloud has been hanging over the team.

additional_notes: Used when you didn’t sleep at all (or barely slept) during the night, often because of work, studying, travel, stress, or a party. Common expression: "faire une nuit blanche" = "to pull an all-nighter."
target_language_example: J’ai fait une nuit blanche à cause de l’examen.
native_language_example: I pulled an all-nighter because of the exam.

meaning: night and day; all the time (around the clock).
additional_notes: Used literally to contrast day vs. night ("like night and day"), or idiomatically to mean continuously/24-7, often with verbs like travailler (to work) or être ouvert (to be open). In comparisons, you can say "C’est la nuit et le jour" = "It’s like night and day."
target_language_example: Ils travaillent nuit et jour pour finir le projet.
native_language_example: They work day and night to finish the project.

meaning: null and void; treated as if it never existed.
additional_notes: Formal/legal phrase used for contracts, decisions, clauses, or actions that are declared invalid. It means the document or act has no legal effect and is considered as though it never happened.
target_language_example: Le contrat a été déclaré nul et non avenu.
native_language_example: The contract was declared null and void.

additional_notes: Means “nowhere,” often used with negation: ne... nulle part (“not... anywhere”). You can also see it without ne in casual spoken French (e.g., Je vais nulle part). It can refer to location (être nulle part), destination (aller nulle part), or where something is found (on ne le trouve nulle part).
target_language_example: Je ne le trouve nulle part.
native_language_example: I can’t find it anywhere.

additional_notes: Used to ask for, give, or confirm a phone number. Often appears with possessives (mon/ton/son numéro de téléphone) or in questions like « Quel est votre numéro de téléphone ? ». In everyday speech, people may shorten it to « numéro » when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Quel est votre numéro de téléphone ?
native_language_example: What is your phone number?

additional_notes: Used to react to something surprising, impressive, annoying, or unfortunate. The exact feeling depends on tone and context (complaint vs. admiration). Often said on its own, or before a comment. Not literally “oh there there” in English.
target_language_example: Oh là là, c’est cher !
native_language_example: Oh wow, it’s expensive!

meaning: "Oh my God!" (an exclamation of surprise, shock, frustration, etc.).
additional_notes: Used as a strong, emotional reaction in spoken French. It can sound intense depending on tone and context; in more formal or less religious language, people may also say "oh là là", "mon Dieu" (without "oh"), or "oh mon gosh" (softer, more playful).
target_language_example: Oh mon Dieu, j’ai oublié mes clés !
native_language_example: Oh my God, I forgot my keys!

meaning: "oh no!" (an exclamation of surprise, disappointment, or worry).
additional_notes: Used as a quick reaction when something goes wrong, when you hear bad news, or when you suddenly realize a problem. Often said alone, or followed by what happened: "Oh non, j’ai oublié mes clés !" You can make it stronger by repeating it ("Oh non, non, non !").
target_language_example: Oh non, j’ai raté le bus !
native_language_example: Oh no, I missed the bus!

additional_notes: Used for hunting birds like eagles, hawks, falcons, and owls. It’s a common general term in nature documentaries and when talking about wildlife.
target_language_example: On a vu un oiseau de proie tourner dans le ciel.
native_language_example: We saw a bird of prey circling in the sky.

additional_notes: Used to talk about birds that travel seasonally from one region/country to another. Often used in nature/travel contexts; plural is "oiseaux migrateurs".
target_language_example: En automne, on voit souvent des oiseaux migrateurs partir vers le sud.
native_language_example: In autumn, you often see migratory birds leaving for the south.

meaning: extremely; so much that it can’t be any more (often used for emphasis).
additional_notes: Commonly used after an adjective or adverb to intensify it: "fatigué on ne peut plus" = "extremely tired". Literally means "one can’t anymore," but in practice it’s an idiomatic way to say something is at the maximum degree. Often used in writing or a slightly formal tone; less common in casual spoken French than "très" or "super".
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué on ne peut plus après cette journée.
native_language_example: I’m extremely tired after this day.

additional_notes: A very common phrase to express uncertainty or a precaution. Often used to justify doing something as a safety measure: « Prends un parapluie, on ne sait jamais. » Literally “one never knows,” but it functions like “you never know” or “just in case” in English.
target_language_example: Prends ta carte d’identité, on ne sait jamais.
native_language_example: Take your ID card, just in case.

additional_notes: A masculine noun: un on-dit / des on-dits. Often used to refer to gossip or unconfirmed information circulating in a group. It comes from the expression « on dit… » (“they say…”), but as a noun it means the rumor itself.
target_language_example: Ce n’est qu’un on-dit : rien n’a été confirmé.
native_language_example: It’s just a rumor—nothing has been confirmed.

additional_notes: Literally “portable computer.” In everyday French, this is the standard term for a laptop. You may also hear “un PC portable” (especially for a Windows laptop). “Ordinateur” = computer; “portable” agrees with it (masculine singular).
target_language_example: J’ai oublié mon ordinateur portable à la maison.
native_language_example: I forgot my laptop at home.

meaning: the order of things; the natural course of events.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how things are normally arranged or how events usually happen (often implying what’s natural, normal, or expected). Common in phrases like « dans l’ordre des choses » (“in the natural order of things”).
target_language_example: C’est dans l’ordre des choses que les enfants grandissent et deviennent indépendants.
native_language_example: It’s the natural course of things that children grow up and become independent.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an alternative or another possibility. It can be a simple "or" in questions (often meaning "or maybe"), or a stronger "or else" meaning "otherwise" when giving a consequence. Common in spoken French.
target_language_example: On peut aller au cinéma, ou alors rester à la maison.
native_language_example: We can go to the movies, or else stay at home.

additional_notes: Used to present an alternative option, often a bit more explicit than just "ou". Common in questions ("A ou bien B ?") and in warnings or consequences ("Fais-le, ou bien…" = "Do it, or else…"). It can also introduce a correction or clarification: "Ou bien plutôt…" ("Or rather…").
target_language_example: Tu veux du thé ou bien du café ?
native_language_example: Do you want tea or coffee?

meaning: "or what?" (a pushy way to ask "or else? / or something?")
additional_notes: Used at the end of a question to pressure someone for an answer or to challenge them. Tone can sound impatient, annoyed, or confrontational (“So… yes or no?”). It can also mean “or what/ or something” when you’re unsure, but it’s still quite direct. Often heard in casual speech; in polite contexts, avoid it and use a softer option like « ou bien ? » or « ou quoi d’autre ? ».
target_language_example: Tu viens ce soir, ou quoi ?
native_language_example: Are you coming tonight, or what?

additional_notes: Means a soft stuffed toy bear. Used with articles like "un/une" (e.g., "un ours en peluche") or possessives ("mon ours en peluche"). Also commonly shortened to "un nounours" (more childlike).
target_language_example: Elle a offert un ours en peluche à son enfant.
native_language_example: She gave her child a teddy bear.

additional_notes: Used with body parts or openings (mouth, eyes, door, window) to mean opening them as wide as possible. Often appears in the imperative: « Ouvre grand… » / « Ouvrez grand… ». Also common with the adjective used alone: « grand ouvert(e) » (“wide open”).
target_language_example: Ouvre grand la bouche !
native_language_example: Open your mouth wide!

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. You can use it as an infinitive (e.g., after pouvoir/devoir/aller) or conjugate ouvrir: « J’ouvre la porte » (I open/am opening the door), « Peux-tu ouvrir la porte ? » (Can you open the door?).
target_language_example: Peux-tu ouvrir la porte, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you open the door, please?

meaning: to open your eyes; (figuratively) to realize / become aware.
additional_notes: Literal: physically open your eyes. Figurative: to understand the truth about something, to stop being naive, or to notice what’s really happening (often used as advice or a warning: "Ouvre les yeux !"). Conjugates like a regular -ir verb: j’ouvre, tu ouvres, il/elle ouvre, nous ouvrons, vous ouvrez, ils/elles ouvrent.
target_language_example: Ouvre les yeux : il te ment depuis le début.
native_language_example: Open your eyes: he’s been lying to you from the beginning.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause meaning that the location doesn’t matter (a concessive idea). It’s typically followed by the subjunctive: « où que + subject + verb (subjunctive) ». Example pattern: « Où que tu ailles… » = “Wherever you go…”.
target_language_example: Où que tu ailles, je te suivrai.
native_language_example: Wherever you go, I’ll follow you.

meaning: “where is the world going?” (expresses worry or disapproval about how things are changing).
additional_notes: Often used as a rhetorical question to comment on society, politics, or bad behavior—similar to “what is the world coming to?” or “where is this world headed?” You’ll also hear it with “Mais…” for emphasis: “Mais où va le monde ?”
target_language_example: Mais où va le monde ? Même les enfants ne disent plus bonjour !
native_language_example: What is the world coming to? Even kids don’t say hello anymore!

additional_notes: Very common spoken/texting abbreviation of “petit déjeuner” (often also written “ptit dej”, “p’tit dej”). Used casually with friends, in messages, and sometimes in informal ads or menus. In more formal situations, use “petit déjeuner”.
target_language_example: On se fait un p'tit déj ensemble demain matin ?
native_language_example: Shall we have breakfast together tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: Written abbreviation used mainly in notes, emails, lists, or parentheses. In speech, you usually say « par exemple » rather than « p. ex. ». Often followed by a comma or used in parentheses.
target_language_example: Tu peux apporter des fruits (p. ex., des pommes ou des bananes).
native_language_example: You can bring fruit (e.g., apples or bananas).

additional_notes: Used for bread that has been toasted. Common at breakfast (e.g., with butter or jam). Also used as a menu item or when describing how you want bread prepared. Related phrases: « une tranche de pain grillé » (a slice of toast), « du pain grillé » (some toast).
target_language_example: Je prends du pain grillé avec du beurre, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’ll have some toast with butter, please.

additional_notes: Used for the building where courts and judicial services are located (trials, hearings, some administrative/legal offices). Common in directions and official contexts: « au palais de justice », « devant le palais de justice ». Not necessarily a “palace” in the luxurious sense; it’s the standard term for a courthouse.
target_language_example: Je dois aller au palais de justice demain matin.
native_language_example: I have to go to the courthouse tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Commonly used in everyday situations (shopping, travel, at home). Often written with a hyphen: "papier-toilette". You may also hear the shorter "PQ" (informal).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, où sont les papiers toilette ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the toilet paper?

additional_notes: Used to say something happened unintentionally (the opposite of "exprès" / "délibérément"). In everyday French, you’ll often hear the more common variant "par inadvertance" (more formal) or simply "accidentellement". Also note: French more commonly says "par accident" than "sur accident" (which is not used).
target_language_example: J’ai supprimé le fichier par accident.
native_language_example: I deleted the file by accident.

additional_notes: Used to express motivation or reason: you do something because you love someone/something (not for money, duty, etc.). Often follows a verb phrase (e.g., faire quelque chose par amour).
target_language_example: Il a déménagé à Paris par amour.
native_language_example: He moved to Paris for love.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens before a particular moment. Very common in polite expressions like "merci par avance" (“thank you in advance”) in emails/messages. Also used with actions you do ahead of time: "prévenir par avance" (to warn in advance), "payer par avance" (to pay in advance).
target_language_example: Merci par avance pour votre réponse.
native_language_example: Thank you in advance for your reply.

meaning: in this kind of weather; in weather like this.
additional_notes: Used to comment on what is (or isn’t) suitable given the current weather conditions. Often followed by something you would/wouldn’t do (e.g., go out, walk, wear something). It can refer to the weather right now or generally “with weather like this.”
target_language_example: Par ce temps, je préfère rester à la maison.
native_language_example: In this kind of weather, I prefer to stay at home.

additional_notes: Used to talk about good luck or a fortunate coincidence. Often interchangeable with "heureusement" (luckily) or "par hasard" (by chance), but "par chance" tends to suggest the outcome was fortunate.
target_language_example: Par chance, j’ai trouvé mes clés.
native_language_example: Luckily, I found my keys.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast with what was just said. Very common in speech and informal writing. In more formal French, you may also see "en revanche" or "cependant."
target_language_example: Je n’aime pas le café ; par contre, j’adore le thé.
native_language_example: I don’t like coffee; however, I love tea.

additional_notes: Used to say you know something from memory and can recite it without looking (a poem, a lesson, a phone number, lyrics, etc.). Common with verbs like apprendre (to learn), savoir (to know), connaître (to know), and réciter (to recite): apprendre par cœur = learn by heart. Literally “by heart,” but it simply means “from memory.”
target_language_example: J’ai appris cette poésie par cœur.
native_language_example: I learned this poem by heart.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened unintentionally. Often comes after the verb: « J’ai envoyé le message par erreur. » You can also use it with « faire »: « J’ai fait ça par erreur. » Similar to « par accident » (also common).
target_language_example: J’ai supprimé le fichier par erreur.
native_language_example: I deleted the file by mistake.

additional_notes: Common abbreviation in writing (texts, notes, emails). In more formal writing you may see "p. ex." as well. When speaking, people usually say the full phrase "par exemple" rather than the abbreviation.
target_language_example: Tu peux venir mardi, par ex., ou mercredi.
native_language_example: You can come Tuesday, for example, or Wednesday.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an example or one item in a list. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence (Par exemple, ...) or after a statement (…, par exemple). Common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: On pourrait aller au cinéma, par exemple.
native_language_example: We could go to the movie theater, for example.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens randomly or without planning. Very common in questions to mean “by any chance…?”: « Par hasard, tu saurais… ? » or « Tu n’aurais pas…, par hasard ? » It can also mean “accidentally” when something was not done on purpose.
target_language_example: Par hasard, tu n'aurais pas son numéro ?
native_language_example: By any chance, you wouldn’t have his number?

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or location near the speaker, often when guiding someone or pointing something out. Common with imperatives like “Venez/Viens par ici” (Come here/this way) or as a standalone direction: “Par ici !” It can also mean “around here” in questions like “Il y a une pharmacie par ici ?”
target_language_example: Par ici, s’il vous plaît : la sortie est à gauche.
native_language_example: This way, please: the exit is on the left.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens after what was just mentioned. Common in storytelling, instructions, and formal writing. Often interchangeable with "ensuite" or "plus tard" depending on context.
target_language_example: Nous avons dîné, puis nous sommes allés au cinéma ; par la suite, nous sommes rentrés.
native_language_example: We had dinner, then we went to the movies; afterwards, we went home.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what was true or happened before, often in a general sense (not a specific date). Common with the imperfect or past tenses: « Par le passé, je travaillais… » / « Il a déjà fait ça par le passé. ». Slightly more formal than « avant » in some contexts.
target_language_example: Par le passé, cette rue était beaucoup plus calme.
native_language_example: In the past, this street was much quieter.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a general direction or area (not a precise point). Common in giving directions ("Par là !") and in approximations ("par là" = roughly/around that amount or time, often with "vers": "vers 8 h, par là"). It can also mean "by/through there" depending on context.
target_language_example: La gare ? C’est par là, au bout de la rue.
native_language_example: The train station? It’s that way, at the end of the street.

additional_notes: Means something happens intermittently (not all the time). Often used to describe feelings, symptoms, weather, or situations that come and go. Similar to "parfois," but "par moments" emphasizes that it happens in certain moments/periods. You can place it at the beginning or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Par moments, j’ai envie de tout arrêter.
native_language_example: At times, I feel like stopping everything.

additional_notes: Used to specify a price, limit, or amount for each individual (common in restaurants, hotels, events, travel). Often follows a number or price: « 20 € par personne », « deux verres par personne ».
target_language_example: Le dîner coûte 25 € par personne.
native_language_example: Dinner costs €25 per person.

additional_notes: Used when you’re strongly asking someone to stop, help, or agree out of compassion. Often sounds dramatic or urgent. Common with imperatives: « Arrête, par pitié ! » or « Aide-moi, par pitié. » You can also use it sarcastically in some contexts, but beginners should treat it as a serious plea.
target_language_example: Arrête, par pitié !
native_language_example: Stop, please!

additional_notes: Used to compare two things or to introduce a reference point/topic. Very common in French for comparisons ("X est grand par rapport à Y" = X is tall compared to Y) and for “regarding/with respect to” ("par rapport à ce sujet" = regarding this subject).
target_language_example: Par rapport à l’année dernière, les prix ont augmenté.
native_language_example: Compared to last year, prices have gone up.

meaning: as a result of; following (because of).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the cause of something, often in formal or written French (similar to « à cause de » but more formal). It is followed by a noun or noun phrase: « par suite de + nom ».
target_language_example: Par suite de la grève, le train a été annulé.
native_language_example: As a result of the strike, the train was cancelled.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened without warning or preparation. Often used with verbs like surprendre (to surprise), attaquer (to attack), arriver (to happen/arrive), or prendre (to take/catch). Common alternatives include "à l’improviste" (unexpectedly) and "par surprise" can also be used like "prendre quelqu’un par surprise" (to catch someone by surprise).
target_language_example: Ils nous ont attaqués par surprise.
native_language_example: They attacked us by surprise.

additional_notes: Often used after verbs to say something is on the ground or has fallen onto the ground: "être par terre" (to be lying on the ground), "tomber par terre" (to fall to the ground), "jeter par terre" (to throw/knock to the ground). Also used figuratively: "Je suis crevé(e), je suis par terre" = I'm exhausted (wiped out).
target_language_example: Mon téléphone est tombé par terre.
native_language_example: My phone fell on the ground.

meaning: by phone; on the phone (phone call).
additional_notes: Used to say something is done using the telephone. Common with verbs like appeler (to call), parler (to talk), contacter (to contact), réserver (to book). Often contrasts with en ligne (online) or en personne (in person).
target_language_example: Je vais te contacter par téléphone demain.
native_language_example: I’m going to contact you by phone tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to specify that something should be written down (an email, letter, form, message), often in formal or administrative contexts. Common with verbs like "confirmer" (to confirm), "envoyer" (to send), "demander" (to request), and "signaler" (to report).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me confirmer cela par écrit ?
native_language_example: Can you confirm that to me in writing?

additional_notes: Most often refers to position or movement above something (synonym of "au-dessus de"): "passer par-dessus le mur" = to go over the wall; "mettre un manteau par-dessus" = to put a coat on over (something you’re wearing). It can also mean "over there" in the sense of "across" or "on the other side" (often said with a gesture): "Là-bas, par-dessus". As a noun, "un par-dessus" can mean an overcoat (a coat worn over other clothes).
target_language_example: Il a mis une veste par-dessus son pull.
native_language_example: He put a jacket on over his sweater.

additional_notes: Used for places with rides and attractions (roller coasters, games, shows). Often said with an article: « un/le parc d'attractions » (plural is common when speaking generally).
target_language_example: On va au parc d'attractions ce week-end ?
native_language_example: Are we going to the amusement park this weekend?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a place with rides and entertainment. Often followed by a name (e.g., "un parc d'attractions Disney") or described with adjectives (e.g., "un grand parc d'attractions"). In everyday French, "parc d'attractions" is more common than the literal-sounding "parc d’amusement".
target_language_example: On va au parc d'attractions samedi avec les enfants.
native_language_example: We’re going to the amusement park on Saturday with the kids.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation or cause. In everyday speech it’s often shortened to "parce qu’" before a vowel sound: "parce qu’il…", "parce qu’on…". Answering a "Pourquoi ?" (Why?) question often starts with "Parce que…". Also common: "parce que" vs "car"—both can mean "because," but "parce que" is more common and can be used in more situations.
target_language_example: Je suis en retard parce que le bus n’est pas venu.
native_language_example: I’m late because the bus didn’t come.

additional_notes: Form of the verb "parler" + "de" to introduce the topic being discussed. It changes with the subject (je parle de…, tu parles de…, il/elle parle de…). With a pronoun, French often uses "en": "Il en parle" = "He talks about it."
target_language_example: Elle parle de son travail.
native_language_example: She talks about her job.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is talking at a speed that’s hard to follow. You can use it about yourself (often as an apology) or about someone else (as a complaint/request). Common requests: « Parlez moins vite, s’il vous plaît. » (Speak more slowly, please.) / « Tu parles trop vite. » (You speak too fast.)
target_language_example: Désolé, je parle trop vite ?
native_language_example: Sorry, am I speaking too fast?

meaning: to talk to; to speak to.
additional_notes: Used with an indirect object (a person/animal you are addressing). The person is introduced by "à" and usually replaced by an indirect object pronoun: me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur. Example: "Je lui parle" = "I’m talking to him/her." (Not to be confused with "parler de" = "to talk about".)
target_language_example: Je vais parler à mon professeur après le cours.
native_language_example: I’m going to talk to my teacher after class.

additional_notes: Standard polite question using inversion (verb + “-vous”). You can ask one person formally or a group. Often used with “Excusez-moi” to start a conversation: “Excusez-moi, parlez-vous français ?”
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, parlez-vous français ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you speak French?

meaning: a share (of the benefits/money); literally “a piece of cake.”
additional_notes: Often used figuratively to mean someone’s portion of profits, credit, or advantages (similar to English “a share of the pie”). Literally, it can also mean an actual slice/piece of cake. In the figurative sense, it’s common with verbs like « avoir », « vouloir », « prendre », « réclamer » (to have/want/take/claim a share).
target_language_example: Tout le monde veut sa part du gâteau.
native_language_example: Everyone wants their share of the pie.

additional_notes: Used to talk about organized political groups in elections and government. Often appears with a specific party name (e.g., un parti politique français) or with verbs like créer/rejoindre/voter pour (to create/join/vote for).
target_language_example: Elle a rejoint un parti politique l'année dernière.
native_language_example: She joined a political party last year.

meaning: "no" / "not any" (used before a noun in negatives).
additional_notes: Used in negative sentences before a noun to mean there isn’t any of something: ne … pas de + noun. After "pas", French typically uses "de" even where you might expect "du / de la / des" (e.g., "pas de pain" = no bread). In everyday speech, "ne" is often dropped: "J’ai pas de…".
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas de voiture.
native_language_example: I don’t have a car.

additional_notes: Common, friendly reply meaning it’s not an issue. Used after someone thanks you (like “you’re welcome”), or to reassure someone (“don’t worry about it”). Literally “no problem.”
target_language_example: — Merci beaucoup ! — Pas de problème.
native_language_example: — Thanks a lot! — No problem.

additional_notes: Used as a polite reply after someone says “merci.” Literally “not of what,” but in everyday French it means “don’t mention it” or “no problem.” Often said casually; you can also hear it as “Y a pas de quoi” or “Mais pas de quoi.”
target_language_example: — Merci pour ton aide ! — Pas de quoi.
native_language_example: — Thanks for your help! — You’re welcome.

meaning: “Not that / none of that.” (as in “don’t do/say that”).
additional_notes: Used to reject or stop something you don’t want (an excuse, an offer, a behavior, a topic), often with an implied “don’t start with that.” Commonly appears as “Pas de ça !” or with more context: “Pas de ça entre nous” (not between us), “Pas de ça ici/maintenant” (not here/now).
