In “Pas de ça !”, “ça” refers to what the other person just did/said.
target_language_example: Pas de ça ! On en parle plus tard.
native_language_example: Not that! We’ll talk about it later.

additional_notes: Common way to give a strong negative answer or to disagree politely. Often used in replies to yes/no questions: « Tu aimes ça ? — Pas du tout. » It can also reassure someone by negating a worry: « Tu es en retard ? — Pas du tout ! »
target_language_example: — Tu veux sortir ce soir ? — Pas du tout, je suis fatigué(e).
native_language_example: — Do you want to go out tonight? — Not at all, I’m tired.

additional_notes: Used to say something hasn’t happened up to now, but may happen later. Often answers a question (e.g., "Tu as fini ?" — "Pas encore.") or appears in a sentence with a verb ("Je n’ai pas encore mangé.").
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas encore fini.
native_language_example: I haven’t finished yet.

additional_notes: Very common. Literally means “not bad,” and is used to say something is pretty good or satisfactory (often in a modest/understated way): « C’est pas mal ! ». It can also mean “quite a lot/many” with quantities: « pas mal de … » = “quite a few/a lot of …”. In casual speech, « ne » is often dropped: « C’est pas mal » (instead of « Ce n’est pas mal »).
target_language_example: On a pas mal de travail aujourd’hui, mais ton idée est pas mal.
native_language_example: We have quite a lot of work today, but your idea is pretty good.

meaning: quite a few; a lot of.
additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean “a good number/amount of,” often with a positive or neutral tone. It can refer to countable things (pas mal de gens = quite a few people) or uncountable things (pas mal de temps = quite a bit of time). In speech, it’s often pronounced like “pa mal de.” Don’t confuse it with “pas mal” alone, which can mean “not bad.”
target_language_example: J’ai pas mal de travail cette semaine.
native_language_example: I have quite a lot of work this week.

meaning: quite a few things; a lot of things.
additional_notes: Common, informal-leaning way to say “many things” or “a fair amount.” Literally “not bad of things,” but it’s usually used to mean “quite a lot.” Often follows verbs like avoir/faire/apprendre/voir: « J’ai pas mal de choses à faire » (“I have quite a few things to do”).
target_language_example: J’ai pas mal de choses à faire aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I have quite a few things to do today.

additional_notes: Common in spoken French. Use it to say something isn’t the only thing: « Il n’y a pas que toi » (“It’s not just you / You’re not the only one”). It can also introduce a clarification in the pattern « C’est pas que + clause, mais… » meaning “It’s not that…, but…”. Often appears after « ne…pas » is dropped in speech (e.g., « c’est pas que… »).
target_language_example: Il n’y a pas que toi qui es fatigué.
native_language_example: It’s not just you who’s tired.

additional_notes: Used to strongly refuse something or say it’s not possible/acceptable. Often followed by "de" + infinitive: "Pas question de sortir" (No way we’re going out). Can also stand alone as a firm answer: "—Tu viens ? —Pas question."
target_language_example: Pas question de te laisser partir tout seul.
native_language_example: No way I’m letting you leave by yourself.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to slow down or not rush into something. Often said as an interjection to stop or moderate what someone is doing or deciding. You can also hear it when someone is speaking too quickly: "Pas si vite, je n’ai pas compris."
target_language_example: Pas si vite ! On va vérifier avant de signer.
native_language_example: Not so fast! We’ll check before signing.

additional_notes: A short, spoken warning meaning you must not touch something (often because it’s fragile, forbidden, or belongs to someone). Common in everyday speech; you can also hear it playfully (e.g., kids or friends). The full form is often "Pas touche !" or "Pas touche à + noun" (e.g., "Pas touche à mon téléphone !").
target_language_example: Pas touche à mon ordinateur !
native_language_example: Hands off my computer!

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something little by little, in stages, often carefully or following instructions. Common with verbs like expliquer (to explain), avancer (to move forward/progress), apprendre (to learn), or with guides/tutorials: un guide pas à pas. Can also describe something happening progressively: la situation évolue pas à pas.
target_language_example: On va le faire pas à pas.
native_language_example: We’re going to do it step by step.

additional_notes: Used to say something is barely acceptable, often with a slight tone of criticism: it’s not great, but you can tolerate it. Commonly said about a price, excuse, or behavior. Can also be used as a short reply: « Passe encore. »
target_language_example: D’accord, tu as oublié une fois, passe encore, mais pas deux fois.
native_language_example: Okay, you forgot once—that’s still acceptable, but not twice.

meaning: sleight of hand; a magic trick (sometimes: a sneaky trick/scam).
additional_notes: Used for quick hand movements used in magic to hide what’s really happening ("sleight of hand"). By extension, it can describe a shady maneuver or trick to deceive people (e.g., in business or politics). Often appears in phrases like "un tour de passe-passe" (a magic trick) or "des tours de passe-passe" (trickery).
target_language_example: Le magicien a fait un tour de passe-passe avec une pièce.
native_language_example: The magician did a sleight-of-hand trick with a coin.

additional_notes: A masculine noun meaning an activity you do for fun in your free time. Often used with the verb « avoir »: « J’ai un passe-temps » / « Quels sont tes passe-temps ? ». Written with a hyphen; plural: « des passe-temps » (often unchanged in writing).
target_language_example: La lecture est mon passe-temps préféré.
native_language_example: Reading is my favorite pastime.

additional_notes: Used when ordering goods or services (online, by phone, or in a store). Often followed by the thing ordered ("passer commande de..."), or used with "chez" for the supplier ("passer commande chez..."), or with "auprès de" (more formal) for the provider. Note: it does not mean “to pass a command.”
target_language_example: Je voudrais passer commande de deux pizzas, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like to place an order for two pizzas, please.

meaning: to pass in front of; to go ahead of (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used for physical movement: "passer devant quelqu’un/quelque chose" = to pass in front of someone/something. It can also mean moving ahead of someone in position (e.g., in a line), sometimes implying "cutting in" depending on context.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je peux passer devant ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I go ahead (in front)?

meaning: to go unnoticed; to slip by without being noticed.
additional_notes: Often used with the auxiliary être in the past tense: « il/elle est passé(e) inaperçu(e) ». The adjective « inaperçu » agrees with the subject: inaperçu (m. sg.), inaperçue (f. sg.), inaperçus (m. pl.), inaperçues (f. pl.). Common when talking about not attracting attention, not being detected, or something being missed.
target_language_example: Il est passé inaperçu dans la foule.
native_language_example: He went unnoticed in the crowd.

meaning: to spread the word; to pass the message along.
additional_notes: Used when you want someone to inform other people about something (news, instructions, an event, etc.). Often said as an imperative: « Passe le mot ! » You can also specify who to: « Passe le mot à tes amis. »
target_language_example: Tu peux passer le mot à tout le monde ?
native_language_example: Can you spread the word to everyone?

meaning: to pass the time; to kill time.
additional_notes: Used when you do something while waiting or to avoid being bored. Common with activities: « passer le temps à + infinitive » (e.g., « à lire »), or « passer le temps en + noun » (e.g., « en voiture »).
target_language_example: Pour passer le temps, j’écoute de la musique dans le train.
native_language_example: To pass the time, I listen to music on the train.

meaning: to cross someone’s mind; to occur to someone.
additional_notes: Usually used with an indirect object to say an idea never even occurred to someone: « Ça ne m’est jamais passé par la tête » (“It never crossed my mind”). Also common in questions: « Ça t’est déjà passé par la tête ? » (“Has it ever crossed your mind?”).
target_language_example: Ça ne m’est jamais passé par la tête de mentir.
native_language_example: It never crossed my mind to lie.

additional_notes: Used when you stop focusing on one thing and start doing or thinking about something else (a new topic, task, or situation). Common in conversation to suggest changing the subject or continuing after a problem: « On passe à autre chose ? »
target_language_example: Après cette dispute, j’ai décidé de passer à autre chose.
native_language_example: After that argument, I decided to move on.

additional_notes: Singular; often used in the plural: « des patins à glace » = ice skates. Used for the footwear with blades for skating on ice (as opposed to « patin à roulettes » for roller skates).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de patins à glace pour aller à la patinoire.
native_language_example: I need ice skates to go to the ice rink.

additional_notes: Highly offensive and confrontational (contains “con,” a vulgar insult). Used to insult someone directly (often shouted in anger). Avoid in polite conversation; you may hear it in arguments or in movies.
target_language_example: Arrête, pauvre con !
native_language_example: Stop it, you idiot!

additional_notes: Used in an exclamation, most often with a pronoun: « pauvre de moi ! » (poor me!), « pauvre de toi ! » (poor you!). It expresses sympathy or compassion (sometimes it can be said ironically, depending on tone). It’s not the normal way to state someone is poor financially (that’s usually « être pauvre »).
target_language_example: Pauvre de toi ! Tu as raté ton train.
native_language_example: Poor you! You missed your train.

meaning: to pay a lot; to pay dearly.
additional_notes: Used when something is expensive or costs more than expected. It can refer to money ("It was pricey") and sometimes, in a broader sense, to consequences ("to pay dearly for a mistake").
target_language_example: On a payé cher ces billets d’avion.
native_language_example: We paid a lot for those plane tickets.

additional_notes: Used in legal, political, and news contexts to talk about the punishment of executing someone for a crime. Often appears with verbs like "abolir" (to abolish), "rétablir" (to reinstate), or "être condamné à" (to be sentenced to).
target_language_example: Beaucoup de pays ont aboli la peine de mort.
native_language_example: Many countries have abolished the death penalty.

additional_notes: Used to show two actions happen at the same time. It’s followed by a clause with a verb (often in the present tense, but any tense is possible). For duration with a noun instead of a clause, use "pendant" alone: "pendant le film" (during the movie).
target_language_example: Je lis pendant que tu cuisines.
native_language_example: I read while you cook.

meaning: to think about (someone/something); to have an opinion of.
additional_notes: Used to ask for or give an opinion about something or someone. Very common in questions like « Qu’est-ce que tu penses de… ? » (“What do you think of…?”). Often followed by a noun or pronoun: « penser de ce film », « penser de lui/elle ». For “think about” in the sense of considering/remembering, French also often uses « penser à ».
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que tu penses de ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: What do you think of this restaurant?

meaning: to be thinking of doing; to intend/plan to do.
additional_notes: Used to express an intention or plan: « Je pense faire… » = “I’m thinking of doing…” / “I plan to…”. In the past (« je pensais faire… »), it often means you intended to do something (but it may or may not have happened). Not the same as « penser à faire » (“to remember to do” / “to think about doing”).
target_language_example: Je pense faire les courses après le travail.
native_language_example: I’m thinking of doing the grocery shopping after work.

meaning: to think about; to remember to (do something).
additional_notes: Used with a direct object (person/thing) to mean “think about”: Je pense à toi. Used with an infinitive to mean “remember to” or “think of doing”: Pense à fermer la porte. In the past tense, it often means “to remember”: J’ai pensé à t’appeler (I remembered to call you / I thought about calling you).
target_language_example: Pense à prendre ton passeport.
native_language_example: Remember to take your passport.

additional_notes: Used when someone passes out (often because of illness, heat, shock, etc.). In the past tense, it’s common as: « Il/Elle a perdu connaissance ». Related phrases: « reprendre connaissance » (to regain consciousness) and « s’évanouir » (to faint).
target_language_example: Il a perdu connaissance pendant quelques secondes.
native_language_example: He lost consciousness for a few seconds.

meaning: to lose sight of; (figuratively) to lose touch with.
additional_notes: Used when you can’t see someone/something anymore (e.g., in a crowd), or when you stop having contact with someone over time. Often used in the past: « J’ai perdu de vue… ». Also common with « ne pas perdre de vue » = “not to lose sight of / not to forget (keep in mind) ».
target_language_example: Dans la foule, j’ai perdu de vue mes amis.
native_language_example: In the crowd, I lost sight of my friends.

additional_notes: Used when an action is not useful or is taking longer than it should. Common in negatives and imperatives: « Je ne veux pas perdre du temps » (I don’t want to waste time), « Ne perds pas ton temps ! » (Don’t waste your time!). You can also use « perdre du temps à + infinitive »: « Il perd du temps à chercher ses clés. »
target_language_example: On perd du temps avec ces formulaires.
native_language_example: We’re wasting time with these forms.

additional_notes: Used to say you stop believing that something good will happen. Often followed by "de" + infinitive: "perdre espoir de réussir" (to lose hope of succeeding). You can also say "Ne perds pas espoir" to encourage someone (Don’t lose hope).
target_language_example: Je commence à perdre espoir, mais je vais continuer à essayer.
native_language_example: I’m starting to lose hope, but I’m going to keep trying.

meaning: to lose face; to be humiliated (lose respect).
additional_notes: Used when someone loses dignity, status, or others’ respect—often in public or in front of others. Common in situations involving embarrassment, shame, or saving one’s reputation (e.g., "sans perdre la face" = "without losing face").
target_language_example: Il ne veut pas admettre son erreur, parce qu’il a peur de perdre la face.
native_language_example: He doesn’t want to admit his mistake because he’s afraid of losing face.

meaning: to lose your head (panic / lose control); also: to go crazy about someone.
additional_notes: Used when someone panics, acts irrationally, or loses self-control. It can also mean becoming infatuated with someone ("Il a perdu la tête pour elle" = "He’s crazy about her"). Often used as an imperative: "Ne perds pas la tête !" (Don’t panic!).
target_language_example: Ne perds pas la tête, tout va s’arranger.
native_language_example: Don’t panic, everything will work out.

meaning: to lose one’s life; to die (often in an accident or conflict).
additional_notes: A formal/serious expression used in news reports or official contexts to say someone died, often emphasizing the circumstances (accident, disaster, war). It conjugates like perdre: "il/elle a perdu la vie" (he/she died), "ils/elles ont perdu la vie" (they died).
target_language_example: Deux personnes ont perdu la vie dans l’accident.
native_language_example: Two people lost their lives in the accident.

meaning: to lose control; to panic; to lose it.
additional_notes: Common idiom meaning you’re no longer thinking clearly or staying in control of a situation (emotionally or practically). Often used about stress, fear, or being overwhelmed. Literally “to lose the pedals” (like on a bike), but it’s not used that way in normal conversation.
target_language_example: Quand j’ai vu la foule, j’ai perdu les pédales et je suis parti.
native_language_example: When I saw the crowd, I panicked and left.

additional_notes: Means to stop being patient (to get annoyed or fed up). It’s very commonly said as « perdre sa patience » (literally “to lose one’s patience”). Often used with « finir par » (to end up) or « ne pas » in the negative: « Je ne perds pas patience. »
target_language_example: Au bout d’une heure, il a perdu patience et il est parti.
native_language_example: After an hour, he lost patience and left.

meaning: to get lost; to lose one’s way.
additional_notes: Used when someone can’t find the right route or direction (literally while traveling, or sometimes figuratively in life). In the literal sense, it’s common with the past tense: « Je me suis perdu(e) » (I got lost) or « On a perdu notre chemin » (We got lost).
target_language_example: On a perdu notre chemin en allant à la gare.
native_language_example: We got lost on the way to the train station.

additional_notes: Used when you feel an activity is useless or not worth doing. The verb is conjugated (je perds, tu perds, il/elle perd, nous perdons, etc.) and the possessive changes with the subject: perdre mon/ton/son/notre/votre/leur temps. Often used with “à” + infinitive: “perdre son temps à faire quelque chose” (to waste time doing something).
target_language_example: Tu perds ton temps à attendre ici.
native_language_example: You’re wasting your time waiting here.

additional_notes: Used for the official document that allows you to drive. Common in practical situations (police check, car rental, administrative forms). Often appears with possessives or articles: « mon/ton/son permis de conduire », « le permis de conduire ».
target_language_example: J’ai oublié mon permis de conduire à la maison.
native_language_example: I forgot my driver’s license at home.

meaning: an elderly person; an older adult.
additional_notes: Polite, neutral term for an older person, often used in public services, healthcare, and everyday conversation. The adjective agrees in gender/number: une personne âgée (feminine), des personnes âgées (plural). Also commonly used as a noun phrase (e.g., aider les personnes âgées = to help elderly people).
target_language_example: Cette association aide les personnes âgées à faire leurs courses.
native_language_example: This organization helps elderly people do their grocery shopping.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not worth doing because it won’t bring results or is unnecessary. Often appears with verbs like être (C’est une perte de temps), trouver (Je trouve ça une perte de temps), or with a possessive (Quelle perte de temps !).
target_language_example: Faire la queue pendant deux heures, c’est une perte de temps.
native_language_example: Waiting in line for two hours is a waste of time.

additional_notes: Literally “little friend,” but it means a romantic partner (male). Feminine: "petite amie" (girlfriend). Often used with possessives (mon/ton/son petit ami) or with "avoir" (J’ai un petit ami).
target_language_example: Elle a un petit ami depuis six mois.
native_language_example: She’s had a boyfriend for six months.

additional_notes: Common euphemism meaning “the toilet/restroom,” especially when you want to sound discreet or polite. You’ll often hear it in the phrase « aller au petit coin » (“to go to the bathroom”). It literally means “little corner,” but it’s used idiomatically to refer to the restroom.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je vais au petit coin.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I’m going to the bathroom.

meaning: boyfriend (often: a young or casual boyfriend).
additional_notes: Common, everyday term for a male romantic partner. Often used by teens/young adults, and can sound a bit "cute" or informal compared with "mon copain" (my boyfriend/partner). In adult contexts, people may prefer "mon copain" or "mon compagnon". Literally "little buddy," but it’s understood as "boyfriend" in context.
target_language_example: Elle a un petit copain depuis deux mois.
native_language_example: She’s had a boyfriend for two months.

additional_notes: Literally “small finger.” You’ll often hear it in the expression « Mon petit doigt m’a dit… » meaning “A little bird told me…” (I heard it from someone, but I won’t say who).
target_language_example: Je me suis coupé le petit doigt.
native_language_example: I cut my little finger.

additional_notes: Literally “small lunch,” but it means the morning meal (breakfast). It’s used as a noun: “le petit déjeuner” (the breakfast) or “prendre le petit déjeuner” (to have breakfast). Also used for “breakfast included” in hotels: “petit déjeuner inclus.”
target_language_example: On prend le petit déjeuner à 8 h.
native_language_example: We have breakfast at 8 a.m.

meaning: small bread roll; small loaf of bread.
additional_notes: Common in bakeries and at breakfast. In many places you’ll more often hear specific names like « un petit pain au chocolat » (a chocolate pastry) or « un pain au lait » (a soft milk roll), and « petit pain » can be a general way to refer to a small bread roll depending on the region.
target_language_example: Je vais acheter des petits pains pour le petit-déjeuner.
native_language_example: I’m going to buy some bread rolls for breakfast.

additional_notes: Usually used in the plural: « des petits pois » = (some) peas. Common in food contexts (as a side dish, in salads, with carrots: « petits pois et carottes »). Literally “little pea,” but it means “pea,” not “small bean.”
target_language_example: Je prends du poulet avec des petits pois.
native_language_example: I’ll have chicken with peas.

additional_notes: Common way to describe something happening slowly over time, step by step. Often used with verbs like avancer (to make progress), apprendre (to learn), s’habituer à (to get used to), and changer (to change). It can appear at the beginning or end of a sentence: Petit à petit, … / …, petit à petit.
target_language_example: Petit à petit, je m’habitue à la vie en France.
native_language_example: Little by little, I’m getting used to life in France.

additional_notes: The everyday word for the morning meal. Often used with "prendre" (to have/eat): "prendre le petit-déjeuner". You’ll also see the shorter form "petit dej" in casual writing/speech. The hyphen is common in the standard spelling: "petit-déjeuner".
target_language_example: Je prends mon petit-déjeuner à 7 h.
native_language_example: I have breakfast at 7 a.m.

additional_notes: Means a son’s or daughter’s child. The plural is "petits-enfants". Don’t confuse it with "petit enfant" (without hyphen), which can mean “a small/young child” in general; "petit-enfant" specifically means “grandchild.”
target_language_example: J’ai deux petits-enfants.
native_language_example: I have two grandchildren.

additional_notes: Means “son of one’s son or daughter.” Feminine form: "petite-fille" (granddaughter). Note the hyphen; plural: "petits-fils". Often used with possessives: "mon/ton/son petit-fils".
target_language_example: Mon petit-fils a cinq ans.
native_language_example: My grandson is five years old.

additional_notes: Literally “little friend,” but it means a girlfriend. Used for a female partner; for a male partner, say “petit ami.” You can use it both for a serious relationship or more generally for “my girlfriend.” Often said with a possessive: “ma petite amie.”
target_language_example: Je te présente ma petite amie, Claire.
native_language_example: Let me introduce you to my girlfriend, Claire.

additional_notes: Used to mean someone’s girlfriend. Literally “little girlfriend,” but in practice it’s just a common way to say “girlfriend,” sometimes with an affectionate tone or implying she’s young. For “my girlfriend,” you’ll usually say: « ma copine » (or « ma petite copine »).
target_language_example: C’est ma petite copine, Julie.
native_language_example: This is my girlfriend, Julie.

additional_notes: Most commonly used for a teaspoon (for stirring coffee/tea or measuring small amounts). Often appears in kitchen/cooking contexts (e.g., in recipes) and in cafés/restaurants. The literal idea is “small spoon,” and it’s also used to contrast with "grande cuillère" (tablespoon/large spoon).
target_language_example: Je prends une petite cuillère de sucre dans mon café.
native_language_example: I take a teaspoon of sugar in my coffee.

meaning: little mouse; also (with “la”) the Tooth Fairy.
additional_notes: Literally means “little mouse.” In French-speaking cultures, “la petite souris” is the character who takes a lost tooth from under a child’s pillow and leaves money (similar to the English “the Tooth Fairy”). Often used with the definite article: “la petite souris.”
target_language_example: Cette nuit, la petite souris va passer si tu mets ta dent sous l’oreiller.
native_language_example: Tonight, the Tooth Fairy will come if you put your tooth under the pillow.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a female sibling who is younger than you. In French, "petit/petite" often means "younger" with family members (not only physically small). You can also say "ma petite sœur" (my younger sister).
target_language_example: Ma petite sœur a dix ans.
native_language_example: My little (younger) sister is ten years old.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “granddaughter.” It can also mean “young girl,” but that meaning is less common and depends on context. Literally “little girl,” and the masculine equivalent is “petit-fils” (grandson).
target_language_example: Ma petite-fille a six ans.
native_language_example: My granddaughter is six years old.

additional_notes: Literally “little people,” but it usually refers to humble/poor or lower-status people (often as seen from an upper-class viewpoint). It can sound condescending depending on context, so use carefully. Often used with an article: « les petites gens ».
target_language_example: Il se dit proche des petites gens.
native_language_example: He says he’s close to ordinary people.

additional_notes: Used to say something is unimportant or that any option is fine. Often followed by a clause: "peu importe + (ce que / qui / où / quand / comment)" = “no matter what/who/where/when/how.” Also commonly used alone as a full reply meaning “whatever / I don’t mind.”
target_language_example: Peu importe où on va, je veux juste sortir un peu.
native_language_example: No matter where we go, I just want to get out a bit.

meaning: to matter little; to be unimportant (often: “it doesn’t matter”).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as the set phrase « Peu importe » (“It doesn’t matter / No matter”). You can follow it with a clause or question word: « Peu importe où/quand/comment… » = “No matter where/when/how…”. Note: « importer » here means “to matter,” not “to import” (false friend).
target_language_example: Peu importe où tu habites, je viendrai.
native_language_example: No matter where you live, I’ll come.

additional_notes: Used to describe a change or progress happening slowly over time. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence. Common near-synonyms: « petit à petit », « progressivement ».
target_language_example: Peu à peu, je comprends mieux le français.
native_language_example: Little by little, I understand French better.

additional_notes: Mostly used in religious or historical contexts, especially to refer to the Israelites/Jewish people as “God’s chosen people” (le peuple élu de Dieu). Can also be used more broadly or ironically to mean a group that sees itself as specially chosen or superior. "Élu" here means “chosen,” not “elected” (as in politics).
target_language_example: Dans la Bible, Israël est souvent présenté comme le peuple élu de Dieu.
native_language_example: In the Bible, Israel is often presented as God’s chosen people.

additional_notes: Fixed idiom meaning very strong fear (stronger than just "peur"). Often used with verbs like "avoir" or "prendre" (e.g., "avoir une peur bleue" = to be terrified). Not a literal "blue fear" in English.
target_language_example: J’ai eu une peur bleue quand j’ai entendu ce bruit.
native_language_example: I was terrified when I heard that noise.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It can be used alone as a short answer (Peut-être.) or placed in a sentence (Il viendra peut-être.). As an adverb, it often comes after the verb or at the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Je viendrai peut-être demain.
native_language_example: Maybe I'll come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about valuable minerals used in jewelry (e.g., diamond, ruby, emerald). Often appears in the plural: « des pierres précieuses ». Note the agreement: « précieux » → « précieuse » because « pierre » is feminine.
target_language_example: Cette bague est décorée de pierres précieuses.
native_language_example: This ring is decorated with precious stones (gemstones).

additional_notes: Used when tossing a coin to choose between two options (like flipping a coin). Literally “pile or face,” referring to the two sides of a coin; in everyday English you say “heads or tails,” so it’s not usually translated word-for-word.
target_language_example: On n’arrive pas à décider, alors on fait pile ou face.
native_language_example: We can’t decide, so we’ll flip a coin.

additional_notes: A very common noun for an outdoor meal (often in a park or countryside). Used with the verb "faire" (to have/do): "faire un pique-nique" = "to have a picnic". Also commonly used as "un pique-nique" (a picnic) or "un déjeuner pique-nique" (a picnic lunch).
target_language_example: On va faire un pique-nique au parc dimanche.
native_language_example: We’re going to have a picnic in the park on Sunday.

meaning: to have a picnic; to picnic.
additional_notes: Verb used for eating outdoors (often in a park or countryside). Usually used with "aller" (to go) or "faire" in the noun form: "aller pique-niquer" = to go have a picnic; "faire un pique-nique" = to have a picnic. Conjugates like a regular -er verb: je pique-nique, nous pique-niquons.
target_language_example: On va pique-niquer au parc dimanche.
native_language_example: We’re going to have a picnic in the park on Sunday.

meaning: to have a tantrum; to throw a fit.
additional_notes: Commonly used for suddenly getting very angry or upset (often in an exaggerated way). You can use it for children or adults. Synonyms include "faire une crise" (more neutral) and "faire une scène" (make a scene).
target_language_example: Il a piqué une crise quand on lui a dit non.
native_language_example: He threw a fit when he was told no.

additional_notes: Used when someone asks you to show official identification (e.g., passport, national ID card, residence permit, driver’s license depending on the context). Common in travel, hotels, banks, and age checks. Often said as: « Vous avez une pièce d’identité ? » or « Je dois vérifier votre pièce d’identité. »
target_language_example: Vous pouvez me montrer une pièce d’identité, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you show me an ID, please?

additional_notes: Used for a physical coin (not a banknote/bill). Often heard in shops or vending situations: « Vous avez de la monnaie ? » (Do you have any change?) and « en pièces » (in coins). You can also say « une pièce » when context makes it clear it’s a coin.
target_language_example: J’ai une pièce de monnaie de deux euros.
native_language_example: I have a two-euro coin.

additional_notes: Used for a theatrical play as a work that is performed on stage (not a movie). You’ll often see it with verbs like voir/aller voir (to see), jouer (to perform), and in contexts like au théâtre (at the theater).
target_language_example: On va voir une pièce de théâtre ce soir.
native_language_example: We’re going to see a play tonight.

additional_notes: A very polite, somewhat formal way to say you didn’t hear or understand. Literally it comes from "plaire" (to please), but in modern French it functions like "Sorry?" or "Come again?" Often used as a question after someone speaks: "Plaît-il ?"
target_language_example: — Je vous ai dit de venir à huit heures. — Plaît-il ?
native_language_example: — I told you to come at eight o’clock. — Pardon?

additional_notes: Used when you didn’t hear or didn’t understand someone. It’s quite formal and can sound old-fashioned; in everyday speech people more often say “Pardon ?”, “Comment ?”, or “Vous pouvez répéter ?”. Written with a hyphen; the verb is from “plaire” (to please), as in “S’il vous plaît ?”.
target_language_example:
— Je n’ai pas compris… Plaît-il ?
— Je disais que le train est en retard.
native_language_example:
— I didn’t understand… Pardon?
— I said the train is late.

additional_notes: Common noun phrase used to talk about the moon’s phase. Often appears with the article: "la pleine lune" (the full moon), or in expressions like "à la pleine lune" (at/during the full moon). Also used in "nuit de pleine lune" (a full-moon night).
target_language_example: On sortira se promener à la pleine lune.
native_language_example: We’ll go out for a walk during the full moon.

meaning: to rain really hard; to pour (with rain).
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression meaning it’s raining very heavily (similar to “it’s raining cats and dogs”). Used with an impersonal subject: « Il pleut des cordes. » You can also change tense: « Il pleuvait des cordes hier. »
target_language_example: Prends un parapluie : il pleut des cordes !
native_language_example: Take an umbrella: it’s pouring (with rain)!

meaning: to pour down (rain); to rain very heavily.
additional_notes: Used to describe very heavy rain (like “it’s pouring” / “it’s raining cats and dogs”). Impersonal verb: you normally say “Il pleut à verse” (not *je pleus*). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Prends un parapluie : il pleut à verse !
native_language_example: Take an umbrella: it’s pouring down!

additional_notes: Used after a negative marker (usually "ne... plus") with "avoir besoin" to say you don’t need something anymore: "Je n’ai plus besoin de...". It can also appear in short answers like "Plus besoin" meaning "No need anymore." Note: without "ne", "plus" is often pronounced [ply] and means "more"; in "ne... plus" it usually means "no more/not anymore" (often pronounced [ply]).
target_language_example: Je n’ai plus besoin de ton aide.
native_language_example: I don’t need your help anymore.

additional_notes: Used with a noun or an infinitive to say something is no longer necessary. It’s often part of the structure: "Je n’ai plus besoin de + noun/infinitive" (I don’t need + anymore). Note the negative "ne ... plus" around the verb: "Je n’ai plus ..."; in casual speech, "ne" is often dropped: "J’ai plus besoin de..." (informal).
target_language_example: Je n’ai plus besoin de ton aide.
native_language_example: I don’t need your help anymore.

additional_notes: Used before a noun or a number to express an increase in quantity or a comparison: "plus de + nom" (more of something) or "plus de + nombre" (more than a number). Example patterns: "plus de temps" = more time; "plus de 20 euros" = more than 20 euros. In negative sentences with "ne… plus de", it means "no more / not any more" (e.g., "Je n’ai plus de pain" = I don’t have any bread left).
target_language_example: Il y a plus de vingt personnes dans la salle.
native_language_example: There are more than twenty people in the room.

additional_notes: Used to intensify what was just said ("and even more" / "what’s more"). Often follows a quantity or comparison to emphasize an increase: "de plus en plus, plus encore". It can also introduce an extra point: "et plus encore" = "and more besides".
target_language_example: J’aime ce film, et j’aime encore plus la musique, plus encore que l’histoire.
native_language_example: I like this movie, and I like the music even more—more than the story.

additional_notes: Used to show approximation (numbers, time, quantities) or uncertainty: "Il est arrivé vers 8 h, plus ou moins" (“around 8, give or take”). It can also mean “so-so / not great” when answering how things are: "Ça va, plus ou moins". Often placed after what it qualifies.
target_language_example: On est arrivés à 20 h, plus ou moins.
native_language_example: We arrived around 8 p.m., more or less.

additional_notes: Means that there is nobody left or nobody present. Often used in the negative: “Il n’y a plus personne” = “There’s no one left.” In everyday speech, “ne” is frequently dropped: “Y a plus personne.” Here, “plus” is usually pronounced with a silent “s” ([ply]) because it means “no more,” not “more.”
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il n’y avait plus personne.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there was nobody left.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities or degrees: plus que + number (plus que dix = more than ten) or plus que + noun/pronoun (plus que moi = more than me). It’s also used in comparisons with adjectives/adverbs: plus ... que (Elle est plus grande que lui. = She is taller than him). In negative comparisons, French often uses moins ... que (less ... than) rather than *pas plus ... que*.
target_language_example: J’ai plus que dix euros.
native_language_example: I have more than ten euros.

meaning: more than ever; now more than ever.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is especially true or important at the present moment, even more than at any time before. Often paired with verbs like "avoir besoin" (to need), "être" (to be), or "falloir" (to be necessary): « On a plus que jamais besoin de… ».
target_language_example: Avec les changements climatiques, il est plus que jamais important d’économiser l’eau.
native_language_example: With climate change, it’s more important than ever to save water.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a time after now. Common in future contexts (Je le ferai plus tard. = I’ll do it later.) and in farewells (À plus tard ! = See you later!). Often shortened in speech to “À plus !” (informal).
target_language_example: Je te rappelle plus tard.
native_language_example: I’ll call you back later.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened more than once (often 2–several). It can go at the beginning or end of a sentence. Note: "fois" (time/occasion) is usually used with numbers and quantities (une fois, deux fois, plusieurs fois).
target_language_example: Je l’ai vu plusieurs fois cette semaine.
native_language_example: I saw him several times this week.

meaning: “I’d rather die” (strong way to say you absolutely refuse).
additional_notes: Used to express a very strong preference or refusal, often dramatically or humorously. Typically appears as “plutôt mourir !” or in a longer phrase like “Je préférerais/plutôt mourir que + infinitive” (“I’d rather die than…”). Not meant literally in most everyday contexts, but it’s intense, so use with care.
target_language_example: Plutôt mourir que de lui demander de l’aide !
native_language_example: I’d rather die than ask him for help!

additional_notes: Common in greetings and formal introductions. Often used with verbs like « serrer la main » (to shake hands) or « donner une poignée de main » (to give a handshake). Plural: « des poignées de main ».
target_language_example: On s’est salués avec une poignée de main.
native_language_example: We greeted each other with a handshake.

meaning: a common point; something in common.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a shared feature, interest, or similarity between people or things. Often appears in the structure «avoir un point commun» (to have something in common) or «le point commun entre X et Y» (the common point between X and Y).
target_language_example: On a un point commun : on adore voyager.
native_language_example: We have something in common: we love traveling.

additional_notes: Used for the place where a trip begins, or more broadly the basis/starting point for a discussion, plan, or analysis. Often followed by "de" + noun (e.g., "le point de départ de notre projet").
target_language_example: Quel est le point de départ de la randonnée ?
native_language_example: What is the starting point of the hike?

meaning: a stitch (a suture) used to close a wound.
additional_notes: Used in medical contexts after an injury or surgery. You’ll often hear it in the plural: « des points de suture » (“stitches”). Common related phrases: « faire des points de suture » (to put in stitches), « enlever/retirer les points de suture » (to remove stitches).
target_language_example: J’ai dû avoir trois points de suture après la coupure.
native_language_example: I had to get three stitches after the cut.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s perspective or opinion. Often appears in set phrases like « du point de vue de… » (from the point of view of…), « à mon point de vue » is less common—prefer « à mon avis » for “in my opinion.” Can also mean a physical “viewpoint” (a spot you look from) in contexts like photography or scenery.
target_language_example: De mon point de vue, c’est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: From my point of view, it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a person’s weakness or a vulnerable/less successful aspect of something (a plan, argument, product, etc.). Common in phrases like « mon point faible, c’est… » (“my weakness is…”) and « le point faible de + noun » (“the weak point of…”). Often contrasts with « point fort » (“strong point”).
target_language_example: Mon point faible, c’est le chocolat.
native_language_example: My weakness is chocolate.

meaning: period (full stop); final point/end of the discussion.
additional_notes: Literally “final point.” In writing/punctuation, it refers to the period/full stop at the end of a sentence (more formally: « point » or « point final »). In conversation or argument, « point final » can mean the last word on the matter, like “that’s final” or “end of discussion,” often used for emphasis: « Et point final ! »
target_language_example: C’est comme ça, point final.
native_language_example: That’s how it is, end of discussion.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an advantage or what someone/something is best at (a strength), or the main highlight of an event or place. Often appears as “un point fort” (a strong point) or in the plural “des points forts” (strengths). In a CV/interview context, it means “strength.”
target_language_example: Mon point fort, c’est la communication.
native_language_example: My strong point is communication.

additional_notes: Often used in the expression « sur la pointe des pieds » (or « à la pointe des pieds ») meaning “on tiptoe,” especially when trying to be quiet. Literally it refers to the tips/balls of the feet rather than the whole foot.
target_language_example: Il est entré sur la pointe des pieds pour ne pas réveiller le bébé.
native_language_example: He came in on tiptoe so as not to wake the baby.

additional_notes: Used mainly in cooking (soups, salads, couscous, hummus). In everyday French you’ll often see the plural: « des pois chiches ». Pronunciation: /pwa ʃiʃ/.
target_language_example: Je vais faire du houmous avec des pois chiches.
native_language_example: I’m going to make hummus with chickpeas.

additional_notes: Literally “red fish.” Used for the common pet fish; it can also refer to the fish in a bowl/pond in general. It’s masculine: un/le poisson rouge; plural: des/les poissons rouges.
target_language_example: J’ai un poisson rouge dans un bocal.
native_language_example: I have a goldfish in a bowl.

additional_notes: A very common food word. Literally “apple of the earth/ground,” but it simply means “potato.” It’s feminine: une pomme de terre; plural: des pommes de terre. Often used in everyday contexts like shopping, cooking, and ordering food.
target_language_example: Je vais acheter des pommes de terre pour faire des frites.
native_language_example: I’m going to buy potatoes to make fries.

additional_notes: Common in everyday French (also written "popcorn"). Usually masculine: "le pop-corn". Often used with "un paquet de" (a bag of) or "un bol de" (a bowl of), especially at the movies.
target_language_example: On prend un grand pop-corn pour le film ?
native_language_example: Shall we get a large popcorn for the movie?

additional_notes: Literally “entry door.” Most often refers to the main door to a house or building. In other contexts, it can mean an “entry point” (e.g., a gateway to a market), but beginners will mostly see it as a physical door.
target_language_example: La porte d'entrée est fermée à clé.
native_language_example: The front door is locked.

meaning: a lucky charm (something that brings good luck).
additional_notes: Used for an object (or sometimes a person) believed to bring good luck. Often with an article: « un porte-bonheur ». Can be hyphenated (« porte-bonheur ») and is invariable in the first part; plural is usually « des porte-bonheur » (often left unchanged in writing).
target_language_example: J’ai toujours un petit porte-bonheur dans mon sac.
native_language_example: I always have a little lucky charm in my bag.

additional_notes: A small case used to carry money (especially coins) and sometimes cards. In everyday French, many people use it like “wallet,” but it can also mean a smaller “coin purse.” It’s a masculine noun: un porte-monnaie. Plural: des porte-monnaie (often invariable in writing).
target_language_example: J’ai oublié mon porte-monnaie à la maison.
native_language_example: I forgot my wallet at home.

meaning: to bring bad luck; to be unlucky.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is considered a bad omen or will cause bad luck. Often said with superstition (e.g., certain actions, objects, or events). You can use it impersonally with “Ça porte malheur de …” (“It’s bad luck to …”).
target_language_example: Ça porte malheur de passer sous une échelle.
native_language_example: It’s bad luck to walk under a ladder.

meaning: to file a complaint (especially to the police); to press charges.
additional_notes: Commonly used in legal/police contexts when someone officially reports an offense. You can specify where: « porter plainte à la police/au commissariat » or against someone: « porter plainte contre quelqu’un ».
target_language_example: Elle a porté plainte contre son voisin après le vol.
native_language_example: She filed a complaint against her neighbor after the theft.

meaning: to pay off; to bear fruit (to produce results).
additional_notes: Used to say that an effort, plan, or investment has finally produced positive results. Often refers to work that takes time: studies, training, a project, etc. You can also use it in the past: « a porté ses fruits » (paid off).
target_language_example: Ses efforts ont fini par porter leurs fruits.
native_language_example: His efforts finally paid off.

additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used to say someone looks exactly like someone else, often in the pattern: « C’est le portrait craché de + person » or « Elle est le portrait craché de sa mère ». It’s a set phrase (not literally “spit portrait”), and it’s common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: C’est le portrait craché de son père.
native_language_example: He’s the spitting image of his father.

meaning: to stand people up (not show up to an appointment).
additional_notes: More commonly used as "poser un lapin à quelqu’un". It means you agree to meet someone and then don’t come, leaving them waiting. Informal, idiomatic expression; the literal words (“to put down rabbits”) don’t help with the meaning.
target_language_example: Il m’a posé un lapin : il n’est jamais venu au rendez-vous.
native_language_example: He stood me up: he never came to the meeting.

meaning: to be a problem; to cause difficulty.
additional_notes: Used when something creates an issue or complication. Often used with an inanimate subject: « Ça pose problème » (“That’s a problem”). Very common in the negative: « Ça ne pose pas de problème » (“No problem / That’s fine”). Can also take an indirect object: « Ça me pose problème » (“That’s a problem for me / I have an issue with that”).
target_language_example: Ça pose problème si on n’a pas les bonnes informations.
native_language_example: It’s a problem if we don’t have the right information.

meaning: to stand someone up (not show up to a planned meeting/date).
additional_notes: Informal idiom. Used when someone doesn’t come to an appointment, meeting, or date without warning. Often said with an indirect object: « poser un lapin à quelqu’un » (to stand someone up).
target_language_example: Il m’a posé un lapin : il n’est jamais venu au rendez-vous.
native_language_example: He stood me up: he never came to the meeting/date.

additional_notes: An adjective used in medical/psychology contexts to describe symptoms or stress that happen after a traumatic event. It agrees with the noun it describes: masculine/feminine is the same form (post-traumatique), plural adds -s (post-traumatiques). Common collocation: « trouble de stress post-traumatique » (PTSD).
target_language_example: Après l’accident, il a souffert de stress post-traumatique.
native_language_example: After the accident, he suffered from post-traumatic stress.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a local police station or police post. You can say "au poste de police" (at the police station) or "aller au poste de police" (to go to the police station).
target_language_example: Je dois aller au poste de police pour déclarer un vol.
native_language_example: I have to go to the police station to report a theft.

additional_notes: Used for money (or a gift) given illegally to influence a decision, often in business or politics. It’s a common, standard term (not slang). You’ll often see it with verbs like « donner » (to give) or « accepter » (to accept): « donner un pot-de-vin », « accepter des pots-de-vin ».
target_language_example: Il a été arrêté pour avoir accepté un pot-de-vin.
native_language_example: He was arrested for having accepted a bribe.

additional_notes: Informal, mildly insulting term for someone who’s scared or won’t take a risk. Often used with "être" ("Il est une poule mouillée") or as a direct insult ("Espèce de poule mouillée !"). It literally means “wet hen,” but that’s not how you translate it in English.
target_language_example: Allez, viens ! Ne fais pas ta poule mouillée.
native_language_example: Come on, come! Don’t be a chicken.

meaning: so to speak; as it were.
additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify what you just said, suggesting it’s an approximate or figurative way of speaking. Often set off by commas in writing and placed after the phrase it comments on.
target_language_example: C’est mon bureau, pour ainsi dire.
native_language_example: It’s my office, so to speak.

meaning: "however" / "that doesn't mean that"; or "for that much" (as much as that).
additional_notes: Most often used after a negative to add a contrast or limitation: "ne ... pas pour autant" = "not ... for all that / not ... however" (i.e., it doesn’t change the conclusion). It can also mean "for that much" in comparisons about quantity (less common for beginners).
target_language_example: Il est fatigué, mais il n’arrête pas pour autant.
native_language_example: He’s tired, but that doesn’t mean he stops.

meaning: "as long as / provided that"; also "as far as" (in fixed phrases).
additional_notes: Used to set a condition, similar to « à condition que ». In that conditional meaning, it’s often followed by the subjunctive: « pour autant que tu sois… ». It can also appear in the common expression « pour autant que je sache » = “as far as I know.”
target_language_example: Tu peux venir, pour autant que tu préviennes à l’avance.
native_language_example: You can come, as long as you let me know in advance.

additional_notes: Used to show that what you’re saying is true to the best of your knowledge, but you’re not 100% sure. Common in conversation and writing; it can soften a statement or correct someone politely.
target_language_example: Pour autant que je sache, le magasin ouvre à 9 h.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the store opens at 9 a.m.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something, often in a formal or written style (administration, notices). It is followed by a noun phrase (e.g., pour cause de maladie). For a full clause with a verb, you usually use "parce que" (because).
target_language_example: Le train est annulé pour cause de grève.
native_language_example: The train is canceled due to a strike.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the first point in a sequence or the first step in an explanation (similar to “to begin with”). Common in speech and writing. Often followed by a comma: “Pour commencer, …”.
target_language_example: Pour commencer, je vais me présenter.
native_language_example: To start, I’m going to introduce myself.

additional_notes: Used to say something is final or genuine, often about stopping/ending something: « C’est fini pour de bon » (it’s over for good), « arrêter pour de bon » (to quit for good). It can also mean “seriously/for real” in questions: « Tu pars pour de bon ? » (Are you really leaving? / Are you leaving for good?).
target_language_example: Cette fois, j’arrête de fumer pour de bon.
native_language_example: This time, I’m quitting smoking for good.

additional_notes: Common in spoken French to confirm something is true or to show you’re not joking. Often used as a short question: « Pour de vrai ? » = « Really? ». Can also be used in a sentence: « C’est pour de vrai » = « It’s real / It’s serious ».
target_language_example: Pour de vrai ? Tu as déjà fini ?
native_language_example: For real? You’ve already finished?

meaning: "to make a long story short" / "in short".
additional_notes: Used to signal you’re about to summarize or skip details and give the short version. Often appears mid-sentence after a pause or comma: « …, pour faire court, … ». Also common with « bref » or « enfin » nearby. Slightly informal/conversational but fine in everyday polite speech.
target_language_example: Pour faire court, on a raté le train et on est rentrés en taxi.
native_language_example: To make a long story short, we missed the train and came home by taxi.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a last point, conclusion, or final action in a list or explanation (similar to “finally” or “to wrap up”). Can also mean “to finish” when followed by an infinitive (e.g., “pour finir de + infinitive” = “to finish (doing)…”).
target_language_example: Pour finir, je voudrais vous remercier.
native_language_example: Finally, I would like to thank you.

meaning: "for the love of" (often: "for the love of God").
additional_notes: Used to beg or insist strongly, often showing frustration or urgency. It can be followed by a noun (pour l'amour de Dieu ! / pour l'amour du ciel !) or used with a request (Pour l'amour de Dieu, arrête !). More dramatic/emphatic than simply "s'il te plaît".
target_language_example: Pour l'amour de Dieu, ferme la porte !
native_language_example: For the love of God, close the door!

additional_notes: Used to talk about a temporary situation or what is true at the present time, often implying it may change later. Common at the beginning or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Pour l'instant, je ne peux pas venir.
native_language_example: For now, I can’t come.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what is true in general for a majority of people or things. Often placed at the beginning or middle of the sentence (e.g., "Pour la plupart, ..." or "Ils sont, pour la plupart, ..."). Can refer to people or things; "la plupart" means "most (of them)" and may be followed by "de" ("la plupart des étudiants").
target_language_example: Pour la plupart, les magasins ferment à 19 h.
native_language_example: For the most part, stores close at 7 p.m.

additional_notes: Often used to talk about something lasting permanently (a commitment, a relationship, a sentence, a membership). It can be literal (lasting until death) or more emotional/figurative (“forever”).
target_language_example: Je t’aimerai pour la vie.
native_language_example: I will love you forever.

meaning: "this time" / "in this case" (emphasizing the specific situation).
additional_notes: Used to highlight that what you’re saying is true specifically in the current situation (often with contrast to other times/cases). Common in spoken French. Often placed at the beginning or end of the clause: « Pour le coup, ... » or « ..., pour le coup. »
target_language_example: Pour le coup, je suis d’accord avec toi.
native_language_example: This time, I agree with you.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true only at the present time, and may change later. Common in everyday speech. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence: "Pour le moment, ..." or "..., pour le moment."
target_language_example: Pour le moment, je n’ai pas le temps.
native_language_example: For now, I don’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to shift to what remains or what’s left to say/do after mentioning something else. Often introduces a general conclusion or a change of topic: *Pour le reste, tout va bien.* It can also mean “otherwise/in other respects.”
target_language_example: Pour le reste, je suis d’accord avec toi.
native_language_example: As for the rest, I agree with you.

meaning: for my part; as for me; personally.
additional_notes: Used to give your own opinion or situation, often to contrast with others (similar to “as for me…” or “personally…”). Common patterns: “Pour ma part, je…” / “Pour ma part, je pense que…”. You can also change the possessive to match the speaker: “pour ta part” (as for you), “pour sa part” (as for him/her), “pour notre part” (as for us), etc.
target_language_example: Pour ma part, je préfère rester à la maison.
native_language_example: As for me, I’d rather stay at home.

meaning: “not to say …” / “almost, if not …” (used to correct or strengthen a description).
additional_notes: Used after an adjective or description to add a stronger word, while sounding a bit cautious or polite. Often translates as “almost” or “practically,” e.g., “It’s expensive—practically outrageous.” You can follow it with an adjective, noun, or phrase: « Il est fatigué, pour ne pas dire épuisé. »
target_language_example: C’est cher, pour ne pas dire hors de prix.
native_language_example: It’s expensive—practically outrageously expensive / almost unaffordable.

meaning: "so that" / "in order that" (followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express purpose or desired result. It introduces a clause that typically uses the subjunctive: pour que + subject + verb (subjunctive). Often corresponds to English "so that" or "in order that." If the subject is the same in both clauses, French usually uses "pour" + infinitive instead (e.g., "Je viens pour te voir").
target_language_example: Je te le répète pour que tu comprennes.
native_language_example: I’m repeating it to you so that you understand.

additional_notes: Used to ask what the purpose or point of an action is. Often said as a follow-up question: someone says they want to do something, and you ask "Pour quoi faire ?" It can sound neutral/curious or skeptical depending on tone. Also written in three words; compare with "pourquoi" (one word) meaning "why?" in general.
target_language_example: — Je vais acheter un nouveau téléphone. — Pour quoi faire ?
native_language_example: — I'm going to buy a new phone. — What for?

meaning: for nothing; not at all (with negation).
additional_notes: Most often used to mean “for nothing / free” (no payment or no reason): « C’est pour rien » = “It’s free.” It can also mean “for no reason”: « Tu cries pour rien » = “You’re yelling for no reason.” With negation (ne… pour rien), it means “not at all / under no circumstances”: « Je ne partirai pour rien au monde » = “I won’t leave for anything in the world.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, c’est pour rien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s free.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize certainty or agreement. Common in conversation; similar to "c'est sûr" or "bien sûr". It can appear at the end of a sentence for emphasis ("... pour sûr").
target_language_example: On va gagner, pour sûr !
native_language_example: We’re going to win, for sure!

additional_notes: Means something lasts indefinitely (often in emotional/romantic promises) or that a situation is permanent. In everyday speech, it can also mean “for good” in the sense of “for the last time / permanently” (e.g., leaving a place).
target_language_example: Je t’aimerai pour toujours.
native_language_example: I will love you forever.

additional_notes: Used to say something is happening unusually or contrary to what is typical. Often implies a contrast with someone’s usual behavior (sometimes with mild criticism or surprise). Can appear at the beginning or end of a sentence: « Pour une fois, … » / « …, pour une fois. »
target_language_example: Pour une fois, il est arrivé à l'heure.
native_language_example: For once, he arrived on time.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a frank opinion, admission, or clarification (often softening what comes next). Common in speech and writing. Can be placed at the start or in the middle of a sentence: « Pour être honnête, … » or « …, pour être honnête. »
target_language_example: Pour être honnête, je n’ai pas envie de sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: To be honest, I don’t feel like going out tonight.

additional_notes: Used to agree casually to a suggestion, accept an invitation, or show openness (“sure, why not”). It can also be used as a real question asking for a reason not to do something, but most often it’s an easygoing way to say yes.
target_language_example: On va au cinéma ce soir ? — Pourquoi pas !
native_language_example: Are we going to the movies tonight? — Why not!

meaning: to sue; to take legal action against (someone).
additional_notes: Used in legal contexts to mean starting or continuing a court case against a person or organization. It commonly appears as “poursuivre quelqu’un en justice” (to sue someone) or “être poursuivi(e) en justice” (to be sued / prosecuted). In criminal cases it can also mean “to prosecute,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Il a décidé de poursuivre l’entreprise en justice.
native_language_example: He decided to sue the company.

meaning: "as long as" / "provided that" (often with a wish: "if only").
additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition: something is true or acceptable on the condition that something else happens. Very commonly followed by the subjunctive: « Pourvu qu’il vienne ! » = “If only he’d come!” It can also mean “as long as” in everyday speech: « Tu peux sortir, pourvu que tu rentres avant minuit. »
target_language_example: Tu peux venir, pourvu que tu me préviennes à l’avance.
native_language_example: You can come, as long as you let me know in advance.

additional_notes: Refers to the first person you fell in love with (often an early/teenage romance). You can use it to talk about a person ("mon premier amour") or more generally as an experience ("un premier amour").
target_language_example: Elle n’a jamais oublié son premier amour.
native_language_example: She never forgot her first love.

additional_notes: Used as an official political title. In French it’s usually written in lowercase in running text (premier ministre), but may be capitalized in headlines or when referring to a specific person’s office (le Premier ministre). Often preceded by the article: le/la premier(e) ministre.
target_language_example: Le premier ministre a annoncé de nouvelles mesures.
native_language_example: The prime minister announced new measures.

additional_notes: Most often used for what is closest or most visible in an image (“au premier plan” = in the foreground). Figuratively, it means being given priority or being the main focus (“mettre au premier plan” = to bring to the forefront). Can also describe a key role or the front line (“être au premier plan”).
target_language_example: Au premier plan, on voit une femme qui lit.
native_language_example: In the foreground, we see a woman reading.

meaning: first class (highest/most expensive category, e.g., on a train/plane).
additional_notes: Used for travel tickets and services (train, plane, sometimes mail): « en première classe » = in first class. Often contrasted with « deuxième classe » (second class). Also used more generally to mean “top-notch/first-rate” (e.g., « un service de première classe »).
target_language_example: J’ai pris un billet en première classe.
native_language_example: I bought a first-class ticket.

additional_notes: Used to talk about doing something for the first time, often in the pattern "C’est la première fois que + subject + verb" (present tense in French even if English uses present perfect). You can also say "pour la première fois" = "for the first time." Feminine form: "première" agrees with "fois" (feminine).
target_language_example: C’est la première fois que je viens à Paris.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve come to Paris.

additional_notes: Used to refer specifically to a woman who holds the role of Prime Minister. For a man, you say "premier ministre". In French, job titles often agree with the person’s gender; you’ll also see it capitalized in official contexts ("la Première ministre").
target_language_example: La Première ministre a annoncé de nouvelles mesures.
native_language_example: The Prime Minister announced new measures.

additional_notes: Most commonly used in grammar: "la première personne" refers to the speaker (je / nous = I / we). In everyday speech it can also mean the first person in a line or group (the first individual). Agreement: "première" changes with gender/number (première personne, premiers/premières personnes).
target_language_example: En français, « je » est à la première personne du singulier.
native_language_example: In French, “I” is in the first person singular.

meaning: to catch off guard; to take by surprise.
additional_notes: Used when someone is surprised because they weren’t prepared (often by a question, situation, or unexpected event). Common patterns: « Ça m’a pris(e) au dépourvu » (It caught me off guard) and « prendre quelqu’un au dépourvu ». The past participle agrees with the object when using « être » (e.g., « j’ai été pris(e) au dépourvu »).
target_language_example: Ta question m’a pris au dépourvu.
native_language_example: Your question caught me off guard.

additional_notes: Used when you mean you consider something/someone important, credible, or worth attention (not as a joke). Often used in the negative: « ne pas prendre (quelqu’un/quelque chose) au sérieux » = “not to take (someone/something) seriously.” Can take a person or a thing as the object: « prendre quelqu’un au sérieux », « prendre une situation au sérieux ».
target_language_example: Il faut prendre ce problème au sérieux.
native_language_example: We need to take this problem seriously.

meaning: to take it well; to react well (to something).
additional_notes: Used mainly with an object pronoun: « le/la/les prendre bien » = to take it/them well (e.g., news, a comment, criticism). Often contrasted with « prendre mal » (to take it badly). You can also use it with a noun: « prendre la nouvelle bien » (less common than using a pronoun).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je le prends bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m taking it well.

meaning: to say goodbye; to take leave.
additional_notes: Used when leaving someone (at the end of a visit, meeting, etc.). It can sound a bit formal/polite, especially in writing or professional contexts. Don’t confuse with “prendre des congés” (to take time off / go on leave).
target_language_example: Je dois prendre congé, à demain.
native_language_example: I have to say goodbye, see you tomorrow.

meaning: to realize; to become aware (of something).
additional_notes: Often used with "de" + noun/infinitive: "prendre conscience de quelque chose" (to become aware of something) or "prendre conscience que" + clause (to realize that...). In everyday speech, it’s also common to use the reflexive form "se rendre compte (de)" with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: J’ai pris conscience que j’avais fait une erreur.
native_language_example: I realized that I had made a mistake.

meaning: to get in touch; to make contact.
additional_notes: Used when you start communicating with someone (by phone, email, etc.), often in more formal contexts. Commonly followed by "avec" + person/organization ("prendre contact avec..."), or seen in the noun form "prendre contact" meaning "getting in touch."
target_language_example: Je vais prendre contact avec le service client.
native_language_example: I’m going to get in touch with customer service.

meaning: to take classes / lessons; to take a course.
additional_notes: Most commonly used with an article: « prendre des cours » (take classes) or « prendre un cours » (take a class). You often add the subject with « de »: « prendre des cours de français » (take French classes).
target_language_example: Je prends des cours de français le soir.
native_language_example: I take French classes in the evening.

meaning: to put on airs; to act pretentious/superior.
additional_notes: Used to criticize someone’s attitude when they seem to think they’re better than others or are showing off. Often said as a reproach (e.g., "Arrête de prendre des airs !").
target_language_example: Depuis qu’il a eu sa promotion, il prend des airs.
native_language_example: Since he got his promotion, he’s been putting on airs.

meaning: to take measures; to take steps (to do something).
additional_notes: Used for actions taken to solve a problem, improve a situation, or prevent something. Very common in formal contexts (government, business, safety), but also usable in everyday speech. Often followed by "pour" + infinitive: "prendre des mesures pour réduire...".
target_language_example: Le gouvernement va prendre des mesures pour réduire la pollution.
native_language_example: The government is going to take steps to reduce pollution.

meaning: to have a good time; to enjoy yourself.
additional_notes: A common, friendly expression meaning to spend time pleasantly (often on vacation, with friends, at a party, etc.). It uses the verb "prendre" (to take), but it’s not meant literally; it’s closer to “enjoy yourself.” Often used with "bien" for emphasis: "prendre du bon temps" / "prendre du bon temps ensemble".
target_language_example: On va à la plage ce week-end pour prendre du bon temps.
native_language_example: We’re going to the beach this weekend to have a good time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about weight gain (people, pets, sometimes objects in a metaphorical way). In the past tense, it’s often "J’ai pris du poids" (I gained weight). Neutral in tone; you can soften it with "un peu" (a bit).
target_language_example: J’ai pris du poids ces derniers mois.
native_language_example: I’ve gained weight these last few months.

meaning: to take a step back; to gain perspective.
additional_notes: Used when you pause, distance yourself (physically or mentally), and look at a situation more calmly or objectively—often before deciding or reacting. Very common in everyday French. With people, it can also imply creating a bit of distance in a relationship (taking some space).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de prendre du recul avant de répondre.
native_language_example: I need to take a step back before replying.

meaning: to take care of; to handle; to cover (costs).
additional_notes: Common in practical contexts meaning to assume responsibility for a person, task, or expense. Often used with an object: prendre en charge un patient (take care of a patient), un dossier (handle a case/file), or des frais (cover expenses). In healthcare it can mean “to treat/care for,” and in insurance/admin contexts “to reimburse/cover.”
target_language_example: L’assurance prend en charge une partie des frais médicaux.
native_language_example: The insurance covers part of the medical costs.

meaning: to take into account; to consider.
additional_notes: Used to say you will consider a factor, opinion, or constraint when deciding or evaluating something. Common in formal and everyday contexts. Often followed by a noun: « prendre en compte + nom » (e.g., la situation, les besoins, les remarques).
target_language_example: Nous devons prendre en compte votre situation avant de décider.
native_language_example: We have to take your situation into account before deciding.

meaning: to take into consideration; to consider.
additional_notes: Used in fairly formal contexts (writing, work, official situations) to mean you will think about something before deciding. Often followed by a direct object: « prendre [quelque chose] en considération ». Common alternatives: « tenir compte de » (to take into account), « considérer » (to consider).
target_language_example: Nous prendrons votre demande en considération.
native_language_example: We will take your request into consideration.

meaning: to catch (someone) in the act; to catch red-handed.
additional_notes: Used when someone is caught while committing a wrongdoing (stealing, cheating, etc.). Often heard in news or legal/police contexts. You can say "prendre quelqu’un en flagrant délit" (catch someone red-handed) or use it in the passive: "être pris(e) en flagrant délit" (to be caught in the act).
target_language_example: Il a été pris en flagrant délit de vol.
native_language_example: He was caught red-handed stealing.

additional_notes: Used with a direct object for the subject being photographed: « prendre quelqu’un/quelque chose en photo ». In everyday French, people also say « prendre une photo » or « prendre une photo de … ». Conjugates like a normal verb phrase: « je prends en photo », « j’ai pris en photo ».
target_language_example: Tu peux me prendre en photo devant la Tour Eiffel ?
native_language_example: Can you take a photo of me in front of the Eiffel Tower?

meaning: to take (someone/something) as an example; to model yourself on.
additional_notes: Used to say you should follow a person’s behavior or use something as a model. Often appears as "prendre exemple sur + quelqu’un/quelque chose" (to take inspiration from / follow the example of). You can also hear "prendre exemple sur lui/elle" or "Il faut prendre exemple sur...".
target_language_example: Tu devrais prendre exemple sur ta sœur : elle travaille tous les jours.
native_language_example: You should take your sister as an example: she works every day.

meaning: to catch fire; to burst into flames.
additional_notes: Used when something starts burning (often suddenly). You can use it for objects, buildings, or even a person’s clothes. Common in news and emergency situations. Past tense often appears as "a pris feu" (caught fire).
target_language_example: La voiture a pris feu après l’accident.
native_language_example: The car caught fire after the accident.

meaning: to come to an end; to end.
additional_notes: Used to say that something (an event, a period of time, a situation) ends. Often used in the past or future: « a pris fin » (came to an end), « va prendre fin » (will come to an end). Slightly formal/common in writing, but also heard in speech.
target_language_example: La réunion va prendre fin à 17 h.
native_language_example: The meeting will end at 5 p.m.

meaning: to take shape; to start becoming real/clear.
additional_notes: Used when an idea, plan, project, or situation is developing and becoming more defined. Often followed by "dans" or "au" + place/time (e.g., "dans mon esprit", "au fil du temps").
target_language_example: Peu à peu, le projet prend forme.
native_language_example: Little by little, the project is taking shape.

meaning: to catch a cold; to get chilled.
additional_notes: Used when you become cold enough that it might make you ill, or when warning someone to dress warmly. Very common with negation and imperatives: « Ne prends pas froid ! » Also appears with “attraper un rhume” (to catch a cold) as a close synonym, but « prendre froid » emphasizes getting cold/chilled.
target_language_example: Mets ton manteau, tu vas prendre froid.
native_language_example: Put on your coat, you’re going to catch a cold.

meaning: to be careful; to watch out.
additional_notes: Used as a warning or advice, often followed by "à" + noun/pronoun ("prendre garde à la marche" = watch your step), or "de" + infinitive ("prendre garde de ne pas..." = be careful not to...). Common in the imperative: "Prenez garde !" / "Prends garde !" (Watch out!). Similar to "faire attention" and slightly more formal/literary in tone.
target_language_example: Prends garde à la marche !
native_language_example: Watch your step!

meaning: to get some fresh air; to go outside for a bit.
additional_notes: Used when you step outside briefly to breathe fresh air, clear your head, or take a short walk. Very common in everyday speech. Literally “to take the air,” but the natural English is “get some fresh air.” Can also imply taking a break: « Je vais prendre l’air » = “I’m going to step outside for some air.”
target_language_example: Je vais prendre l’air cinq minutes, j’ai besoin de souffler.
native_language_example: I’m going to get some fresh air for five minutes; I need to catch my breath.

additional_notes: Used when someone escapes or leaves quickly, often to avoid danger, trouble, or being caught (common in news/police contexts). Conjugates like prendre: "il/elle a pris la fuite" (he/she fled).
target_language_example: Le voleur a pris la fuite quand la police est arrivée.
native_language_example: The thief ran away when the police arrived.

meaning: to take over; to take control (literally: “to take the hand”).
additional_notes: Often used figuratively when someone starts leading an activity or handling a task: *Je prends la main* = “I’ll take it from here.” It can also be literal (taking someone’s hand), but the “take over” meaning is very common in work/tech contexts (e.g., taking control of a situation, a file, or a computer).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je prends la main et je m’en occupe.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll take over and handle it.

prendre la main dans le sac

target_language_multi_word_term: prendre la main dans le sac
meaning: to catch (someone) red-handed; to catch in the act.
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression most often used with a person as the object: « prendre quelqu’un la main dans le sac ». It means catching someone while they are doing something wrong (e.g., stealing, cheating), like being caught “with their hand in the bag.” You’ll also see « être pris(e) la main dans le sac » (“to be caught red-handed”).
target_language_example: Le gardien l’a pris la main dans le sac en train de voler.
native_language_example: The security guard caught him red-handed while he was stealing.

meaning: to measure; to gauge/assess (the extent of something).
