additional_notes: Can be literal (taking measurements) or figurative (understanding the scale/importance of a situation). In the figurative sense, it often implies realizing something clearly: « prendre la mesure de + noun » = “to grasp/fully appreciate the extent of …”.
target_language_example: Il faut prendre la mesure de la situation avant de décider.
native_language_example: We need to assess the situation before deciding.

meaning: to speak up; to take the floor.
additional_notes: Used in meetings, classes, debates, etc. to mean starting to speak (often formally), sometimes after raising your hand or being invited. You’ll also hear it with permission: « Je peux prendre la parole ? » (“May I speak?”).
target_language_example: Je voudrais prendre la parole pour poser une question.
native_language_example: I’d like to speak up to ask a question.

meaning: to take the trouble (to); to bother to.
additional_notes: Often followed by an infinitive: « prendre la peine de + infinitive » (to take the trouble to do something). Used to stress that something required effort, or sometimes to politely (or pointedly) ask someone to make an effort.
target_language_example: Merci d’avoir pris la peine de m’écrire.
native_language_example: Thank you for taking the trouble to write to me.

meaning: to take over; to relieve someone (take over their shift/duties).
additional_notes: Used when someone replaces another person to continue the same task, job, or shift (at work, in caregiving, in a relay race, etc.). Often implies continuity: one person stops and another continues. Common patterns: « prendre la relève de [qqn] » (take over from someone) and « prendre la relève » (take over, without saying from whom).
target_language_example: Je prends la relève de Marie à 18 h, tu peux rentrer chez toi.
native_language_example: I’m taking over from Marie at 6 p.m.; you can go home.

meaning: to hit the road; to set off (by road).
additional_notes: Used when you start a trip or leave somewhere, especially by car. Often implies beginning a journey: « On prend la route à 7h » (We set off at 7). Can also mean being on your way: « Je prends la route » (I’m heading out / I’m leaving).
target_language_example: On prend la route demain matin pour Lyon.
native_language_example: We’re hitting the road tomorrow morning for Lyon.

meaning: to annoy; to be a headache (to deal with).
additional_notes: Informal. Used when something/someone is bothering you, stressing you out, or making things complicated: « Ça me prend la tête » = “It’s doing my head in / It’s driving me crazy.” Often used in the negative: « Ne me prends pas la tête » = “Don’t annoy me / Don’t give me a hard time.”
target_language_example: Arrête de me prendre la tête avec ça.
native_language_example: Stop giving me a hard time about that.

meaning: to take over; to relieve someone and continue (their work).
additional_notes: Used when someone replaces another person and continues what they were doing (at work, in a task, in a discussion, etc.). Very common in the pattern « prendre le relais de + person/thing » (“to take over from…”). Note: it’s usually spelled « relais » (not « relai ») in modern French.
target_language_example: Je dois partir ; tu peux prendre le relais ?
native_language_example: I have to go; can you take over?

meaning: to take over; to take over from someone.
additional_notes: Used when one person (or group) continues a task after another stops, often in work or teamwork contexts. You can add “de + person” to say who you’re taking over from: “prendre le relais de Marie”. Also used in relay/team sports, but very common figuratively (projects, shifts, responsibilities).
target_language_example: Je dois partir, tu peux prendre le relais ?
native_language_example: I have to leave—can you take over?

meaning: to take the wheel; to start driving.
additional_notes: Used when someone begins driving a vehicle (gets behind the wheel), often after switching drivers or at the start of a trip. Can be literal (a car) and sometimes figurative meaning “to take control/lead.”
target_language_example: Après le dîner, c’est Marie qui a pris le volant.
native_language_example: After dinner, Marie took the wheel (started driving).

meaning: to take charge; to take control (e.g., of a team, project, or vehicle).
additional_notes: Used when someone assumes leadership or responsibility: in business/politics it means “take charge / take the reins.” It can also be literal in contexts like driving or flying, meaning “take the controls.”
target_language_example: Après le départ du directeur, elle a pris les commandes de l’entreprise.
native_language_example: After the director left, she took charge of the company.

meaning: to place bets; to take bets.
additional_notes: Used in gambling contexts (sports betting, horse racing, etc.) meaning either to bet yourself or to accept/record other people’s bets (depending on context). It’s also used figuratively to mean “I bet…” / “Let’s bet…” when predicting what will happen. Note that "Paris" here is "bets" (plural of "pari"), not the city.
target_language_example: On peut prendre les paris : il va arriver en retard.
native_language_example: We can bet: he’s going to arrive late.

meaning: to take measures; to take action (or to take a measurement).
additional_notes: In real French you almost always use it with an article: **prendre des mesures** (take measures/take action) or **prendre une mesure** (take a measure; also take a measurement). Very common in formal contexts (government, rules, safety): *prendre des mesures pour…* = “take steps to…”. In the past tense: **j’ai pris**, **il/elle a pris**, **nous avons pris**, etc.
target_language_example: Le gouvernement a pris des mesures pour réduire la pollution.
native_language_example: The government took measures to reduce pollution.

meaning: to take note; to note down.
additional_notes: Used to say you are writing something down or keeping it in mind. Often followed by de + noun (prendre note de l’adresse) or by a clause with que (prendre note que…). Common in polite or formal contexts (emails, meetings): Je prends note de… / Nous prenons note de…. Also appears as an instruction: Prenez note !
target_language_example: Je prends note de votre demande et je vous répondrai demain.
native_language_example: I’m taking note of your request and I’ll reply to you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with à to mean “to participate in” something: prendre part à une réunion, à un débat, à une activité. Often a bit more formal than participer, and it emphasizes being involved in an event or activity.
target_language_example: Je vais prendre part à la réunion demain.
native_language_example: I’m going to take part in the meeting tomorrow.

meaning: to take sides; to take a stand.
additional_notes: Used when you choose one side in a disagreement or debate. Common patterns: « prendre parti pour quelqu’un » (take someone’s side), « prendre parti contre quelqu’un » (take sides against someone), and « sans prendre parti » (without taking sides / staying neutral). Not to be confused with « prendre part (à) », which means “to take part (in) / participate.”
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas prendre parti dans cette dispute.
native_language_example: I don’t want to take sides in this argument.

meaning: to get scared; to become frightened.
additional_notes: Means to suddenly feel fear, often because of something unexpected. It’s very common in everyday French. Can also be used for animals or people who panic or startle easily (e.g., un cheval qui prend peur).
target_language_example: J’ai pris peur quand j’ai entendu un bruit dans la nuit.
native_language_example: I got scared when I heard a noise in the night.

meaning: to take a seat; to sit down.
additional_notes: Used in polite or formal contexts (e.g., a host, teacher, or announcement) to invite someone to sit. It can also mean “to take up a position/role” or “to happen/occur” in more abstract contexts, but beginners will most often see it as “sit down.”
target_language_example: Veuillez prendre place, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please take a seat.

meaning: to take pleasure; to enjoy (doing something).
additional_notes: Used to express enjoyment, often with "à" + infinitive (prendre plaisir à faire qc = to enjoy doing sth). You can also use it with "de" + noun/doing (prendre plaisir de/à qc). Slightly more formal than "s’amuser" (to have fun).
target_language_example: Je prends plaisir à apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I enjoy learning French.

additional_notes: Used when someone permanently stops working, usually because of age (retirement). The possessive changes with the person: prendre ma/ta/sa/notre/votre/leur retraite. Often used with a time reference: prendre sa retraite à 65 ans (“retire at 65”).
target_language_example: Mon père va prendre sa retraite l’année prochaine.
native_language_example: My dad is going to retire next year.

additional_notes: Used with "de" before the person/thing you care for: "prendre soin de + noun/pronoun". Often means looking after someone (health, safety, needs) or taking good care of something. Common in advice and polite requests.
target_language_example: Prends soin de toi !
native_language_example: Take care of yourself!

meaning: to take care of; to look after.
additional_notes: Used to talk about caring for a person, animal, or thing, or about paying attention to something (health, yourself, details). Common patterns: «prendre soin de quelqu’un/de quelque chose» (take care of someone/something) and reflexive «prendre soin de soi» (take care of yourself). Often followed by a noun or stressed pronoun: «de moi/de toi/de lui/d’elle/de nous/de vous/d’eux/d’elles».
target_language_example: Je dois prendre soin de ma grand-mère ce week-end.
native_language_example: I have to take care of my grandmother this weekend.

meaning: to take your time; not to rush.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re going slowly and calmly, or to tell someone there’s no hurry. The possessive changes with the subject: je prends mon temps, tu prends ton temps, il/elle prend son temps, nous prenons notre temps, vous prenez votre temps, ils/elles prennent leur temps.
target_language_example: Ne te presse pas, prends ton temps.
native_language_example: Don’t rush, take your time.

meaning: to catch (someone) in the act; to catch red-handed.
additional_notes: Used when someone is caught while they are doing something (often something wrong, like stealing). Very common in the passive form: « être pris(e) sur le fait » (“to be caught in the act”).
target_language_example: Le voleur a été pris sur le fait.
native_language_example: The thief was caught in the act.

meaning: to have a drink (often: to go for a drink).
additional_notes: Very common invitation to go out casually for a drink (alcoholic or non-alcoholic). Often used with "On va prendre un verre ?" or "Tu veux prendre un verre ?". It can also mean simply having a drink at home, depending on context.
target_language_example: On va prendre un verre après le travail ?
native_language_example: Shall we go for a drink after work?

additional_notes: Used on signs, notices, emails, and formal instructions to politely tell people what to do. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: « Prière de + infinitive » (e.g., « Prière de patienter »). More formal than « s’il vous plaît » and not used much in casual conversation.
target_language_example: Prière de ne pas fumer.
native_language_example: Please do not smoke.

additional_notes: Used to talk about foods made from milk (e.g., milk, cheese, yogurt, butter). Often seen in the plural: « produits laitiers ». You may also hear « produit à base de lait » (milk-based product).
target_language_example: Je suis allergique aux produits laitiers.
native_language_example: I’m allergic to dairy products.

additional_notes: Used in politics/government to refer to a text that is being proposed and debated before it becomes a law. In French, once it is adopted/promulgated, it becomes a "loi" (law). Not the same as "projet" in the everyday sense of a personal project.
target_language_example: Le gouvernement a présenté un projet de loi sur l’immigration.
native_language_example: The government introduced a bill on immigration.

additional_notes: A polite, common wish you say or write to someone who is ill or recovering. Often used in messages/cards, frequently with verbs like « Je te/vous souhaite un prompt rétablissement » (I wish you a speedy recovery). « Prompt » is formal and means “speedy”; in everyday speech people also say « Bon rétablissement ».
target_language_example: Je te souhaite un prompt rétablissement.
native_language_example: I wish you a speedy recovery (get well soon).

additional_notes: Used to say that a place/land/building belongs to a private person or company and is not open to the public. Common on signs (often with: « Défense d’entrer » = “No entry / Keep out”). Feminine noun phrase: une propriété privée.
target_language_example: Attention : propriété privée, défense d’entrer.
native_language_example: Warning: private property, no entry.

meaning: to pay attention; to pay heed.
additional_notes: Common verb phrase meaning to focus or be careful about something. Often followed by "à" + noun/pronoun: « Prête attention à la route. » You can also use it with an indirect object pronoun: « Prête-lui attention » (pay attention to him/her/it), though « fais attention à… » is often more common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Prête attention à ce que je dis.
native_language_example: Pay attention to what I’m saying.

additional_notes: Used in formal contexts (court, government, ceremonies) to mean making a solemn promise, often publicly. It can appear with a person or institution you swear to (e.g., « prêter serment devant le tribunal »).
target_language_example: Avant de témoigner, il doit prêter serment.
native_language_example: Before testifying, he must swear an oath.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask permission or ability. It’s the inverted question form of "je peux" (from the verb "pouvoir"). Commonly followed by an infinitive: "Puis-je + verb" (e.g., "Puis-je entrer ?"). In everyday casual speech, people often say "Est-ce que je peux… ?" or "Je peux… ?" instead.
target_language_example: Puis-je vous poser une question ?
native_language_example: May I ask you a question?

additional_notes: Common word for a sweater you pull on over your head. You’ll often hear it in clothing contexts (shopping, describing what you’re wearing). It’s masculine: un pull-over (or un pull). Plural: des pull-overs. Can be used with "mettre" (to put on) and "enlever" (to take off).
target_language_example: J’ai froid, je vais mettre un pull-over.
native_language_example: I’m cold, I’m going to put on a sweater.

additional_notes: A very vulgar, informal intensifier used before a noun: putain de + noun. It becomes putain d’ before a vowel or silent h (e.g., putain d’idée). Common in angry or frustrated speech; avoid in polite settings. Similar in strength to “fucking” in English.
target_language_example: J’en ai marre de cette putain d’attente !
native_language_example: I’m sick of this fucking wait!

meaning: a very vulgar intensifier: “fucking / damn / bloody”.
additional_notes: Used before a noun to strongly express anger, annoyance, emphasis, or surprise (similar to English “fucking” or “damn”). It’s highly offensive/vulgar in many contexts—avoid in polite situations, with strangers, at work, etc. In pronunciation, the final consonant of *putain* is often not pronounced: roughly “pu-tan de”.
target_language_example: J’en ai marre de ce putain de bus !
native_language_example: I’m sick of this fucking bus!

additional_notes: Used to refer to Santa, especially around Christmas. Often written with capitals as "Père Noël" and used with the definite article: "le Père Noël". You may also see "Père Noël" used like a title when addressing him in stories or letters.
target_language_example: Les enfants ont écrit une lettre au Père Noël.
native_language_example: The children wrote a letter to Santa Claus.

meaning: to lose it; to flip out (suddenly lose control).
additional_notes: Informal idiom. Used when someone suddenly gets very angry, stressed, or panicked and reacts explosively. Often said about yourself or someone else: « Il/Elle a pété les plombs ». Similar in tone to “to blow a fuse” or “to snap.”
target_language_example: Quand il a appris la nouvelle, il a pété les plombs.
native_language_example: When he heard the news, he flipped out.

additional_notes: Contraction of "que aurez-vous" used with subject–verb inversion in formal/written French. Often used when offering or asking what someone would like: "Qu'aurez-vous à boire / à manger ?" It literally means “what will you have?”, and can also be used more generally as “what will you have (done/ready)?” depending on context.
target_language_example: Qu'aurez-vous à boire ?
native_language_example: What will you have to drink?

meaning: "what would you have" / "what would you like?" (very polite, conditional question).
additional_notes: Contraction of « que » + « auriez » + « vous » (inversion). Uses the conditional of « avoir » to sound more polite or hypothetical. Often followed by something like « à déclarer », « à boire », « à dire », etc. (e.g., asking what someone would like or what they would have to say/declare).
target_language_example: Qu'auriez-vous à déclarer ?
native_language_example: What would you like to declare? / Do you have anything to declare?

meaning: "what had you…" / "that you had…" (formal inversion of "que" + "aviez-vous").
additional_notes: Used mainly in writing or very formal speech. It’s a contraction of "que" → "qu’" before a vowel, plus the verb "avoir" in the imperfect ("aviez") with inverted "vous" to form a question. Often appears at the start of a question: "Qu’aviez-vous dit ?" = "What had you said?" In everyday French, people more often use "Qu’est-ce que vous aviez… ?" or "Vous aviez quoi… ?" depending on formality.
target_language_example: Qu’aviez-vous prévu pour ce soir ?
native_language_example: What had you planned for tonight?

additional_notes: Very common question used to ask what the problem is or what is happening. Often said on its own as a reaction, or followed by a noun/pronoun: “Qu’est-ce qu’il y a ?” (What’s wrong?), “Qu’est-ce qu’il y a, Paul ?” (What’s wrong, Paul?), “Qu’est-ce qu’il y a avec toi ?” (What’s wrong with you?). In casual speech you’ll also hear the shortened form “Qu’est-ce qu’y a ?”
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce qu’il y a ? Tu as l’air inquiet.
native_language_example: What’s wrong? You look worried.

additional_notes: Very common question formula in spoken French, usually followed by a subject + verb: « Qu'est-ce que tu fais ? » = “What are you doing?” It’s also used in « Qu’est-ce que c’est ? » = “What is it?” If “what” is the subject of the verb, use « qu’est-ce qui » instead: « Qu’est-ce qui se passe ? » = “What’s happening?”
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que tu veux boire ?
native_language_example: What do you want to drink?

additional_notes: Very common question used to ask what something is (often while pointing at or referring to something). It’s a fixed expression and often followed by a noun: “Qu’est-ce que c’est, ce truc ?” Also used at the start of questions meaning “what…?”: “Qu’est-ce que tu fais ?” (What are you doing?). In speech you may hear it shortened to “c’est quoi ?” (more informal).
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que c’est, cette machine ?
native_language_example: What is this machine?

additional_notes: Used to ask “what” when the thing you’re asking about is doing the action (the subject). Often followed directly by a verb: « Qu'est-ce qui se passe ? » (“What’s happening?”). Contrast with « qu'est-ce que » for “what” as the object: « Qu'est-ce que tu fais ? » (“What are you doing?”).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qui t'arrive ?
native_language_example: What's happening to you? / What's wrong?

additional_notes: "Eûtes" is the passé simple (simple past) form of "avoir" for "vous". You’ll mainly see this in literature or very formal historical writing; in everyday French, people usually say "Qu’avez-vous eu ?" (what did you have / what did you get?) or "Qu’est-ce que vous avez eu ?".
target_language_example: Qu’eûtes-vous à répondre à cette accusation ?
native_language_example: What did you have to say in response to that accusation?

additional_notes: Formal inversion of « qu’est-ce qu’il y a ? » meaning “what is (going on)?” Used to ask what’s happening or what the problem is. Often appears with a complement: « Qu’y a-t-il à manger ? » (What is there to eat?) or « Qu’y a-t-il dans la boîte ? » (What’s in the box?).
target_language_example: Qu’y a-t-il ? Tu as l’air inquiet.
native_language_example: What’s the matter? You look worried.

additional_notes: Used to express a concession: something is true regardless of a condition. Often followed by the conditional (e.g., « quand bien même je pourrais… ») or sometimes the subjunctive in more formal/literary style. It’s fairly formal compared to « même si ».
target_language_example: Quand bien même il pleuvrait, on irait se promener.
native_language_example: Even if it rained, we would go for a walk.

additional_notes: Very common phrase used to add contrast or insistence. Often implies “despite that” or “all the same.” It can soften a disagreement ("Quand même…" = “Come on…/Still…”) or express surprise/insistence ("C’est quand même incroyable" = “It’s still pretty incredible / It’s unbelievable, honestly.”). In conversation it’s frequently placed mid-sentence or at the end.
target_language_example: Il pleut, mais on y va quand même.
native_language_example: It’s raining, but we’re going anyway.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a new topic or shift focus to someone/something already mentioned. Often followed by a noun, pronoun, or an infinitive (e.g., « quant à moi », « quant à faire ça »). Typically used in more formal or written French; in conversation you may also hear « et pour… » or « pour ce qui est de… ». Not used to express quantity, despite « quant » looking like English “quantity”.
target_language_example: Quant à moi, je préfère rester à la maison.
native_language_example: As for me, I prefer to stay at home.

additional_notes: The number 45. Used for age, time, prices, dates, etc. Hyphenated in standard French spelling. For time, you’ll often hear: « Il est quarante-cinq » (rare/ambiguous) or more commonly « Il est une heure quarante-cinq » / « Il est deux heures quarante-cinq ».
target_language_example: J’ai quarante-cinq ans.
native_language_example: I’m forty-five years old.

additional_notes: The number 48. Used for counting, ages, prices, dates, and times. Spelling uses a hyphen. Liaison is common before a vowel sound: « quarante-huit ans » (the final -t is pronounced).
target_language_example: J’ai quarante-huit ans.
native_language_example: I’m forty-eight years old.

meaning: a quarter of an hour (15 minutes).
additional_notes: Used to talk about duration or a time delay. Very common after prepositions like « dans » (in), « depuis » (for/since), and « pendant » (for/during): « dans un quart d’heure » = in 15 minutes; « depuis un quart d’heure » = for 15 minutes; « pendant un quart d’heure » = for 15 minutes. Often you’ll also hear the shorter « un quart d’heure ».
target_language_example: J’arrive dans un quart d’heure.
native_language_example: I’ll be there in 15 minutes.

additional_notes: Used for the main place where a group/organization coordinates activities (military, police, company, campaign, etc.). Often abbreviated as « QG » in writing and speech (e.g., « au QG »). It’s usually used with an article: « le quartier général », and you can specify whose with « de » (e.g., « le quartier général de l’entreprise »).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au quartier général à 18 h pour faire le point.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at headquarters at 6 p.m. to review the situation.

additional_notes: Literally “four twenties.” Used in standard French for 80 and as the base for 81–99 (e.g., quatre-vingt-un = 81). Note the spelling: “quatre-vingts” takes an -s only when it’s exactly 80 with nothing after it (Quatre-vingts.), but no -s when followed by another number (quatre-vingt-deux = 82).
target_language_example: J’ai quatre-vingt-deux euros.
native_language_example: I have eighty-two euros.

additional_notes: Standard French uses a base-20 counting pattern for some numbers: 90 is literally “four twenties ten” (4×20 + 10). You’ll also see the same pattern in 80 (quatre-vingts) and 91–99 (quatre-vingt-onze, quatre-vingt-douze, etc.). In Belgium/Switzerland you may hear “nonante” for 90.
target_language_example: J’ai quatre-vingt-dix euros.
native_language_example: I have ninety euros.

additional_notes: Used in counting and with nouns: "quatre-vingts" has a final -s when it stands alone (80) or is followed by a noun (quatre-vingts euros). The -s disappears when another number follows (81–99): "quatre-vingt-un", "quatre-vingt-dix". Literally means "four twenties" and is part of the standard French number system.
target_language_example: J’ai quatre-vingts euros.
native_language_example: I have eighty euros.

additional_notes: Very informal/slang. Used for emphasis, often with a negative (e.g., "je n’ai que dalle" / "j’ai que dalle" = “I’ve got nothing”). Common in casual speech; avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: J’ai compris que dalle à ce cours.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand a thing in that class.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to express surprise or emphasis about a large quantity. Common in exclamations: "Que de + noun !" (often with no verb). Usually followed by a plural noun: "Que de choses !" You can also use it in a full sentence for emphasis, though it sounds more literary/expressive than neutral "beaucoup de".
target_language_example: Que de monde dans la rue !
native_language_example: So many people in the street!

meaning: "what the heck/what the devil" (expresses surprise, annoyance, or disbelief).
additional_notes: Used in questions to intensify the tone, similar to English "what the heck...?" It’s stronger than plain "que" but not necessarily a swear word; it can sound a bit old-fashioned or dramatic. Often appears as "Que diable fais-tu ?" or "Que diable est-ce que c’est ?"
target_language_example: Que diable fais-tu ici ?
native_language_example: What the heck are you doing here?

meaning: "as far as I know" / "to my knowledge".
additional_notes: Fixed expression using the subjunctive of savoir (sache). Very common with a negative to mean that something is not true or not the case to the best of your knowledge: "pas que je sache" = "not that I know of". It can also appear after other negatives like "rien que je sache" (nothing that I know of).
target_language_example: Il n’y a pas de réunion aujourd’hui, que je sache.
native_language_example: There isn’t a meeting today, as far as I know.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone thinks or believes, usually after a main clause (often negative): « Je ne pense pas que tu crois ça » (“I don’t think you believe that”). « Que » is a conjunction meaning “that,” and « tu crois » is “you think/believe.” The verb can also mean “you think (something is true)” depending on context.
target_language_example: Je ne pense pas que tu crois vraiment ce qu’il dit.
native_language_example: I don’t think you really believe what he says.

additional_notes: Uses the informal subject pronoun "tu" (used with friends, family, children). Common as a direct question, and can sound annoyed depending on tone/context (similar to “What do you want?”). In more polite/formal situations, use "Que voulez-vous ?"
target_language_example: Que veux-tu manger ce soir ?
native_language_example: What do you want to eat tonight?

meaning: “What do you want?” / “What would you like?”
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone wants or needs; can sound blunt on its own, so it’s often softened in polite contexts with things like « Que voulez-vous, s’il vous plaît ? » or « Que voulez-vous dire ? » (What do you mean?). Often followed by « que » + clause: « Que voulez-vous que je fasse ? » (What do you want me to do?).
target_language_example: Que voulez-vous que je fasse ?
native_language_example: What do you want me to do?

additional_notes: Used to express disappointment or sympathy when something unfortunate happens. Often said on its own as an exclamation, or followed by a clause: « Quel dommage que… » (“What a shame that…”).
target_language_example: Quel dommage ! Je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: What a pity! I can’t come tonight.

meaning: “whatever … was / might have been” (concessive: no matter what … was).
additional_notes: Used in the structure **quel(le)(s) que + noun + fût/fussent** (imperfect subjunctive of *être*), common in formal/literary French. In everyday speech, it’s often replaced by **quel que soit / quels que soient** (“whatever … is/are”).
target_language_example: Quel que fût le danger, ils ont continué.
native_language_example: Whatever the danger was, they kept going.

additional_notes: Used to express that something is true regardless of the person/thing/choice. Often followed by a noun or pronoun: « quel que soit le problème » (whatever the problem), « quel que soit ton choix » (whatever your choice). Agreement: « quel que soit » (masc. singular), « quelle que soit » (fem. singular), « quels que soient » (masc. plural), « quelles que soient » (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Quel que soit ton choix, je te soutiendrai.
native_language_example: Whatever your choice, I will support you.

additional_notes: Common, neutral way to ask about the weather. Literally “what weather does it make?”; the “il” is an impersonal/dummy subject (not “he”). Often used with answers like: Il fait beau / Il fait mauvais / Il fait froid / Il fait chaud.
target_language_example: Quel temps fait-il aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: What’s the weather like today?

additional_notes: A common way to ask someone’s age in informal conversation (using "tu"). More formally, use: "Quel âge avez-vous ?" Literally "what age do you have?" In French you use "avoir" (to have) for age: "J’ai 20 ans" = "I’m 20 (years old)."
target_language_example: Quel âge as-tu ?
native_language_example: How old are you?

additional_notes: Standard way to ask for the current time. Often written with a hyphen: « Quelle heure est-il ? ». In conversation you’ll also hear the more informal « Il est quelle heure ? ».
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, quelle heure est-il ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time is it?

additional_notes: Indefinite pronoun used when you don’t know (or don’t want to say) who the person is: « Est-ce que quelqu’un peut m’aider ? ». In negative sentences, French usually switches to « personne »: « Je ne vois personne » (not *« je ne vois pas quelqu’un »*). Grammatically treated as masculine singular even if it refers to any gender; you’ll often see masculine singular agreement: « quelqu’un de gentil ».
target_language_example: Il y a quelqu’un à la porte.
native_language_example: There’s someone at the door.

additional_notes: Very common indefinite pronoun meaning an unknown or unspecified thing. Often used with an infinitive: "quelque chose à + verb" (something to do/eat/see). You can also add a description with "de": "quelque chose de + adjective" (something + adjective), e.g. "quelque chose de spécial" = something special.
target_language_example: Je cherche quelque chose à manger.
native_language_example: I’m looking for something to eat.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an unknown, unspecified, or not-very-important location. It can refer to a physical place (a street, a room) or a more general idea like "somewhere in the world". Often placed at the end of the sentence: "Je l’ai vu quelque part."
target_language_example: J’ai laissé mes clés quelque part.
native_language_example: I left my keys somewhere.

additional_notes: An adverbial phrase meaning “to some extent.” Often used in more formal or written French than "un peu". It typically comes right before an adjective or another adverb: "quelque peu + adjective/adverb" (e.g., "quelque peu fatigué", "quelque peu plus tard").
target_language_example: Je suis quelque peu surpris par ta réponse.
native_language_example: I’m somewhat surprised by your answer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an unspecified duration (often “for a while” or “some time ago”). Often appears with common time expressions like « il y a quelque temps » (some time ago) or « pendant quelque temps » (for a while).
target_language_example: Je vais rester ici quelque temps.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay here for a while.

additional_notes: Feminine plural form of « quelques-uns ». Used to refer to an unspecified small number of feminine things/people, often with « de » + plural noun (« quelques-unes de mes amies ») or on its own when the noun is understood. Hyphen is common when it’s a pronoun meaning “a few (of them)” rather than directly modifying a noun.
target_language_example: J’en connais quelques-unes.
native_language_example: I know a few of them.

additional_notes: A pronoun meaning “some” or “a few” when you mean a specific group already mentioned or understood (like “some of them”). It’s masculine plural; the feminine plural form is **quelques-unes**. Written with a hyphen.
target_language_example: J’ai invité plusieurs collègues, mais seulement quelques-uns viendront.
native_language_example: I invited several coworkers, but only some (of them) will come.

additional_notes: Used as a question, often on the phone or when you can’t see who is talking. You’ll most commonly hear it as « Qui parle ? » or more politely « Qui est à l’appareil ? » (Who’s calling?). Literally means “who speaks.”
target_language_example: Allô ? Qui parle ?
native_language_example: Hello? Who's speaking?

meaning: what’s more; moreover; on top of that.
additional_notes: Used to add an extra point that strengthens what you just said (often an additional reason, advantage, or surprising detail). It’s fairly formal/written and is close in meaning to "de plus" or "en plus," but with a slightly more emphatic tone.
target_language_example: Il est très compétent, et qui plus est, il parle trois langues.
native_language_example: He’s very competent, and what’s more, he speaks three languages.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indefinite person: “whoever …”. It’s often followed by the subjunctive (e.g., « Qui que tu sois… »). Very commonly appears as « qui que ce soit » = “whoever it may be / anyone at all”.
target_language_example: Qui que tu sois, tu es le bienvenu.
native_language_example: Whoever you are, you’re welcome.

additional_notes: Used to mean an unspecified person, often with a negative idea ("anyone at all") or in conditional sentences. Common with negatives like « ne…pas/jamais/plus » and in clauses starting with « si » (if).
target_language_example: Si tu vois qui que ce soit, appelle-moi.
native_language_example: If you see anyone at all, call me.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or possibility. Often stands alone as a short reply, or followed by a clause (sometimes with inversion): "Qui sait ?" (Who knows?) / "Qui sait, peut-être qu’il viendra." (Who knows, maybe he’ll come.)
target_language_example: — Il va accepter ? — Qui sait !
native_language_example: — Will he accept? — Who knows!

meaning: alert; on the lookout (in: être sur le qui-vive).
additional_notes: Mostly used in the fixed expression « être sur le qui-vive », meaning to be watchful and ready to react (e.g., because something might happen). Often used with « rester » as well: « rester sur le qui-vive ». It’s a set phrase; you generally don’t use « qui vive » by itself in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Depuis les cambriolages dans le quartier, tout le monde est sur le qui-vive.
native_language_example: Since the burglaries in the neighborhood, everyone is on the lookout.

meaning: 'look who’s here!' / 'who do we have here!'
additional_notes: An exclamation used when someone arrives or you spot someone, often in a friendly or slightly playful tone. It’s short for the more explicit phrasing like « Qui voilà ? » or « Tiens, qui voilà ! ». You can also hear the plural « Qui voilà ? » addressed to a group. Not a literal translation of English; it’s an idiomatic way to announce someone’s presence.
target_language_example: Tiens, qui voilà ! Ça fait longtemps !
native_language_example: Well, look who’s here! It’s been a long time!

meaning: to leave the ship; (figuratively) to abandon a group/project when things go wrong.
additional_notes: Used literally for leaving a boat/ship, but very often used figuratively meaning “to jump ship” or “to abandon ship” (leave a team, company, relationship, or plan—especially at a difficult moment). Note: "quitter" often means “to leave” (a place/someone), not just “to quit” (stop an activity).
target_language_example: Quand l’entreprise a eu des problèmes, plusieurs employés ont quitté le navire.
native_language_example: When the company had problems, several employees jumped ship.

additional_notes: A very common, informal greeting question. Literally “what’s new?”, but often used like “what’s up?” You can answer with “Pas grand-chose.” (Not much.) or “Rien de spécial.” (Nothing special.).
target_language_example: Salut ! Quoi de neuf ?
native_language_example: Hi! What’s new?

meaning: “What now?” / “What else?” (often showing annoyance or disbelief).
additional_notes: Used as a short reaction when someone asks for more, complains, or says something surprising—similar to “What now?” or “What else is there?” Tone is often impatient or exasperated. In a neutral context it can simply mean “what else?”.
target_language_example: Tu veux encore de l’aide ? Quoi encore ?
native_language_example: You want help again? What now?

meaning: "what to do" / "what to do about it."
additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty about the next action, often after verbs like *savoir* or *dire*: *Je ne sais pas quoi faire* (“I don’t know what to do”), *Il ne sait pas quoi dire* (“He doesn’t know what to say”). It can also be used on its own as a question (*Quoi faire ?*) meaning “What should we do?”
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas quoi faire.
native_language_example: I don’t know what to do.

meaning: "be that as it may" / "whatever the case".
additional_notes: Very formal and literary (and somewhat old-fashioned). It means “in any case / anyway,” often used to move on despite uncertainty or disagreement. In modern everyday French, you’ll much more often see/hear: « quoi qu’il en soit ».
target_language_example: Quoi qu'il en fût, il fallait prendre une décision.
native_language_example: Be that as it may, we had to make a decision.

meaning: "anyway" / "in any case" / "whatever the case may be."
additional_notes: Used to move past a detail or disagreement and continue with the main point. More formal than "bref"; common in spoken and written French. Often followed by a comma: "Quoi qu'il en soit, ..."
target_language_example: Quoi qu'il en soit, on doit prendre une décision aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Anyway, we have to make a decision today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a concession: something is true regardless of the condition that follows (often with the subjunctive), e.g., "Quoi que tu fasses..." = "Whatever you do...". Don’t confuse it with "quoique" (one word), which usually means "although / even though" (e.g., "Quoique fatigué, il est sorti."). A common test: if you can replace it with "peu importe" (“no matter”), it’s usually "quoi que" (two words).
target_language_example: Quoi que tu décides, je te soutiendrai.
native_language_example: Whatever you decide, I’ll support you.

additional_notes: Means “anything at all” or “whatever it may be,” often used after negatives (ne…pas, ne…jamais), in questions, or in conditional sentences. Very common in phrases like: ne…rien faire de quoi que ce soit (“not do anything”), sans quoi que ce soit (“without anything”), or avant de faire quoi que ce soit (“before doing anything”). Not used to mean “something” in affirmative statements (use quelque chose instead).
target_language_example: Je n’ai rien vu ni entendu, quoi que ce soit.
native_language_example: I didn’t see or hear anything at all.

meaning: to tell stories; (often) to make things up / tell lies.
additional_notes: Literally “to tell stories,” but very commonly used to suggest someone is inventing excuses or lying (like “to spin a yarn”). In the negative, it often means “Stop making things up” (e.g., « Ne raconte pas d’histoires ! »).
target_language_example: Arrête de raconter des histoires, je sais que tu as oublié.
native_language_example: Stop making things up, I know you forgot.

meaning: to refresh someone’s memory; to jog someone’s memory.
additional_notes: Used when you want to remind someone of information they may have forgotten. Often followed by “à quelqu’un” (to someone) and/or “sur” (about): « Rafraîchis-moi la mémoire » (Remind me), « Je vais te rafraîchir la mémoire sur… » (I’ll remind you about…). It can be used politely or with a slightly threatening tone depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu ne te souviens pas ? Laisse-moi te rafraîchir la mémoire.
native_language_example: You don’t remember? Let me refresh your memory.

meaning: currant (dried); a small dried grape used in baking.
additional_notes: In everyday English, this corresponds to a dried currant used in cooking (often in cakes, biscuits, or trail mixes). In French, it’s a specific kind of small dried grape; you’ll commonly see it in recipes and on ingredient lists.
target_language_example: Ajoute des raisins de Corinthe dans le gâteau.
native_language_example: Add currants to the cake.

additional_notes: Used for a dried grape, often in baking/cooking (cakes, cookies, cereals) or in mixes like nuts and dried fruit. Singular: un raisin sec; plural: des raisins secs. Note that un raisin means a grape, while un raisin sec means a raisin.
target_language_example: Je voudrais un pain aux raisins secs, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a raisin bread, please.

meaning: the reason for being; main purpose.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the core purpose or justification of something (a person, project, company, rule, etc.). Often appears in the structure "la raison d'être de + noun" ("the purpose of..."). In French it’s a common, fairly formal expression; in English it’s also used as a loanword.
target_language_example: La raison d'être de cette association, c'est d'aider les personnes en difficulté.
native_language_example: The purpose of this organization is to help people in need.

additional_notes: Fairly formal/medical/neutral term (common in health contexts, legal texts, or serious conversation). In everyday speech, people may use other, more colloquial expressions. Often used with verbs like « avoir » (to have) or « avoir eu » (to have had).
target_language_example: Ils ont eu un rapport sexuel sans protection.
native_language_example: They had unprotected sex.

meaning: in relation to; regarding; compared with.
additional_notes: Used mainly in the fixed expression « par rapport à » to mean “compared with / relative to” (often for comparisons: « Par rapport à l’an dernier… » = “Compared with last year…”). Less commonly you may see « (avoir) rapport à » meaning “to relate to / to have to do with” in more formal writing. Note: « rapport » by itself can also mean “report,” but « par rapport à » is about comparison/relationship, not a written report.
target_language_example: Par rapport à l’année dernière, je travaille plus.
native_language_example: Compared with last year, I’m working more.

additional_notes: Common animal name. Literally means “washing little rat” (raton = “little rat”, laveur = “washer”), referring to the raccoon’s habit of handling food as if washing it. Plural: des ratons laveurs.
target_language_example: J’ai vu un raton laveur près des poubelles.
native_language_example: I saw a raccoon near the trash cans.

meaning: to make up for lost time.
additional_notes: Used when you want to compensate for time you didn’t use well or time you were separated from someone, by doing more now. Common in personal goals, work, study, or relationships. Conjugate the verb: je rattrape / tu rattrapes / il rattrape / nous rattrapons, etc.
target_language_example: Après les vacances, je dois rattraper le temps perdu au travail.
native_language_example: After the vacation, I have to make up for lost time at work.

additional_notes: An idiomatic expression meaning to stop being too proud and accept something (apologize, admit you’re wrong, accept help, etc.), even if it feels humiliating. You can conjugate it: « J’ai ravalé ma fierté », « Il va ravaler sa fierté ».
target_language_example: J’ai ravalé ma fierté et je lui ai demandé de l’aide.
native_language_example: I swallowed my pride and asked him for help.

additional_notes: Used for a literal beam of sunlight (often through clouds or a window). Can also be used figuratively to mean “a ray of sunshine” (something or someone that brings cheer). Plural: des rayons de soleil.
target_language_example: Un rayon de soleil entre par la fenêtre.
native_language_example: A ray of sunshine is coming in through the window.

meaning: to turn back; to go back the way you came.
additional_notes: Used when you stop going forward and return in the opposite direction (often because you’re lost, something is blocked, or you changed your mind). Common with "faire demi-tour" (to make a U-turn) as a near-synonym. Often used in the past: "On a rebroussé chemin" (We turned back).
target_language_example: On s’est perdu, alors on a rebroussé chemin.
native_language_example: We got lost, so we turned back.

additional_notes: Usually used as « un regard noir » (a glare). It describes a look that shows anger, disapproval, or annoyance, often without saying anything. You’ll also see the verb phrase « lancer un regard noir (à quelqu’un) » = “to shoot someone a dirty look / glare at someone.”
target_language_example: Quand il a entendu la blague, il m’a lancé un regard noir.
native_language_example: When he heard the joke, he shot me an angry look.

meaning: to come under; to fall within; to be a matter of.
additional_notes: Used to classify something as belonging to a category, field, or responsibility. Common patterns: "relever de + noun" (relever de la médecine = fall under medicine; relever du secret professionnel = be covered by professional secrecy) and "relever de + person/authority" (Ça relève du directeur = it’s up to the director / under the director’s authority). Often sounds formal/administrative and means “is under the jurisdiction/responsibility of.”
target_language_example: Ce dossier relève du service juridique.
native_language_example: This file falls under the legal department.

meaning: to call into question; to challenge.
additional_notes: Used when you question whether something is true, valid, fair, or should continue as it is. Common in formal or neutral contexts (work, school, news). Often followed by a direct object: « remettre en cause une décision / un plan / une théorie ». In the passive: « être remis(e) en cause » = “to be called into question.”
target_language_example: Ils ont remis en cause la décision du chef.
native_language_example: They called the boss’s decision into question.

meaning: to question; to call into question; to challenge (an idea/decision).
additional_notes: Used when you doubt something, reconsider it, or challenge its validity. Common with nouns like une décision, un projet, une méthode, une idée, un principe. Often followed by a direct object: « remettre en question + [thing] ». In everyday speech, it can also mean “to rethink” something.
target_language_example: Il faut remettre en question cette décision.
native_language_example: We need to question (rethink/challenge) this decision.

meaning: to put someone in their place; to set someone straight.
additional_notes: Used when someone is being rude, arrogant, or overstepping, and you (or someone else) respond firmly to stop them and remind them of their proper role/limits. Often implies a sharp verbal response or correction. Can also be reflexive (se remettre à sa place = to remember one’s place).
target_language_example: Il a commencé à critiquer tout le monde, alors je l’ai remis à sa place.
native_language_example: He started criticizing everyone, so I put him in his place.

meaning: to cheer (someone) up; to lift (someone’s) spirits.
additional_notes: Used when someone is sad, discouraged, or tired and you want to make them feel better. Often used as "remonter le moral à quelqu’un" (to boost someone’s morale) or reflexively "se remonter le moral" (to cheer oneself up). Common with verbs like "essayer de" (try to) or in the past: "Ça m’a remonté le moral" (That cheered me up).
target_language_example: J’essaie de lui remonter le moral après sa journée difficile.
native_language_example: I’m trying to cheer him/her up after a tough day.

meaning: to go back in time; to travel back in time.
additional_notes: Used literally for “time travel” (science fiction) and figuratively for “going back” to an earlier period (e.g., looking at old photos, remembering the past). Literally it’s “to go back up time,” so it doesn’t translate word-for-word into natural English.
target_language_example: Avec ces vieilles photos, j’ai l’impression de remonter le temps.
native_language_example: With these old photos, I feel like I’m going back in time.

meaning: to do everything possible; to move heaven and earth.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression meaning you’ll make every effort to achieve something (find someone, solve a problem, get something done). Often used with the idea of trying very hard, even desperately: « Je vais remuer ciel et terre pour… ».
target_language_example: Je vais remuer ciel et terre pour retrouver ton passeport.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything possible to find your passport.

additional_notes: Used for scheduled meetings like a doctor’s appointment (un rendez-vous chez le médecin), a business meeting, or a date. Common with the verb « avoir »: « J’ai un rendez-vous à 15 h. » It can also mean a place/time where people agree to meet: « On se donne rendez-vous à 18 h devant la gare. »
target_language_example: J’ai rendez-vous avec le médecin demain matin.
native_language_example: I have an appointment with the doctor tomorrow morning.

meaning: to report / to give an account (of something).
additional_notes: Often used as **rendre compte de + [thing]** (“to report on / to account for something”) or **rendre compte à + [person]** (“to report to someone”). Very common in formal/work contexts. Related reflexive form: **se rendre compte (de)** means “to realize (that)”.
target_language_example: Je dois rendre compte à mon chef de l’avancement du projet.
native_language_example: I have to report to my boss on the project’s progress.

meaning: to give thanks; to express gratitude (often to God).
additional_notes: Most often used with "à": "rendre grâce à quelqu’un" = to give thanks to someone. The expression is fairly formal/literary and is common in religious contexts (e.g., thanking God). In everyday speech, beginners more often use "remercier" or "dire merci".
target_language_example: Nous rendons grâce à Dieu pour cette chance.
native_language_example: We give thanks to God for this opportunity.

additional_notes: Used to show respect or admiration for someone, often in a formal context (a speech, ceremony, article). Common pattern: « rendre hommage à + person/thing » (e.g., a teacher, a victim, an artist, someone who died, or an achievement). It can also be used after someone’s death: « rendre hommage à sa mémoire » (to pay tribute to their memory).
target_language_example: Nous rendons hommage aux victimes.
native_language_example: We are paying tribute to the victims.

meaning: to do justice (to); to give someone/something the credit they deserve.
additional_notes: Used when you want to say you’re being fair in your judgment or properly recognizing someone/something. Common patterns: « rendre justice à quelqu’un/quelque chose » (do justice to someone/something) and « rendre justice à + [person] » meaning to acknowledge their merit (even if you disagree with them). Can also be used in legal contexts with the idea of justice being carried out, but in everyday speech it often means “give due credit.”
target_language_example: Il faut rendre justice à Marie : elle a beaucoup travaillé sur ce projet.
native_language_example: We have to give Marie credit: she worked a lot on this project.

meaning: to return the favor; repay in kind.
additional_notes: Used when you do something similar in return for what someone did (often a good deed, but it can also mean paying someone back in a negative sense). Often used with an object pronoun: « Je te rendrai la pareille » (“I’ll return the favor / I’ll pay you back”).
target_language_example: Merci pour ton aide hier, je te rendrai la pareille.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help yesterday; I’ll return the favor.

meaning: to do someone a favor; to help out.
additional_notes: Used when you help someone in a practical way. Common patterns: « rendre service à quelqu’un » (do someone a favor) and « Tu peux me rendre service ? » (Can you do me a favor?). Often followed by « en + -ant » to say how you help: « Tu peux me rendre service en gardant les enfants ? ».
target_language_example: Tu peux me rendre service et récupérer mon colis ?
native_language_example: Can you do me a favor and pick up my package?

additional_notes: Used with a direct object (the person): « rendre visite à quelqu’un ». You typically don’t use it for visiting places (for that, use « visiter »). Common in polite or everyday conversation and can imply paying someone a visit.
target_language_example: Je vais rendre visite à mes grands-parents ce week-end.
native_language_example: I’m going to visit my grandparents this weekend.

meaning: to go back to normal; to be put back in order.
additional_notes: Used when a situation becomes calm/organized again after trouble, confusion, or a disruption. Very common in the fixed phrase « Tout rentre dans l’ordre » (“Everything is back to normal”). Can be used about practical situations (a schedule, a system) or about relationships and conflicts.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tout va rentrer dans l’ordre.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything will go back to normal.

meaning: to bump into; to lay into (someone) / be harsh with (someone).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French. With a person: « rentrer dedans à quelqu’un » means to go at someone aggressively (verbally), to scold or pressure them. With a thing/person in an accident context, it can mean to crash into or bump into someone/something. Often used with an indirect object pronoun: « Il lui est rentré dedans » (He laid into him / He bumped into him, depending on context).
target_language_example: Le patron lui est rentré dedans devant tout le monde.
native_language_example: The boss laid into him in front of everyone.

additional_notes: Used when you restart something with nothing kept from before (a project, relationship, training plan, etc.). It often implies resetting everything and building again from the beginning. Common variants: « repartir de zéro » (same meaning) and « repartir à zéro après… » (after…).
target_language_example: Après cet échec, on va repartir à zéro et refaire un plan.
native_language_example: After that failure, we’re going to start over from scratch and make a new plan.

additional_notes: Used to express condolences or to honor someone who has died. Often written as "RIP"/"R.I.P." in French too. In a full sentence you’ll also see: "Qu’il/elle repose en paix" (“May he/she rest in peace”).
target_language_example: Il nous a quittés l’an dernier. Qu’il repose en paix.
native_language_example: He passed away last year. May he rest in peace.

meaning: "rest in peace" (said about someone who has died).
additional_notes: Very common funeral/condolence phrase, often written as « Reposez en paix » or abbreviated « R.I.P. ». The « -ez » ending is the polite/plural command (addressing the person formally or more than one person). You may also see the singular informal version « Repose en paix ».
target_language_example: Reposez en paix, Madame Dupont.
native_language_example: Rest in peace, Mrs. Dupont.

meaning: to regain consciousness; to come to.
additional_notes: Used when someone wakes up after fainting or being knocked out. Often used with "après" (after) or "quand" (when), and commonly in medical or emergency contexts. Related: "perdre connaissance" = to lose consciousness / to faint.
target_language_example: Il a repris connaissance après quelques minutes.
native_language_example: He regained consciousness after a few minutes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about fast-food restaurants or the fast-food sector in general (e.g., a place that serves food quickly, often burgers, sandwiches, fries). It’s a common, neutral term in ads, city signs, and business contexts. You can also say: « un restaurant de restauration rapide » (a fast-food restaurant).
target_language_example: On mange de la restauration rapide ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we eating fast food tonight?

meaning: to remain to be seen; to be decided/confirmed later.
additional_notes: Used to say the outcome is still uncertain or not yet known. Often appears with an impersonal subject: "Reste à voir si..." (= "It remains to be seen whether...").
target_language_example: Reste à voir si on aura le temps.
native_language_example: It remains to be seen whether we’ll have time.

additional_notes: Used literally (stop breathing for a moment) or figuratively (to wait anxiously/in suspense). You can conjugate retenir: je retiens, tu retiens, il/elle retient, nous retenons, vous retenez, ils/elles retiennent. Often used with pendant (for): « Retenez votre souffle pendant dix secondes. »
target_language_example: J’ai retenu mon souffle en attendant les résultats.
native_language_example: I held my breath while waiting for the results.

meaning: back to square one; having to start over.
additional_notes: Used when a plan or process fails and you have to begin again from the beginning. Comes from board games: the “starting square” (case départ). Often said as: « C’est le retour à la case départ. »
target_language_example: Sans les bons documents, c’est le retour à la case départ.
native_language_example: Without the right documents, it’s back to square one.

meaning: to come back to; to revisit (a topic); to go back on (a decision).
additional_notes: Used to return to a subject you mentioned earlier: "revenir sur un point / une question". It can also mean changing your mind about something: "revenir sur sa décision / sa promesse" (= to go back on it, retract it).
target_language_example: Je voudrais revenir sur ce point.
native_language_example: I’d like to come back to that point.

meaning: to come back to; to return to (a place, person, or topic).
additional_notes: Often used for returning to a subject in conversation: « On reviendra à ça plus tard. » It can also mean “to amount to / come to” with prices or totals: « Ça revient à 10 euros. »
target_language_example: On reviendra à ce point plus tard.
native_language_example: We’ll come back to this point later.

additional_notes: Used in buildings to mean the level at street/entrance level. Commonly abbreviated as « RDC » on signs and elevator buttons. In French, « le premier étage » is usually the floor above the rez-de-chaussée (so it may differ from U.S. usage where the ‘first floor’ can be the ground floor).
target_language_example: L’appartement est au rez-de-chaussée.
native_language_example: The apartment is on the ground floor.

meaning: nothing like that; nothing better than that.
additional_notes: Used to say that nothing compares to something (often in a positive, enthusiastic way), or to reject a comparison/idea (“nothing like that!”). Common pattern: « Rien de tel que + noun/infinitive » (Nothing like + ...). Can also be followed by « pour + infinitive » to say it’s the best way to do something.
target_language_example: Rien de tel qu’un bon café le matin.
native_language_example: There’s nothing like a good coffee in the morning.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that there is nothing (often as a short answer). Common in negatives with "ne... rien" (e.g., "Je n’ai rien du tout"), and can also be used alone: "Rien du tout."
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que tu as mangé ? — Rien du tout.
native_language_example: What did you eat? — Nothing at all.

additional_notes: Used before a word or phrase to mean “only/just” and to emphasize exclusivity (similar to “nothing but”). Often followed by a noun, an infinitive, or a clause introduced by “de” (e.g., “rien que de penser…”). You can also see it in set phrases like “rien que ça !” (“just that!” / “that’s all!”).
target_language_example: Je veux rien que dormir.
native_language_example: I just want to sleep.

meaning: nothing to do; nothing can be done.
additional_notes: Common in everyday speech. It can mean you have no tasks/activities ("nothing to do") or that a situation can’t be changed/fixed ("nothing can be done"). Often used with "Il n’y a rien à faire" (There’s nothing we can do) or "Rien à faire !" (No way!/It won’t work!).
target_language_example: Il n’y a rien à faire, le train est déjà parti.
native_language_example: There’s nothing we can do—the train has already left.

meaning: "don’t give a damn" / "don’t care at all" (very vulgar).
additional_notes: A strong, crude way to say you don’t care (about something) or it doesn’t matter to you. Built on the verb « foutre » (vulgar). Often used as « Je m’en fous » (less strong) or « J’en ai rien à foutre » (very strong). Avoid in polite/professional contexts.
target_language_example: J’en ai rien à foutre de ce qu’il pense.
native_language_example: I don’t give a damn what he thinks.

additional_notes: Used to say two things are unrelated or that a comparison doesn’t make sense. Often appears in the longer phrase "ça n’a rien à voir (avec ...)" = "it has nothing to do with ...". In casual speech you may also hear "rien à voir !" meaning "not the same at all!"
target_language_example: Ça n’a rien à voir avec mon problème.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with my problem.

meaning: to laugh out loud; to laugh heartily.
additional_notes: A common idiom for laughing very loudly and openly (often uncontrollably). Literally “to laugh with (one’s) throat wide open,” but the natural English meaning is “to laugh out loud / heartily.” Used in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: En voyant la vidéo, ils ont ri à gorge déployée.
native_language_example: When they saw the video, they laughed out loud.

additional_notes: Common food item; often used when ordering or describing a meal (e.g., as a side dish). Opposite of "riz complet" (brown/whole-grain rice).
target_language_example: Je voudrais du riz blanc, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like some white rice, please.

meaning: evening dress; formal dress for an evening event.
additional_notes: Used for more formal occasions (a party, gala, ceremony, wedding reception). Often implies a nicer, dressier outfit than an everyday dress. You can also hear "une robe de cocktail" for a less formal event.
target_language_example: Pour la cérémonie, elle a mis une robe de soirée noire.
native_language_example: For the ceremony, she wore a black evening dress.

additional_notes: Used for a mystery/crime story in book form (often abbreviated as "un polar" in informal speech). "Policier" here means related to police/crime investigation, not “polite.” Plural: "des romans policiers."
target_language_example: J’adore lire des romans policiers le soir.
native_language_example: I love reading detective novels in the evening.

additional_notes: Used mainly in car/travel contexts for an extra wheel kept in the trunk in case of a flat. By extension, it can also mean a “backup/stand-in” person or solution (similar to “plan B”).
target_language_example: On a eu une crevaison, alors on a mis la roue de secours.
native_language_example: We got a flat tire, so we put on the spare tire.

additional_notes: Common term for the cosmetic you put on your lips. Often used with the verb "mettre" (to put on) or "porter" (to wear): "mettre du rouge à lèvres" / "porter du rouge à lèvres". You can specify a color: "un rouge à lèvres rouge" (a red lipstick).
target_language_example: Elle met du rouge à lèvres avant de sortir.
native_language_example: She puts on lipstick before going out.

additional_notes: Commonly used on French menus for Vietnamese-style fresh spring rolls (often served cold), typically filled with shrimp, pork, vegetables, and noodles; plural: "rouleaux de printemps". Not the same as a fried "nems" (egg rolls).
target_language_example: Je vais prendre deux rouleaux de printemps, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’ll have two spring rolls, please.

additional_notes: Common everyday term for sticky tape used to seal, repair, or attach things (e.g., packing tape, clear tape). You’ll also hear more specific types like "ruban adhésif d’emballage" (packing tape) or "ruban adhésif double face" (double-sided tape).
target_language_example: Tu as du ruban adhésif pour fermer ce carton ?
native_language_example: Do you have any tape to seal this box?

additional_notes: Common in shops, pharmacies, and online shopping to say an item isn’t available right now. Often used with verbs like « être » (être en rupture de stock) or « avoir » (avoir une rupture de stock). It usually implies the product may come back later.
target_language_example: Désolé, ce produit est en rupture de stock pour le moment.
native_language_example: Sorry, this product is out of stock for the moment.

meaning: rule of the game; (by extension) a ground rule.
additional_notes: Most often used in the plural: « les règles du jeu » (“the rules of the game”). Can be literal (sports/board games) or figurative for how a situation works (e.g., in business, politics, relationships): « changer les règles du jeu » = “to change the rules/ground rules.” Note: « règle du jeu » can refer to one specific rule; « règles du jeu » refers to the full set.
target_language_example: Avant de commencer, expliquons les règles du jeu.
native_language_example: Before we start, let’s explain the rules of the game.

additional_notes: A common term in news and science for the long-term rise in Earth’s average temperature and its effects. Often used with verbs like « lutter contre » (to fight against) or « être dû à » (to be due to).
target_language_example: Le réchauffement climatique provoque des phénomènes météorologiques extrêmes.
native_language_example: Global warming causes extreme weather events.

meaning: to reduce to ashes; to burn down completely.
additional_notes: Used literally for something destroyed by fire (a house, a building, a forest). Also used figuratively to mean “to destroy completely” (plans, hopes, a reputation). Common pattern: réduire [quelque chose] en cendres.
target_language_example: L’incendie a réduit la maison en cendres.
native_language_example: The fire reduced the house to ashes.

meaning: to settle scores; to settle one’s accounts (often by confronting someone).
additional_notes: Literally “to settle one’s accounts.” It can be used in a neutral, financial sense (paying what you owe), but very often it’s figurative: to confront someone, get revenge, or finally address an old conflict (“settle scores”). Often used with “avec” (with): « régler ses comptes avec quelqu’un ».
target_language_example: Il a réglé ses comptes avec son ancien patron.
native_language_example: He settled scores with his former boss.

meaning: to settle scores with someone; to “deal with” someone (often threatening).
additional_notes: An idiomatic, often menacing expression meaning to take revenge or punish someone for something. It’s commonly used with an indirect object: « régler son compte à quelqu’un » (to deal with someone). Depending on context (especially in crime/action contexts), it can strongly imply “to kill” or “to finish someone off.”
target_language_example: Il a juré de lui régler son compte.
native_language_example: He swore he’d settle scores with him.

additional_notes: A polite way to ask someone to answer (often in formal situations, in a classroom, on a form, or in a customer-service context). "Répondez" is the imperative form of "répondre" used with "vous" (formal/polite or plural). You can also say "Réponds, s'il te plaît" when speaking to one person informally.
target_language_example: Répondez, s'il vous plaît, à toutes les questions.
native_language_example: Please answer all the questions.

additional_notes: Used for online platforms where people connect and share content. Often appears with verbs like utiliser (to use), publier sur (to post on), and suivre (to follow). Plural: réseaux sociaux.
target_language_example: Je n’utilise pas beaucoup les réseaux sociaux.
native_language_example: I don’t use social media much.

meaning: the American Dream (idea of success and upward mobility in the U.S.).
additional_notes: Used when talking about the belief that anyone can achieve a better life through hard work and opportunity in the United States; often discussed in social/political contexts and can be used neutrally or critically (e.g., saying it’s fading or is a myth). Usually preceded by "le": "le rêve américain".
target_language_example: Beaucoup de gens viennent aux États-Unis pour poursuivre le rêve américain.
native_language_example: Many people come to the United States to pursue the American Dream.

meaning: to be about; to be a question of.
additional_notes: Used mainly in the impersonal form "il s'agit de" to introduce what something is about or what the matter is. Common in more formal or written French. The "de" is required before a noun or infinitive: "Il s'agit d'un problème" / "Il s'agit de choisir". (Unlike English, you generally don’t say *"je m’agis de"*—it’s not used like a normal verb with a personal subject.)
target_language_example: Il s'agit de comprendre le problème avant d'agir.
native_language_example: It’s about understanding the problem before acting.

additional_notes: Very common verb meaning to leave a place or to go away. Often used with a subject pronoun: « je m’en vais », « tu t’en vas », « il/elle s’en va », « nous nous en allons », « vous vous en allez », « ils/elles s’en vont ». In the near future: « Je vais m’en aller » = “I’m going to leave.” Can also mean “to go” (when the idea is leaving): « On s’en va ! » = “Let’s go!”
target_language_example: Je dois m’en aller maintenant.
native_language_example: I have to leave now.

meaning: to not care (at all); to not give a damn.
additional_notes: Very informal and can be vulgar, depending on tone and context (from the verb « foutre »). Commonly used with an indirect object to say you don’t care about something: « Je m’en fous » = “I don’t care,” « Il s’en fout » = “He doesn’t care.” Often followed by « de + noun »: « Je m’en fous de ça » = “I don’t care about that.” Avoid in formal situations; use « je m’en moque » or « ça m’est égal » for a more neutral tone.
target_language_example: Je m’en fous de ce qu’ils pensent.
native_language_example: I don’t care what they think.

meaning: to manage; to get by; to make it through (a difficult situation).
additional_notes: A very common pronominal verb used when talking about coping with a problem, succeeding despite difficulty, or recovering from a tough situation. It conjugates with être in compound tenses (e.g., je m'en suis sorti(e)). Often followed by de + noun: s'en sortir de (cette situation).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tu vas t’en sortir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you’ll get through it.

meaning: “to have …” (passé composé with être), with “en” meaning “of it/about it/from it” and referring back to something already mentioned.
additional_notes: This isn’t usually used alone: it’s the auxiliary part of a longer verb phrase, where the main meaning comes from what follows (often a past participle). The reflexive pronoun changes (me/te/se/nous/vous/se), and “en” replaces a phrase with de (de ça / de ce problème, etc.). Very common patterns include: “s’en être rendu compte” (to have realized it), “s’en être sorti(e)” (to have gotten out of it / managed).
target_language_example: Je m’en suis rendu compte trop tard.
native_language_example: I realized it too late.

meaning: to get along; to understand each other.
additional_notes: Often used with "avec" and an adverb like "bien" or "mal": "s'entendre bien avec quelqu'un" = to get along well with someone. It can also mean “to be able to hear each other” (e.g., on the phone: "On s'entend ?" = "Can you hear me/each other?").
target_language_example: Je m'entends bien avec mes collègues.
native_language_example: I get along well with my coworkers.

additional_notes: Used to make a request politely when speaking to someone you address with 'tu' (a friend, child, someone your age in a casual setting). Literally 'if it pleases you'. For a formal or plural version, use 's'il vous plaît'. Also commonly written without the accent as 's'il te plait', but the correct spelling is 'plaît'.
target_language_example: Passe-moi le sel, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Pass me the salt, please.

additional_notes: Used when asking someone you address as "tu" (a friend, family member, child). Literally means “if it pleases you.” For formal situations or with "vous," use "s'il vous plaît." It can go at the beginning, middle, or end of a request: "S'il te plaît, ..." / "..., s'il te plaît."
target_language_example: Tu peux m'aider, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you help me, please?

additional_notes: Used to make a request more polite. Literally means “if it pleases you.” The spelling includes accents and an apostrophe: s'il vous plaît. For informal situations with one person you know well, you’ll often hear: s'il te plaît.
target_language_example: Un café, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: A coffee, please.

additional_notes: Very common polite phrase used to make requests or ask for something. Literally means “if it pleases you.” Use "s'il vous plaît" with "vous" (formal, strangers, or more than one person). With friends/family (singular "tu"), you often hear "s'il te plaît." It can also be used alone to mean “please?” (as in asking someone to repeat) or “yes, please” when accepting something: "Oui, s'il vous plaît."
target_language_example: Un café, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: A coffee, please.

meaning: to take care of; to deal with.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb: s’occuper de + noun/pronoun. Use it for caring for people/animals/things ("to look after") or handling a task/problem ("to take care of it"). Conjugates like occuper (je m’occupe, tu t’occupes, il/elle s’occupe, nous nous occupons, vous vous occupez, ils/elles s’occupent). Often followed by a person: "Je m’occupe de ma sœur."
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je m’occupe de tout.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll take care of everything.

meaning: to get started (on it); to start doing it.
additional_notes: Uses the pronoun “y” to refer back to what you’re starting (a task, activity, work, etc.). Common in everyday speech to mean you finally begin seriously: “Il faut s’y mettre” = “We’ve got to get started.” In the past: “Je m’y suis mis(e)” (agree with the speaker: mis / mise).
target_language_example: Bon, il est temps de s’y mettre !
native_language_example: Okay, it’s time to get started!

meaning: to go about it; to handle it (how to do something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s method or approach for doing something. Very common in questions with "comment" (how): "Comment tu t’y prends ?" = "How do you go about it?". It conjugates like "prendre" and changes with the subject: je m’y prends, tu t’y prends, il/elle s’y prend, nous nous y prenons, vous vous y prenez, ils/elles s’y prennent. Often followed by "pour" + infinitive: "s’y prendre pour + verb" (to go about doing something).
target_language_example: Comment tu t’y prends pour apprendre le français ?
native_language_example: How do you go about learning French?

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s mother; "sa" agrees with the thing owned (mère is feminine), not with the person (it can mean either “his” or “her”). For emphasis/clarity you can also say "la mère de [person]" (the mother of…).
target_language_example: Il habite avec sa mère.
native_language_example: He lives with his mother.

additional_notes: A common noun meaning a bag you carry on your back. Often used with an article (un sac à dos / le sac à dos). Related: faire son sac à dos = to pack your backpack.
target_language_example: N’oublie pas ton sac à dos pour l’école.
native_language_example: Don’t forget your backpack for school.

additional_notes: A common noun for a bag you carry by hand or on your arm, typically used by women. Often used with a possessive: « mon sac à main ». In everyday speech, « sac » alone may be understood from context, but « sac à main » is the clear term for a handbag (vs. « sac à dos » = backpack).
target_language_example: J’ai oublié mon sac à main dans le taxi.
native_language_example: I forgot my handbag in the taxi.

additional_notes: Used to say someone arrived or escaped without injury or danger. Often follows verbs like "arriver" (to arrive), "rentrer" (to come home), "s'en sortir" (to get out of it), or "retrouver" (to find).
target_language_example: Il est rentré sain et sauf après l'accident.
native_language_example: He came home safe and sound after the accident.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French as a shortened form of « (je) ne sais pas ». In conversation, people often drop « ne » (and sometimes « je »), so you may hear « je sais pas » or just « sais pas ». In writing, the more standard form is « je ne sais pas ».
target_language_example: — Tu viens ce soir ? — Sais pas, peut-être.
native_language_example: — Are you coming tonight? — I don’t know, maybe.

additional_notes: Inversion form of "tu sais ?" used to ask a question. It’s common in writing and in more formal speech than "tu sais ?". Often followed by a question word: "Sais-tu où..." (Do you know where...).
target_language_example: Sais-tu où est la station de métro ?
native_language_example: Do you know where the метро station is?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the time of year when it rains a lot, especially in tropical/subtropical climates. Often used with prepositions like pendant (during), en (in), or avant/après (before/after): « pendant la saison des pluies ».
target_language_example: Pendant la saison des pluies, il pleut presque tous les jours.
native_language_example: During the rainy season, it rains almost every day.

additional_notes: Common in work and pay discussions. Often used with the definite article: « le salaire minimum ». In France, you may also hear the acronym « le SMIC », which refers to the official minimum wage.
