native_language_example: He said he just wanted to get laid.

additional_notes: Emphatic form of "toi" used to stress that it’s you personally (not someone else). Often used after a preposition or at the end of a sentence, and in commands/advice: "Fais-le toi-même" (“Do it yourself”). Also used in the expression "toi-même !" meaning “you too!” (often as a comeback).
target_language_example: Tu peux le faire toi-même.
native_language_example: You can do it yourself.

additional_notes: Used to describe the moment you start being in love with someone: « tomber amoureux de + person » (masculine) / « tomber amoureuse de + person » (feminine). In the plural: « tomber amoureux/amoureuses ». Often used in the past tense: « Je suis tombé(e) amoureux(se) ».
target_language_example: Elle est tombée amoureuse de lui pendant les vacances.
native_language_example: She fell in love with him during the vacation.

meaning: to fall into; (figuratively) to fall for / get caught in.
additional_notes: Used with a noun after it (e.g., un trou, un piège). Literally it means physically falling into something: « tomber dans l’eau ». Very commonly used figuratively with things like « tomber dans le piège » (to fall into the trap), meaning you were tricked or got caught.
target_language_example: Il est tombé dans le piège.
native_language_example: He fell into the trap (he got tricked).

additional_notes: Common idiom in everyday spoken French. It means suddenly losing consciousness (often from heat, shock, seeing blood, etc.). It’s not literal (it doesn’t involve apples). You can also say: « Je suis tombé(e) dans les pommes » (I fainted).
target_language_example: Il faisait tellement chaud que je suis tombée dans les pommes dans le métro.
native_language_example: It was so hot that I fainted on the subway.

meaning: to come out of nowhere; to be totally unexpected (sometimes: a welcome surprise).
additional_notes: Literally “to fall from the sky.” Used to say something arrives unexpectedly, or that you didn’t anticipate it at all. Can also imply something is a lucky stroke (“just what I needed”). Often used in the negative: “Ça ne tombe pas du ciel” = “It doesn’t come out of nowhere / It’s not by magic.”
target_language_example: Son appel m’est tombé du ciel : j’avais justement besoin de parler à quelqu’un.
native_language_example: Her call came out of nowhere—in fact, I really needed to talk to someone.

meaning: to break down; to stop working (for a machine/vehicle).
additional_notes: Used when a car, device, elevator, etc. suddenly stops functioning. Very common with vehicles: « Ma voiture est tombée en panne. » You can also use it in the present: « Ça tombe en panne. » (It keeps breaking down / It’s breaking down.) Related noun: « une panne » = a breakdown/failure.
target_language_example: Ma voiture est tombée en panne sur l’autoroute.
native_language_example: My car broke down on the highway.

meaning: to get pregnant; to become pregnant.
additional_notes: Literally “to fall pregnant,” but it simply means “to get/become pregnant.” Use it mainly for the moment of becoming pregnant (not for being pregnant over time). For “to be pregnant,” you usually say « être enceinte ».
target_language_example: Elle est tombée enceinte à 28 ans.
native_language_example: She got pregnant at 28.

meaning: to get sick; to fall ill.
additional_notes: Used to talk about becoming ill (the change of state), not being ill already. Often used with past tenses to say someone got sick (e.g., "Il est tombé malade"). For being sick, you usually use "être malade" (e.g., "Je suis malade").
target_language_example: Il est tombé malade la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: He got sick last week.

meaning: to run into; to come across (unexpectedly).
additional_notes: Often used for unexpected meetings or discoveries. It can mean meeting someone by chance (Tomber sur quelqu’un) or finding something unexpectedly (Tomber sur quelque chose). Literally it means “to fall on,” but in everyday French it usually has the “stumble upon” meaning.
target_language_example: Je suis tombé sur Marie au supermarché.
native_language_example: I ran into Marie at the supermarket.

meaning: to fall flat; to flop (not have the intended effect).
additional_notes: Used when something (a joke, an idea, a plan, an event) fails or doesn’t get the expected reaction. Often said about humor: « La blague est tombée à plat » = “The joke fell flat.”
target_language_example: J’ai essayé de faire une blague, mais elle est tombée à plat.
native_language_example: I tried to make a joke, but it fell flat.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the moment when it starts getting dark and night arrives. Often appears with prepositions like "à la tombée de la nuit" (at nightfall) or "dès la tombée de la nuit" (as soon as night falls).
target_language_example: À la tombée de la nuit, on est rentrés à la maison.
native_language_example: At nightfall, we went back home.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s upper body is uncovered (no shirt). Often with être: « être torse nu ». You’ll also see it after a noun: « un homme torse nu ». « Nu » agrees with gender/number (e.g., « des hommes torse nu(s) » / « une femme torse nue »).
target_language_example: Il est sorti torse nu malgré le froid.
native_language_example: He went out shirtless despite the cold.

meaning: to knock on wood (to avoid bad luck after saying something optimistic).
additional_notes: Used after mentioning good news or hoping something will continue to go well, as a superstitious way to prevent jinxing it. Often said as a quick aside: « Je n’ai jamais eu d’accident, je touche du bois. »
target_language_example: Tout se passe bien jusqu’ici, je touche du bois.
native_language_example: Everything is going well so far, knock on wood.

meaning: to hit rock bottom (to reach your lowest point).
additional_notes: Often used figuratively for a difficult period (financially, emotionally, addiction, etc.). Literally it means “to touch the bottom,” but in everyday French it commonly means reaching the worst moment before things can improve. You can also use it in the past: « J’ai touché le fond. »
target_language_example: Après avoir perdu son travail, il a touché le fond, mais il s’en est remis.
native_language_example: After losing his job, he hit rock bottom, but he recovered from it.

meaning: to mention (something) briefly; to say a word (about).
additional_notes: Used when you want to bring up a topic quickly or discreetly, often with "à" + person: "toucher un mot à quelqu’un" = to have a quick word with someone / to mention it to them. Can also be used with "de" + topic: "toucher un mot de quelque chose" = to mention something. Slightly informal/colloquial.
target_language_example: Je vais toucher un mot au chef de ce problème.
native_language_example: I’m going to mention this problem to the boss.

meaning: to be coming to an end.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is almost finished (an event, a trip, a meeting, a period of time). Often used in the present tense: « La réunion touche à sa fin » = “The meeting is coming to an end.”
target_language_example: Les vacances touchent à leur fin, il faut rentrer demain.
native_language_example: The vacation is coming to an end; we have to go back tomorrow.

meaning: still just as (…); as … as ever.
additional_notes: Used to say something hasn’t changed: the person/thing is the same as before in degree or quality. It’s usually followed by an adjective or adverb (e.g., toujours aussi fatigué(e), toujours aussi bien). Often used in comparisons or when reacting to something familiar.
target_language_example: Tu es toujours aussi drôle !
native_language_example: You’re still just as funny!

additional_notes: Used for a trick performed by a magician (on stage or close-up). You can say faire un tour de magie (“to do/perform a magic trick”) or montrer un tour de magie (“to show a magic trick”).
target_language_example: Il nous a fait un tour de magie incroyable.
native_language_example: He did an incredible magic trick for us.

meaning: a magic trick; sleight of hand.
additional_notes: Used for tricks done by a magician (often with quick hand movements). It can also be used figuratively to suggest a deceptive or sneaky maneuver (e.g., in business or politics).
target_language_example: Le magicien a fait un tour de passe-passe avec une pièce.
native_language_example: The magician did a sleight-of-hand trick with a coin.

meaning: To beat around the bush; to avoid getting to the point.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used when someone avoids saying something directly (often about an uncomfortable topic). It’s common in spoken French and can sound slightly informal. Often used with the imperative: « Arrête de tourner autour du pot ! »
target_language_example: Arrête de tourner autour du pot et dis-moi la vérité.
native_language_example: Stop beating around the bush and tell me the truth.

meaning: to go around in circles; to make no progress.
additional_notes: Used literally (walking/driving around a circle) and very commonly figuratively to mean being stuck, repeating the same thing, or not moving forward in a discussion or process. Often said with verbs like "on" (we), "je" (I), "ça" (it): "On tourne en rond."
target_language_example: On tourne en rond : on n’a toujours pas trouvé de solution.
native_language_example: We’re going around in circles: we still haven’t found a solution.

meaning: to move on; to put the past behind you.
additional_notes: Used both literally (turning a page in a book) and, very commonly, figuratively to mean leaving a difficult situation, relationship, or period of life behind and starting fresh. Often used with "il faut" or "je veux" (e.g., "Il faut tourner la page").
target_language_example: Après leur rupture, elle a décidé de tourner la page.
native_language_example: After their breakup, she decided to move on.

additional_notes: Used literally (physically turning away) and figuratively (to reject, abandon, or refuse to help). Often followed by "à" + person/thing: "tourner le dos à quelqu’un". Can also appear as "tourner le dos à" in many contexts.
target_language_example: Il a tourné le dos à ses anciens amis.
native_language_example: He turned his back on his old friends.

meaning: both (of them); the two of them.
additional_notes: Used to refer specifically to two people or two things together. Often used with people: "Ils sont tous deux…" = "They are both…". It agrees in gender: tous deux (masculine/mixed), toutes deux (feminine). Similar in meaning to "les deux", but "tous/toutes deux" emphasizes “both” a bit more.
target_language_example: Ils sont tous deux très gentils.
native_language_example: They are both very nice.

additional_notes: Used to talk about two people or things together. It agrees in gender/number: "tous les deux" (masculine or mixed group) and "toutes les deux" (two females). Often placed after the subject or at the end of the sentence: "Ils viennent tous les deux." / "Je les connais tous les deux."
target_language_example: Je les ai vus tous les deux au café.
native_language_example: I saw both of them at the café.

additional_notes: Common time expression meaning something happens daily. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence. Can also be used as an answer to “À quelle fréquence ?” (How often?).
target_language_example: Je vais au travail tous les jours.
native_language_example: I go to work every day.

additional_notes: Used to give an upper limit and to downplay the quantity, time, or likelihood (often implying it won’t be more than that). Common with numbers or durations: "Il y en a tout au plus dix" (no more than ten). It can also soften a statement: "C’est tout au plus une hypothèse" (only a hypothesis at best).
target_language_example: J’arriverai dans dix minutes, quinze tout au plus.
native_language_example: I’ll arrive in ten minutes, fifteen at most.

additional_notes: Used as a short, friendly confirmation that things are okay or completed (similar to “all set” or “good to go”). You’ll often hear it in replies like « C’est tout bon » (“It’s all good / We’re all set”). It can also be said after checking something to mean “Correct!”. Common in everyday spoken French; sounds informal/colloquial.
target_language_example: — J’ai envoyé le mail. — Tout bon, merci !
native_language_example: — I sent the email. — All good, thanks!

additional_notes: Used to refer to the total set of things that satisfy a description. It introduces a relative clause and is followed by a verb: « tout ce qui + verb ». Often corresponds to English “everything that…” (or “anything that…” depending on context).
target_language_example: Je vais te dire tout ce qui s’est passé.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you everything that happened.

meaning: Intended meaning: “anything / every thing” (but this form is incorrect).
additional_notes: In French, the correct phrase is **toute chose** (feminine singular) because **chose** is feminine: *une chose*. You may also see **toutes choses** (plural), but the expression is fairly formal/literary; in everyday speech you more often say **tout** (“everything”) or **n’importe quoi** (“anything/whatever,” often with a casual tone).
target_language_example: Toute chose a son importance.
native_language_example: Everything has its importance.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things or two situations: A is like B. Often followed by a noun/pronoun or a clause (e.g., “tout comme moi / tout comme tu le dis”). It can sound slightly formal compared to “comme”.
target_language_example: Tout comme toi, j’aime le chocolat.
native_language_example: Just like you, I like chocolate.

meaning: "all things considered" / "when all is said and done".
additional_notes: Used to sum up your final opinion after thinking about different factors. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence (Tout compte fait, …) or at the end (…, tout compte fait.). Neutral register.
target_language_example: Tout compte fait, je pense que c’est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: All things considered, I think it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to express contrast or concession: something is true despite what was just said (similar to 'nevertheless'). Often placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il pleuvait, mais on est sortis tout de même.
native_language_example: It was raining, but we went out anyway.

additional_notes: Common time expression meaning something will happen without delay. In everyday speech it can also mean "very soon" (depending on context and tone), but its core meaning is "immediately." Often used to respond to requests: « Oui, tout de suite. »
target_language_example: J’arrive tout de suite.
native_language_example: I’m coming right away.

additional_notes: Commonly used for directions: aller tout droit = to go straight ahead. It can also mean 'directly' in the sense of 'without detour' or 'immediately' (e.g., aller tout droit à la maison = go straight home). Often appears after verbs of movement like aller, continuer, marcher.
target_language_example: Allez tout droit jusqu’au carrefour, puis tournez à gauche.
native_language_example: Go straight ahead to the intersection, then turn left.

meaning: 'that's all there is to say' / 'enough said'.
additional_notes: Used to conclude a discussion or argument: the speaker implies everything important has already been said and there’s nothing more to add (often after giving a key point or summary). Can be neutral but may sound firm or final, sometimes slightly blunt depending on tone.
target_language_example: Je t’ai expliqué la situation : tout est dit.
native_language_example: I’ve explained the situation: that’s all there is to say.

additional_notes: Used to say something is spoken (not just thought). Often with verbs like dire/parler/lire: « dire tout haut », « parler tout haut » (= speak loudly / out loud, depending on context). Also common in the expression « tout haut et tout bas » (“aloud and to oneself/under one’s breath”).
target_language_example: Je ne l’ai pas dit tout haut, mais je le pensais.
native_language_example: I didn’t say it out loud, but I was thinking it.

additional_notes: Means “everyone/ everybody” in a general sense (all people). Often used as the subject of a sentence: “Tout le monde est…” (Everyone is…). Can also be used after prepositions like avec/pour: “avec tout le monde” (with everyone).
target_language_example: Tout le monde est prêt ?
native_language_example: Is everyone ready?

tout le plaisir est pour moi

target_language_multi_word_term: tout le plaisir est pour moi
additional_notes: A polite reply after someone says “Merci” or “Enchanté(e)” (Nice to meet you). It’s a formal/very polite way to say you’re happy to help or happy to meet them. You can also hear “Le plaisir est pour moi.”
target_language_example: — Merci pour votre aide. — Tout le plaisir est pour moi.
native_language_example: — Thank you for your help. — The pleasure is all mine.

additional_notes: Common adverb phrase meaning something happens very often or constantly. Depending on context it can mean literally continuously ("all the time") or more generally "always". Often placed after the verb: « Je travaille tout le temps. » Can also be used at the beginning for emphasis: « Tout le temps, il se plaint. »
target_language_example: Elle est tout le temps en retard.
native_language_example: She is late all the time.

additional_notes: Used with the verb « être » (often « Je suis tout ouïe ») to show you’re ready to listen carefully. « Ouïe » means “hearing” (a noun), so the expression is slightly idiomatic but very common and not slang.
target_language_example: Vas-y, je suis tout ouïe : raconte-moi ce qui s’est passé.
native_language_example: Go ahead, I’m all ears: tell me what happened.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize small size (literally “all small”). Often agrees with the noun: masculine singular tout petit, feminine singular toute petite, masculine plural tout petits, feminine plural toutes petites. Can describe a person/child (very young/small) or an object (tiny).
target_language_example: Quand j’étais tout petit, j’habitais à Lyon.
native_language_example: When I was very little, I lived in Lyon.

additional_notes: Very common spoken filler used at the end of a list to mean “etc.” or “you know, the whole thing.” It’s informal and mainly used in conversation (you’ll sometimes hear it as “tout ça, quoi”).
target_language_example: On a parlé de boulot, de vacances, tout quoi.
native_language_example: We talked about work, vacations, and all that.

additional_notes: Means being alone or doing something without help/without anyone else. It agrees with the person: masculine singular is "tout seul"; feminine singular is "toute seule"; masculine plural "tout seuls"; feminine plural "toutes seules". Often used after the noun/pronoun: "Il est tout seul." / "Je suis tout seul."
target_language_example: Je peux le faire tout seul.
native_language_example: I can do it by myself.

additional_notes: Describes someone who is smiling a lot and looks happy/pleased. Often used with the verb "être" (e.g., "Il est tout sourire") or as a descriptive phrase (e.g., "un visage tout sourire"). It’s a figurative expression rather than literally “everything smile.”
target_language_example: Elle est arrivée tout sourire, heureuse de nous voir.
native_language_example: She arrived all smiles, happy to see us.

additional_notes: A fairly formal/literary way to mean “anyone/everyone,” emphasizing an average person (not a specialist or VIP). Often used with “pour,” “à la portée de,” or “accessible à” (e.g., “accessible à tout un chacun”).
target_language_example: Ce guide est clair et accessible à tout un chacun.
native_language_example: This guide is clear and accessible to everyone.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens unexpectedly, often mid-story or when describing a change. Common in both speaking and writing. Similar idea to "soudain" (more formal/literary) or "d’un coup" (more spoken).
target_language_example: Tout à coup, il s’est mis à pleuvoir.
native_language_example: All of a sudden, it started to rain.

meaning: completely; exactly; (in replies) absolutely / yes, exactly.
additional_notes: Commonly used to agree strongly with what someone said: “Tout à fait !” (“Absolutely!/Exactly!”). It can also mean “completely” before an adjective or phrase: “tout à fait d’accord” (“completely in agreement”), “tout à fait possible” (“completely possible”). Often a bit more formal/neutral than “carrément”.
target_language_example: — Tu es d’accord ? — Oui, tout à fait.
native_language_example: — Do you agree? — Yes, absolutely.

meaning: 'earlier' or 'in a little while' (a short time ago / a short time from now).
additional_notes: Used for a vague, short time period close to the present. It can refer to the recent past ("earlier today") or the near future ("in a little while"), and context (or verb tense) tells you which one. Common with: "à tout à l'heure" = "see you later" (soon).
target_language_example: Je te rappelle tout à l'heure.
native_language_example: I’ll call you back later (in a little while).

meaning: all at once; at the same time.
additional_notes: Used to say that several things happen simultaneously, or that someone has several qualities simultaneously. Common with verbs like "faire", "dire", "être". Can also emphasize that doing everything together is too much (similar to "all at once").
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas tout faire tout à la fois.
native_language_example: I can’t do everything all at once.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a whole set of things just mentioned or understood from context (ideas, problems, events, etc.). Often comes at the end of a sentence for emphasis: "et tout ça" = "and all that" / "and stuff like that". Can refer to "this" or "that" depending on context; in speech it often just means "all that stuff".
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas le temps de faire le ménage, les courses et tout ça.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to do the cleaning, the shopping, and all that.

additional_notes: Adjective meaning “having unlimited power.” Often used in religious contexts for God ("Dieu tout-puissant" = “Almighty God”), but it can also describe a person or organization seen as extremely powerful (sometimes with a critical tone). It agrees in gender/number: tout-puissant (m. sg.), toute-puissante (f. sg.), tout-puissants (m. pl.), toutes-puissantes (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Dieu tout-puissant, protège-nous.
native_language_example: Almighty God, protect us.

additional_notes: Literally “steam-powered train.” Used for historical or tourist trains (often in museums, heritage railways, or old-time travel contexts). In everyday modern travel you’re more likely to hear "train" or "TGV" for high-speed trains.
target_language_example: On a pris un train à vapeur pendant les vacances.
native_language_example: We took a steam train during the vacation.

meaning: word processing (text editing on a computer).
additional_notes: Used for software or tools used to write, edit, and format documents (e.g., Microsoft Word, Google Docs). You may also hear it as part of a longer phrase like « logiciel de traitement de texte » (word-processing software).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin d’un logiciel de traitement de texte pour écrire mon CV.
native_language_example: I need word-processing software to write my resume.

additional_notes: A formal agreement (usually between countries or groups) that officially ends a war or conflict. Very common in history, politics, and news. Often used with a specific treaty name or date (e.g., un traité de paix signé en 1945).
target_language_example: Les deux pays ont signé un traité de paix après la guerre.
native_language_example: The two countries signed a peace treaty after the war.

additional_notes: Common in school and professional contexts. Often used with verbs like « favoriser » (to encourage), « améliorer » (to improve), or « faire » (to do). You can also say « esprit d'équipe » for “team spirit.”
target_language_example: Dans ce projet, le travail d'équipe est essentiel.
native_language_example: In this project, teamwork is essential.

additional_notes: Neutral/formal term for a person who provides sexual services in exchange for money. Often appears in the feminine as « travailleuse du sexe »; plural: « travailleurs/travailleuses du sexe ». « du » = « de + le » (“of the”). You may also see inclusive spelling: « travailleur·se du sexe ».
target_language_example: Elle est travailleuse du sexe et elle veut travailler en sécurité.
native_language_example: She is a sex worker and she wants to work safely.

additional_notes: A neutral, respectful term meaning a woman who does sex work. The masculine is « travailleur du sexe » and the plural is « travailleurs/travailleuses du sexe ». You may also see « personne travailleuse du sexe » as a more gender-neutral option. It’s used in formal contexts (health, social services, news) more than in casual conversation.
target_language_example: Elle dit qu’elle est travailleuse du sexe.
native_language_example: She says she is a sex worker.

meaning: to cross someone’s mind; to occur to someone.
additional_notes: Used for ideas or thoughts that suddenly appear, often briefly. Very common in the past tense: « Ça m’a traversé l’esprit » (“It crossed my mind / It occurred to me”). You can change the indirect object to show who it occurs to: m’ (me), t’ (you), lui (him/her), nous (us), vous (you), leur (them).
target_language_example: Ça m’a traversé l’esprit d’appeler Marie, mais j’ai oublié.
native_language_example: It crossed my mind to call Marie, but I forgot.

additional_notes: The standard, neutral term for an earthquake (often used in news and safety contexts). Also commonly said as "un séisme". Plural: "des tremblements de terre".
target_language_example: Il y a eu un tremblement de terre cette nuit.
native_language_example: There was an earthquake last night.

meaning: to shake like a leaf; to tremble a lot (from fear, cold, etc.).
additional_notes: Common comparison meaning someone is trembling visibly and strongly. Used with emotions (especially fear or nervousness) or physical causes like cold. Structure: "trembler" + "comme" + "une feuille".
target_language_example: Il tremblait comme une feuille avant l’entretien.
native_language_example: He was shaking like a leaf before the interview.

meaning: (slang, vulgar) to have sex (usually said about a man).
additional_notes: A crude, humorous euphemism (literally “to dip one’s cookie/biscuit”). Often used jokingly or as a slightly sexist way to talk about a man having sex; avoid in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Il était tout content parce qu’il avait enfin trempé son biscuit.
native_language_example: He was really happy because he’d finally had sex.

additional_notes: The number 31. In French, compound numbers are usually written with hyphens: trente-et-un. Used for dates (le trente-et-un mai = May 31st), counting, prices, etc.
target_language_example: On est le trente-et-un décembre.
native_language_example: It’s December 31st.

additional_notes: Used to express the number 300. Note the spelling rule: *cent* takes an **-s** (*cents*) when it is multiplied and **not** followed by another number: *trois cents* (300) but *trois cent un* (301) and *trois cent vingt* (320).
target_language_example: J’ai dépensé trois cents euros.
native_language_example: I spent three hundred euros.

additional_notes: Used when something seems so perfect or advantageous that you suspect it isn’t real or won’t happen. Often said about deals, offers, or surprising good news. You can also shorten it in casual speech: « C’est trop beau pour être vrai. »
target_language_example: Cette promo est trop belle pour être vraie, non ?
native_language_example: This sale is too good to be true, isn’t it?

additional_notes: Used before a noun to say the quantity is excessive. Use **trop de + noun** (e.g., trop de travail). The noun can be singular or plural depending on what you’re counting. Often followed by **pour + infinitive** to mean “too much to…”: *trop de bruit pour dormir*.
target_language_example: Il y a trop de monde ici.
native_language_example: There are too many people here.

additional_notes: A very rude, vulgar way to call someone an “asshole” (literally “ass hole”). Stronger than “imbécile” or “idiot” and best avoided in polite situations. Can refer to a person: “C’est un trou de cul.” Plural: “des trous de cul.”
target_language_example: Ne lui parle pas : c’est un trou de cul.
native_language_example: Don’t talk to him: he’s an asshole.

additional_notes: Very crude/vulgar slang used to insult someone (like calling them an “asshole”). Not appropriate in polite conversation; can be offensive and escalate conflict. Literally “hole of the butt/ass.”
target_language_example: Arrête de te comporter comme un trou du cul !
native_language_example: Stop acting like an asshole!

meaning: black hole; (figurative) a place/time where things disappear or are forgotten.
additional_notes: Literal meaning is the astronomical “black hole” (a region in space with very strong gravity). Figuratively, it can describe a memory lapse (“a blank”), or something that absorbs time/money/attention with little result (e.g., paperwork, a project). In everyday speech you might also hear “un trou de mémoire” for “a memory blank,” but “un trou noir” can be used more generally for something that swallows things up.
target_language_example: Depuis que j’ai commencé ce projet, c’est un vrai trou noir : j’y passe des heures et je n’avance pas.
native_language_example: Since I started this project, it’s a real black hole: I spend hours on it and I don’t make progress.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has objections or is critical, often implying they’re being picky. Common pattern: « Je n’ai rien à redire » = “I have nothing to complain about / nothing to criticize.” You can also say « Il y a toujours quelque chose à redire » (there’s always something to criticize).
target_language_example: Je n’ai rien à redire sur ton travail.
native_language_example: I have nothing to criticize about your work.

additional_notes: Used to say something is going well or to show approval (like “very good”/“great”). It can also be a neutral agreement/acknowledgment: “OK, fine.” You’ll hear it in answers to “Ça va ?” (I’m doing very well) and in evaluations (a teacher might say “Très bien !”).
target_language_example: — Ça va ? — Oui, très bien, merci.
native_language_example: — How are you? — Yes, very well, thank you.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree with what someone just said. Literally “you have said it,” where “l’” stands for “it” (the thing that was just said). Often said on its own as a reaction; can also be used with emphasis: “Tu l’as dit !”.
target_language_example: — C’est vraiment cher. — Tu l’as dit !
native_language_example: — It’s really expensive. — You said it!

additional_notes: Literally, it’s like saying “you are missing (to) me.” In French, with "manquer," the person who is missed is the subject: "tu me manques" = I miss you; "je te manque" = you miss me. Can be used with friends, family, or romantically.
target_language_example: Tu me manques beaucoup depuis ton départ.
native_language_example: I miss you a lot since you left.

additional_notes: Often used as an exclamation: « Tu parles ! » to show you don’t believe what was said or you strongly disagree. Very common in spoken French and informal. (Literally it means “you speak/you’re talking,” but the sarcastic meaning is the one learners usually hear.)
target_language_example: Il dit qu’il va arrêter de fumer demain. Tu parles !
native_language_example: He says he’s going to quit smoking tomorrow. Yeah right!

meaning: “you’re talking about…” / “you mean…” (asking what someone is referring to).
additional_notes: Used with the informal subject pronoun tu (“you”) to ask or clarify the topic: Tu parles de quoi ? (“What are you talking about?”). It’s often followed by a noun or pronoun: Tu parles de Marie ? (“Are you talking about Marie?”). In a more formal register, use vous parlez de…. Note: tu parles! (without de) can also mean “Yeah, right!”, but tu parles de is usually literal.
target_language_example: Tu parles de quel film ?
native_language_example: Which movie are you talking about?

meaning: 'you can speak' / 'you can talk' (to one person).
additional_notes: Uses informal singular "tu" (talking to a friend, child, or someone you’re on "tu" terms with). "Peux" is the "tu" form of "pouvoir" (can/to be able to). Often used to invite someone to talk or to ask if they’re able to speak: "Tu peux parler ?" can mean "Can you talk/speak?" or "Is it okay for you to talk (right now)?"
target_language_example: Tu peux parler plus lentement, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you speak more slowly, please?

additional_notes: Common in casual conversation (uses tu). It can be a real question (“Do you know...?”) or a filler/discourse marker like English “you know,” to introduce or soften what you’re saying. In more formal situations, use “vous savez”.
target_language_example: Tu sais, je pense que c’est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: You know, I think it’s a good idea.

meaning: "you know what?" (used to introduce what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Very common in casual conversation to get someone’s attention, build suspense, or announce a decision/idea. Often followed by a pause and then the point you want to make. Can also sound slightly annoyed depending on tone.
target_language_example: Tu sais quoi ? On va au cinéma ce soir.
native_language_example: You know what? We’re going to the movies tonight.

meaning: to kill time; to pass the time.
additional_notes: Common, neutral expression used when you’re waiting or have nothing to do. Often used with "pour" + infinitive to say how you’ll pass the time (e.g., "pour tuer le temps, je…"). Also used with "en" + present participle (e.g., "en lisant").
target_language_example: Pour tuer le temps, j’ai lu un livre en attendant le train.
native_language_example: To kill time, I read a book while waiting for the train.

additional_notes: Used for a person who kills multiple victims in separate incidents over time (often in crime news, books, and documentaries). Literally “killer in series,” but the natural English equivalent is “serial killer.” The feminine form is "tueuse en série".
target_language_example: La police pense qu’il s’agit d’un tueur en série.
native_language_example: The police think it’s a serial killer.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone paid to kill a specific person. Common in news, crime stories, and movies. The structure is literally “killer for wages/fee,” and it’s typically masculine; the feminine form is "tueuse à gages" (less common).
target_language_example: La police pense qu’il s’agit d’un tueur à gages.
native_language_example: The police think it’s a hitman.

additional_notes: Used to describe a woman who has killed multiple people in separate events over time. Feminine form of "tueur en série". Common in news, true-crime, and police contexts; strong/serious topic.
target_language_example: La police pense qu’il s’agit d’une tueuse en série.
native_language_example: The police think it’s a female serial killer.

additional_notes: A common neutral term for a cellphone (often shortened to « mobile »). « Téléphone portable » is also very common; in France, « portable » alone often means a cellphone. In Quebec, you may also hear « cellulaire ».
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mon téléphone mobile à la maison.
native_language_example: I forgot my mobile phone at home.

additional_notes: Common everyday term for a phone you carry with you (as opposed to a landline, "téléphone fixe"). Often shortened to "portable" in conversation ("J’ai oublié mon portable").
target_language_example: Tu as un téléphone portable ?
native_language_example: Do you have a mobile phone?

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object introduced by "à": téléphoner à quelqu’un = to call someone. The person is usually replaced by an indirect object pronoun: "Je lui téléphone" (I’m calling him/her), "Je leur téléphone" (I’m calling them). For phone numbers, you can also say: "téléphoner au + number" or more commonly "appeler au + number".
target_language_example: Je vais téléphoner à ma mère ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to call my mother tonight.

additional_notes: Used in legal/news contexts for someone who personally saw an event happen. Often appears with "un/une" (un témoin oculaire / une témoin oculaire) or in the plural (des témoins oculaires).
target_language_example: La police cherche un témoin oculaire de l’accident.
native_language_example: The police are looking for an eyewitness to the accident.

meaning: lead candidate (at the top of a party list).
additional_notes: Mostly used in politics (elections with party lists). It refers to the person placed first on a party’s list of candidates, often the best-known candidate and the one who ‘leads’ the list. Also used more generally to mean the top/leading name on any list.
target_language_example: Elle est tête de liste aux élections municipales.
native_language_example: She is the lead candidate in the municipal elections.

additional_notes: Informal and rude-ish. Used to insult someone you think is stupid or has done something dumb; sometimes said in a teasing way between friends, but it can easily sound aggressive. Not appropriate in formal situations. Literally “knot head,” but the meaning isn’t literal.
target_language_example: Arrête, tête de nœud ! Tu as encore perdu les clés.
native_language_example: Stop it, you idiot! You lost the keys again.

meaning: one-on-one; private conversation/meeting between two people.
additional_notes: Used for a meeting or conversation with just two people, often in private (e.g., a serious talk, a date, or a private discussion at work). Can be used as a noun (un tête-à-tête) or as an adverbial phrase (en tête-à-tête). Spelling is often with hyphens: tête-à-tête.
target_language_example: On peut parler en tête-à-tête ?
native_language_example: Can we talk one-on-one?

additional_notes: Used to say that something is going to happen at some point in the future, even if you don’t know exactly when. Often paired with the future tense or expressions like "ça arrivera" (it will happen).
target_language_example: Tôt ou tard, il faudra prendre une décision.
native_language_example: Sooner or later, we’ll have to make a decision.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun (or on its own) to mean “another” or “a different one.” It agrees in gender and number: une autre (f.), d’autres (pl.). Often used when asking for a replacement or additional item.
target_language_example: Je veux un autre café, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like another coffee, please.

meaning: a certain number of; a number of (some).
additional_notes: Used to talk about an unspecified but real quantity. Often means “several” or “quite a few,” depending on context. It can refer to countable things (people, items, reasons, etc.) and is followed by a plural noun: un certain nombre de personnes. More formal/neutral than saying quelques.
target_language_example: Un certain nombre de personnes ont annulé leur réservation.
native_language_example: A number of people canceled their reservation.

meaning: a blow/hit; also a single try or action (depending on context).
additional_notes: Very common everyday word. Literally refers to a hit (physical or figurative): « recevoir un coup » (to take a hit). By extension it can mean a single attempt/action: « essayer encore un coup » (try once more). Often appears in set expressions like « tout d’un coup » (all of a sudden) and « du coup » (so / as a result). Note: English “coup” usually means a political takeover, so don’t assume that meaning in French.
target_language_example: Il a reçu un coup au bras.
native_language_example: He took a hit on the arm.

additional_notes: Used to mean you’ll do something at an unspecified time in the near future. Often implies an intention or plan, but without a fixed date. Common with future tense: « Un de ces jours, je vais… » or « Il faudra qu’on se voie un de ces jours. »
target_language_example: On ira au cinéma un de ces jours.
native_language_example: We’ll go to the movies one of these days.

meaning: one of these days; sometime soon (but not a specific date).
additional_notes: Commonly used to suggest doing something in the near or medium future without committing to a precise time. Often appears with verbs like "se voir" (to see each other), "passer" (to stop by), or "se faire" (to do).
target_language_example: On se voit un de ces quatre ?
native_language_example: Shall we see each other one of these days?

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to express quantity. It’s fairly formal/neutral (more formal than "beaucoup de"). Agreement: "nombre" is masculine singular, so you say "un grand nombre", but the verb usually agrees with the plural idea after it (e.g., "Un grand nombre de personnes sont…"). Use "d’" before a vowel sound: "un grand nombre d’étudiants".
target_language_example: Un grand nombre de personnes sont venues à la réunion.
native_language_example: A large number of people came to the meeting.

additional_notes: Often refers to an unspecified day in the future: « Un jour, j’irai à Paris. » It can also mean “one day” in the past when telling a story, similar to “one day…” in English. Literally “a day.”
target_language_example: Un jour, je parlerai français couramment.
native_language_example: Someday, I will speak French fluently.

additional_notes: Used to say that people/things are dealt with separately, in sequence (not all at once). Often follows a verb like "faire", "passer", "entrer", or "prendre".
target_language_example: Entrez un par un, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Come in one by one, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a small amount or degree. Often comes after the verb ("Je parle un peu") or before an adjective/adverb ("un peu fatigué"). With a noun, you usually add "de": "un peu de café" (a little coffee).
target_language_example: Je parle un peu français.
native_language_example: I speak a little French.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to express a small quantity. It’s very common in everyday requests and offers (food, drink, time, etc.). Often followed by a noun without an article: « un peu de pain », « un peu d’eau » (de becomes d’ before a vowel or silent h).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un peu de sucre, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a little sugar, please.

additional_notes: Used to say you need a small amount of time, or to talk generally about having some time available. Often appears after verbs like avoir/prendre/donner (avoir un peu de temps = to have a little time; prendre un peu de temps = to take a little time). You can add "encore" to mean "a bit more time" (encore un peu de temps).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin d’un peu de temps pour réfléchir.
native_language_example: I need a little time to think.

additional_notes: Literally means “a hair,” but it’s commonly used to mean a very small amount (often in informal speech). Frequently appears in expressions like “un poil + adjective” (e.g., un poil trop cher = a bit too expensive) or “un poil de + noun” (e.g., un poil de sel = a pinch/very little salt).
target_language_example: Tu peux parler un poil plus fort, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you speak a tiny bit louder, please?

meaning: a little thing; something very small (often: "nothing much").
additional_notes: Literally “a nothing.” Used to mean something tiny or insignificant, often with verbs like "ce n’est rien" (it’s nothing) or "pour un rien" (over nothing / for the slightest thing). Can also be used positively to mean a small gesture or gift: "un petit rien".
target_language_example: Je me suis fâché pour un rien.
native_language_example: I got angry over nothing / over the slightest thing.

additional_notes: Common, informal-ish way to say there are many things or a large amount. Used with plural nouns (un tas de gens = lots of people) and also with uncountable nouns (un tas de travail = lots of work). Often used in everyday speech instead of more formal "beaucoup de".
target_language_example: J’ai un tas de choses à faire aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I have lots of things to do today.

meaning: “such a” / “someone like that” (a certain person, not named).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean “such a + noun” (often for emphasis): « un tel problème » = “such a problem.” Also used like a placeholder name meaning “a certain person” when you don’t say who: « un tel a appelé » = “so-and-so called.” The feminine form is « une telle »; plural « de tels / de telles ».
target_language_example: Un tel comportement est inacceptable.
native_language_example: Such behavior is unacceptable.

additional_notes: Used to say things happen separately, in sequence, not all at once. Often after a verb: "passer un à un" (go through one by one), "entrer un à un" (enter one by one), "compter un à un" (count one by one). Note the accents: "à".
target_language_example: Les élèves entrent un à un dans la salle.
native_language_example: The students enter the room one by one.

additional_notes: Most often used to talk about something that happened one time in the past (Une fois, j’ai… = Once, I…). It can also be used in counts/instructions (Une fois par jour = once a day). In some contexts it means “once/when” to mark sequence: Une fois arrivé(e), … = Once/when (you are) arrived, …
target_language_example: Une fois par semaine, je vais à la piscine.
native_language_example: Once a week, I go to the pool.

additional_notes: Used to say you want something settled permanently, with no need to repeat it. Often appears with verbs like décider, régler, finir, clarifier: « régler ça une fois pour toutes ». Can sound firm or impatient depending on tone.
target_language_example: Il faut régler ce problème une fois pour toutes.
native_language_example: We need to settle this problem once and for all.

additional_notes: Commonly used to ask someone to wait briefly (often like English “Just a second”). It can be a polite way to pause a conversation: "Une minute, s'il vous plaît." It can also literally mean one minute as a unit of time, but in everyday speech it often just means “wait a moment.”
target_language_example: Une minute, s'il te plaît, j'arrive.
native_language_example: Just a minute, please, I'm coming.

meaning: one of a kind; unique of its kind.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is truly distinctive, with no real equivalent. Often used as a compliment in ads, reviews, or everyday speech. You can also vary it: « unique en son genre » can describe a person, a product, a place, an event, etc.
target_language_example: Ce restaurant est unique en son genre.
native_language_example: This restaurant is one of a kind.

additional_notes: Extremely rude and vulgar insult, used to tell someone to go away or to express angry disbelief (“Yeah, right!” / “No way!”). Avoid in polite conversation; it can easily start a fight. Often heard as “Va chier !” or “Va te faire chier !” (also very vulgar).
target_language_example: Va chier ! Laisse-moi tranquille.
native_language_example: Fuck off! Leave me alone.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or that something is unknowable. Often sounds a bit resigned or dismissive in tone. Common in spoken French, sometimes followed by a clause: “Va savoir pourquoi…” (= “Who knows why…”).
target_language_example: Il n’est pas venu—va savoir pourquoi.
native_language_example: He didn’t come—who knows why.

additional_notes: A very vulgar, aggressive way to tell someone to go away. Use only in extreme situations (or when quoting) and avoid in polite conversation. Much softer alternatives include: “Va-t’en !” (Go away!), “Laisse-moi tranquille.” (Leave me alone.), “Dégage !” (Get out!/Get lost! — still rude but less explicit).
target_language_example: Va te faire foutre !
native_language_example: Fuck off.

additional_notes: An insulting way to tell someone to go away; stronger than “va-t’en” and can be close to “f*** off” depending on tone. Uses the informal "tu" form ("va" + "te"); for more than one person you might hear "allez vous faire voir" (also rude). Avoid in polite or professional situations.
target_language_example: Va te faire voir ! Je ne veux plus te parler.
native_language_example: Get lost! I don’t want to talk to you anymore.

additional_notes: Used for a vehicle designed to travel in space. "Vaisseau" is a fairly general word for a (large) vessel/ship, and "spatial" means "space-related". In everyday French, you may also hear "un vaisseau" in sci‑fi contexts to mean a spaceship.
target_language_example: Dans ce film, le vaisseau spatial décolle vers Mars.
native_language_example: In this movie, the spaceship takes off for Mars.

meaning: to be worth it; to be worth the trouble.
additional_notes: Used to say something deserves the effort, time, or cost. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., « Ça vaut la peine d’essayer. » = “It’s worth trying.”). With people, you’ll more commonly hear « Il/Elle en vaut la peine » (“He/She is worth it”).
target_language_example: Ça vaut la peine de visiter ce musée.
native_language_example: It’s worth visiting this museum.

additional_notes: Used to say that an effort, cost, or experience is worthwhile. Commonly used as “Ça vaut le coup (de + infinitive)” (e.g., “Ça vaut le coup d’essayer.”) or in negative form “Ça ne vaut pas le coup (de…)” = “It’s not worth (it/doing…).” Note: literally “to be worth the blow,” but it’s a fixed expression meaning “worth it.”
target_language_example: Ça vaut le coup de visiter le musée.
native_language_example: It’s worth visiting the museum.

meaning: to be better (to); to be preferable.
additional_notes: Often used in the impersonal structure « Il vaut mieux + infinitive » to give advice or say what is preferable (similar to “You’d better…” / “It’s better to…”). Can also compare two options: « Ça vaut mieux que… » = “That’s better than…”.
target_language_example: Il vaut mieux partir tôt pour éviter les embouteillages.
native_language_example: It’s better to leave early to avoid traffic jams.

additional_notes: From "va" (go) + "y" (there). Used very often in spoken French to encourage someone to start or continue, give permission, or urge them to hurry. Can be said alone as a prompt ("Vas-y !") or used after another phrase ("Vas-y, essaye." = "Go ahead, try."). In fast speech it’s often pronounced like "vazy".
target_language_example: Vas-y, tu peux le faire !
native_language_example: Go ahead, you can do it!

meaning: to spill the beans; to reveal a secret.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used when someone gives away confidential information or reveals the truth too soon (often unintentionally). Common in everyday spoken French. It’s usually used with a subject (e.g., « Il a vendu la mèche ») and can imply that the person “gave the game away.”
target_language_example: Ne vends pas la mèche : c’est une surprise !
native_language_example: Don’t spill the beans: it’s a surprise!

meaning: to come and get / to come pick up (someone or something).
additional_notes: Often used with a direct object: « venir chercher quelqu’un/quelque chose ». In everyday situations it commonly means coming to pick someone/something up (by car, from a place, etc.), not just “come to look for.” You can also hear it in near-future: « Je vais venir te chercher » (“I’m going to come pick you up”).
target_language_example: Je viens te chercher à 18 h devant la gare.
native_language_example: I’m coming to pick you up at 6 p.m. in front of the train station.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as **venir de + infinitive** to express the very recent past (something that happened moments ago). Conjugate **venir** to match the subject, then add **de** + the infinitive: *je viens de partir* (I just left), *nous venons de manger* (we just ate). Note: **venir de + place/person** can also literally mean “to come from” (origin): *Je viens de Paris.*
target_language_example: Je viens de finir mes devoirs.
native_language_example: I just finished my homework.

meaning: to help; to come to someone’s aid.
additional_notes: A fairly formal expression used for offering help or assistance, often in serious situations (accidents, emergencies, support). It’s usually followed by "à" + a person/group: "venir en aide à quelqu’un". You can also use it without saying who: "venir en aide" (to provide assistance).
target_language_example: Les pompiers sont venus en aide aux victimes.
native_language_example: The firefighters came to the victims’ aid.

meaning: to come to mind; to occur to (someone).
additional_notes: Used when an idea, memory, or thought suddenly appears in your mind. Often used with an indirect object pronoun: « Ça me vient à l’esprit » (It comes to mind / It occurs to me), « Ça lui vient à l’esprit » (It occurs to him/her). Common in the present or past: « C’est venu à l’esprit » (It came to mind).
target_language_example: Une idée vient à l’esprit quand je marche.
native_language_example: An idea comes to mind when I walk.

additional_notes: Literally “worm of earth/soil.” Common in gardens and nature contexts. Pronunciation note: the final consonant in “ver” is usually not pronounced (sounds like “vair”). Plural: des vers de terre.
target_language_example: Après la pluie, on voit souvent des vers de terre sur le trottoir.
native_language_example: After the rain, you often see earthworms on the sidewalk.

additional_notes: A common noun for the insect larva that produces silk. Often used with an article (un/une, le/la): « un ver à soie », « le ver à soie ». Note that « ver » (worm) sounds like « vert » (green) and « verre » (glass), but the meaning is different.
target_language_example: Les vers à soie produisent de la soie.
native_language_example: Silkworms produce silk.

additional_notes: A formal historical/political title for a person who governs a country or region in the name of a monarch (the « roi »/king). Used mostly in history books or formal contexts. Feminine form: « vice-reine » (viceroy/vice-queen). Plural: « vice-rois ».
target_language_example: Le vice-roi gouvernait la colonie au nom du roi.
native_language_example: The viceroy governed the colony in the king’s name.

additional_notes: Used when talking about religious or spiritual beliefs about what happens after someone dies. You’ll often hear it in discussions about faith, heaven/hell, reincarnation, etc. The phrase is fairly literal: "vie" (life) + "après" (after) + "la mort" (death).
target_language_example: Certaines religions parlent de la vie après la mort.
native_language_example: Some religions talk about life after death.

additional_notes: Refers to someone’s personal life and things they keep from the public (relationships, home life, personal information). Often used in discussions about privacy rights or protecting personal data: "respecter la vie privée" (respect privacy), "atteinte à la vie privée" (invasion/violation of privacy).
target_language_example: Je veux protéger ma vie privée sur les réseaux sociaux.
native_language_example: I want to protect my privacy on social media.

additional_notes: Used to talk about routine, day-to-day activities and habits (work, school, chores, commuting, etc.). Often appears with words like "dans la vie quotidienne" (in everyday life) or "la vie quotidienne en France" (daily life in France).
target_language_example: Dans ma vie quotidienne, je prends le métro pour aller au travail.
native_language_example: In my everyday life, I take the subway to go to work.

meaning: an “old maid”; an unmarried woman (often with a negative/old-fashioned tone).
additional_notes: Literally “old girl.” In modern French it can sound outdated, judgmental, or insulting because it implies a woman is past the “expected” age to marry. Use cautiously; a more neutral option is often “une femme célibataire” (a single woman). Historically it could also mean “spinster.”
target_language_example: Elle déteste qu’on l’appelle une vieille fille.
native_language_example: She hates being called an old maid.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the older, historic part of a town/city (often with narrow streets, monuments, and tourist areas). Common in travel contexts and on signs/maps. Often appears with a specific city: « la vieille ville de Nice ». Plural: « les vieilles villes ».
target_language_example: On a visité la vieille ville après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: We visited the old town after lunch.

additional_notes: Describes a person, style, or way of doing things that follows traditional methods or values. Often used with "à l’ancienne" or contrasted with something modern ("moderne", "nouvelle école"). Usually positive or neutral (respect for tradition), but can also imply being a bit outdated depending on context.
target_language_example: Mon professeur est un peu vieille école : il préfère les livres papier aux tablettes.
native_language_example: My teacher is a bit old-school: he prefers paper books to tablets.

meaning: as old as the world; age-old.
additional_notes: Used to say something is very old, has existed for a long time, or is nothing new (often about an idea, habit, or problem). Common in phrases like “C’est vieux comme le monde” (“That’s as old as the world”).
target_language_example: La jalousie, c’est vieux comme le monde.
native_language_example: Jealousy is as old as the world.

additional_notes: Used to describe a person, idea, or habit that feels behind the times. It’s mildly critical but often light/teasing depending on tone. Can agree in gender/number in some uses: vieux jeu (masc.), vieille jeu (fem., less common), vieux jeux (plural). Often used with être or in phrases like un style vieux jeu / une mentalité vieux jeu.
target_language_example: Je sais que c’est un peu vieux jeu, mais je préfère appeler plutôt que texter.
native_language_example: I know it’s a bit old-fashioned, but I prefer calling rather than texting.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or talking about wine. In French, the color word follows the noun: vin blanc (white wine), vin rouge (red wine), vin rosé (rosé). You can also say un verre de vin blanc (a glass of white wine) or une bouteille de vin blanc (a bottle of white wine).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un verre de vin blanc, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of white wine, please.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or talking about wine. In French, colors usually come after the noun: vin rouge (red wine), vin blanc (white wine). You can ask for a glass (un verre de vin rouge) or a bottle (une bouteille de vin rouge).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un verre de vin rouge, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I would like a glass of red wine, please.

additional_notes: Used for the number 21. In French, 21 (and similarly 31, 41, 51, 61) takes “et” before “un”: “vingt et un”. Other numbers in the 20s use a hyphen: “vingt-deux”, “vingt-trois”, etc.
target_language_example: J’ai vingt et un ans.
native_language_example: I am twenty-one years old.

additional_notes: A compound number formed from "vingt" (20) + "cinq" (5). Often written with a hyphen in French (vingt-cinq). Used for age, prices, dates, quantities, etc.
target_language_example: J’ai vingt-cinq ans.
native_language_example: I’m twenty-five years old.

additional_notes: A cardinal number. Like other numbers in the 20s, it’s formed as « vingt » (20) + « neuf » (9) and is usually written with a hyphen. Used for age, dates, quantities, prices, etc.
target_language_example: J’ai vingt-neuf ans.
native_language_example: I am twenty-nine years old.

additional_notes: Used for the number 24 in counting, dates, and quantities. With hyphenation as in most compound numbers in French (e.g., vingt-deux, trente-quatre). You may also hear it when talking about time in the 24-hour clock (e.g., vingt-quatre heures = 24 hours).
target_language_example: Il y a vingt-quatre élèves dans la classe.
native_language_example: There are twenty-four students in the class.

meaning: 24 hours a day; around the clock.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is available all the time (often written and said as “24 heures sur 24”, “24h/24”). It’s common with services, shops, or ongoing situations: “ouvert 24h/24”, “service 24h/24”.
target_language_example: La réception est ouverte vingt-quatre heures sur vingt-quatre.
native_language_example: The front desk is open 24 hours a day.

additional_notes: Used to say the number 26 when counting, giving a quantity, age, dates, addresses, prices, etc. Hyphenated in standard spelling: « vingt-six ».
target_language_example: J’ai vingt-six ans.
native_language_example: I’m twenty-six years old.

additional_notes: Commonly used as a preposition/adverb meaning “opposite” or “facing”: « Je suis assis vis-à-vis de toi. » It can also mean “regarding / in relation to” (often with « de »): « Vis-à-vis de la loi… » In conversation you may also hear it used like “in terms of.” The spelling keeps the hyphens and accents: vis-à-vis.
target_language_example: Je suis assis vis-à-vis de la gare.
native_language_example: I’m sitting opposite the train station.

meaning: with regard to; toward; compared with.
additional_notes: Often used in more formal French to talk about a relationship or comparison between two things: « vis-à-vis de » + noun/pronoun. Common equivalents are « concernant », « envers » (toward someone), or « par rapport à » (compared with). The form « vis-à-vis » can also be used on its own in some contexts.
target_language_example: Quelle est la politique de l’entreprise vis-à-vis des clients ?
native_language_example: What is the company’s policy toward customers?

additional_notes: Used in health/nutrition contexts (food labels, supplements, medical advice). In French, vitamins are usually written with the noun + letter (vitamine A, vitamine C).
target_language_example: Ce complément contient de la vitamine A.
native_language_example: This supplement contains vitamin A.

additional_notes: Used in health/nutrition contexts (foods, supplements, immunity). Often appears on product labels and in advice: "riche en vitamine C" (rich in vitamin C), "prendre de la vitamine C" (to take vitamin C). The letter is capitalized (C).
target_language_example: Les oranges sont riches en vitamine C.
native_language_example: Oranges are rich in vitamin C.

meaning: quickly; briefly; in a rough way.
additional_notes: Common in casual speech to mean something is done fast and without much detail or care (similar to “quick and dirty”). Often used with verbs like faire, regarder, expliquer: “Je te l’explique vite fait.” It can also downplay the effort: “J’ai mangé vite fait” (I ate quickly / just grabbed something).
target_language_example: Je te résume ça vite fait.
native_language_example: I’ll summarize that for you quickly.

additional_notes: A formal/technical term for a railway line or the tracks themselves. Often used in transport, signage, or news (more common than everyday “les rails” in casual speech). Example: “traverser la voie ferrée” = to cross the railway tracks; “passage à niveau” is a level crossing.
target_language_example: Ne traversez pas la voie ferrée quand les barrières sont baissées.
native_language_example: Don’t cross the railway tracks when the barriers are down.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation or to show the method or result of doing something. Often followed by a clause describing the process (voilà comment + subject + verb), or used alone to summarize: "Voilà comment !" (= "That’s how!"). Similar to "voilà" + a clarifying word (voilà pourquoi = that’s why, voilà ce que… = here’s what…).
target_language_example: Voilà comment on fait une omelette : d’abord, on bat les œufs.
native_language_example: Here’s how you make an omelette: first, you beat the eggs.

additional_notes: Used to wrap up an explanation, list, or situation (often meaning “nothing more to add”). It can sound final or matter-of-fact; with tone it can be neutral, reassuring, or slightly dismissive. Also commonly said as “Voilà, c’est tout.”
target_language_example: Je t’ai donné toutes les infos, voilà tout.
native_language_example: I gave you all the info, that’s all.

meaning: to check with; to talk to (someone) about it.
additional_notes: Common in everyday French to mean “ask/consult someone” or “arrange something with someone.” Often used in the future or near future: « Je vais voir avec … » (“I’ll check with …”). The person you’ll consult follows « avec » (e.g., « voir avec le chef / ma collègue »). It does not literally mean “see with” in English.
target_language_example: Je vais voir avec mon collègue si on peut avancer la réunion.
native_language_example: I’ll check with my colleague to see if we can move the meeting up.

meaning: to see clearly; to understand clearly.
additional_notes: Often used literally (good visibility) or figuratively (to understand a situation). Very common with the pronoun “y”: “y voir clair” = to see/understand things clearly; in the negative, “Je n’y vois pas clair” can mean “I can’t see well” or “I’m not sure what’s going on.”
target_language_example: Avec ces lunettes, je vois clair.
native_language_example: With these glasses, I can see clearly.

meaning: to think big; to aim high.
additional_notes: Used when talking about ambitious plans or big goals (not being modest or cautious). Often appears in advice or encouragement: « Il faut voir grand. » Literally it’s “to see big,” but the real meaning is “to be ambitious / have big plans.”
target_language_example: Pour réussir, il faut voir grand.
native_language_example: To succeed, you have to think big.

voir le bon côté des choses

target_language_multi_word_term: voir le bon côté des choses
meaning: to look on the bright side (of things).
additional_notes: Used to encourage optimism in a situation, especially when something goes wrong. Often said as advice ("Il faut voir le bon côté des choses") or as a reminder to stay positive.
target_language_example: Je suis déçu, mais j’essaie de voir le bon côté des choses.
native_language_example: I’m disappointed, but I’m trying to look on the bright side.

meaning: to see it coming; to see where this is going.
additional_notes: Used when you anticipate what will happen or what someone is about to do/say (often with a slightly suspicious or knowing tone): « Je te vois venir ! » = “I know what you’re up to / I see what you’re getting at.” It can also be used in the sense of “wait and see how things develop” in « on va voir venir » (less common).
target_language_example: Je te vois venir : tu vas encore me demander de payer.
native_language_example: I see where this is going: you’re going to ask me to pay again.

meaning: “you see?” / “see?” (used to check understanding or introduce an explanation).
additional_notes: Literally “do you see?” (from voir). Used in conversation to draw the listener in, emphasize a point, or make sure they follow what you’re saying—similar to “you know?” or “see?” Can appear mid-sentence or at the end; often set off by commas. Somewhat informal/colloquial.
target_language_example: C’est compliqué, vois-tu, mais je vais t’expliquer.
native_language_example: It’s complicated, you see, but I’m going to explain it to you.

additional_notes: Used for a car you rent from an agency/company. Also commonly said as "une voiture de location" or "une voiture de location" vs. "une voiture de location" in ads; you may also see "location de voiture" (car rental) for the service/activity.
target_language_example: On a pris une voiture de location à l’aéroport.
native_language_example: We got a rental car at the airport.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for a fast, performance-oriented car. Often used with an article (une/la) and can be plural (des voitures de sport). Not to be confused with "voiture de course" (race car).
target_language_example: Il a acheté une voiture de sport rouge.
native_language_example: He bought a red sports car.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: "voiture" (car) + adjective "électrique" (electric), which usually comes after the noun in French. Plural: "voitures électriques". Often used when talking about charging, batteries, or eco-friendly transport.
target_language_example: Je veux acheter une voiture électrique.
native_language_example: I want to buy an electric car.

additional_notes: Used for someone who steals from people’s pockets or bags in crowded places (metros, tourist areas, markets). Often appears in warnings: « Attention aux voleurs à la tire ! ». The word « tire » here refers to “pulling” (like pulling something out), not a “tire” on a car.
target_language_example: Fais attention dans le métro : il y a souvent des voleurs à la tire.
native_language_example: Be careful on the metro: there are often pickpockets.

additional_notes: A sport name; often used with the verb "jouer au" (to play): "jouer au volley-ball". Also commonly shortened in speech to "le volley". In French it’s usually written with a hyphen: "volley-ball".
target_language_example: Je joue au volley-ball le samedi.
native_language_example: I play volleyball on Saturdays.

meaning: to be willing to; to kindly agree to (do something).
additional_notes: Used as a polite way to ask someone to do something or to express consent. Very common in requests, especially in questions like « Voulez-vous bien… ? » (“Would you please…?”) or even more politely « Voudriez-vous bien… ? » (“Would you mind…/Would you please…?”). It doesn’t mean “to want well” literally; « bien » adds politeness/approval (roughly “kindly”).
target_language_example: Voulez-vous bien fermer la porte, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Would you please close the door?

meaning: to mean; to signify (also: to intend to say).
additional_notes: Very common expression used to ask for or give the meaning of something: “Qu’est-ce que ça veut dire ?” = “What does that mean?” It’s conjugated like the verb vouloir (je veux, tu veux, il/elle veut, etc.), often with “ça”: “ça veut dire…”. It can also clarify intent: “Je veux dire…” = “I mean…” / “What I’m trying to say is…”.
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que ça veut dire ?
native_language_example: What does that mean?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize or contrast a group of people addressed with « vous » (e.g., “you, as opposed to us/them”). Common in some regional varieties (especially in Québec French) alongside « nous autres » (“we”). Can sound colloquial and is not required in standard French, where « vous » is usually enough.
target_language_example: Vous autres, vous venez d’où ?
native_language_example: You guys, where are you from?

additional_notes: Uses the verb savoir (“to know”) with vous (“you,” formal singular or plural). Commonly used to ask if someone knows something (often followed by a question), or as a conversational filler/tag meaning “you know?” / “as you know.”
target_language_example: Vous savez où est la gare ?
native_language_example: Do you know where the train station is?

meaning: "You know what…" (used to introduce what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Used to get attention or add emphasis before a statement, suggestion, or decision. Often followed by a pause. With "vous" it sounds neutral/polite; with friends you’ll often hear "tu sais quoi". It can also be used to express a change of mind or mild frustration (like “You know what, forget it”).
target_language_example: Vous savez quoi ? On va y aller demain.
native_language_example: You know what? We’ll go tomorrow.

additional_notes: Emphatic/reflexive pronoun used to stress “you” (formal singular or plural). Often follows the subject pronoun or a noun/pronoun: « Vous-même… », « Vous avez… vous-même ». Can also agree in number/gender: « vous-mêmes » (plural), « vous-même » (singular), though the form « vous-même » is commonly used as the polite singular.
target_language_example: Vous pouvez le faire vous-même.
native_language_example: You can do it yourself.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize “you” (plural or formal) or after a preposition (e.g., avec, pour) to mean “(by) yourselves.” With a mixed or all-male group, use “vous-mêmes”; with an all-female group, use “vous-mêmes” → “vous-mêmes” is still common in mixed groups, but the feminine plural is “vous-mêmes” → actually “vous-mêmes” (masc./mixed) vs “vous-mêmes” (fem.) = “vous-mêmes” / “vous-mêmes” is written differently: masculine/mixed “vous-mêmes”, feminine “vous-mêmes”. Also used as a reflexive pronoun in expressions like “vous vous...” (e.g., Vous vous êtes blessés vous-mêmes.).
target_language_example: Vous pouvez le faire vous-mêmes.
native_language_example: You can do it yourselves.

additional_notes: Used for travel done for work or professional purposes. Very common in formal and everyday contexts (e.g., at work, in hotels, at the airport). Often appears with verbs like « faire un voyage d'affaires » (to go on a business trip) or « être en voyage d'affaires » (to be on a business trip).
target_language_example: Je suis en voyage d'affaires à Lyon cette semaine.
native_language_example: I’m on a business trip in Lyon this week.

additional_notes: Literally “travel in time.” Used for science-fiction or hypothetical situations (going to the past or future). Often appears with verbs like faire (to do), voyager (to travel), or parler de (to talk about): faire un voyage dans le temps, voyager dans le temps.
target_language_example: Dans ce film, les personnages font un voyage dans le temps.
native_language_example: In this movie, the characters time travel.

meaning: "you see" / "see?" (used to explain or check understanding).
additional_notes: From the verb "voir" (to see) in the formal/plural "vous" form: "voyez" = "(do) you see". Often used as a discourse marker to introduce an explanation, add emphasis, or make sure the listener is following. Common in more formal speech or writing; in casual speech you might hear "tu vois". Can appear mid-sentence or at the end like a tag question.
target_language_example: C’est compliqué, voyez-vous, parce que nous n’avons pas le budget.
native_language_example: It’s complicated, you see, because we don’t have the budget.

additional_notes: Used when you’re about to check, think about, or figure something out (often before answering). It can sound mildly impatient or skeptical depending on tone, but it’s common and not rude in neutral contexts. Literally “let’s see” (from "voir" = to see).
target_language_example: Voyons voir… où est mon téléphone ?
native_language_example: Let’s see… where is my phone?

additional_notes: Often used to contrast everyday reality with the internet, social media, gaming, or fiction. You’ll commonly see it with prepositions like « dans la vraie vie » (“in real life”) or « en vraie vie » (more casual).
target_language_example: On se connaît en ligne, mais dans la vraie vie on ne s’est jamais vus.
native_language_example: We know each other online, but in real life we’ve never seen each other.

additional_notes: Very common in French (often written with a hyphen: week-end; plural: week-ends). You can use it with prepositions like "ce week-end" (this weekend), "le week-end" (on the weekend), and "pendant le week-end" (during the weekend).
target_language_example: On se voit ce week-end ?
native_language_example: Are we seeing each other this weekend?

meaning: “there’s only that / that’s all there is” (also: “that’s the best!”).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French; it’s a shortened, informal version of « il n’y a que ça ». Used to say there’s no other option/choice (“that’s all”), or to praise something meaning “nothing beats that / that’s the way to go.”
target_language_example: Tu veux un café ? Désolé, y a que ça.
native_language_example: Do you want a coffee? Sorry, that’s all there is.

meaning: to go there; to head over.
additional_notes: “Y” replaces a place (or sometimes an activity) introduced with “à” or “chez”. It’s used with the verb “aller” and conjugates normally: j’y vais (I’m going), tu y vas (you’re going), on y va ? (Shall we go?). Very common to mean “Let’s go!”: On y va ! / Allez, on y va !
target_language_example: On y va maintenant ?
native_language_example: Shall we go now?

additional_notes: Used as an impersonal expression, most commonly with “il”: “il y a” (present), “il y avait” (past), “il y aura” (future). Very common for stating that something exists or is present somewhere. In negatives: “il n’y a pas …” (“there isn’t/aren’t …”).
target_language_example: Il y a un café près d’ici.
native_language_example: There is a café near here.

additional_notes: Used to add something to a list, meaning “including” or “that includes.” Often follows a noun or pronoun that the “y” refers to (it/there/that). Common in writing and more formal speech. Frequently followed by a noun or pronoun: “y compris moi/toi/lui.”
target_language_example: Tout le monde est invité, y compris les enfants.
native_language_example: Everyone is invited, including the children.

meaning: to count on it; to rely on it.
additional_notes: "Y" replaces "sur + something" ("on + something"). So "y compter" means "compter sur ça" (to count on that). Often used to reassure someone: "Tu peux y compter" = “You can count on it / You can count on me.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tu peux y compter.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you can count on it.

meaning: to believe it; to believe in it.
additional_notes: Uses the pronoun “y” to replace something introduced with “à” (or an idea/situation you’re talking about). Common in the negative: “Je n’y crois pas.” = “I don’t believe it / I don’t buy it.” With “croire à” it can mean “to believe in (an idea, project, someone’s chances)”: “Je crois à ce projet” → “J’y crois.”
target_language_example: Tu penses que ça va marcher ? — Oui, j’y crois.
native_language_example: Do you think it’s going to work? — Yes, I believe it will.

meaning: "there are some people who..." (often implying criticism or disbelief).
additional_notes: Informal spoken contraction of « il y en a des qui… ». Used to introduce a general comment about certain people, often to complain or be ironic: « Y en a, ils comprennent jamais ! » You’ll also see/hear « y en a qui… » without « des ».
target_language_example: Y en a des qui se croient tout permis !
native_language_example: There are some people who think they can do anything they want!

meaning: to die; to be killed (also: to “get it” / suffer the consequences).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French and fairly informal. Literally it contains the pronoun "y" (“there”), but the expression doesn’t mean “to pass there.” Often used as a warning or prediction: "Tu vas y passer" = “You’re going to die / you’re going to get it.” Can also mean to pay a price or lose out: "J’y ai passé mon week-end" = “I spent my weekend on it.”
target_language_example: Si tu continues comme ça, tu vas y passer.
native_language_example: If you keep going like that, you’re going to die / you’re going to get it.
