meaning: to die (especially as a result of an accident, war, etc.).
additional_notes: Literally “to stay there,” but it’s an idiom meaning someone didn’t survive (they were killed). Often used with places or events understood from context: "Il a failli y rester" = "He almost died." Can also refer to something non-living being destroyed (e.g., "Ma voiture a failli y rester" = "My car was nearly wrecked"), but it most commonly refers to a person.
target_language_example: Avec cet accident, il a failli y rester.
native_language_example: With that accident, he almost died.

meaning: to be there; to attend (be present).
additional_notes: Uses the pronoun « y » meaning “there” (or “to it/at it”), plus « être » (to be). Very common to talk about being present at an event or in a place: « J’y suis » (I’m there / I’m here), « J’y serai » (I’ll be there), « Il n’y est pas » (He isn’t there / he’s not present). In some contexts it can also mean “to be into it” or “to get it/understand,” depending on tone and situation.
target_language_example: Tu viens à la réunion ? Oui, j’y serai.
native_language_example: Are you coming to the meeting? Yes, I’ll be there.

additional_notes: Written abbreviation mainly used in formal or space-limited contexts (headlines, tables, forms). In everyday writing, you more often see « États-Unis » or « USA ». It’s typically used with « aux »: « aux É.-U. » = “in the U.S.”
target_language_example: Elle habite aux É.-U. depuis 2019.
native_language_example: She has lived in the U.S. since 2019.

meaning: "Down with…!" / "Down!" (a shout to bring something down or reject it).
additional_notes: Used as an exclamation, often in protests or slogans to express opposition: “À bas + noun” = “Down with + noun.” You can also hear it as a command to bring something down (“À bas les armes !” = “Down with your weapons!”). It’s not the same as “en bas” (“downstairs/down below”), which describes location.
target_language_example: À bas la dictature !
native_language_example: Down with the dictatorship!

additional_notes: Used to describe the main ingredient(s) of a product, recipe, or material, or what something is fundamentally built on. Common in food and cosmetics: «un gâteau à base de chocolat» (a cake made with chocolate). Often followed by a noun; can also be used more abstractly («un système à base de données» = database-based).
target_language_example: C’est une boisson à base de plantes.
native_language_example: It’s a drink made from herbs.

additional_notes: A common, friendly way to say goodbye when you expect to see the person again fairly soon. Used in person, on the phone, and in messages. Often paired with other goodbyes (e.g., "Au revoir, à bientôt !").
target_language_example: Merci pour ton aide, à bientôt !
native_language_example: Thanks for your help, see you soon!

meaning: blank; empty; without content (or without a real shot, in « tirer à blanc »).
additional_notes: Used when something is left empty or unsigned (un chèque à blanc = a blank check; un vote à blanc = a blank/empty ballot). In another common expression, « tirer à blanc » means “to fire blanks” (shoot with no bullet).
target_language_example: Je n’ai rien écrit : j’ai rendu la feuille à blanc.
native_language_example: I didn’t write anything: I handed in the sheet blank.

meaning: flat out; at full speed/effort (also: completely full/packed).
additional_notes: Colloquial adverb used to say someone is doing something at maximum intensity ("y aller à bloc", "bosser à bloc") or that a place/vehicle is completely full ("Le métro est à bloc"). It doesn’t translate literally word-for-word, and "bloc" can look like English "block" but the expression means "full-on/at max".
target_language_example: En ce moment, je bosse à bloc pour finir le projet.
native_language_example: Right now, I’m working flat out to finish the project.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is on or inside a means of transport (train, bus, plane, boat, etc.). Often appears with verbs like monter (to get on), être (to be), or embarquer (to board). In announcements you may hear: « À bord du train… » (“On board the train…”).
target_language_example: Nous sommes déjà à bord de l’avion.
native_language_example: We’re already on board the plane.

meaning: exhausted; at the end of one’s rope.
additional_notes: Often used with être: « Je suis à bout » = “I’m exhausted / I can’t take it anymore.” Very common in « à bout de + noun »: « à bout de forces » (worn out), « à bout de patience » (out of patience). It can also mean “to the end” in some contexts (e.g., « jusqu’au bout » = “all the way/to the end”), but « à bout » alone is most often about being worn out or mentally/physically drained.
target_language_example: Après cette semaine, je suis à bout.
native_language_example: After this week, I’m exhausted.

additional_notes: Often used with nouns like forces, énergie, nerfs, patience to mean someone has no more left (physically or mentally): à bout de forces (exhausted), à bout de nerfs (at the end of one’s rope), à bout de patience (out of patience). Not to be confused with venir à bout de (to manage to overcome/finish).
target_language_example: Après la randonnée, j’étais à bout de forces.
native_language_example: After the hike, I was exhausted.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re breathing hard after physical effort (running, climbing stairs, etc.). It can also be used figuratively to mean completely exhausted or worn out (e.g., a person, a team, or a project). Often used with “être” (être à bout de souffle).
target_language_example: Après avoir couru pour attraper le bus, je suis à bout de souffle.
native_language_example: After running to catch the bus, I’m out of breath.

meaning: because of; due to (usually a cause, often negative).
additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something and followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., à cause du bruit, à cause de lui). Often implies a problem or blame; for neutral/positive reasons, learners often use "grâce à" (thanks to).
target_language_example: Le train est en retard à cause de la neige.
native_language_example: The train is late because of the snow.

additional_notes: Used in formal or neutral contexts to mean "up to the present time". Common in writing and announcements to give an update based on the latest information (often followed by a fact or number). Similar to "jusqu’à présent" or "à ce jour" can introduce something that is still true now.
target_language_example: À ce jour, nous n’avons reçu aucune réponse.
native_language_example: To date, we haven’t received any response.

meaning: at that moment / at that time (then).
additional_notes: Used to point to a specific moment in the past or in a story (“then”). Often contrasts with now: À ce moment-là, je ne savais pas… It can refer to a moment already mentioned, or made clear by context. Also common with the imperfect for background description (À ce moment-là, il habitait à Paris).
target_language_example: À ce moment-là, je ne comprenais pas encore.
native_language_example: At that moment, I still didn’t understand.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or refer back to a topic already mentioned, similar to “by the way” or “speaking of that” (but usually more directly linked to the current subject). Often followed by a question or extra detail: “À ce propos, …”.
target_language_example: À ce propos, tu as des nouvelles de Marie ?
native_language_example: Speaking of that, do you have any news about Marie?

meaning: at this stage; at this point.
additional_notes: Used to say where things stand in a process, project, or situation right now. Common in both spoken and written French, often followed by a statement of the current status or what can/can’t be done now (e.g., « À ce stade, je ne peux pas décider. »).
target_language_example: À ce stade, on attend encore une réponse.
native_language_example: At this point, we’re still waiting for an answer.

meaning: about that; on that topic; regarding that.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific topic already mentioned or understood from context. Common in both spoken and written French, often to introduce information, a comment, or a question related to the topic (e.g., "À ce sujet, ..."). Similar to "à propos de ça" but a bit more neutral/formal.
target_language_example: À ce sujet, j’ai une question.
native_language_example: On that topic, I have a question.

meaning: at this time; by now (at this point).
additional_notes: Means “at this moment” or “at this point (by now)”, depending on context. Often used to comment on what is happening now or what should already be true. Common in spoken French; also appears as “à cette heure-ci” for extra emphasis (“right now”).
target_language_example: À cette heure, il doit déjà être arrivé.
native_language_example: By now, he must have already arrived.

meaning: to be paid for by; to be someone’s responsibility.
additional_notes: Most often used in fixed expressions like « à la charge de + person/organization » (“at the expense of / the responsibility of”) or « être à la charge de quelqu’un » (“to be supported by someone”). Common with costs: « Les frais sont à votre charge » = “You pay the costs.” Not to be confused with English “in charge” (French: « en charge » / « chargé de »).
target_language_example: Les frais de livraison sont à votre charge.
native_language_example: The delivery costs are at your expense.

meaning: "hot" / while still hot; immediately (as a first reaction).
additional_notes: Used in set phrases like "manger/servir à chaud" (eat/serve hot) or "réagir/analyser à chaud" (react/analyze right away, before having time to reflect). In contrast, "à froid" means after the fact, calmly.
target_language_example: On en reparlera à froid ; là, tu réagis à chaud.
native_language_example: We’ll talk about it when things have cooled down; right now, you’re reacting in the heat of the moment.

additional_notes: Used literally for riding a horse (être à cheval = to be on a horse) and for sitting/positioning yourself with one leg on each side of something (s’asseoir à cheval sur une chaise = to sit astride a chair, facing the back). It can also be used more generally for something that spans two things, like being between two dates or categories (à cheval sur deux années = straddling two years).
target_language_example: Il est à cheval depuis ce matin.
native_language_example: He has been on horseback since this morning.

meaning: straddling; spanning across (a border, two periods, two categories).
additional_notes: Literally means “astride/on horseback on,” but it’s very often used figuratively to mean something is split between or covers two things at the same time (e.g., a town on two sides of a border, a project covering two years, a person between two jobs/roles). Typically followed by what is being spanned: à cheval sur + noun.
target_language_example: Ce village est à cheval sur la frontière entre la France et la Belgique.
native_language_example: This village straddles the border between France and Belgium.

additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar expression meaning something is really bad or disappointing. Often used after a noun (“un film à chier”) or with “c’est” (“C’est à chier !”). Avoid in polite situations; use safer alternatives like “nul,” “vraiment mauvais,” or “pas terrible.”
target_language_example: Ce resto est à chier.
native_language_example: This restaurant is shitty/terrible.

meaning: against the current; against the trend.
additional_notes: Used literally for moving against a water/current, and figuratively for going against what most people do or think (contrary, unconventional). Often used with verbs like aller, nager, penser, agir: « aller à contre-courant » = to go against the grain.
target_language_example: Il a toujours pensé à contre-courant.
native_language_example: He has always thought against the trend.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something even though you don’t want to (often out of obligation). Common with verbs like accepter, faire, aller, partir. It describes your attitude, not the action itself.
target_language_example: Il a accepté à contrecœur.
native_language_example: He accepted reluctantly.

meaning: by means of; using (repeated) blows/acts of.
additional_notes: Used before a noun to express doing something by repeatedly using a tool/weapon/force, or by repeatedly doing something: à coup de poing (with punches), à coups de marteau (with hammer blows), à coups de téléphone (with repeated phone calls). Often implies repetition and effort, sometimes violence or insistence. Note the common plural form “à coups de …”.
target_language_example: Il a ouvert la porte à coups de marteau.
native_language_example: He opened the door with hammer blows.

additional_notes: Used to describe something so impressive or beautiful that it ‘takes your breath away’ (a view, scenery, a performance, etc.). Often follows a noun with être: « C’est à couper le souffle » or « La vue est à couper le souffle ». Literally ‘to cut the breath’, so it’s an idiom (not a word-for-word translation in English).
target_language_example: La vue depuis le sommet est à couper le souffle.
native_language_example: The view from the top is breathtaking.

meaning: with repeated blows/strokes of; by hitting with.
additional_notes: Used to describe doing something by repeatedly striking, usually followed by a noun (often a body part or tool): « à coups de poing » (with punches), « à coups de marteau » (with hammer blows), « à coups de pied » (with kicks). It can also be used more figuratively to mean “by means of repeated actions” (e.g., « à coups de publicité » = by repeated advertising).
target_language_example: Il a cassé la porte à coups de marteau.
native_language_example: He broke the door down with hammer blows.

meaning: short of; running out of; at a loss (for ideas).
additional_notes: Used mainly in set phrases like « être à court de + noun » (“to be short of / to run out of”). Common with money or time (« à court d’argent », « à court de temps ») and with ideas/words (« à court d’idées », « à court de mots »).
target_language_example: Je suis à court d’argent ce mois-ci.
native_language_example: I’m short of money this month.

additional_notes: Used after words like plein(e), rempli(e), or bondé(e) to emphasize that something is extremely full/crowded: « une salle bondée à craquer » (a room packed to bursting). It can also be used figuratively, especially with adjectives like « mignon(ne) à craquer » meaning “so cute you could burst.”
target_language_example: Le métro était bondé à craquer ce matin.
native_language_example: The subway was packed to bursting this morning.

meaning: on credit; bought now, paid later.
additional_notes: Used when you don’t pay immediately. Common in shopping and finance contexts: acheter à crédit (to buy on credit), payer à crédit (to pay on credit), vente à crédit (sale on credit). Often implies payment later in installments or after receiving an invoice, depending on context.
target_language_example: On peut acheter cette voiture à crédit.
native_language_example: You can buy this car on credit.

additional_notes: Most often used for location: "à côté de" + noun/pronoun = "next to" (J’habite à côté de la gare. = I live next to the station.). Without "de", it can mean "nearby" (C’est à côté. = It’s nearby.). In some contexts it can also mean "off-topic/way off" (être à côté de la plaque), but that’s a separate idiom.
target_language_example: Le café est à côté de la pharmacie.
native_language_example: The café is next to the pharmacy.

additional_notes: Used to locate something close to something else. It often answers “Where?” (Où ?) and can be used for people, places, or objects. Not to be confused with “à côté” alone, which can mean “nearby” or “wrong/off the mark” depending on context.
target_language_example: La boulangerie est à côté de la banque.
native_language_example: The bakery is next to the bank.

meaning: to heart; deeply / seriously (in set phrases).
additional_notes: Usually appears in fixed expressions, especially: « avoir à cœur de + infinitive » (to be keen to / to be committed to doing something) and « prendre à cœur » (to take to heart, take personally, take seriously). Less commonly, « de tout cœur » means “with all my heart.”
target_language_example: Je prends tes conseils à cœur.
native_language_example: I take your advice to heart.

meaning: “Yeah, right!” / “Tell that to someone else!” (I don’t believe you).
additional_notes: Usually said as an interjection: « À d’autres ! » to reject an excuse or claim and show you’re not fooled. Literally “to others,” but it’s used idiomatically to mean “try that on someone else.” Often followed by something like « On ne me la fait pas. »
target_language_example: — Je te promets que je n’ai rien cassé. — À d’autres !
native_language_example: — I swear I didn’t break anything. — Yeah, right!

additional_notes: A common goodbye used when you expect to see or speak to the person the next day. Can be said on its own or with a goodbye like "Salut" or "Au revoir" (e.g., "Au revoir, à demain !").
target_language_example: Bon, je dois y aller. À demain !
native_language_example: Alright, I have to go. See you tomorrow!

additional_notes: Means “half” or “partially,” often describing something not complete. Common in set phrases like à demi-mot (“indirectly,” “hinting”), à demi-heure (“half an hour”), and with adjectives/participles like à demi ouvert(e) (“half-open”) or à demi endormi(e) (“half-asleep”).
target_language_example: La porte est restée à demi ouverte.
native_language_example: The door stayed half-open.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the recipient or the place something is going to, especially in travel/transport and on labels or mail. Often followed by a city/country or a person/organization: « un train à destination de Lyon », « un colis à destination de Marie ». Similar to « pour », but more formal and common for routes/shipments.
target_language_example: Le vol à destination de Montréal part à 18h30.
native_language_example: The flight to Montreal leaves at 6:30 p.m.

meaning: on the verge of; just about to (very close to).
additional_notes: Usually used to express being extremely close to doing something: « être à deux doigts de + infinitive » (or « être à deux doigts de + noun »). It emphasizes that something almost happened or is about to happen.
target_language_example: J’étais à deux doigts de partir quand tu as appelé.
native_language_example: I was about to leave when you called.

additional_notes: Used as a set phrase to introduce a frank or more personal comment, often to soften what follows. Commonly placed at the beginning of a sentence (followed by a comma), but it can also appear mid-sentence. Similar in meaning to "pour être honnête" and "franchement".
target_language_example: À dire la vérité, je n’ai pas très envie de sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: To be honest, I don’t really feel like going out tonight.

additional_notes: Used for doing something without being physically present (often with work, learning, meetings, or controlling something). Also used literally to mean “from far away.” Common phrases: "travail à distance" (remote work), "cours/enseignement à distance" (distance learning), "télétravail" is a related term.
target_language_example: Je travaille à distance trois jours par semaine.
native_language_example: I work remotely three days a week.

additional_notes: Used for directions and location. Often appears after verbs like aller/être/tourner: « Tournez à droite » (Turn right) and « C’est à droite » (It’s on the right). The opposite is « à gauche » (to the left).
target_language_example: Tournez à droite au prochain carrefour.
native_language_example: Turn right at the next intersection.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is missing, unavailable, or not possible, and that another option will be used instead. Often followed by a noun or infinitive: « à défaut de + nom » (in the absence of…), « à défaut de + infinitif » (failing to…). Common in more formal or written French (instructions, contracts, news).
target_language_example: À défaut de réponse avant vendredi, nous annulerons la réservation.
native_language_example: Failing a reply by Friday, we will cancel the reservation.

meaning: right at the surface of; level with.
additional_notes:
Usually followed by a noun: 
- Literal: "à fleur de terre" / "à fleur d’eau" = right at ground level / right at the water’s surface.
- Very common figurative set phrase: "à fleur de peau" = very sensitive, emotions close to the surface (easily moved or irritated).
target_language_example: Ses nerfs sont à fleur de peau en ce moment.
native_language_example: He’s very on edge / sensitive right now.

meaning: afloat; staying afloat (often: staying financially/mentally stable).
additional_notes: Literally “afloat.” Used in the physical sense (a boat floating) and very often figuratively: "rester à flot" = to stay afloat/keep going, especially financially (to avoid bankruptcy) or emotionally (to cope). Common with verbs like "rester", "se maintenir", "garder".
target_language_example: Avec la hausse des prix, ils ont du mal à rester à flot.
native_language_example: With rising prices, they’re having a hard time staying afloat.

meaning: in streams; in abundance (often of liquid).
additional_notes: Used mainly with liquids (water, blood, tears, sweat, rain) to mean “flowing a lot / pouring out.” Common in set phrases like « pleurer à flots » (to cry a lot) and « transpirer à flots » (to sweat a lot).
target_language_example: Il pleuvait à flots quand je suis sorti.
native_language_example: It was pouring (raining in streams) when I went out.

meaning: fully; completely; all out (as much as possible).
additional_notes: Common in everyday French to mean doing something at maximum intensity (speed/effort/volume) or very strongly (being really into something). Often used with verbs like aller/rouler (go/drive), mettre (turn up), pousser (push), être (be), or with "à fond sur" (really focused on).
target_language_example: On y va à fond !
native_language_example: Let’s go all out!

meaning: by dint of; through (repeated) effort or persistence; from doing something a lot.
additional_notes: Used to say that a result happens because of repeated actions, persistence, or sheer repetition over time. Often followed by **de + infinitive**: *À force de travailler…* (“By working so much…”). It can also be used without *de* to mean “with force/using force,” but the common beginner use is the idiomatic “by dint of / from doing something a lot.”
target_language_example: À force de pratiquer, j’ai fini par comprendre.
native_language_example: By practicing a lot, I ended up understanding.

additional_notes: Used to show that a result happens because of repeated action or persistence over time. Common pattern: « à force de + infinitive » (à force de travailler…) or « à force de + noun » (à force de patience…). Often translates as “eventually” or “in the end” when the emphasis is on repetition leading to an outcome.
target_language_example: À force de travailler tous les jours, il a réussi son examen.
native_language_example: By working every day, he ended up passing his exam.

meaning: cold; without heating; calmly (after the fact).
additional_notes: Used in a few common ways: (1) cooking/food: served or eaten cold (e.g., « se manger à froid »). (2) technical: done without heating or without the machine running hot (e.g., « travailler/former à froid » = cold-working). (3) figurative: thinking about something calmly, after emotions have cooled down (« réfléchir à froid », « analyser à froid »). Often contrasts with « à chaud » (hot / immediately / while it’s happening).
target_language_example: On en reparlera à froid, demain.
native_language_example: We’ll talk about it calmly tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used for directions and location. With movement verbs it often means "to the left" (turn/go left): « Tournez à gauche. » With « être/se trouver », it often means "on the left" (located on the left): « C’est à gauche. »
target_language_example: La banque est à gauche de la pharmacie.
native_language_example: The bank is on the left of the pharmacy.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like être/mettre/se mettre/rester (“to be/get/stay”) to describe someone physically kneeling, or figuratively to mean being brought to their knees (defeated/exhausted). Often appears as “à genoux” (both knees) or “à un genou” (on one knee).
target_language_example: Il s’est mis à genoux pour attacher ses chaussures.
native_language_example: He got down on his knees to tie his shoes.

additional_notes: Used to say something is moving forward fast or is getting closer quickly, often with verbs like « avancer », « approcher », « se rapprocher ». Common in « à grands pas » (plural) as well. Example: « L’été arrive à grands pas » = summer is coming up fast.
target_language_example: Les examens approchent à grands pas.
native_language_example: The exams are coming up fast.

additional_notes: Used to say something is progressing quickly or approaching fast (often with verbs like « avancer », « arriver », « se rapprocher »). Can describe literal walking in long strides, but more often means “fast” in a figurative sense.
target_language_example: L’hiver approche à grands pas.
native_language_example: Winter is fast approaching.

additional_notes: Used to say something is spoken so other people can hear it (as opposed to silently or in your head). Common with verbs like lire (to read) and dire (to say): lire à haute voix = to read aloud.
target_language_example: Peux-tu lire ce passage à haute voix ?
native_language_example: Can you read this passage out loud?

meaning: up to; in the amount of; at the level/height of.
additional_notes: Common in formal contexts (news, admin, finance) to express a quantified level or amount: « jusqu’à concurrence de / à hauteur de 50 € » = up to €50. Also used literally for physical position: « à hauteur de la fenêtre » = level with the window; and for location when passing something: « à hauteur de la gare » = by/near the station (at the point level with it). Often followed by a number, a noun, or a place.
target_language_example: L’aide est accordée à hauteur de 500 € par personne.
native_language_example: The aid is granted in the amount of €500 per person.

additional_notes: Means something will last indefinitely, often with an emotional or poetic tone (e.g., love, memories, vows). Common in set phrases like « à jamais dans mon cœur » (“forever in my heart”). It can also mean “permanently” in the sense of “for good,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Je t’aimerai à jamais.
native_language_example: I will love you forever.

additional_notes: Used to say something (information, accounts, payments, records, software) is updated or not behind. Common phrases: « être à jour » (to be up to date), « se mettre à jour » (to update/catch up), « mettre à jour » (to update something). Also used with money: « être à jour de ses paiements/impôts » = to be up to date on payments/taxes.
target_language_example: Mes informations sont à jour.
native_language_example: My information is up to date.

additional_notes: Used to say that something (often praise, criticism, or a reaction) is justified or deserved. Commonly follows verbs like être (être critiqué/ félicité/ admiré à juste titre) or can be used at the start of a sentence to comment on what was just said.
target_language_example: Il a été critiqué à juste titre pour son retard.
native_language_example: He was rightly criticized for being late.

additional_notes: Used with "être / se mettre / se tenir à l’abri" to mean being or getting into a protected place. Often followed by "de" + what you’re protected from: "à l’abri du vent / de la pluie". Can also be figurative for being safe from something ("à l’abri des critiques" = safe from criticism).
target_language_example: Mets-toi à l’abri de la pluie !
native_language_example: Get out of the rain! (Get somewhere sheltered!)

additional_notes: A common emergency cry used to ask for help or attract attention (stronger and more urgent than "Aidez-moi" in many situations). Often said alone as an exclamation, and frequently written with an exclamation mark: "À l’aide !" You can also say "Au secours !" with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: À l’aide ! On m’a volé mon sac !
native_language_example: Help! Someone stole my bag!

additional_notes: Used to say someone feels comfortable physically or socially (not nervous). Often with "être" (Je suis à l’aise) or "se sentir" (Je me sens à l’aise). Can also describe clothing/shoes that fit comfortably (Je suis à l’aise dans ces chaussures).
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas très à l’aise en public.
native_language_example: I’m not very comfortable in public.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something in a traditional way, or describing food, clothes, decor, etc. Very common with cooking: "pommes frites à l’ancienne" (thick-cut fries), "pâté à l’ancienne" (rustic-style pâté). Literally "in the old way/style."
target_language_example: Je préfère cuisiner à l'ancienne, sans robot.
native_language_example: I prefer to cook the old-fashioned way, without a food processor.

additional_notes: Used for radio/TV (and sometimes livestreams) to mean something is being broadcast, or that a person/program is currently live. Often with verbs like être/passer: « être à l’antenne » (to be on the air), « passer à l’antenne » (to be broadcast/go on the air).
target_language_example: Nous serons à l’antenne à 18 h.
native_language_example: We’ll be on the air at 6 p.m.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what will happen from now on, or to say that something should change starting now. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence: « À l’avenir, … » or « …, à l’avenir. »
target_language_example: À l’avenir, je ferai plus attention.
native_language_example: In the future, I’ll be more careful.

meaning: upside down; the wrong way around; backwards.
additional_notes: Used for something physically reversed (clothes inside out, a picture hung upside down) or for an order/direction reversed (saying something backwards). Often contrasts with "à l'endroit" (the right way up).
target_language_example: Tu as mis ton pull à l'envers.
native_language_example: You put your sweater on inside out.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that something/someone is outside (not inside). Often contrasts with "à l’intérieur" (inside). Can describe location ("Je suis à l’extérieur") or where something happens ("à l’extérieur du bâtiment" = outside the building).
target_language_example: Les enfants jouent à l’extérieur.
native_language_example: The kids are playing outside.

meaning: on time; at the right time.
additional_notes: Often used to say someone is punctual or not: « être à l’heure » (to be on time). You can also use it with « arriver »: « arriver à l’heure » (to arrive on time). With schedules, it can mean “at (a specific) time,” similar to “at … o’clock,” especially in set phrases like « à l’heure du déjeuner » (at lunchtime).
target_language_example: Je serai à l’heure pour le rendez-vous.
native_language_example: I’ll be on time for the appointment.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened very recently (often only moments ago). Common with the past tense: « Je viens de le voir à l’instant. » It can also refer to the immediate present in set phrases like « À l’instant ! » meaning “Right away!” (a bit firm, like a command).
target_language_example: Je l’ai vu à l’instant.
native_language_example: I just saw him a moment ago.

additional_notes: Used to indicate location or movement to a place that is inside something (a building, a room, a box, etc.). Often contrasts with "à l'extérieur" (outside). Common in phrases like "à l'intérieur de" + noun (inside/within) and with verbs of movement: "entrer à l'intérieur" (to go inside).
target_language_example: Il fait froid dehors, restons à l'intérieur.
native_language_example: It’s cold outside; let’s stay indoors.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something is located within a physical space (a room, a bag, a building), or more generally within boundaries/limits. Often followed by a noun: « à l’intérieur de la maison ». In everyday speech, « dans » is frequently used as a simpler alternative for “in/inside.”
target_language_example: Il y a des clés à l’intérieur de mon sac.
native_language_example: There are keys inside my bag.

additional_notes: Used either (1) with "de" + noun/infinitive to mean "on the occasion of" / "for" (a specific event), or (2) alone to mean "occasionally" / "from time to time". Example patterns: "à l'occasion de + noun"; "à l'occasion + verb".
target_language_example: À l'occasion de son anniversaire, on va dîner au restaurant.
native_language_example: On the occasion of his birthday, we're going to have dinner at a restaurant.

additional_notes: Used with "être" ("être à l’écoute") to say you are listening/attentive (often in a helpful, customer-service sense: "I’m here and listening"). Can also describe something that listens/monitors continuously (e.g., a device or service "is on standby, listening").
target_language_example: Je suis à l’écoute si tu veux en parler.
native_language_example: I’m here to listen if you want to talk about it.

meaning: back then; at the time (in that period).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a past period already understood from context ("in those days"). Often followed by the imperfect tense to describe habits or situations in the past. Can also be used more generally as "at the time" when talking about a particular moment in the past.
target_language_example: À l'époque, j'habitais à Lyon et je travaillais dans un café.
native_language_example: Back then, I lived in Lyon and I worked in a café.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is on an upper floor of a building (not on the ground floor). Often appears with verbs like "être" (to be) and "monter" (to go up): "Je suis à l’étage" / "Monte à l’étage". Depending on context it can mean any floor above the ground level (not necessarily the first floor).
target_language_example: Les chambres sont à l’étage.
native_language_example: The bedrooms are upstairs.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being/going/living/studying outside your home country. Common with verbs like vivre, aller, partir, étudier, travailler. It contrasts with en France / dans mon pays (in France / in my country).
target_language_example: J’ai vécu deux ans à l’étranger.
native_language_example: I lived abroad for two years.

additional_notes: Common in the set phrase « C’est à l’œil ! » meaning something is being given for free (often by a shopkeeper, bartender, etc.). It’s fairly informal/colloquial. Note: « à l’œil » can also literally mean “by eye” (e.g., estimating without measuring), but the “free” meaning is the common idiom learners meet.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, c’est à l’œil !
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s on the house!

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is actively working or having an effect. Common with verbs like être/voir/regarder: « être à l'œuvre » (to be at work), « voir … à l'œuvre » (to see … in action). Can also be used as an encouragement: « À l'œuvre ! » = “Get to work!”
target_language_example: On voit déjà la nouvelle équipe à l'œuvre.
native_language_example: You can already see the new team in action.

meaning: "to the" / "at the" (before a feminine singular noun); sometimes "in the style of".
additional_notes: This is the normal combination of the preposition « à » + the feminine singular article « la ». It’s used for destinations or locations (e.g., « aller à la banque » = to go to the bank). For masculine singular, French usually uses « au » (à + le), and for plural « aux » (à + les). In set phrases and in cooking, « à la + adjective/nationality » can mean “in the style of” (e.g., « à la française »).
target_language_example: Je suis à la maison.
native_language_example: I’m at home.

meaning: at the bar (in court); at the helm (of a ship).
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like « être/aller/appeler à la barre » in a courtroom (the witness stand / where someone speaks to the judge). It can also be used literally for boating/sailing to mean being at the helm (steering). Not usually used for ordering drinks at a bar (that would be « au bar »).
target_language_example: Le juge appelle le témoin à la barre.
native_language_example: The judge calls the witness to the stand.

additional_notes: Common in spoken French to introduce the main idea or the original starting point of something (similar to “basically” or “to begin with”). Depending on context, it can mean “originally/at first” (time/starting situation) or “fundamentally” (core reason/idea).
target_language_example: À la base, je voulais juste t’aider, pas te critiquer.
native_language_example: Basically, I just wanted to help you, not criticize you.

meaning: outdoors, under the open sky (often: sleeping outside).
additional_notes: Used especially with dormir/passer la nuit to mean sleeping outside with no shelter (often because you’re camping or because you have nowhere to stay). Literally “under the beautiful star,” i.e., under the stars.
target_language_example: On a raté le dernier train, alors on a dormi à la belle étoile.
native_language_example: We missed the last train, so we slept outside under the stars.

meaning: stupid; dumb; in a really idiotic way.
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar ("con" is a strong insult). Used to criticize something as pointless, badly done, or annoying. Common with nouns ("un truc à la con" = a stupid thing) or after a noun ("une question à la con" = a stupid question). Avoid in polite situations; safer alternatives: "bête", "idiot", "stupide", "nul".
target_language_example: J’ai fait une erreur à la con et j’ai tout supprimé.
native_language_example: I made a stupid mistake and deleted everything.

meaning: on the ropes; in serious difficulty.
additional_notes: Usually used with a verb like « être »: « être à la corde » (literally “to be at the rope”). It comes from boxing (a fighter pushed back against the ring ropes) and is used figuratively for someone who is exhausted, overwhelmed, or close to failing. In horse racing, « à la corde » can also mean “along the inside rail.”
target_language_example: Après des mois de dettes, il est à la corde.
native_language_example: After months of debt, he’s on the ropes.

meaning: at the last minute; at the very last moment.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done very late, just before a deadline or when it’s almost too late. Often implies poor planning or urgency. Commonly used with verbs like faire, décider, changer, réserver: « faire quelque chose à la dernière minute ».
target_language_example: Il a réservé ses billets à la dernière minute.
native_language_example: He booked his tickets at the last minute.

meaning: at the end; in the end; finally.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the end of a time period/event ("at the end") or the final outcome after everything ("in the end"). Often appears with "de": "à la fin de la journée" (at the end of the day).
target_language_example: À la fin du film, tout le monde applaudit.
native_language_example: At the end of the movie, everyone applauds.

meaning: at the same time; both (at once).
additional_notes: Used to say two things are true simultaneously, or that someone/something has two qualities at once. Often appears in patterns like "à la fois... et..." (both... and...). It can also mean "simultaneously" (doing two actions at the same time).
target_language_example: Il est à la fois drôle et gentil.
native_language_example: He is both funny and kind.

meaning: up to (the required standard); at the right level/height.
additional_notes: Often used with “être” or “se sentir” to say you’re capable of meeting expectations (“être à la hauteur de…” = “to be up to…”). It can also be literal for physical height/level depending on context. Common patterns: “être à la hauteur de la tâche/du défi” (be up to the task/challenge), “ne pas être à la hauteur” (not be up to it).
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas sûr d’être à la hauteur du poste.
native_language_example: I’m not sure I’m up to the job.

additional_notes: Means something is done quickly, often without much care or preparation. Common with verbs like faire, partir, écrire, préparer: « faire quelque chose à la hâte ». Slightly more formal/literary than « en vitesse » or « à la va-vite ».
target_language_example: J’ai préparé mon sac à la hâte avant de partir.
native_language_example: I packed my bag in a hurry before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the information you’re basing a decision or opinion on (common in formal or written French). Literally means “by the light of,” but it’s usually understood as “given/considering (this new fact).” Often followed by a noun phrase: « à la lumière des faits », « à la lumière de ce que tu as dit ».
target_language_example: À la lumière des nouvelles informations, nous allons changer de plan.
native_language_example: In light of the new information, we’re going to change our plan.

meaning: carelessly; lightly; without taking it seriously.
additional_notes: Used to describe doing something in a superficial or careless way, without enough attention or seriousness. Often implies criticism (not taking something important seriously). Common with verbs like prendre (to take), traiter (to handle), faire (to do), juger (to judge).
target_language_example: Ne prends pas ça à la légère.
native_language_example: Don’t take that lightly.

meaning: by hand; handmade; within reach (close at hand).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say something is done manually (not by machine): « fait à la main » = handmade. It can also mean something is nearby/available: « avoir … à la main » = to have … close at hand. Often placed after the noun (« un sac à la main » = a bag in (your) hand) or after the past participle (« écrit à la main » = written by hand).
target_language_example: J’ai écrit la carte à la main.
native_language_example: I wrote the card by hand.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is at home or at their place. With some verbs it can imply movement: e.g., "rentrer à la maison" = "to go/come home." Note that "maison" means "house/home" (not "mansion").
target_language_example: Je suis à la maison.
native_language_example: I’m at home.

meaning: at the mercy of; helpless against.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something has no control and depends on another person/thing (or circumstances). Often followed by a noun (à la merci de quelqu’un / de la météo). Common in warnings or negative situations.
target_language_example: Sans téléphone, je suis à la merci de la météo.
native_language_example: Without a phone, I’m at the mercy of the weather.

meaning: fashionable; in style. (Also: served with ice cream.)
additional_notes: Most commonly means “fashionable / trendy”: Elle est très à la mode. In food contexts—especially on menus—“à la mode” can mean “served with ice cream” (often a dessert): une tarte aux pommes à la mode. The literal idea is “in the fashion/style.”
target_language_example: Ces chaussures sont à la mode en ce moment.
native_language_example: These shoes are in fashion right now.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is current and in touch with modern trends (style, ideas, a place, etc.). It’s an idiomatic expression—literally it would be “at the page,” but it doesn’t mean that in normal conversation.
target_language_example: Ce café est vraiment à la page.
native_language_example: This café is really trendy.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done extremely well, without any flaws. Often follows a verb like faire, réaliser, réussir, ou cuire (for food): "cuit à la perfection". Slightly formal/expressive, common in compliments and reviews.
target_language_example: Ton français est prononcé à la perfection.
native_language_example: Your French is pronounced perfectly.

additional_notes: Used to indicate substitution or replacement. Very common with "à la place de" + noun/pronoun (instead of someone/something): "Je prends un thé à la place du café." You can also use it alone when the alternative is understood: "Tu veux venir ? — Non, je reste ici à la place."
target_language_example: On peut prendre le bus à la place du métro.
native_language_example: We can take the bus instead of the subway.

additional_notes: Used to show substitution/replacement: one thing/person is used or happens rather than another. It’s followed by a noun, pronoun, or infinitive verb (e.g., « à la place de toi », « à la place de prendre le bus »). Often similar to « au lieu de », but « à la place de » emphasizes “in someone/something’s place.”
target_language_example: Je vais prendre le train à la place de la voiture.
native_language_example: I’m going to take the train instead of the car.

meaning: within reach of; within someone’s ability/means.
additional_notes: Used both literally (something physically close enough to reach) and figuratively (something achievable or affordable). Common patterns: « à la portée de tous » (within everyone’s reach), « à la portée de chacun » (within anyone’s ability), « à la portée des enfants » (within children’s reach / suitable for children). Often paired with verbs like « être », « mettre », « rester ».
target_language_example: Ce livre est à la portée de tous.
native_language_example: This book is within everyone’s reach (easy enough for anyone).

meaning: first thing (in the morning); at the earliest time.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens very early, often the first possible moment of the day (similar to “first thing tomorrow” / “first thing in the morning”). You can also use it more generally for “at the earliest opportunity.”
target_language_example: Je passerai te voir à la première heure demain matin.
native_language_example: I’ll come by to see you first thing tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: A common, friendly way to say goodbye when you expect to see the person again. It’s often short for “à la prochaine fois” (“until next time”). Used in casual and neutral situations; you can also hear “à la prochaine !” at the end of a conversation, message, or meeting.
target_language_example: Bon, je dois y aller. À la prochaine !
native_language_example: Well, I have to go. See you next time!

additional_notes: Used with the verb « être » to say someone is retired (« Il/Elle est à la retraite »). Also used after nouns like « âge » (« l’âge de la retraite » = retirement age). You can also say « prendre sa retraite » = to retire (literally “to take one’s retirement”).
target_language_example: Mon père est à la retraite depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: My father has been retired for two years.

additional_notes: Literally “in the street.” Common in informal French to say someone has no home or no money. Often used with être: « être à la rue » (to be homeless / to have nothing). Context decides whether it’s about housing (homeless) or finances (completely broke).
target_language_example: Depuis qu’il a perdu son travail, il est à la rue.
native_language_example: Since he lost his job, he’s homeless / he has nothing left.

meaning: after; following; as a result of.
additional_notes: Used to indicate what comes next in time/order ("following") or what happens because of something ("as a result of"). Common in phrases like "à la suite de" (following / after / as a result of) and "à la suite" (in the next/following part, in continuation).
target_language_example: À la suite de l’accident, la route est fermée.
native_language_example: Following the accident, the road is closed.

additional_notes: Used when clinking glasses and making a toast. It’s informal and usually said to one person; to toast several people you often hear "À la vôtre" (more polite) or "À votre santé !" / "Santé !".
target_language_example: Allez, à la tienne !
native_language_example: Come on, cheers!

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is falling behind others (in progress, speed, fashion, etc.). Often used with verbs like être/rester (to be/stay) or laisser (to leave someone behind).
target_language_example: Avec ce rythme, on va rester à la traîne.
native_language_example: At this pace, we’re going to fall behind.

meaning: at work; busy working (on a task).
additional_notes: Often used with "être" or verbs like "se remettre" to say someone is working or has gotten back to work: "Il est à la tâche" (He’s hard at work), "Je me remets à la tâche" (I’m getting back to work). It’s more formal/literary than everyday "au travail" or "en train de travailler".
target_language_example: Après la pause, je me remets à la tâche.
native_language_example: After the break, I’m getting back to work.

meaning: in the headlines; on the front page; featured as the main story.
additional_notes: Used mostly with news/media (newspapers, websites, TV) to say something is the most important or prominently featured item (“la une” = the front page / top story). Common with verbs like « être à la une » (to be in the headlines) and « faire la une » (to make the headlines).
target_language_example: Ce scandale est à la une de tous les journaux.
native_language_example: This scandal is in the headlines of all the newspapers.

meaning: at the sight of; upon seeing.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens when someone sees something. Common with reactions or changes: « À la vue de + noun/pronoun ». A close synonym is « en voyant ».
target_language_example: À la vue de la police, il est parti en courant.
native_language_example: At the sight of the police, he ran off.

additional_notes: Used when clinking glasses or raising a drink. It’s short for “À votre santé !” (“To your health!”). Often said as “À la tienne” (to one person informally) or “À la vôtre” (to several people or to one person formally).
target_language_example: On trinque ? À la vôtre !
native_language_example: Shall we toast? Cheers!

meaning: in the long term; over the long run.
additional_notes: Used to talk about long-term effects, plans, or results (months/years rather than days/weeks). Often contrasted with "à court terme" (short term). You can place it at the start or end of a sentence: "À long terme, ..." / "..., à long terme."
target_language_example: À long terme, ce changement sera bénéfique pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: In the long term, this change will be beneficial for everyone.

additional_notes: Used on signs and ads to indicate something (an apartment, house, car, room, etc.) is available to rent. Often seen as "À louer" on a window or in listings (sometimes with details like price and contact info).
target_language_example: Appartement à louer, proche du métro.
native_language_example: Apartment for rent, near the metro.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re doing something without tools, gloves, or weapons. Often with verbs like attraper (to catch), combattre/se battre (to fight), creuser (to dig). Invariable phrase (no plural or gender changes).
target_language_example: Il a attrapé le poisson à mains nues.
native_language_example: He caught the fish with his bare hands.

additional_notes: Used after a verb to say something works or suits someone very well. Often with verbs like aller (to suit/fit), fonctionner (to work), réussir (to succeed), se passer (to go).
target_language_example: Cette solution me convient à merveille.
native_language_example: This solution suits me perfectly.

additional_notes: Mostly used in set phrases rather than alone. Common patterns: “à mesure que + clause” = “as / while” (as something changes over time); “au fur et à mesure (que)” = “gradually, little by little / as you go.” It comes from “mesure” (measure) and suggests something happening in step with something else.
target_language_example: À mesure que je pratique le français, je comprends mieux.
native_language_example: As I practice French, I understand better.

meaning: "halfway" (midway between two places or two points in time).
additional_notes: Used to say something is in the middle of a route or process. Often followed by de + place/point (à mi-chemin de Paris) or between two things (à mi-chemin entre A et B). It can also be used figuratively for a compromise or something that’s neither one thing nor the other.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à mi-chemin entre chez toi et chez moi.
native_language_example: We’ll meet halfway between your place and mine.

additional_notes: Most often means “to me” after a verb (e.g., donner/montrer/parler à moi), though in everyday French you usually use the stressed pronoun with the preposition: à moi, à toi, à lui/elle, à nous, etc. It can also mean “mine!” to show possession or claim something, especially in short exclamations (often with C’est… or as a standalone).
target_language_example: Donne-le à moi !
native_language_example: Give it to me!

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition that is necessary for something not to happen (often followed by the infinitive with a subject implied, or by “que” + subjunctive when there’s an explicit subject). Common patterns: “à moins de + infinitive” (À moins de partir maintenant, on sera en retard.) and “à moins que + subjunctive” (Je viens, à moins que tu ne préfères être seul.).
target_language_example: Je viendrai demain, à moins de changer d’avis.
native_language_example: I’ll come tomorrow, unless I change my mind.

additional_notes: Used to express an exception/condition: something is true except if another situation happens. It’s normally followed by a clause with the subjunctive: « à moins que + subject + subjunctive » (often with « ne » explétif: « à moins qu’il ne pleuve », where « ne » does not mean “not”). Contrast: « sauf si » + indicative is another common way to say “unless/except if.”
target_language_example: On ira au parc à moins qu’il ne pleuve.
native_language_example: We’ll go to the park unless it rains.

additional_notes: Means “half” in the sense of partially or to the halfway point. Common with adjectives and past participles: « à moitié endormi » (half asleep), « à moitié rempli » (half full). It can also modify a verb: « faire quelque chose à moitié » (do something halfway / only partly).
target_language_example: Je suis à moitié endormi.
native_language_example: I’m half asleep.

additional_notes: Used to give your personal opinion. Often followed by a full sentence: « À mon avis, ... ». You can change the possessive to match the speaker: « à ton avis » (in your opinion), « à son avis » (in his/her opinion), « à notre avis » (in our opinion), etc.
target_language_example: À mon avis, ce restaurant est le meilleur du quartier.
native_language_example: In my opinion, this restaurant is the best in the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Used after a verb. Literally means “to death” (e.g., battre à mort = beat to death). Very commonly used in everyday speech as an exaggeration to mean “really/so much,” often with feelings like boredom or tiredness: s’ennuyer à mort (be bored to death), être crevé à mort (be dead tired).
target_language_example: Je m’ennuie à mort dans ce cours.
native_language_example: I’m bored to death in this class.

meaning: directly on; right on (in contact with a surface).
additional_notes: Used mainly to say something is placed directly on a surface without anything underneath: « à même le sol » (right on the floor), « à même la peau » (directly on the skin). Note: in the common phrase « à même de + infinitive », it means “able to / in a position to” (e.g., « Je ne suis pas à même de répondre. »).
target_language_example: Il a posé le matelas à même le sol.
native_language_example: He put the mattress directly on the floor.

meaning: at the right level; up to standard.
additional_notes: Used to talk about whether something meets the expected level (skills, students, work quality). Common in expressions like « être à niveau » (to be at the right level) and « mettre à niveau » (to bring up to standard / upgrade / update, e.g., equipment or skills).
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas encore à niveau en français.
native_language_example: I’m not up to the right level in French yet.

additional_notes: Means “again” in the sense of repeating an action or doing something once more. Often interchangeable with « encore », but « à nouveau » is a bit more formal and emphasizes starting over or doing it anew.
target_language_example: Peux-tu répéter à nouveau, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you repeat again, please?

additional_notes: Used to separate something from the rest. Common uses: (1) as an adverb meaning "aside" or "separately": Mettre quelque chose à part (set something aside). (2) with "à part" + noun/pronoun meaning "except (for)": À part toi, personne ne le sait (Except you, nobody knows). Often interchangeable with "sauf" in the 'except' meaning, but "à part" can feel like 'setting one thing apart from the group'.
target_language_example: À part toi, je ne connais personne ici.
native_language_example: Except for you, I don’t know anyone here.

meaning: "from" / "starting from" (a time, date, place, age, price, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a starting point in time (from Monday, from 8am), a starting place (from Paris), a minimum threshold (from €10 / starting at €10), or the source of something (made from / based on). Often followed by a noun, date, time, or number. Common in announcements and schedules.
target_language_example: Le magasin est ouvert à partir de 9 h.
native_language_example: The store is open from 9 a.m.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens almost not at all, or only with difficulty, or just a moment ago. Common patterns: "à peine + adjective/adverb" (Je suis à peine réveillé. = I’m barely awake), "à peine + noun/number" (Il a à peine 18 ans. = He’s only just 18), and "à peine ... que" to mean “no sooner ... than” (À peine arrivé, que je suis reparti. = No sooner had I arrived than I left again).
target_language_example: J’ai à peine eu le temps de manger.
native_language_example: I barely had time to eat.

additional_notes: Used to give an approximate number, time, or degree of certainty (similar to “around” or “roughly” in English). It can also mean “almost” in some contexts (e.g., “à peu près fini” = almost finished), but most commonly it means “approximately.” Often placed before the number/time: “à peu près dix minutes.”
target_language_example: J’arrive dans à peu près dix minutes.
native_language_example: I’ll be there in about ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used mainly to describe a slope, street, cliff, or drop: « une pente à pic », « une falaise à pic ». It can also appear in the idiom « tomber/arriver à pic » meaning “to come at just the right time.”
target_language_example: Attention, ce sentier est à pic.
native_language_example: Careful, this path is very steep.

additional_notes: Used to say you go somewhere by walking (not by car/bus/bike). Often with verbs like aller/venir/rentrer: « Je vais à pied. » You can also use it to describe distance/time on foot: « C’est à dix minutes à pied. »
target_language_example: On y va à pied ?
native_language_example: Shall we go there on foot?

additional_notes: Literally “flat.” Used for something physically flat (e.g., a tire), for a battery that’s dead ("La batterie est à plat"), and very commonly about a person meaning they’re worn out: "Je suis à plat" = “I’m exhausted.” Often heard in everyday spoken French.
target_language_example: Je suis à plat après cette journée.
native_language_example: I’m totally exhausted after this day.

meaning: lying flat on your stomach; face down.
additional_notes: Used to describe a position where you are stretched out with your stomach on the ground (the opposite of « sur le dos », on your back). Often used with verbs like « être », « se mettre », « s’allonger »: « être/se mettre/s’allonger à plat ventre ».
target_language_example: Le soldat s’est mis à plat ventre derrière le mur.
native_language_example: The soldier lay flat on his stomach behind the wall.

meaning: “to the point of crying” / “enough to make you cry.”
additional_notes: Used after an adjective (often negative) to intensify it: *triste à pleurer* (“so sad you could cry”), *ennuyeux à pleurer* (“so boring it makes you want to cry”). You can also see it with *de quoi*: *Il y a de quoi pleurer* (“There’s enough to make you cry”).
target_language_example: Ce film est triste à pleurer.
native_language_example: This movie is so sad you could cry.

additional_notes: Very common informal goodbye, often shortened from "à plus tard" (“see you later”). Used with friends, classmates, coworkers, etc. You can also hear/write it as "à plus !", "à+" (texting), or "à plus tard" (a bit more explicit). Not usually used in formal situations.
target_language_example: Bon, je dois y aller. À plus !
native_language_example: Well, I have to go. See you later!

additional_notes: Common, friendly way to say goodbye when you expect to see the person again later (today or another day). Often shortened to "à plus" (more informal). Typically used in casual conversation; in more formal settings you might use "au revoir" instead.
target_language_example: Bon, je dois y aller. À plus tard !
native_language_example: Well, I have to go. See you later!

additional_notes: Informal/colloquial and can sound crude, so avoid in formal situations. Common with être (être à poil = to be naked) or se mettre (se mettre à poil = to get undressed). It can also be used jokingly/exaggeratedly to mean “without any clothes on” (not just “without a coat”).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas ouvrir la porte, je suis à poil !
native_language_example: I can’t open the door, I’m naked!

meaning: done just right; perfectly cooked (especially meat).
additional_notes: Most commonly used when talking about cooking, especially steak: "un steak à point" means cooked to a medium doneness (between "saignant" = rare and "bien cuit" = well-done). More generally, it can also mean something is ready at the right moment (e.g., a plan or preparation is "à point").
target_language_example: Je voudrais un steak à point, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a steak cooked medium, please.

meaning: at just the right time; very appropriately.
additional_notes: Rather formal/literary. Used to say something arrives or happens exactly when needed (often with verbs like arriver, venir, tomber): « Ça tombe à point nommé » = “That comes at exactly the right time.”
target_language_example: Ton aide arrive à point nommé, merci !
native_language_example: Your help is coming at just the right time—thank you!

additional_notes: Used to say something is close enough to grab without moving much. Often followed by "de" + a noun or pronoun: "à portée de main de/du/de la..." Less commonly, it can be used more generally to mean something is readily available.
target_language_example: Garde ton passeport à portée de main.
native_language_example: Keep your passport within reach.

additional_notes: Used to describe a first impression based on initial information or appearance; it can imply that your opinion may change after looking more closely. Often followed by a comma or used with verbs like "sembler" (to seem) or expressions like "mais" (but) to contrast with a later judgment.
target_language_example: À première vue, ce restaurant a l'air cher, mais les prix sont raisonnables.
native_language_example: At first glance, this restaurant looks expensive, but the prices are reasonable.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like vendre (to sell), exploiter (to run/use), or être (to be) to indicate that something makes money rather than causing a loss. Often appears in phrases like vendre à profit (sell at a profit) or exploiter une activité à profit (run a business profitably).
target_language_example: Il a revendu sa voiture à profit.
native_language_example: He resold his car at a profit.

additional_notes: Most commonly used to introduce the topic you’re talking about: “à propos de + noun/pronoun” = “about/regarding …”. It can also be used alone to mean “by the way” when you’re adding something related or changing topic slightly: “À propos, …”.
target_language_example: À propos de ton voyage, tu pars quand ?
native_language_example: About your trip, when are you leaving?

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic of what you’re talking about. Common in speech and writing. Often followed by a noun or an infinitive: « À propos de ton projet… » (about your project), « À propos de venir demain… » (about coming tomorrow). Can also introduce a side note or new topic, similar to “by the way”: « À propos, … » (without « de »).
target_language_example: J’ai une question à propos de ton cours de français.
native_language_example: I have a question about your French class.

additional_notes: Used to say something is at a short distance. Common with "de" + place/person ("à proximité de l’hôtel" = near the hotel) or with "d’ici" ("à proximité d’ici" = nearby). Often interchangeable with "près"/"près de", but "à proximité" is a bit more neutral/formal.
target_language_example: Il y a une pharmacie à proximité de la gare.
native_language_example: There is a pharmacy near the train station.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the current moment, often to contrast with the past or to move a conversation forward. Common in writing and formal speech; in everyday conversation you’ll also hear "maintenant".
target_language_example: À présent, je comprends mieux.
native_language_example: Now, I understand better.

meaning: on all fours (on hands and knees).
additional_notes: Used to describe a person (or animal) moving or positioned with both hands and both knees/feet on the ground—common for babies crawling, looking for something under furniture, etc. You can use it with verbs like être (to be), marcher (to walk), or se mettre (to get) : « se mettre à quatre pattes » = to get down on all fours.
target_language_example: Le bébé avance à quatre pattes dans le salon.
native_language_example: The baby is crawling on all fours in the living room.

additional_notes: Used in questions and exclamations to ask/emphasize the degree or intensity of something. Often followed by a clause (à quel point + subject + verb) or by an adjective/adverb (à quel point c’est important).
target_language_example: Tu sais à quel point c’est important pour moi ?
native_language_example: Do you know how important it is to me?

additional_notes: Used to say something feels useless or not worth doing, often with a resigned or pessimistic tone. It’s a set phrase and is usually followed by an infinitive (à quoi bon essayer ?) or can be used alone as a question.
target_language_example: À quoi bon continuer si personne ne m’écoute ?
native_language_example: What’s the point of continuing if no one is listening to me?

meaning: at a rate of; at the rate of.
additional_notes: Used to express a ratio or frequency (price per unit, speed, quantity per time, etc.). Often followed by a number + unit: « à raison de 10 € par personne », « à raison de 3 fois par semaine ». Common in formal or written contexts (instructions, contracts, reports).
target_language_example: Le cours est facturé à raison de 50 € de l’heure.
native_language_example: The lesson is billed at a rate of €50 per hour.

meaning: filled to the brim; completely full.
additional_notes: Used to say a container is so full the contents are level with the rim (or almost overflowing). Often used with verbs like « remplir » (to fill) and with words like « verre », « tasse », « baignoire ». It can also be used figuratively for being full/overwhelmed (e.g., « à ras bord de travail » = up to your ears in work).
target_language_example: Elle a rempli le verre à ras bord.
native_language_example: She filled the glass to the brim.

additional_notes: Often used after verbs like être (to be) or avoir l’air (to look/seem) to say someone is very pleased. You’ll also see it in the fixed phrase « être à ravir » (to be delighted).
target_language_example: Elle était à ravir de te revoir.
native_language_example: She was delighted to see you again.

additional_notes: Means moving/doing something in the opposite direction or order. Common with time for a countdown: "compte à rebours" (countdown). Also used with verbs like "marcher à rebours" (walk backwards) or "compter à rebours" (count down).
target_language_example: On a lancé le compte à rebours avant le décollage.
native_language_example: They started the countdown before takeoff.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something powered by a jet engine (propulsion by reaction), especially in technical or transport contexts. Very common in fixed phrases like « moteur à réaction » (jet engine) and « avion à réaction » (jet plane).
target_language_example: Cet avion à réaction est beaucoup plus rapide.
native_language_example: This jet plane is much faster.

additional_notes: Means doing something freely, according to one’s own preference. It can change with the subject: « à mon/ton/son/notre/votre/leur guise » (as I/you/he-we/you all/they please). Often used after a verb like « faire », « agir », or « disposer ».
target_language_example: Tu peux organiser la soirée à ta guise.
native_language_example: You can organize the evening however you like.

additional_notes: Means someone does something in their personal style, not necessarily the usual or expected way. It can be positive (unique style) or gently critical (not the best way). Often varies with the person: « à ma manière » (my way), « à ta manière » (your way), « à leur manière » (their way).
target_language_example: Il aide les autres à sa manière.
native_language_example: He helps others in his own way.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clarification or a list of specific details after a general statement. Common in writing and formal speech. Often appears after a comma: « ..., à savoir ... ». Also used after verbs like « expliquer/préciser », as in « Il faut préciser, à savoir que... ».
target_language_example: Nous avons deux options, à savoir prendre le train ou louer une voiture.
native_language_example: We have two options, namely taking the train or renting a car.

additional_notes: Commonly means having nothing left: "à sec" (out of money), "à sec" (out of fuel), or after drinking a glass "boire cul sec" (drink it all at once). It can also mean "dry" (with no water/liquid), e.g. a riverbed "à sec" or hair "sécher à sec". Meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Je suis à sec, je ne peux pas payer le restaurant.
native_language_example: I’m broke; I can’t pay for the restaurant.

meaning: successful; popular; hit (said of a product, movie, book, etc.).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something that sells well or is widely popular (un livre à succès, une série à succès). Often translated as “bestselling” (for books) or “hit” (for songs/movies). Not usually used to describe a person directly.
target_language_example: C’est une série à succès en France.
native_language_example: It’s a hit TV series in France.

additional_notes: Used to say that the rest will come later (like at the end of an episode or article). Also common in messages or emails to mean “more details to follow.” You may also see it abbreviated as “à suivre…”
target_language_example: Je t’explique la suite demain — à suivre.
native_language_example: I’ll explain the rest to you tomorrow—to be continued.

additional_notes: Used when clinking glasses/drinking with friends. « ta » is informal singular “your” (to one person you know well); the more formal/plural version is « à votre santé ».
target_language_example: Allez, à ta santé !
native_language_example: Cheers— to your health!

additional_notes: Literally means "at the table." Often used as a call to come and sit down because the meal is ready (similar to "Dinner's ready!"). You can also use it to describe someone who is seated for a meal: "Nous sommes à table" (we’re at the table/eating).
target_language_example: À table ! Le dîner est prêt.
native_language_example: Time to eat! Dinner is ready.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens at the planned time (on time) or before it’s too late (in time). Often used with verbs like arriver (to arrive) or être (to be). Contrast: en retard = late.
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé à temps pour le train.
native_language_example: I arrived in time for the train.

additional_notes: Used to describe a job, work schedule, or study arrangement that is not full-time. Often appears with “travailler” (to work) or “un emploi/un travail” (a job): “travailler à temps partiel”, “un emploi à temps partiel”. The opposite is “à plein temps” (full-time).
target_language_example: Je travaille à temps partiel le mercredi et le vendredi.
native_language_example: I work part-time on Wednesday and Friday.

additional_notes: Used mainly for jobs, work schedules, or study programs. Often paired with verbs like travailler (to work) or être (to be): travailler à temps plein = to work full-time. Contrast: à temps partiel = part-time.
target_language_example: Je travaille à temps plein.
native_language_example: I work full-time.

meaning: "in the long run" / "eventually"; also "due" (at maturity, for a payment/debt).
additional_notes: Common in formal or written French. With time/plan results: "à terme" means the final outcome after some time (like “eventually” or “in the long run”). In finance/bills: "à terme" means a payment or debt is due at a set date (matures). Also used in the phrase "à terme" vs "à court terme" (short-term).
target_language_example: À terme, cette décision sera bénéfique.
native_language_example: In the long run, this decision will be beneficial.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is on the ground, often after falling or being knocked over. Also common figuratively to mean exhausted or worn out: « Je suis à terre » = “I’m wiped out.” With objects, it can mean “down” or “knocked over”: « La chaise est à terre ».
target_language_example: Après la chute, il était à terre.
native_language_example: After the fall, he was on the ground.

meaning: as (in the capacity of); as a (e.g., as an example/temporary measure).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the role/status in which someone acts (à titre de directeur = as director), or the purpose/justification of something (à titre d’exemple = as an example; à titre provisoire = temporarily). Common in formal or written French. Often followed by a noun: à titre de + noun (or à titre + adjective like provisoire).
target_language_example: Elle travaille à titre de consultante.
native_language_example: She works as a consultant.

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular pronoun toi (for someone you address as tu). Common after verbs like donner, dire, envoyer: Je te donne ça, à toi. Also used on its own to pass the turn in a game or conversation: À toi ! (Your turn!). For the formal/plural version, use à vous.
target_language_example: À toi ! C’est ton tour.
native_language_example: Your turn! It’s your turn.

meaning: Your turn! / It’s up to you (to do it).
additional_notes: Used to pass the turn in a game or activity, or to tell someone they should act next or take responsibility. You can change the pronoun: « à vous de jouer » (to one person politely or to a group), « à moi de jouer » (my turn). Also common outside games: « À toi de jouer, montre-nous ce que tu sais faire. »
target_language_example: Bon, j’ai terminé. À toi de jouer !
native_language_example: Okay, I’m done. Your turn!

meaning: in your opinion; what do you think?
additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to someone’s opinion. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence: « À ton avis, … ? » or « …, à ton avis ? ». Can be made formal with « à votre avis » (to one person formally or to a group).
target_language_example: À ton avis, on part à quelle heure ?
native_language_example: In your opinion, what time should we leave?

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is wrong, or that something was done/said unfairly or by mistake. Often appears with verbs like avoir tort (to be wrong) or accuser/condamner à tort (to accuse/convict wrongly). Opposite: à raison (rightly).
target_language_example: Il a été accusé à tort.
native_language_example: He was accused wrongly.

additional_notes: Used to say that people do something alternately, taking turns (often fairly or in an agreed order). Common with verbs like "passer" (to pass), "parler" (to speak), or "faire" (to do): "On parle à tour de rôle."
target_language_example: On répond à tour de rôle aux questions.
native_language_example: We answer the questions in turn.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens each time or is almost guaranteed (often with a slightly emphatic tone). Common with verbs like "ça marche", "je gagne", "il arrive", etc. Not about "blows"—"coup" here is like an "attempt/instance".
target_language_example: À tous les coups, il oublie ses clés.
native_language_example: Every time, he forgets his keys.

meaning: at any time; at any moment.
additional_notes: Used to say something can happen whenever (now or later), often implying it could happen unexpectedly. Common in offers/help (“Call me any time”) or warnings (“It could happen at any moment”).
target_language_example: Tu peux m’appeler à tout moment.
native_language_example: You can call me at any time.

meaning: at all costs; no matter what.
additional_notes: Means you are determined to do something, even if it’s difficult, expensive, or involves sacrifice. Often used with verbs like vouloir (to want), obtenir (to get), éviter (to avoid), or empêcher (to prevent).
target_language_example: Je veux à tout prix éviter les embouteillages.
native_language_example: I want to avoid traffic jams at all costs.

additional_notes: Common way to say goodbye when you expect to see the person again later the same day. Often shortened in speech to "à tout". Not used for "see you tomorrow" or longer time spans (use "à bientôt" or "à demain").
target_language_example: Je dois y aller—à tout à l'heure !
native_language_example: I have to go—see you later!

meaning: See you later! (short for "à tout à l’heure")
additional_notes: Very informal, mostly spoken or in texts/messages. It’s a shortened goodbye meaning you’ll see the person again soon (later today). Not to be confused with the literal "à toute" meaning "to every/each (feminine noun)", which is uncommon on its own.
target_language_example: Bon, j’y vais. À toute !
native_language_example: Alright, I’m off. See you later!

additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something moving or happening very quickly (running, driving, speaking, time passing, etc.). It’s common and neutral in tone. Often paired with verbs like aller, courir, rouler: « Il roulait à toute allure. »
target_language_example: Le train est parti à toute allure.
native_language_example: The train left at full speed.

meaning: at full speed; as fast as possible.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is going very fast. Common with verbs like aller, rouler, foncer, courir. It can be literal (a car) or figurative (working very quickly).
target_language_example: Il roulait à toute vitesse sur l’autoroute.
native_language_example: He was driving at full speed on the highway.
