meaning: 'through' / 'across' (moving from one side to the other, or passing through something).
additional_notes: Used for movement through a place, space, or obstacle: « marcher à travers la forêt » (through the forest), « regarder à travers la fenêtre » (through the window). It can also be used more abstractly meaning 'throughout' or 'across' a period/topic: « à travers les siècles » (through the centuries). Often corresponds to English 'through' or 'across' depending on context.
target_language_example: On a marché à travers la ville pour aller au musée.
native_language_example: We walked across the city to go to the museum.

additional_notes: Used for moving directly through the countryside (e.g., walking/running) rather than staying on paths or roads. Often contrasts with taking the long way around on roads. Related adjective: « une course à travers champs » (a cross-country race).
target_language_example: On est rentrés à travers champs pour éviter la route.
native_language_example: We went back across the fields to avoid the road.

additional_notes: Used on signs, listings, and ads to indicate an item/property is available to buy. Often placed after the noun: "maison à vendre" (house for sale), "voiture à vendre" (car for sale).
target_language_example: Il y a une maison à vendre dans cette rue.
native_language_example: There is a house for sale on this street.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean something is scheduled/expected in the future (often in announcements, agendas, and listings). Common with nouns like "événements" (events), "prochaines dates" (upcoming dates), or "informations" (information) in the sense of "more to come".
target_language_example: Des informations à venir seront publiées la semaine prochaine.
native_language_example: More information will be published next week.

additional_notes: Used to mean that something lasts until the end of someone’s life (a commitment, a ban, a contract, a sentence, etc.). Often follows a noun: "un abonnement à vie" (a lifetime subscription), "interdit à vie" (banned for life), "condamné à vie" (sentenced for life).
target_language_example: Il a été condamné à vie.
native_language_example: He was sentenced for life.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is speaking softly, often so others won’t hear (e.g., in a library, during a meeting, or to share something discreetly). Common with verbs like parler / dire / murmurer: « parler à voix basse », « dire à voix basse ». Contrast: « à haute voix » = out loud.
target_language_example: Parle à voix basse, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Speak quietly, please.

additional_notes: Used to say something is spoken so others can hear it (often for reading or repeating). Common with verbs like lire (to read) and dire (to say): lire à voix haute = to read aloud.
target_language_example: Peux-tu lire ce texte à voix haute ?
native_language_example: Can you read this text out loud?

meaning: as much as you want; unlimited.
additional_notes: Used to mean there’s no set limit: you can take/consume as much as you like. Common in food contexts (e.g., buffet, drinks) and with quantities like "café à volonté" (unlimited coffee). It can also mean "at will" (whenever you want), though in everyday situations it most often refers to an unlimited amount.
target_language_example: Dans ce restaurant, les frites sont à volonté.
native_language_example: In this restaurant, the fries are unlimited (all you can eat).

meaning: At your service; yes, sir/ma’am (ready to obey).
additional_notes: A polite, somewhat formal expression used to show you are ready to do what someone asks. Common in customer service, the military, or when speaking respectfully to a superior. You can also say « à votre service » (more neutral) or « à tes ordres » (to one person you address with tu).
target_language_example: — Pourriez-vous m’aider avec ces cartons ? — Bien sûr, à vos ordres.
native_language_example: — Could you help me with these boxes? — Of course, at your service.

additional_notes: Polite way to ask for someone’s opinion or to introduce their viewpoint. Often used as a question ("À votre avis ?") or in a longer question ("À votre avis, … ?"). Can also appear in statements: "À votre avis, c’est une bonne idée." Informal equivalent: "à ton avis" (with friends/family).
target_language_example: À votre avis, quel est le meilleur restaurant du quartier ?
native_language_example: In your opinion, what’s the best restaurant in the neighborhood?

meaning: "At your service"; "How can I help you?"
additional_notes: A polite, formal set phrase used by staff (waiters, customer service, hotel reception) to show readiness to help. It can also be used when you’ve done something for someone to mean “happy to help.” Often said as a response to thanks (similar to “you’re welcome / my pleasure”), though common alternatives are « je vous en prie » and « avec plaisir ». The informal version is « à ton service ».
target_language_example: Bonjour, Madame. À votre service : que puis-je faire pour vous ?
native_language_example: Hello, ma’am. At your service—what can I do for you?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a frank or clarifying comment (often something you admit or a correction to what was just said). Common in both spoken and written French. Often followed by a pause: « À vrai dire, ... ».
target_language_example: À vrai dire, je n’ai pas très envie de sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: To tell the truth, I don’t really feel like going out tonight.

additional_notes: Used mostly in formal or technical contexts, especially banking and payments. In phrases like « payable à vue », it means the money must be paid immediately when presented (no waiting period). Literally « at sight », close to English « on sight ».
target_language_example: Ce chèque est payable à vue.
native_language_example: This check is payable on demand (on sight).

additional_notes: Refers to a person you feel a deep, natural connection with—often (but not always) romantic. Commonly used with possessives (mon/ma/mes): « mon âme sœur ». Can also be used more broadly for a best friend or someone who “gets you.”
target_language_example: Je pense qu’elle est mon âme sœur.
native_language_example: I think she is my soulmate.

meaning: 'it was' / 'it has been'; also 'it was okay' (as an answer).
additional_notes: Literally "ça" (it/that) + "a été" (has been / was). Used to talk about how something went: "Ça a été" can mean "It was fine/okay" (often implying 'not amazing, but alright'). In context it can also mean something is over/done: "Ça a été" = "That’s done/That’s over".
target_language_example: — Ça s’est bien passé ? — Oui, ça a été.
native_language_example: — Did it go well? — Yeah, it was okay.

additional_notes: Used as an exclamation when you’re surprised (pleasantly or not), like “Well, well!” or “Would you look at that!”. Often said on its own, or before a comment: “Ça alors, tu es déjà là !” Slightly old-fashioned/expressive rather than slang.
target_language_example: Ça alors ! Je ne m’attendais pas à te voir ici.
native_language_example: Wow! I wasn’t expecting to see you here.

additional_notes: Very common informal spoken expression to say a situation is lousy, disappointing, unfair, or not going well. Literally it comes from *craindre* (“to fear”), but the meaning is idiomatic (not “that fears”). Often used as a standalone reaction: *Ah mince… ça craint.*
target_language_example: On a raté le dernier métro… ça craint.
native_language_example: We missed the last subway… that sucks.

additional_notes: Informal, conversational expression meaning things are going fine. Often used as a short answer to “Ça gaze ?” (“How’s it going?”). You’ll mostly hear it in casual speech; in more neutral French you can say “Ça va (bien).”
target_language_example: — Ça gaze ? — Oui, ça gaze, merci !
native_language_example: — How’s it going? — Yeah, it’s going well, thanks!

meaning: it’ll be fine / it’ll work out.
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or say a situation will turn out OK. Literally “it will go,” but the natural meaning is closer to “it’ll be fine.” Often said on its own after someone worries: « Ça ira. »
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, ça ira.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’ll be fine.

additional_notes: Informal, spoken expression used to say something is acceptable, suitable, or good enough for a need (“it’ll do”). Often said after a suggestion or when choosing between options. You may also hear it in the negative: “Ça le fait pas” = “That’s not OK / that doesn’t look good / that’s not appropriate.”
target_language_example: On prend cette table ? Oui, ça le fait.
native_language_example: Shall we take this table? Yes, that works.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French. Used to agree to a plan (“OK, sounds good”) or to say something is functioning (“it works”). Also used on the phone/in audio checks to mean “can you hear me / it’s working.”
target_language_example: On se retrouve à 18 h ? — Oui, ça marche.
native_language_example: Shall we meet at 6 p.m.? — Yes, that works / OK.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not important or not a big deal, often to reassure someone after a small mistake or inconvenience. Similar in meaning to "ce n’est pas grave" and can also be used as a response to an apology or thanks (like “that’s okay” / “don’t mention it”).
target_language_example: Désolé, je suis en retard. — Ça ne fait rien.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm late. — No problem.

additional_notes: Common informal reply to “Ça va ?” or “Comment ça va ?” meaning things are going well. Can also be used to confirm that something works or is agreed: “OK, sounds good.” Literally means “it rolls,” but it’s usually used idiomatically.
target_language_example: — Ça va ? — Oui, ça roule !
native_language_example: — How are you? — Yeah, all good!

additional_notes: Used to say something should stop because it’s too much or you’re annoyed. Can be firm or angry depending on tone. Often said as an exclamation: « Ça suffit ! ».
target_language_example: Ça suffit ! Arrête de crier.
native_language_example: That’s enough! Stop yelling.

meaning: "That suits you" / "That looks good on you."
additional_notes: Used to say that something (often clothing, a color, a haircut, a style) suits someone or looks good on them. It can also mean something "fits" someone (their personality or role): e.g., a job or a nickname. In pronunciation, "ça" often sounds like "sa" and the whole phrase is commonly said quickly.
target_language_example: Cette robe, ça te va bien !
native_language_example: That dress really suits you!

meaning: "it’s running" / "it’s working" (said about a machine, system, or process).
additional_notes: Literally “it turns,” but very often used to mean something is operating normally (a motor, computer, business, etc.). In everyday speech it can also mean “things are going/rolling along.” In a film set context, you may hear "Ça tourne !" meaning “We’re filming!” (the camera is rolling).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : l’ordinateur a redémarré, ça tourne.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: the computer restarted, it’s working.

additional_notes: Very common, casual expression. As a question (“Ça va ?”), it means “How are you?/How’s it going?” As an answer (“Ça va.”), it means “I’m OK/Fine.” You can add details: “Ça va bien” (I’m doing well), “Ça va mal” (I’m not doing well). More formal: “Comment allez-vous ?”
target_language_example: —Salut ! Ça va ? —Oui, ça va, merci.
native_language_example: —Hi! How’s it going? —Yeah, I’m good, thanks.

additional_notes: Used to say that things are going well or that you’re fine. Often answers "Ça va ?" (How’s it going?). You can also use it about a situation: "Ça va bien se passer" (It will go well). Slightly more positive/enthusiastic than just "Ça va."
target_language_example: — Ça va ? — Oui, ça va bien, merci.
native_language_example: — How’s it going? — Yes, I’m doing well, thanks.

additional_notes: Used to announce that something is finished, finally ready, or has just happened (often with relief or satisfaction). Common in spoken French. Can also be a response meaning “yes, I’ve got it / I understand now.”
target_language_example: Ça y est, j’ai trouvé mes clés !
native_language_example: There we go, I found my keys!

additional_notes: Used in chess to announce the game-ending position where the king is in check and has no legal move to escape. You can say it as an exclamation after making the final move (often without the article: “Échec et mat !”). Occasionally used figuratively to mean someone has been completely defeated or left with no options.
target_language_example: Échec et mat ! J’ai gagné la partie.
native_language_example: Checkmate! I won the game.

additional_notes: A common, neutral expression for suddenly starting to laugh (often because something is very funny or surprising). Used with conjugated forms of « éclater »: « j’éclate de rire », « il a éclaté de rire ».
target_language_example: Quand il a raconté la blague, tout le monde a éclaté de rire.
native_language_example: When he told the joke, everyone burst out laughing.

meaning: to burst into tears; to break down crying.
additional_notes: A fairly strong, vivid expression for starting to cry suddenly and intensely (often because of shock, sadness, or overwhelming emotion). Used with people: "Elle a éclaté en sanglots." In the past tense you’ll often see "a éclaté" (passé composé).
target_language_example: En apprenant la nouvelle, elle a éclaté en sanglots.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she burst into tears.

additional_notes: Refers to a school or institute where people learn a foreign language (often for adults, but not always). Commonly used with a specific language: « une école de langue française / une école de langues ».
target_language_example: Je cherche une école de langue pour apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a language school to learn French.

additional_notes: A place where you learn foreign languages (often as classes or courses). Usually appears with an article (une/l’/cette école de langues) and can be followed by the language: « une école de langues (où on apprend) l’anglais / le français ».
target_language_example: Je me suis inscrit à une école de langues pour apprendre l’espagnol.
native_language_example: I enrolled in a language school to learn Spanish.

additional_notes: Used in science contexts to talk about elements on the periodic table (like oxygen, iron, gold). Often appears with an article: « un élément chimique » (a chemical element) or « l’élément chimique » (the chemical element).
target_language_example: L’oxygène est un élément chimique.
native_language_example: Oxygen is a chemical element.

additional_notes: Common in formal or written French. Often followed by a noun or clause to introduce a reason or context: « étant donné + noun » (given/considering…) or « étant donné que + clause » (given that / since…). Means the same idea as « vu » or « puisque » in many contexts.
target_language_example: Étant donné que tu es fatigué, on peut rentrer plus tôt.
native_language_example: Given that you’re tired, we can go home earlier.

meaning: a state of shock (medical or emotional).
additional_notes: Used for both medical shock (a medical emergency) and severe emotional shock after a traumatic event. Often appears with verbs like « être en état de choc » (to be in a state of shock) or « se trouver en état de choc » (to be in a state of shock). In everyday speech it can mean “really shaken up,” but it can also be a serious medical term in news or hospital contexts.
target_language_example: Après l’accident, elle était en état de choc.
native_language_example: After the accident, she was in a state of shock.

additional_notes: Common in medical or administrative contexts to talk about someone’s overall health condition. Often used with possessives (mon/ton/son état de santé) or with "l’" (l’état de santé).
target_language_example: Quel est votre état de santé en ce moment ?
native_language_example: What is your health status at the moment?

additional_notes: Literally “flying star,” but in French it means a meteor seen as a streak of light in the night sky. Commonly used with verbs like voir (to see) or souhaiter (to wish): “faire un vœu en voyant une étoile filante” (make a wish when you see a shooting star).
target_language_example: J’ai vu une étoile filante et j’ai fait un vœu.
native_language_example: I saw a shooting star and I made a wish.

meaning: to be delighted; to be over the moon.
additional_notes: An idiom meaning you’re extremely happy or thrilled (often because something good happened). Used with conjugated forms of « être »: « Je suis aux anges », « Elle était aux anges », etc. It’s fairly common and not slang, but it’s figurative (not literally “with the angels”).
target_language_example: Quand j’ai appris la nouvelle, j’étais aux anges.
native_language_example: When I heard the news, I was over the moon.

meaning: To be in trouble; to be in a difficult situation.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression meaning you’re in a mess or predicament (often because of something you did). It’s fairly informal and a bit ironic: literally it means “to be in nice sheets,” but the real meaning is the opposite.
target_language_example: Si mes parents découvrent ça, je vais être dans de beaux draps.
native_language_example: If my parents find out, I’ll be in big trouble.

meaning: to be in the same situation (often a difficult one).
additional_notes: Used to say that two or more people share the same problem or circumstances, so they should understand each other or work together. Very common metaphor; can also appear as: « On est tous dans le même bateau. »
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : on est dans le même bateau, on va trouver une solution.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we’re in the same boat, we’ll find a solution.

meaning: to be standing; to be up (out of bed).
additional_notes: Used for a person (or sometimes an object) in an upright position. Very common to talk about being awake and out of bed: « Je suis debout » = “I’m up.” Contrast with « être assis(e) » (to be sitting) and « être couché(e) » (to be lying down/in bed). « Debout ! » is also used as an instruction meaning “Stand up!”
target_language_example: Je suis déjà debout, je prépare le café.
native_language_example: I’m already up; I’m making coffee.

meaning: to be really easy (“a piece of cake”).
additional_notes: Idiomatic (often said as « C’est du gâteau ! »). Used to say something is simple or no problem. You can also use it with an infinitive: « Pour lui, résoudre ce problème, c’est du gâteau. »
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, l’examen va être du gâteau.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, the exam is going to be a piece of cake.

meaning: to be on good terms (with someone).
additional_notes: Used to say that two people (or groups) have a good relationship and get along well. Often followed by « avec » + person: « être en bons termes avec quelqu’un ». It can describe friendly relations even if they aren’t close friends.
target_language_example: Je suis en bons termes avec mon ancien collègue.
native_language_example: I’m on good terms with my former coworker.

meaning: to be in the middle of (doing something); to be (currently) doing something.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that an action is happening right now (progressive aspect). It’s followed by an infinitive: « être en train de + infinitive ». Conjugate « être » to match the subject and tense (e.g., « je suis en train de… », « il était en train de… »). Often translates as the English present continuous (“am/is/are doing”), but French can also use the simple present without it; this phrase adds emphasis on “right now/in the process.”
target_language_example: Je suis en train de préparer le dîner.
native_language_example: I’m (in the middle of) making dinner.

meaning: to be high time (to do something).
additional_notes: Used almost always in the pattern « Il est grand temps de + infinitive » to say something is overdue or should happen now. It expresses urgency (similar to “It’s about time…”). You can also see « Il est grand temps que + subjunctive » in more formal French.
target_language_example: Il est grand temps de partir.
native_language_example: It’s high time to leave.

additional_notes: A common, neutral term meaning “human being,” often used in general statements (about humanity, rights, science, etc.). It can refer to any person and is slightly more formal than "personne" in some contexts. Plural: "des êtres humains".
target_language_example: Chaque être humain mérite le respect.
native_language_example: Every human being deserves respect.

meaning: to be the case; to be true.
additional_notes: Used to confirm whether something is true or applies in a situation. Often appears after a conditional or a statement (e.g., « Si c’est le cas… » = « If that’s the case… »). Also commonly used in the negative: « ce n’est pas le cas » = « that’s not the case ».
target_language_example: Si c’est le cas, on peut partir maintenant.
native_language_example: If that’s the case, we can leave now.

meaning: to be there; to be present.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s presence/availability (physical or sometimes emotional support). Depending on context, it can mean “to be there” or “to be here.” Common forms: je suis là (I’m here/there), tu es là, il/elle est là, on est là, nous sommes là, vous êtes là, ils/elles sont là.
target_language_example: Je serai là à 8 heures.
native_language_example: I’ll be there at 8 o’clock.

meaning: to be about; to be a matter of; (negative) to be out of the question.
additional_notes: Usually used with **de** and often in the impersonal form **il est question de...** (“it’s about...”) or **il n’est pas question de...** (“there’s no question of... / no way...”). In the negative, it’s a strong refusal or impossibility. Not used much by itself without context.
target_language_example: Il n’est pas question de sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: There’s no way we’re going out tonight.

meaning: to be dressed up (to the nines); to be wearing your best clothes.
additional_notes: An idiomatic, fairly informal way to say someone is very well dressed for a special occasion (party, wedding, date, etc.). Often used with the verb phrase "se mettre sur son 31" (to get dressed up). You can also say "être sur son trente-et-un".
target_language_example: Pour le mariage, il était sur son 31.
native_language_example: For the wedding, he was dressed to the nines.

meaning: a living being; a living creature.
additional_notes: Usually used as a noun phrase (often with an article): un/une être vivant. Common in biology and general speech to contrast with something non-living (inerte) or not alive. Note: don’t confuse with the verb phrase être vivant (“to be alive”), which describes someone/something’s state (e.g., Il est vivant).
target_language_example: Tous les êtres vivants ont besoin d’eau.
native_language_example: All living beings need water.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone/something is, especially with cities or specific places: «être à Paris», «être au travail». With articles, à contracts: à + le → au, à + les → aux (e.g., «au café», «aux États-Unis»). For countries, French often uses «être en» (e.g., «en France») rather than «à».
target_language_example: Je suis au bureau.
native_language_example: I’m at the office.

meaning: to be at the door; (figurative) to be out/asked to leave.
additional_notes: Often literal: someone is physically at the door (arriving, waiting, knocking). It can also be used figuratively to mean someone has been (or is about to be) kicked out or fired, especially in contexts like « mettre quelqu’un à la porte » (“to throw someone out”).
target_language_example: Dépêche-toi, le taxi est à la porte.
native_language_example: Hurry up, the taxi is at the door.

meaning: (to have) very sharp eyesight; a keen eye.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used to say someone notices tiny details or sees things from far away. Often used with the verb "avoir": "avoir un œil de lynx" (to have a keen eye). You can also use it to compliment someone who spotted something others missed.
target_language_example: Tu as un œil de lynx : tu as tout de suite vu l’erreur.
native_language_example: You have a keen eye: you spotted the mistake right away.

meaning: “an eye for an eye” (revenge/punishment in equal measure).
additional_notes: Fixed expression meaning retaliation: you repay a harm with the same harm. Often used when talking about justice, vengeance, or arguing against revenge (e.g., quoting “œil pour œil, dent pour dent”). Note: œil is pronounced like “uh-y” (singular), and the plural is yeux.
target_language_example: Il croit à la justice « œil pour œil ».
native_language_example: He believes in “an eye for an eye” justice.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an artistic creation (a painting, sculpture, etc.). Often used with articles: « une œuvre d’art », « des œuvres d’art ». In museums you might also hear it more generally for notable pieces.
target_language_example: Cette œuvre d’art est exposée au musée.
native_language_example: This work of art is on display at the museum.
